As smart glasses capable of capturing images and recording video become more affordable and accessible, community concerns are also growing about privacy, surveillance and the potential for misuse. Recent media reports suggest a discounted AI enabled version has sold out across Australia. Last week, I asked the Privacy Commissioner to prioritise consideration of the privacy implications associated with this technology. The potential for these devices to be used to covertly record, track, stalk and harass requires prompt and careful consideration. Their discreet design can make it difficult for people to know when they are being filmed, increasing the risk of unwanted surveillance and undermining Australians' ability to control how their personal information and images are collected.

The increasing availability of this technology could have significant implications, particularly for women and children, who may be disproportionately exposed to inappropriate recording, harassment, intimidation or other harmful conduct. Research from the University of Sydney found many women are being filmed in gyms, workplaces, shops and university campuses, despite expressing discomfort or refusing consent. Analysis of hundreds of Instagram videos captured using these devices found a staggering 60 per cent of point-of-view content contained behaviour classified as potential harassment. Let me be clear—this government stands against the use of smart glasses for nefarious purposes.

While state and territory laws already restrict the use of recording devices in some circumstances, the commissioner's expertise is critical in identifying emerging privacy risks and appropriate safeguards. The commissioner has noted that, where technology companies receive and store personal information collected through wearable devices, they must comply with privacy laws, but there are real questions as to whether they will be able to do so. Robust privacy laws are essential to Australians' trust and confidence in the digital economy and the services provided by governments and industry. In our first term, we created a new statutory tort against serious invasions of privacy. We outlawed doxxing, and we significantly increased penalties for breaches. The government will continue to progress work on a second tranche of legislative reforms to ensure our privacy laws are fit for the digital age. Australians rightly expect their privacy to be respected, and that is exactly what this government is focused on delivering.

speaker: Katy Gallagher
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank Senator Hume for the question about productivity, because it is an important issue across our economy, and we've been upfront about that since we came to government, when the government that Senator Hume was a member of had a productivity assumption of 1.5 per cent every year across their budget and failed to meet it each time. Treasury advice to the incoming government was that a more realistic figure should be lower than that, and we have adopted that Treasury advice.

But we have had a productivity issue in our economy for decades, including for the entire time that those opposite were in government. That's why we've put productivity and addressing productivity at the centre of our economic thinking and into the decisions we've taken in the budget. In particular, I would urge those who will have the opportunity, to vote this week so we can get the bill done. In another regulatory reform bill, the first regulatory reform bill which was brought to this parliament, those opposite voted against it. I hope that the second bill that we bring forward, which is about reducing red tape and has, as one of our measures, addressing productivity, will be in the Senate and listed on the program this week, and it should be passed by the Senate this week.

But we also have a range of other measures in the budget that specifically go to looking at ways that we can improve productivity across the economy, and we will continue to do that. We will probably continue to be frustrated by those opposite, who don't support a lot of it, whether it's building homes, modernising energy markets, better recognising skills, unlocking data and AI— (Time expired)

speaker: Mehreen Faruqi
heading: MATTERS OF URGENCY
text:
Are you coming to the Prime Minister's 118th birthday? It's going to be a big day. As well as celebrating making it all the way to 2081, he will finally get to mark the closure of gas wells he approved while Prime Minister more than five and a half decades earlier—all 1,695 of them. These wells are just one of the 36 new and expanded coal, oil and gas projects the Albanese government has approved—new projects harming the planet, harming the environment and health for decades to come.

I've got some investment advice so good that you'll think this clip is an AI scam. Here's what to do: first, be a big gas corporation. Then drop some cash into Labor's election accounts—$100,000 or so will do. In return, Labor will let you make billions and get away with exporting over half of Australia's gas without paying a cent in royalties. In fact, this government collects more money slugging you with student debt than these big gas companies pay in tax. And when the Greens, who don't take a single cent of these dirty donations, sided with Australians, saying we should have a minimum 25 per cent export tax on gas revenue, Labor chose to side with the billionaires. Seriously!

Polluting gas corporations love Labor in the same way that Gina loves One Nation. If you're sick of Labor working for their donors instead of you, now is the time to stick it to them and join the Greens. Together we are capable of massive change. Join us and help make this happen.

speaker: Peter Stuart Whish-Wilson
heading: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
text:
Every day here, we begin by paying our respects to Aboriginal people, the traditional custodians of this land. Words are cheap without actions. If we really respected our First Nations people, we would do so much more to walk the path towards reconciliation and justice and heal the wounds of the past. I rarely hear the words 'truth and treaty' spoken these days—or 'closing the gap', for that matter. We know what needs to be done; let's get on and do it.

I want to make an important disclaimer suitable for this day and age, and that is that this speech has been written without the use of AI—and also probably that viewer discretion might be required for the bros in the manosphere, because there will be some real men tears today and it may be triggering to some of them.

Last autumn, in my home town of Bicheno, we copped one of the biggest swells I've ever witnessed on the east coast of Tasmania. And, by the way, Bicheno, my home town, just got voted the No. 1 small town in Australia by Australian Traveller magazine—not to mention there have been some recent UFO sightings off the coast that have been well publicised. That has nothing to do with my retirement—or I hope it's got nothing to do with my retirement! Nevertheless, it appeared the force of this swell picked up the sand and pushed the barway connected to Redbill Beach across to beautiful Diamond Island, a hundred metres north. When another massive swell hit a few weeks later, this time from the north, a whisper began about town that something very special and magical was going to happen—underground rumours and whispers that a mythical wave might come to life.

I'd heard it all before, but, looking through my telescope, there it was. I could barely believe my eyes. Through the pines and the afternoon sea mist, long walls of ocean energy were rolling perfectly off the island, the dark figures of a few local surfers flying down their faces—and they're okay with me doing this tonight, because it's a public place and everyone knows where it is. With only a few hours of light left, my son, Finn, who's here tonight, and I couldn't get out there fast enough. My local beach that I feel deeply connected to had transformed into one of the best waves in the world, and that afternoon I shared some of the best waves of my life with my son.

Getting back on the beach in the fading light, the ocean a perfect mirror of an intense magenta sunset, I remember putting my arm around Finn and saying, 'This is as good as it gets for me.' I couldn't help thinking, 'How many of these moments have I missed over the years, always travelling, constantly away from home?' Walking back in the dark, surrounded by the thunder and energy of the surf, my decision to leave politics was made. I reckon I've got at least 10 good years of surfing left in me, so I am going to make hay while the sun shines.

I'm only too aware that the deep connection that I share with my coastline is a blessing and a source of inspiration. But, truth be known, it can also be a burden. David Attenborough recently stated:

After … 100 years on this planet, I now understand the most important place on earth is not on land but at sea … If we save the sea, we save our world.

Those of us who have eyes wide open to what's happening in our oceans know that it's going to take a lot of saving. When you're connected to nature, you see the wounds of the world—wounds that are largely self-inflicted in places like this and the other parliaments of the world. That makes them more painful, harder to bear, especially when you're one of the rare, privileged few who get elected to parliament but struggle to turn the tide.

As I was sitting on my surfboard in that autumn dusk, the lights from Nic's famous little penguin-viewing platform and rookery should have been flickering on. The sandbar should have been alive with these iconic creatures—and I have one of them on my lapel tonight—returning from fishing in the open ocean to feed their chicks. But the lights were off. The penguins vanished that summer. For the first time in its 35-year history, the Bicheno Penguin Tours closed up shop. This was the biggest tourist attraction in town, and it was distressing and devastating to my community. My wife, Natalie, and daughter, Bronte, who are also here tonight, and I went for walks through the penguin rookeries that summer and watched helplessly as the penguin chicks left behind slowly starved to death waiting for parents who wouldn't return, wandering around dazed in the sun, eating sticks, desperate with hunger. Not one survived. A marine heatwave had forced their parents too far out to sea in the search for food. Some of them eventually returned, towards winter, as the water cooled, but far too few and far too late. The marine heatwave, I remind you, is linked to the burning of fossil fuels.

Looking north from that same sandbar, this area of coastline was historically so full of giant kelp that it was famously difficult to get boats into the area. It was so thick it would foul their props. In 1839, Charles Darwin, on the voyage of the Beagle, visited Tasmania and the Southern Ocean, falling in love with these exact same giant kelp forests, stating:

I can only compare these great aquatic forests … with the terrestrial ones in the intertropical regions. Yet if in any country a forest was destroyed, I do not believe so many species of animals would perish as would here, from the destruction of the kelp.

How prophetic. Darwin was hauntingly right. It took less than two centuries. The giant kelp has now long vanished from my coastline, along with the profound loss of biodiversity he predicted. Ninety-five per cent of all Tasmania's giant kelp forests have disappeared. This loss is directly linked to the warming of the East Australian Current and the march of marine invasive species. Both are tied to climate change.

Bicheno, typical of so many small towns on Australia's east coast, used to have dozens of operating fishing boats. Only a few remain now. The loss of this habitat has had devastating consequences for Tasmania's fisheries and the communities that rely on them. The loss of fisheries and tourism income in just one small town among many along the Great Southern Reef is one of the economic consequences being felt because of the greed of the fossil fuel industry and our corrupted political system that has for decades refused to act meaningfully on climate change. I've spent the last chapter of my Senate career travelling the nation working with scientists, other inspiring individuals—many of them here tonight—community and environment groups; using my platform to bear witness to the sad decline in our natural world; raising awareness on the devastating impacts that our addiction to fossil fuels is having on our oceans; and advocating in here for the strongest possible climate action.

That 2025 summer, that marine heatwave, smashed also our World Heritage coral reefs, and for the first time we recorded mass coral bleachings on both the east and west coasts at the same time. I joined scientists at Ningaloo Reef and out at Heron Island on the Great Barrier Reef—also with Penny, Steph and Larissa—and saw the devastation caused by water temperatures that reached as high as 36 to 38 degrees Celsius. That's bathwater. If a bushfire destroyed millions of hectares of precious World Heritage biodiversity on land, it would be declared a national emergency—but not heatwaves at sea, apparently.

Senators, look at what else is happening around our coastlines. Six hundred and fifty thousand shearwaters washed up dead on Australia's east coast beaches last summer, believed to have starved to death because of a marine heatwave. Travel west to witness the algal bloom and dead sea in areas of coastal South Australia—also linked to a marine heatwave. And it is with great sadness that I relate that, while I was writing this speech yesterday, new counts on South Australia's giant cuttlefish have plummeted to record lows. Just like with Bicheno's penguins, tourism operators in Whyalla have cancelled cuttlefish season, with millions in expected losses, while populations of fur seals are declining and other species are weakened further as the new strain of pathogenic bird flu also arrives on these shores.

Go further west and witness the massive decadal loss of seagrasses in central Western Australia—a thousand square kilometres—and up, across the Top End to North Queensland, to witness catastrophic mangrove diebacks. An estimated 40 million trees across thousands of kilometres are believed to have perished.

It's official. As of yesterday, July again was the warmest month our oceans have had globally on record. They are literally off the charts. Models now show the strong likelihood of a record El Nino and the real possibility we will all get a taste of two degrees warming above pre-industrial levels next year, in 2027.

But you won't hear any of these truths in the Murdoch press misinformation machine. A death cult of powerful corporations and elites in and outside of parliaments continue to do what they've done for more than 40 years—either deny climate change altogether or lie, deceive, delay and distract from what's necessary to decarbonise our economies and radically reduce emissions in line with what the science tells us.

We are all collectively the frog in the pot, metaphorically and literally on top of a gas stove, and we can't climb out or extinguish the flame because a bunch of lying, greedy bastards won't let us do it. They will go to any lengths to protect their profits, including legalised bribery and blackmailing of corruptible political parties. This is happening globally. It's frightening, and it's bloody infuriating. If you told me, as a senator starting 14 years ago, about what I'm seeing now—especially this ongoing stubborn denial, greed and disregard in the face of our safe climate breaking down—I wouldn't have believed you. And I came in here as a climate ocean campaigner.

But, then again, in 2012, I hadn't witnessed the historic Clean Energy Future Package—legislated by the Labor and the Greens' power-sharing government and held up as a global standard in climate policy—defeated by the climate denial machine in this country. I hadn't witnessed with my own eyes LNP senators laughing as they did a joyful 'ring o'Rosie', dancing on the grave of this same legislation in this chamber and in the other one. That legislation has turned out to be the only real historic climate action ever seen in this country.

I hadn't yet worked and lived through a decade of the swamp and desert years of climate policy paralysis under the LNP, which I note continues to this day, or witnessed three prime ministers toppled over climate policy or witnessed a Labor government, elected in 2022 after campaigning on climate action, repose national climate targets whose ambition equated to two degrees of global warming—a death sentence for most of the world's coral reefs. Even today, astonishingly, the Labor Party is still approving new fossil fuel projects. In particular, the clock is ticking on the approval of fossil fuel giant Woodside's Browse project to drill and risk pristine Scott Reef and fuel the recent shameful expansion of the North West Shelf extension out to 2070.

Twice, I've watched Donald Trump get elected and become arguably the most important man on planet politics, the narcissist-in-chief of our ally the United States, an antiscience climate denier totally corrupted by big money from his fossil fuel and billionaire donors and a puppet for powerful interests dividing us and risking our future. The question I keep asking myself—and everyone I know, by the way—is: how did our system get infected by this mass political psychosis? Information is power, and those who control this control the agenda. But our information environment, which dictates the daily decisions we make, has changed radically since I started as a senator. It's official that most of us now get our news from social media platforms, a system set up to incentivise engagement and that rewards anger, outrage, fringe views and the spreading of lies. Politics has itself become entertainment that feeds on this anger, these lies and fringe views. Engagement hackers use rage baiting to lure voters and channel them towards more extreme, dangerous political views.

I remind senators the World Economic Forum, two years in a row, in 2024 and 2025, said that disinformation, the poisoning of our information system, is the biggest threat facing humanity. This disinformation, combined with the physical threats posed by climate change, they labelled as humanity's biggest long-term threat. While politicians and parliamentarians are at the pointy end of our climate wars, there exists a well-oiled denial machine behind the defeat of climate policy globally. PR firms, consultancies, think tanks, compliant conservative media outlets like the Murdoch press, and mercenary online armies funded by billions of dark money are often linked to fossil fuel interests coordinating global efforts to obstruct climate action. Don't take my word for this as a Greens senator. Ex-Chief of the Defence Force, Admiral Chris Barrie, and his climate security experts group, recently released a report stating this organised campaign to be akin to information warfare. In a world where AI provides an industrial platform for endless dis- and misinformation, we have to restore trust in science, our democratic institutions, public policy and polity.

Senators, if we lose this fight, we lose everything. There is much we can do as a parliament to tackle this and reset the agenda. There is hope. I'm proud of the work and the recommendations of the Senate select committee I recently chaired that looked into this clear and present danger, and I want to acknowledge some of the other members here tonight—Senator Pocock, Senator Darmanin, Senator Ananda-Rajah and Senator McLachlan—for working cross-party on getting this report done. I urge you all, please, in the years ahead, to jump into this critical work before this cancer on climate action and our democracy becomes terminal.

I feel like I've given it a good crack over the last 14 years. Some political waves caught, some missed. Some people have said to me, 'Peter, it's a good time to be leaving politics.' I know it's the right decision for me and my family, but, truthfully, it doesn't feel like a good time. But I accept there probably never is a good time. If you care about the environment, the ongoing genocide in Gaza, the need to fight for a pathway for justice and reconciliation for our First Nations people, to unshackle ourselves from the US military industrial complex and so many more issues, your work is never done. But it gives me great comfort on the eve of my departure that other warriors in this chamber, across political lines, and this parliament are willing to stand up and carry the torch on such critical issues.

I'd like to take this opportunity to congratulate my successor, Vanessa Bleyer, who's over here in the chamber today. You'll be all getting very familiar with Vanessa shortly. She will be a formidable senator for the Greens, for Tasmania and for nature. Murray, I think I can say confidently you'll probably be wishing I was back in six months time after you've been grilled by Vanessa a few times.

Senators, we really do have one of the best jobs in the world to build platforms for change. We get to poke our noses into nearly everyone's business. We have incredible tools, powers and resources at our disposal, especially the committee system. Clerk, President, I've been so fortunate to have initiated and chaired dozens of Senate inquiries in the past 14 years, and I'm in awe of the committee staff that I've worked with over the years. I'm sure all senators in this chamber feel the same way. But I wanted to give a special shout out to Patrick, Stephen, Tas, Alan and Kate to just name a few.

I'd also like to thank you and all the Senate staff, especially in the chamber here tonight—the parliamentary staff, the COMCAR drivers and security guards—from the bottom of my heart. Of course senators would be nothing without our staff—overworked, underpaid and often unrecognised, consistently going beyond the call of duty. And it is a calling for our staffers.

Thanks and respect to Jess McColl for the work she does in Larissa's leader's office and to all Greens staffers for what they do—in fact, to all staffers. But to my crew especially—Megan Jolly, Eddie Gray and Chloe Preston, Jack Fittler and Lily Mimica, who are currently working with me, and it's great to see some of the old gang back in the building tonight, in particular Charlie Goldberg, Thomas Moore and Tim Beshara. Also a big thanks to Emma Anglesey and Matti Rose, who couldn't make it.

Now, I didn't want to write this bit, because I felt like it was too scripted, so I'm going to kind of speak off the cuff here. Megan, my chief of staff, has been with me since I started, which is a massive, massive task, let me tell you. And I don't think I can remember that she's ever taken a day's sick leave, but I'm sure she has! She's an absolute trooper. Thank you for protecting me. Your intuition is legendary. I've learnt to take advice because of you, and you're nearly always right—just like my wife too, by the way! I wanted to say this is as much your journey here tonight as it is mine, and it absolutely couldn't have happened without you.

To Chloe and Eddie: someone once said to me that I was lucky to have hired the daughters of two fishermen—brought up on the coast, down to earth, straight shooters, salt of the earth and more than a bit of salt in their blood, lovers of the ocean. I just wanted to say to you both tonight—there you are, Eddie—enjoy your break that you're going to have and time with your beautiful partner, Gandy, and with your dogs and time in the ocean. I'll look forward to seeing you in the soup! I feel like we've been to war together. You followed me all around the country and you've always had my back. Thank you. Chloe, I kind of feel like your time with me is only going to be a footnote in one chapter of your book. You've had such a fascinating life. You're such an incredible individual, and I'm so fortunate that you have consistently saved my bacon on so many occasions—although you're vegan, and I shouldn't have used the word bacon! But I'm eternally in your debt, and I look forward to keeping our relationship going.

Jack, when you joined me, you had twins. You came to my office. You started an MPP. You took out a mortgage. We all looked at you and thought: 'What the hell. This guy is incredible.' Mate, you should be so proud of what you've achieved. You have not only turned up day in, day out and been an incredible friend and confidant, but you have achieved great things and you should be very, very proud of that.

Lily, thank you for the million views that you've got me on social media in the couple of years that you've been with me! It's been really good to work with you, and the Greens are very lucky to have you. Libby especially is lucky that you're now going to go and join her office.

I wanted to say, more broadly, thank you for your loyalty—that means so much to me—and your respect, your humanity and your good advice. You stuck with me till the end and you never wavered, and I'll be forever grateful. Not yet! I'm close. I wanted to say tonight a big shout-out to Fraser Brindley, who, sadly, passed away while working in this building three years ago to this week. I dearly wish he was here with us tonight. Working for Nick and me and the Greens for many, many years, Fraser proved MPs weren't the only ones driving change in this place. He turned up every day and he did change the world. He was a leader and a giant in our movement. His inspiration and memory is a compass that we still take our bearings from. His mum, Helen, is with us here tonight. Please know your son is dearly missed and was loved and respected by so many of us.

Sorry; this is called a circuit breaker—because I knew this was going to be a struggle. That one's for the manosphere, President!

Our team, over the years, has got some serious work done. We've helped people almost every day, and together we've had a powerful platform to fight for change. But I wanted to say tonight that any achievements we've made have been collaborative efforts, working across our party room and across the political aisles. Getting Senate work into policy outcomes and legislation isn't easy. Forget the making sausages analogy; it's more like baking a cake. You can have all the best policy ingredients added and mixed in the right way, but if the oven is not set to the right temperature, it will flop or be inedible. That temperature is the politics of the day, and this building is the oven. I'd like to think my team has baked a few delights over the years.

I'm proud that we got an effects test, arguably one of the biggest competition policy reforms in a decade, and we did that working with the Nationals. I'm proud that we've legislated in this place tranche 2 anti-money-laundering laws, and I wanted to especially shout out to Deb O'Neill, who's not here tonight, for her decades of work on this, and to Senator McKim and to Fraser. Multinational tax transparency and multinational tax avoidance laws—working with the coalition over many years, we've got billions of dollars from big corporations to help pay for schools and hospitals. A royal commission into banking and financial services shook corporate Australia and led to significant legislation in this place. Crikey, there's a whole book in the telling of how that royal commission came together. I did want to say it was a combined effort, working across the aisle with the Labor Party and with the coalition—especially Wacka Williams, who I wanted to give a very special mention to tonight, and to Sam Dastyari for the work and the leadership he showed on this. I'm proud that we solved the backpacker tax impasse in return for $100 million for Landcare and Indigenous Protected Areas. A levy on the big banks to help pay for services that protect our most vulnerable—I could go on.

I'm also proud my team and I have initiated some groundbreaking world's first Senate inquiries into tackling marine plastic pollution, shark protection and risk mitigation, exploring the impacts of warming oceans on our coral reefs and marine habitat, the dangers of seismic blasting in our oceans and, of course, the need to tackle climate driven marine invasive pests like the long-spined sea urchins that are doing so much damage to my precious coastline. There was also an inquiry into how we stop illegal fishing in the Southern Ocean—which I think, Senator Colbeck, you were involved with—and whaling in the Southern Ocean. The last inquiry, I think, stood me in good stead for probably the best and most challenging experiences of my parliamentary career, being the only politician willing or stupid enough to self-fund a trip to Tokyo and directly lobby the Japanese parliament to stop this barbaric practice. I'm confident our parliamentary work has helped communities and campaigners better protect their oceans, coastlines and wild places, and it's a solid foundation for others to continue to build on.

Last night I did an adjournment speech, shouting out some of the important fellow travellers on my journey, like the many scientists I've been lucky enough to work and campaign with. I also have very fond memories, and will always have fond memories, of the environmental campaigners I've been privileged enough to work with. There are too many to list here tonight, but a special thanks to Darren Kindleysides, the previous CEO of the Australian Marine Conservation Society and, in the chamber tonight, Paul Gamblin, the new CEO. Thanks for arranging a beer with Tim Winton, too; I'll be eternally grateful for that, Paul. Also Alexia Wellbelove, who I've worked with now for well over a decade. Thanks for being here tonight, Alexia, and thanks to all the crew at AMCS for all you do, and, in fact, to all the marine conservation organisations.

Of course, my other tribe are surfers. I'd like to shout out tonight to Josh Kirkman and Tim Silverwood, who are here tonight. Tim, you get a double mention because I'm about to talk about plastics in a second. Thank you for being here tonight. At Surfrider Foundation, where I was a board member before I came into politics, Drew McPherson, Damo Cole, Brendan Donohoe, Wendy Harmer and Paul Maddock, to name a few.

My last act in the Senate tomorrow is bringing on a private member's bill for debate to make producers of plastic packaging responsible for their pollution. I'll be thanking many folks tomorrow when we talk about this issue, but a special thanks to Jeff Angel, Tim Silverwood again, Gayle Sloan and Suzanne Toumbourou, who are here tonight. I really appreciate you being here, and I hope you come along tomorrow too. I'm proud to have worked and fought with so many legends, and I hope post politics we can continue to work together in some way.

Reflecting on the last 14 years in this place, there is one thing I'm especially proud of. It was the opportunity to play a small leadership role working with so many of my heroes and campaign to get Australian journalist Julian Assange out of his Belmarsh prison hell and back home to Australia. I have a spray painting by Tasmanian artist Jamin of Australian father of the year Terry Hicks, the father of David Hicks, on my office wall here in parliament. Terry has always been a hero of mine because of his love for his son, a love that conquered all. When Julian Assange's father, John Shipton, came to parliament in 2018 seeking help to get his son safely back to Australia, we discussed Terry's odyssean efforts against all odds to get his son David out of Guantanamo Bay so he could face a fair trial and extradition back to Australia. The first Trump presidency made it clear they were out to get Julian Assange and WikiLeaks. They wanted his head on a pike. They set out to extradite him to the US to face a bogus trial behind closed doors and a probable virtual death sentence. It was a dark and trying time for Julian's family and his supporters, who, like Terry Hicks, were up against some of the most powerful forces on the planet.

But this wasn't just an attack on Julian Assange; it was an attack on press freedoms and universal human rights, an attack on all of us. It was meant to send a message. And, as we warned at the time, it was a taste of things to come. If I recall correctly, John, who's here with Julian's brother, Gabriel, you were only able to get a few meetings in your first trip to parliament. I think they were with myself and Andrew Wilkie. It seemed Julian was persona non grata in this building back then. Great revolutionaries threaten entrenched powers with an inevitable backlash. The political assassination of Julian's character and freedom over the years meant few politicians wanted to lend him a hand at the time, including, to be fair, amongst my own mob.

John and I had many discussions over the years about how we could humanise Julian and rebuild his reputation, such as documenting his family's fight to free him and establishing a Parliamentary Friends of the Bring Julian Assange Home Group. Within five years of the establishment of that parliamentary friends group, a handful of MPs grew to 65 senators and MPs from across the political divide—and it's a deep political divide—calling for Julian's release and return home. The motion backing his return to Australia passed the House of Representatives. Our parliamentary friends group also embarked on the most unlikely parliamentary delegation to Washington, I'll wager, ever seen by this institution, including Senator David Shoebridge and Senator Alex Antic—who also said he was going to come tonight; sorry, Alex!—Monique Ryan, Tony Zappia and Barnaby Joyce. Because we were able to put our political differences aside to campaign for the release of an Australian who was being tortured in a maximum security prison, so too did the Democrats and Republicans, and an alliance was built across the Pacific.

Gabriel, you did a magnificent job, including by, I understand, accidentally bumping into senators and congressmen on trains and at the coffee cart, getting us meetings and building the most unholy of alliances. That was very successful in the end. Our presence was certainly noted in Washington prior to an important visit from our prime minister. Tonight, I would like to personally thank the Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, for the quiet diplomacy and leadership he showed when getting Julian Assange home, which, by the way, I'm sure our not-so-quiet diplomacy from the parliamentary friends group aided and abetted. I thank Kevin Rudd, who hosted us in Washington, and the British high commissioner at the time, Stephen Jones, both of whom played a significant role in Julian's return home to his family. And, of course, this wouldn't have been possible without his wonderful wife, Stella, brother, Gabriel, and father, John, and so many other champions, like Jennifer Robinson, Greg Barns, Stephen Kenny, Barry Pollack, Geoffrey Robertson, Nils Melzer, Scott Ludlam, who has also joined us tonight, Flick Ruby and way too many others to mention here tonight, who all took up the campaign and legal battles that ultimately got Julian released. While Julian is home with Stella and their boys, Gabriel and Max, the campaign continues to clear his name of charges negotiated during a plea deal to return home.

I helped start this political campaign because I could see John loved his son, as I do mine, and would do anything to help him. That's what inspired me. It was nothing more complicated than that. Sometimes you need to be true to yourself and follow your heart, listen to your humanity, ignore political expediency, be inspired by great people and never give up fighting.

On that note, I want to acknowledge Bernard Collaery, who is also here tonight—thank you for being here, Bernard—and what he sacrificed personally to get justice for whistleblower Witness K and the people of East Timor. On the topic of whistleblowers, I understand Gabriel has now established the Information Rights Project, which fights for whistleblowers facing persecution. And, importantly, David McBride has his parole decision tomorrow. Good luck, David. There are many in this parliament who support you.

Speaking of love and family, I'm so lucky to have had such strong women in my family life: my mum, Rosemary; sister, Kerri; wife, Natalie; and daughter, Bronte. Mum, who can't be here tonight—I'm looking forward to spending a lot more time with her—was always the original greenie and a loving, empathetic mother to all. She could also be really bolshie, and that's absolutely where I get it from.

To my kids, Bronte and Finn: Bronte, I actually found this note this afternoon, serendipitously. 'I love you, Daddy'—this is 2012, the very first week I started and gave my first speech—'Just remember: don't listen to them. Just think of surfing with Finn and I in Bicheno. Don't forget us.' I've never forgotten either of you. I'm so proud of who you've become and proud of the fact that I can say that you and Finn are two of my best mates. I'm so sorry I was away so much of your life. I hope I've done you proud. I might get that box off you again in a second.

Love and gratitude also to my brother, Dave, in Freo, to my sister, Kerri, who is watching this live with Martu mob out in the Little Sandy Desert tonight, and to my father, Tony, a man of principles and deep conviction who worked hard with my mum to give all our family the best chance in life.

Nat, my beautiful wife—not just my soulmate but also my best mate—I'm grateful for your love every single day and I would be lost without you. I remember dragging you over to Tasmania 23 years ago. We'd lived in seven cities in 10 years and you wanted to put down roots in WA, which is fair enough, but I remember you eventually relenting and saying to me, 'I think we've got one last adventure left in us.' Here we are in the Australian Senate 23 years later, and I hope we've got more adventures ahead. I love you. Thank you.

In 2022, the Australian Greens celebrated 50 years since the world's first green environmental party, the United Tasmania Group, was established—I apologise to Mehreen and David from the New South Wales Greens, because this is often very controversial—in the Hobart Town Hall in 1972. And if I speak loudly enough, hopefully I can talk over them. Could you bring them to order, please, President! Could you bring my colleagues to order! I often say that Tasmania's most important export to the planet was the green political movement, and I feel so proud every day that I'm part of a movement that turns up day in, day out, rain, hail or shine, to change the world.

Obama was right when he said politics is hope in motion. That's why I joined the Greens in 2008. I thank each and every Greens member and supporter from the bottom of my heart, and a special mention for the Tasmanian Greens' long-term and long-suffering convenor Damien Irving. Thank you for your steadfast support over many years, and to each and every Tasmanian who voted for me, giving me this opportunity of a lifetime.

The forces rigging our economy, undermining our democracy, polluting our planet and stoking hatred and grievance for their own ends are counting on you, me and all of us to give up. That's their strategy. I can say with confidence tonight that there is no bloody way that is going to happen—not a chance in hell. The Greens will never ever give up.

So to my comrades and fellow green warriors and mates—to each and every one of you—you're all wonderful. It's been an honour and a privilege to serve with you and those who have gone before. I think the ultimate compliment to all of you is that I actually genuinely do feel like I'm a better human for the time that I've spent with you, and I'm so grateful. I thank you for your support and your respect.

I want to give a special shout-out to leaders of political parties—and this is all leaders of political parties; I don't think there is a harder job on the planet—and especially to previous party room leaders Bob Brown, who I replaced; Christine Milne, who was a mentor to me; Richard, who's a good mate; Adam, who's a good mate; Larissa; and Nick, with your time being the leader of the Tasmanian Greens. It is literally the hardest job on the planet. It's completely thankless. The buck stops with you and you are a lightning rod for so much discontent, including in your own party. It's the most difficult job.

Everyone has different theories of leadership, but, in my opinion, a leader—a true leader—enables and works to bring out the best in each and every member of their team. If we all shine so do you, and our movement benefits. Larissa, you've done such a wonderful job doing that, and you've got this, mate; you've got this. I'm nearly finished, thank God!

This is not an easy job—we all know that—especially when you care deeply. I know most people here—in fact, all people here—do. The wheel moves slowly in this place, and it can be a heavy burden to bear sometimes. So please look after yourselves, comrades. May all your journeys bring you wisdom in the struggles of the heart and courage in the heart of the struggles ahead.

Lastly, to all my fellow senators—for at least another 48 hours, anyway!—all of us here are ordinary people who have been given an extraordinary opportunity. One day, you will likely also be standing here giving your valedictory. I ask you to reflect this afternoon on how you want to feel when this happens, whenever that may be. Here's a little message from over thousands of years for you, some stoic wisdom and reflection from Marcus Aurelius that I think is particularly and especially important for all of our time here in the Senate: 'Whatever you do, you're going to be forgotten anyway. So live your life in such a manner that, while you remain, you belong to yourself.' Adios and thank you.

speaker: Larissa Waters
heading: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
text:
Well, Senator Pete Whish-Wilson had some pretty big shoes to fill when he entered the Senate to replace Bob Brown as a Greens senator for Tasmania in 2012. Big shoes, but, as our resident surfer, Pete always seemed more comfortable barefoot. Nevertheless, over the last 14 years I have been proud to watch him fill those shoes. He's brought to this place a rare combination: the analytical mind of an economist, the instincts of a campaigner, a huge heart and care for people, and a deep and abiding love of the ocean.

Pete's path to parliament didn't begin as a staffer or a bureaucrat but in Tasmania's pristine environment and alongside hundreds of thousands of people fighting for a better world. Standing among more than 200,000 people marching against the Iraq War, Pete realised that caring deeply wasn't enough; he had to be prepared to act. He was moved to fight for our common future, both for people and for the planet, and he had the courage to turn that conviction into action. Back home in Tassie, that determination drew him into the community campaign to protect the Tamar Valley from the proposed pulp mill, and it ultimately brought him into this chamber.

During his time in parliament, he's been a relentless advocate for nature, the climate, ecosystems and wildlife, and fairness. That commitment has shaped much of Pete's work in this place. In 2012, he was the first-ever senator to raise in the Australian parliament the scourge of plastic pollution choking our oceans. He has since led the charge in parliament by establishing three landmark Senate inquiries into marine plastic pollution and Australia's recycling crisis. When it came to commercial whaling in 2013, Pete gatecrashed a diplomatic function in Canberra and gave the Japanese prime minister a handwritten letter from Sea Shepherd captain Paul Watson urging Japan to cease its commercial whaling in the Antarctic. He's the only Australian politician to visit Japan and lobby its politicians and parliament directly to end this cruel and unnecessary practice.

He was also the first MP in the Australian parliament to oppose the introduction of industrial supertrawlers, leading the parliamentary campaign to have them banned from Australian waters. His work included establishing a historic Senate inquiry in March 2014 into the Southern Ocean and Antarctic waters, including illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, after which the government agreed to carry out two 40-day customs patrols in the Southern Ocean.

Whether the threat came from plastic pollution, industrial fishing or commercial whaling, Pete brought the same qualities to the fight: deep knowledge, persistence and an absolute unwillingness to accept that protecting our oceans was too difficult. Pete brought that same persistence to his work in the Treasury portfolio. Drawing on his own experience in economics and finance, he challenged concentrated corporate power from a position of real authority. He secured the effects test in competition law reform. His work was fundamental in pushing for and establishing the banking royal commission, which led to more than 70 pieces of legislation, including tightening the screws on banks and insurance companies; a levy on big banks to pay for schools and hospitals; multinational anti-tax-avoidance laws; new, sweeping anti-money-laundering laws; and multiple tax-transparency measures.

He's also been a prominent, longstanding critic of investor-state dispute settlement clauses in trade agreements, which give big corporates control over domestic laws that might seek to protect the environment ahead of corporate profits. He introduced a private member's bill to ban these ISDS clauses in 2014, and his advocacy has had an impact. These clauses are now tainted, and they're used less frequently.

Pete understood that markets are created by political choices and that governments can choose whether they serve entrenched corporate interests or the public good. And he brought that same determination to causes that were difficult, unfashionable or too easily ignored. He's been a strong voice on medicinal cannabis for pain management, and he never shied away from sharing his own personal experiences to help reduce the stigma for others.

There are, in fact, few challenges that Pete has ever shied away from. He's been calling out the manosphere—and I love that 'real man tears' tissue box!—and he's been calling out the toxic stereotypes that rob men of the full experience of human emotion and often drive violence against women. Just a few weeks ago, he stood in this place and demanded that we 'wake the eff up' to the avalanche of AI slop and foreign bots in our social media feeds. His work on the Senate select committee inquiry into information integrity on climate change and energy showed just how strong the denial machine of conservative think tanks, PR firms, consultancies, third-party campaign groups and some conservative media outlets was working to throw sand in the gears of climate and energy policy in this country. And now we're seeing that same denial machine invading every area of our democracy.

Pete was also a vocal opponent of the detention and potential extradition of Julian Assange and a founding member of the Parliamentary Friends of the Bring Julian Assange Home campaign, along with our former colleague Senator Scott Ludlam, up there in the gallery. In December 2019, Pete tabled a petition with more than 200,000 signatures, one of the largest petitions ever presented to the Senate, calling on the government to intervene and to ensure Julian's safe passage home. For Pete, this was never an abstract argument about diplomacy or process. It was about an Australian citizen whose freedom and wellbeing had been left hanging in the balance. I too would like to acknowledge that we had Julian's dad, John, and his brother, Gabriel, in the gallery just before for his speech.

That willingness to take up a cause before others were ready to act is just as evident in his work back home in Tasmania. Pete was campaigning against salmon farming and in defence of the Maugean skate well before most others. At his 2015 Senate inquiry into this issue, another Tasmanian senator stormed out halfway through the first day, calling it a witch-hunt. Last year, that same senator joined Pete in demanding an end to salmon farming in Macquarie Harbour.

That kind of advocacy is rarely comfortable. It means being dismissed, attacked and sometimes standing almost alone. Pete has never let that deter him. And that story captures something essential about Pete. He's never needed an issue to be fashionable, easy or immediately winnable. He does the work, he builds the case and he keeps going until others catch up. And, when they do catch up, the debate has often shifted because Pete has refused to let it disappear.

Pete's connection to the ocean has been evident throughout his work in the Senate. In fact, he might be the only senator whose policy toolkit has ranged from establishing landmark inquiries to encouraging Australians to eat more sea urchins. That perspective has been especially evident in the debate over shark mitigation. He's rejected the fear driven calls for culls and lethal control programs, without ever dismissing the anxiety and trauma experienced by coastal communities. Instead, he's championed practical, evidence based measures that better protect people without indiscriminately killing marine life, including shark-spotting drones, personal deterrent devices and improved public education. He led a Senate inquiry into shark mitigation and, right up to his final weeks in parliament, continued calling for the federal leadership needed to make our beaches safer for ocean users and wildlife alike.

But, beyond the inquiries and the campaigns and the reforms, I will miss the person behind them—his conviction, his humour, his passion and clarity—and the certainty that, when Pete took up a cause, he would see it through. Our oceans need defending, and I will miss having Pete here to fight for them. I will particularly miss having him here just behind me, with a ready, warm smile, the support of a friend and the humanity that he always brings to his work. He is a good man, and the Greens have been lucky to have him, and the Senate has been lucky to have him. His duty to help the world is not done, but he will do it in a way that ensures that the other pulls on his heart—his family and the wild places of Lutruwita—have more of him than we do.

Pete entered this chamber with Bob Brown's very big shoes to fill, and 14 years later he leaves with a legacy entirely his own. Our oceans still need defending. Corporate power still needs challenging. Governments still need reminding that justice is not optional. But every one of those fights is stronger because Peter Whish-Wilson has been part of it.

Pete, thank you for your courage, your tenacity and your friendship, and for showing what can be achieved when conviction is matched by persistence. Tasmania and the parliament are better for your service. We will all deeply miss our senator surfer, but the tide has shifted because you were here.

speaker: Mehreen Faruqi
heading: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
text:
Well, Senator Surfer, I can already see you riding away on a wave, and it's really well deserved as well. That was such a beautiful valedictory speech. I think it's really difficult to condense 14 years of politics and activism and life into 45 minutes or so, but you did it so beautifully. You did it with such heart and soul. And you did it like you always do—by being yourself. And along the way you did give us a lesson in climate science and climate history, as well as the history of the Greens. But some of us might agree to disagree with that. And you sure have given it such a good crack, Pete—an incredible crack.

I actually didn't know you, Pete, until I got to this place in 2019, but I did know quite a few people who did know you, and this is what they always told me, 'You'll get what you see; you'll get a real human—a really nice bloke, someone who wears his heart on his sleeve, a bloke's bloke but also a person's person.' And now we know you are a little bit of a 'wife guy' as well in the best possible feminist way—and really good on you! I was also told that you have humanity, integrity and honesty and a real fire to protect Mother Nature and the climate. I have only seen that fire burn even more brightly in the time that I have known you, and that has really inspired me. So thank you, Pete.

From day one, to be honest, I found everything that I was told to be exactly true. On top of that, I admire so much your commitment to really fight hard for the issues that you care about. I have been lucky enough to be part of those fights and partner with you in some of those fights about the common things that we both care about. I'll just mention two of those things. One is, of course, the privilege to campaign with you protecting sharks in our oceans and the other is joining tens of thousands of people in New South Wales to protect our coastlines from that horrific PEP-11, which was going to blast and drill off the pristine coast of New South Wales. That was one of those fights we did win, alongside the fierce, fierce campaigning of communities. PEP11 was indeed rejected in 2025. I've been very proud to stand alongside you and thousands of people in that fight, and I will continue the fight to end the barbaric cruelty against sharks while also making sure that people who love to go into the ocean are protected as well.

One thing that I think I will never forget is the fierce passion with which you, Senator Whish-Wilson, have tried to unmask the perils of misinformation and disinformation in this age of AI slop and of bot farms funded by those which you so eloquently mentioned in your speech and who deliberately try to undermine climate protection and our democracy. I do hope that there are others in this place who can assume the mantle in the way that you have done. So thank you so much, Pete. We love you. Happy surfing.

speaker: Michelle Ananda-Rajah
heading: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
text:
Colleagues, I had the great privilege of collaborating with Pete on the Senate Select Committee on Information Integrity on Climate Change and Energy. Pete, I regard this as a seminal piece of work—as groundbreaking work which I think has opened the door for a really rich vein of inquiry which will now branch out from the work we did.

I can't tell you all what this work was like for us. We were in the trenches. I felt at times that we were under attack, and it was like you and me against the world. I felt, sitting next to you as a newbie, really unfamiliar with the processes of the Senate and, frankly, the powers of the Senate. I was unfamiliar. This was uncharted territory for me, but you were a steadying influence. You had my back at times when I was faced with some pretty unsavoury commentary. I was going to say 'unsavoury characters', but let's not attack the man. Play the ball, not the man, right? I will say 'unsavoury commentary'. You had my back, and you called that stuff out publicly. Frankly, some of that stuff was misogyny. It was, and it was directed at me, which was something unfamiliar to me, because I came from medicine. I didn't really deal with that stuff. To have to deal with this in a public forum was confronting, but you stood up against that stuff, and I will forever be grateful.

But the work itself was incredible. We pulled back the veil on what you and I—and now, I think, a lot of other people in the commentariat—call the denial machine. We never found a smoking gun, but we certainly mapped out the actors and we showed how this network effectively operates and who the key players are. We identified some of their backers—absolutely fossil fuel interests—but we also revealed the vector, and that is the social media platforms. We revealed the technical and financial architecture that allows this stuff to be propagated and amplified and then to divide and sow doubt. You're absolutely right: we are in a polluted information environment and it is information warfare. It is a frontier where we will either win or end up on our knees.

The work that we did on this report, led by you and the strength of your conviction, has meant that it is now being picked up by other committees. It's been picked up by the electoral matters committee, who can see synergies, and it's also been picked up, I think, by the departments and institutions that underpin this place in communications, in the AI Safety Institute that has been stood up and in the climate and energy space. Certainly I was so proud of this work that I sent this book—I'm such a nerd—to all our key stakeholders. If I were to die tomorrow, I'd die happy because of my children but also this work, and that's because of you, my friend. So go well. Go strong. You are a warrior. Thank you.

speaker: Josh Burns
heading: BILLS
subheading: Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026, National Self-exclusion Register (Cost Recovery Levy) Amendment Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
The former member for Dunkley, Peta Murphy, was a great friend of mine. In fact, she liked to tease me from time to time. When I was giving speeches in this place, if I didn't focus on the material, she used to call it 'story time with Josh', and only Peta could distil it down to that in such a great way. But I will try not to have 'story time with Josh', Peta. I will try and do your incredible report justice.

I want to start my speech by paying tribute to Peta Murphy, who, through the work of a committee report, has left an incredible legacy. All of us in this place feel a sense of responsibility and a sense of duty to honour Peta, and I know the minister, who is next to me, feels that deeply. She also was a great friend of Peta's. We miss Peta very much and we will continue on with the work she has left us—and that can't be said of every member of parliament—via a committee report. This parliament feels so strongly about the work that was done in that committee report, and that shows the intellectual bravery that Peta Murphy brought when she came into this place to this and her skill as a parliamentarian. We miss her very much.

The toxic relationship between gambling and sport is one that, frankly, every single member of this place understands we need to do something about it. The way in which it has really ingrained itself in the culture of sport in this country has meant that not only is there a cultural aspect of it but also a reliance on it, There is a toxic reliance on gambling—on gambling advertising, on this cycle of companies looking to target the most vulnerable people who are susceptible to their advertising, and sporting codes and organisations who are reliant on the money that gambling produces. Football clubs, with their pokie licences; commercial television; local sporting clubs; stadiums—it is everywhere.

There will be repercussions from this bill. This is not a bill where there aren't going to be any consequences in making the changes that we are putting forward in this bill. This will have an impact and it is real, but we have to do it. We have to break this nexus and this connection between gambling advertising and sport. When I think about my eight-year-old daughter, who loves the Carlton Football Club—that is one of the proudest things that I have been able to impart on her. We watch games together; I love watching the footy with her. And then you see the ads pop up—the multies, the betting, the celebrity endorsements—and you think, 'What is going to be left inside this child's mind about what she is actually watching?' It should be all about the game, not about the odds. We need to do something about that and that is what this bill does.

Unfortunately, it is not easy. The number of reforms that we have in this bill—I'm going to run through them in a moment—is significant. And, like every piece of legislation where we sit down with people across the parliament and we work out how we're going to pass it through the Senate, I know there has been a huge amount of work done by the minister and members in this place. Hopefully, it will be a great moment where we can make significant changes to improve the situation where gambling isn't investing in our sport and our TV channels.

I also want to mention a bit of history. The closest example of what we're trying to do here is when our country got rid of tobacco advertising. Actually, if you look at the timeline of how long it took for us, as a country, to take out tobacco advertising, it was significant. The first health warnings in Australia about tobacco were introduced in 1973. There was a radio advertising ban on tobacco three years later, in 1976. Australia subsequently banned tobacco advertising in newspapers and magazines in 1990—14 years later. The Tobacco Advertising Prohibition Act 1992 imposed much broader national restrictions on the broadcasting and publication of tobacco advertising from 1993.

It took Australia 20 years to take away tobacco advertising. Think about the media markets and the state of journalism in Australia in the nineties versus what it is now. If you look at the commercial advertising in the newspaper classifieds—around $4 billion a year was going into classified advertising back then; it's now about $200 million. All of that directly funds journalism in this country. All of that directly funds free and independent media. All of that funds commercial television and the sort of other advertising that funds Australian programs, and Australian content and kids programs, Australian industry and Australian jobs. It took 20 years to take away tobacco advertising, at a time when media advertising revenue was going up.

Right now, we are seeing the greatest transition away from independent news, from journalism, from the advertising that funds the important pillars of our democracy, not to mention our local sporting clubs and our sporting codes. And we're entering into a time when money is being moved into large tech companies and being invested in artificial intelligence. It's moving away from holding people and moving away from being invested back into the institutions that help create all of the different parts of our democracy and is moving towards other parts that make our democracy and our truth and our politics so much more difficult.

This is not simple. This is actually really difficult. I know that people out there ask: 'Well, why not just do a full ban? Why not just do it?' They are legitimate questions, and Peta Murphy laid the groundwork and the pathway against which we all must hold ourselves. But this also is real, and the consequences of this will be real: there will be millions of dollars less for journalism, for institutions, for sport—to invest in women's sport, in the AFLW. All of these things are going to need time to adjust. But we need to make sure that we are true to the point of what this bill is all about, and that is breaking the nexus and the connection between gambling and sport. Even though there will be consequences, we need to push on with these reforms.

The bill will make a significant number of changes to the number of ads on TV, making sure that gambling ads won't be on TV during sport, especially during specific hours. There'll be frequency caps outside of those hours. I also want to mention the fact that, whenever you're watching sport and you see these celebrity endorsements parading as being part of the television coverage, it's actually just an endorsement by Sportsbet or Ladbrokes or one of these other companies. All of that will be banned. Gambling advertising is not going to be normalised—this culture of 'what's happening over at the odds?' All that part of our radio and television coverage of sport is going to be gone.

When kids walk into a stadium, they're not going to see advertising all around the stadium. They're not going to see it on jerseys. They're not going to hear it on the radio while they're going to and from school. The way this bill outlines the online ban basically means that, as a parent, I am going to be able to opt out or switch off all gambling advertising on the streaming platforms in my home. That is a power that we want to give to each and every parent around Australia: if you don't want your kids to see gambling advertising, you can do something pretty simple and click 'opt out'.

If platforms choose not to have that function, the alternative is no gambling advertising on their platforms; they have to comply with this, or the answer is no gambling advertising. Here is the choice that this bill gives parents: either, if online platforms, social media and tech companies choose to not comply with the law and not provide these three steps of verification and options for parents, they will have no gambling advertising or, if they want to have gambling advertising on their platforms, they have to give parents and other people the choice and the ability to turn it off. That is a power that does not exist right now.

When you think about all of that and you think about my eight-year-old daughter, when we go to the footy and the MCG, there will be no gambling around the MCG anymore. There will be no gambling on the stadium. There will be no gambling advertising on the uniforms. When we travel to and from school, there will be no gambling advertising. When we're watching the footy at home, when we're watching it on 7plus, there will be no gambling advertising. We will have created a gambling advertising free home. That sounds pretty good to me, and that's exactly what this bill will be able to do.

There are also much broader reforms that are contained in this bill that I don't want to run out of time on, because they are significant and they have required a lot of work, and I'm really proud that we are taking them. We are going to ensure that illegal offshore gambling providers are reducing their gambling harm and ensure that anyone participating in gambling in Australia is doing so within the safety of Australian consumer protections. We're strengthening BetStop, which has helped thousands of Australians pull themselves out of problem gambling. We are going to address harmful and emerging online gambling products, including banning online keno and foreign match lotteries.

If you want to just pause on online keno, these are online pocket pokies where people can just click pokie and pokie time and time again. We see the ways in which people lose themselves in casinos until all hours of the morning. Well, just imagine lying in bed, pressing the pokie over and over again. People are losing thousands of dollars. All of that will be banned under this bill, and I think that is a fantastic reform. I've never spent a cent at a pokie. I've never spent a cent with any of these companies. I've never spent a cent on Sportsbet or Ladbrokes or any of them. That's a personal choice I make. But I think this is a wonderful thing, where we are not making it easy for these companies to just take money off people lying in bed with an algorithm and a formula that is not designed for people to win. It is designed for companies to make money.

The impact on foreign match lotteries also will mean that the local small businesses that are selling lottery tickets aren't going to have these foreign lotteries able to undercut them and have situations where people can buy tickets in offshore lotteries. People want to be a part of the lotto. My grandmother used to love doing that. I've never really seen the appeal, but at least we will ensure that Australians are buying from local newsagencies, and I think that's a good thing. There are many other things that this bill does. It closes regulatory gaps that allow some operators to offer lottery-style products under the guise of trade promotions and reward clubs. There are a number of other things that we're going to ensure that this bill does.

But I want to make this point: when negotiating anything in this parliament, we don't have the numbers, as the Labor Party, to pass everything through the Senate. That requires us to sit down with people and negotiate. It requires us to negotiate with either the Liberal Party or the Greens. There have been bills where we've gone through one, and there have been bills where we've gone through the other. Ultimately, that's about respecting our democracy. Obviously, I want to see a whole range of things that this bill makes an incredible contribution to. One of the things that we passed in our national conference was around inducements and the way in which these companies are offering people extra incentives to continue gambling and targeting the most susceptible people on that. I think that in the negotiations that is obviously something that the Labor Party in our conference said that we want to see included in the bill, and I know that there is a lot of work going on behind the scenes. I am working as closely as I can with my colleagues, and I know everyone is working to make sure we get something through this House and we get these reforms in.

That is because they will make a difference. They will make a profound difference. They'll give parents the power to turn off gambling advertising. They'll mean that, when young kids are walking into the colosseum of Australian football, they're not looking around seeing BetStop and Ladbrokes; they're walking around and seeing the great Australian athletes, men and women competing on the best sporting field in the country and possibly the world. It took 20 years from the moment in which tobacco advertising and health warnings were issued in Australia for a bill to come in. Well, we are doing this. This has never been done before, and this is a huge set of reforms that will have a big impact on breaking that nexus between gambling and sport. I thank every member who has contributed to this, the minister and so many others. Most of all, I thank Peta Murphy, who laid down the path, and now it's our job to walk down it.

speaker: Andrew Wallace
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
There are real problems in higher education. No-one should pretend otherwise. There are concerns about quality, student experience, workforce shortages, artificial intelligence, antisemitism and social cohesion on campus, international student numbers, access for students in the outer suburbs and in the regions, and the position of private higher education providers. The coalition recognises that a future government may need stronger tools to respond to these problems. For example, powers over international student allocations could be used to align international education with national capacity in housing, infrastructure and services. Powers attached to public funding could, if appropriately designed, be used to require stronger standards on antisemitism, social cohesion and institutional accountability. A more flexible pathway for Commonwealth-supported places could assist private providers in priority workforce fields, and place allocations could be used to support regional and outer-suburban opportunity where it is genuinely needed. Those are legitimate objectives, but good objectives don't automatically justify unlimited powers. The question for this parliament is whether the bill gets the balance right between national stewardship, institutional autonomy, student choice, accountability and parliamentary oversight.

On the evidence already received by the Senate Education and Employment Legislation Committee, there are significant reasons to doubt that the bill has that right balance. Universities Australia, the peak body for Australia's universities, says:

The Bill shifts significant decision-making authority to the Minister and the ATEC, with many of the framework's most important features left to Guidelines, non-disallowable instruments and administrative decision-making rather than primary legislation.

Universities Australia supports the broad direction of reform but recommends passage only with substantial amendments.

QUT, my old university, makes the point even more directly. It says:

The case for the Bill's funding reforms is clear. The case for these extraordinary Ministerial powers has not been made.

QUT warns that a measured delay to improve the bill would be preferable to legislation that permanently weakens university governance, autonomy and parliamentary scrutiny.

UniSC, in my electorate of Fisher, also provided a submission. They are in general support of the bill's objectives but they also warned that a centrally managed system may fail to keep pace with local population growth, workforce need and student demand. Now, as one of the members for the Sunshine Coast, many students tell me—in fact, I was at Chancellor College just recently—that moving away to study under this government's cost-of-living crisis is just not a realistic option. Travel, accommodation costs, caring responsibilities and lost income mean that, if a local place is unavailable, university may simply be unavailable to them.

UniSC rightly argues that decisions cannot be made solely from Canberra using lagged data; they must reflect local knowledge, local demand and the needs of high-growth communities just like mine. If we want more young people in Fisher to study locally, uniSC needs the certainty to plan, invest and grow with our community. I want to send a shout-out at this opportunity to Helen Bartlett, the vice-chancellor. She is doing a great job at uniSC as she embarks, on behalf of the university, on developing our very own medical school that the member for Fairfax and I worked so very hard for 10 years to develop with Griffith University. The time has now come for UniSC to have its own medical school, and the member for Fairfax and I will be continuing to push that very hard.

Most of the submissions raise legitimate concerns, including excessive ministerial discretion, insufficient transparency, weak parliamentary oversight, threats to institutional autonomy, rigid allocation settings or risks created by the overenrolment penalty regime. The bill's treatment of the Australian Tertiary Education Commission deserves particular attention. Labor presents ATEC as an independent steward, but independence from the sector is not the same thing as independence from the executive government. ATEC commissioners can be removed by the minister where their performance has been unsatisfactory for a significant period—terms which are not defined. ATEC cannot employ its own staff. It relies on APS staff made available by the department. It cannot independently engage contractors or consultants. It must have regard to ministerial priorities, and it remains subject to ministerial directions. These things should be ringing alarm bells in the broader education community.

More concerningly, the bill creates additional avenues for the minister to influence international student allocations, including by specifying matters with which ATEC must comply and by directing it to consider varying provider-level allocations. It is a body which may administer decisions but is structurally constrained by the executive by design—by this Labor government's design. The international student provisions require particularly close examination. Universities Australia states in its submission that the minister should set the broad framework but ATEC should make provider-level decisions independently according to transparent criteria. It also argues that the international allocation framework should be subject to independent statutory review. The coalition will examine those proposals seriously before we reach a position on these.

There's also a fundamental practical concern with the new managed-growth model. Under the current system, universities can enrol more students than the Commonwealth directly funds. They do not receive additional Commonwealth funding for those students, but they can retain the student contribution. That system is not perfect, but it has allowed universities to respond to genuine demand and educate more students using the same taxpayer contribution. This bill treats that flexibility as overenrolment and imposes a financial penalty. It changes a capped-funding model into a capped-places model. Why should parliament penalise an institution that educates more Australian students for the same taxpayer contribution? Universities have warned that the likely response will be more cautious offers, higher entry thresholds, early closure of applications and fewer opportunities for capable students.

The bill's fiscal claims also require a clear explanation from the minister. The minister's public pitch has referred to $3.6 billion over a decade and 230,000 additional places, yet the explanatory memorandum refers to $2.5 billion in additional net funding over 11 years from 2024-25 and 200,000 additional commencing domestic students over the decade. Those are not trivial differences. Where does the additional $1.1 billion come from? How did an additional 30,000 places appear? Why do the MYEFO papers refer to $2.5 billion over 11 years while the minister now promotes $3.6 billion over a decade? Was the new funding included in the budget? Was it being offset, cut or repurposed to pay for it? What protections exist against a funding announcement today becoming an unfunded liability tomorrow?

The Parliamentary Library's Bills Digest notes that the $2.5 billion MYEFO measure was partly offset through $16.4 billion in repurposed funding and efficiencies over 11 years. That makes transparent scrutiny of the government's new claims all the more important. The bill's needs based funding provisions also need closer scrutiny.

The principle of better support for First Nations students, low SES students and regional delivery is sound. The coalition supports genuine opportunities for Australians who have historically been locked out of higher education, but the practical operation of the scheme will turn heavily on ministerial guidelines, eligibility criteria, modifier amounts, regional classifications, conditions of grant, and expenditure rules. Adelaide uni says important policy settings are left to guidelines, and recommends a legislative requirement for genuine consultation before they are made or varied.

This is exactly why the committee process matters. Parliament should not be asked to sign a blank cheque and discover the real scheme later, in guidelines drafted behind closed doors in ministerial offices. The coalition will approach this bill constructively but not casually. The coalition will make its final decision after the work of the committee is complete. Our standard will be straightforward: does this bill expand opportunity without centralising— (Time expired)

speaker: Tim Watts
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
There are plenty of Australians who hate the idea of data centres being built in Australia at the moment. For many people, they are the physical embodiment of everything that they're worried about with the arrival of AI. Others are worried about the local impacts of a specific data centre that's being built or proposed for the community that they live in. The development of AI and the rollout of the data centres to support it is a big change. It's happening around the world, and it's natural for people to feel anxiety about it.
