But, while the world is changing, we can't afford to hide under the bed. We can't just hit the stop button and hope for the best as the world moves on around us. We need to take control and shape these changes in Australia's interests, to take control so that Australia can benefit from the upside of AI while protecting our community from the potential downsides. That's why, earlier this year, our government announced a set of expectations for large AI data centres and why the Prime Minister has announced that we will be delivering a set of binding Australian standards for AI. As the Prime Minister said, 'This is about Australia shaping the future, rather than letting the future shape us.'

If we get this right, Australia has everything it needs for Australians to realise the benefits of AI: the smartest minds, the biggest renewable energy opportunities, proximity to Asia and a predictable and reliable legal system buttressed by a robust democracy. Australia is home to some of the world's best healthcare researchers, and access to AI and computing power in Australian data centres can help them make life-saving medical breakthroughs. AI and Australian computing power can enable cutting-edge scientific research on some of the most complex challenges we face.

Australia's first university led AI supercomputer, MAVERIC, from Monash University, sits in the CDC data centre in my electorate in Melbourne's west. Australian scientists are using it for research on cancer, infectious diseases and antimicrobial resistance, and new medicine discovery, as well as enhanced skin cancer detection, simulation of star and planet formation and analysis of Antarctic imagery for environmental modelling. AI and Australian computing is also vital to ensuring that Australia's defence forces and security agencies are able to keep up with the rapidly evolving and increasing challenges they're confronting to keep us safe.

Australian standards for AI will ensure that all Australians are able to benefit from these opportunities while being protected from the potential harms. Australian standards for AI will set clear rules for the construction of data centres, including where they're built and the power and water they use. They will include a legal obligation for the next generation of large-scale data centres to underwrite new power supply. They'll be required to cover their full share of grid connections so no costs are passed on to homes or businesses. We'll create an obligation for these data centres to build new renewable energy generation and to put at least as much energy into our grid as they take out of it, and we'll require data centres to minimise their water use and pay for any additional water infrastructure required.

Many current and proposed data centres across Australia already meet these requirements. I know this from my own experience of the data centres in my electorate, in Truganina, Laverton and Brooklyn. I've followed the construction and operation of these data centres closely, and a number of them have now been operating for years. I can't recall receiving a single complaint about them since they started operation, and I'm certain that I've received more complaints about the abattoirs, chemical manufacturers and trucking and shipping container parks that operate in the surrounding industrial areas. These data centres create less smell, less dust and less traffic than the existing industrial land uses in this area, and they support good jobs in our community. Nearly 4,000 jobs have been created in the construction of the Australian owned and operated CDC Laverton data centre. I've spoken to the workers and unions on site, and I know they're good jobs with good conditions. Once it's finished, it'll support 1,750 ongoing roles in our community—jobs for locals who don't have to drive to the CBD to do them.

Best practice data centres, like the CDC data centres in Brooklyn and Laverton, utilise an advanced liquid cooling system to maximise their water efficiency. They use a single volume of water which is continuously recirculated. That means the Brooklyn and Laverton data centres don't use any water for cooling. They're some of the most water efficient data centres in Australia and New Zealand. The result of innovations like this is that Australian data centres account for just 0.04 per cent of Australia's total water use. Public swimming pools use six times more; golf courses use 10 times more. Last financial year, Australian data centres consumed 3.9 terawatt hours of electricity, around two per cent of Australia's national energy market consumption. They've supported 1.5 terawatt hours of renewable energy generation per year and have invested $3.1 billion in grid infrastructure, and they'll invest a further $7.2 billion in grid infrastructure by 2030.

Done right, data centre rollouts can help fund our renewable energy transition, bring down costs for consumers and improve the reliability of our grid, but only if we take control of our future instead of hiding under the bed. We're not America. We want to manage AI and data centres the Australian way. That's what the Albanese government is doing.

speaker: Alison Penfold
heading: COMMITTEES
text:
This is a completely last minute decision to speak, but it is an important one. I welcome the report of the Standing Committee on Education, Security and Prosperity in Asia titled Building Asia capability in Australia through the education system and beyond. The reason that I've chosen to speak on this particular report is my own experience both as a university student and also in my professional career. I was a European humanities student at school, and I studied French and German, but, for a couple of reasons, when I went to university I chose to study Korean language.

There are two reasons for that. One is that I have a goddaughter who was adopted from Korea and my hope was that one day, if she ever wanted to go to Korea and learn about the country of her heritage, that I could go and that I could help her engage with the country. Secondly, I had a lot of friends and colleagues at the time—I'm gen X, and I finished high school in 1989—who were studying Japanese. I had this sense, well before K-pop and K-dramas, that Korea was a country that Australia needed to deepen its relationship with.

So I chose to study Korean language at the Australian National University. I have to say that, despite the fact that some 30 years later my Korean is not much beyond being able to say 'maekju juseyo' to order a beer and 'ajumma, ppalli wa', come here I need a beer quickly, I still very much value the relationship and that experience that I had. Indeed, I had the opportunity through an Asian languages scholarship to actually go and study for a year at Sogang University where not only did I spend time learning Korean in a language school but I also had the opportunity to actually study with Koreans in the classroom. This is the sort of experience that is critical and a key point of the report.

Then in my own professional life, when I was the CEO of the Australian Livestock Exporters' Council, part of my job was spending time in Indonesia, Vietnam and Malaysia. I came to that job at quite a turbulent time in the industry—after Labor's ban on live cattle to Indonesia. I was responsible to help bridge the divide between our countries, rebuild the trade and help our customers understand the animal welfare requirements that Australia was placing on Australian exporters through the Exporter Supply Chain Assurance System. When you go and have those conversations business to business, people to people, it's not just about trade numbers. It's actually about having a deeper understanding of the culture. One of the things I learnt with Korean is you can't directly translate from English to Korean if you don't understand the cultural context in which you are having to explain and get your point across.

As I say, when we're engaging with Asia, it's far more than numbers on a trade balance sheet. It means understanding languages, cultures, history and politics. It means building relationships and networks. Wherever possible, it means actually spending the time in the region. I'm incredibly grateful now, as a member of parliament, to come to this place having that experience and that exposure—having studied Korean language at the ANU and having spent time in Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam.

The report describes this capability as a combination of cultural knowledge, language skills and professional networks that allow Australians to engage effectively with our region, and that resonates very strongly with me. When you learn another country's language, you inevitably learn much more than words. You begin to understand how people think, how their history has shaped them, how their society works and how they see Australia and the world. That understanding became so practical to me and, as I say, to bring to my work here in the parliament.

Those experiences reinforced for me that successful engagement in Asia depends on relationships, trust and cultural understanding. You cannot build those things from Canberra, Wauchope, Taree or Tea Gardens. You have to spend time in country, to listen, to understand how business is done, and it's done quite differently. I learnt that very clearly, particularly in my engagement with Vietnamese cattle importers, trying to explain the Exporter Supply Chain Assurance System, why Australia was implementing it, how decisions are made and what matters to the people that you're dealing with. As I say, in the live export industry, that meant working very directly with businesses, officials and communities across Southeast Asia. It meant understanding not just commercial arrangements but also local expectations, cultural sensitivities and the importance of long-term relationships. That experience taught me that Australian businesses are at their strongest in Asia when we turn up, build trust and invest in understanding our partners.

That's difficult to replicate in a classroom and impossible to replace with an app or an AI translation tool. Indeed, the committee made precisely that point: technology can make translation easier, but it cannot substitute for the cultural understanding and human relationships that allow diplomats, businesses and governments to operate effectively. That is why I'm concerned by some of the figures contained in this report. In 2023, only 3.3 per cent of Australian year 12 students studied one of the previously designated priority Asian languages—Japanese, Chinese or Indonesian. Australia ranked second last among 64 countries for the proportion of year 10 students learning a second language, and only 38 per cent of Australians speak two or more languages, compared with an OECD average of 68 per cent. The situation at university is no better. The report found Asian language enrolments are at a historic low. Only around one per cent of domestic university students were studying an Asian language in 2023, while enrolments at the ANU have fallen substantially across all of the 16 languages it teaches. That certainly concerns me, as an alumni of Asian language study at ANU—an incredible program that ANU has invested in over many decades.

There's a practical economic dimension to this. Australia is a trading nation. Our farmers, miners and regional businesses produce some of the best products in the world, but future prosperity will increasingly depend on our ability not simply to sell into Asian markets but to understand those markets and build enduring relationships with them, which I've seen myself. A businessperson who understands the language, customs and commercial culture of Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia or Vietnam certainly has an advantage. A diplomat or a Defence official who understands the history and perspectives of our neighbours is better equipped to represent Australia's interests. Indeed, on a recent trip to East Timor as part of the Australian Regional Leadership Initiative, I worked with some of our officials from the Australian embassy in East Timor who spoke some Tetum, and that made such a difference when we were up in remote villages and increased that engagement, which made the experience for me. I think those other MPs and senators, who were on the delegation, got so much more out of the visit.

A young Australian who's lived and studied in Asia comes home with knowledge, networks and experience that can benefit this country for decades. That's why I particularly support the report's emphasis on immersion and in-country experience.

The committee recommends continuing support for longer term, language focused study through the New Colombo Plan and considering opportunities for postgraduate students and researchers spending time in Asia. My own experience—I'll finish on this point—tells me that this is money well spent: giving young Australians the opportunity to learn the language and to go and practise it in-country, from just ordering the food to trying to attend a lecture learning about Korean political economy. I tell you what—that was a hell of a class and one of the most difficult language-learning experiences of my life. But I learnt so much not only about Korea but also about the importance of this investment in young people for the future, for building our relationship with Asia.

speaker: Andrew Leigh
heading: COMMITTEES
text:
I have to say what a pleasure it is to be speaking in this debate after the member for Banks, Zhi Soon and just before the members for Reid, Sally Sitou, and Menzies, Gabriel Ng. The Labor caucus has become a better caucus in the 16 years that I've served in it. One of the ways it's become better has not only been your entry into the caucus, Deputy Speaker, but also the greater diversity that we now have in our caucus—a caucus which now looks more like the community that it serves.

When I was five, I briefly attended a primary school in Banda Aceh in the north of Sumatra. Our lessons were conducted in Indonesian, and much of the school day consisted of learning nation-building songs, because the national government wanted to ensure that all Acehnese thought of themselves as Indonesian first and Acehnese second. We played in the muddy playground, and my mother recalls at the time that the sole white child in the class was also the only child whose white shirt came home brown at the end of every day.

My father, Michael Leigh AM, was working at Syiah Kuala University helping strengthen social science research across Indonesian universities and Islamic institutes. My mother was beginning her research on Acehnese crafts, which she turned into a book, Tangan-Tangan Trampil: Seni Kerajinan Aceh = Hands of Time: The Crafts of Aceh, and then on Indonesian education, including the Pancasila principles, which became her doctoral thesis. We lived in Aceh for two years and in Jakarta for a year, and that helped shape how I see our region and the value of Australia engaging with the world.

Australia is at its best when we see multiculturalism as a strength and international engagement as a quality. We benefit from those person-to-person links, which allow Australians to be more secure, to be more economically prosperous and to enjoy so much of what the region has to offer through our outbound tourism and the benefits that inbound tourism brings to Australia in jobs and prosperity. The government has placed the Indo-Pacific at the centre of our foreign policy. The Prime Minister chose Indonesia for his first bilateral visit after the 2022 election. Foreign Minister Wong set herself the task of visiting every ASEAN country except Myanmar in her first year, along with every member of the Pacific Islands Forum. And since we came to office, Australian ministers have made more than 140 visits to South-East Asia, including 20 by the Prime Minister and 31 by the Foreign minister. The PM has attended every summit with ASEAN leaders. The foreign minister has attended every ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting. Showing up is a statement of intent in our region. We have also invited the region to Australia, hosting the ASEAN-Australia Special Summit in Melbourne in 2024, marking 50 years since Australia became ASEAN's first dialogue partner and creating the largest diplomatic gathering Australia had hosted in more than a decade.

We have continued to engage with the region through the Jakarta treaty signed this year—the Australia-Indonesia Treaty on Common Security—and through the third Australia-India annual summit held in Melbourne last month, during which Prime Minister Modi visited Australia and agreed to expand the comprehensive strategic partnership and pursue fresh areas of economic cooperation. Australia has supported Timor-Leste's accession as ASEAN's 11th member and stabilised the relationship with China while protecting Australian interests and without compromising what matters to Australians.

Our foreign policy is also strengthened through our strong engagement with First Nations Australians. A point that I remember former Foreign minister Bob Carr making to me is that, when you engage in international meetings, your domestic policies and particularly your policies as they relate to First Nations people are taken into account in how other nations engage. Asia accounts for some 60 per cent of our two-way trade, and we benefit from Asia being such a fast-growing region and from our engagement in the region.

It's in that context that the government commissioned the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Education to complete a report titled Security and prosperity in Asia: building Asia capability in Australia through the education system and beyond. I commend the member for Gellibrand, Tim Watts, for his leadership on this report. It received some 195 submissions and held 11 public hearings. It defines Asia capability broadly, including language proficiency and cultural literacy, country knowledge and regional experience. Its main argument is that Asia capability is a sovereign capability, one that Australia can exercise in its own right.

There are some really troubling statistics in the report. Domestic university enrolments in South-East Asian languages fell 75 per cent between 2005 and 2024. Of Australia's one million domestic university students, just 500 are studying Indonesian. At the year 12 level, enrolments in Indonesian fell from 1,161 in 2010 to 486 in 2024. I confess that my own Bahasa has faded over the years, though I do sometimes like to remind my children that, while English just has the word 'hot', Indonesian has 'panas' meaning hot in temperature and 'pedas' meaning spicy. That can help us at dinner. It doesn't help that my Indonesian proficiency is sadly unequal to that of the 500 Australians who are studying at Australian universities.

We have the example of great scholars such as Herb Feith and Jamie Mackie, whose work built stronger ties, but we need more of that kind of Indonesian engagement. The problem comes too in China expertise. In the five years to 2021, only 17 students completed honours in Chinese studies with language, and, among more than 2,300 postgraduate coursework programs offered by Australian universities, only 21 include an Asia focused specialisation. Hindi is taught at only two Australian universities despite the fact that Australia's Indian diaspora is around a million people, including a terrific community in my electorate of Fenner. The report recommends stronger pathways through schools and university language hubs supported by better national data. It understands that, while AI translation is getting better, it doesn't bring the cultural literacy that bilingualism does. It acknowledges how important it is to have school exchange or university placements. A homestay can create those relationships and memories that can sustain years of study. The report also recognised the way in which Australian institutions can sometimes overlook expertise that is already inside their workplace. Employees notice who gets promoted based on their language skills or their regional networks that sit outside their formal job descriptions.

The report also notes that, while Asian-language learning is declining at the school and university levels, we have a great strength in our community language schools. In 2023, 631 community language schools taught more than a hundred languages to over a hundred thousand students. I see in my own electorate the terrific work of community language schools being done. But that is not translated into formal skills recognition or into community teachers having workable pathways into qualified classroom teaching.

We need to see more Australian business leaders championing Australian capability in position descriptions. We need to see more board members asking whether regional strategy draws on people with genuine country knowledge. We need to have universities and employers maintaining a closer conversation about demand which allows students to see clear pathways into great jobs as a result of studying Indonesian or Hindi. We need to support more Asian Australian staff into senior roles through peak bodies such that exist in the legal services sector. Organisations such as Asialink, with whom I spoke last Friday, are doing a power of good in building these skills across the region.

When I sat in that Banda Aceh classroom, my understanding of Indonesian came through songs and stories. Today, we need that expertise built through business ties, and this terrific report is a great place to start.

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: COMMITTEES
text:
Our minister for education called education the great equaliser in an unequal world. I strongly share that belief, and I'm confident that it's shared by many members in this place. Many years ago, I completed my own teacher training. I'm also a mother to two young boys. I know education shapes every child's future. Every child deserves the best education Australia can offer, whatever school their family chooses. Good teachers shape learning outcomes, civics education and media literacy protect our democracy, and, importantly, languages open up other parts of the world.

These beliefs are why I am so pleased to serve on the House Standing Committee on Education. I am proud of the report our committee has presented, Security and prosperity in Asia:building Asia capability in Australia through the education system and beyond. At the outset, I want to thank our chair, the member for Gellibrand, and the deputy chair, the member for Nicholls, for leading all of my committee colleagues through this process.

Australia's security and prosperity are tied to our region. We need people who speak its languages, understand its cultures and histories and have built trusted relationships there. We refer to this as 'Asia capability'. It is a national capability built in classrooms, universities and workplaces and through time spent in the region. The evidence of our nation's capability showed a pipeline deep in trouble. Domestic enrolments in South-East Asian languages at Australian universities fell by 75 per cent from 2005 to 2024. Take the study of Indonesian, for example, where we heard some of the most concerning evidence. Barely 500 of Australia's one million domestic university students study Indonesian. At school, 3.3 per cent of Australian year 12 students studied a priority Asian language in 2023. Year 12 Indonesian enrolments fell from 1,160 students in 2010 to 486 nationwide in 2024. In my home state of Queensland, the figures are even more stark. Four students across our state were projected to sit a year 12 Indonesian exam in 2026. Witnesses to our inquiry warned that Indonesian teaching faces functional extinction in Australia by 2031. Indonesia is one of Australia's closest and most consequential neighbours. Losing our ability to teach Indonesian weakens our ability to understand the country and build strong relationships with its people.

Translation technology in the age of AI just cannot fill that gap. We heard evidence that software can translate words, but it can't read a room, understand history and build trust and relationships. The Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority, ACARA, conveyed this to our committee very well. A calculator can produce an answer, but the user still needs enough mathematics to know whether that answer makes sense.

Australia's Asian Australian communities hold deep language skills and cultural knowledge, yet heritage language skills often fall across generations. Families told our inquiry they want formal study for their children. Many South Asian Australian students have little access to Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali or Tamil. We have wonderful language programs right across my community of Griffith through so many of our schools. Of the 19 state schools in and around Griffith, 11 offer at least one Asian language. Japanese is taught at nine of these state schools and Chinese at five. That gives us a good base, but the full picture shows how narrow the choices remain. Those 19 state schools provide 35 language offerings; 14 offer Chinese or Japanese, and the remaining 21 are European or other languages. The gap is clearer among 13 schools that offer only one language. Just five teach an Asian language.

We have strong foundations across Griffith, but the pathway can break as soon as a student changes school. A child may begin Japanese at primary school and then enter a secondary school where it is unavailable. Another student may study Chinese through to year 12 and then find no clear university course or career path. A passionate teacher can spark a lifelong interest in a language and culture, but we cannot ask individual teachers to carry a national capability on their shoulders alone.

We have local examples of learning experiences that this report seeks to support. We've got so many great state schools offering fabulous programs, including West End State School, East Brisbane State School and Brisbane State High School. Among other colleges in my area, Cannon Hill Anglican College has run Japan tours for their students for more than 20 years. Senior students visit Tokyo, Kyoto and Hiroshima. They complete a four-day homestay. Peter Nakamura, the college's head of faculty for languages, has seen students use their Japanese in daily life. Some return as adults to reconnect with host families.

Last year at Villanova College, students joined more than 450 language learners from 20 schools at the University of Queensland's Go Borderless Languages Experience Day. Villanova students then took part in a 13-day China immersion tour, using their Chinese in Beijing and attending school in Nanjing. These experiences give students a reason to keep studying, but not all students and all families are able to afford access to these types of programs. We know interest grows through real contact. The proposed Asia leader schools draw on this practice and act as hubs for high-quality teaching. The proposed Australian Schools in Asia Consortium will help schools run immersion and exchange programs. ATAR incentives and university credit pathways will reward continued study.

I know the effect of cultural immersion from my own life. For me, that particular exposure was in the Pacific. At 16, I travelled to the Solomon Islands, and I stayed at the Melanesian Brotherhood Central Headquarters at Tabalia and at Selwyn College near Maravovo as part of my school trip. I fell in love with the Solomon Islands language and culture, and I made lifelong friends. Anyone who knew me as a teenager can probably picture the Solomon Islands material that filled my bedroom.

I had the great honour of meeting the new Prime Minister of the Solomon Islands, the Hon. Matthew Wale, during his visit to Australia earlier this year, in June. The Solomon Islands sit in the Pacific, and the same lesson applies across our broader region. Time in another country builds understanding that no app can reproduce. Australia and the Solomon Islands share ancient cultural links, close geography and a history of standing together through hard times. Meeting the Prime Minister brought me back to the friendships and curiosity that began when I was 16 years old. We need to make sure our future generations of young people have that same chance to form those connections in our region too, particularly in Asia.

The committee made 34 recommendations. The report recommends a national Asia capability strategy, backed by a national data framework and dashboard. Australia needs clear goals and reliable information on subjects, enrolments, teachers and pathways. It recommends Asia leader schools and the Australian Schools in Asia Consortium. It recommends the recognition of heritage language learning in classrooms. It backs targeted support for language teachers, a larger supply of specialist teachers and continuing professional development.

For universities, the report recommends placing Asia capability among the priorities set by the Australian Tertiary Education Commission. It seeks protection for nationally strategic Asian languages in university funding agreements and shared language hubs for cross-institutional study. The report calls on the Commonwealth to lead through its own recruitment. Government agencies should recognise Asia capability as a priority in relevant jobs. Students need to see where language and regional knowledge can take them. Together, these recommendations connect primary school interest with secondary study, university courses and real careers. They support the teachers and institutions needed at each stage.

I would like to take this opportunity to thank every person and organisation that made a submission and attended our public hearings. The committee received hundreds of contributions and heard from dozens of witnesses, many of whom have spent their working lives helping Australians learn about our region. Teachers kept small classes open; researchers protected courses under pressure. Their participation shows parliamentary committees at their very best. Members tested evidence, asked questions and weighed different views. Good policy grows from this exchange. It helps us as elected representatives make better decisions. I offer special thanks to the outstanding staff in the committee secretariats as well, Joel Bateman and Lisa Deans. Their expertise helped turn hundreds of submissions, hearing transcripts and policy ideas into a clear report for our parliament, with the member for Gellibrand's leadership.

For local students, this report highlights the opportunity before us. It is about the child learning Japanese at East Brisbane State School, who deserves a path through secondary school. It's about the student studying Chinese at Brisbane State High School, who deserves to see a future for that skill. Australia needs the knowledge and confidence to make its own way in Asia. The capability starts with a teacher, a classroom and the chance to meet people in our region. To every teacher, academic, student and community leader who contributed: thank you. You kept these subjects alive through years of uneven policy attention. This report is for you and for the students you have yet to teach.

speaker: Claire Clutterham
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise today to speak in support of the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026. There can be no argument that giving more Australians the chance to go to university and succeed is essential to meeting the nation's future skills and economic needs. Backgrounds, postcodes and bank balances cannot stand in the way of more Australians going to university to attain a higher education degree, to allow them to participate in the critical nation building endeavours our country needs to embark on, to ensure a secure, sustainable and prosperous future, to allow us to compete in an increasingly competitive global marketplace, to enable us to innovate and enjoy the benefits of targeted research and development and to ensure that our national security is properly prosecuted.

Australia needs more university educated workers, not fewer. More opportunity is good for students, good for their families, good for communities, good for the economy and good for our country. The Australian Universities Accord made it clear that, if Australia is to prosper in the years ahead, we must grow Australia's participation, performance and investment in tertiary education so we can generate the knowledge, skills and research our nation needs. The final report recommended that the tertiary attainment rate of all working age people with at least one certificate III qualification or higher be lifted from 60 per cent currently to at least 80 per cent by 2050. It also recommended increasing the proportion of university educated Australians aged 25 to 34 from 45 per cent currently to 55 per cent by 2050. In making these recommendations, the final report noted that the tertiary system will need to more than double the number of Commonwealth supported students in universities from 860,000 currently to 1.8 million by 2050.

As well as increasing the number of skilled workers in our country ready to contribute to our economy and our communities, higher education provides many other essential benefits to Australian society. By encouraging intellectual endeavour, creativity and personal accomplishment, universities also promote democracy, critical thinking, debate, the embrace of different perspectives and the fostering of civic values. A university degree can also lead to expanded professional and personal networks, more defined career goals and, of course, employment. Further, the world faces a host of challenges ranging from economic inequality to climate change and geopolitical conflict to ongoing wars, and universities and graduates play a key role in helping to address some of these challenges. Given these benefits, creating accessible educational opportunities for students of all postcodes, backgrounds and bank balances to develop responsive skills is critical for a vibrant future workforce, for responding to challenges through innovation and for ensuring our communities are resilient.

Universities also encourage critical thinking and the consideration of different perspectives. You might not agree with a particular perspective that is being put, but you must consider it. You may dismiss it, but you've heard it and you've thought about why you might be dismissing it. You don't just accept it. You evaluate it, check it, challenge it and develop your own independent view on it. And you're actively encouraged to do this. You know that, if you don't, you might have missed something or you might be misinformed or disinformed. And we know that misinformation and disinformation, either deliberate or by virtue of laziness, are one of the biggest dangers facing our country, because they draw on inaccurate or incomplete information, depriving the information consumer of the facts and distorting the decisions that the consumer of the information might then make.

People who have been taught to think critically, to assess and challenge information, to not simply agree with the first thing that is said to them and to not simply accept the contentions of those who shout the loudest are better placed. The overarching negative effect of misinformation is that, without an accurately informed public, democracy cannot function. Again, you might not agree with the information, but if it is accurate—based on facts, data and evidence—you can at least make your next decision and make your choice with the comfort of knowing that you had the relevant information you needed.

We know that misinformation and disinformation create division. They create polarisation. And sometimes misinformation or disinformation based on rumour, gossip or a malicious agenda can have devastating consequences: disengagement with democratic processes, hostility to political figures, and violence. Disinformation has a competitive advantage over accurate information in the attention economy, because it is not constrained by the truth. The effort required is minimal, and the digitisation of media and the explosion of social media has also enabled producers of misinformation and disinformation to access sophisticated and extremely convincing tools of digital forgery, such as deepfakes, the digital alteration of an image or video that convincingly replaces the voice, face or body of one individual with that of another. That's not just a tech problem or a communications issue. It's a crisis of trust.

Tackling this means protecting communities from harm while upholding freedom of expression and other human rights. Freedom of expression and other human rights need to be protected at the same time as countering disinformation because of its capacity to unravel the threads that hold societies together. In settings with increased instability it can tip societies into violence. It can also corrode the norms of debate and science-backed evidence that societies have typically taken for granted. Countering this is difficult, because the monumental challenge facing us is structural. The information ecosystem simply was not designed with truth or safety as its key features. It was designed for engagement, which comes in many forms, including hate.

Well-developed critical thinking skills by virtue of a university degree can play a key role in countering these challenges, because these skills allow one to assess the strength and appropriateness of the information being presented through questioning, examining and evaluating different positions. These skills are not just useful with respect to misinformation and disinformation. Questioning, challenging and evaluating have a place in every profession. It was my full-time job, in my pre-politics career as a lawyer. Doctors, nurses and engineers do it all day. Goodness knows, teachers do it all day, as well as mechanics, plumbers, electricians and business owners. The ability to challenge, evaluate, question and go beyond the algorithm is fundamental to the success of our economy, our community and our liberal democracy.

Universities that produce graduates with a thirst for knowledge, a thirst for facts, a love of learning, a determination or arm themselves with the evidence they need to justify a decision they are working towards reduces the impact misinformation has on our democracy. I'm not saying that it is only those with a university degree who can counter misinformation because, with effort, we all can, but we know that universities arm students with the tools to do this, and the more people who are armed with a desire for facts and accuracy, the better.

This bill will see additional funding to the tune of $3.6 billion invested into the tertiary sector over the next decade to increase the number of students at university and to meet Australia's future skills needs. It does this through a new managed growth funding system and demand driven needs based funding to support students from underrepresented backgrounds to access and succeed at university. The estimated impact of these changes is that there will be an extra 230,000 domestic students commencing study over the next decade, getting those crucial critical thinking skills, developing the capacity to examine different perspectives and to reach an informed and evidence based view. This can only be a good thing for our democracy and our communities.

Labor is the party of education. We know that education lifts people out of poverty and gives people an opportunity: an opportunity to contribute to their communities, to do something for their families and to do something for themselves. We know that opportunities like this should not be limited to those with means or those who live in metropolitan areas. Everyone should have this opportunity. To be pro-education is to be pro-business, pro-private-sector, pro-public-sector, pro-productivity and pro-economic-prosperity because, without an educated population, you don't have any of those things.

This bill, which opens the doors of educational opportunity to a more diverse range of people, is not the only step that the Albanese Labor government has taken to ensure education is accessible and affordable. I will never forget 3 November 2024 and being in the Norwood International High School in my electorate of Sturt when the Prime Minister announced that a re-elected Albanese Labor government would make HECS better and fairer by cutting 20 per cent off of HECS debts. We have delivered that.

That is in addition to the indexation of HECS debts, moving to a marginal repayment system and raising the minimum repayment threshold. People should not be put in a position where they decide they will not go to university because it will be too hard to pay off the corresponding debt.

People should not be put in a position where they decide not to study for teaching, nursing and midwifery degrees because they cannot afford to take time off to complete the practical component of their degree. Paid prac is a delivered Albanese Labor government policy of which I am particularly proud. I completed a Master of Teaching and Secondary Education about a decade ago as a mature-age student who was able to take a combination of unpaid and paid leave from my employment to complete the prac. The unpaid portion hit even though I was in my late 30s. Imagine being a young student in your early 20s living out of home and being asked to give up your income for weeks at a time so you can complete a degree in a critical industry. Paid prac is meaningful change and meaningful action to ensure that students who want to can enrol to study to become teachers, nurses and midwives—and now, significantly, additional allied health professions.

This bill represents the seventh accord bill that the Minister for Education has introduced. There were 47 recommendations in the Australian universities accord, and, with the passage of this bill, the Albanese Labor government will have implemented 36 in full or in part. Prompt yet careful progress is being made as the Albanese Labor government seeks to shore up our tertiary education sector so that it's primed to deliver the skilled workforce Australia needs to advance its national security and economic prosperity and contribute to a Future Made in Australia. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Monique Ryan
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
text:
There is a clear and increasingly urgent need for Australian governments to set the conditions for safe and effective adoption of AI services in health care. AI is already reading our scans and biopsies, drafting clinical notes and triaging patients. But our response so far has been siloed and fragmented. There is no single oversight body across health care. The new office of AI will need dedicated senior health leadership.

We need a national AI health strategy covering tiered safety and evidence standards across the AI lifecycle; clear liability and an independent body empowered to audit or halt deployed systems; mandatory equity testing across rural, First Nations, non-English-speaking and older populations; national data sharing and benchmark data sets; and clinician training in model uncertainty, not in generic AI literacy.

We need investment in sovereign AI capability and genuine protections of transparency and consent for all patients of all ages in our healthcare system. AI is already opening doors to a more efficient and more adaptive healthcare system, but it also has the potential to be a very major disruptor of that system. We have to move with innovation and agility to get ahead of this historic challenge.

speaker: Tanya Joan Plibersek
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
Thank you so much, Mr Speaker, and thank you for meeting Conor Pall yesterday. He is a unique young man, as the Prime Minister said. Thank you also to the member for Boothby for her question and for her advocacy on this issue. As someone who worked on the front line of homelessness, she knows the impact of family, domestic and sexual violence on our community.

Ending gender based violence is a priority for our government. As the Prime Minister said, yesterday was another devastating reminder of why this is so important. As we sat yesterday and listened to those frontline service delivery organisations talk about what we need to do in the next phase of our work on violence against women and children, I think we heard some really important and some really consistent insights. We heard that we have to do more and better for children. Children tell us that they are not just witnessing domestic violence; they are experiencing it, and they need the services to support them.

We know that escalating rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are a huge concern that we need to address. Almost 40 per cent of victims of sexual assault are between the ages of 10 and 17. And we know that online harms are spilling into real-life harm. As the Prime Minister said, sexual strangulation is becoming commonplace because children are seeing violent and degrading pornography before they've had their first kiss. It's where they're getting their sex education from.

Tech facilitated abuse is exploding. Just as we deal with one thing, like undetectable stalking apps or nudify apps, the next challenge emerges, as the Attorney-General spoke about yesterday—with those AI glasses that can record people even without their knowledge.

And, of course, we need to work with people who use violence—help those who are willing to change. And, for those who aren't willing to change, who go on and harm one woman after another—throw them in jail, actually deal with them.

Of course, we're not waiting for the second action plan to take action. You heard from the Minister for Housing yesterday about her $308 million to deliver safe, secure homes for women and children escaping family and domestic violence, which will help 22,000 people. Our government's $4.4 billion investment has helped 1,400 organisations help close to half-a-million people. But, while one woman or one child is frightened at home at night, while one person fears sexual assault, while one person is ground down by coercive control, we won't rest; we won't stop. Every one of us here, every level of government, every community organisation, every school and every family has a role to play in our aim of ending violence against women and children.
