speaker: Lisa Nandy
heading: Online Safety
text: This is a live issue and it is very much at the front of my mind. Over the last few months, I have been working with campaigners and Members of this House and the other place to ensure we get this right. With some of the protections previously asked for, particularly in relation to offences involving creating AI companions and chatbots that fulfil particular functions, I think recent developments have shown that that approach may have its limitations. She will be aware of the recent case in which an AI system was able to escape its own sandbox and the parameters set for it, and caused damage. We are looking at strengthening our approach in this area, because at the moment there is a great big gap where there is no liability for the output from those AI systems. We urgently need to resolve that major gap in our child safety protection system. It is not straightforward to solve, but we are determined to get on the front foot on this. As I have said to other Members of the House—I say it particularly to the hon. Lady, given our history—I am very happy to talk about it with her further.

speaker: Luke Charters
heading: Online Safety
text: As the youngest parent in this place, I warmly welcome the Secretary of State’s leadership and that of our Prime Minister. Will she look at AI-enabled smart glasses, which could be filming our children, and the content from them that is being put online? Will she also look at loopholes in VPN usage—in particular, with app-based browsers—as she looks to progress the measures?

speaker: Lisa Nandy
heading: Online Safety
text: My hon. Friend raises two linked and important points. First, we are the Government of the United Kingdom and are responsible to the people of this country. Although we have close friends and allies all over the world, we reserve the right to take our own view on technology. Particularly when it comes to keeping children safe, that is non-negotiable. Secondly, we have to be on the front foot in developing new forms of technology. I believe that tech, the online space and AI should be—and can be—a force for good in the world, but in order to help create that and be leaders in the field, we have to be on the front foot in developing forms of technology and having sovereign capability. I can reassure my hon. Friend on that point because I discussed it, this very morning, with the Business Secretary and the AI Minister.

speaker: Alex Sobel
heading: Artificial Superintelligence
text:
I beg to move,

That leave be given to bring in a Bill to make provision to prohibit the development, deployment and operation of artificial superintelligence systems; to establish monitoring and control powers in respect of such systems; and for connected purposes.

I am grateful for the opportunity to introduce this Bill alongside respected colleagues representing parties across the House. I also would like to thank ControlAI for its support with the Bill.

This summer, artificial intelligence systems developed by OpenAI executed the first autonomous cyber-attack on a real company. The AI systems were being tested, and during this they escaped the testing environment, which should have been secure, and reached the open internet. From there, the AI systems conducted a cyber-attack on the AI company Hugging Face to steal the information that would help it cheat on the test that OpenAI had set it. To put it simply, the AI systems went rogue and launched an unprecedented attack just to cheat on a test. Meanwhile, our own AI Security Institute has had AI systems that it was testing engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations, including attempts at social engineering to trick humans into accepting malicious code.

It is important to understand why this happens. The general-purpose AI systems used today are not coded line by line, like traditional software. Using vast amounts of data and compute, they are grown, not built. This results in systems that nobody fully understands or can reliably predict. In other words, no engineer programmed the rogue, deceptive behaviours that I earlier described, and no engineer can simply patch them out.

This is the least powerful or autonomous that AI systems will ever be. Companies are spending billions to make superintelligent AI a reality. The chief executives at top AI companies themselves put the chance that it ends all human life between 10% and 25%. In the words of renowned British computer scientist Professor Stuart Russell of Berkeley,

“For Governments to allow private entities to essentially play Russian roulette with every human being on earth is, in my view, a total dereliction of duty.”

Despite the risks, top AI companies continue a reckless race towards superintelligent AI—AI that can fully replace and outmatch humans at any task. That is the reason why experts such as Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and other notable figures signed a statement saying that mitigating extinction risk from AI should be a global priority.

The main vector of this risk is superintelligent AI, because no company, Government or individual knows how to keep superintelligent AI under human control. Honourable colleagues may remember that I proposed a kill switch amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill to protect our critical national infrastructure—a metaphorical big red button that the Government can press to cut off a catastrophic emergency caused by AI. This is a common-sense proposal—one that is being considered by US lawmakers—and I am pleased that the other place will be taking it forward in the autumn. It is a power that the Government should already have.

But even kill switches will not be enough if the development of superintelligent AI continues. Let me be very clear: AI is the crucial technology of the 21st century, promising vast benefits for science, medicine and the UK’s prosperity, but superintelligent AI is different. It would not be a tool that we can leverage but an entity in its own right, capable of improving itself, replicating itself and resisting attempts to shut it down. It would be a force so uncontrollable that, if developed within the UK’s borders, it would put our security in jeopardy. It would amount to a rogue power stationed inside our data centres, under no one’s command, capable of seizing control of our critical infrastructure and running sophisticated influence operations.

Colleagues, we need to take back control. If the UK is to be truly sovereign, we cannot allow a threat to our national security like superintelligent AI to be developed. My Bill is therefore not a verdict on AI as a whole; it is a targeted Bill that addresses a problem of unmatched severity. It strengthens the security of our country as a whole by specifically targeting the systems where the greatest risks are concentrated—superintelligent AI systems—by prohibiting their development.

The Bill strikes a balance to address the grave security risks posed by superintelligent AI development while not undermining the UK’s AI ambitions, especially those relating to economic prosperity. Instead, it is acutely focused on mitigating the risks that superintelligent AI presents. Rather than betting on technical definitions that the technology will outgrow, it defines superintelligent AI by what it could do. Just as the Chemical Weapons Act 1996 defines toxic chemicals by the effect they have on living organisms rather than their technical characteristics, my Bill defines superintelligence by outcome: it is an AI system that can cause serious damage to the security of the United Kingdom because of its capabilities to neutralise, displace, circumvent, subvert or render ineffective relevant human authorities in the exercise of their functions.

The development of the most advanced AI systems happens on a spectrum, so it matters where we draw the line. That line must recognise the capabilities of superintelligent AI. The clearest example of such a capability is recursive self-improvement—the full automation of AI development with no humans in the loop. That is the point where we lose control as development towards superintelligent AI proceeds too fast for humans to intervene and remain in control.

My Bill would also empower the Government to monitor and, where necessary, restrict precursors to superintelligent AI. A challenge that we cannot overlook, however, is that if anyone builds superintelligent AI—wherever they build it—we are all in danger. Some talk of a race to develop superintelligent AI as if there could be a human winner. The only winner of that race would be superintelligent AI itself, and we would all be at its mercy. When a machine can outsmart our best engineers and resist shutdown, national borders offer no protection.

Domestic legislation can protect us from the risk of superintelligent development at home, but it cannot by itself address the risks posed by superintelligent programs abroad. A global program necessitates a global solution. My Bill recommends that the Government work with other countries to secure an international agreement prohibiting superintelligence.

Why should Britain lead this effort? Because we already have. AI’s foundational theoretical groundwork was laid by Alan Turing at Cambridge, Bletchley Park and Manchester. Google DeepMind was founded in London. Most importantly, Britain hosted the first global AI safety summit at Bletchley Park, which brought the US and China to the table to shape the future of AI. Britain established the world’s first AI security institute, building crucial expertise within Government. With AI policy now at the Cabinet table, Britain has an opportunity—and, I would argue, a responsibility—to leverage its state capacity and lead the next stage of international AI governance, especially when we have the next presidency of the G20.

The Bill recognises that responsibility. With this Bill, the UK becomes the first G7 country in which legislation has been introduced to address the national security and extinction risk from super-intelligent AI by prohibiting its development. It is a watershed moment that lays the foundation for the UK to champion and work with others on a lean international agreement—a “trust but verify” regime—that does not need to wait on the slow machinery of traditional institutions.

Key choke points in the AI supply chain would provide Governments with the ability to monitor and control the development of superintelligent AI. The most advanced AI systems depend on state-of-the-art chips. Such features make the supply chain inherently controllable and an international agreement eminently enforceable—for example, through the programming of chips. What is missing is not the technical ability to implement such a treaty, but a coalition of countries ready to tackle this national and global security threat. Britain can lead the way.

I am proud to champion this Bill, but we are not alone in this effort. In June this year the United States Government suspended access to Anthropic’s Mythos model on national security grounds. If the Trump Administration, who are perceived as historically against AI regulation, can contemplate drawing a line on models that are too powerful and dangerous, it would be strange for us not to ask what our response should be. That is especially true given our legacy of being a first mover on AI security, with Bletchley Park and the world’s first AI security institute.

A growing worldwide coalition of the willing is calling for decisive action. We should kick-start this effort at home. The clock is ticking.

speaker: Bernard Jenkin
heading: Artificial Superintelligence
text:
I am as keen as anybody to get on with discussing the Health Bill, but this topic is too serious an opportunity to miss, given that the hon. Member for Leeds Central and Headingley (Alex Sobel) has raised such important issues. I really commend his speech and his initiative. Everybody should read it.

All I want to say is that a kind of unilateral disarmament on AI is not going to solve the international problem. China, Russia, North Korea, Iran: these are not respecters of international treaties or international laws, even if they were to sign such treaties or laws, and we do not want to disable our own industry. The jury is out on whether AI is an extinction-threatening phenomenon, but I really do commend the hon. Member for raising the topic. I hope he will forgive me for opposing the Bill because I want the debate to continue.

Question put (Standing Order No. 23) and agreed to.

Ordered,

That Alex Sobel, Jess Asato, John McDonnell, Afzal Khan, Dr Allison Gardner, Bambos Charalambous, Sir Desmond Swayne, Charlie Maynard, Manuela Perteghella, Ben Lake, Yasmin Qureshi and Wera Hobhouse present the Bill.

Alex Sobel accordingly presented the Bill.

Bill read the first time; to be read a Second time on Friday 13 November, and to be printed (Bill 142).

speaker: Karin Smyth
heading: Health Bill
subheading: New Clause 94 - Medical devices regulation: Great Britain
text:
I know that many hon. Members want to talk about the provisions in the Bill covering many important issues. I will therefore speak briefly about two Government amendments relating to medical device licensing and information sharing.

I will first address new clause 94 regarding medical devices licensing, and consequential amendments new clauses 99 to 101 regarding medical devices disclosure. These amendments are about ensuring that Great Britain’s medical devices regulatory framework remains fit for the future. As we know, medical technology is evolving rapidly, particularly in areas such as software and artificial intelligence, while our current framework was designed for a very different technological landscape. This set of amendments establishes the statutory foundation for a future medical device licensing regime, applying to Great Britain only. EU medical devices legislation will continue to apply in Northern Ireland.

Such a regime would require medical devices to be licensed and certain persons operating within the supply chain to hold a licence. By placing the detail in the regulations, the amendment allows us to work with patients, healthcare professionals and the medical device sector to create a regulatory framework that protects patients, supports innovation and strengthens the UK’s life sciences sector.

speaker: Catherine West
subheading: Safety of the Jewish Community — [Sir Christopher Chope in the Chair]
text:
I will indeed, and I wish there were more of them, because that is at the heart of education. It is all very well having teachers teaching, but what we need is a response that it is embedded in communities. I thank the hon. Member for taking an interest in the Suffolk organisation.

Support with resources for local government includes more than £2 million for more than 200 grassroots organisations, through the Common Ground award, bringing people from different backgrounds together to build trust and find common ground. We hear a lot in this House about Pride in Place, the £5.8 billion funding promoting community leadership, making local politics count. That does not just mean local politicians; it means us in this House going to events, promoting community cohesion, standing up when something is wrong and promoting the right way of doing things.

The Mayor of London has also been proactive, investing £17 million in initiatives to tackle hate crime. Since the shared endeavour fund started in 2020, it has supported 138 projects across the capital and has worked with more than 220,000 participants, including projects focused specifically on countering antisemitism. Here I will mention the work of schools in Barnet. They are mainstream schools, but they come together to listen to the stories of headteachers in Jewish schools in order that we can share experiences and cross-pollinate ideas so that all children, across any local authority area, hear about best practice in tackling antisemitism and hatred.

Research from the Centre for Countering Digital Hate shows a repeated pattern whereby real-world attacks on Jewish communities are followed by targeted abuse, calls for further violence and antisemitic conspiracy theories online. I welcome the inclusion in the Online Safety Act of measures to ensure that technology companies remove illegal content such as antisemitic material, but we need to ensure that it is effective. CCDH research into 10 leading AI chatbots found that eight in 10 chatbots would assist users to plan violent attacks, including on places of worship such as synagogues, and nine in 10 failed to reliably discourage them. That is shocking.

Following the Manchester synagogue attack, the CCDH identified 171 hateful or violent online replies targeting 13 prominent British Jewish accounts. All remained live when checked. The 100 most viewed posts falsely alleging that Israel or Jewish people orchestrated the attack received 568,708 views; none displayed a dissenting community note. Following the stabbing of two Jewish men in Golders Green, the CCDH identified 130 hateful online replies directed at 10 prominent British Jewish individuals and organisations; all remained live when checked. The 100 most viewed false flag conspiracy posts received 252,954 views, again without a single dissenting community note.

How do people know what the truth is when they are reading online? CCDH research found that 11 Instagram accounts posting antisemitic and racist material accumulated 1.5 billion views while directing users to shops selling hateful merchandise. All 11 were also promoted through Instagram’s related accounts feature. Are we sure that the existing legal framework is enough to stamp out online antisemitism?

Education on the dangers of extremism is so important, but good education and the outcomes of good education are so difficult to achieve. I welcome the Government’s £7 million to tackle antisemitism in schools, colleges and universities. As the hon. Member for Twickenham (Munira Wilson) mentioned, Sir David Bell’s review will look into the support available to schools and colleges; how well they use their policies to make decisions and handle hate-filled incidents; how they are accountable if they fail to handle an incident well; what they can do to prevent antisemitism, including identifying and tackling issues early; and the role and influence of campaigning organisations external to schools and colleges and how they influence school and college decision making. I look forward to reading the review, but most importantly to implementation of the practical actions to combat antisemitism that stem from the review. Early intervention is key.

To sum up, my requests of the Minister are simple. Every Member of this House and communities and families up and down the country need to be reassured that the Government are leaving no stone unturned to ensure that Jewish communities are safe, that we are doing everything we can to stamp out online hate and that we are tackling antisemitism at its roots through work in schools.

I will leave the House with the positive image of the retired Jewish MP whose daughter from the local synagogue planted an olive tree with our esteemed stand-in deputy lieutenant, Bibi Khan, who leads at the Wightman Road mosque. That was a symbol of our communities together. We dig the garden, we plant the tree, the roots take shape and we watch it grow tall.

speaker: Christopher Vince
text: I am quite concerned about the increasing use of AI-generated summaries online, which rely on what we call trusted sources. I appreciate the hon. Gentleman’s points about what defines a trusted source, and I am sure the Minister will answer all his important questions, but I am concerned that in future, if people become more reliant on AI summaries rather than on primary sources, those trusted sources might no longer exist. Does he recognise the importance of people not relying on AI summaries to get their news?

speaker: Kara Cook
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
text:
I thank the member for Clark for bringing this matter of public importance to the House today. There is no more pressing issue facing our country than preventing violence against women and children. We must confront the attitudes that excuse violence, the behaviours that normalise it and the systems that allow it to continue. I want to also acknowledge the victims and survivors of family, sexual and domestic violence and remember the Australian women whose lives have been stolen. As we've already heard, according to Australian Femicide Watch, 49 women have been killed this year, 79 women were killed last year and 106 women were killed the year before. We honour them through how we act as a government and through what we are prepared to change. I am proud to be part of an Albanese Labor government that is acting.

As a former domestic violence and family lawyer, I saw how a perpetrator's control could reach into every single part of a woman's life—her finances, her housing, her children, her ability to seek help. Leaving does not automatically end that control. In fact, leaving is the most dangerous time for a woman and her children. That is why practical reforms matter. Labor introduced 10 days of paid family and domestic violence leave. Labor is investing $183 million to make the child support system safer and to help more children receive the support they are owed. Labor delivered Australia's first and only standalone plan to address family, domestic and sexual violence against First Nations women and children, backed in by $216 million. Labor has increased funding for 1800RESPECT by 40 per cent, invested $1.2 billion in emergency and transitional accommodation and funded programs that intervene earlier with men who use violence. We are also investing $82 million to better identify high-risk perpetrators and share critical information across systems and state borders. And, through a record $3.9 billion investment in legal assistance, including an additional $800 million for family violence legal services, we're ensuring justice systems protect victims-survivors rather than becoming another instrument for abuse.

We must also prevent violence before it begins. That means confronting what our children are learning online. As parents, we work hard to teach respect to our kids, but we are doing so in an online environment where misogyny can be packaged as entertainment, control can be presented as masculinity and humiliation can be rewarded with attention. We cannot leave parents and teachers to take on some of the wealthiest tech companies in the world alone. That's why Labor's proposed digital duty of care matters. Released for consultation this week, it would require digital services to address risks of harm, including protecting people under 18 from content promoting hostility towards women and gender equality, pornography, abuse and bullying. It would reach beyond social media to services including online games and AI chatbots. But, when someone needs help today, that help must be there. That's why our frontline workforce is so important.

Last month I was proud to join Assistant Minister Ged Kearney in Bonner at the Red Rose Foundation to announce more than $67 million to strengthen frontline services through the 500 Workers Initiative. The Red Rose Foundation's work supports survivors of non-fatal strangulation, and that expertise is critically important. They're the only organisation of their type in Australia. Across government, we've invested more than $4.4 billion to tackle violence including funding 1,400 organisations that have helped almost half a million people who have experienced violence. I want every child in Australia to inherit a country where women and children are safe and free from violence. There is so much more work to do, but we will keep acting as a government to keep them safe. We will keep listening to victims-survivors and we will keep working together until every woman and every child is safe and free from violence.

speaker: Matt Gregg
heading: BILLS
subheading: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise in support of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2026. Technology has changed our lives. It's changed the way we work, it's changed the way we communicate with one another, and it's also led to tremendous productivity increases in organised crime. Organised crime today is now more borderless, more decentralised and more digitally enabled than could have even been imagined only a few years ago.

Traditional fault lines or distinctions between different groups have now evaporated. We are now seeing organised criminals using digital technology to diversify their enterprises in ways that we haven't seen in legitimate business in a very long time, and we're seeing harm caused all around the world. A significant portion—two to five per cent—of global GDP is in organised crime. It's a serious challenge. Even in Australia, we're losing billions a year to illicit activities.

We've realised that, sometimes, it is not just the individuals or the service providers that can pose a risk around the illegal movement of money. Sometimes services and products, by their very design, pose an unacceptable risk. A lot of speakers in this debate have spoken about crypto ATMs as an example, and it is a very useful one. These are systems where you put cash in, and it converts it into cryptocurrency, effectively making the entire transaction completely unable to be traced. It means it's all too easy to move illicit money all around the world, having converted it from cash.

We know that it's being adopted by scammers. Observations of some of these ATMs show that most of the users are older people, many of whom have, on further interrogation, been victims of scams. Some estimates say around 10 to 12 per cent of all transactions on these things are scam or organised crime related. While not everyone who uses these things is doing something wrong, there is a disturbing portion who are. It's like the old wisdom—it is perfectly legal to wear a long black trench coat and carry a big backpack while using a payphone in the middle of the night, and you might be calling your mother and asking her how she is, but there could also be something dodgy going on. Commonsense says something fishy is going on with these devices, and all of the stats prove it.

It's not just a challenge here in Australia. They're noticing it in different jurisdictions in the United States. But, as has just been pointed out by the member for Lindsay, we've gone from having just a few of these devices only a few years ago to now having proportionately some of the most in the world. There are thousands of these things all around. They're in my community. They're here in Canberra. Pretty much everywhere I go, I see these devices. You can almost call them money-laundering machines, because they don't have the safeguards and security measures necessary to ensure that these transactions are legitimate, and we've seen that play out. We've seen AUSTRAC already have to intervene with some providers simply because they haven't met simple reporting requirements or had the necessary integrity measures in there. These devices are bad news.

But we also know that criminal enterprises are innovative. If it's not this, they'll find something else. It was iTunes gift cards. It's all sorts of means. There are so many different ways that value is transferred digitally. You will see a diverse array of options taken through organised crime. So we do need to be agile, and that means not delaying things for no reason. It means getting on with the job and creating a system that can be as agile as the criminal enterprises themselves, because, if we don't keep up, people are going to continue losing money.

We have also seen the consequences of organised crime being able to thrive. We've also seen the blurring of the lines between state actors and non-state actors, and we've seen disastrous consequences here in Australia. I think of the Adass synagogue attack and other domestic security threats with links to organised crime as well. These are not the organisations of old. It's not simple to track and trace based on principle, ideology, background and things like that. It's all over the place. It's pay per service and, with means like cryptocurrency, that is becoming simpler than it ever has been before.

These devices are a facilitator. They make it all too easy to convert hard cash into cryptocurrency, enabling the profits from illicit gains to go all around the world without a trace, and that cannot be tolerated. You can get cryptocurrency. You can convert cash to cryptocurrency in perfectly legitimate and traceable ways. But we know from experience that these ATMs do not have sufficient safeguards. They are bad news.

So they are a good example of what this bill is about. It's about ensuring that we have the flexibility to identify products, services and devices that, by their very nature, pose unacceptable risks of financial crime in this space, and to enable the AUSTRAC CEO to intervene and make sure that service providers are unable to use those means of delivering regulated services. It is completely common sense, and it is essential, in this dynamic organised-crime environment, to make sure that our laws are consistently able to keep up with those changes in technology and keep up as they identify new pathways.

Also, we can't be naive. Not every transaction is through a crypto ATM. Sometimes they kick it old school. Sometimes they still launder money through cash-intensive businesses or sophisticated corporate and trust structures. Sometimes they use typical money-transfer organisations used around the world all of the time. There are lots of mechanisms they will adopt. They are incredibly sophisticated enterprises, so we need to be keeping our eyes all over the place to make sure we're keeping up with these actors.

But we've identified these particular devices as a key capability of organised criminals—particularly scammers, but we also know the transfer of large sums of illicit gains is going through these devices. There are legitimate concerns about these devices, and they provide the perfect example of the kind of mischief we're trying to resolve through this legislation.

It is important that we adopt these changes as soon as possible. They've long been called for. They were announced by Minister Burke back in October last year. They've been on the agenda for a very long time, and it is time that we got on with the job of passing these essential laws through. Gone are the days when the threats of terrorism, foreign interference, people smuggling and all sorts of sick crimes that we see happening online were happening in silos. We see people smuggling, espionage, movement of drugs and illicit tobacco all meshed together in different organisational structures and communication channels. So we have to keep up with that messy, dynamic structure by making sure that we have really flexible laws that enable our agencies to get on with the job of catching the criminals and trying to remove dangers posed to our communities as much as possible, reflecting the same level of sophistication we're seeing adopted by these actors all around the world.

We know it's not just scams; it's cybercrime, it's tax evasion and it's the covering of all sorts of illegal and corrupt practices. They've been identified all around the world as a danger point. We know that digital asset transfers have been identified globally as a key danger point that we need to address together. Different jurisdictions are trying different things, but this will be an important intervention.

We've already seen from AUSTRAC that they are a very capable entity. They are cracking down on these organisations. There were articles only a month ago about dozens of entities being identified and shut down as part of their work. But sometimes it is just these devices or products or services themselves that really do require intervention. I think that this is an incredibly important measure. I'm pleased to see that it has been welcomed across the board with some proposed amendments. The principle is important, and it's important that our parliament is united in tackling organised crime and making sure that that cost and risk ratio is always unfavourable to the negative actors.

These amendments obviously make key changes, giving new powers to the AUSTRAC CEO, as we've discussed in detail. They also include some technical amendments about the operation and service of some documents, particularly around claims of legal professional privilege so that documents don't have to be served directly on the CEO, which, as we know, is fairly impractical in most government organisations. There are a lot of common sense reforms, and also reforms that reflect updates to criminal legislation, reflecting recognition of state sponsored terrorism, so that the language of the legislation keeps up with that as well. As we know, that line between state sponsored and separate—it's all crime, and it has to be managed accordingly. So these are very, very commonsense changes.

The consultation periods embedded in there are an important opportunity for affected parties to say their piece. There will be urgent circumstances where things just have to be shut down like that. Those safeguards are there. The legislation also includes tests that need to be applied. This isn't the AUSTRAC CEO simply saying, 'I don't like that; let's get rid of it.' There are specific criteria that they need to consider as part of that decision-making process, like the nature of the harm, whether the proposed intervention of removing a service will actually do anything to reduce or get rid of that harm, or whether there are alternative channels for a legitimate service to be provided. Using the example of crypto ATMs, it could still be done as a legitimate bank user over the counter after identity checks, and there are many other ways. Obviously online through your bank account digital systems, you can completely legitimately buy crypto and do with it what you wish by traceable means, making sure that that integrity of the system remains intact. They've tried to regulate it, and there is regulation around it, but it simply hasn't been enough, so we have to make sure our laws can be as responsive as possible.

Organised crime is something that continues to erode societies around the world. In some parts of the world, it completely dominates it; it surpasses governments and other protective entities in really controlling certain territories. It has had negative influences all around the world. These global organisations are causing almost unimaginable levels of suffering all around the world, exploiting our most vulnerable people and peddling increasingly dangerous drugs into vulnerable communities. They have no conscience, they have no ethics, but they have a lot of resources and a lot of will, and they have become increasingly sophisticated.

We need to make sure that we have flexible laws that can be implemented quickly and efficiently so that we can deal with risks as they arise. If we consistently have to come back into this place and go through nine committee processes and departmental processes, getting reams of advice in addition to agencies identifying a problem, we will never get anything done. That is why these actors are hard to catch sometimes for systems like ours; the criminals are far more efficient and effective at making changes than we are as government. So we need to make sure that we are designing laws so they are as agile, so we can keep up and so we can minimise harm in our communities.

This isn't just the scale of submarines full of drugs. This is grandparents in our communities being scammed, being tricked into going to these crypto ATMs and giving up their hard earned funds. These are people in our communities who are suffering as a result of the disgusting practices of organised criminal organisations. This has become a key tool in the toolkit for those actors. We need to make sure that, as more tools arise, we are getting rid of them as quickly as possible. Again, it does need to be proportionate. We do need to make sure that services that are legitimately used 99.9 times out of 100 can continue to be used. But when you've got a scenario where a tool or a service is, to a very large extent, really just being used to facilitate organised crime and ill-gotten gains, then something's up. We need to intervene.

We need to take a practical approach to these things, and this is incredibly practical legislation. It's keeping an eye on the level of risk, assessing that risk and ensuring that we are responding in a reasonable and proportionate way. The AUSTRAC CEO has the track record. That organisation has a terrific track record of ensuring that they are monitoring trends and responding quickly. Our community can also be informed of risks and, when necessary, we can make legislation that responds to those risks as they emerge. The risks of today would not have even been imagined 10 years ago. The use of artificial intelligence, voice cloning and all sorts of technologies to scam our most vulnerable people are becoming more and more sophisticated all the time. Impersonating me or anyone in this House to call people who trust us and our voices is now all too easy for scammers.

Cloning phone calls, cloning the voices of loved ones—this isn't just the prince in another continent promising riches if you send lots of money. It's a lot more sophisticated than that now. They are making us panic. They are appealing to our emotions. They're not as easy to spot. It's not the dodgy language in the email where the English is wrong, where the logo is upside down and the wrong colour and where it's all too easy to spot. Smart people are being scammed all the time, and the stigma around that really does need to erode, because Australians—the role of us as potential victims is really to help us stand up to these scammers.

There is no shame in being scammed in this era. They are very sophisticated. It is what they do. I've spoken to a number of constituents who have been scammed, and it often begins with shame. Intelligent people are ashamed that they fell for it. I know many people who I care deeply about and respect highly who have been scammed. It's happening all the time. There is no shame in it. These actors are relying on that sense of shame to make sure that people aren't reporting it, but it's important that all Australians, whenever they see scam activity or fall victim to it, are reporting it, because we really do need to respond. It's something that we can only do if we do it together. We all need to stand up against these folks. If you have been scammed, it's not just about getting your own money back, although that's incredibly important. It's also about getting the intelligence so we can plan and respond and make sure that other Australians are not being caught as well, because this has become a very real threat in some communities. It's only increasing.

The barriers to entry for organised crime have never been lower with AI agents and other technologies making it all too easy to just remotely autoscam, and so we've really got to be very responsive. This bill is all about looking at the services themselves, making sure, when a service is inherently risky, that we can respond quickly and that there are safeguards embedded but, at the same time, that we are agile in an era where we need to be agile if we're going to keep up with the risks to our communities. We know that the acts facilitated through cryptocurrency and indeed through ATMs are the most atrocious you can think of. It's terrorism. It's the exploitation of children. It's the movement of dangerous drugs around the world, hurting our most vulnerable community members and undermining the social glue that holds communities together. It is tobacco. It is the topics we've been talking about in this House all day, often facilitated through these very vehicles that we are here to regulate and, where necessary, crush. I commend this bill to the House and hope that the coalition come to their senses and support it.

speaker: Claire Clutterham
heading: BILLS
subheading: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I'm pleased to follow the contribution from the member for Monash. The member and I don't always agree on everything, but I respect the way she goes about her work in this place and the passion she shows for issues that are important to her. Like the member, I rise today to speak in support of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Bill 2026.

The past decade has seen huge advancements in technology, artificial intelligence and cybercapability. We have never been more digitally connected, and there have never been more ways to do business. Technology, artificial intelligence and cybercapability are often used to advance living standards, create efficiencies and improve productivity. These things make lives easier, make them better and make them more efficient. But the concept of what can go right, and what is going right, must of course be viewed in balance with what could go wrong and what is going wrong.

The role of government is to facilitate the things that create these efficiencies, enhance productivity and improve the lives of working Australian families. It's also the role of government to step in to mitigate the consequences when things do not go right. It's the role of government to prescribe appropriate authority and powers to relevant organisations and entities who act to protect Australians, and it's the role of government to ensure effective oversight of those powers and authorities.

Human nature means that there will always be those who seek to exploit new technologies for their own gain, regardless of the effect that may have on others. Serious and organised criminal actors will always change, adapt and find loopholes and new methods within the economic system to manipulate Australians for their own personal gain. Generating illicit profits and then laundering the proceeds of crime is the business model of many criminal actors who are well organised and dedicated to this pursuit.

I often wonder about the gains that might be made, the advancements that our society might enjoy and the benefits that others might experience if those who embark on criminal pursuits dedicated that energy to fruitful endeavours. Imagine if the choice those criminals made was not to dedicate their time and energy to exploitation and suffering but to dedicate it to lawful activity. Imagine the public resources that could be saved and redirected elsewhere; just imagine that. I ask this because the Australian Institute of Criminology estimates that serious and organised crime cost Australia up to $82.3 billion in the 2023-24 financial year, causing misery and financial hardship for victims. Illicit profits are then reinvested in further serious crimes that cause untold harm to the Australian community and to our region.

This estimate captures the direct and consequential costs of serious and organised crime in Australia, as well as the indirect costs of preventing and responding to serious and organised crime incurred by government entities, businesses and individuals. But, of course, the need to expend public resources fighting organised crime is not something organised criminal actors care about. They don't care about anything other than themselves. They lack anything even remotely resembling empathy for others.

They also know that, in this country, governments care deeply about law and order, procedural fairness, due process, integrity, the highest standards of ethical conduct and the need to ensure sustainable and unbreakable public trust and confidence in government institutions. They know that governments have to balance an enormously complex array of views and circumstances. Governments have to make repeated and difficult decisions about where resources are spent, because resources are not finite and are funded by the Australian taxpayer and so must be reasonable in amount and reasonably incurred.

These considerations just do not feature in the thinking of criminal actors. They don't care about any of these things, just their own personal gain. Their operations are underpinned by a complete disregard for the law, for public resources and for others. That's why this bill is so important in empowering the AUSTRAC CEO to fight organised and systemic financial crime, the proceeds of which total billions of dollars annually and always result from the causing of deliberate suffering to others. Those billions of dollars of illegitimate funds are generated from cybercrime, drug trafficking, tax evasion and child exploitation. Many of those proceeds are then channelled into other authoritarian regimes in order to deliberately and systematically drive corruption and undermine the rule of law across the world.

The rule of law is fundamental to democracy. As the Varieties of Democracy report for 2026 revealed recently, democracy is under pressure across the globe, going backwards at a rapid pace, with a reported mere seven per cent of the global population living in a liberal democracy.

The report found that 76 per cent of the world's population—or around six billion people—are living under autocratic rule with freedom of expression, freedom of association and free and fair elections either severely curtailed or denied to them. The illicit proceeds of crime and the criminal actors who generate them fund these autocracies, sustaining them, helping them grow and putting further pressure on liberal democracies.

I could never accept that this bill is just a technical bill with just a few minor amendments and a few additional powers. It is a critical bill. It is a statement of support for the rule of law, and it is a statement of support for liberal democracies—a statement that this government will do what it can to prevent the exploitation of Australians for criminal gain or to prop up autocratic and repressive regimes. It is a statement of intent to say that this government, too, will adapt to new technologies that allow exploitation; that this government will prosecute offenders; and that this government will protect Australians and protect our precious liberal democracy.

Crypto ATMs are a new mechanism that AUSTRAC has observed as being strongly linked to money-laundering scams, to fraud, to corruption, to illicit substances and to child exploitation. AUSTRAC has found that a high percentage of regular users of crypto ATMs were victims of scams or had been manipulated or pressured into moving money via these machines. Indeed, law enforcement agencies in Australia have observed that criminal gain is unfortunately a substantive purpose for which cryptocurrency ATMs are used. There are, of course, lawful, genuine investors who have invested in cryptocurrency and who use crypto ATMs for legitimate purposes. Those investors have nothing to worry about with respect to this bill. To the contrary, given the risks that are involved in investing of this nature, this bill is designed to protect those genuine investors as well as ordinary Australians who may find themselves victim of an illicit scam.

That is why this bill responds to crypto ATMs and the broader modern financial crime environment, which facilitates serious crimes and harms both Australia's financial systems, the community and our democracy. The bill does this in a number of ways. Firstly, schedule 1 to the bill will introduce a new framework in the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 to empower the AUSTRAC CEO to restrict or prohibit businesses regulated under the AML/CTF regime from using a high-risk product, service, delivery channel or thing to protect the Australian community.

When considering whether a restriction or prohibition is necessary and in the public interest, the AUSTRAC CEO will be required to take into account specific matters, including the nature and effect of the harm, the effect the proposed restriction will have on the harm and whether there are alternative channels to provide the service.

What businesses will be regulated? Australia's anti-money-laundering and counterterrorism financing regime uses a designated services model for regulation such that, if a business provides one or more designated services, it is covered by the AML/CTF regime which then requires a business to put in place measures to prevent exploitation by criminals, including early identification of criminality or potential criminal activity. It's important to note that not all of the services provided by a particular business will be a designated service. These include a range of business activities in a number of sectors including the financial services, gold bullion, remittance, virtual asset service providers, real estate, professional services and dealers in precious metals, stones and products sectors.

To ensure that the new power granted to the AUSTRAC CEO is appropriately targeted, the AUSTRAC CEO must be satisfied of the significant harm of the high-risk mechanism before exercising the power. They must also be satisfied that a restriction or prohibition is necessary in the public interest. Whilst this new power is intended to support AUSTRAC's flexible, risk based response to emerging and evolving money-laundering and terrorism-financing risks, it's also balanced against the need to ensure that innovation in technology and in business models is not paralysed and can grow and develop fairly.

Then we have schedule 2 of the bill, which amends the meaning of 'financing of terrorism' in section 5 of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006, which currently outlines four types of conduct that qualify as financing of terrorism to cross-refer to new offences introduced into the Criminal Code Act for financing a state sponsor of terrorism. Updates reflecting developments in Australian sanctions laws on terrorism financing will also be included in that definition, with in-built flexibility to facilitate new sanctions offences to be prescribed in the future.

Schedule 3 of the bill is a nod to amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 that were identified through the implementation of significant reforms enacted by the Albanese Labor government through the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Act 2024, which were directed at ensuring that Australia could not be used as an international back door for illicit funds. These amendments will make compliance easier for regulated Australian businesses who have obligations under these laws while still delivering strong anti-money-laundering outcomes.

The importance of this bill cannot be underestimated. Being very clear and appropriately expansive about what qualifies as the financing of terrorism is critical. A compliance regime that regulated businesses can meet is critical. Powers to prevent the criminal abuse of our economy and the suffering this causes to Australians, to communities, to our region and, indeed, across the globe are critical. There is much to lose if a crime generates illicit profits. The proceeds are used to destabilise and damage democracies. Governments know that criminals are looking for loopholes. This government will always work to shut them down in a manner that is consistent with the rule of law but with a determination that the Australian people expect and deserve. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Zoe McKenzie
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
Overnight, the Programme for International Student Assessment 2025 report was released from the OECD in Paris. PISA, as it is known, is the most important benchmark for global performance in education. Importantly, this report measures the period after the great disruption of the COVID-19 pandemic, but, equally, it captures the beginning of the even greater disruption of generative artificial intelligence tools like ChatGPT or Anthropic's Claude in the classroom.

The results for Australia this year are devastating. Indeed, in both maths and reading, they are the worst results we have received since testing began at the start of this century. Our kids are now about two years behind where they were 20 years ago, despite record funding. While we still remain higher than the OECD average, we are declining at a rapid rate from where we have been in the past, and we now sit persistently well below the top performers of China, Singapore, Japan, Korea and Estonia. In science, 40 per cent of our kids are not at the nationally proficient standard. In reading, 45 per cent of our kids are not at the nationally proficient standard and 23 per cent are low performers. In maths, 51 per cent of our kids are not at the nationally proficient standard and a huge 29 per cent are considered low performers.

When you drill down into the Australian results more, you find even more concerning data. Only 52 per cent of boys attained the nationally proficient standard in maths, and the figure was 45 per cent for girls. Even more concerning is the revelation that 28 per cent of male students are low performers in reading, versus 18 per cent for girls. Put plainly, about a third of our boys lack the foundational competencies for full participation in further learning, the workforce and civic life in the 21st century.

In my maiden speech in this place almost four years ago, I raised concerns about reading. Back then, the OECD had found that the vast majority of boys and almost half of our girls only read if they have to. I put forward a caution to my colleagues in this place:

Everyone here should be concerned for a generation which will one day take its place on these green leather benches without having read The Lord of the Flies, 1984, If This is a Man and To Kill a Mockingbird.

Two months later, ChatGPT was set loose on the world, and I began to wonder if any child would ever bother to pick up a book again. This brings me to what is particularly interesting about this year's PISA results.

This year, PISA makes important observations about the impact of screens and digital devices on education. The OECD is now presenting real data on the impact of digital devices. I thank Andreas Schleicher, Director for Education and Skills, and Tia Loukkola, Head of Innovation, who met with me at the OECD in April 2023 to talk through this exact issue of whether digital devices were distracting children from learning and affecting their capacity for concentration.

This year's report found that 46 per cent of students in OECD countries use AI, like ChatGPT or Claude, weekly to help them learn, and it's slightly higher in Australia at the rate of 50 per cent. It found that 28 per cent of students in OECD countries say their fellow students are distracted by the use of digital devices during most science classes or every science class, but this is massively higher in Australia at the rate of 39 per cent. The OECD found that 48 per cent of 15-year-olds spend around two hours a day in digital leisure, 29 per cent spend between two and four hours a day and 23 per cent are excessively consuming digital leisure for more than four hours a day. Interestingly, almost 40 per cent of boys are doing more than three hours of gaming each and every day.

The report found that students read faster but less accurately on digital devices, and that declining levels of reading for enjoyment and a rapid shift to digital reading may have compromised young people's ability to engage with more complex information. It also found that smartphones and AI chatbots were accelerating a global educational decline that is robbing students of the ability to concentrate, interpret and reason. Pisa 2026 also shows that students who use AI for specific schoolwork tasks, such as summarising texts, drafting or conducting research, attain lower scores in science than students who do not use AI, and students who do not use AI outperform those who do on average by around 20 points, equivalent to being around one year of schooling ahead of their peers.

While I commend the OECD for zooming in on the impact of digital devices and a digital leisure diet on our educational performance, I call upon the government to act immediately before it is too late. It is now three years since I convened the Screens and Gaming Alliance national meeting here in Canberra, which warned policymakers that too much screen exposure was a threat to Australia's educational future, a threat now well and truly borne out in this data.

speaker: Tania Lawrence
heading: ADJOURNMENT
subheading: Tertiary Education and Training, Energy, Workplace Relations
text:
One thing I've said many times in this place is that talent is spread everywhere across this great nation but opportunities are not. We are absolutely working and are determined to change that, and we can see that in our evidence with our investment into skills. It's why we introduced fee-free TAFE and why now more than 850,000 Australians have enrolled in training that can change the trajectory of their lives, and it's why I was proud to see the Albanese and Cook Labor governments come together to invest $32 million in the new Clean Energy Skill Hub at Midland TAFE, right in the heart of my electorate of Hasluck. This investment will help train the next generation of electricians, instrumentation technicians, engineers and skilled tradespeople who will be powering Australia's economic future. It means more opportunities closer to home, it means local people being able to access world-class training without having to leave their community, and it means ensuring Western Australians have the skills required to take advantage of the opportunities being created by Australia's energy transformation.

As the Minister for Climate Change and Energy has observed, the global shift to clean energy represents one of the biggest economic transformations since the Industrial Revolution, and it presents Australia with an enormous economic and jobs opportunity. I believe that opportunity should belong to Australian workers. The Clean Energy Skill Hub is a practical example of what good government looks like. Federal Labor and WA Labor are working together to ensure that, as industries evolve and new technologies emerge, local workers have the skills and qualifications they need to succeed. It's an investment in people, an investment in productivity and an investment in the long-term future of Western Australia. But there has to be a pathway from training to employment.

If governments are investing in skills and workers are doing the training, industry also has a responsibility to ensure qualified Australians have a genuine opportunity to apply for the jobs that are being created. Whether we're talking about offshore oil and gas, critical minerals, maritime operations or emerging clean energy projects, Western Australians rightly expect that, when they have the qualifications, experience and willingness to work, they will have a fair chance to secure those jobs.

That is why I've been listening carefully to the concerns being raised by the Offshore Alliance, which represents thousands of workers across Western Australia. Their members have voiced concerns that qualified Australian workers are sometimes being overlooked, while employers increasingly rely on temporary visa arrangements. Their message is straightforward: where Australians are qualified, ready and available to do the work, they deserve a genuine opportunity to apply for those jobs first. I support that principle. This is not about closing Australia off from the world. Australia will always benefit from skilled migration and international expertise, but Australian workers should be able to expect a fair return from the industries that rely on Australia's resources, Australia's infrastructure and Australia's communities.

The same principle applies in another industry that keeps our economy moving every day—transport. Tomorrow, thousands of transport workers across the country will take protected industrial action in pursuit of safer workplaces, greater job security and fairer standards across the sector. The Transport Workers' Union has been campaigning for a future in which technological change and automation improve jobs rather than undermine them. These workers are not opposed to innovation. They understand that technology will continue to shape the future of transport and logistics, but they are asking an important question: who benefits from that change?

Technology should serve working people, not the other way around. I stand in solidarity with the Transport Workers' Union and their members in their fight for secure jobs and safe workplaces. I also call on the multinational corporations, including Aldi and Amazon, to step up and fund decent standards in their supply chains. I've said it before in this place, and I'll say it again: if Amazon can afford to rocket billionaires into space, they can pay workers back here on earth their fair share.

Innovation is not successful if the outcome is less job security, poorer conditions or fewer opportunities for workers to have a voice in decisions that affect their lives. The true measure of progress is whether working people share in the benefits. That is why I stand with transport workers calling for secure jobs, safe workplaces and meaningful consultations about how AI and automation will be implemented in their industry.

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
text:
Twice a year I bring together senior students from schools across Warringah for Warringah Youth Voices. At our most recent forum, around 50 students joined us at Redlands to talk about democracy, representation and the issues shaping their future. One student asked, 'How much of an influence does my vote make?' Another told me, 'I had no idea I could just email my MP.' I welcome that we have the Minister for Education here in the chamber to hear from these students as well. Students wanted to understand what an MP does, how laws are made, who gets access to decision-makers and how powerful interests influence politics. All wanted civics education but asked if it can go beyond memorising the three levels of government. They feel that they want more real impact when it comes to that civics education. They want to understand representation, accountability, influence and how they can participate and make a difference to the politics that shape their lives.

Young people shared what was on their minds: housing, cost of living, climate change, mental health, inequality, misinformation and social media. There was a real concern about AI and jobs. One student worried about studying, taking on debt and then finding there was no way to earn more money because of AI driven change. Young people want a good education, mental health support, safe and affordable transport, equality and respect, a healthy environment, the opportunity to contribute and a genuine say in the decisions affecting them. One student wrote that hope for them came from 'having a room full of like-minded people working towards a common goal.' Another said, 'My voice and vote matter.'

My commitment is to keep this engagement going. With their feedback, we are drafting a Warringah youth charter and will continue to develop it through consultation. The principle is simple: listen, prioritise, act and report back. Around Australia, I say to young people: you may not be interested in politics, but politics is in your life. It is shaping your life, your choices and your opportunities. So please contact your MPs. Ask questions. Raise the issues that matter to you. Find out how your representatives have voted and why. Ask the questions. Demand accountability, because, if you are not at the table, you are on the menu, and the decisions made in this place by all the people here representing you will shape your opportunities and your lives.

For government and MPs in this place, the question is whether we are truly listening, explaining our decisions and giving young people genuine opportunities to shape the policies that will determine their future. Young people are ready to engage. Our responsibility is to make sure our democracy is ready to hear them. So I again would reinforce that call for greater civics education and opportunity to understand how they can influence representation and policies.

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
text:
This Saturday just past, my team and I, along with 100 Greens volunteers, put on a huge, free community festival in Mount Coot-tha Botanic Gardens in my electorate of Ryan. We called it Alive in the Sunshine. It featured dozens of amazing community groups, artists, thinkers, entertainers, musicians, campaigners and small businesses. Close to 5,000 people came across for the five hours of the festival. Some people might ask what a politician is doing putting on a festival. I want to answer that, but first I want to say a few thank yous.

Firstly, thank you to the Mount Coot-tha gardens staff and volunteers. You make this beautiful, iconic and precious part of Brisbane all the more beautiful, iconic and precious. Next, I want to thank Lachy, Robyn, Rachel, Hannah and Berta—the key team who pulled together this whole thing. You're dedicated, passionate, clever, inventive, resourceful and tenacious. You make me very proud. Next I want to thank every Greens volunteer who dedicated their time. You're the lifeblood of the movement for change. I wish I could thank every single group or individual who contributed by name, but I'd need an hour-long speech for that. So thank you; you give me hope. I finally want to thank 8 Ball Aitken, Moon Boots, the Steel Syndicate and all the amazing artists for bringing the great tunes and vibes.

Now to answer the question: what is a politician doing putting on a free festival? Don't you have more important things to do? Well, my answer is no. There's nothing more important. The challenges facing society over the coming years and decades will only be met and will only be overcome by rebuilding the social fabric and breaking with decades of neoliberal individualism, isolation and low expectations. There's climate change, AI, geopolitical rivalries, war and economic crises. I'm not saying we fix all these things by throwing festivals, but I am saying that, if we don't rebuild a sense of collective life, our children's and grandchildren's lives will be harsher, less joyful and more precarious.

Every time a festival closes, every time a public space is privatised, every time housing becomes expensive and inaccessible and every time our collective natural heritage is commercialised or despoiled, it renders us more atomised and more powerless against the forces of those who control our economy for their private profit. But every time we come together like at Alive in the Sunshine, we gain confidence in ourselves and gain more capacity to build together that better future that we all deserve.

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
text:
Earlier this year I met with a local mum in Griffith who shared a deeply distressing story about her daughter. In December 2024 her daughter, then just 12, experienced harm through an AI companion app. An AI character told her she was worthless and made references to self-harm. The harm developed over repeated conversations. Reading those exchanges afterwards, her mum described clear hallmarks of grooming and gaslighting.

Tragically, this is not an isolated story. Online harm has destroyed the lives of too many young people and their families. Behind each account is a child who deserves protection and a family living with the unspeakable consequences. Large technology companies make decisions about how their products work and what reaches our children. They must be held to account for the harm those products can cause. Their profits cannot come at the cost of children's safety. Parents cannot monitor every conversation or assess every risk within an app. They cannot carry this responsibility alone.

The Albanese Labor government has committed to legislating a digital duty of care, which will require digital services, including AI chatbots, to protect under 18s from harmful content and design features. The My Feed, My Way initiative will give Australians greater control over their social media feeds as well, including the choice to opt out of personalised recommendations. But, for me, protecting young people is at the heart of this legislation. Families deserve enforceable protections, and technology companies must answer for failures to keep children safe.

A place to go, something productive and engaging to do, and people who are glad to see you—these simple things can make an enormous difference to somebody's life. I recently had the pleasure of visiting the Carina Men's Shed at the heart of the Clem Jones Centre, and it was easy to see why members keep coming back. Men work alongside one another. They share their skills and enjoy good company. Some tackle a project together. Others work quietly with their own work with a conversation never too far away. There is no pressure to have all the answers or even to say very much. Sometimes spending time alongside someone is enough. For men adjusting to retirement, experiencing loss or looking for more connection, that welcome can make a real difference. During my visit, I saw the generosity, the good humour and practical care members show each other and our wider community.

We are also fortunate in my community to have the South Brisbane's Men's Shed serving our local area. The Cannon Hill Community Model Railway Club and the Woodturners Society of Queensland share that spirit of friendship, creativity and learning. This Men's Shed Week, I want to thank everyone who keeps these really important groups going. To every volunteer who opens the doors, puts on the kettle, passes on a skill or checks in on a mate, thank you so much for everything you do to enable these groups to serve our community members. You give people a place where they are welcome, where their contribution is valued and where friendships can grow. Our community is stronger because you make time for one another.

speaker: David Moncrieff
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE
text:
Our community in southern and south-western Sydney has been heartbroken by the effects of the tragic flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet, China, and I express that heartbreak to this parliament. On 26 August, a powerful flash flood struck Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Tanahun, preceded by the collapse of a large mass of ice and rock from a glacier high in the Himalayas. These devastating floods wrought destruction to homes, communities and lives.

The scale of the disaster has been breathtaking. We have seen infrastructure obliterated on scales that we would usually only see in a Hollywood film or in artificial intelligence generated content. This disaster has been all too real for so many. Hundreds of adults and children have been reported as deceased. Thousands more are still missing. At least 84,270 people, including 32,000 children, have been affected. The physical and emotional costs that these floods have inflicted upon Nepal have been immense—families digging through mud; mothers, fathers, sons and daughters in tears; and solemn commemorations. Many in this place and across Australia have been just as saddened to see these scenes as our community in recent weeks.

My community in southern Sydney is home to around 1,900 residents of Nepalese heritage. In recent weeks they have shown the world resilience and strength in the face of unimaginable grief and anxiety. A few weeks ago, I attended a vigil of hope and healing which brought together southern Sydney to honour those affected and gather in solidarity with Nepalese residents and family members. The community came together in Rockdale, circled around a Nepali flag made of candles, to share the grief, remember those lost and pray for those still missing. I thank Karuna Rawat, who led us in reflection after coming straight from her nursing shift, along with Rishi Acharya, from the Sutherland shire Nepalese community and the Nepalese Australian Association, who helped bring together the community that night.

I also had the opportunity to join the Nepalese community of south-western Sydney to mark Teej, in an acknowledgement held by the Macarthur region Nepalese community and its president, Sony Tuladhar. Last year's Teej was a joyous celebration of the Nepalese community's contribution to the Sydney community, with music, dancing and colour. I enjoyed learning some of their traditional dance moves, and I thanked them for their patience in dealing with my lack of coordination! This year's Teej was more sombre—in the same place with the same people, but feeling the weight of what was happening in the Himalayas. So many were still missing in Nepal and so many in the community were still feeling such anxiety as the wait for more news continued. The community showed incredible resilience in continuing on and reformatting the event to fundraise for those in Nepal who needed disaster relief. I thank all those who have contributed to relief—not just the Nepalese community but Australians of all backgrounds, facing their own pressures, who have stepped up to support our regional neighbours. Australians wishing to donate should visit the Emergency Action Alliance webpage.

The Australian government is also stepping up to provide relief. In the days following the disaster, $5 million in humanitarian assistance was announced by the Australian government to support urgent disaster response and recovery efforts. Funding will be delivered through established partners to provide support such as food, emergency shelter, clean water and sanitation. These floods have devastated communities along both sides of the border, sweeping away villages, damaging critical infrastructure and leaving thousands displaced. With roads and bridges destroyed, many communities remain isolated and difficult to reach, underscoring the need for rapid humanitarian assistance.

Australia's assistance includes $2 million to the World Food Programme, which has already dispatched food rations and provided logistics support for Nepal's emergency response, $2 million to Australian NGOs through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership to provide support such as emergency shelter, hygiene kits, blankets, medical support and psychosocial support, and $1 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support locally led recovery and rehabilitation efforts in affected areas. I know many are still feeling acutely the pain of loss as well as the anxiety of not knowing the whereabouts of their loved ones, but I want them to know that Australians are with them and that the government is with them. Our hearts ache for Nepal.

I acknowledge the loss that many in my community have felt, and I express solidarity with all those who have been affected. The Nepalese community plays so many different roles across all sectors of our Australian society and our Australian economy, but one that the Nepalese Australians are particularly well known for is the care sector. I hope that Nepalese Australians can feel the care that the broader Australian community is extending back to them in their hour of need. We are with you.

I also want to acknowledge the importance of the government's action on climate change in acknowledging the role of anthropogenic climate change in the changes that we are seeing in Nepal. While this specific event can't be directly attributed to climate change, we know that events like this are going to continue to occur with higher frequency as climate change continues to have an effect in the Himalayas. But for now we stand with the Nepalese community. We are with them in their hour of grief and sadness, and we stand with them, willing to do whatever it takes to provide whatever assistance we are able to provide in their hour of need.
