They use staggering amounts of water and electricity. Estimates show that, by 2035, data centres in Sydney could use 250 megalitres of water a day. That's equal to Canberra's drinking water supply. They could also swallow 15 to 20 per cent of Sydney's water supply in a decade. That is a massive amount of water use and power use. Their electricity use could triple in five years, driving power and water prices through the roof.

Currently, data centres use two per cent of the national power off the grid, but it could more than triple in just five years to over six per cent. We need a moratorium on new data centres that builds safeguards and controls them, to protect productive agricultural land, to protect our water resources, to protect households and businesses from higher power and water bills, to protect the environment, to protect public health and to empower local communities by letting them have a say over whether or not they want these energy sources in their areas—in our areas. Out in country Australia, we're struggling to keep up with the amount of water we've got. We go through these debilitating cycles of drought, and everyone in country Australia is very concerned that these data centres are going to suck up more water and that our power bills and our water bills will keep going up.

The bill also delivers national AI safety oversight by ensuring that the Commonwealth approves and reviews AI systems before those systems are released into Australia. If they're coming from the United States or anywhere else, the Commonwealth will have oversight over it. It helps ensure that AI systems are safe and effective and do not present unacceptable risks to the health and wellbeing of Australians, to the privacy of Australians or to the civil rights of Australians, and that they do not pose a threat to the very future of humanity and humankind. We need this national safety oversight, and we need to ensure the Commonwealth reviews and approves AI systems before they are released in Australia.

The rush to AI must be controlled. It cannot come at the expense of our natural resources, our regional communities or the safety of humanity. Australia can play a leading role here. I don't think any countries have been proactive enough in regulating advanced AI, but I think the world is waking up to this and we need to lead the way. We need to show the United States and the President of the United States that, if they will not lead, Australia will lead and other right-thinking countries will lead on this, and if enough people do it and if enough people speak out we will get action and be able to control this new technology that we are hurtling towards without proper controls. We urgently need kill switches on the technology and commonsense guardrails around data centres on the ground.

I urge all members to support the suspension of standing orders and pass this game-changing bill. We need to put human oversight back at the centre of artificial intelligence. We owe it to our communities, we owe it to our children and grandchildren, and we owe it to humanity itself.

speaker: Dai Le
heading: BUSINESS
text:
I second the motion of the member for Calare. I spoke last week about the good and the bad of this new world we're living in of artificial intelligence—its ability to make us work more efficiently and more productively but also its potential harm to humanity.

Let me start with what artificial intelligence gets right. It can reduce paperwork for small businesses, improve services and help people work more productively, if used well. For small-business owners in Fowler, that matters. A task that once took a day may take an hour. Paperwork that kept someone at the kitchen table late at night can be dealt with before they open the shop in the morning. I, too, want the people of Fowler to have every safe AI tool that helps them compete, grow and spend more time with their families. I'm not here to stand in the way of that.

But a tool this powerful needs rules and guardrails. We are already seeing the harm. For a community like Fowler, the risk can be even greater. More than six in 10 people in Fowler speak a language other than English at home. A scam can arrive in someone's first language sounding urgent and convincing while a legitimate warning does not reach them the same way and at the same speed. An increasing example is AI voice cloning imitating loved ones and demanding money. Once that content spreads, it is hard to pull back. And when people cannot tell what is real, trust breaks down—trust in information, trust in institutions and trust in our democracy.

That's why I support this motion and the member for Calare's bill. It is not about banning AI; it is about keeping people in control of a powerful technology. The bill requires providers of certain advanced AI systems to maintain the ability to intervene, stop a system's outputs, suspend access, restrict dangerous uses or shut the system down when necessary. This is not a one-big-red-button action. It is a graduated response—restrict a harmful capability; slow the system down; suspend access; move to a safe backup; shut it down when there is no safe alternative. That is not anti innovation; it is common sense.

For example, many of you who use today's cars would have—my car at least has it—a reversing safety sensor. So, when I'm reversing out of a car park or my driveway for instance, even though I can see an oncoming car, my car senses an oncoming car and automatically stops my car from reversing further. That way, we do not collide, or there's a prediction that we can collide. Sometimes, it's annoying to use, because I think I have my driving under control. But it has been designed to protect me and others from a mistake that I may not see coming. So we accept that safety feature because we understand the cost of getting it wrong. If we expect safety systems in cars on our driveways, surely we should expect meaningful safety systems from the companies developing the most powerful technology of our time.

There's also a physical side to the AI revolution—data centres, as the member for Calare mentioned. AI does not exist only on our screen; it needs enormous infrastructure, using electricity and water and land. Australia has around 165 operational data centres, with at least 225 more proposed or under development, and they are being fast-tracked before any legislation to safeguard them is in place. They are being built as we speak. Much of that growth is in New South Wales and Victoria. At least two data centres have been approved in Fowler, with more proposed. People deserve answers. Who pays for the electricity, the water and the infrastructure? Can the government guarantee that Fowler families will not face higher power bills? This needs to be addressed, and the member for Calare has done so in this bill.

I welcome innovation. But innovation must serve the people, not leave them behind. And this bill is a sensible step towards responsible planning, stronger safeguards and putting ethics back into infrastructure like data centres and AI development. We need to have that in place, and we have to do that—if we're taking the lead in the world with other legislation, such as the banning of social media for under-16s, surely this is more critical. This will have wider impact on our community and our society.

That is how we can make AI work for Australians. Rather than asking Australians to simply adjust to AI, we need to ensure that the Australian public can trust this new technology that's being rolled out so fast in front of us. Thank you.

speaker: David Farley
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
My adjournment speech tonight is going to focus on debt—but debt is not the problem; neglect is. Debt needs no sunshine, no water, no power and no human hand. Leave it in the dark, untended, unloved, and it still grows—interest upon interest—silently and relentlessly. Borrowing is not inherently bad; managed with discipline, it builds productive assets. It carries a nation through crisis. It bridges a shock that would otherwise break us. Neglected, it becomes a burden inherited by people who never voted for it—people who had no seat at the table when the decisions were made. I ask this chamber: are we borrowing to make Australia stronger or are we leaving the next generation a larger bill?

Commonwealth debt is forecast to reach $1.1 trillion during 2027-28 and is continuing to climb. Interest costs rise with it. Every dollar consumed servicing yesterday's debt is a dollar unavailable to build a hospital, strengthen defence, construct a dam, improve a road or reduce the burden on taxpayers. Debt has an opportunity cost. That cost is paid in things we did not build.

On housing, Australia desperately needs more homes. Yet dwelling commencements fell 11.2 per cent in the March quarter, new housing loan commitments fell 5.4 per cent in the June quarter and dwelling approvals fell 3.6 per cent in the quarter—three quarters, three falls, one direction. Canberra can announce housing targets until the cows come home. Announcements do not build houses; builders build houses, and builders need capital, trades, material, land and an approvals system that lets them get on with the job.

On infrastructure, Snowy 2.0 was estimated at $6.1 billion in 2018. That estimate was reset to $12 billion in 2023, and by March this year $11.1 billion had already been spent, with the project reported to be only 73 per cent complete. On the Inland Rail operational sections and constructions, the completed Melbourne-to-Brisbane vision still remains unfinished. Infrastructure cannot be measured by announcements, sod turnings or appropriations; it must be measured by three questions: 'What did you build? When did you finish it? What did the taxpayer finally pay?'

Moving to energy, the current regulated energy reference price has fallen, and that is welcome, but what is the whole-of-system cost of transforming Australia's electricity system—generation, transmission, storage, firming and network augmentation? What do we do while maintaining reliable, affordable, internationally competitive energy? Without competitive energy, there is no competitive manufacturing sector, no strong industrial economy and no sovereign capacity.

On productivity, productivity is not just an economist's abstraction; it's a foundation beneath sustainable wages, investment and living standards. Yet Australia's businesses confront regulation upon regulation, approval upon approval and compliance cost upon compliance cost. Red tape consumes time. Green tape delays investment. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence, automation and advanced manufacturing reshape the global economy of our competitors, and our competitors build the future while we debate the process.

Governments do not create prosperity by decree. We mine. We farm. We manufacture. We build. We transport. We export. Government's responsibility is to create conditions, affordable capital, reliable energy, secure water, efficient infrastructure, skilled people, sensible regulation and confidence. Sovereign security is not created by policy documents; it's created by capacity—fuel, food, energy, water, transport, industry and people—the capacity to sustain ourselves when the world around us becomes difficult. This is an intergenerational judgement. What will our children inherit, greater productivity capacity or greater liabilities? Infrastructure or invoices? Industry or regulation? Food security or dependency?

Debt itself is not immoral, but allowing debt to grow without building the productive capacity required to service it is a total abdication of responsibility. Debt does not need our permission to grow; it only needs our neglect. Our responsibility is not merely to leave our children the debt accumulated in our time; it is to leave them a productive nation capable of paying for it.

(a) that RSL Australia, based on data from the Department of Veterans' Affairs, estimates approximately 25,000 veterans spend an average of $9,700 per year, well above the proposed $5,000 annual cap;

(c) rising costs relative to revenue have driven hospital closures and sales, with obstetrics and mental health services under particular pressure;

(d) hundreds of thousands of Australians are downgrading their private cover as its value erodes, a trend the Government's cut to the seniors' private health insurance rebate will accelerate, adding further pressure to the public system;

(e) private health regulation was designed for an earlier era of high membership, not-for-profit insurers and larger hospital numbers, and now lacks flexibility to respond to demographic change, contract imbalances and economic shocks;

(f) no dedicated, whole-of-system mechanism exists to balance the interests of patients, doctors, hospitals, insurers and device manufacturers; and

(g) selective contracting and vertical integration increasingly threaten patient choice and the doctor-patient relationship; and

(2) calls on the Government to establish an independent statutory Private Health System Authority within the Health portfolio to:

(b) ensure fair insurer-hospital and insurer-practitioner contracting, including sustainable payment arrangements given bargaining power discrepancies;

(c) safeguard against managed care by assessing arrangements on their actual effect, not stated intent, where they restrict patient choice, interfere with clinically appropriate care, or distort clinical decisions, including in emerging hospital-in-the-home care;

(e) oversee safe, clinically-led expansion of out-of-hospital care that is properly funded and benchmarked, without shifting cost or risk to patients and families.

speaker: Anika Wells
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Corangamite for her question and for many constructive discussions about improving women's safety online. The Albanese Labor government is committed to working with the tech industry to ensure that Australia can capture the opportunities and spread the benefits of AI. But, on behalf of Australian parents, one issue we are not willing to negotiate on is online safety, particularly for young people.

If tech companies want to do business in Australia, they must obey Australian laws, and Australia's state and federal laws prohibit the publishing and distributing of sexualised, non-consensual deepfake material and AI generated child sexual abuse material. I commend the Attorney-General for that work. But an ongoing issue is the heavy reliance on victims reporting the deepfakes after the harm has already occurred.

We must move the burden of reporting online harm from the shoulders of victims and stop that harm at the source. We must hold big tech accountable for the tools they are creating and putting out to market, including to children. We must create basic safety standards for big tech just like every other industry in this country, like cars or food or toys. And, under our draft digital duty of care, the Albanese government will create basic safety standards and ban so-called nudify apps. The digital duty of care will require all online service providers to ensure that there are systemic and pre-emptive measures in place to restrict the use of nudify services, and the bill will give the eSafety Commissioner the power to issue take-down notices to search engines and to app stores that house these nudify apps.

These apps are solely designed to abuse, to bully, to harass and to intimidate. The Albanese government is determined to restrict them because, whilst the image might be fake, the abuse and the harm is real. Parents know this all too well. One child in every classroom in Australia has now been the victim of deepfake material. Four out of five of those reported cases are young girls. In one Melbourne case, investigators found 50 female students at a single high school were the victims of sexually explicit deepfakes. The scale of this harm is escalating. The eSafety Commissioner has found a 550 per cent increase year on year in this conduct since 2019. While AI has the power to move Australia forward, there is no place in our country for apps and technologies that are solely used to abuse, to humiliate and to harm people—especially our young people.

Australian parents are desperate for help against this scourge which hides in phones, in bedrooms and in schoolyards. The Albanese government hears their calls, and that is why the draft digital duty of care legislation will force big tech to listen as well.

speaker: Josh Burns
heading: COMMITTEES
subheading: Public Accounts and Audit Joint Committee; Report
text:
On behalf of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit, I present the following reports: Report 516: Inquiry into Commonwealth financial statements 2023-24 and 2024-25 and Report 517: Annual report 2025-26.

Report made a parliamentary paper in accordance with standing order 39(e).

by leave—First of all, I present the report of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit No. 516: Inquiry into Commonwealth financial statements 2023-24 and 2024-25.

The annual auditing of financial accounting and reporting by Commonwealth entities by the Australian National Audit Office provides assurance to the parliament on the financial position of the Australian government and the expenditure of taxpayer money.

This report considers the findings of both the 2023-24 and 2024-25 financial statements audits, with a particular focus on three areas of interest to the committee: compliance with legislation, including section 83 of the Australian Constitution; the information technology environment; and the governance of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.

Legislative non-compliance has increased across the two audit periods. While the committee welcomes evidence that entities have accepted the seriousness of issues identified by the ANAO, and are taking active steps toward remediation, the committee remains concerned by the number of breaches that persist across multiple audit cycles.

The IT control environment continues to account for the largest proportion of audit findings. It is clear to the committee that IT governance and controls continue to be a persistent challenge for entities.

The committee was encouraged by the approaches undertaken by the Department of Defence and NBN Co, both of which have successfully resolved findings relating to unauthorised post-separation access of IT networks. In these cases, resolution was achieved by addressing the issue as a whole-of-business issue rather than one confined to IT alone. The committee considers this approach instructive for the broader public sector and encourages other entities to apply similar methods.

The committee also considered the continued growth in the use of AI and other emerging technologies across the public sector. While the committee did not investigate the use of AI across the public sector in depth, it will continue to monitor whether governance frameworks are keeping pace with the rate of adoption and the range of emerging use cases.

One recommendation made by the committee was that the ANAO tables at least annually a report that examines public sector entities use and preparedness for emerging digital technologies.

I want to acknowledge and thank Senator Matt O'Sullivan for his service as deputy chair until March 2026 and thank the current deputy chair, the Hon. Scott Buchholz MP, for his help, commitment and support.

I thank all committee members for their contributions to this inquiry, and I commend that report to the House.

I am also pleased to present Report 517: Annual report 2025-26I've already given it to the clerks.

Under the Public Accounts and Audit Committee Act 1951, the committee is required to report annually to the parliament on the work it has undertaken.

The committee's work includes reviewing Australian National Audit Office reports and conducting inquiries where it identifies issues needing further examination. The committee determines the audit priorities of the parliament and makes recommendations to the government on the budget estimates of the Australian National Audit Office and the Parliamentary Budget Office. The committee can request a post-election review of the PBO's operations and did so following the 2025 election.

In 2025-26, the committee held 27 meetings, including seven public hearings. The committee commenced eight inquiries, tabled three reports, undertook a range of non-inquiry activities in line with legislative responsibilities and met with delegations from Kiribati and Cambodia, both highly successful. We completed inquiries in 2025-26, including into the effectiveness of Australia's National Anti-Doping Scheme and the procurement processes for supporting services for victims of child sexual abuse.

Again, I thank the deputy chair and all of the committee members, and I also want to pay a special tribute to the secretariat, who are outstanding public servants and serve the committee with distinction.

I commend the report to the House.

I ask leave of the House to present executive minutes on reports of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit, if that's possible.

Leave granted.

I present the executive minutes on reports 463, 472, 477, 479, 485, 486, 488, 491, 492, 498, 502, 504, 509, 511, 512, 514 and 515 of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit.

speaker: Mehreen Faruqi
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Universities should be fee free and fully funded for teaching, learning and research. No student should live in poverty while studying or be burdened with a lifetime of debt. Higher education, like all education, should be a public good built on equity and democracy. These are the basic propositions that shouldn't be hard to achieve in a country as wealthy as ours. But this Labor government keeps choosing to keep students poor and in debt. Labor's decision to continue the Liberals' uni fee hikes and funding cuts forces students to take on crushing debts in crowded classrooms at unis too often beset by governance crises. Staff are battling wage theft, job insecurity, course cuts and, increasingly, the threat of executives seeking to replace them with AI.

As the cost of living worsens and students cry out for help, the test for any higher education legislation that speaks the language of opportunity is whether it rises to these challenges. The Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026, as it stands today, does not meet that challenge. It falls far short of delivering the change university students and staff deserve, both in policy design and in funding. The bill promises equity, yet, four years after being elected, the Albanese government still refuses to address higher education's most egregiously inequitable policy—the Liberals' fee hikes and funding cuts, which have sentenced students to forever debts and fifty-four thousand dollar arts degrees and priced out low-SES students, whose commencements have decreased by almost 10 per cent. This policy alone has cost students at least $2.1 billion in the past four years.

How can you all sit here and tell students that you are opening the doors of opportunity when support payments like youth allowance and Austudy are well below the poverty line? When you're forcing students to starve just to afford their degrees, all while with the cost-of-living crisis is increasing under your watch, how is that opportunity? Tell me, what door is it that you are opening for students? It certainly isn't a door to an affordable home with food on the table. Labor can dress this bill up in words like 'equity' all it likes, but the bill itself does nothing to change the fact that too many young people are struggling through uni or have stopped going to uni altogether.

The committee inquiry into this bill made clear that there are many things in this bill that need to change, relating to student choice, growth, ministerial powers, postgraduate students, international students, equity students—and on the list goes. My team and I have been through these with the minister and his office, with good faith from both sides, I might say, and I will be moving amendments to address many of these issues. It's not just a couple of amendments but pages and pages of amendments. You do have to wonder why a bill that needs so many changes was even brought into parliament in the first place.

The higher education sector is in such crisis that it has been cornered into accepting the bare minimum, cornered into accepting crumbs when what is needed is a bigger pie of funding. If the Albanese government is serious about improving equity, then it needs to get serious about fully funding fee-free higher education. I urge the education minister to keep pushing the Prime Minister to invest much more in the future of higher education and our young people and our country. Otherwise, we'll always be doing gymnastics without actually solving the real problem.

A primary concern I and many others have had from the start is the bill's potential to curtail student choice. Students may not get a Commonwealth supported place, CSP, at the university and course of their choosing because places are capped. Instead, the minister and ATEC are attempting to funnel students into institutions and courses they may not want to go to—and to do what? To patch funding holes of the government's own making because they refuse to fund universities. The Greens will be protecting student choice by ensuring that ATEC must take student demand into account when setting allocations and by expanding the overenrolment provision from a hard cap to a buffer.

This bill also allows the minister to set CSPs for a designated course to zero. You can just imagine that under—God forbid!—a coalition or One Nation government they would seek to ban degrees and courses that they don't like in the name of being against 'wokeness'. No minister should ever be able to tell a student what they can and cannot study. The Greens will be bringing an amendment to remove this provision.

The problem is not where students are choosing to study but decades of Labor and the coalition deliberately underfunding and cutting funds to higher education. Universities, staff and students are bearing the brunt of this. Our regional universities are also suffering. If regional universities are to thrive and be attractive to students, they must be fully funded, including through dedicating funding for infrastructure and research investment. That is actually what the accord recommended, not this half-assed response that we have today. Tying funding to student places and hoping that they will come is not really a solution.

The Greens support needs based funding, yet the funding could all be squashed by one single section that allows the minister to set the equity support amount provided to university to zero dollars. You cannot say that you are providing needs based funding and then leave it open for a future government to make that funding zero. The Greens will be moving an amendment to fix this.

In the inquiry, we also heard countless witnesses share the absurdity of the bill calculating the applicability of needs based funding at the time the person enrols in the unit. This means that a low-SES student living in a regional area who moves to the inner city for university is apparently no longer disadvantaged. So we are going to rectify this perverse application as well.

It appears that Labor has sought to limit the eligibility of needs based funding to as small a cohort as possible. The only reason for this is their refusal to fund universities properly and fully or even fund every equity student a Commonwealth supported place in the degree and university of their choosing. Instead, they would rather splurge and waste hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars on fossil fuel subsidies and non-existent nuclear submarines.

Numerous submissions from universities, students, the NTEU and academics raised concerns that the current definition of a low-socioeconomic student is inadequate and unfit for purpose, utilising an outdated postcode determinant. The planned definition does not account for income, employment, family education history, occupation, housing, caring responsibilities, cultural barriers, disability or language proficiency. The Albanese government's response is, 'We'll look into it.' Well, you've had four years in government to look into it and you have fallen short yet again. This bill was the perfect opportunity to fix this outdated and blunt measure. I do hope that Labor is sincere when it says that it will now start this work.

A highly criticised aspect of this bill is an overall lack of accountability and transparency combined with excessive ministerial powers. We will be moving a number of amendments that go some way to addressing these issues. ATEC will be required to publish its reasons when making allocations, and the minister's unfettered power to make conditions on funding grants will be removed. This power could have been used to further crack down on students raising their voices for justice for Palestine, for example, or even forced universities to adopt the highly controversial IHRA definition of antisemitism, which conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism. The interventionist precedent this power would create should alarm everyone, and it is unacceptable to the Greens. We will be removing the section.

The bill, as it stands, allows the minister to set a course and provide a level of allocations for international students. There are people in this chamber who, if they had this power, would actually set this allocation to zero. I think you all know who I am talking about here. Unsurprisingly, this is the Albanese government having another swing at migration policy and trying to disguise it as education policy. As Mr Richard Lee from the Council of Australian Postgraduate Associations shared, 'International students are not a tap to turn on and off.' The continual scapegoating of international students for the government's own policy failures is damaging. It causes harm to students and migrants. Minister Clare has admitted that international-student visa fees, tripled since 2024, are being used to fund the accord reforms. International students are not cash cows or political playthings.

The Albanese government must stop wrecking international education to pander to One Nation's racist, antimigrant stance. It is disappointing that the government decided not to support expanding the evaluation of the act to include reviewing the allocation of international students. Their politicisation of international students trumps good policy once again, and it is students and universities who will suffer. The Prime Minister is really in a shameful race to the bottom with One Nation on migration, and he's made it clear that he doesn't care about international students being collateral damage or about our higher education system suffering.

I want to go to postgraduate students for a minute. With the exception of First Nations students, the bill excludes postgraduate students from needs based funding. While the bill allows a university to determine how it uses its allocation of CSPs, tying needs based funding only to undergraduate students creates a perverse incentive for universities to use all, or a large portion, of their allocated CSPs for undergraduate students. Needs based funding must cover the full pipeline of university education and all equity students, without which the door will remain tightly shut to postgraduate degrees and to research as well.

Without the Greens in the Senate, this bill would have handed the minister of the day diabolical interventionist powers over higher education, placed unacceptable limits on student choice and failed to deliver equity. I want to thank my team, especially Sienna and Lauren, who have worked so hard for us to get to this outcome today, with 12 amendments being made in the Senate and a couple in the House. The 12 amendments we have secured demonstrate the importance of the Greens in the Senate.

I'll finish where I started. This bill has no additional funding beyond what is already budgeted for universities. For a sector whose expenditure totalled $43.1 billion in 2024, a mere $3.66 billion over the next decade is crumbs. If the Albanese government wants to improve equity, they must repeal the fee hikes and funding cuts they've kept on the books for four years—not in two years time, but today. We will not see true equity in Australia's higher education system until universities are fee-free and fully funded for learning, teaching and research. All I ask is that the Prime Minister give young people what he himself enjoyed: free education at a well-funded public university.

Opening a door will not do much good until and unless the government addresses student poverty, abolishes student debt and increases student support payments, PhD stipends and housing affordability, all of which impact students' ability to walk through the door and out the other end having completed their degrees. We know there is so much work to be done to ensure staff have the governance structures to be able to run their universities democratically and the resources, pay and conditions for world-class teaching and research and to ensure students have the best learning conditions and are not crushed by ever-increasing fees and debt.

It is possible; the only thing standing in the way is the Albanese government. The Greens will always put students first. We will continue to fight for universities and institutions to serve the public good, not to serve the government or the corporations of the day.

With that, I move the Greens' second reading amendment:

At the end of the motion, add ", but the Senate:

(a) notes that:

(i) students and young people are facing the worst of the cost of living crisis, and 'opening doors' for students is not enough if they are not supported to complete their studies,

(ii) students are being shackled by a lifetime of debt which is making the cost of living crisis worse, locking people out of the housing market and crushing dreams of going to university,

(iii) the punitive Job-ready Graduates scheme fee hikes, which have led to $54,000 arts degrees, have now been in place for longer under Albanese's Labor Government than they were under the Morrison Government,

(iv) while degree costs skyrocket, student payments like Austudy and Youth Allowance remain well below the poverty line,

(v) higher education, like education at every level, is an essential public good that should be free, accessible and equitable, and

(vi) all students undertaking mandatory placements should be paid for every hour of work they are required to do, at least at minimum wage, not a lesser supplementary amount; and

(b) calls on the Government to:

(i) invest in, and fully fund, higher education for leaning, teaching and research,

(ii) increase Austudy and Youth Allowance,

(iii) wipe all student debt and make university and TAFE fee-free for all,

(iv) urgently reverse the fee hikes and funding cuts of the Job-ready Graduates scheme, and

(v) pay all students doing mandatory placements at no less than minimum wage rates".

speaker: Marielle Smith
heading: MATTERS OF URGENCY
text:
I also rise to contribute to the debate on this urgency motion. The Albanese Labor government fights to keep Australian industry. We fight for good industrial jobs in Australia and for Australians. That is why we're building a modern energy system and reserving Australian gas for Australian industry. We're putting our shoulder to the wheel and rebuilding Australia's industrial base, and we're doing that because we know that a stronger Australia is an Australia that can make more of what it needs here at home. Australia has the workers, the resources, the energy and the ideas that the world needs, and our government's Future Made in Australia agenda is turning those strengths into jobs, investment and resilient supply chains.

This is not about making everything; it is about making more here in Australia, adding more value to Australian resources and ensuring that the benefits flow to workers, to local businesses and to local communities. It's about backing the strategic capabilities Australia needs: renewable and reliable energy, critical minerals processing, green metals, defence and advanced technologies, and world-class research and innovation. Rebuilding and strengthening Australia's industrial base is hard work. Establishing new industries is not a linear process. But our government unashamedly backs Australian industry, we back Australian jobs and we back Australian workers, just as we have in Whyalla.

Of course, this is a very difficult time for the people of Whyalla. The announcement by the administrator of the steelworks that the efforts to restart the blast furnace over recent months were unsuccessful will impact on workers, their families and the broader community. And it is clear that years of failure to invest in the steelworks mean that it is now beyond repair. What these workers in Whyalla need now more than ever is a government that backs them in, that acknowledges how tirelessly they have worked throughout this challenging period. They need a government that is committed to a domestic steel manufacturing industry and a government that is securing the long-term future of the Whyalla steelworks alongside the local jobs and the local families who rely on it.

We believe in a future made in Australia, we believe in a strong future for Whyalla and we believe in Australian industry and all of its potential. That's why our government established the national reconstruction fund, a $15 billion investment fund to back Australian industry and to drive the industries of tomorrow. To date, that fund has announced 32 investments, totalling some $1.83 billion across resources, biotech, artificial intelligence, food and beverage manufacturing, housing and quantum development. The work of that fund to grow domestic industrial capabilities is central to our economic security, and it's central to our resilience. This work is more important now than ever.

Together, through the national reconstruction fund, targeted Future Made in Australia programs and smelter interventions, the Albanese Labor government is making Australia stronger and ensuring that our resources, energy, skills and ideas are creating value for Australians. We are strengthening supply chains, crowding in private investment and building the industrial base our country will need for decades to come. We're supporting jobs in our industrial heartlands, and we are creating the jobs of the future. What workers want and what industry needs right now is a government that backs them in. What they need is a government that believes in their potential and that believes in a future for local manufacturing—and one that not just believes in it but is prepared to stand up for it.

What they don't need is an opposition that talks them down. What they don't need is an opposition that abandons them. They don't need representation like they've had from the Liberal Party in the past. We all remember Joe Hockey, on the floor of the other place, goading the car industry to leave Australia, to leave my home state of South Australia, to turn their back on South Australian workers, to turn their back on Elizabeth and to turn their back on our state. And do you know what? After they goaded them to do it, they did. Our state has lived with the consequences of that. Our government and the Malinauskas government have been trying to do something about it. Workers in our state remember the Liberal Party's record on that. We remember how you behaved then. We'll remember how you respond now. Workers in my state want a government that will back them in, not an opposition that will talk them down.

speaker: Malcolm Roberts
heading: MATTERS OF URGENCY
text:
I thank Senator Blyth for this matter of urgency, which One Nation supports. Last night I read a list of large job losses from the last few months here in Australia. Today there's one more to add. The retailer Cue, or Veronika Maine, has now gone into receivership. They may be saved, and I hope for the sake of their 69 stores and hundreds of people that they are. Other retailers in administration or liquidation recently include Betts, Lincraft, Barbeques Galore, Aussie Disposals, Stateside Sports, AH Beard, Harold's and regional retailer Proud Poppy. These are names familiar to all Australians. I've shopped at them. This is personal. These are people in their communities that are now out of work.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, in the 12 months prior to February 2026, nationwide retrenchments rose to 257,900 people. That is more than a quarter of a million people—Australians who no longer have a job, families without a breadwinner. Every community is suffering. Every retailer is feeling it. Unemployment has risen under the Albanese government from 3.4 per cent to 4.5 per cent. This follows on from the 14,152 business insolvencies last financial year—the second highest on record after the all-time high of 14,700 recorded under Treasurer Chalmers the year before. Australians having a go to provide for themselves and people we know in our communities keeping our local shops in business? No longer. There are 691,500 Australians without a job and looking for one.

Another million Australians on top of that are working and not getting all the hours they need to keep their heads above water. Imagine how hard that will be with another one million planned new arrivals to compete with thanks to Labor's mass immigration program. Those still with jobs are increasingly classified as the working poor, dependent on government handouts to survive, which is exactly how totalitarian governments throughout time have wanted their citizens: desperate, broke and totally reliant on government.

The bailout offered to keep Tomago aluminium smelter in business will, in my experience, only be temporary. Labor and the Liberals did the same thing with the Australian car industry. Remember when we made cars? Remember all those union jobs? Subsidies were used to keep the car industry alive long enough to transition from local manufacturing to a fully imported supply chain. Then the subsidies ended. They were pulled.

With modern, computerised, AI driven automated assembly lines, cost-efficient manufacturing is possible here in Australia and has been for years. Modern manufacturing does not need cheap labour. It needs proximity to raw materials, which we have, and capital to build our facilities. We have $4.5 trillion in capital stored in superannuation funds looking for profitable, safe investments. It needs a regulatory environment to free up that investment. A One Nation government will deliver that.

American industry has worked all this out. In the last few years, Apple, GE, Samsung, General Motors, Eli Lilly, Intel and Micron have all moved manufacturing back to the United States. Why? Because they're on a track back to cheap power. If they can do it, so can we. Of course, this does need steel, and this Labor government just allowed our steel mill in Whyalla to close, with 600 jobs lost. That's 600 jobs gone. That's another heavy industry facility where subsidies were used as a bridge to allow the plant to be hollowed out and then replaced with imports. The LIBERTY Bell Bay manganese smelter closed in July—another 250 jobs gone. Instead of encouraging investment in manufacturing and heavy industry to bring jobs home, this government is growing the Chinese economy. When did unions stop worrying about Australian workers and start cheering on the Chinese Communist Party? Or was the $15 billion ripped out of Victoria's Big Build a pay-off for silence? Who knows?

India is emerging as a major source of steel, using iron ore and coal. Where do they get theirs? Oh, that's right! They get their iron ore and coal from Australia, of course. Australian workers are wondering how it could be possible to ship iron ore from Western Australia and coal from New South Wales and Queensland to China and India, make the steel using automated production and then ship it back here. I'll tell you. It's a one-word answer—energy. It turns out weather-dependent-power windmills can't sustain manufacturing and heavy industry and can't sustain an economy. This government's insistence on advancing ideology over enterprise is costing everyday Australians their jobs, their homes, their marriages, their families and their dignity. The next election can't come soon enough.

speaker: David Shoebridge
heading: MATTERS OF URGENCY
text:
What I never hear in this debate is how anyone is going to materially improve the lives of people here. They phrase this debate about housing, about wages—never do they put forward how they're going to take on the one per cent and make people's lives better. The parties in here—Labor, One Nation and those of the coalition—and their ultrawealthy backers have targeted migrants repeatedly over decades of underinvestment in housing, public health and core services because migrants are an easy distraction for them and their billionaire backers. Migrants don't tend to be massively rich. Some are, but they don't tend to be. Many of them don't vote, and they're just the perfect scapegoat for a political class that refuses to take on the ultrawealthy, so One Nation and Labor are more than happy to gang up on them. We'll see the same thing tomorrow when Minister Burke stands up, with One Nation grinning over his shoulder. We know it's all dog whistling.

We've actually lived through an experience of net negative migration. During COVID, Australia's population went down—and Australia's house prices rose by more than 20 per cent in just 18 months. Everyone forgets that because it disturbs the narrative. Let's be clear. Your mum's friend from the Philippines who's an emergency nurse at the local hospital had no say over how much of the federal budget went into public housing or health. The family down on the corner who run the grocery shop aren't in cabinet when the government decides to cut NDIS funding. Your friend's partner who moved from Canada to get married wasn't on the phone to Albanese telling him to fast-track AI. The bloke in your local football team who fled war in Iraq wasn't in charge of setting interest rates.

speaker: David Pocock
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I'd like to start by saying that I welcome the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026 and the reforms it contains to how we fund universities, and I intend to support it. However, the very clear consensus from evidence presented to the Senate committee inquiry is that it needs amendments before it should pass the Senate.

First and foremost, while fixing how we fund universities, the bill does nothing to address student contributions and the crushing debt impacts from Job-Ready Graduates. After four years in power and having railed against Job-ready Graduates in opposition, it should be unbelievable—unfortunately, it isn't—that the Albanese government have failed to act on JRG. First they kicked it to ATEC. Now ATEC is saying there'll be no advice until next year and no change until 2028 at the earliest. In that time, students will continue to accrue $50,000-plus debts for a humanities degree, a degree that we know is more important than ever in the face of AI.

I'm moving an amendment that would seek to expedite this process. The overwhelming consensus from the Senate inquiry was that the most concerning thing about this bill is the extraordinary powers that it gives the current minister and any future minister to intervene in our universities. While some of these powers have been wound back, they remain excessive. I believe further amendment is required specifically to remove ministerial power to set course-level caps for international students, cap demand-driven places for Indigenous students and set provider-specific funding conditions. As a Senate, we should be a check on executive power and we should fight tooth and nail not to provide this level of power to any future minister. These sorts of changes should be subject to scrutiny. They should have to come through this parliament and be judged by elected representatives on behalf of the people that send them to this place.

In circumstances where this bill passes unamended, QUT highlighted the potential perils and vulnerability to politicisation of standard university operational decisions. I'll quote from their submission. It said:

The Bill would create an avenue for stakeholders dissatisfied with such decisions to seek Ministerial intervention in operational matters that should remain within established institutional governance processes.

It said the existence of these powers:

… would encourage stakeholders to seek Ministerial intervention whenever an institutional decision becomes contentious. Refusing to intervene could then become as politically consequential as intervening.

I don't understand why the minister would even want these powers. Can you imagine the lobbying that it opens them up to and the public criticism where they do or don't make a decision that may or may not be ideologically aligned with a certain group? Not only could a minister ban a specific course for ideological reasons or at the behest of a vested interest; they could also mandate that certain courses be taught. Given what we've seen overseas, it's really not hard to imagine a government banning all sorts of things, such as welcomes to country or pride events on campus, or interfering with what universities teach about climate change, genocide or the Holocaust. No government should have this sort of power to impose ideologies on our universities. As Doctor Byron succinctly put it, while the government could be worried about a future rogue Senate, the Senate should be worried about a future rogue government. That encapsulates the concerns about handing this sort of extraordinary power to the minister.

Both I and the coalition will move an amendment that would seek to remove these powers. In my second reading amendment, I talk about the need to better define equity. The University of Canberra highlighted the shortcomings with the current definition:

… the ACT is largely excluded from the Government's Needs-based Funding model, with no support for Low Socio-Economic Status (Low SES) or regional students. Proposed methodology of using Low SES does not recognise any disadvantaged University of Canberra students from the ACT. We have not received support funding in 2026 for most of our disadvantaged students and now expect to be underfunded into 2027.

The 2021 Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA) are not adequate in identifying disadvantage in the ACT. Using these tables there are no Low-SES areas in the ACT. This is a product of good urban planning but statistically hides disadvantaged individuals.

Canberra has pockets of extreme disadvantage, and this needs to be recognised. We have to have a system where students who need more support get it and universities who need to provide that support are provided with additional funding to do exactly that. This really rough way of calculating low-SES or regional students just doesn't cut it. We have to do better as a country in terms of collecting data and ensuring that universities like the University of Canberra aren't missing out.

The purpose of this bill is managed growth, but, as experts like Doctor Andrew Norton highlighted, 'the bill does not appropriate any new funding for additional student places'. He said:

By contrast, the bill has two new features that will reduce how many student places universities can offer.

This clearly stands in contrast to the stated aim of managed growth. Another of my amendments seeks to set a floor in the total allocation pool. A further concern is around parliamentary oversight. The two determinations that set the size of the whole system, the domestic total allocation pool and the international pool are expressly exempt from disallowance. Every decision beneath them is declared not to be a legislative instrument, including place allocations, core and growth determinations, and international allocations. We should not be allowing this as a Senate. We should have a say on these decisions of the executive. They should be up for debate. They should be up for disallowance. I urge fellow senators to ensure that we do not hand these powers to the executive in perpetuity. One of my amendments seeks to change this and give the parliament, rather than the minister of the day, oversight of these crucial matters—crucial not just for our university sector but for the future of our country.

I'd like to thank my team for the huge amount of work that they put into this bill and this inquiry. Based on the evidence provided to the Senate Committee, I requested 23 amendments to this bill, all based on what I'd heard from the university sector and from experts. Unfortunately, at the time of making these remarks, only five have been circulated, and I note the Greens are yet to circulate any amendments. For a bill this important, I think it speaks to a failure of process. As senators, we need to have the opportunity to move amendments to bills, and that requires access to drafting in a timely way that enables us to discuss with colleagues and to seek support before the bill is in the Senate like this. I'd like to thank those in the drafting office for the amazing work that they do. We know that you're under the pump.

But, as a crossbencher, again I would like to raise with the government, with the President, the lack of drafting resources for the crossbench. I can't speak of how the major parties experience it, but, as a crossbencher, it is incredibly difficult to get anything drafted in a timely manner, and I don't think that's good enough for our democracy. Elected representatives, regardless of where you're from, who you're here representing or which state or territory you're representing, should have access to drafting, where you can put forward your amendments in good faith, have conversations with colleagues, and then, when it comes down to it, they're either supported or not supported.

Finally, I'd like to thank the committee for all their work and stakeholders for their comprehensive, detailed and constructive submissions on this legislation. Too often the public does not see the genuinely good faith work that happens in this place—the collaboration and the collegiate way that Senate committees can work a lot of the time, obviously not all of the time. I think we should continue to highlight that as senators. So while I have these concerns, I thank the government for the direction they are heading in, and I commend my amendments to the Senate. I foreshadow my second reading amendments.

speaker: David Shoebridge
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise first of all to acknowledge the work of my colleague Senator Faruqi in this space, endorse her comments and particularly note the raft of concerns about this bill that remain unaddressed including the genuine cost-of-living crisis that we know students are facing with ever mounting HECS debt. I haven't spoken to a student who remembers getting a haircut on the HECS debt, but I've spoken to plenty of students who are looking at a lifetime of debt for simply wanting to get an education to contribute to society.

We still don't see a solution for the so-called Job-Ready Graduates scheme that saw these appalling cost hikes for arts degrees. It was a conscious attack from the coalition to dumb down our universities and to attack critical thinking. We're five years—it feels like forever—into a Labor government, and they still haven't addressed that despite repeated offers from the Greens to solve that. Degree costs have continued on their upward path. Student payments remain below the poverty line. These are the core issues in the university sector that despite the name on the box of this bill—it's called the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026. Again, as we know, the doors of opportunity are very narrowly open under Labor, particularly for students who don't have family support, those who are first generation at university, those who are considering career that isn't in the finance sector or a highly paying sector but is essential for our society like teaching, nursing, social work, critical thinking. They're the ones who continue to be under the gun despite five years of a Labor government.

There's one other thing that I think absolutely needs to be addressed with urgency in the university sector, and it's playing out in university campuses in my home state of New South Wales. It's playing out on the campuses of the University of New South Wales, of the University of Sydney, of UTS, of Macquarie University, but I know it's playing out across universities Australia wide. While there's talk of building opportunities—what this bill talks about—what students and academics are facing right now are universities reaching for AI to dumb down degrees, to replace staff and to put at risk the reputations of some of our finest institutions. Last week, the University of New South Wales said it had signed this so-called strategic partnership with OpenAI—a US owned, tech-bro owned vampire company who has no interest in building Australia's education sector, who has no interest in educating Australians and who definitely has no interest in our universities being competitive. Without putting any guardrails in, without talking to the staff and without articulating what the strategic partnership will mean for job security, for the quality of degrees, for teaching, they make this big announcement. This is the statement that UNSW made:

The collaboration, one of the largest AI education deployments in the Asia-Pacific region, aims to help ensure graduates are equipped to use AI critically, ethically and effectively.

Who are they partnering with? OpenAI, the same US tech-bro owned corporation that let its agents escape the sandbox and run wild.

What are the what are the checks and balances being proposed here? Where are the restraints in how our university sector rolls out AI to endanger our research capability? It's not all upside with AI. There's serious risk of deskilling our researchers, rogue AI agents taking that research and heading off heaven knows where. There's complete silence from this government about—not a whisper about one of our premier universities and, at different times, one of our highest ranked university on global ratings uncritically rolling out a foreign multinational AI player right throughout its universities in what it describes as 'the largest AI education deployment in the Asia-Pacific'.

That's not a good news story. That's a flashing-lights warning story. It's not just that. Less than a week after that, the University of Sydney made an announcement as well. The University of Sydney comes out and talks about 'a university-wide investment in AI to ensure every student and staff member has free and equitable access to advanced AI tools'. And then we get this guff:

Tomorrow's leaders will also need to understand AI's ethical, social and environmental impacts, and possess the ability to work with this technology critically and responsibly. We will support you for that future by providing equitable access to advanced AI tools.

Whatever the University of Sydney's Vice President of Operations, Ms Gower, might say about it being a human centred approach to AI, ask the staff—the academics, the people who are going to have to deliver for this. How they see this deal of the University of Sydney with the same bunch of US tech-bro AI vampires is as a threat. Because, at the same time that the university went out and made its announcement that they're going to be incorporating a foreign owned AI into every aspect of the university's operations, the NTEU members, the people who actually have to teach, do the research and undertake the critical thinking at University of Sydney, were out on strike seeking enforceable consultation protections around AI. This is how this is how managerial and out of touch management at our universities is—these vice-chancellors and their cronies that hang around them, paid a million bucks a year and more. I think, in Sydney, they also get a free, posh residence. You get a million bucks in your bank account and a free, posh residence if you're the vice-chancellor in Sydney, and then you use that privilege to roll out AI and take away the jobs of the actual teaching staff.

And we get Labor coming in here with their—what is it named?—Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill. Well, under Labor, the door's been opened to vampire, US owned AI to come and march through our universities and take away jobs, destroy the critical thinking that we're going to need for our students and continue to empower the managerial class to run through our universities.

I want to say, on behalf of my party, the Greens, that we stand in solidarity with the NTEU members who are on strike, asking for genuine, enforceable consultation protections before universities like Sydney or UNSW enter into these multiyear deals. And we want to make sure that they're enforceable rights so that the vice-chancellors on their million bucks a year and their $500,000, $700,000, $800,000 per annum human-development staff-squashing managerial teams don't get to destroy our universities. The only door of opportunity that seems to be opening here is the door of opportunity for US big tech to come in, deskill and put at enormous risk some of our most important institutions.

I would urge the government to go and look at what the community thinks about this and the lack of action on protecting our universities from the rollout of US owned AI, because you have a look at the comments on social media about Sydney university's post and they're not saying: 'Oh, amazing—wonderful opportunity. I'm glad you've invited these robber barons in to come and attack our university.' They're calling it 'despicable garbage'. They're calling it 'fascism-maxxing'. They're naming it for what it is.

There's some marginal good in this bill. The marginal good is great. But there's this massive risk, and it's not academic; it happened last week—the week before this bill got rolled in to literally destroy the integrity, the reputation, the qualities of our universities, because, under Labor, US big tech, US AI companies, are marching through our universities, and the staff are on the front lines fighting it, going into industrial action, saying, 'You can't do this without us.'

What's the answer from Labor? Nothing, because it turns out that the same big tech companies that are talking to the vice-chancellor at Sydney university and schmoozing with the vice-chancellor at UNSW are in there with a ready-access door to the Prime Minister, trying to do a job on creatives and trying to get a red carpet to roll out their AI vision right across this country—to steal our water, our power and our data and, in this case, to have that march through some of our most important institutions.

Unless this government is willing to come and work with the Greens to address the risk of AI through our universities—you can pass as many 'opening the doors of opportunity' bills as you like, but, unless we address the risk of foreign owned AI through the march of our institutions, this won't amount to a hill of beans.

speaker: Vanessa Bleyer
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
Off the far north-west coast of Tasmania is an island, Robbins Island. Its traditional Palawa name is Pilitika. It is rich in Aboriginal cultural heritage and of profound significance to the Palawa Pakana people. It contains landforms of global geological and geomorphological significance. Its complex coastal systems serve as an international index site for studying past climate changes and sea-level histories. It is on the migratory pathway of the critically endangered orange-bellied parrot, which doesn't just instinctively fly over but stops and forages on the island. It is home to the last remaining disease-free population of the endangered Tasmanian devil in the world. Elsewhere in Tasmania, a facial tumour disease is decimating Tasmanian devil populations.

Now, wait for this, and I hope you're all sitting down: last year, in 2025, this Labor government approved a wind farm at Pilitika/Robbins Island. Construction of turbines will destroy sites of Aboriginal cultural heritage, destroy sites of global geological significance and cause the extinction of the orange-bellied parrot as the turbine blades pulverise the last parrots that survive. Construction of a bridge from mainland Tasmania to Pilitika/Robbins Island will introduce diseased Tasmanian devils and decimate the last healthy wild population. Construction of a wharf will deprive us forever of studying sea-level histories at a time of climate crisis, when we need it most. Like every development, there's a right place and a wrong place. This is simply the wrong place for a wind farm.

You'll be pleased to know I'm the bearer of good news. Something has just happened which means that this government should now bring the proposed wind farm at Pilitika/Robbins Island to an end. It was a condition of this government's approval of the Robbins Island wind farm that, within six months of the date of approval, the proponent of the wind farm—backed by a megarich Philippines based company, by the way—must submit an orange-bellied parrot survey plan to this government for approval. The proponent did not. It was a condition of this government's approval that the proponent notify this government within two business days of failing to comply with the condition. The proponent did not. The big foreign corporation behind the proposed wind farm obviously cares not for the laws of this nation, just like it obviously cares not for the irreplaceable natural and cultural wonders of Pilitika-Robbins Island.

On the other hand, we hear this government talking so much about how it upholds the rule of law and that the rule of law is a foundational principle of Australia's democracy. It follows that it must care very much for the laws of this nation. So, no doubt, this government is going to do what the law says that it should because of the breached conditions and immediately revoke the approval of the wind farm at Pilitika-Robbins Island. No doubt, this government is going to do what the law says it should and prosecute the proponent for its serious statutory offence in breaching the conditions. Surely this government is not more concerned about appeasing a big corporation and making decisions for that big corporation instead of for us. I and so many whom I represent in Tasmania eagerly await the news from this Labor government that it will adhere to the rule of law and that this monstrosity of a wind farm—100 turbines, each over 200 metres high, and in absolutely the wrong place—is over.

Speaking of developments that are absolutely in the wrong place, I note a proposed data centre in the Tamar Valley in northern Tasmania that remains controversial. Recently, a local council in Tasmania approved that AI data centre at what was previously the site for Gunns proposed pulp mill. Let me tell you, that place and I go way back. When I was a lawyer, we ran more court cases to stop that proposed dirty, stinking pulp mill than to stop any other proposed development in this nation. We challenged every single state and federal government approval. This was because that site in the Tamar Valley is not the place for a pulp mill. The noise that the pulp mill would have generated and the light that the pulp mill would have emitted would have been grossly disruptive to the residents of the Tamar Valley, and it would have permanently damaged the then $50-million-a-year tourism industry. The massive amounts of water that the pulp mill would have needed could not have been delivered, because the presence of threatened flora species where the pipeline was intended to be built would have prohibited it. For all these reasons, the pulp mill failed.

For the same reasons, a noisy, light-emitting and water intensive AI data centre at the same site as the proposed Gunns pulp mill cannot proceed, in what is now a $100-million-a-year tourism industry. It might have local council approval, but I can't see how it could get federal government approval under our national environment laws. Big business and the Tasmanian government sought to ram through the pulp mill, but, as a community, we stood up and saw it off. As a community, we can and we will do the same for this AI data centre.

We know that data centres are deeply unpopular across the whole of Australia, particularly in Tasmania. A petition tabled this month by my Greens colleagues in Tasmania's state parliament opposing the development of AI data centres was one of the largest in the state's history. Tasmanians called for an immediate moratorium on non-complete artificial intelligence and data facilities until strict protective guardrails are put in place.

We need a moratorium on AI data centre developments across the whole nation now. That is the Greens position and that is the public's expectation of all of us in this place. We can't wait until next year, when this government says it's going to introduce proposed laws, because, in the meantime, companies like Firmus are going to ram their proposals through local planning processes. Local councils aren't even equipped to deal with that. AI data centres were not even a sparkle in anyone's eye when the planning schemes were prepared. The only people that benefit from these developments are the big tech corporations.

The company that is seeking to build the data centre in Tasmania's Tamar Valley, Firmus, is run by a convicted fraudster. Can we really take him at his word? We can't, and I'll give you some evidence as to why. Firmus has just appealed the local council decision to approve the data centre at the proposed Gunns pulp mill site in an effort to allow it to run diesel powered generators at the site. It had promised that its data centres would be powered by renewable energy.

These big tech corporations are misleading our communities. They are misleading our governments, and they are proposing developments that are in the wrong place. The community won the fight against Gunns proposed pulp mill and the community will win this fight against this proposed AI data centre.

speaker: Michelle Ananda-Rajah
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
The Albanese Labor government is turning the screws on the social media platforms. Those arguing against it call it censorship; I reject that completely. What we have right now is not free speech; it is the illusion of freedom. We don't know what we are seeing or why we are seeing it. We are force-fed content, with no idea of whether it is real or AI slop, who made it, where it came from or why we are seeing it. Depending on your profile, it might be dogs, food, misogyny, eating disorders, radicalisation or pro-measles or pro-self-harm content.

When Australians don't know what they are seeing or why, that's not freedom. That's tech authoritarianism. Tech oligarchs have been running the show. They are the controllers behind our screens. And these harms are not trivial—women bleeding to death after freebirths, election interference, climate misinformation dividing communities and scams that are making us poorer. But it's the harms to our kids that keep me up at night—too many suicides, too much cyberbullying and online shaming and youth radicalisation making our boys hostile to women and girls. The digital duty of care gives us back choice and control. Now Australians will be able to switch off the algorithm and control what they see. That's real freedom.

With one in five Australians paying for AI, including one in three Aussie firms, our dependency on AI is growing. A former Anthropic researcher has warned that AI could precipitate human extinction and that no other human activity posed this level of danger. Days later, the Anthropic CEO called on the industry to slow down, warning that, if left unchecked, AI risks advancing beyond our capacity to control it. This assumes, of course, that we understand its preferences. We do not.

On 7 July, OpenAI made public a fully automated autonomous AI cyberattack on an external company called Hugging Face. It was a milestone, and not in a good way. One AI agent, working in a team or a swarm, exclaimed, 'Oh, my God! There's a shared message board. We've found other agents.' That's what the AI actually said. AI agents are conniving and collaborating while covering their tracks from human oversight to achieve their goals. We shouldn't be surprised. After all, these agents are trained on our human foibles. Warnings were quickly corroborated by AI oligarchs Sam Altman and Elon Musk. When the warnings are coming from inside the tent, we should listen.

The Albanese Labor government is taking this seriously. We announced our national AI plan last year, and the Prime Minister, in July of this year, foreshadowed that world-first AI standards are coming. We have established an AI safety institute. We have also signed a memorandum of understanding with Anthropic and Microsoft to encourage responsible development of AI and set out standards that force new data centres to underwrite their own power, pay their own connection costs, use water sustainably and deliver jobs. All these elements will come under a new office of AI, established under the Prime Minister's wing to better coordinate a whole-of-government response.

But maybe it's time to ask if we need to go further. Comparable global threats have produced global conventions. The 1997 chemical weapons convention ended the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons, following the gas attacks of World War I. This time we do not have 80 years to coordinate a global response. When insiders are saying that AI could precipitate human extinction, and some are saying that could happen a lot sooner than we think, an international convention is not such a crazy idea.

Continuing, I'm really proud of the fact that the Albanese Labor government has delivered a women's health package of nearly $1 billion. This package was born out of the fact that we are a female-dominant government, with 56 per cent female representation in our federal Labor caucus.

speaker: Sarah Hanson-Young
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
Big AI companies are trying to blackmail the Australian government and this very parliament. They want to get the government to agree to sell out Australia's intellectual property rights. It is absolutely disgraceful that these companies, trillion-dollar companies, want a free cheque to come and scrape, steal and thieve on Australia's culture and on our intellectual property. The Albanese government had promised to stand strong against this push from big AI to take whatever they want without consent and without payment from Australians. But what do we see? We see the Albanese government going weak at the knees. Big AI is blackmailing the Albanese government and wanting to make sure this parliament follows suit. Frankly, Australians are sick and tired of being told that big tech can just get whatever it wants. Australians are rightly sceptical of AI and the enormous amount of power it has and the bullying that goes on. Australians are right to be sceptical of what AI wants to do here on Australian soil. We know, of course, they want to build their big data-mining centres. They want carve-outs on rules and fast-tracking for buildings. And now we hear that they're trying to push the government to give them a carve-out on copyright as well.

Australians are looking at this and they're saying, 'Hang on a minute—how come these big American companies think they can just come to Australia, set up shop, take our water, take our energy, take our land and, now, take our culture and our intellectual property for free?' This option that the government is seemingly pushing around is for an opt-out—that is, that Australians are going to be expected to opt out of having their work stolen, opt out of having their rights protected and opt out of being paid for their creativity and their lifetime's work. An opt-out is a cop-out, and it's about time that the Albanese government showed some muscle. The big tech companies and big AI are coming to Australia with their big dollar signs, dazzling state and federal governments and promising the world. Meanwhile, they're actually giving a dire warning of what this technology is capable of. We saw the biggest AI CEOs only in the last week say that they don't even know how to control this technology, but they want Australians to roll over and give them carte blanche access here in Australia, and we'll worry about the consequences later.

Australians are not patsies. We're not AI's patsy and we're not America's patsy. We want a government who's willing to stand up for our rights, our culture and our intellectual property. If the Albanese government cannot do that, then they should fess up and tell Australians that they're too weak to run these negotiations and too weak to take on big AI and big tech. Pretending that you're cutting a good deal while you're being screwed is laughable at best but dangerous at worst. Australians know that big AI has no right to a social licence unless it earns it, so the Albanese government must force AI to earn it. We need a moratorium on these big AI data-mining centres so that these laws can be put in place first, to protect Australians, to protect our culture, to protect our water, to protect our energy, to protect our rights and to protect Australia's sovereignty. (Time expired)

speaker: Jacqui Lambie
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
Every time big corporations get a sniff of any regulation, they threaten to leave the country. Now big tech is jumping on the bandwagon. Open AI—that's ChatGPT, by the way—has issued an ultimatum to our government, telling the Prime Minister that, if he doesn't walk away from his promise to the Australian people to protect our copyright laws, it won't even consider investing in training in this country. Basically, they said, 'Let AI suck up all the Aussie music, books, movies and art or we won't be investing in this country.' That's their ultimatum.'

They tried this on in the UK, but the British government told them they weren't changing their copyright laws. They are trying it on here. Big tech is trying this on all over the world. They're like dinosaurs from Jurassic Park. They're testing the fences. They tried it on in Europe, and Europe also said no. Denmark have gone one further. They've been bigger. They are passing laws that give people control over their voices and their images. With other Western countries standing up for their copyright laws, we are next. As OpenAI's senior vice-president told the Australian newspaper, we are 'a good target'.
