You'll get the arguments out of DFAT, Treasury, Finance and the Productivity Commission—which are occupied by people who are stuck in ideological permafrost and who find it hard to believe these types of powers should come in. In fact, there was an article in InnovationAus that talked about Treasury analysis of the economic implications of AI, and it quoted the Treasury, saying:

"In Australia, most productivity growth at the firm level related to AI will likely come from adopting and adapting technologies developed elsewhere."

That's the mentality for all parliamentarians. Like I said, regardless of who occupies the Treasury benches, you get advice from these types of people that believe the best way for us to use technology is to import it quickly and not develop it here. God forbid we spend our own money developing sovereign capability on anything!

Similarly in terms of safeguards, they take the view that free trade should occur unencumbered: if someone can price a product in a particular way, competition will be good, will strengthen local firms and will ensure that lower prices flow through the economy, and that's got to be a good thing. That's very superficial and does not factor in how bigger economies, bigger players, can undercut the prices at which they offer product for trade. When I say this bill has been 30 years in the making, it's going through that journey—the journey of recognising that the free trade mantra is only good if it's not superficial. It's got to be fair dinkum, and you've got to be able to test whether the prices for product are legitimate and not deliberately undercut.

There'll be a lot of people in this place and outside that talk about impending conflict with China and talk about having to get ready for some sort of military conflict, one they've concocted in their head and believe will occur any time soon. China don't need to fire a missile; they just fire product our way. And they fire product because we set up a world trade system where they took on so much of the work that we used to do, and they price it in such a way that creates dependencies. China don't have to fire a shot; they just fire a product at us.

If we don't think seriously, in a sustained way and in a determined way, about building sovereign capability, if we continue to listen to the same voices in Canberra—the PM&C, Treasury, Finance, DFAT and the Productivity Commission—and if we take as gospel what is put to us, we will always be dependent. Make no mistake. We will not build up serious sovereign capability. We will not be able to stand on our own two feet. All we will ever be is the best customer on an app store, buying someone else's product from some other land, instead of actually building the capabilities that matter here.

Having an economically diverse country, where we don't have all our eggs in one basket, where we build our wealth through different sectors and different activities, is really important. And, if you want to build greater productivity, look at the countries that are more economically complex in their make up and see how much more productive and stronger they are. That's the challenge for us.

I maintain the position that our commitment to sovereign capability has to be deeper than talk. It requires serious coordination across government at cabinet level, where all relevant portfolios are committed, on a yearly basis reporting, what has been done to advance sovereign capability in the key areas. We cannot do everything on our own, and it's certainly not something I would urge.

On the big, important things we have to have depth in capability. That can be across our existing behemoths of resources and agriculture, as well as energy production, medical sciences, advanced manufacturing and advanced tech. We need to be able to build our capabilities. And we have to do it in a way acknowledging the way that other countries do it, instead of having the ideological nineties version of the way in which we back industry, because the nineties version was that you don't put any government funding in. Other countries have been doing it and working smart in building up capability, and we have been the outpost that has ignored the way the rest of the world is working. It means investing more in R&D. It means investing more in grants to help grow companies at the relevant points of the technology readiness levels. It involves a scale-up approach that sees more small businesses become medium-sized enterprises and seeing the productivity uplift that occurs from there. Having a national scale-up strategy is really important. It's being able to keep a central tab on how we are developing capability. All this is critical for the long-term good of the country.

This type of legislation and this type of activity, where we take an important power out of the Productivity Commission, put it into the ADC and protect ourselves in a quicker way from dumping activity, is a big part of that process as well. So I congratulate the industry minister on landing this and the government in bringing forward this legislation, because it is very important and it does correct a behaviour that we have supinely just sat here and let the world dictate the terms in which trade occurs, comforting ourselves in the notion that we've chanted the mantra of free trade without recognising that that doesn't always occur that way and that sometimes you've got to step in and protect yourselves from the behaviours of others. Trade is important. It builds stronger relationships between countries. It does absolutely improve the strength of economies and the strength of incomes of the workers within those economies. But we can't be purist about it. We have to be pragmatic, and we have to step in where it's necessary to do so. This is one example of just that, and I absolutely commend the bill to the House.

Question agreed to.

Bill read a second time.

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: My question is to the Prime Minister. Prime Minister, Anthropic plans to build a giant data centre in the Western Downs, potentially increasing Queensland's energy use by 25 per cent, the equivalent usage of 1.5 million homes, therefore pushing up power prices. Will you legislate requirements for data centres to build renewable infrastructure at least equal to their energy consumption? In the meantime, will you place a moratorium on data centre approvals?

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Ryan for her question. It goes to artificial intelligence and its impact in local communities, which is something that has caused an issue around the world, it must be said. We think that there is enormous benefit to come from artificial intelligence in areas such as health care, health provision and doing analysis to make a difference. There are benefits in education and potentially benefits in productivity as well. But that doesn't mean that there are not risks which need to be mitigated, which is why I announced that we would legislate for Australian standards to make sure that artificial intelligence works in our national interests.

This was raised as well at our National Cabinet meeting, and it was agreed there that we would progress the legislation, which, because of the corporations power, the Commonwealth will have power to legislate to ensure that the suggestion that has been made that it would increase power prices, that it won't do that, and that it will need renewables. If there is surplus energy in, for example, gas, in some areas, then we would allow that to be used on the proviso that it does not put pressure on the system and therefore put pressure on the prices that ordinary Australians are paying.

Why is that important? That's important because you need social licence for these institutions, and we're working constructively to make sure that that social licence is available—is absolutely critical. We've said very clearly that we must shape AI or it will shape us. Areas such as sovereign capability, our capacity to provide for the defence and security of Australia is absolutely essential. There's the idea that we just say, 'We'll have a moratorium on new technology,' which is one option that has been put forward, I know, by the Greens political party. What I want to do is not have a moratorium. I want us to be at the forefront of shaping it in our national interest, because this is a technology that is happening. You can engage in ChatGPT, or any of these facilities right now. It is having an impact. That is why we can't afford to sit on the sidelines, because if we sit on the sidelines we won't have any impact on how this rolls out.

Next week, at the United Nations, I expect that this will be a major topic of conversation on the way. I leave tomorrow night. I leave and arrive on the same night because of the way that it works in San Francisco, for meetings to take place. I'll engage constructively, and I would encourage all of the parliament to engage with the committee chaired by the member for Maribyrnong and deputy chaired by Senator Duniam, in the other place, and engage constructively. This should not be a partisan issue. This is one which really requires the national interest to be first and foremost.

speaker: Jim Chalmers
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
They've got a lot of nerve asking about productivity assumptions, given they presided over the weakest decade for productivity growth in the last 60 years. The weakest decade for productivity growth in the last 60 years was the decade that they presided over, and their budgets weren't worth the paper they were written on, because they deliberately kept productivity assumptions at 1.5 per cent.The June quarter of 2022—the quarter that they left office—was the weakest quarter for productivity in over 40 years, so they've got a lot of nerve asking about productivity. They did nothing about productivity in their wasted decade of missed opportunities in office.

The assumption in the budget and the assumption in the Intergenerational report is set by Treasury based on all the available data here and abroad. It is a long-run assumption. It's not common to constantly change long-run assumptions. One of the first things I did as Treasurer was to get rid of the coalition's dodgy productivity assumption and make it more realistic, on the advice of the Treasury department. I accepted their advice to downgrade the long-run assumption to 1.2 per cent. As I said, they're not changed frequently. While productivity growth has been weak for the last couple of decades, there are some potential upsides, including from artificial intelligence. The productivity assumption is consistent with international forecasts. The UK uses 1½, the US uses 1.4, New Zealand uses 0.9, and we are in the middle of those assumptions. The Treasury changed the transition path from two years to five years, recognising how volatile short-term movements can be.

But, more broadly, as I said, this country has had a productivity challenge not for the last couple of years but for the last couple of decades. That's why this government, more than our predecessors over there, takes this productivity challenge seriously. We take responsibility for trying to turn it around over time, and that's why the budget had the broadest and biggest productivity agenda of any budget in recent decades. It's an agenda which is all about approvals being faster, working with the federation, foreign investment reform, all of the agenda that the Prime Minister ran through on AI and the technological revolution—all of the important ways set out in the Intergenerational report on Monday that we can try and turn this productivity performance around. But to finish where I started, of all of the people that I would take advice from on productivity, those opposite would not be anywhere near the top of the list.

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: Prime Minister, this week the leaders of the major AI developers have publicly agreed that AI is developing faster than our ability to control it. The Australian AI Safety Institute is our frontline defence against these risks to test models, support our regulators and work with international partners. We invest only $8 million a year in the institute, half of one per cent of what we invest in biosecurity. In light of growing public concern, will you commit to increasing the funding for the AI Safety Institute?

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Curtin for her question and for her interest in what is an absolutely vital issue. We do want more of a stake in where AI is made and how it is made. We want more Australian companies and global companies developing AI here, on our terms, in our interests. That is how we will have influence over these issues. As I said at Sydney university, in the speech I gave there, we want to make sure that the creativity created by our writers and our musicians is actually valued and that they have some control. If we do not participate in this process, we will not have any control. We won't have a say, which is why we have prioritised this as an issue.

We created the AI Safety Institute in November 2025, and I table the media release from Dr Andrew Charlton and Tim Ayres, 'Establishment of Australian AI Safety Institute'. That was an important organisation which is working closely with partner institutes in the UK and Canada. It's also working very closely with the Australian Signals Directorate. You would have seen the comments by Abigail from ASD this week as well, who has also warned of some of the risks which are there. This institute will provide our agencies and security experts with up-to-date information and testing to respond to emerging risks. AI safety is a whole-of-government responsibility, but that's also why we will be legislating for Australian standards on AI. All of that will be fed into the process through the committee chaired by the member for Maribyrnong, and I encourage all members to really participate in this. We want to make sure that we follow best practice.

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: The question was about increasing funding for the AI Safety Institute.

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: It's just been established. It's just been established less than one year ago. Funding decisions are made through our ERC and budget process. So we think that we want to make sure this follows best practice AI safety and security standards. We want to make sure that it works in ways that ensure Australian creators are in control of and retain ownership of their work and payment. And we want to make sure that data centres used for AI training aren't pushing up energy bills, impacting water resources or being built without meaningful community engagement.

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Hughes for his question. Indeed, global uncertainty and conflict overseas is putting Australians under real pressure, and that's why I'll always show up to shape a better future and for Australia to have a say in these forums.

Tomorrow I will travel to the United States. It will be an opportunity to talk our nation up, showing the world everything we have to offer. On Saturday I will have meetings in San Francisco, including with Tim Cook, the head of Apple, and other meetings will take place in the United States with the private sector, as well as my obviously representing Australia at the United Nations General Assembly, along with the Foreign Minister.

I'll be working with our partners as well to build on the record which has seen now 20 countries since we announced our social media ban for under-16s engage in action themselves. And of course also, as has been raised a number of times now during this question time, it is important that we have dialogue about governance arrangements with regard to artificial intelligence, making sure that we get the economic and security benefits that can come with AI but doing it in a way that protects Australia's national interests. Now, to do that, we have to be engaged with our friends in the United States, because the two big countries that are engaged, of course, are the United States and China in what is this extraordinary emerging technology that will change the way that society functions over our lifetime. But over the next decade, if we don't get this right in the next few years, it can get away from us, and we need to make sure that doesn't occur.

When Australia is overseas, we also represent our region, the Pacific family. And there will be engagement with them about issues including, of course, climate change, which is the number one issue for our Pacific family. It's also talking about the opportunities which are there, given that Australia has the resources, technology and people to drive the world's clean energy transition, including the critical minerals and rare earths that we have. I'll be discussing with our American friends the agreement that was put in place by me and President Trump and how that is progressing.

While there, I'll also launch our bid for a seat on the UN Security Council. It is vital that, as a middle power, Australia play its role. We are respected around the world. The biggest challenges that Australia faces are global ones, and that's why us having a say at the UN Security Council table is very much in Australia's national interests.

And on that note, Mr Speaker, I ask that further questions be placed on the Notice Paper.

speaker: Sue Lines
heading: COMMITTEES
subheading: Artificial Intelligence Joint Select Committee; Membership
text:
Yesterday, I informed the Senate that I had received nominations from Senator David Pocock and Senator Shoebridge seeking appointment to a single crossbench position on the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. In accordance with standing orders, a ballot will be held to determine which of the two senators is to be appointed to the committee. Before proceeding to a ballot, the bells will be rung for four minutes.

The bells having been rung—

The Senate will now proceed to a ballot. Ballot papers will be distributed to all senators, who are requested to write the name of the candidate they wish to vote for. The candidates are Senator David Pocock and Senator Shoebridge. Senator Sheldon?

speaker: David Shoebridge
heading: COMMITTEES
subheading: Artificial Intelligence Joint Select Committee; Membership
text:
Thanks to the chamber. It's a bloody outrage that the majors in this place are not letting there be two representatives from the crossbench. I know that there's probably a committee of secretaries who are desperately keen not to have more crossbenchers actually asking the questions. We can see a stitch-up when you do it. We know what you want to do. You don't want people actually testing what happens in this committee.

I've got to tell you this. Joint select committees are places where hope goes to die, so you actually do me a great favour in not sending me down onto this select committee. We've all been on them, right? Some drones and deadheads from the lower house come in and bore you to death. If anyone thinks a joint select committee on AI is how we're going to get ahead of the tidal wave of disaster that's coming, wake up and smell the roses! But, mainly, the crossbench can see a stitch-up, and we're not going to fight amongst ourselves.

speaker: David Pocock
heading: COMMITTEES
subheading: Artificial Intelligence Joint Select Committee; Membership
text: I thank the Senate for this opportunity. One of the criticisms of the AI industry is that it still remains overwhelmingly white and male, so the irony is not lost on me that the Senate is provided with an opportunity to vote between two white dudes named David. Senator David Shoebridge does outstanding work at estimates and on committees, so I think, whatever the Senate decides, there will be a crossbencher engaging in good faith on this issue, which is one of the huge challenges we face. We're facing an exponential technology that is clearly difficult to deal with for legislators and difficult to deal with as a society. I think either David will make a good contribution to this community.

speaker: Lord Harper
heading: G20 Summit 2027: Objectives - Question
text: My Lords, I got the message from the Minister that she is not able to tell us what is going to be on the Government’s list on priorities, so can I just make a suggestion? All I am asking is that she will at least say she will go away and consider it. Given the leadership we have demonstrated since 2023 on artificial intelligence, and the global respect for the AI Security Institute, this would be a great opportunity for the UK to show international leadership on regulating AI globally. I urge the Minister to think about that as we put our policy objectives together.

speaker: Lord Whitty
heading: Education and Skills Reform - Statement
text: My Lords, while I welcome many of the aspects of this Statement and much of what my noble friend the Minister said, I still feel that it lacks an overall strategy in relation to future changes of demands on the employment and skills markets. In particular, will the Government produce a strategy which is central to their economic policy and deals with the impact that AI will have on the employment and skills requirements in the medium term? One does not have to be a total pessimist and say that AI is going to destroy millions of jobs, but it will change millions of them dramatically, not least entry-level jobs. Will there be a strategy from the department for dealing with AI and its impact on the needs of our education and skills system?

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Education and Skills Reform - Statement
text: It is precisely in order to equip children to respond to the changing needs in the labour market that we are making some of these changes, but those build, of course, on the introduction by this Government of Skills England. I hope that my noble friend will have seen some of the important work that Skills England has done on the way in which AI skills will be necessary for the future workforce, and how they are likely to change the nature of the skills that young people and, in fact, adults need. The Government have responded to that through additional skills training to support not just young people but people throughout their lives to develop those AI skills. I agree that this is a wide-ranging challenge to both the labour market and our education system and that more work needs to be done, but we have certainly made an important start.

speaker: Lord Brooke of Alverthorpe
heading: Prison and Probation Service - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I congratulate the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, on securing this debate and I am grateful for how he opened it. I thought he was going to be a little more critical and, in turn, I have written a counter speech. I want to speak primarily about rehabilitation, which he mainly focused on. As he said, one of the big influencing factors has been 30 years of sentence inflation, with more and more, and longer and longer, sentences being handed out. I too look forward to the maiden speech of the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, with great interest in what he may say on this.

There have been 30 years of underinvestment, by all Governments, in the courts, prisons, the probation services and of course rehabilitation, which has been the Cinderella right at the end of the line. However, services have been particularly hollowed out since 2010, when George Osborne’s austerity programme was introduced. Then there was the calamitous, I believe, social experiment of the part-privatisation of the probation service by the Conservative Government, as well as a failure to build new prison places—we are still waiting for new ones to come on stream, as has just been mentioned.

In 2024, Labour inherited a demoralised and understaffed workforce, with prisons almost full to capacity. We were almost at a point where, without radical action, the country faced the prospect that courts would not be able to send criminals to jail, because there were no places to incarcerate them. I am glad to say that we have not shied away from that challenge. I congratulate all those who have been involved in trying to right the wrongs, especially the now departed Prisons Minister, my noble friend Lord Timpson; he did outstanding work, which was recognised across the whole Chamber. He did it with enthusiasm and endeavoured—this particularly appealed to the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, and me—to re-energise the work on rehabilitation of prisoners, especially those with addiction problems relating to drugs, alcohol or the recent growth in problem gambling, on which the noble Lord, Lord Foster of Bath, has done such valiant work. I am sure that we will hear more on that from him today.

My noble friend Lord Timpson also recruited Professor Dame Carol Black. She was brought in, with her particular expertise, to assist with these long-standing addiction problems and with rehabilitation. The rehabilitation of offenders whose crimes are driven by drug or alcohol addiction is a crucial part of any strategy to reduce reoffending. Currently, services are still not fit for purpose. For example, half of all people on probation have a drug or alcohol problem, and over half of those arriving in prison are assessed as needing drug or alcohol treatment. Intensive drug or alcohol rehabilitation programmes in prisons were delivered to 11,000 people in 2012. We do not keep the figures now on what is being done, but the guess is that is in the order of as low as 2,000 a year—that is a terrible fall-away.

The Sentencing Act envisages increased early release, or community sentences instead of short periods of imprisonment, for offenders addicted to drugs or alcohol, but there are no plans to ensure that these people get adequate treatment. If their addictions are not treated, we will see high rates of reoffending and licence breaches. Dame Carol will be giving an update on progress in her report entitled From Hope to Delivery: Drug and Alcohol Treatment Under a New Government. She will be doing this in Committee Room 5 on Wednesday, 14 October. I hope that many of us present today, and others, will be there to hear about the work she has been done to try to address, in particular, addiction issues linked to rehabilitation so that we can then, in turn, look forward to a more detailed programme of action on rehabilitation and recovery. I would be grateful if the Minister could give us an indication of how the Government are likely to respond to the report that will be coming from Dame Carol.

I am also involved in some rehabilitation work being trialled shortly in a Kent addiction recovery centre that welcomes prisoners in its numbers. We are endeavouring to develop an AI companion linked to the 12-step recovery programme—I assure noble Lords that it will be entirely safe—so that prisoners there will be given a companion 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 52 weeks a year, if they are in need of someone to give them advice that has been based on the 12-step programme. We have managed to interest Stanford University in the USA in this, and we are hoping that King’s in London will also be associated, to validate a doctoral research project that is being set up alongside it.

We also have enthusiastic support from the charity Forward Trust, which I am sure the Minister will know does valuable work in recovery and rehabilitation within, and for those leaving, prisons. We see this project as having considerable potential in assisting with rehabilitation. I wonder therefore whether the Minister can give an indication of whether, if we get this off the ground, there may be a possibility to trial it in prison. It has great prospects of meeting some of the many deficiencies we currently have from not having the numbers around to help people with rehabilitation.

speaker: Lord Lemos
heading: Prison and Probation Service - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I begin by thanking the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, for securing this important debate and all noble Lords who have contributed this afternoon to what has been a sober but very humane debate. Noble Lords will know that not every debate about prisons has those characteristics, so I very much appreciate that.

For many years, the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, has brought sustained attention to the purpose of imprisonment and to the vital role that families and strong, stable relationships can play in rehabilitation. We are very grateful to him. I declare my own interest: I was the lead non-executive director of HMPPS until 2025. I chaired its agency board and had the pleasure and the privilege of meeting the noble Lord and talking with him, particularly about the work my then colleagues at HMPPS were doing on the relational model, which he was a champion of and is at the heart of what we are all discussing.

I congratulate the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, on a magnificent maiden speech. I am proud to say that I have read both parts of the noble and learned Lord’s court review, twice. He looks shocked, but I have, and I look forward to working with him very closely, as does everyone at the Ministry of Justice.

I will start with the most immediate pressure on prison capacity. I take the challenge from the noble and learned Lord, Lord Garnier, not to indulge in the blame game very seriously, and I will try not to. I will also try not to recite lots of things other people have said before and that your Lordships already know. I am all too conscious that I alone stand between noble Lords and Recess, so I shall be concise but thorough.

On all these comments about prison capacity, I am not, as I say, going to indulge in the blame game. In two regards, the comments many noble Lords have made highlight the heart of this problem and the theme we will return to again and again. The noble and learned Lord, Lord Thomas, and the noble and learned Baroness, Lady Butler-Sloss, mentioned the great increase in sentence length. This is at the heart of the long-running difficulty with prison capacity. Noble Lords do not need me to tell them that, in the context of a prison capacity crisis, many if not all the things noble Lords have said they value in prisons—such as education, regime, healthcare and rehabilitation—are the first to suffer in overcrowded prisons with overstretched staff. So, we have to get the capacity crisis under control.

I am not going to bandy figures around, but we are providing 14,000 additional prison places and we will continue to make a commitment to prison building. On that, I just say to the noble Lord, Lord Marks, that we are not suggesting that the prison numbers will come down or that the prison building programme may, in the end, not prove adequate. We recognise that this is an ongoing thing and will go on for a very long time, perhaps even for a decade. I entirely agree with the comment by the noble Lord, Lord Marks, that we cannot build our way out of this capacity challenge, though build we must.

On sentencing, measures already in force include the presumption to suspend prison sentences of 12 months or less. The noble Lord, Lord Farmer, talked about short sentences, and those are subject to important exceptions. Our view is that short spells in custody disrupt housing arrangements, employment and drug treatment. They are not good for mental health and, crucially, as the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, said, the family ties that are at the heart of preventing further offending.

Where offenders can be punished and managed safely in the community—I do not apologise for the use of the word “punishment”—we should use that opportunity to both supervise them effectively and tackle the underlying causes of their offending, reserving prisons for those who most need to be there and from whom the public need to be protected. Over the coming months, we will implement the progression model that was at the heart of David Gauke's recommendations and at the heart of the Sentencing Act. I have had the opportunity to discuss that with many noble Lords before today. This is almost the most important building block to a changed landscape for prisons.

I make this offer to noble Lords in the spirit of my noble friend Lord Timpson; noble Lords can consider me a sort of polyester version of my noble friend. We need to make sure that the whole approach of the Sentencing Act—a third in custody, a third under intensive supervision—is understood much better by the public, as the noble Lord, Lord Marks, and others have said. I would be very happy to arrange a presentation from our officials on exactly how this is going to work and how we are preparing for it.

It means a tougher probation service. I was very mindful of the comments made by the noble Baroness, Lady Sater, who I am working with on youth custody, as well. We are asking the Probation Service to do something really quite difficult, as the noble Lord, Lord Marks, made clear. We are asking it to improve itself after a long history of troubles that started with the failed privatisation, and to take on many new responsibilities under the intensive supervision model. We know that is challenging.

I have talked about the money. The noble Lord, Lord Marks, has asked me again about contingency planning. The question of government funding and the need for more funding is something we talk about all the time in the Ministry of Justice, as noble Lords can imagine. We will approach the spending review in the usual optimistic spirit.

I want to recognise, finally, on this question of the progression model, that we listened to some of the concerns of victims and their families about the changes. As noble Lords know, we changed some of the exemptions, but we recognise that changing release arrangements can cause victims and their families a great deal of uncertainty and distress. That is why stronger supervision and support for victims are so important in the Government’s approach.

I now turn to prison safety and security, which a number of noble Lords have mentioned. Prisons must be places of safety, security and order, where staff can do their jobs, prisoners can engage in a constructive regime—particularly in education and training for employment—and genuine rehabilitation can take place. As I have said, all this is made much more difficult by serious overcrowding, overstretched staff and inadequate facilities. Drugs, illicit mobile phones and drones fuel violence, criminal activity, debt and intimidation; they undermine staff authority and make turning lives around substantially harder.

At the heart of what we need to do is ensuring effective security. It is essential. That is why we are investing in both the fabric and the security of our prisons, including an additional £35 million this financial year—we get some money out of the Treasury—to strengthen counter-drone security in prisons where there is the greatest threat. We are also working closely with law enforcement partners to disrupt those bringing drugs, weapons and other contraband into prisons.

Our prison officers perform a demanding public service and I take my hat off to them. They need the confidence, training and support to maintain order and build the constructive relationships that help offenders turn their backs on crime for good.

In response to the noble Lord, Lord Reay, as of June this year, prison officer staffing stood at 92% of our target level and prison officer resignation rates are at their lowest in five years. It is obviously a difficult labour market, as the noble Lord, Lord Foster, highlighted. Many pressures remain, particularly in hard-to-staff prisons, but we have made an enormous effort—going back to my days in HMPPS—on recruitment, as I am sure the noble Lord, Lord Foster, would recognise.

Many noble Lords have highlighted that a safe prison must also be a purposeful one. Most people who enter prison, as the noble and learned Lord, Lord Thomas, highlighted, will eventually return to the community. This is a simple statement of fact that is too readily ignored. Nearly 80% of offenders are reoffenders and therefore we have a responsibility to use the time spent in custody as effectively as we can, as many noble Lords have emphasised. Our approach is to help individuals develop skills and secure employment and stable accommodation, and to provide access to treatment for substance misuse and mental health needs.

In response to the noble Lord, Lord Brooke, we meet regularly with Dame Carol Black and are working with her on the findings of her report. My colleagues and I would be very happy to meet the noble Lord and his colleagues to discuss the AI tool he was describing. All these efforts in health care and accommodation go to the heart of the proposition of the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, that through all these things we are trying to maintain positive relationships. That is a good and humane thing to do, regardless of anything else: it is a good in itself. Effective rehabilitation nevertheless sits alongside punishment and robust supervision as an essential part of protecting the public. Every offence prevented means one fewer victim.

I recognise the comments made by my noble friend Lord Winston, which were utterly compelling, about the effect on the brain. I have seen research along those lines, and this is a very important area for us to develop. The noble Lord, Lord Foster, will know that we have discussed previously the whole question of gambling and gambling addiction. My noble friend Lord Timpson made some progress on that, and I hope we can continue that. I have no doubt that I will have many opportunities to discuss that with the noble Lord, Lord Foster.

Purposeful activity can have a transformative effect. We are expanding vocational training and apprenticeships and improving links with employers and access to education. Our track record on getting prisoners into jobs when they leave has improved. My noble friend Lord Timpson put a great deal of emphasis on that. We are seeing progress. The proportion of prison leavers in employment six months after release increased to 36.5% in the year to March 2026. We know we have a long way to go, but we are making some progress.

I turn to the question of family and other relationships, which the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, described as the golden thread. The evidence bears this out. Research shows that prisoners who received visits were three percentage points less likely to reoffend within one year of release. But as I have said, I regard that as a good thing in itself, whatever the statistics are telling us. I am delighted that they confirm my view. The prison gates should not be a cliff edge, for all the reasons I have set out. Prisons, probation, local authorities, health services and employment support must work as one system. Of course, there are many difficulties and that is why, alongside MHCLG, we have committed to halve the proportion of prison leavers released to no fixed abode and to increase the proportion in settled accommodation by the end of this Parliament.

I want to say a few words about probation. I thank probation staff for the vital work they do every day to protect the public and support rehabilitation. It is easy to be critical, but we also need to recognise their efforts and their achievements. They have been asked to carry too much for too long. We are responding with the investment that a number of noble Lords have referred to. We have already recruited 2,300 new probation officers over the past year and are recruiting at least 1,300 more in 2026-27. We are rebuilding the service and asking it to take on new responsibilities. Probation officers will have more on their plate, as the noble Baroness, Lady Sater, said. There is much to be learned from the experience in youth custody—I entirely agree with her about that.

Moving part of a sentence from custody into the community, as we are, does not mean the end of punishment. We are giving probation the toughest range of tools ever to manage offenders, including tough licence conditions, electronic tagging on a scale never seen before, curfews, restriction zones, and recall to prison where those conditions are breached. The noble and learned Lord, Lord Bellamy, spoke about recalls, and I answered a question yesterday from the noble and learned Lord, Lord Garnier, on IPPs and recalls. I am very happy to take that away and get back to the noble and learned Lord and everyone who has spoken in this debate about exactly what we are doing to address that trend.

One of the things we are already aware of is that, once someone has been recalled, the time taken to get to a parole decision before they can be released is something we need to address. But I do not at all demur from the general challenge, and I will return to it. Again, as I have said about this progression model, my officials will be very happy to arrange a session on the changes to probation so that noble Lords can feel more confident, at least, of the steps we are taking to build a Probation Service for the future.

I will say something about women offenders and female offenders, as raised by the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, and the noble and learned Baroness, Lady Butler-Sloss. Female offenders often have distinct and complex needs. Many are victims themselves, with histories of trauma, abuse, mental health and addiction, and many are mothers. That is why our long-term aim is to reduce the number of women in prison and, in particular, pregnant women and mothers of young children. That is a particular commitment of ours, to which we shall be addressing ourselves with energy. We have announced—this refers to what the noble and learned Baroness, Lady Butler-Sloss, was talking about—the expansion of intensive supervision courts for women, which will use a multi-agency approach to address the root causes of offending. This is an important development, which we shall watch very carefully to see if it may help in other areas too. We are also investing in voluntary and community sector provision to help prevent offending and divert women away from the criminal justice system in the first place. The Sentencing Act’s presumption to suspend sentences is expected to reduce the number of women entering prison by about a third. However, custody will, of course, remain necessary when the seriousness of the offence or the protection of the public requires it.

The noble and learned Lord, Lord Garnier, and one or two other noble Lords mentioned the Government’s decision on IPPs. I am very proud of that. We are continuing the regular meetings with interested Peers. Indeed, the Lord Chancellor himself is attending the next one—the noble and learned Lord, Lord Garnier, looks very impressed. The independent review of the prison system, chaired by Amber Rudd, will examine the long-term reforms needed to build a prison system fit for the future, as the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, has challenged us to do. She will report later this year, and I and my ministerial colleagues will be working closely with her on that.

We must protect the public, and we must stand with victims. Serious offenders must be punished appropriately. Those released into the community must be robustly supervised, and we must reduce the likelihood of further offending. If we succeed in this, that will mean fewer crimes and fewer victims. I note the comments noble Lords have made on foreign national offenders and on remand. This is all part of the approach we need for getting prison numbers to a more sustainable future.

I hope I have addressed the principal points raised, but I will read Hansard with my officials carefully and write on points I have failed to address. I will say this: in my short time in this job, and indeed before, I have worked with many noble Lords in this House on these issues. I regard this as a collaborative, cross-party venture—I was going to say adventure; it is certainly a venture. I know noble Lords from across the House are working with us on IPPs, but I hope we can continue to work together more widely.

In closing, I reiterate my thanks to the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, for tabling this Motion and giving us the opportunity to have this debate. None of the problems that noble Lords have highlighted should prevent us paying tribute to those who work tirelessly across our Prison and Probation Service. They undertake, as the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, noted, difficult and demanding work on behalf of us all. I wish noble Lords a very good Recess. I hope you do not go to too many conferences, but before that the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, will respond.

speaker: Claire Clutterham
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
Artificial intelligence and efficient and effective regulation can coexist. Government and industry can collaborate with respect to AI for the benefit of the Australian people. The private sector and public sector can realise a shared vision and goals when it comes to artificial intelligence. But all of this takes leadership underpinned by three critical things: decisiveness, targeted stakeholder consultation and expertise.

That is the approach this government is taking with respect to AI. By bringing government and industry together to develop policy solutions, it's possible to harness the opportunities, reduce the known risks and plan for future ones. Partnerships of this nature mean there's no need to choose between letting innovation grow and flourish without controls or regulating to paralyse development. Regulation or innovation is a false choice. Both are important, with regulation needing to safely facilitate innovation, creativity, competition and entrepreneurship, not paralyse them.

Another false choice is deciding now whether AI will be an existential threat to the human race and then regulating on the basis of that choice. This is lazy, populist, apocalyptic thinking that helps no-one, creates unnecessary fear and discourages populations from embracing opportunity. It also paints industry as the bad guys when, in actual fact, it is industry that has the technology we want and that the Australian people expect we will have.

Most reasonable Australians will also accept that accessing and using artificial intelligence does require a level of regulation. It does not mean more government or bigger government for the sake of it. It means targeted government action informed by public sector and private sector industrial expertise, so that relevant issues like urban and regional planning, energy and water use, economic development, workforce planning, education, service delivery, organisational accountability and community confidence can be confidently and expertly managed. This is to make sure that once a particular aspect of artificial intelligence really gets going, we have the understanding and means to intervene—not to paralyse it but to manage it in the event that unintended consequences begin to play out.

First and foremost, regulation with respect to artificial intelligence must have two key objectives. Regulation must both reduce harm and promote timely access to evidence based technological resources that benefit people. Achieving these two objectives requires consideration of different criteria.

Firstly, regulation must be proportionately incremental, integrating lessons learned from measurable data at each step along the technology's development. It must also recognise and reflect that there are different regulatory layers and address them in a tailored way. Regulating the AI infrastructure layer, the AI frontier layer and then the AI application layer will require different approaches, and some layers may require less regulation than others.

Regulation must also reflect and speak to existing public policy frameworks such as competition, industrial relations and energy. And, in this sense, it must be developed in a way which does not impose disproportionate or new and excessive compliance and reporting burdens on industry. It must be developed in a way that is proportionate to the actual risk and the actual evidence based opportunity. It should be designed in the way that the technology should be—with gateways, so a single regulatory action does not lead to an irreversible outcome or cause unnecessary paralysis. Finally, regulation must encourage trust and confidence between government and industry because it's only through effective and efficient partnerships between government and industry that we will be able to build the foundations upon which the benefits can be safely harnessed and the risks minimised.

We are already seeing a divergence of regulatory approaches across the globe. The EU is proceeding by prioritising rights based safeguards, the US is prioritising innovation and China is prioritising strategic control. But global collaboration is crucial. International interoperability is crucial to ensure that regulation is not only compatible but fair, allowing all nations the opportunity to harness the benefits of artificial intelligence. That is the challenge before us and that is what the Prime Minister was calling for in Australia's national statement at the UN last month. That call was urgent and that call was right.

speaker: Pat Conaghan
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
text:
I move:

That this House:

(1) notes that despite the Government increasing the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) workforce by more than 5,700 public servants since the 2022 election, participant complaints, funding disputes, fraud investigations and demands on parliamentary electorate offices continue to grow;

(2) further notes with concern, the increasing seriousness and urgency of matters being raised, including cases involving loss of essential supports, participant safety, housing insecurity, hospital discharge delays and risks to health and wellbeing;

(3) expresses concern that administrative failures within the NDIA are placing an increasing burden on carers, providers, support workers and electorate offices, to resolve participant matters that should be addressed promptly by the NDIA; and

(4) calls on the Government to:

(a) urgently reduce the backlog of reviews, reassessments and participant decisions;

(b) prioritise participant-facing service and decision-making roles over administrative growth;

(c) reduce waste, inefficiency and unnecessary bureaucracy within the NDIA;

(d) strengthen accountability, timeliness and transparency in decision-making; and

(e) ensure that investment in staffing, technology and artificial intelligence delivers better and more timely outcomes for participants rather than greater administrative burden.

On this side of the floor, we know that bigger government doesn't necessarily mean better outcomes, and nowhere is this more obvious and evident than in the National Disability Insurance Agency.

I understand the logic here. You think putting more staff means more hands on deck, which should mean that those decks are cleared more swiftly and more effectively, but anyone working in an electorate office right now—it's a job that I would not like to do. It's a very difficult job, but we've got great people doing it. Anyone in an electorate office right now will tell you that they have never received more urgent and justifiable pleas for assistance from their constituents than they have in the past few months. Electorate staff have increasingly become an emergency escalation point at levels that they have not experienced before, particularly in regional seats like mine in Cowper. You've got to ask how that can be.

The NDIA has more than doubled its public service workforce since 2022, from just over 5,000 to a whopping 11,052. They've doubled it. They're now working on the federal scheme at a federal level, and they should be clearing it at twice the rate. This isn't just anecdotal feedback. You only have to look at the complaints lodged over a three-year period to see the outcome erosion in black and white.

As of 30 June 2024, around 71 per cent of requests undertaken that year were completed within 60 days. Seventy-one percent—that's not too bad. But that number fell to 54 per cent in June 2025 and then fell to just 30 per cent by 20 December 2025—30 per cent! It's a disgrace, considering that the workforce has doubled. These stats are taken from the government's own performance dashboard, and we need to remember these aren't just numbers on a page or a screen. These are people in need waiting for months and months and months for care, desperate care and, in many cases, people who have previously received care and have been unceremoniously cut off. We've all had examples of that.

Again, you just need to look at the government's own reports to validate this. The latest report shows a clear split between simpler front-end decisions and more complex matters for existing participants. Only 48 per cent of internal reviews were completed within 60 days, and only 32 per cent of participant requested assessments and 44 per cent of scheduled reassessments were completed on time. With the further impending changes to the scheme, this situation is only going to get worse. Foundational supports are capped at $10 billion over five years, jointly funded by the Commonwealths and states. Thriving Kids accounts for $4 billion of that amount, but not all states have signed up to the Thriving Kids, leaving implementation gaps.

Continued poor transition and implementation rollouts like these—we've seen service restrictions and closures and workforce losses and gaps in support, particularly in regional communities. This issue has to be addressed. Today, I'm calling on the government to publish the size and age-of-review reassessment and decision backlogs, show how many additional staff are participating in face-to-face roles and what results and efficiencies they have delivered, provide transparency over service standards for decisions, reviews and complaints, and report performance publicly. The government has doubled the NDIA workforce and is now reshaping how billions of dollars in disability support are delivered, but the results for participants most in need are already speaking for themselves. The government are failing on the NDIS, and they need to do better.

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
text:
We cannot trust OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies to regulate themselves, and we can't trust the US government to do it either. This is my clear takeaway from the first week of hearings in the newly established Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. OpenAI's breaches of Australian government websites and the Hugging Face hack have shown the level of risk and the insufficiency of internal safeguards within these companies. Australia cannot manage all of the risks, but we can take meaningful steps to improve our chances of making AI a positive force, rather than a dystopian one.

For me, three no-brainers came out of the first week of hearings. The first is increasing investment in the Australian AI Safety Institute so we have a credible and useful voice in international standard setting and can futureproof our own regulations. The second is requiring AI companies to monitor and report key incidents so we know when something goes wrong, rather than waiting months for the companies to decide to tell us. The third is requiring screening of imported nucleic acid sequences to reduce the threat of a terrorist using AI to produce a new virus or pandemic. More will come out of this committee, but the government needs to move quickly to keep up with the escalating risks. These three actions are no-brainers, Prime Minister; it's time to act.

speaker: Mary Doyle
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
text:
I will now read a speech from a girl in my community of Aston as part of the Raise Our Voice competition. Sanvi was the winner of this competition. It reads:

Dear Parliament, my name is Sanvi and I'm a 16 year old student from Melbourne.

I am writing to express my concern about an issue shaping my generation's future, the rapid development of artificial intelligence.

AI has enormous potential to improve education, healthcare and the way we work, so I don't believe the answer is to simply restrict it.

Instead, Parliament should invest in AI education and establish clear guidelines for its responsible use, particularly in schools.

Young people should be taught how to use AI as a resource while still developing independent thinking, creativity and digital literacy.

AI will most likely become a major part of our lives, and we have an opportunity to use it to our advantage. But we also need to ask, what happens if AI changes the jobs we are preparing for?

If technology can do more of what we are learning, how do we ensure our education remains meaningful?

We cannot stop AI from developing, but we can prepare ourselves for it.

I urge Parliament to invest in comprehensive AI education and introduce clear, practical guidelines for its responsible use in schools, ensuring my generation is prepared to work alongside AI and shape the future it creates.

Those are the words of 16-year-old Sanvi from Aston, and I congratulate her.

speaker: Garth Hamilton
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
subheading: Mort's Mates Gala Fundraising Dinner 2026, Young Australians, Groom Electorate: Artificial Intelligence
text:
A quick shout-out to Charlie Moreton and the iconic brand of Moreton & Co. for the Mort's Mates fundraiser we held in our region. It's a great night out, the third iteration of it. They raised money for the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health, which is a brain research centre that particularly focuses on the impacts on mental health. I think it's such an important and crucial conversation we're having. Thank you very much, Charlie, Merida and the team.

What do you want to change about Australia? It's a question that I ask everywhere I go when I knock on doors throughout my electorate. What heartens me is when I speak to the older generation. What they say is they want a better future for the younger generations. They want there to be structural advantages for being Australians. That's why I'm here, and I think we can bring about that change that Australia needs.

I want to raise my concerns and the concerns of many people that I've met doorknocking around not just the AI data centre that's being proposed for Dalby but the actual impact of AI on our community. These are genuine concerns from people in my electorate. Firstly, on AI, we've seen blue-collar jobs stripped from our regions and I just want to raise their voice. I'm concerned that if we aren't in control of this change we'll see white-collar jobs stripped from our region. I'm all for good jobs and good pay, and these are genuine concerns of people in my electorate. Speaking with regard to the data centre itself, whilst there are concerns around water, it's a 2.1-gigawatt data centre. If you want to give me 2.1 gigawatts of extra data, I think I'd probably spend it on something more useful.

speaker: Tom French
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
text:
There's a quote attributed to Walter Isaacson that I've been thinking about. He wrote:

The technology that promised to connect us found a better business model in dividing us.

I reckon that captures one of the biggest problems facing our society. Social media was supposed to bring people together. Instead the business model rewards outrage, anger and division because keeping people angry keeps them engaged and keeping them engaged makes money. Now we're watching artificial intelligence accelerate this problem. Content can be produced almost instantly, fake news sites imitate genuine journalism, and the distinction between reporting and manufactured content is becoming difficult to identify. Meanwhile, local newspapers have been disappearing. The journalists who attended council meetings, reported on local businesses and held decision-makers accountable have increasingly been replaced by algorithms.

That's why it's encouraging to see local publications, like the North Coast Post in my electorate, serving communities like Moore, because journalism isn't just about producing words on a screen. It's about having someone who knows their community, asks difficult questions and takes responsibility for what they publish. Technology should serve the public, but, when the companies that control the technology make more money from dividing us than informing us, we've got a serious problem. We need a digital economy that rewards reliable information, not manufactured outrage. And we need to make sure artificial intelligence strengthens Australian communities rather than further undermining the institutions they depend on.

speaker: Ash Ambihaipahar
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: My question is to the Prime Minister. How is the Albanese Labor government making sure artificial intelligence works in Australia's interest, and why is this agenda so important?

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Barton for her question. Indeed, AI offers extraordinary opportunities for Australia, for our growth, for investment, for productivity and for businesses such as those I'll speak with tonight at the Australian Industry Group about using AI to benefit their productivity and therefore to be able to grow. Our government knows that, and that's why we're legislating Australian standards for AI. That's why we're also consulting across the board, engaging seriously with other nations as well as with AI companies themselves, so we can make sure that AI stands for Australia's interests, harnessing its power as a tool to help us build a stronger economy.

We know that we need humanity to shape AI rather than the other way around. That is why we've established the AI committee that has been stood-up in a bipartisan fashion and has already begun its work under the leadership of the member for Maribyrnong and Senator Duniam in the other place. The hack by a frontier AI agent into government websites brought home to Australians that some of the risks which are there are very real indeed. We took strong action on that and made our nation's view clear that the breach was completely unacceptable.

It is clear for everyone to see that the AI genie is well and truly out of the bottle. We can't pretend that it doesn't exist and isn't already having an impact on the way that we work, the way that we engage and, indeed, the way that politics is conducted as well. That is why what really matters is how we respond to it and how we intervene and shape it. That is also why we are engaging with domestic and global companies and with other nations as well. We did that at the United Nations General Assembly last month. We did that as well in the meetings that we have continued to hold with major companies. We're going to make sure that Australia can gain from the benefits that can come from AI whilst mitigating the risks. That is the way forward, that is what is in Australia's national interest, and that is what we will continue to do. I encourage every member of this House to engage with this process because this will be one of the dominant issues over the next decade and beyond.

speaker: Jo Briskey
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: My question is to the Minister for Communications. How is the Albanese Labor government working to protect Australians from online harms? Why is it particularly important to protect young people from the harm on social media, online games and AI chatbots?

speaker: Anika Wells
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Maribyrnong for her question and for her lifelong commitment to better understanding and to combating the psychological harm that Australian children face each and every day. Mr Speaker, may I add my congratulations to you. Almost two years ago today, parliament came together and voted to give Australian kids a break from the pervasive pool of social media. We called out the harmful and addictive design features that were being used against them—targeted algorithms, doomscrolling, persistent notifications and toxic popularity metres that were stealing their attention for hours every day. I've heard from parents all over Australia who are so relieved that we have delayed access to social media until the age of 16, but they are understandably still worried about how they can protect their kids on other platforms like online games and like AI chatbots.

Parents are calling on the parliament to do more, and they're not alone. Experts and advocates are urging parliament to come together and take the next step in protecting young Australians from online harm by legislating a digital duty of care. A recent report by the National Mental Health Commission found it is not just content but platform design features that are linked to harm. The commission called for greater responsibility on tech providers to create safer digital environments. Headspace welcomed the proposed digital duty of care because the weight of trying to avoid online harms should not just sit with the young person or their family. The digital duty of care recognises that the responsibility should sit with the platforms. The Butterfly Foundation has backed the proposed digital duty of care because online content is an increasingly significant driver of harm for Australians experiencing eating disorders.

Last week, the Alannah & Madeline Foundation wrote to every member of parliament, calling on us all to support the digital duty of care. The foundation did a survey of primary school students across Australia. They were asked: what should the internet be like? Their answers included: 'safe', 'trustworthy', 'truthful', 'respect', 'learning', 'social interaction', 'integrity' and 'responsibility. I think if a few hundred primary school students can work it out, the adults in this place can too. Online safety should not be a political issue. All sides of parliament need to work together to deliver a digital duty of care. There is no reason why we can't work together to get this done.

speaker: Raff Ciccone
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: My positive question is to the minister representing the Prime Minister, Senator Wong. Last month, the minister joined the Prime Minister as he led Australia's delegation to the United Nations, where Australia launched its bid for a seat at the UN Security Council for the year 2029-30. The Albanese Labor government has also showed global leadership when it comes to AI and digital security and safety, bringing together world leaders to shape the future of this technology. Minister, how does the government's approach to international engagement make Australia safer and more secure in an increasingly contested world?

speaker: Penny Ying Yen Wong
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
And we congratulate the Speaker too—absolutely. He did a great job. Thanks to Senator Ciccone, who understands very well, from the work that he does in chairing the senate committee, the circumstances that we live in. In a time of global uncertainty, it is a fact that Australia's peace and security rely on working with others, playing our part to shape the kind of world Australians want to see. We take the world as it is and seek to shape it for the better, and we do this best by working with international partners. That is the approach we took at the UN last month, and it's why the Prime Minister launched our campaign for a seat on the UN Security Council for 2029-30—to give Australians a stronger say in the decisions that affect us and our region. Our priority is to work to prevent conflict, uphold the rules to protect us all and promote peaceful, resilient digital futures.

Australia is an active and ambitious middle power, and we've seen Australian leadership on digital safety and on AI regulation being adopted around the world. Prime Minister Albanese introduced our world-leading under-16 social media ban and led the way again with the digital-duty-of-care announcement. At the United Nations, the Prime Minister joined with more than 20 world leaders to support control over frontier AI models. I was pleased to co-chair the inaugural meeting of signatories of the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel with the Deputy Prime Minister of Jordan. One year after its launch, in honour of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, we achieved historic support from more than two-thirds of the United Nations, and 132 countries are now signed on to support our efforts to drive safer conditions for aid workers. Australia listens with respect, partners as equals and protects what matters most.

speaker: Anne Ruston
heading: BILLS
subheading: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise to speak to the Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026. We acknowledge that this bill establishes a permanent Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander aged-care commissioner and the bill also makes a long list of repairs to Labor's new Aged Care Act. And since the bill's introduction, it has been amended to establish a new escalation pathway for decisions regarding Labor's algorithm, which it so often gets wrong. Disappointingly, this amendment that's been put forward does not fix the flawed tool itself. Together, this bill tells you a great deal about the state of aged care in this country.

First—the commissioner. This bill gives effect to a key recommendation of the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety, a royal commission established by the coalition. The royal commission said that this role should be in place by 1 July 2023. However, it's taken this government four years to even bring this particular issue to the parliament, so it's important that the government is held to account on making sure that it meets the commitments that it makes. A new title on the door by itself does not shorten a single wait.

Second—the repairs. Much of this bill is machinery. A large part of it writes into law interim arrangements the government had already put into place using Henry VIII powers. Those are the powers that let a minister change the effect of an act by regulation without coming back to the parliament. The government leaned on them just to keep its new system running. Those powers are due to sunset this month, so the government is here, asking the parliament to make its emergency arrangements permanent before the clock runs out.

On top of that, there are 13 technical amendments—contributions, means assessments, refundable deposits, payment methods, reviews and overpayments. Some are welcome. Clearer obligations on providers to refund fees that were overcharged and stronger powers for the regulator to deal with unreasonable prices are sensible protections for older Australians, and we absolutely support them. But this is a clean-up, not a cure. In three weeks, Labor's new Aged Care Act turns one. It is a reform this government promised would make aged care simpler, fairer and more responsive, and, within months, ministers needed emergency powers just to keep the act working. This is not the mark of a system that was ready when it first began; it's the mark of reform that was rushed.

That brings me to the third and most revealing part of the bill. For months, the government told this Senate, assessors and older Australians that a trained human was involved in every step of the assessment process. That was not true. Documents released under freedom of information show the department's own staff regarded human override as a settled position, and then it was removed from the top down, with officials learning of it three days before the tool went live. Now, nearly a year later, the government has added schedule 4 to this bill, an escalation pathway for what it calls exceptional cases. Let me be clear about what this pathway actually is. An assessor who knows the algorithm has got it wrong cannot fix it. They must get the older person's consent within seven days and they must refer the case to the department of health and aged care in Canberra, and the criteria for who even qualifies will be set out in the rules the government has not actually yet written. Schedule 4 does not put a human back in charge; it gives the computer a supervisor in Canberra.

The Senate has already passed the fix for this problem. On 2 July, this chamber passed the coalition's Aged Care Amendment (Restoring Human Override for Aged Care Needs Assessments) Bill 2026 with the support of the Australian Greens and the crossbench. It would let a qualified assessor override the algorithm on the spot, require decisions to explain how the tool was used and give every older Australian assessed since it began the right to a reassessment. In the other place, Labor used its numbers to vote down urgent consideration of it—that is, they wouldn't even let this urgent issue be debated. They simply said no and refused any further conversation. The government should remember the words of one of its own senior ministers:

… in every case there needs to be human oversight of any use of AI. We don't just hand over decision-making to abstract computer programs …

Those were the words of Minister Plibersek in the House of Representatives on 27 May. Labor set the standard. Labor did not meet it in aged care.

When the committee examined the bill, the sector told us it had lost confidence in the tool because it produced strange outcomes that were causing harm. Advocates told us the existing reconsideration process can take more than 90 days, and still the department would not accept the tool is flawed. No algorithm has ever grown old, and no older Australians should be reduced to a score generated by a computer.

While this bill tidies up some paperwork, it does nothing for older Australians who are waiting and waiting and waiting. According to the department's last report, last financial year, more than 325,000 older Australians spent time in the home-care queue. In Labor's first full year in office, it was 199,000. And last financial year, 6,436 of them died while they were waiting for care. That's more than 17 people every single day dying while waiting in a queue for aged care. That's up 93 per cent on Labor's first full year in office. Think about that. It's someone's mother or someone's husband, someone who has already been told that they need care, and this government only handed over those figures after failing to comply with two orders of this Senate.

For those who do get a package, providers tell us that many are placed on a minimum-service offering—a convenient way of just saying that they haven't been given their full package. Just 60 per cent of the funding is allocated of the assessed need. Sixty per cent of the funding is allocated to just about everyone who receives a part package for the first time. And the department has admitted it changed how it counts the waitlist so that someone on a part package no longer counts as waiting. Prior to 1 November 2025, those people remained counted on the waitlist until they received their full package. When you can't shorten a queue, the Labor Party's answer is: you refine it and you redefine it.

On home support, the government has finally retained the Commonwealth Home Support Program until at least 2029, after providers, advocates and a Senate inquiry told them. I suppose it's better late than never. On residential care, the sector needs around 10,500 new beds a year to keep pace with demand. In 2024-25, just 802 new beds were built. That is why more than 3,000 older Australians are stuck in public hospital beds with nowhere to go, and the government's answer is an increase of just 2.55 per cent, against a 4.75 per cent wage increase providers are already paying. The former Inspector-General of Aged Care put it plainly: 'The way this government is implementing aged-care reform is causing harm.'

Let's be plain about what this bill does not do. It does not restore human judgement to assessments. It does not clear the waitlist. It does not fund a single new aged-care bed. And it does not get one older Australian out of a hospital bed and into a place to receive the care they need. Behind every assessment, every review and every funding decision in this bill is an older Australian—someone who's worked, raised a family and built this country, someone now waiting for a package, an assessment, a bed or an answer. The coalition believes the person must come before the process. That means restoring human judgement to assessments. It means telling older Australians the truth about how long they will wait. And it means judging this government not by how tidy its legislation looks but by whether an older Australian can get the care that they need when they need it.

We welcome this bill, as it fixes so many problems that this government was warned of on the passage of the Aged Care Bill in the first instance, but Labor has got a very, very long way to go, because older Australians deserve better from this government. It's time this government backed in its promise of putting the care back into aged care instead of putting the 'wait' into 'waitlists'.

speaker: Malcolm Roberts
heading: BILLS
subheading: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
The Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026 amends the Aged Care Act 2024 to, firstly, establish yet another permanent statutory office, the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner, within the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission; secondly, to incorporate temporary modifications made to the Aged Care (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) (Aged Care System Modification) Rules 2025 into the Aged Care Act and Aged Care Rules 2025 and repeal the instrument; and, thirdly, to vary arrangements concerning refundable deposits, including their use while an individual awaits a means-test assessment, the ability to transfer deposits between providers and the treatment of deposits in aged-care means-testing. One Nation is in support of these long-overdue changes. Fourthly, it will make other administrative and regulatory amendments concerning direct-care staff, local government providers, specialised residential care homes, residential care subsidies, fee advice notices, deemed decisions and the recovery of Commonwealth overpayments.

This bill has been referred to two committees for reporting—the second because the government added a new schedule late in the passage of the bill. Both reports recommend the bill be passed. I note once again that the Labor government has packaged something we do agree with—the improvements and technical clean-up in schedules 2, 3 and 4 of the bill—with something we do not agree with, the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner. This is designed to force One Nation to oppose the bill and, in so doing, provide social media fodder for the ALP and the Greens at the next election.
