They want to claim One Nation opposed reforms to help our elderly. It's a wedge, another bloody wedge—one of the many wedges this cynical Labor government have used lately to entertain themselves while everyday Australians continue to go backwards. You don't care about the people.

One Nation has moved an amendment on sheet No. 4177 to remove the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander commissioner provisions and leave the remainder of the bill intact. One Nation opposes discriminating against Australians based on physical characteristics, including ethnicity, age, sex, sexual orientation and disability. Positive discrimination is still discrimination. It seeks to present a morally superior position which inevitably fails in a perfect storm of cost escalation, empire building, self-interest, mission creep and unexpected consequences that the taxpayers pay for.

According to the Guardian newspaper, Aboriginal children in Australia have historically been murdered at roughly three times the rate of non-Aboriginal counterparts—three times. Aboriginal children experience rape at five times the rate of non-Aboriginal children, a figure that's underreported to the point of official data being useless—bloody useless. Aboriginal children are being left in squalor without adult supervision. All of this is under the watchful gaze of the virtue-signalling elites who advance bills like this and then crack open the chardonnay to celebrate how worthy they are. This government and state governments won't stop Aboriginal children being raped and murdered, yet they have the money for a dedicated Aboriginal aged-care commissioner and their staff. This will of course lead to more regulations and higher costs for everyone. The entire idea, of course, will have no KPIs—not one—to measure progress, because for Labor it's not about the outcome; it's about feelings.

We do not need an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner. We need our aged-care system to support everyone that it's tasked with supporting. A One Nation government will send its attorney-general into Aboriginal communities, along with ministers for housing, health and infrastructure, to fix the crime and the structural problems behind these heartbreaking, unacceptable statistics—unacceptable to most Australians but not the government.

We will create jobs to restore the future of Aboriginal communities, using mining and value-adding of raw production, including in agriculture. We will oversee Australia's largest infrastructure project, the northern rail crossing from east to west, part of the national rail loop, to bring rail transport, water, electricity and the internet to remote communities. That's our idea of helping the Aboriginal community, not this window dressing BS.

Anyone who thinks this is a good idea need only look at Closing the Gap. A measure there intended to reduce the life expectancy gap between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Australians has in part failed, completely failed, with life expectancy in recent data getting worse for Aboriginals, not better. An analysis of government outlays over the first eight years of the strategy alone, from 2008 to 2016, calculated that total combined spending towards meeting the Closing the Gap targets exceeded—wait for it—$130.2 billion. The source of that data is Adam Creighton in the Australian quoting the Productivity Commission data on 12 February 2018. The Productivity Commission estimated in 2017 that federal government spending on Aboriginal affairs was $25 billion a year. I see nothing to suggest that that number has been going down since then. And then add the state spending.

I hope the Senate will realise it's time to change course on the Aboriginal industry. Stop funding more parasites in consultants, academics, lawyers, bureaucrats and larger top-end supervisors. Instead, directly fund the communities where it's needed. I'll say it again. This is what we're advocating: instead of the parasites getting the money, let's get it to the communities, to fund the communities, where it's needed directly.

Moving on, the new schedule 4, added in the House of Reps, makes changes to take account of criticism of the government's use of AI for decision-making. Applications for aged care have for the last year been determined using AI, not human beings. The Albanese government implemented a system last year which featured strict prohibition of human override. Expert, qualified human-needs assessors were explicitly barred from altering or overriding the algorithm's outputs, even when they knew a decision was clinically wrong. Second was the systemic under-assessment of vulnerable people. Critics noted that the rigid computer program frequently failed to capture the complex realities of ageing, leaving vulnerable older Australians without adequate funding or essential homecare packages. Without their packages—so much for care! Third was the lack of consultation and transparency. The automated tool was introduced quietly with no public consultation, no industry trials and no transparency regarding the underlying algorithm—no openness; just a secretive AI. Fourth was the severe bureaucratic backlogs. Appeals against robodecisions ballooned sixfold after the system rolled out, meaning many elderly citizens faced extensive waiting lists, with some tragically dying before their reviews were resolved. Robo decision-making is a counterproductive efficiency measure, and I wonder about the real motivation for robo decision-making.

This Labor government has declared war on the elderly. Just listen to these: removing their health insurance discount rebate, forcing more elderly Australians into the public health system and, in the end, costing taxpayers at least $2 billion more a year in public health to save $350 million on the rebate. That $2 billion figure is likely conservative, with up to 75,000 elderly Australians being forced to give up private health, almost double the government estimate—your estimate, doubled. The Albanese government tried to introduce co-contributions on personal care for aged pensioners. This was so badly received that the government backed down—you backed down—and agreed that vital personal care, like bathing and dressing, would not require out-of-pocket fees. Increased costs for capital and daily living—self-funded retirees and part pensioners must pay significantly higher means tested fees for everyday accommodation, capital contributions and clinical assistance.

The Support at Home mess—the government absorbed existing homecare packages into the new Support at Home framework. Seniors groups have heavily criticised the measure for severe package backlogs, long wait times and plans to fold the entry-level Commonwealth Home Support Program into it, which critics say threatens independent living in regional and remote communities. The government lifted social security deeming rates by 0.5 per cent—half a per cent!—which means that, even if pensioners' bank accounts are not yielding high interest, Centrelink now legally assumes they are anyway and adds made up unpaid interest to their income, reducing their pension. That's what you're doing. You're basically stealing money from pensioners. For older veterans reliant on specialised treatments, the government produced a $5,000 annual cap on allied health services. Older veterans who require year-round support were told to pay for it themselves—'Just pay for it yourself'—a measure that the Senate forced the government to withdraw. It's no wonder the government wanted to use robo decision-making to deflect the blame for this attack on elderly Australians away from themselves—cowardly, dishonest, a lie.

Schedule 4 in this bill will help in improving rules around robodecisions. It must be the law that any decision taken using AI be subject to human review. A One Nation government will introduce legislation to prevent computerised decision-making anywhere in the government. AI can do the legwork, sure. It should never, though, be used to make a decision, let alone make final decisions that a qualified staff member cannot overturn when an error is detected.

I foreshadow second reading amendment 4176, which has been advanced in response to many constituent concerns around the expansion of and advocacy for voluntary assisted dying. Voluntary assisted dying is now legal in all states. Nothing in our amendment advocates against voluntary assisted dying occurring. It simply seeks to protect aged-care providers who have a conscientious objection to providing voluntary assisted dying services on their premises. A religious objection is the most common conscientious objection. New South Wales, Queensland and South Australia have a law in place which explicitly regulates institutional objections. They mandate that residential aged-care facilities must not block external voluntary assisted dying practitioners from entering the premises. Because an aged-care room is legally considered a resident's home, facilities are required to allow all stages of the voluntary assisted dying process, from consultations to death, to take place onsite. In Ontario and British Columbia, provincial governments in Canada have removed the right for aged-care facilities and hospitals to refuse voluntary assisted dying. This is very troubling to me, and it's troubling my constituents. Our amendment seeks to provide support for aged-care facilities with encouragement that they're not alone and to hold the line and uphold their convictions.

This amendment is not about voluntary assisted dying as much as it's about freedom of conscience and freedom of religion. Currently, in South Australia, healthcare providers can opt out of voluntary assisted dying if they advise residents that the facility does not offer voluntary assisted dying. This allows the resident a transfer to a facility that does offer voluntary assisted dying. My amendment reflects this sensible compromise. The South Australian model works and should be the national model. In the very difficult, emotive space of euthanasia, it's very important to respect the differing views in the community and to allow residents to choose a non-voluntary-assisted-dying facility if they so want and for providers to opt out of voluntary assisted dying if it conflicts with their values. I ask the Senate to support my amendment 4176.

speaker: Vanessa Bleyer
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
This Labor government has a habit of approving big developments that communities are opposed to. Look at how this federal Labor government is refusing to put a moratorium on mega AI data centres until there are proper regulations in place. These are big developments that destroy our natural environment, adversely impact our tourism industry, and interfere with a person's right to live peacefully at home and in their community. So as this Labor government keeps approving big developments in the interests of big corporations who line their pockets with donations, the community is going to have to do more of what this federal Labor government isn't.

I know what it's like. There was a day where at my home, in my community, in what was then a $50-million-a year tourism industry, when a federal Labor government approved a big dirty, stinking pulp mill in my backyard. The community rose up and stopped that big development. So let me tell communities across Australia how we went about it to stop that dirty, stinking pulp mill and how we've gone about stopping other big developments that should never have been approved.

First, you must involve yourself in a community and political engagement campaign. Get the community together. You will not be the only one that has identified that our federal Labor government is doing something that's not in our interests and in the interests of the environment that we depend on. Organise a town hall meeting, call everyone together, organise for there to be appropriately qualified persons speaking at those community events and then keep the community organised. Engage politically. Speak to your elected representatives. They have been elected to make decisions that are in our best interests, and, when they're not doing so, we should let them know.

Second of three pillars to stop a big development that shouldn't proceed is litigation. When it came to the pulp mill, we challenged state and federal government approval decisions more so than any other project in the country. Often when a government makes a decision in the interests of a big corporation that lines its pockets, it's prone to make mistakes, as was my experience as a lawyer. So get legal advice. If there are grounds to run a case challenging a government decision then take the opportunity if you can.

Third, there's direct action. If that soil starts to turn, stand outside with a placard representing the position that you rightly hold if a big development has been approved that is in the wrong place and is not in the best interests of the community and our natural environment. So now, community, you know what you can do to do what the government isn't—to stand up for your rights, to stand up for your backyards and to stand up for your natural environment.

But of course, this federal Labor government can instead choose to make decisions for people rather than profit. My message to the community is: if the day comes when you are fed up with a federal Labor government who is not making decisions that you think they should, the Greens are here to make decisions for the community before corporations. Join the movement.

speaker: Alicia Kearns
heading: Baby Loss Awareness Week
text:
I thank the hon. Gentleman. Our little ones must be very close in age; I hope that his is doing very well. The Prime Minister said, “We are sorry,” but opening up the records would show that we meant it. It would release those mothers from the shame that was forced on them, and allow them to finally find their baby, name them, and lay them to rest.

Often in this place, we talk about what should be done, or what we could do, so I will end very briefly on a positive note. We cannot undo a family’s heartache, or the loss that they will carry for all their lives, but what drives most of us to come here is a determination to stop the same thing happening to someone else. I made that promise to my best friend in 2022, when she lost her baby Siena at nine months. I took my promise and secured £1.8 million in funding from the then Conservative Health Secretary to roll out a new technology designed to reduce stillbirths and premature births. The Tommy’s app—or Siena app—is a clinical decision support tool that accurately assesses women’s chance of having a premature birth, or developing complications with the placenta that can lead to stillbirth, and it is proven that it is saving lives. The trial began in 2024 and is running in 26 NHS maternity units, involving 39,000 women a year.

My request to the Health Secretary is to roll out the app across every single hospital. We have proven that it works. It essentially gives midwives an artificial intelligence equivalent. It gives them all the information that they may not know or understand about someone because they come from a different heritage, have a different background or have a complicated medical history. This tool can save lives, and can save more families from the heartache that too many suffer.

We must do better. We are failing women on too many accounts. Almost all of us in this room can probably share a trauma, or a time when something went wrong in the NHS because we were not listened to, and we must do more. I thank everyone for their frankness, and for sharing their stories this evening, and I thank the Health Secretary for agreeing to meet me in a few days; I am really grateful.

speaker: Andy Burnham
heading: International Update
text:
With permission, I wish to make a statement on the United Nations General Assembly and related international events that have occurred since the House last met.

Before I do so, let me first welcome my hon. Friend the new Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Sagal Abdi-Wali) to her place. What a journey, from child refugee to Parliament, and what a country—that this story of hope could happen here. I know my hon. Friend will enhance this House in so many ways, and I look forward to working with her.

I took a clear message to the United Nations: after a decade of turbulence, Britain is back and can be relied upon as a consistent and stable partner in an uncertain world, always upholding the shared values set out in the UN charter, rejecting aggression wherever we see it, and always steadfast in our support for Ukraine, as I assured President Zelensky at our meeting in New York.

In the three weeks since that meeting, Russian strikes have intensified even further, with more attacks on civilians: on apartment blocks housing innocent families; on buses carrying innocent children. When I spoke to President Zelensky on Saturday, he described the step change from Russia, including daylight attacks intended to break the will of Ukraine and ours. I can tell you, Mr Speaker, that that will never happen. In recent days, we have announced new funding to help Ukraine get through its fifth winter under Russian bombardment and a new sanctions package so that over 90% of Russia’s oil-producing capacity is now covered by UK sanctions.

The quickest way to get diesel back on to world markets without rewarding the aggressor is an energy ceasefire, with both sides stopping their attacks. I raised this with President Trump in New York. It is what Ukraine wants to see, so I welcome President Trump’s announcement yesterday of a reciprocal energy ceasefire. President Zelensky has assured me that Ukraine would immediately implement it when a start date is confirmed, and I will be discussing this further with him in the coming days.

NATO is a defensive alliance. We do not seek confrontation, but our resolve to defend our allies and ourselves is absolute, and I was clear in all of my meetings, including with the NATO Secretary-General in Oxfordshire, that we will meet our NATO commitments in full.

We know that Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe. In Berlin last week, Chancellor Merz and I agreed a new partnership to tackle these hybrid threats. We must be clear-eyed about attempts to destabilise our democracies. It is why, in my speech to the UN General Assembly, I confirmed our commitment to establish a new centre for information defence, as recommended by the Foreign Affairs Select Committee. More broadly, this is a moment to deepen collaboration with our partners, which is why in Berlin I indicated Britain’s openness to Germany joining the global combat air programme alongside Italy and Japan.

In my meeting with President Trump, we discussed the situation in the middle east. I confirmed Britain’s decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling support. I can confirm today that it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.

Since UNGA, we have been in close contact with the US about protective security at our shared bases. I thank our police and military personnel for their swift response to the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth. My right hon. Friend the Home Secretary will update the House on the incident at RAF Fairford, but I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.

In my meeting with the President, I also raised the Falkland Islands and the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British. I emphasised that point in my speech to the General Assembly and that we will also always do whatever it takes to uphold their will.

In New York, I also had a positive meeting with the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, about the forthcoming UK-EU summit. I can confirm to the House today that it will take place in Brussels on 20 November. This summit presents an opportunity to make progress on two crucial issues: boosting UK growth and controlling illegal immigration. On the table is a trade deal on food and drink products, a deal on emissions trading, progress towards linking our energy systems, a new youth experience scheme, and deeper co-operation on immigration.

This summit presents an opportunity to make progress on two crucial issues: boosting UK growth and controlling illegal immigration. On the table is a trade deal on food and drink products, a deal on emissions trading, progress towards linking our energy systems, a new youth experience scheme and deeper co-operation on immigration. The summit will also be an opportunity to raise our concerns about “Made in Europe”, and it is clear to me that there is an opportunity to make progress in all of these areas. Together, these deals will add the equivalent of over £10 billion per year to the UK economy by 2040, with the potential to add significantly more. We should not turn our backs on this opportunity, and I hope Members from all sides of this House will get behind the Government’s efforts to land a positive outcome. It is a chance to cut costs and bureaucracy for sectors like farming.

At present, entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay. Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100 million in lost exports. British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU. Seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned. This is having a real impact on businesses, and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage. For farmers and food producers, it would lift a burden that can reach £1,400 on a single shipment. For our small businesses, it would mean no more export health certificates, which can cost up to £200 each time. For households, it would ease the pressure on prices in the supermarket. It could help lower energy costs for households and businesses alike.

In Northern Ireland, the proposed energy deal could cut wholesale energy costs by 20%. On immigration, we could link up our law enforcement efforts once again, sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals, as well as ensuring faster electronic evidence from the phones of those behind the gangs. It is in Britain’s interests to secure a deal along these lines, and I will work hard over the next five weeks to achieve that. I believe that our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term. If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation that we must have. Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today, to consider what is best for our country.

Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term. At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach, like the one I am suggesting, but if we go into this further phase, we will proceed with care and complete transparency. This is the leadership we need to draw a line under a decade of drift and division, and to take the country forward.

Beyond Europe, a confident Britain is ready to play our part on the global stage as we take up the presidency of the G20 in 2027. I confirmed in New York that we will place artificial intelligence centre stage in our presidency, to capture the incredible opportunities it presents while guarding against the risks. Leading voices like the president of Microsoft are saying Britain is the world leader on AI safety, so we are well placed to take on this role, and to work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards on AI, in our G20 presidency year.

The message to the world is clear: Britain is back. On so many fronts, we are playing our part and looking confidently to the future. We are leading again, so our country can hope again. I commend this statement to the House.

speaker: Edward Davey
heading: International Update
text:
Following the loss of his father, Roy, may I start by offering the Prime Minister’s family my deepest sympathies? I am sure that we were all moved by his words about his dad, and his determination to fix social care and tackle the devastating impact of dementia on sufferers and their families. I hope that we can work across this House to make that happen.

Let me now turn to the Prime Minister’s words about Europe. His predecessors turned a blind eye to the disastrous consequences of the Conservatives’ Brexit deal, so it was welcome to hear him recognise that damage today. We on these Liberal Democrat Benches have consistently argued that their Brexit deal has made us all poorer, weaker and less safe, so I am glad that the Prime Minister has arrived at the same conclusion, but now it is time to do something about it.

The test of the Prime Minister’s ambition is straightforward, if he wants growth and if he wants to cut the cost of living. Will he drop Labour’s red lines now, and open negotiations on joining the single market and a customs union? It would be a real dereliction of duty to refuse now to fix a deal that we know is not working. Every day, every week, every month of delay means more unnecessary costs for British businesses, more pointless red tape, more pain for British families. Being outside negotiations on AI safety, “Made in Europe” regulations and migration agreements does this country real harm. Fixing our relationship with Europe is more important now than ever, especially at a time when President Trump is waging a trade war with Canada while signing a new trade deal with Putin. Never before have we seen a US President so hostile to the UK and our allies, and so friendly to our adversaries. We cannot afford to fudge or dodge on this issue, and especially on Ukraine, so will the Minister bring together a coalition of the willing behind a joint statement condemning Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and calling on him to cancel it?

Let me finally refer to the Prime Minister’s comments about Russian interference in the Brexit referendum. That took courage, after the Conservatives had spent so long suppressing the evidence. Will the Prime Minister now present it to the House in full, alongside any evidence of interference in other UK votes, so that we can understand the threat and make it a national security priority to protect our democracy from attacks such as that?

speaker: Victoria Collins
heading: International Update
text: As Liberal Democrats, we have long been calling for global leadership on AI from the UK, so I am pleased to hear the Prime Minister talk of that. We cannot get the best out of AI if we cannot protect people from the worst, and the UK should be leading on that. We also need to learn from online safety, and it needs to be Governments that lead the charge, not big tech. Will the Prime Minister listen to the Lib Dem call for an international AI safety institute, based on the International Atomic Energy Agency, based here in the UK?

speaker: Andy Burnham
heading: International Update
text: We already have the AI Security Institute, and to be fair, I pay tribute to the previous Conservative Prime Minister, the right hon. Member for Richmond and Northallerton (Rishi Sunak), who was instrumental in the establishment of that institute. It is because of that that the president of Microsoft was on the radio this morning saying that Britain is now regarded as the world leader in AI safety. What we must not be, however, is complacent, which is why I am putting AI at the top of the agenda for Britain’s presidency of the G20. I look forward to working with the hon. Lady and Members from across the House to ensure that Britain brings together a global code of standards and principles that can capture the benefits of AI while guarding against the risks it poses.

speaker: Anneliese Dodds
heading: International Update
text: I also was pleased to hear what the Prime Minister had to say about AI, both in New York and this afternoon in the Chamber. Can he confirm that it remains his view that decisions about global principles and standards for AI should be taken by democratically elected Governments representing working people and not by industry alone?

speaker: Andy Burnham
heading: International Update
text: I agree with my right hon. Friend very forcefully. I am setting up a process under the banner of the G20 presidency that mirrors what this country did in 2008, when international agreement was needed about how to handle the financial crisis. The Canadian Prime Minister, who was very much involved at that time, has been in discussions with me about how we could create a process to mirror that for AI so that individual countries could go back and embed those principles in their own laws and statutes. That is what we are trying to achieve. I would be really pleased if the whole House would get behind this endeavour, as the UK is in the global spotlight.

speaker: Gordon McKee
heading: International Update
text: Britain has enormous strengths in AI. We attracted almost as much private investment as the EU 27 combined last year, but in an industry dominated by the United States and China, it is only by co-operating with our friends in Europe that we can achieve the scale necessary to keep ourselves safe and to thrive. Does the Prime Minister agree that a technology partnership is one of the ways in which we could rebuild our relationship with the EU?

speaker: Andy Burnham
heading: International Update
text: That is an excellent thought, and that is exactly what we may be able to strengthen as part of our G20 presidency year. I point my hon. Friend towards the actions of the AI Minister, who has regained access to US AI frontier models for the AI Security Institute. That shows that we are in a good position to broker new standards on AI across the world and make arrangements with all our partners.

speaker: Cat Smith
heading: Procedure Committee
text:
The Procedure Committee has concluded its in-depth review of the written parliamentary questions system, and we were pleased to be able to publish our report just before the conference recess. I thank the Backbench Business Committee for granting time for this statement, and I also thank current and former members of the Procedure Committee for their thoughtful consideration throughout the inquiry.

My Committee regularly reviews the performance of Departments in answering written parliamentary questions, but there was a sense that a wider review was needed, because the written parliamentary questions system really was not working for Members. The number of questions had risen drastically, and the responses were not keeping pace or, indeed, meeting our expectations in terms of quality. Equally, we knew that the Government and the House administration were under pressure to deliver in a system that was at risk of being overwhelmed. We launched our inquiry in November 2025; we organised a survey of MPs, received written evidence, and heard in person from Opposition Front Benchers and groups of Back Benchers. I thank the many Members on both sides of the House who gave evidence to the Committee.

We know that our colleagues are not always satisfied with Government responses to WPQs, and we also know that that feeling has increased as the number of WPQs has also increased sharply. We heard that there were frustrations among colleagues about a small number of MPs submitting a disproportionate number of questions, which could be construed as an abuse of the system. Members who make restrained and focused use of the WPQs system for their parliamentary work are, effectively, being adversely affected. The system, overall, needs to be based on a lower volume of input but a higher quality of output when it comes to responses from the Government. The flip side of our efforts is to alleviate some of the pressures in the system, but we think that MPs should expect better responses from the Government.

We heard of concern about the tabling of some WPQs with limited Member involvement. We are clear about the fact that WPQs are a proceeding in Parliament, and should therefore always be initiated by elected Members. We cannot send our staff to speak in oral questions for us; nor should we expect our staff to table WPQs without our seeing them. At present, that is reflected by the need for our wet signatures on the hard-copy WPQs if we are to table them in that way at the Table Office. We believe that this should be reflected in the modern e-tabling system, and we recommend that Members be required to approve personally, in MemberHub, questions submitted by their staff. The fundamental e-tabling limit should remain at 20 per Member per sitting day, but limits should be introduced for recesses.

It is, in our view, an anomaly that this limit applies in sitting times but not in recesses. Members will understandably wish to scrutinise developing events during a recess, but as WPQs submitted during recesses cannot be answered until the House returns, there is often a better way of doing this, such as corresponding directly with Ministers. We recommended a limit in recesses of 20 WPQs per Member for the first calendar week, and a further 10 for each additional full calendar week. In other words, the longer the recess, the more questions a Member will get. We remind Members that these are very much maximums, not targets to be hit, and that when we increase quantity, we may see a decline in quality. Moreover, looking busy by tabling more WPQs than the neighbouring MP is not an indication of how well someone is working as an MP.

We also heard concerns about “carding”. We found that the process generally works well, but the terminology could be modernised. A card is not a red card, and it is not a block; it is merely a query that can generally be resolved very quickly if a Member nips into the Table Office. We recommended that carding be renamed “querying” to reflect that. When a Member accumulates a large number of unresolved queries—in old money, cards—at any one time, it creates a blockage in the system, and reduces the Table Office’s ability to advise other Members. When Members have 20 live unaddressed queries at any one time, they should be required to address those before submitting further WPQs.

At present there is a cut-off time for same-day e-tabling of WPQs, but it is different on different days of the week, and it falls outside the normal working day. The Committee believes that a uniform time of 4 pm should be set between Mondays and Thursdays. That would be more straightforward for Members, and it would also mean that the focus of Table Office staff in the evenings, when far fewer staff are available, would rightly be on advising Members on matters such as motions and amendments for the following day, rather than marshalling WPQs. It would also allow questions to be considered over more time, thus supporting our goal of improving the consistency of colleagues’ experiences. Given the Friday sitting hours, we recommend that we retain the 2.30 pm cut-off on Fridays.

Having an exceptional route to an urgent answer is very useful to Members, but we found that “named day” was a very confusing term for some. We thought that for the sake of modernisation, we could replace it with “priority questions”, which would better reflect the core purpose of a named-day question and would probably be simpler and easier for colleagues to understand. However, we recommend that the deadline for answers to priority questions be set automatically at three working days after tabling, which is the earliest that a Member can receive an answer to a named-day question. The limit for priority questions should remain unchanged at five per Member per sitting day. Colleagues should consider using an ordinary question to receive a detailed response, and using priority questions when speed is of the essence.

We heard of a range of concerns about Government responses to WPQs from Members on both sides of the House. The Government should address those concerns, particularly by ensuring that questions are grouped sparingly and always individually addressed within a combined response. We recommend that references to information published elsewhere be used sparingly—there should be relevant extracts, not just hyperlinks—and that the Government communicate with Members and the Table Office when there is a block on questions on a particular topic. There should also be more transparency and accountability in the Government’s performance in answering WPQs. To that end, we have recommended that a public-facing dashboard be introduced on the parliamentary website, to be updated monthly, showing the performance of each Department in answering WPQs on time. That will empower Members, the public and even the press to pursue inadequate performance, and we hope that it will also help the Government to drive forward improvements.

We recommend that Members consider how we use WPQs. We are best placed to decide, as individual elected representatives, when we need to ask a particular question, but we should also consider the cost to the public purse. There are many alternatives, including other parliamentary proceedings, ministerial correspondence, and the excellent services provided by the House of Commons Library, and sometimes we might actually obtain a better outcome from those.

Artificial intelligence was an emerging theme in our inquiry, and we appreciate the concerns raised by Members. We are a forward-thinking Committee, and we see the benefit of AI in improving the processes, but we are more cautious about its use for content. It is most important for Members to check and remain responsible for their questions, and for Ministers to check and remain responsible for their answers.

Ultimately, as we set out in the report, we recognise the importance of bringing the House with us, given the importance of WPQs to Members across the House. For that reason, we have recommended that the Government bring forward a motion endorsing the report as a whole. This would allow the House to endorse the report’s findings, recommendations and statements of principle, and allow the House administration, the Government and all of us to get on with implementing it. We hope that colleagues will support that motion when it comes before the House.

We have overhauled the WPQ system in a modernising direction. Although we have not been able to take up every suggestion that was made to us, we have sought to give colleagues a better experience of WPQs and to make them a more valuable tool, including for the important function of scrutinising Government. Our Committee will review its findings and the implementation of the recommendations as we continue our regular work of monitoring departmental performance in answering WPQs. I commend this report to the House.

speaker: Danny Kruger
subheading: Rejoining the EU — [Sir Edward Leigh in the Chair]
text:
I am just going to keep going. I do not think we are actually having a debate; we are just exchanging our speeches, so I will not give way.

I sympathise with the points we have heard, such as those made about zoos, Spanish delis or Freddy and his band. It is clearly very frustrating how the EU has treated its close friend, the UK, after Brexit, and that has had very unfortunate consequences for those businesses.

We need to look at this issue from a much bigger perspective, and here the facts are much more contested about the overall benefits and costs of Brexit. When we talk about these always cited statistics on the decline in GDP since 2026, we are comparing an unknowable counterfactual with what has actually happened in the real European Union and the UK. Here, as the Member for Harwich and North Essex (Sir Bernard Jenkin) said, the UK has done better than our European competitors.

Let us just be straightforward about this: the whole of Europe, including the United Kingdom, has suffered economically over the last decade. Different sectors have prospered and suffered in different ways. Although we have not suffered in services exports, we have suffered in goods exports, and I recognise that. However, those goods losses overlap with stupid political choices made by our sovereign United Kingdom, particularly in respect of energy policy.

Where we have also suffered and struggled is where our regulations have remained aligned with the EU. The fact is that European regulations have caused Europe to decline, and where we have also declined, it is because we have remained aligned with them. Mario Draghi, the former Italian Prime Minister and chairman of the European Central Bank, wrote a brilliant report that conclusively demonstrated how much it is the EU itself that holds back European growth, and why it is so regrettable that Britain has remained aligned in so many sectors.

Let me quickly state what actually works for prosperity and what drives economic growth. Last year’s Nobel prize winners won for their brilliant work demonstrating why there has been sustained growth in the world for the last 200 years. It is not because of market share or market access, as valuable as that is; it is because of innovation and technology. It is because of a regulatory system, largely derived from the United Kingdom, that enables businesses to prosper.

The key aspects of that system are light-touch regulation and legal certainty, which are features of common law and the United Kingdom’s economy. Legal systems matter, and the civil law system that the EU operates and applied to the UK is different, as it involves heavy regulation and legal uncertainty. Where we have remained constrained by EU law, such as in electric or self-driving cars, we do just as badly as the EU. However, where we have diverged—where we have used our Brexit freedoms—that is where we are prospering. Of course, AI technology is the key evidence of that.

speaker: Danny Kruger
subheading: Rejoining the EU — [Sir Edward Leigh in the Chair]
text:
The AI that the hon. Lady used to write her speech is the benefit of Brexit, and we all benefit enormously from the UK’s leadership in this enormous sector. We attract as much investment in our AI sector as the whole EU27 combined. That is what divergence looks like, and that is what growth looks like.

What is happening is that the EU—and I am afraid the Government—is deliberately locking the United Kingdom into its regulatory system, so that it becomes increasingly apparent that there will be no opportunity to leave. [Interruption.] I am very unclear about the speech times, Sir Edward. Have I gone over?

speaker: Iqbal Mohamed
subheading: Rejoining the EU — [Sir Edward Leigh in the Chair]
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Mrs Barker. I am a democrat, and I respect the will of the people. But to be blunt, Brexit has been the biggest fraud in the history of Britain. Ten years ago, the British people were sold a fantasy. They were told that Brexit would make us richer, but almost every person in my constituency is worse off today than they were before 2016. They were told that it would reduce red tape, but we have heard from across this Chamber that many businesses have stopped trading with the EU. Dewsbury and Batley, the bed capital of the UK, has seen trade reduced. People were told that Brexit would restore national sovereignty and allow Britain to take back control. Instead of taking back control, we lost the control we already had.

Instead, Brexit has been an unmitigated disaster. The British public were deceived and failed by their politicians. Charlatans peddled falsehoods masquerading as truisms. The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson toured the country on a red bus promising an extra £350 million per week for the NHS—where is he? What about the hon. Member for Clacton (Nigel Farage), who spent decades insisting that Brexit would transform Britain’s financial fortunes? Liam Fox, the former International Trade Secretary, said that the Brexit trade negotiation

“would be one of the easiest in human history.”

How did that work out?

We were told by various leave campaigners, including Michael Gove, that the UK would retain essentially frictionless trade access to the EU market while escaping EU rules, and that Brexit would produce a large fiscal dividend—we are still looking for that money behind the sofa. We were also promised that new trade deals would more than compensate for any loss of EU trade, but we have heard about the miniscule benefits of the trade deals we signed.

Some would say that we should not reopen old wounds or that the referendum was a once-in-a-generation event and disregarding its outcome undermines the legitimacy of the democratic process. But in this instance, I fundamentally disagree. When a referendum is decided on the back of half-truths, lies and downright deceit, we must be willing to look at the evidence again.

This is not just a matter of economics; it is about the kind of geopolitical world we now find ourselves in. Across the Atlantic, the United States no longer provides the political, economic, and strategic certainty that Britain has relied on since the end of the second world war. We are living in an age of unprecedented global instability. At the same time, transnational challenges such as frontier AI systems and climate change demand co-operation. In this brave new world, fragmentation is a weakness. Unity brings strength.

Europe’s nations face the same challenges as us. We share the same democratic values, security interests and economic future. The question that faces us, then, is simple: will we be honest enough to say that Britain’s long-term future lies inside the European family of nations? Britain would be stronger, safer and more prosperous inside the EU. The sooner we have that national conversation, the better.

speaker: Monica Harding
subheading: Rejoining the EU — [Sir Edward Leigh in the Chair]
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Mrs Barker. In the 2016 Brexit referendum, there were many who argued that our future must involve aligning with the USA—a stable and reliable partner that shared our values—and those who thought that the days of Russian aggression were over. Now we are in the world of Trump and war in Europe. The US is waging its own war that is hurting all our wallets, and Brexit has made the UK economy smaller.

The world in which we voted in 2016 has changed, and we must make decisions based on the world as it is. But even in 2016, we were promised that voting for Brexit would usher in an economic boom, open the funding floodgates for our NHS and other cash-strapped services, and put an end to immigration. The then Prime Minister hoped that the referendum would settle the issue of EU membership for a generation, yet here we are, 10 years on, still debating this very subject at the public’s request. Let us look at the impact that Brexit has had on the country—and on constituencies such as my own, Esher and Walton—on its own terms, as it was sold to us.

On the economy, one recent publication argued that:

“We left the European Union without the economic plan that should have gone with it.”

That would have been a damning indictment coming from my side of the argument, but it came from the right hon. Member for North West Essex (Mrs Badenoch), the leader of the party that delivered Brexit. By ripping us out of the single market and customs union, the Conservatives blew an enormous hole in the UK economy, costing us roughly £90 billion in lost tax revenue in 2025 alone. That is money that could otherwise have been used to lower the tax burden on workers and fund our public services.

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that Brexit

“will reduce long-run productivity by 4 per cent relative to remaining in the EU”,

and that

“Both exports and imports will be around 15 per cent lower in the long run”.

Brexit has stifled investment and job creation. It is handicapping our economy and failing British businesses and workers. The funding windfall for our NHS and other public services has not materialised; we would have more money to fund our public services had we not embarked on this failed experiment.

On the question of immigration, which was so central to the Brexiteers’ case for leaving the EU, after Brexit—and under a Government run by the very people who had pushed for Brexit—net migration reached a record level of nearly 1 million people in the year to June 2023. As we have heard, we also left the Dublin agreement.

Brexit has failed on its own terms. I know from the many conversations I have had over the last decade that many of my constituents, the majority of whom voted to remain, foresaw those problems and take no pleasure in being proved right. Brexit has failed on its own terms.

What is the case for the EU, then, as we stand here today? The challenges we face today are not confined to national borders, and our solutions must reflect that. I could point to our strength in numbers in tackling climate change, terrorism and people smugglers, or in regulating the risks from AI and taking on the tech giants. Cross-border problems need cross-border solutions and strength in numbers. The EU is far from perfect, but it represents an important ideal: it is worth working together to find common solutions that benefit all of us.

Secondly, there is the economic case. We recognise that, when it comes to economics, geography matters. The EU is our largest trading partner for a good reason. Trade deals with countries on the other side of the world cannot replace a market of millions of people right here on our doorstep.

Lastly, as the Prime Minister says, let us give the next generation real hope. The last decade has been a difficult one for young people, so let us give them back their ski seasons or their right to tour Europe. I have just come from the Chamber where the Prime Minister talked in positive terms about Europe. It is good, at last, to hear a Labour leader making the case for Europe. It has been a long decade.

speaker: Tony Zappia
heading: GRIEVANCE DEBATE
text:
We live in the most uncertain times that I can recall in my lifetime, from the life-changing impacts of a three-year global COVID pandemic to the war in Ukraine, the rise of China's global influence, the recent military attack on Iran and, now, the fear of AI. People are understandably fearful of what the future holds. Simultaneously, essential, basic needs like housing are out of reach for many new, aspiring homeowners and the national health system struggles with daily demands. Not surprisingly for most people in both Australia and throughout the world, daily survival has become a priority.

A regrettable fallout of the current pressures is that the critical issue of climate change and global warming are being sidelined. Recent polling confirms that climate change is dropping down the list of voters' most important issues, with only five per cent nominating it as their most important issue compared to nearly 30 per cent in 2022. Even worse, in many parts of the world, climate change initiatives are being scaled back or put on ice, in turn adding to the pace and threats of climate change. Within the broader community, discourse about global warming and climate change has stalled. Yet scientists tell us that the risks have in no way diminished and the consequences can be devastating and irreversible. A recent UK national assessment highlighted the alarming level of biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse and the dire consequences for humanity that flow from that. The fact remains that the Earth is getting hotter, and the dominant cause is the burning of fossil fuels.

Whilst Australians generally welcome renewable energy initiatives, we simultaneously continue to export record amounts of coal and gas, with Australia now being the third-largest fossil-fuel exporter. However, renewable energy technology, whilst welcome and effective, is hardly meeting growing energy demand when, in reality, total carbon emissions should be trending downwards if threats of climate change are to be reversed. Annual global temperatures over the next five years are predicted to be between 1.3 degrees centigrade and 1.9 degrees centigrade above preindustrial levels according to the World Meteorological Organisation. The consequences include melting ice sheets, coral bleaching, rising sea levels, water scarcity, disappearing flora and fauna, more extreme weather events that occur more frequently, a substantial increase in human heat stress and many, many others.

The devastating fires in recent times, which saw 150 million hectares burned globally in the first four months of 2026 alone, with more since across Europe and North America, and the terrifying and destructive water and landslide in Nepal are confronting realities of climate change, whilst the human and financial costs of those events add to global financial pressures and stresses. It is also predicted that, in the years ahead, hundreds of millions of people will become climate change refugees, adding to the global refugee problem that we currently face. Australia's near neighbours in the Pacific will be some of the first and worst affected, and their problems will become Australia's problems. In the meantime, here in Australia, the Liberals', the Nationals' and One Nation's members openly backtrack from efforts to reduce carbon emissions, invest in renewable energy or accept the work of our global climate scientists. They are doing their best to prolong fossil-fuel use and constantly talk down the transition to electric vehicles, the Albanese government's investment in batteries and Australia's participation in the COP31 climate change conference.

Climate change is real and, whilst climate change deniers, backed by the fossil fuel companies, run their dishonest, self-serving campaigns, the hard decisions are being left to future generations. Not surprisingly, the younger generations have now become the most active advocates for climate change action. They are the ones who will inherit the failures of today's generations. Survey after survey confirms that younger people are not dismissive of climate change consequences and feel betrayed by the lack of global climate change actions. It is understandable that dealing with the immediate cost-of-living pressures would be a priority for governments; however, there is no reason why climate change responses should be put on hold, as they have been in so many places. Good government means dealing with both. Doing so need not be contradictory.

The Iran war and its subsequent ongoing disruption to global oil supplies highlights Australia's enormous reliance and vulnerability when it comes to diesel, petrol and jet fuel. Transitioning to electric vehicles can save Australians on ever-increasing fuel costs while simultaneously reducing carbon emissions. Large-scale production of sustainable aviation fuels in Australia could reduce greenhouse gas emissions from our aviation sector, create jobs and increase our resilience to supply shocks from events overseas. There are opportunities for farmers to electrify farm equipment—such as irrigation pumps, which often account for a substantial amount of on-farm diesel use—which could then be run on solar and batteries. I'm pleased to say that we're actually seeing some of that transition, with the sale of electric vehicles now growing at a much faster pace than had been predicted only a couple of years ago. That is good because, again, it not only diminishes the amount of carbon that is produced and released into the air but accelerates the transition that we need to go through if we are to reverse the effects of climate change.

For all the criticism that I often hear about what countries are doing about climate change, the one country that is actually still sticking to its plan and agenda and probably doing more than any other country when it comes to climate change adaptation is in fact China, a country that is quite often in the firing line of the critics.

Climate change is real, and the effects are already with us. The consequences are real and they are devastating. Governments know that. But, in many cases, they are too timid to act. Our younger generations know that climate change is real, and they have every right not only to be concerned but to expect stronger action across the world. They don't want just words and reports and they don't want just one conference. They want meaningful action and long-term climate change adaptation policies, something we have been talking about ever since I came to this place in 2007. But I haven't seen enough real work being done.

I stand with those young people in calling for stronger action globally on climate change and global warming. The longer we delay our response, the more destruction will occur and the more drastic and costly the response in the future will be. It is a great injustice to future generations to burden them with that responsibility.

speaker: Sarah Witty
heading: GRIEVANCE DEBATE
subheading: Melbourne Electorate: Community Events, Artificial Intelligence
text:
When I gave my first speech in this place, I spoke about Melbourne as a city that pulses with live music, breathes a soul of theatre and has creativity running through it. I've had plenty of reasons since then to feel even more strongly about that. I have the enormous privilege of representing a part of Australia where you can walk a few streets and come across live music, theatre, comedy, galleries, record shops, games, fashion and people making things you probably wouldn't find anywhere else. Melbourne has built that reputation over generations. A lot of it has happened in small venues, rehearsal rooms and studios above pubs, behind shopfronts and in places where somebody was prepared to give an artist a go.

I was reminded of that recently when I toured the Melbourne Fringe Festival. Fringe has been part of Melbourne for more than 40 years. This year's festival has more than 450 events, and its open-access model means an independent artist does not have to go through a selection committee or audition before registering a show. There is theatre, comedy, circus, cabaret, music, dance and visual arts. There are established artists and people putting something in front of an audience for the first time. For 20 days, that work takes over theatres, pubs, shopfronts and community halls across Melbourne. You can see people trying things out. Some of it's funny. Some of it's strange. Some of it is even challenging. That willingness to experiment has always been part of Melbourne's culture.

Earlier this year I visited St Martins Youth Arts Centre in South Yarra. They have worked with children and young people since 1980, putting them in rehearsal rooms with professionals and treating them as artists in their own right. They help create the work themselves and develop scenes, movement, sound, characters and performance. I really enjoyed seeing how seriously they take young people's ideas and creativity. People including Ben Mendelsohn, Catherine McClements, Gina Riley and Jane Turner have come through St Martins.

Another area where Melbourne exceeds is gaming, and I recently saw the launch of Melbourne International Games Week at ACMI in Federation Square. ACMI is Australia's only museum dedicated to screen culture, bringing film, television, video games and screen based art together in the middle of Melbourne and welcoming around one million visitors each year. It has also taken video games seriously as an art form for more than 20 years. It exhibits and collects games, supports developers and hosts Melbourne International Games Week, a 10-day celebration of Australian and international video game culture and industry. Digital games development recorded average annual growth of 13.1 per cent over the decade of 2024 to 2025, the strongest growth across Australia's culture and creative sector. The broader cultural and creative economy contributed $70.3 billion in 2024-25.

Another organisation I've been proud to support is the Social Studio. The Social Studio has been part of Melbourne's scene since 2009, creating training, employment and creative opportunities for people from refugee and migrant backgrounds through fashion, design and the arts. Their school, manufacturing studio and retail store give emerging creatives somewhere to build skills and find meaningful opportunities.

When talking about art, I often come back to music. Melbourne's music scene is one of the things I love most about representing this city. On almost any night, you can find someone playing somewhere. There are rooms packed with people and rooms where the audiences can practically lean on the stage. There are musicians playing their first proper gig and others who have spent their lives performing. Around them are sound engineers, bookers, promoters, producers, venue staff, good audience members like me and all the people who keep live music running.

Those smaller venues have a practical place in Melbourne. Long before an artist can fill a festival stage, they need somewhere to play in front of a much smaller group of people, and hopefully that's more than one. They need someone willing to book them and audiences willing to take a chance. The Albanese Labor government knows the pressure the live music sector has been under. We established Revive Live to support Australian owned venues and festivals and give Australian artists more opportunities to perform, develop an audience, hone their craft and earn an income.

Some of the Melbourne organisations and venues supported, including the Grace Darling Hotel, the Bodriggy Brewing Company, Yah Yahs and Punters Club alongside Ability Fest and Glo Glo in Fitzroy. Across Australia, Revive Live has provided $19.3 million to 221 live music businesses, including 100 venues and 121 festival activities. Our government has committed a further $12.5 million for 2026-27. Labor's cultural policy, Revive, also established Music Australia within Creative Australia to support and promote contemporary Australian music and help Australian artists develop audiences and markets.

As incredible as Melbourne's arts and culture scene is, it is under pressure and threat from unregulated AI training. If you make music, write, illustrate, photograph, design or perform, your work is your intellectual property. Australian copyright law gives copyright owners economic rights over their material, while creators and performers also have moral rights including attribution and protection against false attribution. Generative AI has raised serious questions about what happens when copyright work is used to train AI systems. The Albanese Labor government has already made clear it supports artists and their work by ruling out a broad text and data mining exception in Australian copyright law. Parts of the technology sector had called for such an exception. It could have allowed AI developers to use Australian creatives' copyright work, for free and without permission, to train AI systems. The government has ruled that out and has been clear that it has no plan to weaken copyright protection because of AI.

The government's Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Reference Group is bringing creators, industry and experts together to work through what comes next, including how copyright material is used as inputs for AI and questions around transparency. The government is considering different ways of addressing this emerging technology—for example, whether Australia should establish a paid collective licence framework for AI or continue with voluntary licence agreements. It is also examining whether copyright law needs greater clarity around AI generated material and whether a small-claims forum could make it cheaper for copyright owners to pursue lower-value infringements. These discussions are ongoing, and I am pleased to know that artists and creative workers are at the heart of these talks.

Melbourne gives me the chance to see how broad our arts scene really is—independent performers at Fringe; young people making theatre at St Martins; designers at the Social Studio; game developers, musicians, technicians and the people keeping local venues alive. The mix has taken generations of people to build. I am incredibly proud to represent them and proud to be part of a government that backs Australian artists and wants the next generation to have the opportunity to make a life and a career from their creativity.

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
subheading: Curtin Electorate: Raise Our Voice Australia
text:
Raise Our Voice provides an opportunity for young Australians to draw the parliament's attention to the issues shaping their future and the action they want parliament to take. I'm proud to share from some young people in Curtin. Toni, aged 14, had this to say about disability justice:

I am not a burden. I am not a joke. I am not lesser. I am the same as anyone else, I just need a little help sometimes. I am autistic.

I need Parliament to understand that I have so much to give this world. I play sport, I volunteer in my community, I row for my school, I play basketball for my state, I can play an instrument, and I have an amazing group of friends.

The NDIS has given me support, and without it I may not have been able to do these things. I need Parliament to understand that every dollar you spend on me matters and makes a difference.

Sometimes people say things that make it sound like we aren't worthy. I am lucky. I go to a school that gives me lots of support and makes sure I am treated well. Not every autistic child gets this, but they should.

Autistic teenagers like me need a hospital system that understands our needs, an education system that looks after us, and politicians who see us as adding value to our communities.

I am autistic and I am proud. I need Parliament to be proud of us and to take real action for disabled people.

Meg, aged 18, shared her views on AI:

Hi, I'm Meg. I'm 18, I'm from the Curtin electorate, and my brain is shrinking. This is not hyperbole; this is AI.

While artificial intelligence has created large-scale changes in society that improve everyday life, it is also slowly eating away at what makes us human. Creativity, innovation and critical thinking are all fried and atrophied as AI replaces them with a click or a tap.

As a member of the generation most affected by this change, I refuse to watch corporations profit from AI as it strips away our future. We need this to be managed. We need change.

At university, I have watched my peers compete for grades, only to see the top marks go to essays written by AI. We are fighting robots, and we are losing.

To win this fight, we need to learn how to use AI strategically to expand our thinking instead of limiting it. Creating education programs in schools could be a crucial step—

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
subheading: Curtin Electorate: Raise Our Voice Australia
text:
Meg said:

To win this fight, we need to learn how to use AI strategically to expand our thinking instead of limiting it. Creating education programs in schools could be a crucial step towards a world where society isn't paralysed by AI.

So, for a smarter future, limit the use of AI. Limit the erosion of your children's brains. And act to save humanity.

Thanks, Tony and Meg. Parliament hears your voices.

speaker: Monique Ryan
heading: BILLS
subheading: Private Health Insurance (National Joint Replacement Register Levy) Amendment Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
The Private Health Insurance (National Joint Replacement Register Levy) Amendment Bill 2026 removes the $5,000 cap on the levy payable per device per financial year by sponsors of joint replacement prostheses. The levy funds the Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry. To date, the cap has meant that small and medium sized device companies have been forced to carry a disproportionate share of the registry's costs. Removal of the cap will ensure that the levy paid is proportional to the number of devices sold by each company.

The National Joint Replacement Registry is an excellent demonstration of what can be achieved with good clinical data, but its success reflects how Australia is failing in other ways with our health data. In 2002, Australian surgeons performed more than 50,000 hip and knee replacements. At that time, we had no good data on the long-term effect of those devices. The best estimate was that one in five hip replacements would eventually need revision. Australian orthopaedic surgeons decided that that wasn't good enough. They built a registry which now collects data from every relevant hospital in Australia, public and private, on every joint replacement performed. That registry has saved Australians from real harm. In 2007, the registry identified the ASR metal-on-metal hip resurfacing device as an outlier, with a revision rate more than double that of comparable prostheses. By the end of 2009, the manufacturer had withdrawn both ASR devices from the Australian market.

Australia now has more than 140 clinical registries operating nationally and across jurisdictions. They inform best-practice care, quality improvements, health policy and resource planning. Some of them are world leading. But they're a patchwork, established at different times for different reasons and funded in different ways. The Joint Replacement Registry is funded by an industry levy collected under its own legislation. Other registries are funded through time limited Commonwealth grants. The National Clinical Quality Registry Program provides $40 million over four years to support 10 existing national registries. Other registries rely on the Medical Research Future Fund or on time limited NHMRC grants. Some are funded by state governments. Some are funded by specialist colleges or universities, charities or patient groups. Others are funded by pharmaceutical companies with a commercial interest in their outcomes. Many, if not most, survive on the goodwill of clinicians who enter data into those registries in their own time, and I know this from personal experience.

I founded the Australian Neuromuscular Disease Registry in 2020. It's housed at the Murdoch Children's Research Institute. It's one of 70 registries in the TREAT-NMD global network, which harmonises datasets so researchers across the world can pull data across borders, which was essential when every one of the conditions that we were studying was rare. The registry is funded by patient groups like Muscular Dystrophy Australia and Save Our Sons, with some support from pharma. It largely depends on the dedication of clinicians like my former colleagues Dr Eppie Yiu and Mrs Robin Forbes.

The reality is that long-term data has never mattered more. If we look at the gene therapies and genetic therapies now being given to Australian children with neuromuscular disease, which are given once and meant to last a lifetime, approvals are largely based on short-term data from small clinical trials. The TGA has adopted the European guideline on the quality and clinical aspects of gene therapy medicines—

A division having been called in the House of Representatives—

Sitting suspended from 17:44 to 17:57

The TGA has adopted the European guidelines on the quality and clinical aspects of gene therapy medicines but has not adopted the companion European guidelines on long-term safety and efficacy follow-up, which recommend that patients receiving gene therapies be followed for up to 15 years. The long-term follow-up that those patients need falls back on registries like ours, registries run on goodwill and short-term grants. When the Commonwealth consulted on a national clinical-quality registry strategy, stakeholders were unified in saying that our approach to registries is ad hoc and fragmented and that the sector needs sustainable national funding.

But funding was absent when the national Clinical Quality Registry Strategy was finally released in 2021 and is still absent five years later, so whether a condition, a device or a procedure is properly monitored in Australia depends less on its importance to public health than on whether a group of committed clinicians start a registry of their own. Australian women harmed by transvaginal mesh implants know what that costs. So do those who received defective breast implants produced by Dow Corning and those placed at risk by the now recalled Philips sleep apnoea devices.

Last week in Kooyong I met with Catherine Shang, the CEO of the Australian Cardiovascular Alliance. Heart disease and stroke account for one in four deaths in Australia, but we have no national profile of them. Cardiovascular data is held in hospital records and standalone registries in different formats in different jurisdictions. Compare that with cancer, where mandatory reporting of every diagnosis has supported a national database since 1982. The gap is most stark in sudden cardiac death. Sudden cardiac arrest affects over 25,000 Australians every year. On average, one Australian under 35 suffers a sudden cardiac arrest every day. Those statistics are derived from a Victorian registry that was enabled through a philanthropic donation but has now stalled.

Kooyong constituents Gordon and Bronwyn Thoms know the cost of that. In 2023, their daughter, Alexandra, died from sudden cardiac arrest at just 23 years of age. Alexandra was a happy 23-year-old who had recently completed her double degree. She died in her sleep without warning. Before losing Alexandra, the Thoms family had no concept that a seemingly healthy young person could die suddenly from an undiagnosed cardiac condition. That lack of awareness is itself part of the challenge that we face. Tragically, it took Alexandra's death to find the underlying genetic cause that then enabled preventive monitoring and potentially life-saving intervention for other family members. Alexandra's brother, Charlie, was diagnosed with the same cardiomyopathy and subsequently received an implanted defibrillator.

The Australian Sudden Cardiac Arrest Alliance has brought the sudden cardiac arrest community together to identify what we need to do. Working with clinicians, researchers, survivors and bereaved families, they have developed evidence based recommendations for a coordinated national sudden cardiac arrest plan. One of AuSCAA's central recommendations is a near-real-time registry of cardiac arrest cases able to identify risks, measure outcomes and drive continuous improvement. Victorian researchers were tracking every arrest in people aged one to 50, determining the cause and circumstances of each to target prevention. A similar registry being established in New South Wales now is struggling to connect emergency services with forensic information, and its ongoing funding is uncertainty. Organisations like AuSCAA shouldn't have to fight for data infrastructure and coordinated action. The Commonwealth should be providing that. It now needs to meet with AuSCAA. It needs to act urgently to fund and implement a national sudden cardiac arrest plan.

Another problem is the fact that our registries and the larger government data collection don't speak to each other. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare holds national hospital mortality and cancer data. Communicable diseases are reported through the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System. Occupational lung diseases, like silicosis, are captured in the National Occupational Respiratory Disease Registry. Each of these have their own legal basis, governance, data standards and custodians. But, when registries want to link data with hospital records or death records, they're often forced to do that as a one-off project. They have to seek approvals in each jurisdiction, negotiate with multiple data custodians and satisfy multiple ethics committees. One-off linkages are labour intensive, slow and expensive.

This country collects enormous amounts of healthcare data but then walls it up in separate silos. Look at Medicare. Every time an Australian sees a GP or a specialist, undergoes a procedure, has a pathology test or an imaging study or fills a PBS script, the Commonwealth has a record of that. Medicare and the PBS constitute one of the biggest and most complete longitudinal, population-wide health datasets in the world. But our clinical registries struggle to access that data. Think about what routine access to that data could do. A registry tracking a new hip or knee device could see, without asking a single extra question of the surgeon or the patient, whether recipients go on to need more physiotherapy, less pain medication, more imaging or more specialist reviews than recipients of other devices. A registry for a chronic condition could measure in real time whether the care that Australians receive matches the guidelines that we spent so much time and money writing. The Commonwealth is already paying for this data. It has the legal authority to share it safely and under strict privacy considerations, but it's lacked the infrastructure, the will and the single focus for it until now.

This year, after nearly four decades of advocacy from public health experts, Australia has finally established the Australian Centre for Disease Control. The CDC was created to be a data-driven organisation, one able to modernise our surveillance systems and enable data sharing and linkage across the Commonwealth, the states and the territories. It already houses the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System and the National Occupational Respiratory Disease Registry. The COVID-19 response inquiry recommended that the CDC be expanded to include non-communicable diseases, building on that data infrastructure and that linkage capacity.

I believe that clinical and disease registries should be part of that expansion. Imagine if, instead of 140 separate registries, each with its own funding fights, IT systems, data standards and linkage negotiations, we had a national registry platform hosted by the CDC, working closely with the AIHW and the safety and quality commission. Registries could keep their own clinical leadership.
