They should, but the infrastructure, the secure data environment, the common standards and the enduring links to Medicare and the PBS, to hospital records, to other registries and to the National Death Index could be built once and shared by all. That would mean routine rather than one-off data linkage and a sustainable, transparent funding model which doesn't depend on which registries happen to have their own act of parliament. Australians are rightly cautious about how their health information is used. A national platform would need strong legislative safeguards, independent oversight and genuine transparency about who accesses what data and why, but I think it's fair to say, given my experience of the milieu, that a single well-governed, well-secured national system could well be safer than dozens of underresourced ones, each managing sensitive data on its own.

As it stands, progress in the health portfolio is slow. I would argue too slow. The government's health technology assessment review made 50 recommendations more than two years ago, and its implementation advisory groups roadmap has been in limbo since the end of last year. The strategic examination of research and development handed the Albanese government 20 recommendations last December. We're still waiting for a government response to those. There are more reasons for urgency. The government is now working through how artificial intelligence should and could be adopted and used in our healthcare system. AI is only ever as good as the data that it learns from. Coordinated, high-quality national health data should be the foundation of the government's AI agenda in health, not an afterthought.

The national joint replacement registry has shown us what Australian doctors are capable of. This bill helps to make that registry sustainable. I support it, and I thank the government for introducing it, but I'd urge the minister to see this bill as a start of the conversation. Every Australian who has a hip replacement deserves to know that someone is watching to see how well it works—that's happening—but so does every Australian who receives a heart valve, a breast implant, a new cancer treatment or the diagnosis of a rare disease. We have that data. We have that expertise, and we now have a national centre for disease control. What we need is the ambition to bring them together in the interests of data interoperability to further advance our healthcare system. With that in mind, I move the amendment as circulated in my name:

That all words after "reading" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:

"the House:

(1) notes that:

(a) for more than two decades, the National Joint Replacement Registry has demonstrated the value of high-quality clinical registry data to patient safety;

(b) Australia's more than 140 clinical registries are fragmented and poorly integrated, and rely on inconsistent and often insecure funding; and

(c) Medicare Benefits Schedule (MBS) and Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) data remain largely unused by clinical registries despite their unique value as population-wide, longitudinal health records; and

(2) calls on the Government to urgently:

(a) develop a coordinated national approach to health data collection, including for clinical quality registries;

(b) establish common data standards and enduring, privacy-protected linkage between clinical registries, MBS and PBS data, hospital, cancer and death records, and national genomic data resources;

(c) house a national clinical registry in the Australian Centre for Disease Control;

(d) prioritise the development of coordinated, high-quality national health data so that the research potential of artificial intelligence in health can be fully realised; and

(e) release and respond to the Health Technology Assessment Review Implementation Advisory Group's final report and respond to the Strategic Examination of Research and Development report".

speaker: Matt Smith
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: My question is to the Prime Minister. How is the Albanese Labor government making sure we shape artificial intelligence in our national interest, and why is this agenda so important?

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Leichhardt for the question. He certainly understands that artificial intelligence is changing the way that we work, the way that we live and the way that society functions. It'll shift the way that we think about our economy, how we deal with the productivity challenge and how we deal with defence and national security issues as well.

The role of technology itself in government and politics will have a significant impact over coming years. There are massive benefits there, potentially, for governments and businesses to harness. Last night, I spoke at the Australian Industry Group about the potential productivity benefits that will come from a harnessing of artificial intelligence in the manufacturing sector, for example, that the AIG very much represents.

Above all, though, we must be clear eyed that the development and deployment of AI need to serve our national interest and need to reflect our values. Legislating Australian standards for AI is crucial to making that the case. Overnight, the President of Microsoft himself made the point that, at the moment, AI is less regulated than a bottle of milk or a washing machine. And it shows. Right around the world, an unacceptable pattern has developed where companies with AI agents undertaking routine tasks end up breaking out of test environments or accessing restricted systems and data they should never have even attempted to access in the first place. Because, even though frontier agents are the latest development in AI, the fact is they are tools built by humans and they are not beyond that human reach. That is a challenge for us: to make sure that humans stay in charge of this technology. Companies can, and they should, be putting safety first. It is the role of governments to hold them to account. That is how humans remain in control of AI, shaping this change instead of letting it shape us.

Our work on these issues spans the work of government and the parliament, as it should. Yesterday, the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, updating us on their work to date, wrote to us. There are areas of consensus being worked through, and I thank the members of the committee, both from government and from opposition. I note the member for Curtin, as well, is playing a constructive role in this committee. But I'd urge the entire parliament to engage on these issues. Once again, this is an important issue. It brings the parliament together. It certainly should not be an area of partisanship. It needs to be something in which we all engage as much as possible, because this is a very new development, but it is a revolution that will have an enormous impact on the way society functions. (Time expired)

speaker: Anika Wells
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Bean for his question and for the opportunity to join him at St Mary MacKillop College Canberra to talk to students about their own experiences online. Social media can have a devastating impact on people with eating disorders and body image issues. Toxic and predatory algorithms expose Australians to fitspiration and thinspiration content, blasting images and advice that reinforce unrealistic ideals and harmful behaviour. That is why, building on Australia's social media minimum age law, our proposed digital duty of care calls out material and conduct that encourages, promotes or instructs disordered eating as being harmful to under-18s. Social media platforms, online games and AI chatbots will be required to have systems in place to prevent young people from being exposed to pro-eating-disorder content.

To make sure companies are following their duty, the eSafety Commissioner and accredited Australian researchers need the ability to check the homework of these platforms—Australian researchers like Dr Rys Farthing of Reset.Tech and Dr Hannah Jarman of Deakin University. Dr Farthing and Dr Jarman conducted a study of 1,204 pieces of pro-eating-disorder content on social media. They created under-18 and over-18 sock-puppet accounts and reported the 1,204 pieces of content on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube and Pinterest to see whether the platforms took them down. What they found was shocking but, unfortunately, unsurprising. On Instagram, only 10.7 per cent of that material was taken down. When reported to YouTube, only seven per cent of the pro-eating-disorder content was taken down. On X, it was 4.5 per cent. This is the kind of mystery-shopping-style test that social media platforms, online games and AI chatbots should be accountable for in Australia. But these Australian researchers had to conduct their study in Italy, in Poland and in Germany, because, right now, in Australia, they have no protection from legal threats.

That is the kind of transparency and accountability that the coalition want to block when they say sock puppets are an Orwellian spy operation. The coalition have asked for an explanation of why sock-puppet accounts are needed. This is why: to hold these companies to account for the harm they are causing young Australians, to not just listen to what the companies are saying but to check what they are actually doing. This is what the digital duty of care will deliver and why the coalition needs to put politics to the side and work with the parliament to get this done. (Time expired)

speaker: Nick McKim
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE: TAKE NOTE OF ANSWERS
subheading: International Relations: Australia and the United States of America
text:
I move:

That the Senate take note of Senator Wong's response to Senator Shoebridge's question.

speaker: David Pocock
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE: TAKE NOTE OF ANSWERS
text:
I move:

That the Senate take note of the answer given by the Minister for Industry and Innovation (Senator Ayres) to a question without notice I asked today relating to artificial intelligence.

It's really of no comfort that the minister's first instinct is to downplay the incident, given what we've seen with the Hugging Face incident in the US and what we've seen with bots breaking out of testing environments and OpenAI having no idea that this was happening until after the fact. It seems like we're in a situation now where we potentially have to pay OpenAI to have access to a program to help protect us from OpenAI. It doesn't make a lot of sense to me. I would love to see the minister have more answers in his answers to Senate questions generally but, specifically, more answers when it comes to AI and the threat of AI.

The government has not been able to answer why they put on hold, or shelved, an AI safety act that had started consultation in 2024.This is not a new issue. We've known for many years that we need safeguards in place. The government said: 'We don't need safeguards. We're basically just going to see how this plays out.' It's not playing out that well. Now they're scrambling. They did the same thing on data centres, where they said: 'We have standards. They're on a website. Check them out'—and it was basically all the existing regulations that they'd put on a website. It's not good enough. They are now scrambling to put in national standards. People expect governments to be more proactive, to actually take on vested interests and to put Australians first, and I'm really concerned that we're not seeing that when it comes to artificial intelligence, given everything that is at stake.

Question agreed to.

speaker: Slade Brockman
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
I rise tonight to thank the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office for hosting me and some of my fellow parliamentarians on a delegation to Taiwan. It was an extraordinary experience, and I am one who is fortunate enough to say that it was not my first time in Taiwan. I was fortunate enough to go before. For me, it was very much like going back and visiting an old friend. It felt very familiar, it felt very friendly, and it felt like there was much that Taiwan and Australia could learn from each other and could teach each other.

We were extraordinarily privileged to meet and spend time with Vice President Hsiao; President Han of the Legislative Yuan; Dr Joseph Wu, who is the Secretary-General of Taiwan's National Security Council; and many others. We were given a very deep appreciation of the strategic challenges faced by Taiwan and also the complementarity and future possibilities of our already strong economic relationships. Many people are very well aware of the complementarity of the economies of Australia and Taiwan. Australia obviously has produced raw materials and food and energy that have been exported to Taiwan. In return, Taiwan is obviously a manufacturer of many high-tech goods that are being utilised here in Australia.

It's good to see that it is not just the positives of the past. It is not just a relationship that is based on past success. It is actually one that has a pathway to future success. Taiwan obviously is a significant player in the space of AI and data centres and the possibilities of those being built in Australia. Meanwhile we see the increased development of Australia's rare earths and critical minerals, which obviously are vitally important to things like AI and data centres and also to the production of batteries and so many other of the high-tech products that we so desire.

It was a wonderful opportunity to sit down with many good friends to relearn some of the challenges they face and to see how committed Taiwan is to their democratic institution and how engaged they are. One of the visits that we had was to the two main parties, the DPP and the KMT. Obviously hearing from those two main parties, in a political sense, was very important to the delegation as was hearing from the senior members of the government and the parliament. It was an extraordinary opportunity to renew those friendships, renew those relationships and learn more about the future of the relationship between Australia and Taiwan. I sincerely thank the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office here in Canberra for their assistance in putting this program together. I hope that, before my time here comes to an end, I have the opportunity to visit Taiwan again.

speaker: Penny Allman-Payne
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
Tonight I'll be reading speeches written by young people across Queensland on the issues that are important to them. I feel very privileged to help elevate the voices of these young people, and I hope they stay engaged and continue to push for positive change. To these young people: thank you, and I hope I do your speeches justice.

Grace, who is 14 years old, writes: 'The issue shaping my future is the lack of accessible health care in rural and regional Australia. While many Australians can visit a doctor just minutes from home, some rural families must travel for hours to reach a GP or a hospital. In an emergency, that time can make all the difference between life and death. This could affect someone's friend, child or sibling—someone who is cared for. This issue impacts not only rural communities but all Australians. As major cities become more crowded and expensive, many people would consider moving to regional areas. However, without reliable health care, schools and essential services, relocating is not a realistic option for many young Australians building their futures. Parliament can help create this change by funding more hospitals and medical centres in regional areas, encouraging doctors and nurses to work outside major cities and expanding telehealth services and transport options for patients who live far from specialist care. If students like myself can think of practical ways to improve Australia's future, why can't our leaders? Health care shouldn't depend on your postcode. It's a right, not a privilege, and it's time for parliament to ensure every Australian has access to care they deserve.'

Poppy, who is 11 years old, writes: 'Imagine growing up knowing your great-grandmother, hearing her stories and learning about her life. Just as you are old enough to appreciate those moments, her memories begin to disappear. She no longer recognises you or remembers your name. This is my reality. My Nana is the matriarch of our family, but dementia is slowly taking her memories and independence away. My family is not alone. Almost 450,000 Australians are living with dementia. This is expected to rise to more than one million by 2065. There are also around 29,000 younger Australians between 18 and 65 living with early dementia. Australia's National Dementia Action Plan talks about promoting equality and human rights for people with dementia. But what does this actually look like? In countries like the Netherlands, dementia villages provide safe neighbourhoods where residents can walk, visit cafes and go shopping while receiving support. My Nana has always been active and loves her daily walks. Now it is unsafe for her to walk alone. What if she could live somewhere designed around what she can do rather than what she can't? That is why I am calling on parliament to invest in dementia villages in Australia and to explore better models of care that allow people to remain active, connected and independent for as long as possible because people living with dementia deserve more than simply being kept safe; they deserve to keep living.'

Nabiha, who is 15 years old, writes: 'Hi, my name is Nabiha, and I am a Muslim Australian. I wasn't born here, but I still consider Australia my country. I moved here when I was three years old and have lived here for most of my life. I have never known a home other than Australia. The issue I wanted to bring up is racism—specifically the discrimination and hostility directed towards Muslims. When I go out, I'm always self-conscious about myself experiencing judgement from others due to the fact that I dress modestly and choose to cover my face with a niqab. Australia is a multicultural, multiracial country where people from all over the world come in hopes of living a safe and peaceful life without the fear of racism and discrimination over how they look or dress or act. However, at the moment this is not Australia. To solve this issue, I want the Racial Discrimination Act to be updated. I want it to explicitly cover religious discrimination, not just race or ethnicity, because right now Islamophobia is falling through the legal gaps. I urge the parliament to support school based programs that bring Muslim speakers, community leaders and youth ambassadors into classrooms. I would encourage MPs to visit mosques, meet Muslim youth and publicly challenge misinformation. I don't want a society where Muslims are treated differently than others. I want to live in a society where I, as a Muslim girl, can go out and feel safe, respected and fully accepted, where my identity isn't questioned, my beliefs aren't judged and my presence doesn't need defending—a society where diversity is normal, equality is expected and every person, regardless of faith, can be belong without fear or hesitation.'

Naeem, who is 15 years old, writes: 'Did you know Australia currently hosts 162 operational data centres, with more on the way? These data centres take up on average 20,000 to 100,000 feet and store thousands of files and servers required to run programs like ChatGPT. Data centres globally already consume enough water to fill 1.8 million Olympic sized swimming pools. Australia currently has the national AI plan rolled out in December of last year, which addresses some of the dangers of AI, including deepfakes and potential copyright infringements, but neglects environmental factors. The plan talks of building AI infrastructure with no regard to the strain it puts on our energy and water usage, and this excess consumption is likely to increase in the next couple of years. What I propose is adding to the national AI plan, adding regulations on excess water and electricity usage in AI data centres. Parliament should introduce strict environmental regulations on water and energy usage for data centres. AI infrastructure as a whole, with the current rapid expansion, could place enormous pressure on Australia's already stressed water supplies and rapidly growing energy demand. Introducing strict environmental regulations today would protect young Australians like me from inheriting an AI driven environmental crisis tomorrow.'

Thank you to Grace for her contributions on regional healthcare, to Poppy for her thoughts on dementia care, to Nabiha for her views on racism and discrimination and to Naeem on data centres and AI. We look forward to you staying engaged as you get older.

speaker: Malcolm Roberts
heading: ADJOURNMENT
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026
text:
Right here. The Albanese Labor government has circulated the most onerous, terrifying bill presented to parliament this century. The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 exposure draft gives the government power to censor not just social media but the entire internet, using powers that exceed anything available anywhere in the world. The bill enacts a new statutory digital duty of care which would impose a proactive obligation on a broad range of online service providers to protect users from so-called harm. These include every social media platform; every communication platform, like Signal and WhatsApp; search engines including Google and Bing; app stores like Apple and Google Play; hosting services, meaning every website, every web-hosting company, in Australia, covering every website in Australia; code-hosting sites like GitHub; cloud services like Cloudflare; telcos including Telstra, Optus and Aussie Broadband; software like Oracle, Adobe, HubSpot, SAP and Monday—it's a bloody long list; AI systems like Grok, Claude and ChatGPT; any and every site that generates or edits pictures or videos; and other designated internet services—a catch-all for anything you guys forgot. And, wait for it, it includes equipment suppliers for internet hardware, including routers, servers, desktop computers, laptops and internet enabled phones. Worse, it can extend to BIOS or software updates on your computer which can be used to block websites, words or phrases at machine level. Even anonymous platforms like Tails will be caught up in this bill, which intends to give Australian citizens nowhere to hide from the eSafety commissar's quest for power.

What does a digital duty of care look like? The bill requires any person responsible for an online service to 'ensure, so far as is reasonably practical, a safe online environment'. This has three elements. All persons are protected from a variety of harms, including harassment. This has a legal meaning from general criminal law which would exclude a single critical post, although a pattern of critical posts from one person or one person participating in a campaign of critical posts from others would breach this section—one person. If the eSafety commissar or commissioner writes guidelines stating that certain political discussions or hostile online discourse creates an environment ripe for harassment, tech companies are legally forced to react and ban the user, group or topic—topic! This gives the eSafety commissar sweeping powers to defend approved government opinions, voter blocs or movements, while slapping down anyone critical of the government.

Secondly, children attract broader protections, including any material or behaviour capable of inflicting serious harm—capable of inflicting harm in the judgement of the eSafety commissar, the arbiter. There is no place for intent, let alone causing actual harm. 'Capable' is the new, low threshold. It's absurd.

Thirdly, it covers harms arising from platform design. These can flow from material or conduct. This includes infinity scrolling, which is the one thing in the bill One Nation would like to see removed from social media.

In fairness, I say the digital duty of care is not absolute. The 'reasonably practical' qualifier, which largely reflects principles from workplace safety legislation, requires weighing up all relevant matters, including the likelihood and degree of harm; what's known or ought reasonably to be known about the risk; the availability of mitigation measures and the cost of those measures; or the impact on user privacy, including whether that cost or impact would be grossly disproportionate to the risk. Exemptions—the duty does not require platforms to police or take action regarding lawful communications occurring in private solely between consenting adults. This ensures end-to-end encrypted messaging services or standard private adult emails are not forced to actively monitor private conversations for general harmful content.

The bill does include the word adult, meaning a digital ID will be necessary to prove you are an adult before allowing you to have a chat or email chain without monitoring from the government, so you have a digital ID to get away from monitoring. These things are private anyway. What does it matter what you say amongst friends? Apparently, it does to this Labor government. When the government is provided with this much power with no suitable checks and balances, abuse will occur.

Now, we get to another terrifying aspect of the Albanese government's digital duty of care. Section 205G to 205K of the bill allow the government to create fake accounts called sock puppets or liar puppets that appear to be a person yet are in fact a government run account. These clauses allow the eSafety commissar and approved researchers to assume false or fictitious online identities.

speaker: Malcolm Roberts
heading: ADJOURNMENT
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026
text:
These clauses allow the eSafety commissar and approved researchers to assume false or fictitious online identities; use AI to make up images, videos or memes; post under the fake names; and watch what happens—in other words, all the things they ban you from doing. The exposure draft states that the eSafety commissar's testing powers operate without limitation. There's no mechanism requiring eSafety to seek an independent warrant before deploying fake accounts nor is there a statutory requirement to publicly report on how many liar identities they operate, what they said, who they impersonated or whose images they deepfake—nothing. This provision will allow the government to make any claim, promote any agenda and attack any person, party or idea without consequence. The only limit to fraudulent identities is the provisional liar accounts can't do something which is a criminal offence. How reassuring.

The bill explicitly states that this authority applies despite anything to the contrary in other federal, state or territory privacy and identity laws. This is despite section 3 of the Privacy Act 1988 explicitly stating federal law is not intended to exclude or limit the operation of state or territory laws that protect personal information, provided those laws can operate concurrently with it. Section 109 of the federal Constitution provides, where the state law is stricter than the Commonwealth law, the state law generally applies, except now where the government is impersonating people to sway public opinion.

Section 25C of the act provides the minister with the power to add anything she wants to the list of harms and then require the eSafety commissar to have that removed from the internet. There's no guidance at all on the use of this power. It's a blank cheque. The minister's decisions under this section are under a legislative instrument. Woe betide Australia if a government ever gets a majority in both houses again. This is terrifying. The UK shows how this provision can be used to eliminate political dissent. In two years, 19,883 UK residents, almost 20,000, have been arrested for saying things on the internet the government did not like. Examples of this so-called hate speech include 11 Britons tracked down and arrested for abusing England players in the World Cup for missing penalties only for abusing black skinned players, abusing white skinned players was considered just fine. This is an example of the single post and company rule I mentioned earlier. A woman was arrested for posting rap lyrics that included the N-word, despite her not having any ill intent. She posted song lyrics for goodness sake. That N-word is ubiquitous in rap, yet, on social media, it's hate speech. Graham Lineham was arrested for saying trans men are still men, which is true. This is where legislation like this always ends up: in policing thought and opinion, rather than worrying about actual harm.

Our major defence ally, the United States, expressed concern. In a communique issued on 22 September, it said, as to the exposure draft:

A framework that empowers governments to enforce vague definitions of "harm" risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship …

The United States nails this reason for this bill: viewpoint based censorship. Their concerns are threefold. Firstly, this is a mechanism of overcensorship, which pre-emptively censors free speech. Secondly, it explicitly warns that such a framework risks reducing the reach of independent journalists and alternative voices. Thirdly, the White House registered its strong opposition to foreign measures that result in the extraterritorial censorship of protected speech.

You all laughed when One Nation said we were heading down the same path as Communist China. Now look: according to the Supreme People's Court public blacklists, 23 million Chinese are now non-persons, unable to access the internet or public transport or leave the country. Five million people have their employment, their income and their spending limited, under the control of the state.

Meanwhile, most of the companies caught up in this power grab are out there taking care of business, thinking Australia is a democracy, blissfully unaware of our descent from democracy to totalitarian communism in just four years. Four years—that's all it took.

Never in the history of humanity has a ruler had this level of power—never. One Nation strongly opposes this bill. In government, we will repeal it.

speaker: Karen Grogan
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
Today I'm proud to read a speech from Breanne, a 17-year-old from the federal electorate of Grey, who has submitted her speech through the Raise Our Voice campaign. The following are Breanne's words to our parliament and to our country:

There are many concerning issues that will shape my future, such as the cost of living, housing affordability, and financial disadvantage for higher education. But the major issue is the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday life.

Now don't get me wrong, AI is a highly beneficial tool that I myself use, whether it be finding the right word, breaking down concepts or getting feedback. But the technology that supports me now is also changing the future that I am preparing for. From job automation and loss of human agency to deepfakes and more, this tool is becoming increasingly capable of learning the ways we work, write and live. The question is: If AI becomes more capable, how much control are we willing to give it?

AI can mimic the way that I have been taught to write in school, automate my future job, steal my human agency, and make us question whether something is real or not.

Therefore, I put forward that Parliament introduce laws that hold Big Tech companies accountable for the AI technology they create and release into our lives. Don't let my future, and the bright futures of all young people, be shadowed by a technology we cannot regulate. Protect our human agency, so we can move forward into a future we can trust.

Thank you, Breanne. I'm very proud to have read out your words today and delighted to see so many of my colleagues doing the same for the raise our voices campaign.

speaker: David Pocock
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: I've got another question for the Minister for Industry and Innovation, Senator Ayres. Minister, OpenAI told the Joint Select Committee on AI that they would be providing Australia with red-level access to their Daybreak cyber program. When will Australia get this access, and how much will it cost us?

speaker: Tim Ayres
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I can speak to that with some generality and then, if I can come back to you on the specific reference that you've made, I will and, if I can come back to the chamber, I will. This government has a world-leading approach here. It was the Albanese government and the Prime Minister himself who raised these issues directly with OpenAI and their CEO and raised them publicly on behalf of all Australians. It underscores the rationale for the position that the government has adopted. I think the work that the joint select committee has been undertaking over the last period has done that as well, and I'm grateful for the work that's happening across the parliament to make sure that we elevate these questions.

There are issues here in relation to cybersecurity around artificial intelligence, but they are by no means the only issues in relation to safety and security, and the safety and security issues are by no means the only issues in terms of our future resilience and our future security. We're making sure that, through legislation here and in the House of Representatives, we deliver a clear legislative framework that makes sure that artificial intelligence investment here in Australia happens on Australia's terms in Australia's interests and we're lifting our capability for all of the economic and resilience reasons that have been outlined.

speaker: David Pocock
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: On the one hand, you tell us that you're world leading. On the other hand, you can't even tell us if we have access to Daybreak or when we have access to Daybreak. The government is clearly now scrambling to put some safeguards in place. Why did the Albanese government shelve an AI safety act after the election?

speaker: Tim Ayres
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: It's certainly not the case that there is anything happening here but a very clear and very calm and effective response on behalf of Australia. Our AI Safety Institute is a world-leading part of a network of 10 AI safety institutes doing that work. And the approach that we are taking is about ensuring that we get the investment and the capability here, not just in our economic interest but also the interests of our security and our resilience. These tools are required—

speaker: David Pocock
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: It's just on relevance. I've let the last two questions go, but I'd love to know why the government shelved an AI safety act.

speaker: Tim Ayres
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: What we're doing, Senator Pocock—we outlined Australia's artificial intelligence national plan last year. We set out standards for data centre investment, which have been signed up to by the major firms. (Time expired)

speaker: Alex Mayer
heading: Energy Security and Net Zero
text: I recently met Paul Hughes, who proudly showed me his AI-enabled heat battery boiler. I am delighted that the Government have made that tech eligible for the boiler upgrade scheme. Would the Minister consider speaking to Treasury colleagues about this technology being part of the energy-saving materials VAT relief framework?

speaker: Gordon McKee
heading: Iran: Threats to British Interests
text: Just this morning, the chief of MI5 warned about the implications of artificial intelligence reducing the barrier to advance terror and cyber-attacks on the United Kingdom, so what work have the Minister and his colleagues done to assess how Iran is using this technology and how we can defend ourselves?

speaker: Stephen Doughty
heading: Iran: Threats to British Interests
text: The implications of AI for our defence and security are obviously significant. My hon. Friend knows that important work is being done by my right hon. Friend the Minister for Artificial Intelligence on this issue. It is crucial that we look at this not just in any one context—he rightly mentions the risk of Iran or others using this technology—because it of course applies more broadly. I can assure him that we are leading international conversations on these issues.

speaker: Sarah Sackman
heading: Courts and Tribunals Bill
text:
I was glad to meet the hon. Member to discuss the situation at Taunton, which I know has been a deep source of frustration. Nothing could more exemplify the years of neglect of our justice system than our crumbling court estate that was presided over by the Conservatives. This Government are investing in the fabric of our court estate. That is not just in the bricks and mortar, but in the digital upgrades that are so important, and I will speak to those now.

We have the technology for remote hearings; we need to be deploying it. This Government will develop a pilot of virtual remand hearings, so that we do not need as many prisoner transfers as before. We will work with our judiciary to develop a new pioneering national video model. The model will allow suitable cases to be allocated to available judges across different locations. It might be that a judge in Cardiff is hearing a matter based down in London, helping to alleviate the pressures there, to make much more effective use of capacity and to target those areas facing the greatest backlogs.

We are also adopting a new national listing tool, harnessing the capacity of AI to schedule cases more efficiently. We will have case progression officers in every single Crown court, making the more complex cases progress further and faster. We are working with the judiciary to set up short trial courts, which hear similar cases together over concentrated periods so that they can be dealt with more quickly. We are also expanding a scheme already used in Manchester, Bristol and Nottingham to allow prison vans to use bus lanes. I agree entirely with those who say we need to make the system more efficient, and we are stretching and straining every sinew to do exactly that, with the investment to go with it. We welcome in particular the judiciary’s reforms to prioritise rape and serious sexual offences and to end the unacceptable practice of floating trials for such cases, giving victims greater certainty about when their case will be heard.

Lord Leveson’s review was clear that investment and modernisation can only take us so far. No single lever can fix a crisis that has been years in the making. We have had decades of under-investment in a system that has simply not kept pace with the 21st century, where cases now take twice as long as they did 25 years ago. So our third lever is pragmatic, principled structural reform to ease the pressure on the Crown court and ensure that its time is concentrated on the most serious cases, and that is precisely what the Bill delivers.

The case for reform remains as strong as ever, but good government requires us to listen, and this place exists to scrutinise and improve legislation. When concerns are raised, it is right that the Government reflect and react. When the Prime Minister took office he committed himself to looking at these proposals again, and that is why over recent months the Prime Minister, the Lord Chancellor and I have listened carefully to stakeholders, to Members on both sides of the House, and to people who work within the system. We have heard that strength of feeling, and we have acted. I can confirm today that the Government have tabled an amendment to remove clause 3, relating to the bench division. The effect will be that all defendants facing a trial in the Crown court will be heard with a jury. That decision does not change the destination or the ambition of the Bill, which has always remained the same: swifter justice for victims.

Simplifying our approach and avoiding some of the operational reforms that would have come with a new division in the Crown court gives us the opportunity to move faster in implementing the changes set out in the Bill. Implementing those changes more efficiently will free up court capacity and make better use of court time, helping us to bring about fast, fair justice for victims. We remain confident that the guts of the Bill—the package of reforms backed by the record financial investment that I have described, along with our ambitious programme of modernisation—will be sufficient to free up Crown court time to turn the tide on the backlog within the current Parliament. This is the right decision for victims, and it is the right decision for the justice system.

I know that the Opposition have tabled amendments to remove the remaining clauses relating to Lord Leveson’s review, but I am afraid that doing so would be to bury one’s head in the sand. We are proceeding with other structural reforms in the Bill, including the removal of defendants’ right to choose whether their cases are heard in the magistrates court or the Crown court when they involve an either-way offence. The reform that we have always proposed is that, as in Scotland, it should be the court rather than the defendant that triages cases. This has a double effect. Not only is it more efficient, ensuring that when the prosecution and the court decide that a case can be heard in the magistrates court, that is where it is heard; it is also fairer. It is about putting the power in the hands of the court rather than those of the defendant and giving a far greater say to victims whose voice can be heard through the prosecution, which puts its case as to what venue the case should be heard in, as well as hearing from the defence. It means that cases will be heard on the basis of their seriousness and not simply the preference of the defendant, as is the case in Scotland.

This is exactly the right thing to do. These measures will not only reduce the demand on the Crown court, but will prevent defendants from gaming the system, electing for a jury trial in the simple hope that delays will drag on and the case will fall apart when the victims or witnesses withdraw. Our reforms are not only pragmatic but principled. For instance, giving magistrates courts greater sentencing powers means that more cases can be dealt with more quickly. The magistrates court is an efficient jurisdiction. It currently deals with triable either way cases about four times faster than the Crown court.

speaker: Kieran Mullan
heading: Courts and Tribunals Bill
text:
Lucky you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I take that point.

The schedule 1 powers that I have talked about are a significant Henry VIII power. Under proposed statutory instrument powers, the Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State will have the authority to add further categories of offences to schedule 1 by secondary legislation. I am not aware of any time before in this place when the Secretary of State could use secondary legislation to erode and remove the right to a jury trial from a particular defendant. That is completely unprecedented and indefensible.

The Conservatives do not merely criticise this bad package of legislation; we have repeatedly sought to put forward practical, evidence-based alternatives that tackle the delays without taking a sledgehammer to our constitutional rights. The Government must fix the operational failures that currently waste thousands of court hours every year. Last year, between 23% and 26% of Crown court trials were ineffective. Rather than stripping citizens of jury trial rights, the Minister should be focused instead on failures in prisoner transport, which result in hundreds of trials being derailed, simply because defendants are late to the dock.

The Government must keep all existing courtrooms open and fully funded, and must use new artificial intelligence tools for disclosure and listing, and they must expand live-link video participation. [Interruption.] Ministers on the Front Bench chunter that they are already doing that. If that is the case, why is the Crown court backlog going up? They are clearly not succeeding with the measures that they are bringing forward, and a number of things are getting worse.

We must improve case management and incentivise earlier case resolution, instead of forcing complex cases into the overburdened summary courts, where there are backlogs too. Extraordinarily, the Minister claimed that there was no backlog in the magistrates courts. I do not know how she decides what is or is not a backlog. Cases going up by 10% in one year is a backlog by any measure. I visited Liverpool Crown court, where the wait for trial is roughly half the length of the wait for trial in other parts of the country. The Government should replicate the proactive case management model successfully pioneered in courts like Liverpool, Preston and Cardiff, where active Crown Prosecution Service case ownership and early trial-readiness reviews have driven down backlogs.

Our sunset clause draws attention to the true motivations of this Government. If the Government sincerely feel that these measures are a necessity to bring the backlog down, as they have argued repeatedly to their Back Benchers, our clause is quite clear that when the backlog is down to the pre-covid average for a period of four quarters, these damaging, rights-eroding measures should be withdrawn. I do not expect that the Government will support that proposal today, because fundamentally they do not have the same faith that we do in the importance and value of a jury trial.

The Government’s partial U-turn demonstrates that sustained scrutiny can force a rethink, but a partial U-turn is not enough. The central flaws of the Bill remain: the abolition of the right to elect trial by jury, the risky expansion of summary jurisdiction, the restriction of appeal rights and the creation of secondary powers to expand juryless trials. We should not erode centuries of procedural safeguards to achieve marginal administrative speed gains. I urge hon. Members across the House, and especially those who have previously spoken out against these measures, to stand by their previous words, to stand by their principles, and to reject these remaining clauses tonight.

speaker: Alex Norris
heading: Courts and Tribunals Bill
text:
I beg to move, That the Bill be now read the Third time.

Before I turn to the substance of this important Bill, let me recognise those who have helped bring it to this stage: those who have sat in the Chair, both in this Chamber and in Committee; the excellent Clerks of the House, who serve us so well; the Whips on all sides; the hon. and right hon. Members who served in Committee with such vigour; the Minister for Courts; my predecessor, my right hon. Friend the Member for Tottenham (Mr Lammy); Members from across the House for their contributions to debate on the Bill, today and at previous stages, especially those who shared their or their constituents’ experiences; and those legal professionals from outside who have engaged with us.

I give specific recognition to the artist formerly known as Sir Brian Leveson for his landmark review. During this process, he has been elevated to the other place, where he is the noble Lord Leveson of Liverpool. What a public servant he is, and what work he did in his review! I recognise his efforts, in this area and in many other aspects of British life. It is a real pleasure to work with him, and we are grateful for his work, which underpins the Bill. Crucially, I recognise the victims and survivors who have shaped the reforms, including those who join us today in the Public Gallery. They should be proud of what they have done. I know that they bring forward their stories at a cost to themselves, in order to make change, and we are very lucky that they do so.

The Bill has victims at its heart. Its purpose is urgent and long overdue: to ensure that justice in this country is fast and fair, because victims today face intolerable delays. People suffer appalling crimes; they summon extraordinary courage to come forward; they relive their most traumatic experiences; and they put their trust in the system, and hope that justice will be done. What happens next is that they wait, and wait, and wait. Trials are pushed back. Cases drift further into the future, and there are years of anxiety before a trial can even begin, while confidence in the system drains away. All too often, victims give up because the process is unbearable.

As the Minister for Courts said—and as the age-old maxim goes—justice delayed is justice denied. This Government cannot and will not accept that. The Bill grips a problem that the previous Government simply would not. It tackles the record and rising Crown court backlog that we inherited, which now sits at nearly 81,000 cases—more than double the level in 2019. I am afraid that is testament to the Conservative party’s record in government, and their failure to grasp the nettle and tackle the reform needed to wrestle our criminal justice system back on track. Again, today we have seen the Conservatives simply deny the reality; they refuse to be reconciled with their record.

Our modelling shows exactly where this trajectory leads, if things are left unchecked: to even deeper delays, collapsing confidence, and a justice system that cannot fulfil its most basic promise, which is that justice will be done swiftly and fairly. This Government will not normalise that delay and allow victims, witnesses and defendants to bear the burden of a system under strain. We cannot continue to try to meet 21st-century pressures with a 20th-century model.

On Report and throughout this process, we have heard colleagues call for greater investment. They are right, and we are investing at record levels. There are unlimited sitting days for our criminal courts.

Others have called for modernisation. They are right to do so, and we are modernising. Through greater use of technology and AI to maximise our capacity, we can speed up justice and ensure that our system responds to the changing nature of crime, which has meant massive increases in digital evidence and demands on court time. But investment alone will not solve the crisis, nor will modernisation. As the noble Lord Leveson of Liverpool made clear, and as all the evidence shows, only when we have structural reform in the form of pragmatic changes can we really begin to turn the tide on the backlog. That is what this Bill will deliver.

I make no apology for looking again at this proposal— I myself as the new Lord Chancellor and my right hon. Friend as the new Prime Minister. Of course we looked again at some of the measures in the Bill. We listened to the strength of feeling from across the House and the legal sector, and we have made changes that mean that now almost all defendants facing trial in the Crown court will continue to be tried by a jury.

The Bill is not solely about bringing down the backlog. It is about making the system work better. I am proud that through other legislation alongside this Bill we have already been able to bring forward measures to improve victims’ experiences of court, with new specialist courts for survivors of rape and sexual offences. I want to recognise, as other colleagues did, the work of my hon. Friend the Member for Warrington North (Charlotte Nichols) at previous stages of the legislation to bring us to this point.

The Bill goes further in supporting that wider effort and challenging the damaging myths that have so often silenced rape victims. It makes it easier for victims to access special measures in order to give their best and proper evidence. Crucially, in the family courts it will finally repeal the presumption of parental involvement. The safety of children must always come first. I recognise the incredible efforts of Claire Throssell to bring this change forward and make it a reality today. It has come at extraordinary cost. I hope that this is a day of pride at what is a significant step forward.

Much of the debate around this Bill has invoked tradition, but the history of our justice system has never been a history of standing still. It has always been a history of adaptation and institutions evolving to meet the demands of a changing society and a changing age. This Bill represents those timeless values applied in a modern context. We are acting to put the interests of the British people first, because the status quo, which would take our courts to a point of no return, which continues to deny fast and fair justice to those who need it, and which damages public confidence and consent, is simply unacceptable to us.

The Government are the only ones with the courage to address the challenges we face head-on, and we have heard that in debates at all stages of the Bill. We are pulling every lever within our power to rebuild a court system capable of delivering justice fairly, swiftly and sustainably. With this Bill, we choose that path, because the cost of doing nothing is simply too high. I commend the Bill to the House.

speaker: Lord Kennedy of Southwark
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, before we move on to the Second Reading of the Health Bill, I want to stress the importance of all noble Lords speaking to be here for the majority of the debate. Equally important is that noble Lords who speak must return at the end of the debate to hear the Front-Bench responses. The advisory speaking time is five minutes.

During this debate, the noble Baroness, Lady Campbell of Surbiton, will address the House using an AI-generated voice. This is a first in a British Parliament. As it is a first, I have advised the Whips that some leeway in the advisory time for the noble Baroness should be allowed as this is the first use of this technology. I am sure the House will agree with me.

speaker: Baroness Merron
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, the NHS matters deeply to people across our country; it profoundly touches all our lives. Every one of us will have our own experience of the National Health Service and our appreciation of the care it provides, and we will all have hopes for its future. As the needs of patients are evolving, so must the National Health Service. Our job is twofold: first, getting the NHS treating patients on time again; and, secondly, reforming the health service so it is fit for the future. These ambitions run throughout the core of the Bill.

Modernisation does not mean change simply for its own sake, but making considered changes that drive real and tangible benefits to patients, who are at the heart of all we do. It means making better use of technology, empowering local leaders to meet patient needs, and taking a clear view of what needs to be done nationally so that more funding and resource reach the front line.

Before turning to the substance of the legislation, I will make a few points of gratitude and note: first, to all Peers who have engaged constructively with the development and scrutiny of the Bill, and who I know will continue to do so. I also want to appreciate the work of my ministerial colleague, the Minister of State for Health, Karin Smyth MP, who led the Bill through the other place, where there was considered debate of more than 400 amendments in Committee, Report and Third Reading. The Bill was approved at both Second and Third Reading without dividing, which is a sign of the broad consensus on its central aims.

On a number of issues, the Government have listened to concerns and amended the Bill. We remain committed to working with both noble Lords and the other place as the Bill continues its passage. I am confident that this House will take a characteristically constructive approach to its important role of scrutinising every line of the Bill. I thank all noble Lords who have already discussed the Bill with me and who attended the information session after First Reading; I look forward to further discussions in the days and weeks ahead.

I am sure noble Lords would also want me to congratulate no fewer than five noble Lords—which I understand is a most unusual number, in a good way—on the occasion of their maiden speeches. I thank them for choosing this Bill in which to make their own introduction to this House. I look forward to hearing from them and I warmly welcome them to your Lordships’ House. As the Chief Whip said, we have a world-first today. I am most grateful to the noble Baroness, Lady Campbell, for making this happen, and for making AI help her make her speech. I am grateful not just to the noble Baroness for choosing this Bill in which to do this, but to the parliamentary authorities for making this possible and ensuring that accessibility prevails in this House.

I turn first to what I believe is one of the most important reforms in the Bill: the single patient record. For many years, patients, carers, clinicians and campaigners have spoken to the shortcomings of fragmented information systems. Too often, information follows institutions rather than individuals; too often, patients and carers repeat the same story over and over again to different professionals; and all too often, healthcare staff make decisions without a complete picture of a patient’s needs. When records are incomplete or inaccessible, opportunities for mistakes increase and continuity of care can be compromised; at worst, these consequences can be deadly. A report on maternal deaths published in 2025 found that failures to share critical information between providers were a significant factor in nearly half of the cases examined; this could have been avoided.

The Bill establishes the legal foundations for the single patient record to create a single, secure and authoritative account of patient information. It will bring together health and social care records so that those providing care can access the information that they need, when they need it. It will empower patients to make informed decisions about their health, while supporting clinicians to provide safer, more joined-up care.

Public support, I am glad to say, is strong. Independent public deliberations show that 76% of participants supported the principle of a single patient record. The benefits are real, including every year: 20,000 fewer A&E attendances, 6,000 fewer hospital admissions, more than £20 million in medicines savings and the release of around half a million hours of doctors’ time. This surely is a prize worth having.

I am grateful to noble Lords who attended the single patient record round table. I recognise the concerns that were expressed about privacy, confidentiality and public trust, so I can assure your Lordships’ House that the single patient record will operate with strict safeguards, strong cybersecurity measures, clear controls over access, robust oversight arrangements and full compliance with existing legal protections. The Bill is about safer care, not weaker protections. It is about empowering patients; it is not about diminishing their rights.

I turn to the abolition of NHS England and the guiding principle of the democratic accountability of our health system. Since NHS England was established, the number of staff working across NHS England and the Department of Health and Social Care has increased substantially. I have experienced the overlapping responsibilities and convoluted processes that slow up decision-making and divert attention away from patient care—something that I know none of us wants. This Bill will return the functions of NHS England to government and the wider NHS system where appropriate. In doing so, it will provide greater clarity for the system. It will restore democratic accountability and free up resources to be reinvested on the front line, where we want to see them. There will also be greater clarity about where responsibility lies, ensuring that Ministers are accountable for national decisions while devolving more power to local NHS organisations.

On that point, let me turn to the matter of devolution and local leadership. This Government believe that a more devolved NHS will be a more effective NHS. Those closest to patients are best placed to understand their needs. That is why the Bill devolves decision-making, empowers integrated care boards, strengthens strategic commissioning and provides greater flexibility for local leaders. Having said all that, I also recognise concerns around local representation and expertise. We listened carefully to those concerns during the passage of the Bill in the other place. As a result, the Government amended the Bill to restore the requirement that every ICB includes a local authority member, jointly nominated by relevant upper-tier local authorities. I believe that this amendment strengthens the Bill. It ensures that important expertise on social care and public health continues to inform decision-making and helps to lay the ground for future social care reform.

Looking ahead, integrated care boards will act increasingly as strategic commissioners of local health services, with responsibility for a broader range of services and resources, while holding that responsibility in their own right rather than as duties delegated to them by others. We want decisions to be made as close to communities as is feasible, with the ICBs providing strategic leadership while working closely with local authorities and other local partners. Neighbourhood health will be at the very heart of this approach.

I know that patient safety is a concern shared by noble Lords across the House. Before turning to that issue, I extend my congratulations to the noble Baroness, Lady Neuberger, on her appointment as chair of the Care Quality Commission. I look forward to working with her and I am sure we all wish her well.

No Government should ever pretend that things do not go wrong in the NHS. When they do, patients, families and the public must have confidence that lessons will be learned and acted upon. The independent review, led by Dr Penny Dash, identified a patient safety landscape that has become cluttered and confusing. The sheer number of recommendations to health bodies in this landscape—over 1,400 in the last 30 years—can make it very difficult for them to focus on doing the right thing. The Bill streamlines that landscape. It transfers the functions of the Health Services Safety Investigations Body to the Care Quality Commission, helping to create a clearer connection between learning from failures and improving care. At the same time, we will ensure that vital safe space protections remain in place.

The Government also recognise the importance of ensuring that the CQC is ready to take on these functions, and that is why we are taking a carefully managed approach to implementation and have been working closely with the CQC to monitor its operational readiness. This transfer will happen only when the CQC is ready. I want to assure your Lordships’ House how seriously we take consideration of patient safety. We will listen to noble Lords’ concerns and keep them updated on any and all progress in this important area.

The Dash review also spelled out how to simplify the arrangements for the patient voice. The Bill abolishes Healthwatch England and local Healthwatch, placing responsibility for listening and responding to patients and the public with the organisations that plan and commission services: ICBs and local authorities. Again, I recognise that noble Lords have raised concerns about these reforms, and I am grateful to my noble friend Lord Hunt for meeting me to discuss them. I look forward to continuing discussions with noble Lords as part of our review of these measures.

Let me take a moment to remind the House of the additional amendments that the Government have made during the passage of the Bill thus far. They relate to pharmacy regulations, visiting in health and care settings and reforms relating to medicines and medical devices. Together, these changes support patient well-being and access to high-quality care and innovation.

In bringing my remarks to a close, I wish to highlight one further commitment relating to a statutory maternity and neonatal commissioner. The Government accepted the recommendation of my noble friend Lady Amos, and I thank her and her team for all their hard work in delivering the national maternity and neonatal investigation. The Secretary of State has made it a priority to bring forward an amendment to establish a statutory maternity and neonatal commissioner to provide independent leadership, oversight and accountability for maternity and neonatal care in England. This is an important opportunity to strengthen accountability and champion the interests of women, babies and families throughout the system. I thank noble Lords for the questions and points they have raised about the role, and I look forward to working with them on this important development.

The Bill will not solve every challenge facing the NHS, but it will be a significant and necessary step towards a modern, accountable and patient-centred health service. It will help information to follow patients rather than institutions. It will reduce bureaucracy and strengthen accountability. It will give local leaders greater freedom to deliver for their communities, and it will place the patient voice closer to decision-making. I, for one, welcome all of that, and I beg to move.

speaker: Baroness Campbell of Surbiton
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, before I contribute to this debate, I would like to thank the Procedure Committee for allowing me to bring my AI-generated voice into the Chamber, and the technical department and the other members of the House of Lords staff who have made this possible. This is cutting-edge technology that will enable me to contribute to debates in my own, once-clear voice before it begins to deteriorate due to my disability. I hope that your Lordships will agree with me that this is an exciting development for the House of Lords, showcasing to the world inclusion in democracy at its best. With that, may I introduce noble Lords to Baroness Campbell mark 2?

I welcome the Bill and share much of its vision. The Government’s commitment to integrated, personalised care and support is long overdue. If implemented correctly, it could transform thousands of lives. However, I also feel compelled to deliver a warning against the potential re-emergence of an institutional medical model. For decades, the disabled people’s Independent Living Movement has fought clinical paternalism, which defines us by our medical condition. We are individuals with the right to control our lives, choosing what we do and who supports us.

NHS personal health budgets—PHBs—were designed to give individuals support to lead ordinary lives on their own terms, however complex their medical needs. The 2019 guidance promised greater choice and control and enhanced independent living. Direct payments enable people to employ personal assistants, or PAs, and to decide how and when they are supported, so I am nervous when I hear the Prime Minister speaking of healthcare and social care staff as one workforce. We must not replace personal control with a one-size-fits-all service. Notional personal health budgets in a national care service could squeeze out direct payments in favour of standardised care packages. Where a PHB is a direct payment, individuals have greater control over NHS funding, and it offers better value, with average savings of 12% to 16% compared with conventional services.

Some ICBs are showing creeping rigidity over the use of PHBs. As I recently highlighted in the Guardian, individuals have been prevented using budgets to enable their PA/carer to support them when they are away from home. Lucinda Ritchie was forced into residential care from hospital against her will, rather than returning to her adapted bungalow and her experienced PA team. Only after we raised the alarm and involved the BBC did her ICB change its mind. This will not do.

In July, the Minister and I discussed my proposal for an inquiry into ICB practices to address these issues. Perhaps she could update me on this, and on whether the Government remain committed to PHBs for 1 million people by 2030 and for anyone who would benefit from them by 2035. Sadly, evidence from the Coalition for Personalised Care tells a different story. Since the restructure, hardly any ICBs have a named lead for PHB expansion. Without the dedicated NHS England team, PHBs have declined from 188,489 in 2023-24.

An NHS-funded PA/carer provides essential support for people with complex needs. I am here today contributing equally with your Lordships as a result of a PHB. I am fortunate. Denying portability effectively institutionalises a person at home. When systems dictate that people cannot travel or place rigid rules around support, they treat the home like a hospital ward, flying in the face of Article 19 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, ratified by the UK in 2009. I will therefore be scrutinising the Bill to ensure that integration and devolution to ICBs does not weaken PHB protections and freedoms. Choice must be safeguarded through stronger guidance, including a right to portability and flexibility. ICBs must not use residential care or budget withdrawal to coerce individuals.

Let us ensure that the medical model does not swallow decades of progress on disability rights and independent living. I am not a medical diagnosis but a wife, grandparent and working member of the House of Lords. ICBs would do well to reflect on that.

speaker: Lord Tarassenko
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, I also congratulate my noble friend Lord Wormald on his excellent and engaging speech informed by his eight and a half years as Permanent Secretary of the Department of Health and Social Care, working with, I believe, seven Secretaries of State during that time. I declare an interest as I have held an honorary contract with the Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust for the past decade enabling me to be an investigator on research projects involving patient data.

I welcome this Bill, especially the legal framework for sharing information through a single patient record. This represents a wonderful opportunity to improve patient care through the linking of multiple sources of health data, but delivering on this objective is fraught with technical difficulties and not just reading PDF files. Interoperability is an issue which continues to plague the NHS, and it is not clear yet how the single patient record data standards will be set, maintained and made binding on suppliers. There is also an opportunity to expand the legal framework underpinning the single patient record by giving our NHS data the status it deserves, making it a sovereign data asset at the core of an NHS digital sovereignty strategy. The first consequence of this would be a binding requirement for the single patient record data to be stored in servers located on British soil.

Secondly, we have been told by DHSC that there will be multiple contracts awarded for the development of the single patient record. An NHS digital sovereignty strategy would prioritise those technologies whose data, control and support remain within UK jurisdiction to reduce our reliance on foreign technologies within the NHS. The selection of Kainos Software Limited, a subsidiary of a FTSE 250 company, as the development partner for UK Biobank’s output checking system after a public procurement process shows that there are UK-owned companies capable of delivering state-of-the-art software solutions for the NHS.

We have been told that the use of data for research is not within the scope of the Bill, but the SPR systems, datasets and governance arrangements will also shape how health data is accessed and used for research. It would be a mistake, as the Health Data Research Service develops, not to address the barriers affecting this access. For example, the control of patient information—COPI—regulatory framework was first introduced as a temporary measure in 2002, more than 20 years ago, and we cannot wait for its reform to happen at some indeterminate time in the future. The Bill needs to set out a timetable for the Secretary of State to complete the process of reforming the COPI regime, following public consultation, within a fixed period of Royal Assent.

Recent polling has put the percentage of those willing to share their de-identified health records for research at between 75% and 80%, but such a high percentage depends on the public maintaining a high level of trust. Again, this will be easier if the single patient record is given the status of sovereign data asset that we all own within an NHS digital sovereignty strategy. A further implication of this status would be to set up a hierarchy of access to de-identified patient data from the single patient record for research, similar to that operated by MHRA for the primary care CPRD datasets, but expanded.

That should soon be followed by the development of our own sovereign AI model capability for the NHS, using longitudinal datasets from the single patient record, linking primary care and secondary care data with outcome data. These models would enable the early detection of diseases such as cancer and cardiovascular disease, and would contribute to the prevention agenda.

The use of the single patient record has the potential to improve direct patient care, but it is also an opportunity, through health data research, to make the UK a healthier nation at the end of the current 10-year plan for the NHS. We must not miss either opportunity.

speaker: Baroness Crawley
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, many congratulations to all our maiden speakers today. It is a special pleasure to follow the exceptional maiden speech of my noble friend Lord Smith of Ranmoor. His CV reads like the making of modern British food standards, but his emphasis on obesity means that I cannot now say that all of us who enjoy eating are very grateful to him.

A son of Sheffield and an alum of Leeds University, of which he is obviously extremely proud, my noble friend started his career at Northern Foods. He was appointed to the Food Standards Agency as CEO in 2008, after which he accepted a senior role at Tesco. He is now chair of Cranswick plc and one of the UK’s most experienced people in food retail.

Throughout his work with several Governments across parties, my noble friend has chaired the Trade and Agriculture Commission and has been co-chair of the Food and Drink Sector Council, among other significant posts. He is also a trustee of Natasha’s Foundation, the food allergy charity, which is very important in food safety today. I am sure all noble Lords will welcome my noble friend’s immense experience to our House and look forward to his many contributions to come.

I usually stay away from giving my opinion on health Bills; it is not my area of expertise and the NHS is challenged enough without my tuppence-worth. However, I could not stop myself with the Bill in front of us, because I was struck by its plan to enhance patient safety and the patient’s experience through a new single patient record—long in the making, as my noble friend Lady Jay said.

This record could transform patient care. As long as safeguards exist against cyber attacks and AI going rogue, and as long as transparency is always at the forefront of our mind with the creation of this record, patients will welcome it as much as we do tonight. I welcome my noble friend the Minister’s commitment to this specific part of the Bill in her opening remarks.

I support the Bill and its ambition. Of course, it has its critics. The trade union UNISON is concerned that the 10-year plan, which the Bill will make law, could produce a larger role for private healthcare. The Patients Association, while welcoming the Bill’s stated intention to put patients first and reduce bureaucracy, points out—as many noble Lords have—that

“any period of organisational change risks distracting from immediate patient care”.

I am sure my noble friend the Minister, who has a well-earned reputation for listening, will be aware of such concerns and will address them in her summing up.

As vice-president of RoSPA, the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents, along with the noble Baroness, Lady Watkins of Tavistock, and the noble Lord, Lord Jordan, our president, I saw in the proposed single patient record an opportunity for far more accurate and meaningful data than is currently the case: data from across the health service, to be used more effectively for patients’ well-being. As noble Lords will know, RoSPA’s mission is to campaign to prevent serious injury and save lives. However, as it stands, injury prevention is hindered by fragmented, incomplete and inconsistent NHS data. Data is often missing or provides only surface-level detail, which makes comprehensive injury prevention policies extremely difficult. As we know, information on injuries comes from multiple sources and agencies: hospitals, ambulance services, primary care, public health data, and so on. The Bill’s new information-sharing powers create a real opportunity not merely to further modernise digital records—to be fair, the old digital record has not always gone super smoothly—but to provide a stronger and safer evidence base for the prevention of accidents.

I will give noble Lords a couple of current examples. According to the latest NHS data, in 2024, seven people were admitted to hospital as a result of being bitten by a crocodile, two people were admitted for being bitten by a scorpion, and 53 people for being bitten by a rat. Three people were the victims of a volcanic eruption and 22 people were admitted to hospital due to a long stay in a weightless environment—I do not know what that means either. However, when it comes to falls, which are the biggest cause of accidental death and injury in this country, more than a third of admissions are recorded simply as “unspecified”. It cannot be right that we know more about injuries caused by crocodiles than we do about hundreds of thousands of falls, many of them affecting our ever-ageing population. During the passage of the Bill, will my noble friend the Minister meet me, the noble Baroness, Lady Watkins, and perhaps representatives of RoSPA to discuss how the Bill will improve the quality of injury data and, in doing so, enable prevention, save lives and reduce avoidable pressure on our overstretched NHS?

speaker: Baroness Martin of Brockley
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, it sounds like I am not alone in broadly welcoming the Bill. Many of its ambitions, not least the single patient record, are ones that I strongly support. Done well, the SPR will transform patient care, streamline decision-making and help realise the potential of the UK’s incredible health data, so I am delighted that this Government are grasping the nettle and getting on with it. The SPR helps to pave the way to use technology, specifically AI, more effectively to spot disease earlier, to personalise treatment and to help people stay well for longer.
