I would like us all to think more ambitiously about AI in health and across our public services.

But today I want to focus my remarks on two opportunities created by this Bill that can help support our economy. The first is research. Commercial clinical trials are a crucial feature of our health system. Just this morning I was at the Oak Cancer Centre at the Royal Marsden where they are researching and testing cutting-edge treatments that will improve survival rates and can transform the quality of life of cancer patients. However, clinical trials are important not only for patient outcomes. According to research for the ABPI by Frontier Economics, in 2022 alone industry clinical trials generated £7.4 billion-worth of GVA for the UK economy and created 65,000 jobs. The Bill rightly places a new duty on the Secretary of State to promote innovation, but it is essential that this duty at the top translates into delivery on the ground. That is why we need robust accountability mechanisms to ensure that ICBs build real capacity for clinical trial infrastructure. How will the Secretary of State work with ICBs to deliver on this vital duty?

The second opportunity is how we use health spending to help grow our economy. Health is one of the largest areas of public spending in this country. How that money is spent is one of the most powerful levers the Government possess to support innovation, back UK entrepreneurs and create good jobs in every part of the country. The Prime Minister understands this. At the innovation summit in Manchester on Friday, he was clear that this Government will, in his words,

“make British public procurement work harder”.

Indeed, the First Secretary of State has already taken welcome steps to reform central government procurement rules, and through the life sciences sector plan and DHSC’s SME action plan the direction of travel is clear. My concern is whether this Bill does enough to support the Government’s goal to use procurement to strengthen our economy.

As I have discovered over several increasingly acronym-heavy weeks, health procurement is pretty complicated, but the thing that is clear is that the Bill transfers vast commissioning responsibilities from NHS England to ICBs. The DHSC’s figures show that ICBs will control around 93% of NHS healthcare commissioning budgets. That is about £179 billion in the next financial year alone. That represents huge purchasing power. I asked my noble friend the Minister in correspondence whether ICBs fall within the Government’s SME procurement targets. I am grateful for her reply, but, sadly, it confirmed that they do not.

That is not the only area where there is a risk of a mismatch between rhetoric and action. When asked whether it would encourage contracts for the single patient record to be awarded to UK firms, the DHSC said that this was a matter for the Cabinet Office and that it was taking a “supplier-agnostic approach”. I understand and totally respect the importance of open competition, but if our flagship health technology programme cannot be used to back homegrown innovation, what can? I ask my noble friend the Minister whether the department will consider a system-wide stocktake of how health commissioning and procurement can better support UK enterprise and innovation so that this House and the public can see where the opportunities lie and how we can realise them.

Both points come down to a single principle: turning ambition into delivery. This Government have set out bold goals for an innovative NHS and for public procurement that drives British growth. I support both wholeheartedly, and I look forward to working constructively with my noble friend to help make them happen.

speaker: Baroness Kidron
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, I feel I should start by declaring that I have a son who is a senior civil servant in the Department of Health and Social Care, and also that I am not a health expert, so both he and the House will be pleased to know that my comments are entirely about the question of data.

The UK holds one of the world’s most valuable research assets in its health data, yet we risk both underusing and undervaluing it. Only this morning, 30 medical researchers wrote to me about their health data research service, a significant investment that promises to enable approved researchers to access UK health data safely and securely. These researchers, echoing concerns from NHS trusts, charities and the private sector, described a current environment with fragmented datasets, burdensome approvals and lengthy delays, sometimes requiring permissions for each dataset. They also suggest that these proposals come after research proposals in the 10-year health plan, the life sciences sector plan and the industrial strategy—plans that span departments and commitments from other arms-length bodies. Therefore, how the data is saved, secured and shared is material. Better access could transform UK research, discovery and growth, as the noble Baroness, Lady Martin, powerfully set out.

Our health data is not only underused but also undervalued. During the passage of the Data (Use and Access) Bill, I proposed, with the support of my noble friend Lord Tarassenko, a sovereign data asset class with NHS data a prime example. Since that time, contracts and memoranda of understanding have been signed with Palantir, OpenAI, Microsoft and Anthropic, each involving access to aspects of data held in trust for the public, including that in the NHS. The controversy over Palantir usefully illustrates worries of vendor lock-in, excessive access to UK datasets and products that underdeliver or cost too much. But my concern is more fundamental. We are spending hundreds of millions of pounds on technology that creates capability elsewhere. Why not use the expenditure on that scale to build sovereign capability of our own? We are an enormous purchaser of technology. Government procurement should not mean accepting whatever the market offers in health or anywhere else. It should establish purpose, contractual conditions, data standards and privacy, and help create capability that we retain here in the UK.

My third point of concern is about inquest data. Coroners identify patterns where systems have failed catastrophically. Taken together, their prevention of future death reports could provide a valuable resource for public health research, identifying emerging risks and preventable deaths. Yet, unlike Canada and Australia, the UK has no systematic means of collecting and accessing them. Dr Georgia Richards of King’s College London has set up the national coronial database to gather evidence. Her herculean task could become an effective system of prevention and public health and address the inequality that the Bill sets at its heart. I hope the Government will support an amendment to collect coronial reports systematically. It is a small measure with enormous consequences.

Finally, I want briefly to talk about emerging forms of data. Neurotechnology, including consumer devices capable of reading brain activity, is developing rapidly. According to UNESCO, global private investment in neurotechnology companies increased twentytwofold between 2010 and 2020, reaching approximately $7.3 billion annually. Harry Lambert, a barrister, founder of the Centre for Neurotechnology and Law, has written a series of fantastic articles in the New Law Journal about technology that we once associated with science fiction but is already here. It offers enormous opportunities for healthcare, but without swift action risks a dystopian future with unprecedented threats to privacy and freedom of thought.

Improving access to health data, retaining its value for the public, learning systematically from preventable death reports and updating the law for emerging technologies would ease frustration, prevent harm and create opportunity for the UK.

speaker: Lord Kamall
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, I begin by thinking the Minister for the way she introduced the Bill, and all noble Lords who spoke in this debate. For reasons which noble Lords will understand, I will not name them all, but I was particularly touched by the speech of the noble Baroness, Lady Campbell of Surbiton, in her own voice thanks to AI, and moved by the speech of the noble Baroness, Lady Barker, in which she shared her personal sad experience.

I thank those who made their maiden speeches, including the noble Lord, Lord Jabbar, who spoke of the need for accountability; the noble Baroness, Lady Lowe of Armley, who shared her experience of Touchstone in Leeds and the importance of the independent patient voice; the noble Lord, Lord Wormald, with whom I worked when I was a Health Minister; the noble Lord, Lord Smith of Ranmoor, who spoke of the importance of a healthy diet; and my noble friend Lord Singh of Solihull, who humbly shared a hint of his considerable experience in psychiatry. Each maiden speech demonstrated the experience and wisdom that we can look forward to in future debates. If it is any reassurance to the noble Lords, I often still wonder what I am doing here—and, frankly, if I go over my speaking time I fear that many noble Lords will ask the same question.

Before I go further, I declare my interest as a professor of politics and international relations at St Mary’s University in Twickenham, where I recently taught an MBA course in healthcare policy. I am also helping the university with its new medical school.

As my noble friend Lord Howe said, we on these Benches support removing the unnecessary duplication of functions between NHS England and DHSC, as most noble Lords do. But as we heard from the noble Lord, Lord Stevens, and others, the reorganisation was announced without any clear idea of the costs and benefits. My first question to the Minister is this: when will these costs and benefits be explicitly published, and when will the operational model referred to by the noble Baroness, Lady Pidgeon, be published, so that we can have a clearer idea of how this new world will work?

I do not doubt the Government’s good intentions, but legislation must be judged not on intentions but on whether it improves the patient experience and health outcomes. This means listening to patients when they tell us something is wrong and ensuring that those warnings result in change. That is precisely why an independent patient voice matters. As noble Lords have said, Healthwatch organisations provide that independent patient voice, gathering the experiences of patients and communities and ensuring that they are heard by those responsible. They speak truth to power.

While not perfect, the independent patient voice for health should not be seen as simply measuring satisfaction. It warns of failures in the quality and safety of care, and it raises flags for others to look at. Look at the volume of compensation from NHS Resolution, to the value of billions of pounds: behind each one of those figures are patients and families whose lives have been profoundly changed and, sadly, in many cases scarred. They may take many years to recover, if ever.

The Government’s proposals to bring that patient voice in-house to integrated care boards and local authorities raises important questions about independence. I understand the reasons for returning powers to Ministers, but if those responsible for a system are also responsible for gathering criticism of it, how can Ministers guarantee that patients will have the same confidence to speak candidly, especially those from more deprived communities who do not often get a chance to speak to those in power?

Given that the Prime Minister, when Mayor of Greater Manchester, wrote to the Secretary of State warning that dissolving Healthwatch would risk losing an independent and trusted patient voice, I wonder what conversations are ongoing within the new Government on proceeding with its abolition.

Similarly, we share the concerns of the noble Lord, Lord Hunt, about proposals to abolish independent health governors. They provide an important role in accountability and we must think very carefully about what happens if you remove that level of accountability.

That question of independence leads me to the proposed abolition of the Health Services Safety Investigations Body and transferring its functions to the CQC. HSSIB performs a different but equally important function, investigating patient safety concerns not to apportion blame or liability, and not to point fingers, but to understand systemic failures and prevent them happening again. Its investigations operate within statutory confidentiality protections.

Ministers have offered reassurance about maintaining autonomy, but legitimate questions remain. Will patients, families and healthcare professionals have the same confidence in the safe space principle when the investigating body sits within the regulator? How will its genuine independence be protected? These are questions that need to be answered.

And, frankly, is the CQC able and competent to take on these functions? During the Mental Health Bill, these Benches supported the Government on resisting calls for an independent mental health commissioner, instead supporting beefing up the CQC’s capacity on mental health. However, as the noble Lord, Lord Bradley, remarked, it is interesting that the Government have since decided to establish an independent maternity commissioner, rather than ask the Patient Safety Commissioner or the CQC to take on that role. Even more recently, I and other noble Lords have repeatedly tried to engage with the CQC on concerns that many healthcare providers have over the CQC’s understanding of, and its ability to regulate, sports and public events. To be frank, I have not been impressed. I do not say this lightly, but I currently have no confidence in the CQC to regulate these events.

It is worth noting that the widely respected incoming chair of the CQC, the noble Baroness, Lady Neuberger, told the Health and Social Care Committee only last month that the CQC was not currently a trusted and respected regulator. Given that assessment, what evidence can the Minister point to that demonstrates that the CQC is ready to take on the responsibilities currently held by HSSIB? The objective should be fewer safety failures, not fewer safety organisations.

A number of noble Lords have heard, and perhaps repeated, the mantra that you cannot solve healthcare until you fix social care. So we welcome the Prime Minister’s commitment to bring forward the Casey review, but I am sure that noble Lords will want to probe the Government further on their plans for social care during this Bill.

Like many other noble Lords, we support in principle the single patient record. As I found to my frustration when I was a Health Minister, patient information remains unconnected across different parts of the health and care system. The Government themselves note that clinicians can be left working with an incomplete picture while patients find themselves repeatedly giving the same medical history. A properly implemented single patient record could be transformative, giving clinicians access to the right information at the right time, improving continuity of care, supporting early intervention and ultimately improving patient safety.

But that does not mean that we will give the Government a blank cheque on this. There remain legitimate questions. Noble Lords may be aware of questions around what can be described as voyeur medical staff who access patient records after national scandals even though they have no medical reason to do so. Or there is the case of the senior consultant, as reported in the Guardian recently, who accessed and inappropriately shared the medical of information of her ex-boyfriend’s current girlfriend. Such stories beg the question of who will be able to access and edit a patient’s record. How will patients know who has accessed their records? In addition, how can inaccurate information be corrected, and what additional safeguards will protect particularly sensitive information?

I was contacted by a lady who found that notes from her psychotherapy at a south London trust, including correspondence on her concerns about a GP practice, were available through the London Care Record, including to the practice about which she had complained. She had been previously assured that this would not happen and she had to pause her therapy after making this discovery.

We are not against a single patient record. In fact, we are in favour of it, but there have to be the right safeguards. Different parts of the NHS continue to use different systems. Indeed, the Government acknowledge this, and so we have to look at this system of interoperability. While patients will benefit from a single patient record, they must have confidence that the most sensitive information that they provide will remain properly protected. Otherwise, we will be creating a health service that is better in sharing information but in which patients have less confidence.

We are discussing these reforms in the context of an ageing population, increased demand for health and care, a decline in people paying into the system relative to those who take out, and public scepticism about immigration to replace our ageing workforce and taxpayers. We have more doctors and nurses than ever before, but we need more capacity. The former Health and Social Care Secretary, Wes Streeting, recognised this and thought that AI could be the solution. But what are patients doing? They are turning to independent healthcare providers. This is not new. My father’s membership of the Transport and General Workers’ Union included treatment for him and my mother at an independent Premier Health hospital. Today, trade unions offer private health insurance or health plans as part of their membership package.

In seeking to increase the capacity supply of healthcare, is there a way that we can work together across the political divide on an increased role for non-state providers to complement the NHS, especially healthcare mutuals such as Benenden Health, charities, friendly societies, co-operatives, social enterprises, non-profit private providers and, where appropriate, private providers? If and where appropriate in this Bill, I hope we can agree to increase independent healthcare capacity to complement, not replace, the National Health Service. This will of course include appropriate access to the single patient record and appropriate safeguards.

These Benches accept that reform may deliver savings, yet we await a timeline and proper cost-benefit analysis. Removing unnecessary duplication, improving productivity and making better use of technology are objectives that we support, but the measure of successful reform is whether taxpayers receive value and patients receive better care. The prize is considerable, but so too is the responsibility. On these Benches, we will be constructive in our approach. Where the Government make a clear case, we will support them. Where we have concerns, we will challenge and scrutinise. We will work together with noble Lords across the House to deliver a Bill that enables a better system of healthcare for patients, no matter where they live and whatever their background.

speaker: Baroness Merron
heading: Health Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, I am grateful for the considered contributions from all sides of the House. They have, to put it mildly, been wide ranging, informative and challenging, as I would expect. I ask for the understanding of noble Lords that the time available to me will not allow me to answer every point made. Indeed, more questions will doubtless be unanswered than answered. But I restate my commitment to work with noble Lords as the Bill progresses and we will revisit many of the topics in the weeks to come.

I will also reflect on the points made, particularly those that are not within the remit of the Bill, because a number of them were extremely helpful. I make the general point that not all matters that have been raised, as I know noble Lords are aware, are for primary legislation or necessarily for this Bill, though I blame not one noble Lord for taking the opportunity to raise them. Again, that is as I would expect. We should also resist the urge to do something here in legislation when there are other means that could achieve the same outcome, as is usual when it comes to legislation. There are quite a lot of health warnings there.

I particularly thank noble Lords who brought not only their professional experience but their personal experience or that of those who are near and dear to them. They included my noble friend Lord Winston, the noble Baronesses, Lady Maclean, Lady Barker and Lady Grey-Thompson, and the noble Lords, Lord Bird and Lord Scriven. Our personal experiences absolutely inform how we see the way forward. I also associate myself with the congratulations on five excellent maiden speeches, from my noble friends Lord Jabbar, Lady Lowe and Lord Smith, and the noble Lords, Lord Wormald and Lord Singh. I associate myself with many of the points made by our new colleagues, including that where we start does not determine where we have to end up—that resonates very much with me—and that we should be proud of those who work in public service, and indeed we are. We are blessed to have all five of our new colleagues join us in your Lordships’ House and we very much look forward to hearing more from them.

A number of points have been made about where the National Health Service is at present, and it is important to make a few comments. I welcome those who have acknowledged the improvements that we have made and the position that we started from. As of March this year, we had met the interim target of 65% of patients waiting up to 18 weeks, when we were nowhere near that just over two years ago, and we will go further. Patient satisfaction is rising. When I was a Health Minister in the previous Labour Government, it was at its highest, but sadly it went to its lowest. We are rebuilding that, and I am glad about the improvement.

Similarly, this summer, in June, July and August—noble Lords will know the extra pressure of the heatwaves that were experienced then—a record 4.7 million-plus treatments, procedures and appointments were carried out, more than in any previous summer. I would be happy to bore your Lordships’ House, if that is what it does to the House, with more evidence of the upward trajectory, but it is only fair not to talk down the NHS where we have improvements, and I am glad that so many noble Lords acknowledged that.

I shall run through some of the points that were raised. I was most grateful for what I will call broad support for the Bill. There were many supporters, including my noble friends Lord Hunt and Lady Thornton, who both set out better than I would—so I do not need to repeat it—the impact of previous legislation and changes to the structure of the NHS. I also heard support from the noble Baronesses, Lady Coffey and Lady Neville-Rolfe, among others.

I have heard the argument that much of this could be done without legislation. I suggest that it is far better for the law to reflect the reality of the system that we want, one that has clear roles and responsibilities. To make the point, as many noble Lords have supported the abolition of NHS England: that cannot be abolished without primary legislation.

With regard to transition arrangements, points were raised by the noble Baronesses, Lady Gerada and Lady Wyld, and the noble Lord, Lord Scriven, among others. We are committed to transparency and parliamentary scrutiny throughout this process. We will continue to publish updates and revised impact assessments, and we will expect to be held to account, as I know noble Lords would expect.

There are strong arrangements in place to monitor delivery, including oversight of workforce risks, knowledge transfer and service continuity, but these changes are not distracting from our focus on performance. I understand why that concern was raised, as I understand the reasons for all the concerns that were raised today, and I know we will work through them all. This summer, as I mentioned, has been the busiest in the history of the NHS, yet more patients than ever before were seen within four hours in A&E despite record demand.

With regard to costs, savings and benefits, which were raised particularly by the noble Earl, Lord Howe, and the noble Lords, Lord Stevens and Lord Kamall, with the abolition of NHSE and the restructuring of ICBs we expect savings of up to £1 billion a year by the end of this Parliament. That will be driven primarily by reductions in headcount, and we expect that savings will build year on year rather than being realised immediately.

On the impact assessment, as usual the focus will be on the impacts of primary legislation rather than secondary and consequential decisions. Our approach to the impact assessment—which the noble Lord, Lord Stevens, kindly raised—is in line with the HM Treasury Green Book guidance and the Better Regulation Framework, as I am sure noble Lords recognise.

I was glad that my noble friend Lord Carter made the point about the need to rightly be focused on outputs. The input of money has clearly not delivered what any of us would have wanted over some considerable time, and our focus on and measurement of outputs is absolutely crucial.

I confirm to my noble friend Lady Nargund that, as I said earlier, integrated care boards will be the strategic commissioners of health services. They will take ownership of areas that are currently delegated to them, such as primary medical care and dentistry, as well as delegated specialist services, such as adult HIV services—as was raised by the noble Lord, Lord Black, and the noble Baroness, Lady Barker—and dialysis. To support ICBs and ensure national consistency, we will use the power of direction over ICBs to set out the expectations of, for example, access criteria or the types of services to be commissioned.

On ICB membership, the Bill will reform the required membership of ICB boards to align them more closely with their role as strategic commissioners. I assure my noble friend Lord Bradley that the requirement for a member of an ICB to have mental health experience—as he referred to—remains unchanged.

On the accountability of ICBs—which was raised by the noble Earl, Lord Howe, and the noble Baronesses, Lady Redfern, Lady Walmsley, and Lady Shawcross-Wolfson—integrated care board commissioning will continue to have clear performance and accountability arrangements in legislation, including a requirement to publish annual reports and accounts setting out how they have discharged their functions and delivered against their targets.

I wrote a very long list of noble Lords who referred to Healthwatch and the patient voice. I had to strike a pen through that, because, unsurprisingly, nearly every noble Lord referred to it. We do not believe that the current structures consistently and effectively connect patient voice or lived experience to the decisions that shape services and deliver outcomes. As I mentioned earlier, our feeling is that, by placing responsibility directly with ICBs and local authorities, we will enable patient insight to inform commissioning, service planning and improvement. That said, we recognise—as I said at the outset and re-emphasise now—the strength of feeling about these changes and the reasons that noble Lords are raising their concerns. I have already stated our commitment to work with noble Lords to review these measures and ensure that any arrangements really do empower local communities and provide transparency on what people have told the system and on how it responded. This is an area for further work.

A number of noble Lords—including the noble Baronesses, Lady Manzoor, Lady Pidgeon and Lady Watkins, and the noble Lords, Lord Patel and Lord Lansley—raised HSSIB and patient safety. As I stated at the outset, I cannot overemphasise our commitment to listening to noble Lords on this important matter. I want to see a strong link between investigation, system learning and improvement, and helping safety insights lead more directly to lasting change. I agree that patient safety depends on a culture in which concerns can be raised, lessons are learned and meaningful improvement follows. I therefore emphasise our commitment to listening further to noble Lords.

Most noble Lords, rightly, also raised the single patient record. I am grateful to the noble Lord, Lord Kamall, and the noble Baroness, Lady Pidgeon, for their support from their Front Benches for this, which is central to our ambition for a modern, joined-up NHS. I know that noble Lords understand the reason that we have raised it.

The noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, was helpful in raising the important issue of health data for research. We know that data from the single patient record could offer significant opportunities, including more intelligently planning our health services and conducting life-saving research. However, the primary focus of the SPR is to offer and support direct care. The Bill does not create any new legal gateways to accessing health data for secondary purposes, such as planning and research, important though they are; nor does it enable data to be collected for these purposes. But it does contain a savings provision that the SPR can be a source of data for secondary uses, such as planning and research, where there is a separate legal basis to do so. This will ensure that we do not miss opportunities but guarantee that strict legal security and confidentiality standards—which are the concerns, rightly, of noble Lords—are met. That will include existing data protection legislation.

I heard noble Lords, including the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, and the noble Lord, Lord Kamall, among others, raise important points about data, security, public trust and privacy. When it comes to health data in particular, trust is everything, as many noble Lords, including the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, have said, which is why the SPR will be designed with the highest standards of cybersecurity and information governance. Let me emphasise this: access to patient information will be restricted to authorised users only, with an audit trail of who has accessed the patient’s data, to clamp down on some of the serious transgressions that we have seen of late. I will come back to the noble Lord, Lord Patel, on the point about the common law duty of confidentiality.

With regard to the federated data platform, I heard concerns from the noble Lord, Lord Scriven, and the noble Baroness, Lady Bennett, about Palantir. Let me say again that the single patient record is different; it is intended that it will be delivered through contracts with multiple suppliers. I heard my noble friend Lady Martin’s wish that those would be UK providers, on which I certainly would share her wish and intent.

On women’s health and maternity, I am grateful for the acknowledgement from a number of noble Lords, including the noble Baronesses, Lady Wyld, Lady Sugg, Lady Manzoor, Lady Pidgeon, Lady Hodgson, and others. I appreciate the acknowledgement of the work that has already taken place and the direction that the Government are taking. We are, as we speak, working up the amendments for the maternity and neonatal commissioner. I look forward to engaging further on this, because it is a priority of this Government to urgently tackle the systemic issues across maternity and neonatal care which have been going on for so many years and are totally unacceptable.

By the end of the year, we will be publishing a single national action plan. It will be overseen by the national maternity and neonatal taskforce, and it will drive improvement in maternity and neonatal care exactly where it matters—to families, to clinicians and to others. The plan will include recommendations from the independent investigation of the noble Baroness, Lady Amos. We are most grateful to the noble Baroness for her work. It will include findings from the Thirlwall report and from the reviews led by Donna Ockenden. We need a single national action plan which will fundamentally drive a systemic and sustained improvement that we have not seen. The taskforce will hold the system to account, and I look forward to this House holding us to account as well.

The issue of health inequalities was raised by the right reverend Prelate, the noble Baronesses, Lady Hollins, Lady Cass and Lady Tyler, and my noble friend Lord Sahota. The Bill reaffirms our commitment to achieving greater equality in the provision of health services—both the ability to access these services and the outcomes achieved. ICBs will lead on improving services because of their clarified role as strategic commissioners. However, they have to deliver demonstrable improvements for disadvantaged groups and underserved communities, including those in the rural, coastal and deprived urban areas.

We will also, as part of our 10-year health plan, distribute NHS funding to better align it with health need. That includes establishing a neighbourhood health centre in every community, beginning with—not ending with—places where health and life expectancy is lowest.

Briefly, on adult social care, our commitment, emphasised by the Prime Minister, is on building a national care service, and that is why we have brought forward the timetable for the vital independent commission of the noble Baroness, Lady Casey. In the meantime, we are acting on early recommendations, including on dementia, motor neurone disease and safeguarding.

I assure your Lordships’ House that the mental health investment standard will continue to apply, in the same way that this Government are committed to improving outcomes and reducing health inequalities for those with learning disabilities, autistic people and people with ADHD, as acknowledged by the noble Baronesses, Lady Hollins, Lady Browning and Lady Leaman.

I am immensely grateful to noble Lords for their contributions in what has been a very helpful debate. I note, as others have done, that the Bill marks another ground-breaking moment for this House: the first use of AI, to give voice to the noble Baroness, Lady Campbell—I know that she is watching us online. I pay tribute, as we all do, to the work that the noble Baroness has done to make the rules of this Chamber more accessible. We are all very fond of Baroness Campbell mark 1, and we are looking forward to getting even more fond of Baroness Campbell mark 2, as she referred to her AI voice. Let us hear more of it. I assure her that we remain committed to personalisation and personal health budgets, as in the 10-year plan.

I know that we will continue these discussions in Committee, both in and outside the Chamber. For now, I commend the Bill to the House.

Bill read a second time.

speaker: Max Wilkinson
subheading: Police Funding: North-east England — [Pete Wishart in the Chair]
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Mr Wishart. I commend the hon. Member for North Durham (Luke Akehurst) for securing this debate. I begin by putting on the record my party’s thanks and admiration for our police services up and down the country, and for the vital role that officers play in keeping our communities safe.

The tragic A66 collision that claimed the lives of two police officers, Matthew Blades and Tom Clough, horrified us all. The disorder that followed in the days after that tragedy disturbed people far beyond the north-east, and we must hope it has brought renewed focus on the area’s safety. I commend all the MPs from the region who have spoken so powerfully with one voice in this debate today.

This summer’s disorder underlines the importance of having a police service that is properly resourced, that is visible and that is trusted by the communities it serves. We have long called for a return to genuine community policing, focused on preventing crime through policing that builds relationships with local communities.

Just a few days ago, I was in the north-east, in Peterlee, to appear on a televised political panel debate. It was clear that crime is a real concern for residents in that area. Indeed, it was raised by the audience member who asked the first question. The audience spoke about the impact on their communities and the underlying causes, including the fact that many communities have been hollowed out economically over the last few decades. What came across was a deep frustration and, very sadly, a sense of helplessness from those in the room.

Police presence must be part of the focus to address the concerns of residents across the north-east. Under the Conservatives, Cleveland police lost hundreds of officers—I think around 400—and after the disorder this summer, 200 officers had to be drafted in to deal with what unfolded. This is not an acceptable state of affairs. The Liberal Democrats welcome the Government’s pledge to recruit 13,000 additional police officers, but police numbers have sadly not matched the Government’s ambition. If the Government are serious about restoring neighbourhood policing, they must get more officers back on to our streets, and they will need to recruit many more. We cannot expect overstretched officers to do more with less, as other Members have said, and too many crimes go unsolved.

We hear about these issues regularly in relation to the north-east and elsewhere; they are common to so many places across the country. The Government will tell us that they have increased national police funding, but with reference to the north-east, Cleveland’s funding increase is the lowest in the country, worth £1.65 million a year less than if it had received the 4.5% average increase. On top of that, Cleveland police is being asked to find £3.88 million of savings to balance its budget. Regardless of the regional issue, it is clear that policing must refocus on finding more resources and making the best of the resources it has.

There is also the issue that a huge amount of police time is taken up by online crime, principally fraud but also including child sexual exploitation and violence against women and girls. Unfortunately, the companies that facilitate this behaviour have not acted strongly enough to prevent it from happening. That is why the Liberal Democrats are calling for a new police agency to tackle serious online crime, funded by a levy on big tech and AI companies. Will the Minister commit to taking steps to ensure that the companies that facilitate online crime are called to account and asked to pay for some of the problems that they create, on a “polluter pays” basis? That would help to redirect police resourcing to the frontline, to build and maintain the physical policing presence that our communities rightly expect. It would help to restore a police counter in every community, giving people accessible, convenient places to share information and engage with the police within their communities.

The Government talk about their neighbourhood policing guarantee, but we now need to see change in our communities. We believe that our proposals can help. One other concern lies in police force reorganisation. If merging forces means that officers become more distant from the communities they serve or are less able to respond to local crime—or, indeed, if three underfunded forces become one massive underfunded force—the reforms will have failed. Will the Minister ensure that police reform does not lead to resources being directed away from smaller communities, which are often in rural areas, to larger urban centres? That is particularly important for the rural communities we have heard about today, where crime has become increasingly organised, serious and persistent. We are calling for a countryside copper guarantee, with properly resourced, dedicated rural crime teams or specialists in every police force. Will the Minister commit to ensuring that forces serving rural areas have the resources they need?

Finally, transferring police and crime commissioners’ powers to mayors without sufficient democratic scrutiny risks replacing one flawed model with another. Local crime and police boards made up of local residents and representatives of the community can provide meaningful local accountability and oversight of policing. Is that being considered by Ministers in their police reforms? That is vital, because only by empowering communities to work with local police will we reduce crime across the country, including in the north-east.

speaker: Anne Webster
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
text:
I will speak about this government's utter disregard for our farmers shortly, but I want to focus now on small businesses because the warning lights are flashing and the sirens are going off. Labor's attacks on small business have reached emergency levels. Over 29,000 companies have entered external administration for the first time in the last two years, and nearly 25 per cent of those companies are in construction. I thought that was important to this government. Accommodation and food service accounted for nearly 15 per cent. This equates to about 39 companies per day going into administration. While the Treasurer wants to tell us and his party what a magnificent job he's doing, the facts do not lie. I want to point out to those opposite that the figures I've just quoted are about people. They're about families. They're about communities. When a business closes its doors, it impacts many, who no longer can have a job and can no longer pay their mortgage or their rent or children's school fees.

New COSBOA research released today paints a sobering picture. The typical small-business revenue has been swallowed up by inflation—revenue, not profit, for those opposite that are business illiterate. Only around one in four owners are paying themselves more than they were a year ago. What are the other three quarters actually paying themselves? Those opposite like to go on about minimum wages. Is there a minimum wage for a small-business owner? No, there isn't. Around two in five small-business owners are working more hours, and one in four worked longer hours for no additional pay. It's little wonder business owners turned to AI after Labor's toxic taxes on trusts to depict their new business partner, the Prime Minister, demanding his cut of the business. All the while, the Albanese Labor government has presided over 16 interest rate rises since taking office, which again undermines business profitability through higher debt costs and makes supplies more expensive.

Those opposite appear to be utterly against business profit altogether, as though even one cent of profit is a bad thing. Of course, none of the Labor cabinet have small-business experience. Talk about a lack of diversity! Small-business owners have rapidly shrinking profits to draw a wage for their own labour in the business and that of their spouse, partner or other family members. Even if they take some wage from the business, can the small-business owner deliver some return on the family's investment and the risk they carry, like putting their savings or home on the line?

And now the Albanese Labor government is forcing small-business owners to absorb more costs. Nobody likes credit card surcharges, but abolishing the surcharge does not abolish the merchant fee. The Reserve Bank says small businesses tend to pay the highest card payment fees. Banning businesses imposing surcharges from 1 October is not immediately matched with the savings intended for small businesses—the quid pro quo, if you like, to reduce interchange fees and similar costs. Over 97 per cent of all Australian businesses are small businesses. There are over 2.6 million of them employing 5.1 million people and generating $600 billion in economic value. Small businesses are left with no choice but to raise prices.

This toxic, untruthful Albanese Labor government is adding insult to injury, at first defending the ATO's credit card payment ban, which would mean more costs brought forward for small businesses. Following the backlash, Labor has reached into taxpayer pockets to postpone that ATO policy bomb until 30 June 2027. They have the power to call it off for six months. That means they have the power to stop it altogether. Where is the Treasurer on this? Labor is starving small business to death.

speaker: David Farley
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
text:
Australia faces a test of governance that has received far too little attention. It's not a test of ambition. Our ambitions are aspirational. It's a test of whether anyone is actually doing the planning. The nation has set itself a series of goals, like stronger GDP growth. We're committed to population growth and all the demands of housing and food production that come with it. We have embraced with considerable enthusiasm the rise of artificial intelligence and the data centres that sustain it—defensible goals. Yet each draws on the same two finite resources: water and electricity. That is the policy problem that has not been confronted.

AEMO forecasts that data centres will rise from about three per cent of grid demand today to 13 per cent by 2036, totalling 34 terawatt hours a year. That is roughly the consumption of every household in New South Wales and Victoria combined. Meeting it will clearly require eight to 10 gigawatts of new generation and storage at a cost of $20 billion to $30 billion before the substantial investment in transmission lines estimated at circa $150 billion of total capital requirement. Sydney Water warns that under evaporative cooling data centres' demands could reach 90 billion litres a year by 2035, between 15 and 20 per cent of Sydney's drinking supply.

These figures raise three questions that go to the heart of national policy. First, who is forecasting, designing and costing this demand and who will finance the supply? Second, who are the customers that will service that capital? Investment of this scale is always repaid by someone. Third and more importantly, who will be displaced? Food producing irrigators, manufacturers and households all face the prospect of higher costs or exclusion as new demand bids for the same resources. Markets are efficient at price discovery. They are not designed to weigh fairness, regional consequence or national cohesion. That is the proper role of government. Either government asserts a planning framework with the foresight, investment and pricing policy to preserve a level playing field for food production, food processing, homes and business, or it allows the market to allocate our water and power by price alone and accepts the casualties that follow.

A nation is more than a balance sheet; it's a compact between its people, its elected government and its enterprise. So I ask the question: who is the architect of Australia's supply and demand? It's obviously not the government continually caught on the back step, chasing the future instead of making it.

speaker: Gabriel Ng
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
text:
I rise today to deliver a speech written by Zihan, a young person from my community as part of the Raise Our Voices campaign. Zihan writes:

Misinformation, hallucinations, AI slop. This is what your average Australian high school student is consuming daily. As a 16-year-old, I see the consequences of AI abuse everywhere. My classmates struggling in maths turn to AI, receive completely wrong answers, yet trust them completely simply because they came from AI. This is unacceptable and will only plague our education system moving forward. We are still students. But when I check the news, I constantly see companies laying off workers because of AI.

As our world becomes increasingly AI-driven, one crucial skill we all need is AI literacy: the ability to understand AI, use it safely and effectively and critically evaluate its outputs. That is why I advocate for AI literacy education to be implemented in the curriculum for all Australian high school students. I want a future where students use AI to aid their learning, not replace it. I want a future where they can safely use AI in their careers rather than fear it. I want a future where AI is not an enemy of teachers, but a tool that works alongside them to help students build a better future. Thank you.

Thank you, Zihan, for your intelligent and thoughtful contribution. Parliament really appreciates it.

speaker: Jason Dean Clare
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank my friend the magnetic member for Menzies for his question. If you want to get an idea about the impact that artificial intelligence has in our schools, check this out. China has just done a study on artificial intelligence involving 26,000 high school students. What it found is that, when they used AI, homework marks increased by 18 per cent and it reduced exam marks by 20 per cent. So you can see what's happening here in terms of what kids are learning and what they're not. I've spoken here in the parliament and outside the parliament in the last few weeks about why we need a digital detox in our schools, about how the evidence is showing us that the more time children have behind a screen the more likely it is that their results will decline and that they'll fall behind, about the impact it has on concentration and about how it's frying the attention spans of our kids.

There's a reckoning coming here. It's not just about screen time or screen limits in our schools. It's also about what we do with AI. There's a reason why we don't give kids calculators in kindergarten. They've got to learn how to count before we give them the tools to do it at speed. They've also got to learn how to think. Working things out manually is a bit like taking your brain to the gym. You've got to develop those mental muscles and learn critical-thinking and problem-solving skills. There's a fair bit of evidence now that AI can undermine this. It what's called cognitive stunting. That's why a number of jurisdictions across the world, including New York and LA, have just hit the pause button on the use of AI in primary schools. So, when ministers come together in a couple of weeks to talk about a digital detox, we'll look at all of these things, including screen times and AI. This is all about helping to make sure that our kids learn when they're at school.

We've also got to make sure that we protect them when they're online. That's what the digital duty of care bill that is getting introduced tomorrow is all about. It puts the onus on tech companies to take reasonable steps to make sure that our children aren't exposed to pornography, things that glorify crime, things that promote eating disorders or things that teach boys to hate girls. No parent wants their kids exposed to this sort of sick stuff. They expect us to act here. This is not political censorship. This is about protecting our kids.

speaker: David Farley
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: My question is to the Minister of Communications. Can you confirm that sections 205H and 205J of the draft digital duty of care bill provide an absolute exemption from all laws and civil proceedings, including the Privacy Act, for the government to use false and fictitious AI powered sock puppet accounts to post information and engage with and surveil conversations with Australians online?

speaker: Fatima Payman
heading: DOCUMENTS
subheading: Cybersafety Legislation; Order for the Production of Documents
text:
I move:

That the Senate take note of the explanation.

When you make a mistake, you should own up to it. In August, officials from the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts told the Senate Environment and Communications Legislation Committee that certain broken links in the Ageassurance technology trial report were not broken at the time the report was handed over. This evidence, the department said, was based on evidence from the company behind the report, the UK-based Age Check Certification Scheme. It was later revealed that ACCS had lied to the Guardian Australia and Australian age-check provider KJR by claiming that AI had not been used in the preparation of the report when, in fact, it had. When asked whether the department had verified that the links had only become broken after the report was presented, an official grumbled, 'It's very difficult to go back and check what may have been replaced a year ago.'

Now, I'm not normally one to put on the tinfoil hijab, but there was something off about all this. So I took on this 'difficult task' and investigated the department's claim. Using a digital library of archived webpages, I was able to confirm that these links pointed to the wrong papers when they were supposedly accessed and when the report was handed to government. Dr Reuben Kirkham, a former computer science academic, told the committee that the existence of this archival evidence 'puts the position beyond any real doubt'.

I noted in a dissenting report that, on evidence I had seen, ACCS had misled the department and that, based on this misleading advice, the department had misled the committee. I do not believe that the department set out to mislead the committee, but I did describe the failure of the department to verify ACCS's claim as a serious dereliction of duty and recommended that the department review the incident to determine whether a breach of the APS Code of Conduct had occurred. Not only was I able to disprove the department's claim but I was able to do it so very easily. Aren't these guys supposed to be the experts? I understand that these are very serious allegations, and I do not make them lightly.

In response, the secretary of the department wrote to the chair of the committee about this issue. The secretary wrote:

I do not accept the conclusion that officials are failing in their duties if they give evidence to a committee based on advice provided to them that, at face value, can be accepted as accurate.

The representations made by officials were based on information available to them at the time and were honestly and reasonably held.

There was not one word contesting what I had said, but nor was there one word taking accountability for providing misleading evidence to a committee of the Senate. There was no acknowledgement that these officials had provided false evidence based on advice from ACCS, who have lied to multiple parties, including the government, about this report. It doesn't seem like ACCS will be penalised for this, which sends an unacceptable message: you can win contracts paid by the taxpayer, deliver shoddy work, lie to the government about it and get away with it. There won't even be a departmental investigation. It just isn't good enough. It's inevitable that the department's evidence will be revealed to be, without a doubt, incorrect. Despite this, the department has yet to acknowledge its misleading evidence, let alone apologise to the committee. Even the liars at ACCS have come out and apologised for what they now describe as 'outdated or incorrect links'. This saga of obfuscation will be for nothing.

When I brought to the attention of the Commonwealth Grants Commission that it appeared to have provided misleading evidence to the Economics Legislation Committee during estimates, it was quick to not only clarify what its evidence should have been but apologise for the error. This is the gold standard for APS accountability. Meanwhile, the department has provided incomplete responses to questions on notice and dragged out FOI timelines. It has failed to take accountability for the mistakes it has made. Years from now, these actions will make for an unseemly tale of resistance to scrutiny.

speaker: Don Farrell
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: I thank Senator Polley for her first supplementary question. As you say, the opposition may not be listening, but the Australian people are. The Australian people are listening because the Albanese government backed parents when it came to delaying access to social media for children under 16, and we have heard from them about how relieved they are. But we know they still are worried about how they can protect their kids on other platforms, like online games and AI chatbots. Under the digital duty of care, platforms, like social media, online games and AI chatbots, must protect under-18s from harmful content, like content that promotes or encourages eating disorders, misogynistic content that promotes hostile ideas about women and gender—

speaker: Tim Ayres
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE: ADDITIONAL ANSWERS

speaker: Jonathon Duniam
heading: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION
text:
Well, thank you, President. What a segue! It's always a big job to follow Senator McGrath—what can I say—but what a wonderful introduction.

Ten years, one month and 13 days ago, I stood not here in this place but somewhere over there and I delivered my first speech to the Senate. In that first speech, I finished up by quoting my late grandmother, a former Labor candidate—and of course everyone has their flaws! She was a super mum and also Burnie councillor, Iris Graham OAM, whose motto for life was 'deeds, not words'. For the last 10 years, that expression has stayed with me and has been a guide on how I hoped to conduct myself as a senator for the state of Tasmania. And, while of course it will be for others to judge—and I'm sure they will—whether or not I've done that, I can say today that I've actually given this job everything I have. Nonetheless, it seems only fair that the words of my grandmother that she lived by should be the test against which I am judged.

I should point out that, in preparing for today and looking back at my first speech those years ago, it was clear to me just how very little I knew about life on the day I arrived, how ill-prepared I was for what awaited me. Still, as I reflected, I think my north star was right and my hopes for my country and the people I was going to represent remained the right ones.

In trying to sum up my time in this place and bring it to an end, I'm not sure my words will ever adequately cover the many reflections, the thoughts and feelings I have as I prepare to leave. To represent one's fellow Australians in this place is a serious role, and it is truly the honour of a lifetime. If you take it seriously, it in turn will take most of you. And that is indeed what actually puts a use-by date on this job.

When a new senator arrives, you never know what to expect—what challenges you'll confront, what opportunities will present themselves, how difficult some days will be or, indeed, how satisfying it is when you get things done for your community. Indeed, when I arrived 10 years ago, I could not have predicted the twists and turns or the challenges our country would face during my time here. I should have known, though, because when I came in I came in as part of that upheaval that was the double dissolution election. I should have known right then that nothing was going to be straightforward. It was only about a year later that, of course, we had the massive change through our parliament as a result of the constitutional and citizenship crisis that turned our parliament on its head. We then had the seismic events of COVID that changed how we lived and how our country functioned. Some of the scars of that time I don't think many Australians will ever heal from. Indeed, along this journey there have been challenges we face globally, including conflict overseas and international economic challenges that we can't hide from, no matter how well insulated we think we are. There of course has also been the odd leadership change too, just in case anyone was bored with Australian politics at any given point; they certainly do spice things up!

I, for one, can't forget the events of the end of last year, when 15 innocent people lost their lives simply because of who they were. The road that led to those events and the pain felt since that time—the most significant terror attack on our shores in our nation's history—has left a mark on our nation forever. All of this has been against the backdrop of a media landscape that is very different to how it was when I arrived. At an ever-increasing pace, we have a vociferously hungry press gallery needing updates and answers to questions 24 hours a day. While I've enjoyed having my weekends interrupted by my friends in the press gallery, I'm not so sure I'm going to miss your Sunday morning calls anymore. Social media, too, has become a hungry beast that needs to be fed lest the void be filled by others who may not share your views or interests.

Challenge and change have been a hallmark of recent times in Australian politics, like never before, and how we handle these tests is how we will be judged. Right now, the challenges that face us are many and varied, and it doesn't matter where you sit on the political spectrum; there is generally an acceptance of what the problems are. The difference comes in how we respond, which, in our adversarial parliamentary system, is what writes our political epitaph. I've long said that there are three parts to being a politician: (1) travel, which sucks, (2) politics, and I don't mean the good kind, and (3) being a problem-solver, which I think is the best part of the job. The most important role any of us will ever have, no matter where we actually sit in this chamber, is that of problem-solver—perhaps for an individual constituent, a community group, a part of the economy or maybe the entire nation. Sometimes I think that role does get lost in the work that we do here, but it's important to remind ourselves of that essential anchor in elected life.

I've had the tremendous blessing of being appointed to various leadership, ministerial and shadow ministerial roles over my decade here, and I do thank the leaders of my party for entrusting me with these roles over time. I certainly did become a jack-of-all-trades while I was here, whether it was forestry, fisheries, tourism, industry development, education and early learning, Home Affairs or immigration. All those different portfolios always required the same discipline and the same KPI: understand your portfolio, identify the problems, find a solution, communicate it to the electorate and hope it translates into trust. Then, hopefully, people will cast a vote for you and your party. While I've prided myself on my own work ethic and on abiding by those rules, that pattern has obviously only worked to a limited degree, given I find myself in opposition. I'm not going to rattle off a mundane list of things I've done or policies or projects I've been a part of delivering; they stand for themselves. But I do want to thank the hundreds, maybe thousands, of amazing Australians I've met, over time, who've driven change and innovation and were the inspiration behind the projects that I've supported.

Not wasting time and getting the most out of the time we have here, which is limited for all of us, is paramount. Indeed, right up until my last day, I've been making the most of the time I have. Last week, I was proud to be a part of the work led by Angus Taylor on the coalition's immigration policy. While not everyone will agree with our approach or the intended outcome, I'm proud of the work and the professional, robust policy that the opposition has put forward. The problem our country is facing is patently clear, and now we've offered our solution for Australians to consider ahead of the next election.

Earlier, I mentioned the unexpected nature of the challenges and opportunities we confront over time. As my time as a member of this parliament draws to a close, we are presented with one of the most capacious opportunities I believe we will see in our lifetimes, and that is the rise and proliferation of artificial intelligence. It is coming whether we like it or not, and, to some extent, it is already here. The choice we have is whether we take the opportunity that AI is presenting on our terms or have those terms dictated to us. It is my ardent belief that we as a nation must chart our course this year—lay down the rules, structures, policies and arrangements to facilitate the best possible outcome for AI take-up in our country. The work I've been able to help lead on the multipartisan committee examining AI has provided a blueprint for us to follow, and I want to thank the Prime Minister's Office for spellchecking my work and for leaving track changes on. I'm also grateful to a certain crossbench senator for picking up on the PMO's work picking up my typos.

Seriously, though, the economic opportunities and the national security imperative depend on us getting this right. That was the aim of the committee's letter. We should not be distracted from that. If we don't get it right, we will not only miss the boat on enormous potential, but we will also be exposed to our adversaries who will, with malevolent intent, take advantage and equip themselves with the power of AI. This is not a call for a blank cheque but a call to recognise the urgency to get this done on our terms.

Good friends are essential in this place and—contrary to popular belief—there are good people here. Indeed, in my view, they are the majority. It's impossible to be friends with everyone, and indeed anyone who tries is a fool, though it's not impossible to seek to find ways to get along despite the differences that may exist. Of course, we all have our trusted friends and colleagues, people we confide in, people we turn to for advice and those we can vent to at the end of a long day. Having a war cabinet you can rely on is essential, and I want to turn to my Canberra family. Matt O'Sullivan and Andrew Hastie have been brothers that have given me a boost and helped me grow in ways that are hard to describe. Your godly counsel and friendship will remain a cornerstone for me in life well beyond parliament. Though I have to say it remains one of life's great mysteries: how did two men with full heads of hair—I'm exhibit A—end up sharing a bathroom when the man with no hair got a bathroom of his own? To what is left of that original grouping of formerly younger senators, soon to be known as the G4, James Paterson, Claire Chandler, who is soon to be a mother, and Slade Brockman, thank you for your friendship. I look forward to supporting you from outside this place.

Indeed, I spoke earlier about the unknowns and uncertainties when you come into this place. All of this has been softened and made easier by those who sit around me. My colleagues from the Liberal and National parties have very much become family, from mad uncles to annoying cousins through to siblings you look forward to seeing. This team of whom I'm proud to be a part has helped me get the most out of every day here and actually enjoy it more than I otherwise would have. I say thank you to my team for your grace when I stuff up, for laughing at my jokes on cue, but importantly for making up the fantastic team that works so well together. I'd love to name all of you, but I think, given our bond, you know how special you are all to me. Of course to my friends who ventured to the rarefied air of the Senate from the other place—while at times we speak different languages, your friendship and support have been invaluable.

To my own leadership team here in the Senate—Michaelia Cash, whose source of energy still mystifies me. For someone who has limited caffeine intake and doesn't drink wine, you amaze me. Your leadership has been tremendous in the Senate. To Anne Ruston, Jane Hume and our whips team led by Maria Kovacic and of course formerly by Wendy Askew, thank you for the roles you've played in keeping this train on the rails. To Matt Canavan and Bridget McKenzie, I'm sorry I never joined the Nats. I think I would have fitted in, though the only downside is that cowboy hats ruin my hair. To Angus Taylor, I want to thank you for entrusting me with the important work that you asked me to do and for being so very supportive of me in my decision to leave when I know it is probably not what you wanted. Thank you.

People tune into question time—I'm not sure how many, but some do—and they see a fair degree of acrimony. It's only fair that people would assume that no-one in this place is friends, especially when it comes to the party divide. I have the very good fortune of being able to say that I leave this place with friendships with a number of people who disagree with me on nearly everything. I look down the government frontbench, and I see people I would call friends despite being formidable opponents, like the government leader, Senator Wong, who of course—and I'm going to let the cat out of the bag now—colluded with me to rein in and almost kill off formal business motions. Sorry, crossbench! There's my Tasmanian colleague Carol Brown, who conspired with me to get funding for Foodbank in Tasmania a couple of elections ago. I don't think we ever told our headquarters that we did that! Well done! I look down to the Greens there and I see my opposite number, Senator Hanson-Young, with whom I found much in common, mainly through trying to outwit the government, sometimes with success.

Some people say that the Senate is like a French film. It seems like it makes sense, but then it doesn't—even to us. However, a functioning Senate is an important thing, and I think people often overlook how important we actually are. In trying to make this place function, there is one person from the other team I've come to build a tremendous friendship with, and that is Katy Gallagher. You wouldn't read about it—a left-wing Labor lady and a right-wing Liberal bloke striking up a great relationship. When difficult discussions were to be had between warring parties, your humanity has made the difference.

None of us admit this until our valedictory speeches—and I'm not going to be any different here—but the fact is that staff make this place tick and frankly save us from ourselves most of the time. To my staff team over the years, I want to thank you. To John Polack, John Klonaris, Jono Maran—yes, we had some name variation in my office—Mary Seselja, Danielle Fontane, Claire and Nick Dunham, Will Calvert-Jones, Bec Dunham, Danielle McKay, Jack Morgan and the many wonderful people who have done their best to make me not look like a fool over the last decade, I want to thank you. I'm grateful for the patience you've all shown me, the hard work you've put in and your willingness to take my late night, early morning and weekend phone calls, which often don't have a point. But I'm especially grateful that you all realise that too many cooks spoil the broth.

Of course, for most of us, we don't get here without our parties—the organisations we believe in and that we unite behind as we go to the people seeking their trust. The Liberal Party in Tasmania means a lot to me and has given me all I have. The gratitude I have for every role I've fulfilled by virtue of my great party is immeasurable. Indeed, I would never have been able to contribute as a senator but for my Tasmanian Liberal Party. That includes our party president, Michael McKenna, who made some extremely difficult decisions to strengthen our party; our treasurer, Jackie Martin; our state director, Sam McQuestin; and the many members who supported me and our party in a number of ways over so many years, including and especially people like Dorothy Dehais and, of course, my first boss, Paul Calvert, former president. To every single member of the Tasmanian Liberal Party who pay their fees each year because they love and want to advance Tasmania, thank you for what you do for our state, our country and our great party.

We all have tutors in life, and I want to single out a few people here tonight. Don Morris, Darcy Tronson and Brad Stansfield are three political professionals who've imparted to me great knowledge and who've been some of the greatest assets to the Tasmanian division of the party. My parents-in-law, Tina and Zekri Palushi, imparted to me the stories and lessons arising from a life without freedom and democracy. Their support and wisdom—and, of course, sharing with me the story of my wife's great-grandfather, Fran Mirakaj, who I referred to in my first speech, who was martyred for his stance on democracy and Christianity in Albania—have all helped me to fight the good fight for freedom in this place. Of course, also, to Abby, Ben and Endrit, thank you for your love and support and for being here today as well.

To my own family—my mum, Mary, who is a force of nature and who incidentally is also retiring from public life this month, so there are going to be a lot of Duniams with spare time on their hands; my dad, Roy, who has been the most steady and tremendous support to all of us in all that we do; and my siblings, Matt, who is here and thank you for coming, and my sister, Paula, who can't be here—thank you for your love and good humour through the last decade of this journey.

When I entered this place, my sons were just young boys. I remember looking up, and I could barely see them poking over the edge of the barrier there. In fact, my youngest, Spencer, was so young that he was in care on the other side of the building in the early learning centre during my first speech. But, as usual, time did what time does. Today, one of them, my son Hugo, is an adult, and my middle son, Henry, is well on the way. Along with my wife, Anisa, my boys are the joy of my life. They are three young men of whom I am proud and who I dearly love.

My family are the biggest blessing from God that any man could ever ask for. For 10 years, boys, I've been doing this—plus all the time prior. You've been missing out on holidays with dad, time at home with him and all the normal things that many of your friends got. You've done it all with grace and maturity. I am grateful for the support that you've shown me through how you've handled this, and I know it hasn't been easy. But it's over now. For 10 years I've given this everything, but I dedicate the rest of my life to supporting you, nurturing you and helping you as you go on to your own adult lives.

Now, for anyone who's worried, my boys were not left alone at home. They benefited from the care and love of their mother, my wife, Anisa. The reality is, as everyone in this place who has children knows, that the absence means it falls to the other parent to do family—to raise, to correct, to educate, to discipline, to run around, to feed, to do everything. When things go wrong, that parent is on their own. It is difficult. Politicians' families are just like every other family. There are problems. There's illness. There are things that need dealing with. In our case, it was Anisa who kept the home fires burning bright and made sure everyone had what they needed when they needed it. Being able to contribute at all in public life for me would not have been possible without Anisa's support and her fearless and extremely frank feedback, which has certainly aided in my personal and professional growth, shall we say. Anisa, as I said in my speech 10 years ago, I will be thanking you for the rest of my life. And I think that's right, although I have this sneaking suspicion that those thankyous are going to become more expensive as time goes on.

Speaking of famous Albanian women, Mother Teresa, in her 1979 Nobel Prize acceptance speech, reflected on where goodness and love start in the world, from a Christian perspective. She said, and I quote:

And if we really believe, we will begin to love. And if we love, naturally, we will try to do something. First in our own home, our next door neighbor, in the country we live, in the whole world.

That is a reminder to me that first getting it right at home, having the love in a family, is where change in the world really does begin. So, to that question that I've been asked more times than I care to remember, 'Why are you going,' I think the answer for you all tonight is abundantly clear. But, President, I can tell you I'd rather have people asking me why I'm going than when I am going to go! Although, given it's been four months since I announced my retirement, it is getting a bit to that time!

Everyone likes free stuff, so I thought I'd throw in some free advice today. Our adversarial system of politics is a breeding ground for division, where points of difference and argument are increasingly the only way to cut through. That's necessary and healthy in a contest of ideas, but it shouldn't be at the expense of resolving issues in the national interest. It's incumbent upon all of us to find ways to resolve issues that confront Australia. We will and we should always have our counterarguments. But Australians are looking for mature debate, where Australia's best interests come first.

Former US prosecutor Roy Cohn from the McCarthy, reds-under-the-bed era, is credited with coming up with the 'three nevers' rule: never apologise, never admit, and never back down. With trust in politics at a low ebb, his advice could not be a bigger bum steer. There is nothing wrong with admitting when we get something wrong. And, in fact, I think it should be applauded. I note, though, I say this from opposition, where of course it's an art form to seize on admissions of failure and defeat. But I believe it is in the country's interest to admit when things don't work and change course if needed.

As part of this free advice, it wouldn't be complete without at least one Bible reference from me. Jesus said in the Parable of the Faithful Servant in Luke 12, 'To whom much is given, much is expected.' To all of us in this place, much has been given, without exception. Therefore, from all of us much is expected by our community and by our country. And I hope every day those who go on to occupy this place remember this and live it out in whatever form they can.

As I conclude, I must acknowledge that the challenge for my party is real, and no-one can deny that. But this challenge is not insurmountable. I come from a proud party with strong foundations. The Liberal heritage, the legacy and the record are all things to be proud of. Having just handed down our methodically crafted and strong immigration policy, I've been reflecting on the legacy of our party when it comes to strong borders. I've been reflecting on how we've been the only party in the past to end the people-smuggling trade and fix a broken migration system. I've been reflecting on how my party remains the party of fiscal prudence and strong economic management. One doesn't have to cast their mind back too far to recall the debt the Howard government was left with, which they paid off and turned into the Future Fund money set aside for the advancement of our country.

We have a history, and we should be proud of it. My party can give Australians what they need, not by pretending to be someone else or seeking to appease certain actors but by returning to our roots—by backing in with conviction our values framework the We Believe statement offers and explaining why it is better than the alternative. We should never wave the white flag. We should always put forward our plan and make the case for people to vote for us. My party has been around for decades. It isn't populist. It isn't flash in the pan. It is here to stay.
