And, sure, we may have spent some time in the wilderness, but we have our bearings now, and I know we will be able to get back over there into government.

I commenced by quoting my late grandmother. I conclude by quoting my great-great-grandfather Tasman Underhill Duniam I—I'm a history buff—who, when being asked by a committee of the Tasmanian parliament in 1882 about the success or otherwise of his farming venture in the new farming district of Mount Hicks in north-west Tasmania, having given up the comfort of his paid employment, said: 'People said I would starve. I have not yet starved'—and, to be clear, he never starved, otherwise I wouldn't be here today! People can choose to do what is comfortable forever or they can challenge themselves and go on to do new and different things. I don't know what awaits me outside this chamber, but they do tell me that there is life after politics. Whatever it is, I'm very much looking forward to it. It's time for me to go now, President. I thank the Senate.

speaker: Michelle Ananda-Rajah
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
I notice we have a lot of children in the gallery. This speech is very much for them, and it's for their parents and carers right around Australia. There is a taboo in our country that is targeting our children, and we need to speak its name. Thousands of boys and young men are suffering in silence, stigmatised and ashamed, after falling prey to sextortion. This is sexual extortion and blackmail in response to image based abuse. Sextortion is one of the fastest-growing online crimes we face. A national study found that one in 10 Australian adolescents have experienced it, with over half occurring before the age of 16—children. Our kids are being targeted by this.

In the second half of last year, our eSafety Commissioner received more than 2,200 complaints of sexual extortion, and victims are overwhelmingly male. Nine in 10 victims of sexual extortion, or sextortion, are either young men or boys. It heavily affects those in the 18- to 24-year-old age group. That is the danger age, as well as kids under 16. It's part of the reason why the Albanese Labor government introduced the social media delay, which kicks in from the age of 16. We need to protect and shield our children from these kinds of harm, because these harms are driving our kids, but especially our boys, towards depression, anxiety and, worse, suicidality.

This is how the playbook works. A boy is contacted online by someone posing as a friend, a peer or a young woman. They may also pose as a celebrity or a social media influencer and set up a lookalike social media account to make the child believe that they're interacting with a real person. Kids may receive unsolicited 'friend' or 'follow' requests from unknown persons. They will ask personal questions like, 'How old are you?', 'Where do you go to school?' or 'Do you have any brothers and sisters?' They may ask for something in exchange for images from that child; they may offer likes or gaming codes in exchange for images. Some may even pretend to represent a company and tell the child or the young person that they have the potential to become a model or a social media influencer, and the child is asked to send photos. Other warning signs are getting a direct message on one app and then being asked to continue chatting in another app, or that English may be a second language to this person—in other words, the language may not be crisp. The criminal might say that their webcam or microphone are not working on video calls or chats—so there's no real way of confirming the identity of the person on the other side. Then the criminal says that they promise to delete your content. However, once the images are shared, things take a turn for the worse, with escalating threats: 'Pay up or these pictures will go to your family, to your friends, to your school, to everyone who follows you on social media'—because they harvest your contacts from social media. Increasingly, criminals are using AI to fabricate images that were never even real—in other words, using nudify apps, which we have banned.

This is the business model of organised crime. Shame is weaponised to make millions. But the consequences are driving our boys to the brink and sending families to the brink. If you think you are a victim, or you know someone who is a victim of sextortion, do stop the chat. Do take screenshots of the text and the profile. Do block the account and report it to the platform. Do get support from a trusted friend, family member or professional support services. Call the kids helpline, for example. Get onto the eSafety Commissioner's website and request a takedown. They have a 98 per cent success rate. Contact the Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation, ACCCE, which is run by the AFP, the Australian Federal Police. They will catch these crooks. Don't send any more images or pay as this will lead to more demands. Don't respond to the demands. Shut this down and, most importantly, don't think that you are alone. You are not alone.

It is important that we back our boys and our young men to speak up, because speaking up robs this crime of its shame and stigma. It's important for all Australians to be upstanders and to support our boys and our girls. (Time expired)

speaker: Tammy Tyrrell
heading: STATEMENTS BY SENATORS
text:
Seventy per cent of young people get their news from social media. For an entire generation, social media isn't just entertainment. It's where they learn about the world, form opinions and, increasingly, engage with politics, and that should matter to all of us, because young, impressionable people are learning about politics through algorithms that aren't designed to inform them but are designed to keep them scrolling. Right now, One Nation is actively recruiting young people, not with policy—we know they have none—but with grievance. They use fast, emotional and algorithm-friendly content to draw young people in and feed them misinformation. We know that the algorithm rewards cheaply made rage bait with the most clicks online, and this is exactly what One Nation is using to grab people's attention. Our democracy shouldn't be at the mercy of AI made memes and misinformation that spreads simply because it makes people angry. But the answer isn't to tell young people to switch off from politics; it's the absolute opposite.

I've spoken with young people in Tassie who tell me they don't want to ignore politics. They want to understand the issues that affect their lives. They want to have a say in their future. And social media can help with that. It can make politics more accessible than ever before. But there is a very large difference between using social media to get people involved in politics and allowing algorithms to decide what political content they see. We should encourage the first and regulate the second, because, when algorithms reward outrage, misinformation and division, reasonable political discussions can get drowned out.

We cannot and will not respond to that by becoming louder and angrier. Instead, our government is increasingly using social media to explain policy, challenge misinformation and give young people a reason to engage with politics in the first place. That's the positive role social media can play in our democracy. But it's also why the government's My Feed, My Way reform matters. Under the digital duty of care, Australians will have greater choice over their default social media feed. They could continue using an algorithm to shape their feed, or they could choose to see content from the friends and creators they've actually chosen to follow. That's not about the government deciding what Australians can see; it's about Australians deciding for themselves. It doesn't tell people what political opinions they can hold. It doesn't tell them which party they can support. It gives people a choice about how their feed is made. It gives people back control.

Misinformation is deliberately made for clicks, and dangerous, hateful content is rewarded because it gets people engaged. We have to question whether that's really the kind of online environment we want, especially for our kids. That's why protecting children and protecting democracy are not separate conversations. Australia has already taken action to protect under-16s from social media accounts and the harmful design features that come with it. Now, we need to make the online environment safer for everyone, and that means putting responsibility back on the tech companies that design these systems.

We shouldn't be asking whether social media is good or bad. We should be asking what we want it to do. Do we want it to push people into increasingly extreme bubbles? Do we want it to reward whoever can produce the angriest 30-second video? Or do we want it to help Australians understand their communities, engage with their democracy and hear from people they've actually chosen to follow? I know which kind of social media I want to see—one where kids can engage with politics without being manipulated, one where misinformation can be challenged rather than spread, one where healthy debate happens based on sources you trust, not an unknown algorithm, one where children are protected and one where Australians, not big tech, control their feeds.

speaker: Ian Sollom
heading: Attorney General’s Office
text: Fraud is growing, and artificial intelligence is making it easier for it to be committed at scale. While cases can be complex, all too often victims tell me that they feel abandoned by the system. The CPS strategy folds fraud into organised crime and national security issues, and none of its seven priorities is actually about victims; in that regard, it differs from the previous economic crime strategy. How will the Solicitor General ensure that fraud victims are not lost in the CPS’s new approach?

speaker: Victoria Atkins
heading: Inheritance Tax
text:
No, if the hon. Gentleman sits down—[Interruption.] I have some words about his AI-generated speech in a moment.

The Conservatives have the answer: we will scrap stamp duty on primary residences. That is how we help people back on the housing ladder. The hon. Member for Macclesfield also described his own constituents who want to pass on their family homes or family businesses to their children as the “idle rich”. I hope that was just the AI.

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text:
Before answering the noble Lord’s Question, I refer Members to my ministerial declaration of interests. My husband works for the Government Digital Service.

The redistribution of the function of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology is independent of decisions on overall Civil Service headcount, as is the case with all machinery of government changes. Artificial intelligence, science and technology are major priorities that cut across the whole of government and are vital for the country’s future economic prosperity. DSIT’s functions have been accordingly redistributed so that policy relating to science and technology is better aligned across government.

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: We absolutely have a focus on science and technology, which is why the Minister for AI has a seat at the Cabinet table. I agree with the noble Lord that the UK stands at a critical juncture, where unprecedented global changes mean that we need to secure our position in relation to these areas, but we cannot see science and technology as an isolated issue that is limited to one department; it is a fundamental priority that cuts across the whole of government and is crucial to the UK’s future economic prosperity.

speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: My Lords, the Government were doing reasonably well through DSIT in helping a booming industry in UK AI find its way through the plethora of initiatives and policies, including the AI growth zones, the AI opportunity action plan and sovereign AI. As well as for civil servants, the removal of DSIT has caused confusion in industry, and I declare my interest as a co-founder of the Business AI Alliance and an adviser to a number of AI businesses. All these businesses have said the same thing to me: where do they go now? Where are all these policy areas sitting? How can they navigate their way as they try to bring that key element of growth to the UK economy?

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: As I said in my initial response to the noble Lord, Lord Empey, we have a Minister for AI at the Cabinet table. We also have a new and renewed BIST, which has been created to signify the UK’s global leadership in innovation and maximise the growth potential that can be contributed to the UK economy by emerging strategic sectors. This is part of our reindustrialisation agenda. BIST is now responsible for emerging and frontier technologies, and I am confident that this will be part of its key work going forward.

speaker: Lord Pack
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: My Lords, we have in recent weeks had yet more evidence of AI agents going rogue, including hacking websites and even sending a fake tip about a real crime to the US police. Can I ask not about overall headcount, but specifically what the impact of these changes will be on the headcount for AI regulation? Is that headcount going to go up, go down, or stay the same?

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: The percentage of staff in digital and data roles is projected to increase. We are clear that when we are looking at overall responsibilities, functions and roles within the Civil Service, we need to make sure that we are ready for future opportunities, but also future threats, as the noble Lord made clear. I had the pleasure of going to talk to AISI last week and I was impressed by the calibre of civil servants there and the work they are doing to protect us and to build a rigorous scientific understanding of both the capabilities and the risks associated with AI.

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: I am unclear about how I am going to come up with an exact figure for somebody who covers a cross-government function, albeit that he will have teams such as AISI working specifically with him. I cannot stress enough that this Government see AI as so crucial that we have a Cabinet-level Minister who has responsibility for drawing all these threads together and for making sure that we are well equipped for both the opportunities that are presented and the well-documented risks associated with AI.

speaker: Lord Moylan
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: My Lords, a large number of civil servants, paid as civil servants, are in fact working for trade unions. Have the Government considered prioritising replacing them with AI?

speaker: Lord Spellar
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: My Lords, we are concentrating a lot on the impact of AI on outside industry. To what extent is the Civil Service looking at using AI in its own internal operations? In particular, what impact will it have on the increased headcount that we have post Covid?

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: We have a huge amount of work going on across government to make sure that we use AI to its potential, from the Department of Health and Social Care looking at how it will use it in a cutting-edge AI trial to transform cancer care—albeit that that is within the health service. We are confident that AI will improve public services and boost productivity, from identifying fraud and potential fraud to making sure that we have automated policy analysts and AI tutoring tools. We are rolling out AI tools that will save time and money to get the most effective Civil Service for the public.

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology: Abolition - Question
text: I am going to repeat myself, with apologies to your Lordships’ House. Not just the UK but the whole world is at such a critical juncture in relation to the rapid increase and developments in AI science and technology. I understand on one level why people think “Well, we’ll put it all in one department and one box”, but putting it across government and making sure somebody is driving that progress across government is critical to making sure that this is embedded and part of everybody’s work across every department, rather than it sitting in DSIT.

speaker: Baroness Taylor of Stevenage
heading: Housing: National Targets - Question
text: It is very important across the planning system. The noble Baroness raises the important issue of how we balance the needs of our economic infrastructure, of which data centres are an increasingly important part. We just had a whole debate on AI. We cannot operate AI without data centres. That needs to be balanced with the need for housing, and this Government are committed to a streamlined planning system that is plan led, pro-growth, accessible and understandable to all, and delivers that balance as far as possible. We work with our colleagues in Defra on the land use framework to make sure that we take account of all the needs for land.

speaker: Lord Forbes of Newcastle
heading: International Update - Statement
text: My Lords, I have been struck during my relatively short time in your Lordships’ House by the increasing frequency with which AI contributes to discussions and questions in this Chamber. I therefore ask my noble friend the Leader of the House if she can confirm that it is the Government’s view and position that decisions about the regulation of AI should be taken by democratically elected Governments expressing sovereign intent on behalf of their citizens, rather than by industry leaders alone. If that is the case, this will require significant international collaboration, through a variety of mechanisms. Is this therefore a position that the Government are prepared to advocate in their international discussions, especially in the forthcoming G20 summit?

speaker: Baroness Smith of Basildon
heading: International Update - Statement
text:
The short answer is yes. The slightly longer answer is that the Government have already said that this will be a key focus when we are holding the chair of the G20 that is coming up. It will be discussed in the summit, no doubt, at the G20 meetings. The issues we have to look at are security, the benefits that can accrue, where the dangers are and how we work together internationally. This is not something that any one country can deal with on its own; it has to be a global effort. It has to be Governments looking at how they can benefit their citizens through AI and how they can protect their citizens from AI when essential. The work is going on.

I think this is the first time the Government have a dedicated AI Minister who sits around the Cabinet table. We also have across every department—indeed, we have discussed it at Cabinet on more than one occasion already—responsibilities around AI. It is not, as I think my noble friend Lady Twycross said earlier today, something that you can put in a box and say it is in just one area. It has to be across government and across nations. It will be a key focus for our Prime Minister at the G20.

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
During my time here, I've had the privilege of receiving dozens of wonderful speeches written by young Australians as part of the Raise Our Voice program. Thanks to everyone who submitted a speech. It was really difficult to choose which one to read. I've got some very passionate and articulate young constituents.

Here is Alice's speech:

Dear members of parliament, my name is Alice. I'm 10 and I live in Brisbane. To me, climate change is the biggest issue shaping our future. Oceans are warming, coral is bleaching and ecosystems are suffering. All around the world today these horrible occurrences are happening and some events that are even worse. Do you care about this planet? The planet that gives food, water and a home to everything? The planet that gives us life. The planet that our own kind is destroying. If you do care then why isn't more being done as we approach the unrecoverable tipping point of climate change? Why are humans so resistant to positive change?

Well, I care. My friends care. My generation cares. This is because if we don't do something now, we will have to face the consequences of the future. We will have to pay the price, not you. So if you do care about Australia's future then start making an impact. Some things you could do include: increasing government incentives for renewable energy sources; investing in more solar farms, wind turbine farms and hydroelectricity projects, including working towards harnessing tidal power to generate electricity.

There are many things you, me and all Australians can do to make more sustainable choices such as using environmentally friendly products, recycling and composting. So what are you waiting for?

Thanks, Alice, for that excellent speech. Alice is completely right, of course, and it's her generation that inspires me.

Sadly, our political system allows big corporations, including fossil fuel companies, to donate huge sums of money to political parties. Then those political parties do as they're told by big corporations—they are bought. It's a fundamental structural, moral and ethical problem destroying trust in our politics, and it shouldn't be allowed. Later this month, I will present a bill to fix exactly this problem. It would ban fossil fuel corporations from making political donations, removing one of the worst corrupting influences on our government, poisoning our politics. I hope the other parties will support it. But of course, they've profited from this system forever, so I'm not holding my breath. In the meantime, I encourage young people like Alice to keep up the fight. The most powerful thing ordinary people can do is take on these big companies whose undue influence is corrupting our politics and damaging our future, and we should all stand up together for what is right.

I'm also thinking about the future and what AI means for our minds, our planet, our lives. Many Australians are understandably sceptical of AI. The government just can't keep up with the technology. We have seen across many sectors the huge damage that rapacious, profit driven, unregulated corporations can do—massive water-guzzling data centres, a new frontier of resource extraction. Is generative AI a useful tool or a quandary for education and learning? Will AI be beneficial to our society? These are the questions I am asking my community in Ryan to think about.

I want to know how real people feel about AI and its impact on their lives. If AI is here to stay, we've got to ensure that it's regulated and useful to us, not just to corporations. It can't be yet another drain on our communities. We can't let massive global corporations write the rules on this—companies like Microsoft's data centre company, who, by the way, paid no tax in the last financial year. The government have one chance to get this right, and they should know that regular Australians are watching closely. I'm looking forward to reading through the responses to my AI survey in the coming weeks, and to sharing Ryan's view in parliament.

speaker: Ash Ambihaipahar
heading: ADJOURNMENT
text:
I rise to share 16-year-old Dion's speech, provided to me through the Raise Our Voice program. Dion writes:

An issue that requires immediate attention is the growing uncertainty surrounding the nature of AI in both workplace and educational institutions. As AI advances significantly with every passing year, its implications on society have become increasingly unpredictable.

To be told that the future you have prepared for may soon be made redundant has caused me, and many of my peers, considerable anxiety. We are encouraged to develop qualifications for pathways that may fundamentally differ by the time we enter them. For many young Australians, decisions surrounding their futures are being shaped by speculation rather than by genuine interest.

I implore the parliament to consider my propositions. In doing so, they ensure that Australians are prepared for, rather than displaced by, its future implications. Firstly, educational institutions should teach basic comprehension skills surrounding AI and its use. Secondly, large-scale businesses should have mandatory requirements surrounding employment for entry-level positions. Finally, small businesses should be granted tax incentives or subsidies to educate young workers, promoting employee development over AI alternatives.

AI will shape all of our futures, though the future should not be one where young Australians are left wondering of their place in the world. Parliament must act.

I share Dion's concerns about AI. When the developers directly behind the technology say that there is a 10 per cent chance it could wipe out humanity, Australians are right to be worried. When we hear about an AI arms race between superpowers, the restructuring of our workforce and the demands that data centres place on energy and water, again, Australians are right to be worried. But when used properly, AI could accelerate medical research by decades. It could help address the productivity challenges that have caused so many national economies to stagnate. It could help scale and stabilise renewable energy so that we can properly transition away from fossil fuels. It is both a threat and an opportunity.

I was elected to this parliament to take difficult issues by the horns, so my job is to represent the human interest in policymaking and to put real people at the centre of the AI challenge, not to bow down to the demands of big foreign companies or to praise the pursuit of profit. Government can often be a slow beast, but not in this case. The current AI inquiry, with its short deadline and bipartisan support, will inform our world-leading artificial intelligence framework. That framework starts with the promise that AI will not undercut working conditions, divide communities or damage our environment. We'll also ensure that data centres are legally required to underwrite their own new power supply, pay their full share of connection costs so that household energy bills are not affected, reduce their power use when needed to support the grid and operate as efficiently as possible in their use of water. The detail on how to achieve these things can be delivered through the inquiry, which is due to report before the end of this year.

I don't want communities to feel like they have been blindsided by developments that care more about building in the name of profit rather than to the benefit of people. I applaud the work of the Bayside and Inner West councils in their advocacy around the proposed data centre at the old Kogarah Golf Club. Because of them, submissions to the project were extended, people got to have their say, and the councils' own submissions represented the community's concerns about the scale of the development, its impact on Cooks River and the unacceptable flooding impacts it may have. Such concerns and others are reflected in the 593 submissions that object to the plan as it stands. I've also written to the state member for Rockdale and to the state planning minister. I share these concerns and I look forward to the response through the State Significant Development process. AI is the biggest challenge of our time. Dion knows this, Barton knows this, I know this and this parliament knows this, and we will tackle it head-on.

speaker: Zaneta Mascarenhas
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
text:
In my first term, there was a private member's motion on eating disorders. I remember sitting in this chamber listening to coalition members who had gone through the painful experience of their daughters having had an eating disorder. I can't imagine how difficult that would have been, particularly as a parent that is away for 20 weeks of the year.

As a parent, one of the reasons why I am here is that I want to make a structural difference to our children's lives, and that includes reducing the influences that increase the likelihood of an eating disorder. We know that social media algorithms are teaching boys and girls to hate their bodies. When the government released the draft laws, the Minister for Communications described what is happening right now. Girls are getting advice from chatbots on how to exist on only 600 calories a day. For those who don't calorie count, you need about 1,600 to 3,000. Today, the Albanese government is introducing a digital duty of care bill, which gives Australians control over their feed and protects kids online. I ask those opposite: what are you prepared to do to stop this scourge? We have a moment. As Senator Jonno Duniam said, there are moments where we can have bipartisanship. This could be that.

speaker: Anika Wells
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I move:

That this bill be now read a second time.

I ntroduction

Australia has one of the most comprehensive online safety frameworks in the world.

It protects Australian children from cyberbullying and adults from cyber abuse.

It empowers the eSafety Commissioner to take down seriously harmful material, including image based abuse.

It requires online services to report how they are keeping Australians safe.

And it has 17 industry-drafted codes and standards that were designed by big tech to protect Australians from illegal and restricted content.

This network of protections has helped many Australians.

But an independent statutory review found, in a constantly evolving digital world, we are playing whack-a-mole.

That is why, today, the Albanese government is introducing a digital duty of care.

Australia's digital duty of care will set basic safety standards for the online services we use every day, just like we have in every other industry.

Illegal a nd r estricted m aterial

The core of the digital duty of care is to provide a safe online environment, where all Australians are protected from seriously harmful and illegal content.

It moves the safety net upstream to the people who design the product to stop the harm, before it ever reaches an Australian user.

It is not about controlling adults online—it is about getting illegal and seriously harmful material offline and giving adults choice.

Like when you buy a new appliance—the government sets minimum safety standards, but ultimately what you choose to buy is up to you, as long as it's legal and safe.

The digital duty of care also sets minimum standards for the features and tools that tech companies use.

Online service providers will have to conduct annual risk assessments of the harms the features on their service could cause to Australians—features like algorithmic recommender systems, the ability to livestream incognito from your glasses, or the ability to artificially generate text and pictures.

Then they will need to put systems in place to prevent those risky features from causing harm to Australians, because the architecture matters. The business model matters. The incentives matter.

Platforms are not passive. They decide what is amplified, what captures us, what behaviours get rewarded.

They have been optimised for engagement and for attachment, not for wellbeing, because the longer we stay, the more valuable we are.

And, through My Feed, My Way, social media companies will have to provide user empowerment tools that give people over the age of 16 choice about what they see in their feed.

If someone wants their feed to be filled with friends and creators they follow, the social media platforms must let them do that by default. You shouldn't be thrown into an algorithm filled with people you don't follow or subscribe to if you don't want to.

And, if you're happy to keep getting personally recommended content in your primary feed, you should have choice about the specific kind of content you do and don't want to see.

Today, the Albanese government has released the proposed rules for user empowerment tools.

They contain four principles that address some of the malicious compliance that we have seen in other jurisdictions.

First, we must be able to opt into the algorithm, with social media platforms required to send users a proactive notification about this choice.

Second, the tools must be accessible, easy to use, prominently available, functional, clear and in simple language.

Third, the choice must stick—platforms can't revert back to their default every time you open the app.

Fourth, choosing to opt out of the algorithm must not make your feed harder to navigate. The experience must be similar to those who have chosen to opt in.

M aterial harmful to children

I've heard from parents all over Australia who are so relieved that we have delayed access to social media until the age of 16.

But parents are understandably still worried about how they can protect their kids on other platforms, like online games and AI chatbots.

And that is a rational fear.

Just last week, we heard about a 14-year-old girl from Western Australia who was approached by an adult on Roblox. He told her she was really good at the game and they started chatting. That chat moved to Discord and changed tone.

He asked for pictures, then blackmailed her. He told her to write his name in her blood, to self-harm, to send pornographic images. He asked her to livestream her suicide.

Another is a 13-year-old boy from Victoria who was lonely and struggling to make friends, and when his counsellor looked at his browser history, he had 50 different tabs of AI chatbots open so he could flick between them.

It was a way for him to feel connected—after all, how can you feel lonely if you're connected with 50 different chats?

But some of the chatbots told him he was ugly and would never make friends. Some egged him on towards self-loathing and some egged him towards self harm. That is a report.

Under Australia's digital duty of care, under-18s must be protected from content and features that are harmful to young people: content that promotes or encourages eating disorders; content that glorifies crime or dangerous stunts; pornography or content that promotes hostile ideas about women and gender equality; content that causes serious distress, including abuse and bullying.

We know many kids don't tell parents that they are seeing harmful content on social media, often because they worry parents will 'overreact' and deny access.

Sometimes they don't even recognise what is happening to them is harmful.

But it shouldn't be on the kid to stop or report the harm.

It should be on the companies that create these online environments to make them safe and to stop the harm before it occurs.

Transitional a rrangements

If the digital duty of care passes through parliament and royal assent, a 12-month transitional period will be in place before the digital duty of care comes into effect.

This transitional period will provide time for the making of any necessary rules and regulatory guidance material to ensure industry is able to put in place measures to meet the new compliance requirements in time for the digital duty of care to come into effect.

Online services that are currently complying with the basic online safety expectations and the relevant codes and standards will be well placed to comply with their digital duty of care obligations.

Noting that not all online services share the same level of risk and type of risks, the extent of a service's obligation, including the need to conduct a full risk assessment, and the level of detail required will vary as determined by the eSafety Commissioner.

To be determined 'low risk', an online service provider will need to conduct a self-assessment process to certify that it does not do things such as:

Providers of low-risk services will have minimal obligations under the digital duty of care, including websites and applications run by small businesses, services that predominantly or exclusively share exempt material, as well as information conduit services, like internet service providers.

Providers of low-risk services must continue to monitor any changes to their service or features and reassess the risk profile of their service when/if significant changes are made.

Conclusion

I would like to finish with a letter I received from an eight-year-old boy named Angus, who lives in Yeronga, in Queensland.

Angus wrote to me because he was worried about what Roblox was doing to friends, and what it might do to his little brother.

He said:

I have a friend who used to be a great friend who would play with me on playdates and we would have a great time. He got Roblox when he was about six years old, after he got Roblox he wasn't interested in playing with me anymore, all he wanted to do was play Roblox and it feels like he is addicted to it.

My friends say weird things that they have learnt from the game and I don't like it.

It isn't safe that it is an online game and strangers can play with you, and I worry about my friends being online with strangers who might be dangerous.

There are horror games on Roblox and it can be really scary for kids. When I have asked my friends to stop playing these types of games they don't listen.

I think that Roblox rots kids brains because it has terrible graphics, there is horror and shooting games and they learn very silly things.

If eight-year-old Angus from Yeronga understands why we need to make the internet safer, then I believe 60-year-old Angus from Cooma might be able to as well.

Online safety should not be a political issue.

All sides of parliament need to work together to deliver a digital duty of care.

There is no reason why we can't work together to get this done.

Debate adjourned.

speaker: Mr Tony Stephen Burke
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Reid for the question and, in particular, for the work that the member for Reid is leading on cybersecurity with the House of Representatives Committee. When we talk about different threats to the country, particularly in terms of terrorism, we often talk about whether a threat is 'possible' or 'probable'. We don't tend to use that language with respect to cybersecurity, because the threat is always certain. Our critical infrastructure and our government institutions are constantly under attack. Some of those cyberattacks come from criminal gangs and some of them come from state actors. But the work in particular of the Australian Signals Directorate in making sure that we help critical infrastructure and government institutions be able to have the strongest possible cyber defences is as much part of our national security as anything else that we do.

The work of the Signals Directorate has traditionally provided advice to government and to critical infrastructure through a process known as the Essential Eight. That process and those essential eight documents have now been updated, and the new documents were released today. Effectively, we need to constantly update them with the new methods that people, those who want to do us harm, are using. The simplest example I'd give would be artificial intelligence. The gap between a hostile actor finding a vulnerability and being able to exploit it used to be roughly 2½ years. It's now 10 hours between finding the vulnerability and exploiting it. We need to make sure that we have the best possible cybersecurity across government and critical infrastructure to be able to keep Australians safe.

The new advice that's come from the Signals Directorate has a series of different themes that are part of it, but there are three new areas in particular that I would highlight. The first is the focus on the human firewall. We've started to find that businesses can invest extraordinary amounts of money in the technical firewall only to find that a well-meaning member of their own staff has inadvertently opened the door. There are gangs like Scattered Spider that exist throughout the English-speaking world that are trained at basically building relationships and pretending they're the help desk so that eventually somebody will unwittingly upload something that never would have made it through the technical firewall.

The second area that the new documents deal with, importantly, is legacy technology. Legacy technology is not just something that's old. It could be new or old, but it's something that can't be updated and can't be patched. Those constant patches and regular updates are a big part of how we make sure that new vulnerabilities, as they're found, are quickly shut down. But legacy technology and edge devices—sometimes people wonder why we are worried about all these other sorts of devices—often, if they can't be patched and updated, then become a pathway to infecting an entire system.

Finally, the supply chain—a business itself can have great cybersecurity, but if parts of their supply chain, businesses that they rely on or other operators who plug into their devices don't have the same level of cybersecurity, you can get a similar threat. I want to congratulate the Signals Directorate, thank them for the extraordinary work they do, and remind everybody about the importance of constantly checking and updating on these issues.

speaker: Jacqui Lambie
heading: MOTIONS
text:
I move:

That the Senate—

a. acknowledges the growing threat posed by artificial intelligence (AI), deepfakes, voice cloning and other emerging technologies, which are increasingly being exploited to impersonate individuals and organisations, spread disinformation, manipulate the public and facilitate sophisticated scams and fraud;

b. expresses serious concern regarding the lack of protection from AI-generated political advertising which undermines electoral integrity, democratic accountability and public trust; and

c. calls on the Government to urgently strengthen Australia's legislative and regulatory framework to address the misuse of AI, deepfakes and voice cloning and prevent their malicious use in scams, fraud and impersonation, including in political advertising.

Before the last election, the ABC asked me to take part in an AI experiment. They asked if I could clone my voice using cheap AI tools. They wanted to see if people in Burnie, in my own backyard, would know my voice from an 'AI fake Jacqui', as they called it. Well, that was scary enough. But here we are two years later, and the deepfake technology is even scarier. A deepfake video of Angus Taylor and me having an argument on ABC TV's Insiders show has been doing the rounds on social media for months. My office has done all the right things. We got straight out on the socials, warning people, but it's still popping up. Just for the record, Australians, I don't endorse any companies, especially not insurance companies. I work for the people of Tasmania, full stop—no endorsing.

In the last sitting, an AI deepfake video of me popped up, and it's doing the rounds again. It's an even nastier one. It's a video of a fake AI Jacqui telling One Nation supporters they are vile and disgusting. And who is sharing this nasty AI slop? Well, you wouldn't guess. After our investigation—a One Nation supporter, of course. We have also alerted the AFP. This is the sort of vile political advertising that just causes more division. I would like to ask every One Nation senator in this place if you support this sort of rubbish. Is this what you call free speech, is it? When we reported it to Facebook Meta, you wouldn't guess what they said. They told us that this video didn't breach their community standards. You know why they said that? Because, let's face it, when it comes to Meta and Facebook, they have no standards, full stop.

I'm looking forward to seeing the government's duty of care bill. This kind of fake, hideous content causes hatred and division, so I get why One Nation likes it; hatred and division are all they've got up their sleeve. As I've said before, I don't care about me, but I do care about my staff who have to deal with the One Nation troll army almost every day—every day! And I care about Australians who are seeing this and might think that it's real.

Australia has strong laws to protect consumers from false claims made in advertisements. Pharmaceutical companies can't claim to have a cure for cancer, food companies can't claim that sugary foods are good for our children, and lawyers cannot guarantee they will win every personal injury case. But it's still okay in this country and legal to lie in political ads. But we can change that. South Australia has had truth-in-political-advertising laws since the 1980s. In 2020, the ACT Legislative Assembly unanimously passed truth-in-political-advertising laws that came into effect in July 2021. Parties and candidates in Australia get a lot of taxpayer money with very few strings attached. What if some of that money gets turned into political ads that are misleading or deceptive? Truth-in-political-advertising laws are extremely popular. There's been a lot of polling on this, and nine out of 10 Australians want truth-in-political-advertising rules, full stop.

Professor Terry Flew is the coordinator of the centre for artificial intelligence at Sydney university. The professor told the Joint Select Committee on AI that his one immediate recommendation is 'that the current political advertising laws be changed to prohibit the use of AI generated deepfakes in election campaigns'—in other words, truth-in-political-advertising laws. Professor Flew told the committee that political deepfakes go way beyond 'the legitimate bounds of public campaigning and prove to be genuinely threatening to the individuals and groups who are the targets of them'.

AI is completely out of control. We know that because the big tech bros are the ones warning the world that there needs to be more regulation and guardrails. It's coming from them. Now, it would appear that our government has finally woken up—well, maybe. I'm hoping. In February this year, when I asked the minister why we weren't investing in our own Australian made AI, all the minister could say was that Australia was a great place to invest, and he pointed to the AI Safety Institute, which has no actual powers, Australians—just another little bunch of people up there getting paid some cash. By the way, this was just days after Labor got rid of the independent AI advisory group. Go figure. So the only place they were getting their information from was big tech.

Last weekend's TheSaturday Paper had a very interesting story about the number of top-level staffers with close ties to the Labor Party who have left the Labor Party and are now working with big tech. The article spoke to insiders who pointed to big tech using the same tactics as big tobacco. Aren't you disgusting little people? That involves hiring multiple former Labor staff. And Ed Husic, the former industry minister who led the government's initial response to AI, said:

What we're witnessing is nothing more than a shock and awe lobbying approach by US tech, designed to swamp government decision-making.

An AI strategist who has worked inside and outside government made a similar point:

The amount of power these people have is incomprehensible … This isn't just a product that's being sold. This is dual-use capability. This is the equivalent of a private company developing nuclear weapons.

This government and the last Liberal government let social media get out of control. Well, you're on notice now. Australia is watching. We need controls on AI now, and we need to ban political deepfake ads. There is already a huge problem with trust in our politicians and this place up here. Having strong truth in political advertising laws and banning political deepfakes would go a long way to having a very good start. I have to ask: what are you waiting for? What I see as the form of policing out there is that you're actually putting the lives of all these parliamentarians and their staff in danger. You are doing that.

Until you bring in some rules and regulations, this is going to continue to uplift. You are setting a very dangerous precedent for one of us to be hurt. God help us if someone goes at me and one of my staff gets hurt. It's gone too far! You have to do something about this, for God's sake, for at least the safety and welfare of our own staff in our offices who travel with us all the time. We are not the PM. We don't have security around us. It is getting that vicious out there. It might be okay for a backbencher who is not known out there, and that is no disrespect to you. But, for an Independent like myself who's been up here for over 10 years and whose face is out there everywhere, and everyone knows who I am, I am extremely worried about my staff being around me. That is a problem. I am really worried. So, please, before one of us or one of our staff actually gets hurt, before it is too late, I'm begging you to do something about this.

Question agreed to.

speaker: Anne Ruston
heading: BILLS
subheading: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026; Direction to Committee
text:
I stand here today because we will support the government in the bill that is before the chamber, because older Australians cannot wait any longer—not because the problem is fixed, because it is not. Make no mistake about what this is. This is an admission by the government that its assessment system is failing older Australians. For almost 12 months, older Australians and their families, assessors and providers have been telling the government that the computer generated algorithm that has no human override is getting it wrong time and time again. They told the Senate inquiry. They've been telling our electorate offices. They were telling anybody who would listen. And, for almost 12 months, this government told them the system was working. Now, under the weight of sheer evidence, the government has finally capitulated. It has agreed to an independent review of the very algorithm it spent a year defending.

I'll remind the Senate what that evidence looks like. In the full year before the algorithm was put in place, 170 people asked for their assessments to be reviewed. In just the first five months after the algorithm was in place, 834 people asked for a review, and we heard of many more that would have asked for a review but were just so tired of fighting the system.

Australia's peak bodies for geriatric medicine called the tool a clinical safety risk, the Commonwealth Ombudsman launched an investigation, and documents released under freedom of information show the human override was stripped out from the top down, with the department's own staff finding out just days before the system went live.

Then there are the people. A man living with motor neurone disease was told by a computer he needed less help, not more—a cruel progressive terminal illness, and the computer said no. The government has since had to change the rules to recognise motor neurone disease as warranting urgent priority. That is not a refinement; that is an admission the system is getting it wrong. So why support these changes? It's because we've listened. We've listened to stakeholders, to advocates and to older Australians who live with this system every single day. And what they've told us is clear. The system is so bad right now we cannot afford to walk away from even the most modest of improvements. But they told us something else as well. Any improvement of the nature that is being put forward by schedule 4 of this bill must only be interim. It cannot become this government's excuse to stop this process from being fixed. We were not prepared to leave older Australians stuck with the current system while this government takes its time producing a perfect bill that we know will never come. So we've done what stakeholders asked of us. We have supported this improvement, but we've made sure it is interim.

In return for our support, the coalition have received two things. As I said, the first is an independent review of the aged-care assessment tool—a clinically informed review backed by experts in geriatric medicine, dementia care and allied health—examining how the algorithm classifies older Australians and who gets priority. That review must inform the rebuilding of any assessment tool. We're pleased that the government has agreed to it and agreed to publish the results of that review in full so it's there for everybody to see. But a review is not worth the paper it is written on unless its results are turned into action.

Older Australians have had enough waiting under this government, and that is why the second thing we secured matters so much: a sunset clause. These provisions will sunset after 12 months. So the government has 12 months to fix the problems that have been identified by so many people. If it does, older Australians will be better off and we will herald that as a welcome advancement. But if it doesn't, these provisions will lapse and the government will have to come back into this place and explain why it has continued to fail older Australians, why it has failed to give them the care that this government has assessed them as needing. That's our mechanism, and we will force the government to act.

Let me be very clear about one more thing. The coalition is not stepping away from our fight for human override. A computer, and a computer alone, cannot be left to make the decisions about the care needs and care priorities of older Australians. I know the Greens have moved an amendment on human override, and, in principle, we support the Greens. We do not believe that what the government have put forward today is adequate when it comes to human override. What they're putting forward today is an escalation pathway run by the department for people in exceptional circumstances. It is a step—it is an improvement on what we have now—but it is not the same thing as letting a qualified assessor, sitting across the table from an older Australian, correct the computer when it gets it wrong. And we know it is getting it wrong time and time again.

The Senate has already passed the coalition's bill to restore human override, with the support of the Greens and the crossbench, and I acknowledge the incredible support of the crossbench, particularly the Greens and Senator Allman-Payne, on forcing this issue. Earlier this year, a senior minister in the Albanese government told the parliament:

… in every case there needs to be human oversight of any use of AI. We don't just hand over decision-making to abstract computer programs…

Well, guess what. We agree with you, Minister. We are simply asking this government to apply that standard to older Australians when it's assessing their care needs and their care need priorities. The government has now said it will review the algorithm, and that is what we expect it to deliver.

We're giving the government the opportunity to go away and do that work. Get it done. But, if it does not, we will be back, and I'm confident that the Greens and the crossbench will be back with us. Together, we have the power to force the government to do the right thing. Remember when Prime Minister Albanese was the opposition leader prior to the 2022 election and told Australians he was going to come in here and put 'the care back into aged care'. Nothing could be further from the reality that older Australians are facing right now. So, today, we're putting the government on notice. The clock is ticking. The coalition will never step away from older Australians. We will never step away from supporting older Australians getting the care they need when they need it. We will keep pushing for a permanent fix, and what we're doing today is telling the government 'you have the chance to come back with a permanent fix, so you'd better do it'.

We will always back a human being able to override a decision when the computer, quite frankly, has made a botch of it. No algorithm has ever grown old. Older Australians deserve a system that sees them as people and not as data. We know, as we stand here today, that 250,000 older Australians are currently waiting to either be assessed or get the package that they've been assessed as needing. We know that, last year, over 6,400 older Australians died while they were waiting to get the home-care package they had been assessed as needing. And we know that right now in excess of 3½ thousand older Australians have been assessed as clinically able to be discharged from our hospitals, yet they languish in hospital beds because this government has rationed care when it comes to aged-care packages. It has failed the sector and the sector's viability with its actions—other actions apart from in this bill—so we're not seeing aged-care beds being built. They need 10½ thousand aged-care beds every year for the next 10 years. Last year, the government's incentives managed to deliver, through the private sector, 802. The government is a long way short of delivering for older Australians, and we believe older Australians need better. That's why we are asking the government to make good on its promise. Fix this absolutely disastrous system. Fix this algorithm that is producing terrible results for older Australians. Quite frankly, older Australians deserve more from their government than they're currently getting.

speaker: Kerrynne Liddle
heading: BILLS
subheading: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026; Direction to Committee
text:
I rise to speak on the Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner) and Other Measures Bill 2026. The coalition welcomes the commissioner, and I have said so in this place earlier this week. Today I want to speak about the government's changes to aged-care assessment and why the coalition will support them. Let me be clear at the outset. We are supporting the changes in this bill because older Australians cannot afford to wait any longer. They can't afford to wait any longer. They're telling us that right around the country, when you listen to them and you listen to their families. The problem is not fixed. It is absolutely not fixed. Make no mistake about what this is: an admission by the government that its assessment system is failing older Australians. For almost 12 months, older Australians, their families, assessors and providers have been telling this government that the algorithm is getting it wrong. They told the Senate inquiry. They told our electorate offices. They told anyone who would listen. For almost 12 months, this government told them the system was working.

Now, under the sheer weight of evidence, the government, which talks about caring for vulnerable people, has finally capitulated. It has agreed to an independent review of the very algorithm it spent a year defending. I'm not sure how you could defend it with the weight of evidence that said the algorithm was just the wrong thing to do. It wasn't assessing people appropriately. It was unfair. It was making mistakes. There was the removal of human override. How much more wrong can you get it?

We are giving the government the opportunity to go away, do that work and get it done, but if it does not, we will be back, and I'm confident the Greens and the crossbench will be with us. Together, we will force this government to do the right thing. The coalition won't step away from this fight for human override. That's because we have heard it time and time again. Senator Ruston and I have been speaking to people in communities across South Australia and everywhere else in this country, and we're hearing exactly the same message. The only people that don't seem to be hearing that are on the opposite side. We won't move one inch from pushing for this to happen.

I know the Greens have moved an amendment on human override. We do not believe what the government has put forward is adequate when it comes to human override. An escalation pathway run by the department for people in exceptional circumstances is a step, but it is not the same as letting a qualified assessor sit across the table from an older Australian and correct the computer when it gets it wrong. This Senate has already passed the coalition's bill to restore human override with the support of the Greens and the crossbench. Earlier this year, a senior minister in this government told the parliament:

… in every case there needs to be human oversight of any use of AI. We don't just hand over decision-making to abstract computer programs …

Of course the coalition agrees; it's common sense. Today, we are putting this government on notice. The clock is ticking. The coalition will never step away from older Australians. We will keep pushing for a permanent fix, and we will always back human override, because no algorithm has ever grown old. Every Australian is different, and older Australians deserve a system that sees them as people, not as data. They deserve nothing less.

speaker: Kanishka Narayan
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: We work closely with the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and Departments across Government to ensure that critical infrastructure developments are sustainable for local resource capacity. The planning system takes into account a number of those questions and ought to account for the long-term implications for water and wider resource supply. We have specifically designed our AI growth zones to be investments in areas where there is sufficient energy capacity and where infrastructure can be enhanced.

speaker: Neil Duncan-Jordan
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: There are environmental consequences caused by the emergence of data centres. There are also overblown claims as to their ability to create large numbers of jobs. The biggest concern, however, is in whose interests they will operate. What steps are the Government taking to ensure that AI works for the people, not just for big tech companies?

speaker: Kanishka Narayan
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: I thank my hon. Friend, whose question is one we have discussed at length. The central point is that in the last wave of technology, we built neither public trust nor British technology. In this wave of AI, we are focused on building both trust and technology so we can have sovereign control over what we are building here.

speaker: Olly Glover
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: What steps his Department is taking with Cabinet colleagues to regulate artificial intelligence.

speaker: Kanishka Narayan
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: We already have a series of areas of regulatory focus for artificial intelligence—data protection, competition policy, equality legislation and online safety. I was particularly proud that we were one of the first countries to ensure that the egregious impacts of AI chatbots on our children were mitigated. As I mentioned earlier in the week, I am looking forward to working right across the House on any further regulatory measures required to tackle any harms from artificial intelligence.

speaker: Olly Glover
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: AI has the potential to transform science and research, including on campuses such as Harwell and Culham in my Oxfordshire constituency. However, those benefits will be realised only if the risks of AI are taken seriously. Will the Minister support the call of over 85 parliamentarians for the Government to use our 2027 G20 presidency to champion an international agreement to properly regulate AI and prohibit super-intelligent AI development?

speaker: Kanishka Narayan
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: I thank the hon. Member for raising the advances of Culham in particular. I visited the site; I take great pride in it, as a national asset when it comes to nuclear fusion and the combination of AI and energy innovation. On his point about the G20, I am proud that the Prime Minister has set out that AI will be top of the agenda. We will look to play a leadership role in ensuring that we arrive at a global code and principles for safe AI.

speaker: Liam Byrne
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: On Tuesday, the head of MI5 warned that AI could help terrorists to develop bioweapons. In the Select Committee, OpenAI and Anthropic told us that statutory AI safety controls are now essential. We are blessed to have the AI Security Institute in this country, but it is no longer enough. Will Ministers confirm that we will have Government amendments on Report of the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill to ensure that we have statutory AI protections to keep this country safe?

speaker: Kanishka Narayan
heading: Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
text: I thank my right hon. Friend for his advocacy and leadership on this matter over the course of the last many weeks. I have mentioned already this week that I want to work with parliamentarians across the House, including him and members of his Committee, on ideas for the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, looking in particular at AI security protections.
