speaker: Simon Lightwood
heading: Highways (Financing) Bill
text:
There will indeed be a stakeholder group and opportunities for people to feed into that.

My hon. Friend the Member for Brentford and Isleworth (Ruth Cadbury), the Chair of the Transport Committee, was right that transport works best when there is a clear sense of direction and purpose. The Government are committed to providing that through a coherent programme of investment, reform and delivery that will create a more reliable, integrated and sustainable transport network. Indeed, that is exactly why we published our “Better Connected” strategy in April, which set out for the first time a single vision of how roads, rail, buses and active travel should work together to serve the people and places across England.

I want to address directly the reasoned amendment before the House, because it goes to the heart of what the Bill is and what it is not. To be honest, it is as if the Opposition have pleaded with ChatGPT to find any conceivable reason why they could disagree with the Bill. The first thing to note is that while the immediate context for the Bill is, of course, to aid the delivery of the lower Thames crossing, the Bill is about far more than that, so I will not be talking about the budget or project timelines. I will not dwell on the frankly shocking hypocrisy of the Conservative party, which oversaw ballooning costs to HS2, lecturing this Government on financial management. There are other times and places for that kind of discussion. Let me simply say this: the project is progressing, with construction activity already under way. Decisions on the project continue to be subject to rigorous scrutiny, with value for money remaining at the heart of decision making. The project already has its necessary planning approvals, which included the approval to charge tolls for use. In bringing forward the Bill, Parliament is not changing that approved scheme; it will just be providing another option in a suite of tools that the Government have to fund major road projects.

I am confused, Madam Deputy Speaker, because I do not understand why the Opposition want to withdraw from the Aarhus convention at this stage of the process for the lower Thames crossing. The main thing the convention does is to allow public participation in the planning process and ensure that environmental information is made available. It protects public access to reasoning and decision making during the planning process. That stage has already passed in the case of the lower Thames crossing. Withdrawing from the convention now, on behalf of the lower Thames crossing, would do absolutely nothing. The environmental information has already been produced. It has already been scrutinised publicly and published. That stage has passed, so it would not save money now.

The third thing to note is that, as I have just explained, there are already Acts that have been approved by this place that allow the Secretary of State, and indeed local government, to introduce new road schemes that involve charging or tolling without recourse to parliamentary approval.

Finally and most importantly, I must address what can only be described as misunderstandings contained in the reasoned amendment. It is important that this House takes its responsibilities for clear and fair communication with the public seriously, and I want to address that head-on. The Bill provides a mechanism for new infrastructure to be funded through future tolls in a way that regulates the potential impact on road users and provides certainty for investors. It also allows for existing physical tolls to be replaced by free-flowing virtual toll systems. The Opposition support both those measures as far as I understand. There is nothing else in the Bill: it has got nothing to say about applying new tolls on existing roads; nothing to say about wider road-user charging; nothing to say about low-traffic neighbourhoods, 15-minute cites or who shot JFK! There are no conspiracies here. I know the Opposition like to whip up the culture wars whenever they see the opportunity, but their rantings and ravings about the war on motorists, in this place and outside it, are obviously wide of the mark.

What sensible hon. Members will see in the Bill is a common-sense approach to managing our road infrastructure, now and in the future—nothing more; nothing less. Frankly, our constituents would be better served if we scrutinised what was in the Bill, rather than harping on about things that are not. Ultimately, the debate comes down to a simple question: should the Government have another tool to help deliver nationally significant infrastructure; a tool that enables practical partnership with the private sector that, in the right circumstances, can offer a good deal for taxpayers and users, and that comes with a strong regulatory protection. I believe that the Government should have that tool.

The Bill does not require the Government to use that model in every case, it does not place private finance above public finance, and nor does it ask the House to make an ideological choice between the two. It simply ensures that where private investment can help deliver nationally important infrastructure, with strong, independent regulation and robust safeguards for users, the Government have the option. That is pragmatic, proportionate and, above all, focused on delivery. I commend the Bill to the House.

Question put, That the amendment be made.

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Russian Interference in the Brexit Referendum - Question
text: That is absolutely not what the Prime Minister said and it is not what I have said from this Dispatch Box. Ten years on from the Brexit referendum, it is reasonable to have a conversation about whether Brexit has been good for this country, including leave voters, who voted in good faith that this would be the best outcome for the country. We are not talking about relitigating the referendum at this point. Nobody is suggesting that the interference by Russia was successful. However, it is clear that, when a foreign state is spending £1.3 billion a year on attempts to spread misinformation and disinformation—through deepfakes to bots to false statements, all of which circulate in the media and on social media—we as a Government have a duty to ensure we defend our democracy, our economy and people of all opinions, whether they voted for Brexit or not, from foreign state interference. I am surprised that this is apparently not the view of noble Lords opposite.

speaker: Lord Leong
heading: Support for Family Businesses - Question for Short Debate
text:
My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Cameron of Dillington, for securing this debate and all noble Lords for their contributions. I congratulate my noble friend Lord McTague on his maiden speech. With 30 years’ experience of running his own businesses and as a former chair of the Federation of Small Businesses, he will bring an enormous contribution to our debates in this House. We look forward to hearing much more from him.

This is a timed debate, so I will endeavour to answer as many questions as I can. If I do not have time, I will write to all noble Lords and place a copy of the letter in the Library.

Family businesses touch our lives every single day: the milk in our tea, the bread on our table, the shop on the high street. Consider how many family business might touch our lives before we have even stepped outside our front door: the Harrison Spinks mattress we wake up on; the Baylis & Harding handwash in the bathroom; the Yorkshire Tea in our cup; the Mornflake porridge in our bowl; and the Warburtons bread in our toaster. Then, perhaps, we put on a pair of Crockett & Jones shoes and a Barbour jacket before we leave the house. Behind each family product is families who have invested, taken risks, created jobs and built reputations over generations. Their businesses are woven into our daily lives. Their futures matter in every community where they employ, supply and serve. Behind each is a family that has taken a risk, built a reputation and accepted responsibility for other people’s livelihoods. When a family manufacturer invests in a market town or a village business takes on an apprentice, the benefits remain in that community for many years to come.

These businesses often measure success in generations. Having spent more than 45 years building and running businesses, I understand something of that outlook. I know the satisfaction of winning a customer and seeing an employee develop. I also know the pressure of meeting payroll when an invoice remains unpaid. When your family’s savings, livelihood and reputation are invested in the business, those pressures follow you home, so I recognise why owners worry about energy bills, borrowing costs, business rates and employment costs, including national insurance. They experience those pressures together, alongside the time required to understand changing rules. For a small firm without a finance department or an HR team, the owner bears the burden directly.

Government must understand that reality: our support must be accessible, our requirements proportionate and our implementation workable. That is the purpose behind our small business plan: helping firms manage today’s pressures while building the confidence and capacity to grow.

Let me set out what that means in practice. First, on getting paid, a business can have a healthy order book and still face a cash flow crisis. An overdue invoice can mean postponing equipment, turning down work or abandoning plans to recruit. Through our Commercial Payments Bill and the support of the noble Lord opposite, we are pursuing a maximum payment period of 60 days for contracts within scope, stronger powers for the Small Business Commissioner and a ban on construction retentions. A small family supplier should be able to challenge poor payment practices with confidence. Work delivered should mean payment received.

Secondly, on access to finance and advice, family owners may want to expand while retaining control of the enterprise they have built. Finance must respond to that ambition. The British Business Bank’s five-year strategy includes 85,000 new start-up loans. For established smaller firms, the growth guarantee scheme supports access to lending for investment and growth. Through the business growth service and the growth hubs throughout the country, we are also making advice easier to find.

Mid-market businesses face their own challenges around investment, management and exporting. The Northern 500 initiative will bring ambitious mid-sized northern businesses together with mayors, government and private sector partners to support their growth.

Thirdly, on investing in people and productivity, succession requires preparation, developing future leaders, bringing in expertise and giving the next generation room to contribute. The Government’s Help to Grow: Management programme provides eligible leaders with training and mentoring backed by a 90% government subsidy. Our digital adoption work helps business to assess how technology and AI can improve productivity.

Family firms also give many young people their first chance. Many noble Lords have asked about skills. In England, apprenticeship training is fully funded for eligible under-25s at non-levy paying employers, with a £2,000 hiring payment for eligible new apprentices from this month. These measures help small employers to develop the skills they need.

Fourthly, on opportunities to win business, departmental procurement targets are intended to deliver more than £7.4 billion in annual direct spending with small and medium-sized businesses by 2028. The Procurement Act and the central digital platform are designed to reduce barriers to participation. The test is whether a capable family business can compete fairly without the bidding process consuming resources it cannot spare.

Place matters too. A successful high street brings customers to the family café, retailer and service business. Our £210 million high street package will help bring neglected buildings back into use and support community assets and businesses alongside the forthcoming high street strategy.

Let me now turn to inheritance and succession. I understand why this matters so much. A business value may be tied up in premises, machinery or land. That is not the same as having cash available, although an estate can, where appropriate, pay its tax liability from other assets. Some families are asking what a potential future liability means for today’s investment and how it affects succession planning, recognising that business owners have a range of options, including making lifetime gifts. The Government must balance support for enterprises with fair taxation and sustainable public services.

We have also listened and changed the arrangements. The allowance for assets eligible for 100% agricultural and business property relief is £2.5 million, and any unused allowance can be transferred between spouses and civil partners. This means a couple can pass on up to £5 million in qualifying assets tax-free, alongside existing allowances and exemptions. Qualifying assets above the allowance receive 50% relief, and tax attributed to property eligible for this relief can be paid over 10 years in interest-free instalments. However, I will ensure that the concerns raised today are conveyed to my Treasury colleagues.

Family Business UK also contributes to our work on small business growth and mid-market regulation, and I, my team and my ministerial colleagues meet with them regularly. That dialogue matters, and I look forward to taking part in Family Business Week, which is coming up very soon. Families who build businesses invest far more than money: they invest their time, hopes and often a lifetime of work. They deserve a Government who understand that commitment and who take their concerns seriously. Our task is to help turn ambition into investment, investment into good jobs, and years of hard work into a business the next generation can carry forward. When family businesses succeed, employees, suppliers and whole communities share in that success. That is why their future matters to us all.

speaker: Baroness Teather
heading: Food Security - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, it is a huge privilege to open this debate. Food security is incredibly complex. Addressing it has also never been more pressing. We now face multiple global threats that could create profound food shocks—shocks that will fall unequally on our population. The question is how we can best prepare as a nation and make our food system more resilient.

Planning effective interventions on food security requires us to think systemically across silos—from farming and the environment to foreign and defence policy, international trade, public health, local government, planning regulations, business logistics, behavioural science and much more besides. I am certainly no expert in all these areas, but one thing I have learnt as a new Member is that breadth of expertise is something this House has in spades. I suggested this title for debate because this kind of urgent, vital and knotty challenge plays to the strengths of the House. I am grateful to noble Lords who have given their time and experience to participate, and I look forward to hearing what they have to say.

As the topic is huge, I want to focus my remarks on three areas: first, the threats to our food system and our national response; secondly, efforts to build resilience for the longer term; and thirdly, the need to involve the whole of society in the effort.

Multiple reports in recent years have warned that the UK is dangerously unprepared for potentially catastrophic shocks to our food system. Professor Tim Lang’s impressive report for the National Preparedness Commission last year paints a comprehensive picture of current vulnerabilities. The National Audit Office warned last month that the sector’s ability to withstand events has not been tested. Farmers tell us that climate change is already a reality, creating huge unpredictability. Crops this year have been affected by drought, flooding, excessive rain and extreme heat, which of course has sometimes made it too hot to harvest. While some yields have held up, we have seen the worst cereal harvest on record, and with a supercharged El Niño, it is only likely to get worse. The Joint Intelligence Committee has given stark warnings about the potential for the collapse of ecosystems within five years and the threat to national security and food supply.

In addition, there are new crises emerging. Attacks on international shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have sharply increased the cost of diesel and fertiliser for UK farmers, and threaten critical shortages in Africa and Asia, from which we import. Of course, Hormuz is not the only international choke point we should worry about. We have seen cyber attacks on supermarkets and distributors. This week, the director-general of MI5 warned about the risk of AI-enabled drone attacks on UK soil, a real concern when almost 95% of retail food moves through just 131 distribution centres.

In this new reality, it is naive to assume that private sector switching of supply chains alone will be enough to keep food flowing. It is certainly the case that supermarkets responded with impressive speed to maintain supplies during Covid, but Covid also exposed structural failings in our system, which we have not yet addressed. First, adequate food supply does not equate to all the people being fed. The Food Foundation estimates that one in eight households are already food insecure. I saw during Covid, while I was running a charity for people facing destitution, that global food shocks fall unequally and can have devastating health impacts. Secondly, none of the national food security assessments considers how the public might actually behave in a food shock scenario. The flipside of highly optimised, just-in-time logistics is that very small changes in consumer behaviour can quickly empty shelves. Thirdly, the same efficient logistics have all but eliminated the need for storage. We could have just a few days of food available in the face of a catastrophic interruption to supply.

We import around 40% of our food and more than 80% of our fruit. It is vital that we increase the proportion of food that we grow in the UK, but this is only part of the story. Food ingredients are often passed along lengthy, tortuous supply chains before they end up on the plate, with processing, manufacturing and distribution happening in different locations. Disruptions anywhere can cascade and amplify along the route. Given this context, our national assessment of risk looks dangerously complacent. The national risk register, for example, has very little on the food system and, where it does consider food, the focus is on risk of contamination rather than interruptions to supply or access.

So, what is needed? First, the Cabinet Office frankly needs to up its game and update the way in which we assess and think about food security in the light of the new threats. We need a special national risk register study that includes consideration of public reactions and dynamics. Secondly, the Government’s post-implementation review of the Civil Contingencies Act provides an opportunity to integrate food resilience and to think about the kinds of structures that we need at local and regional level to co-ordinate efforts. Local areas need plans to get food to the vulnerable and an understanding of community assets and networks that could help. We also need a more grown-up conversation with the public than a website telling people to stock up on tins. Thirdly, while there are legal duties to ensure that food is safe, there are no duties to ensure that everyone gets fed. It really is not clear who would hold responsibility for this in a crisis. Finally, we need a rapid assessment of what storage is available at national, regional and local levels and a plan to improve it. This is not an easy fix. Can the Government convene a cross-sector taskforce, for example, to wrestle with it? Other countries, everywhere from Switzerland to China, have national stores and many European nations are developing plans to store food.

A key theme from Professor Lang’s report for the National Preparedness Commission was the need to move our peacetime food system to a more distributed and diverse model, to boost domestic production and to enhance regional food systems. The UK is unusual in having an underdeveloped regional food system compared with, say, France or Italy.

Long-term sustainability in our food system depends on protecting the natural resources that farming depends on—soil health and biodiversity—and transitioning from reliance on globally imported fertiliser. Yesterday, the Government published a new Organic Action Plan for England, to boost the share of food farmed organically. My first reading of it suggests that there is much in it that is welcome, including backing organic farming to boost resilience to climate change. We have to support farmers to transition to new ways of farming. That means backing those willing to experiment with organic and regenerative farming models that focus on soil health and are not tied to inorganic fertilisers. We must fund rigorous scientific research into crop yields, soil, nature and profitability and share those lessons widely.

However, the new organic plan also leaves lots of questions. There has been exasperation from farmers at the chaos of the sustainable farming incentive scheme. Small growers told me that, even if the scheme had been well managed, it left them out by design. They are a critical component of a regional food system and often already farming in sustainable ways. For example, Vallis Veg in Somerset, an established small farm, told me that the economics of the food system currently relies on farmers in effect exploiting themselves. Its owners are deeply committed to agroecological farming but do not have the resources to certify as organic, which the organic action plan acknowledges is a problem. Vallis Veg’s commitment to the cause extends to supporting new entrants. It provides a small plot of land for free to a local grower to run a market garden, who is allowed to live on site for below-market rent, but even with all that generosity he struggles to make a living. According to a recent McCain Foods survey, one in four farmers made a loss or barely broke even in the past year, and two in five considered quitting farming altogether. We know that those financial pressures are particularly acute for small farmers. Those who make it work often rely on additional funding streams.

The inspirational Prospects Trust on the Cambridge-Suffolk border includes an accessible nature reserve, organic farm, shop and retail outlet and provides placements for people with learning disabilities or autism, funded through social care. It employs 51 local people part time and grows delicious fruit and veg. Over decades, it has built trusted relationships with a local organic wholesaler and a Cambridge college chef willing to cook veg that it cannot sell elsewhere, reducing food waste. It told me that relationships are key to its ability to adapt to shifting weather, because constant communication allows it to agree with the customer on what it can crop. It is a remarkable success story, but there was frustration that it could not access the agricultural water resilience grant to replace its leaky irrigation system because it could not quickly raise the 50% capital contribution needed. Can the Minister say what the Government will do to support small farms such as these?

Incidentally, Cambridge is an example of a city with a vibrant local food partnership, much enthusiasm and fertile arable land. But without capital investment in the missing middle of infrastructure on storage and distribution, it is difficult to turn ambition into a functioning regional food system. The founder of the fledgling Cambridge Food Hub has been trying to secure investment for that missing middle for 13 years. He illustrated the problem that he is seeking to fix by explaining that, even though one of the largest strawberry farmers in the country is based just outside the city, local businesses must buy their produce from New Covent Garden Market. That means that fruit grown six miles away must travel 120 miles—Cambridge to London and then back to Cambridge—in a refrigerated lorry. That is madness.

It is worth contrasting that with the success of the Welsh Veg in Schools initiative. With Welsh Government backing, Food Sense Wales to broker deals and local infrastructure donated by Castell Howell, local growers have been able to co-ordinate what they grow. More veg is being grown and local farms now supply over half of Wales’s councils.

The new organic action plan restates the Government’s ambitions to use public sector procurement to support domestic growing and it references Sustain’s Bridging the Gap programme, but it is short on detail about how the Government will invest in the so-called missing middle infrastructure to make regional food systems fly. Will the Minister tell me what plans her department has to make good on Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledge to boost local food procurement?

The final theme that I want to touch on is how we can ensure that our efforts on food security involve the whole of society. We have a long-standing problem with food inequality and it is getting worse. The Government announced small pots of funding for the Good Food Neighbourhoods programme to tackle fruit and veg deserts, but what is missing is a coherent national strategy with teeth that draws together public health, planning policy, housing strategies, local government, agricultural policy and public attitudes.

Now is the moment for a good food Bill—something that covers the full arc of the food system, allowing co-ordinated decision-making at national and local levels. It would allow us to set targets on childhood obesity, food security and domestic production and would provide certainty about the direction of travel for farmers, businesses, investors and consumers. It would also kick-start a consultation about what we mean when we talk about a healthy nutritious sustainable diet. What would a reference diet look like? What implications would it have for our agricultural strategy? What needs to shift in public attitudes if we are to consume more of the foods that we can grow here, such as beans and pulses? A consensus on these elements would guide policy-making priorities in peacetime, but it would also be critical in an emergency.

Joined-up policy-making would also give more creative projects a chance, such as peri-urban growing and land for community gardens and allotments. No one is arguing that community growing projects will fill the gap in domestic production, but what it can do is build solidarity, narrow the distance between farmers and urban populations, build knowledge and shape attitudes to what we eat and cook. In the end, in an emergency, it is only communities acting together that can provide civil resilience. Everything we do now to invest in conditions for deeper community bonds will reap dividends.

The need to address Britain’s food security cannot wait. I look forward to the Minister’s response and the debate. I beg to move.

speaker: Lord Docherty of Milngavie
heading: Food Security - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the noble Baroness, Lady Teather, for this timely and important debate. I also thank the noble Lord, Lord Trees, and the other noble Lords who have spoken with such knowledge and insight today.

Food security is clearly essential to the well-being—indeed, the survival, as the noble Baroness, Lady Shephard, said—of this and every other nation. It is something that, in our globalised world, we have taken for granted for too long. It is especially timely when one considers the increasing geopolitical threats we face, with all the dislocation and turbulence that they could bring to food security, as well as what emergency planners might call the slow rising tide of climate change.

We discuss food security at the same time the country faces the most dangerous and volatile international situation since World War II. Europe is rearming at a variable pace, led by Poland and Germany, but it is rearming none the less. There is a superpower arms race in AI and compute, with all the risks, known and unknowable, which that entails, including the risk of new bioweapons, which has been much reported. Alongside this geopolitical landscape, the impact of climate change continues, with all the demands that will place on agriculture and food production, as so many noble Lords have mentioned.

As has been said, today the UK imports just over 40% of our food, with by far the largest element—around three-quarters of total imports—coming from mainland Europe. Our level of food imports places the UK among the least self-sufficient developed nations in food production. We have been here before. In 1939, the UK imported 70% of the food required to sustain the population—which was then 50 million—and much of that came from the Empire. Some data suggests that imports were responsible for nearer 90% of the total calorie intake—a remarkable sum. This reliance on imported food became a strategic vulnerability when German U-boats attacked merchant shipping in the Battle of the Atlantic, threatening supplies of grain, meat, sugar and other essentials. Incidentally, that was a battle in which my uncle, Able Seaman David McGroarty, serving in the Royal Navy, died aged 19.

The best-known element of the government response was called Dig for Victory, which encouraged people to cultivate gardens, allotments and unusable land to grow vegetables. However, much more importantly, farmers were encouraged to switch production to grow wheat, potatoes and other crops rather than maintain pasture for livestock. Mechanisation, including a greater use of tractors, helped compensate for labour shortages. The Government transformed how food production and consumption were managed. They exercised extensive control over agriculture through guaranteed prices, subsidies, compulsory cropping requirements and the direction of farming resources.

Food rationing—which was mentioned by the noble Lord, Lord Teverson; I was not alive at the time—ensured that scarce supplies were distributed more fairly and reduced waste. Scientific advances improved farming techniques and more intensive land use contributed to higher output. I do not suggest that exactly the same thing would or should happen now, but, as has been mentioned, we do not have to look far for examples of where conflict can bring to a halt the shipping of essential global commodities. Today, things can be halted by much cheaper and more agile autonomous boats, drones, submersibles, et cetera.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 caused a major shock to global food supplies. Ukraine was and is one of the world’s most important exporters of wheat, maize, sunflower oil and other commodities. The invasion disrupted production, blocked ports, damaged infrastructure and made shipping through the Black Sea dangerous. The result was not only a shortage of food worldwide but higher prices and reduced access to affordable food, especially for poorer countries, some of which had sourced over 80% of their wheat from Ukraine prior to the invasion.

Given our disproportionate reliance on food imports, I, like the noble Lord, Lord Smith, would like reassurance that contingency plans are in place for how we would respond to systemic shocks to those imports. The threat is real, and we need to plan accordingly.

As has been mentioned, climate change will also require a major rethink of UK food production and whole-system change. One obvious example is the viability of grass as animal feed in a warming climate and the impact of that on livestock production. We need only to think back a few months to those images of a scorched Hyde Park to understand the impact climate change is having.

Over time, different sources of protein may be required, all of which, as has been mentioned, will require producers, retailers and consumers to work together. New technology today might mean gene editing rather than tractors, but I am optimistic, as our agricultural sector has seen whole-system change at pace before and may have to do again.

Before I conclude, I will raise one other issue which impacts upon both geopolitical risk and climate change: our sovereign capacity to produce ammonia, the essential element in the production of fertiliser and in what the defence industry calls energetics—what noble Lords and I would call explosives. In 2021, the then Government allowed the only ammonia production plant in the UK to close, citing market forces. This was not long after the same Government allowed one of our last virgin steel-making plants—also in Teesside—to close, but that is another story.

The ammonia plant based in Billingham in Teesside still produces fertiliser, but since 2021, it has been entirely dependent on ammonia produced in and imported from the USA. To repeat, the UK no longer has sovereign capability in the production of one of the most important base chemicals—an essential ingredient to both food security and national security.

I have two questions for my noble friend the Minister. Do the Government have a live and active contingency plan for how they would respond to major disruptions to food imports to this country caused by major geopolitical shocks? Are those plans kept up to date? Are they active or under review? Is there a plan to restart ammonia production in the UK, and if so, what are the timescales for that? I look forward to the Minister’s response.

speaker: Paula Barker
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text: We begin with the Select Committee statement. Alex Sobel will speak on the publication of the fourth report of the Joint Committee on Human Rights, “Human Rights and the Regulation of AI”, HC 160, for up to 10 minutes, during which no interventions may be taken. At the conclusion of his statement, I will call Members to put questions on the subject of the statement, and call Alex Sobel to respond to these in turn. Questions should be brief and Members may ask only one question each. I call Alex Sobel, chair of the Joint Committee on Human Rights.

speaker: Alex Sobel
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text:
Thank you very much, Mrs Barker. As the newly elected Chair, I am proud to be presenting the significant findings of the fourth report of the Joint Committee on Human Rights, on human rights and the regulation of artificial intelligence. I thank Lord Alton for his exemplary leadership and service as the Chair of our Committee.

All the evidence suggests that the world is at the precipice of the outcomes of a reckless race towards superintelligent AI—AI that can fully replace and outmatch humans at any task. Our report found that no cross-economy regulators, agencies or bodies have systemic powers to prevent AI models or systems from being deployed, even if they pose significant risks.

Regulators lack the power to test and evaluate AI systems before they are publicly released or to prevent their release if they are considered to pose unacceptable risks, except in very limited circumstances. Our existing copyright laws will not stop the onset of superintelligent AI in the UK. Model developers engage the AI Security Institute on a voluntary basis. The AI Security Institute has no statutory power.

The Committee found that AI indeed threatens the human rights of people in the UK and elsewhere. We welcome the Prime Minister accepting one of our key recommendations that the Government should use its G20 presidency to address AI harms. That being said, with the speed and turbulence that frontier developers are hurtling towards unleashing superintelligent AI, we must regulate now—not in a year, not in five years, but now. With the G20 in mind, we should seek a global agreement on standards and regulations next year.

The Committee has concentrated on the key principles identified in the Council of Europe’s framework convention as being fundamental to the protection of human rights— equality and non-discrimination, and privacy and personal data protection. The Committee defined that AI systems are machine systems that perceive, learn and act.

AI is now widely used across a diverse range of purposes, from email spam filters through to powerful tools for scientific discovery. AI systems are being incorporated into more complex AI agents. These are small, specialised pieces of software that can make decisions and operate co-operatively or independently to achieve pre-specified objectives. A fundamental aspect of current AI systems is their capacity to operate with varying degrees of autonomy and adaptiveness. Some AI models operate in ways that are so mathematically complex that their outputs are opaque, even to an informed expert.

The general-purpose AI systems used today are not coded line by line, but use vast amounts of data and are grown, not built. This results in systems that nobody fully understands or can reliably predict.

Let me be clear: AI is the crucial technology of the 21st century. It is vital to effective defence and promotes vast benefits for science, medicine and the UK’s prosperity. However, there are many ways in which AI may adversely affect human rights. In particular, witnesses during our inquiry told us of the potential impact on the treatment and condition of workers, workers’ rights generally and on the environment.

Furthermore, companies are spending billions to make superintelligent AI reality. The chief executives of top AI companies themselves put the chance that it ends all human life at between 10% and 25%. In any other industry, with that level of risk, this development would be ruled out. How have we allowed frontier developers to create the rules in which they govern themselves?

On the first principle of the framework convention—equality and non-discrimination—we heard that intentional abuses committed using AI systems such as deepfakes can have a disproportionate effect on people from minoritised groups, compounding existing structural and systemic racism and sexism that impacts victims’ personal and professional lives. The Safety Not Surveillance coalition told us:

“AI is having a chilling effect on communities of colour in the UK.”

Discrimination can arise when AI systems are deployed, because of these baked-in biases and choices made by those deploying AI systems. We heard explicit examples of AI facial recognition software having racial basis and of AI recruitment tools discriminating against women applicants. AI systems are prone to producing unfairly discriminatory outcomes because of biased training data. That threatens the human rights of people in the UK and elsewhere.

Next, we looked at the second principle of the framework convention, which is that AI systems pose particular risks to privacy and personal data. The Committee found that because of the prevalence of web scraping to collect personal data to train large language models, there is potential for AI systems to be used in highly intrusive ways. That threatens the article 8 right to privacy of people in the UK and is given particular expression in data protection law in relation to personal data. Between January and October 2025, about 3 million people would have had their faces scanned by police facial recognition technology in the UK without their consent.

Human rights principles must inform all aspects of the Government’s policies and practices relating to AI systems, including their approach to the regulation of AI. The Committee recommends that the Government encourage the development of AI use cases that can demonstrably improve human rights.

Although the AI action plan commissioned by the previous Administration brings a welcome focus on innovation and economic opportunity, it fails to pay sufficient attention to the need to secure the protection of human rights from AI-generated interference throughout the supply chain.

The UK’s leading position as the third largest AI market in the world affords opportunities not only for economic growth, but for setting strong standards on the responsible adoption and development of new technologies. The Committee is encouraged by the prominence given to AI by the new Administration and urges the Government to seize the opportunity to regulate AI in a way that puts human rights first. To address the global nature of AI harms and protect human rights, Governments need to collaborate to identify risks and promote consistent standards. The UK can be justifiably proud of its record of leadership on AI. That has been maintained across Administrations from different sides of the debate. An appropriate regulatory regime would not only enhance human rights protections but help to reinforce the UK’s leadership position in AI safety.

The Committee recommends that the Government introduce a new AI Bill, as promised in the 2024 King’s Speech, to place AI regulation on a sound basis and give full effect to the framework convention. A risk-based approach is needed to address AI harms. The Hugging Face incident and others illustrate the significant risks that can arise from the newest and most advanced AI models, and legislation should address those risks on a precautionary basis with a view to avoiding harm, as with the regulation of pharmaceuticals. Low-risk AI systems should be subject to fewer and less demanding legal requirements. To ensure that regulation can keep pace with technological developments, it is preferable for legislation to take the form of broadly framed principles. The AI Bill that we recommend should provide for a regulatory regime that would classify different risk levels and mandate proportionately more demanding obligations for higher-risk AI systems and models.

Some uses of AI should be prohibited because they are incompatible with human rights. I believe that to be the case when it comes to superintelligent AI. Once developers reach superintelligent AI, it will be too late to slow anything down in time for us to regulate. The development of the most advanced AI systems happens on a spectrum, so where we draw the line matters. That line must be able to recognise the capabilities of superintelligent AI. The clearest example of such a capability is recursive self-improvement—the full automation of AI development, with no humans in the loop. That is the point at which we lose control, as development towards superintelligent AI would proceed too fast for humans to intervene and remain in control.

Frontier developers are heeding standards, rather than statute, for their own AI models. These are the same developers who are deliberately training their models to hack and deceive, as we heard this week during the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee inquiry session, which I guested at as JCHR Chair. We heard from ex-employees of frontier developers OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic. We heard about non-existent safety cultures in these organisations. Some whistleblowers put the chance of AI destroying humanity at 50%—a coin flip as to whether we survive. This is not a human rights model that we should ever be working with. These frontier developers believe that they will not get stopped by Government in their race to superintelligence. Let us put a stop to that and regulate now.

In the words of David Krueger, previously at the UK AI Security Institute,

“My dream is that in 10 years people will look back and say: ‘Remember when there were all these people building AI that could’ve killed everybody? That was CRAZY! What were we thinking!?’”

speaker: Euan Stainbank
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text: This is a fast-moving topic that has continued to be of deep concern to my constituents since the publication of the report. Subsequent to its publication, has my hon. Friend seen any further evidence of the need for mandatory testing of AI frontier models?

speaker: Alex Sobel
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text:
I thank my fellow Committee member for that question. In the report, we said:

“Many AI systems developed for a specific purpose can be deployed or adapted for use for different purposes and contexts from those intended by the AI developer. Those deploying the system may lack understanding of the risks arising from the way in which the AI system has been designed and developed”.

We also recommend that the AI Bill should

“impose proportionate obligations on actors at all stages of the AI lifecycle and supply chain to ensure that risks are identified, evaluated and effectively addressed at the appropriate stage.”

On Tuesday, at the BIST Committee, we heard from Daniel Kokotajlo, a whistleblower, who said that pre-deployment training was insufficient and AISI or other safety institutes should be undertaking internal testing during all stages of development.

speaker: Chi Onwurah
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text:
I thank my hon. Friend the Chair of the Joint Committee for this report. I should declare an interest as the Chair of the Science and Technology Committee. I guested on the inquiry, and I share the concerns regarding the potential harms to human rights and support the report’s call for effective principle-based regulation now.

Does my hon. Friend agree with me, and with His Holiness the Pope in his “Magnificent Humanity” encyclical, that human rights are for humans, that the anthropomorphising of AI—going as far as ascribing human consciousness and human rights to AI—is an attempt by tech companies to limit their own liability as well as boosting the potential value of their shares?

speaker: Alex Sobel
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text: I thank my hon. Friend the Chair of the Science and Technology Committee. It has been my great privilege to twice hear Pope Leo address an audience in the Vatican. The second time, at the Jubilee of Governments, last year in June, he addressed this exact issue. This is not a recent development for the Pope. I read his encyclical and think that every Government should study it. It is interesting that—although he is technically a head of state, because the Vatican is a state—a faith leader such as the Pope has such an incisive view on an issue such as this and brings it back to the central principle that human rights are for humans. We have already seen the anthropocentric effects on the climate. We cannot have the same pervade every area of life through AI. These AI companies are now at a stage where they are trying to replace Governments and not be regulated by Governments. That is, exactly as my hon Friend says, because they can then limit their liabilities, maximise their profits and act without any scope from the state. That should concern us all.

speaker: Peter Swallow
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text: My hon. Friend will not have failed to clock the comments from the president of Microsoft this week that the UK is best placed to lead on AI governance. That is something that we found in our report, not least because of the AI Security Institute, which our report recommends strengthening further. Does he agree that it is not about limiting the very real benefits that AI may bring to the UK’s economy, our healthcare system or even, as we found in our report, to human rights, but about leading the world in realising those benefits safely while recognising and mitigating the very real risks that exist?

speaker: Alex Sobel
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text:
I absolutely agree. We continually heard evidence right across the industry, both here in the House and externally, about the excellent work that the AISI does. I am pleased that the AI Minister, who is here in the Chamber, has played another leading role in developing AISI as the world’s leading AI safety institute.

However, my hon. Friend is absolutely right. There are two things. The first, as the report found, is about human utilisation of AI tools through, for instance, deepfakes, which affect people’s human rights, or through employment practices, which we can probably very easily regulate, control and legislate for, but that need Government action.

Then, secondly, there are the frontier models. We need a very different level of regulation and legislation for those than we have for individual assistive tools. I am not really worried about ChatGPT 2.0. It is not going to create an existential crisis but, without regulation, future models that are being developed can and will.

speaker: Jim Shannon
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text:
I thank the Committee Chair and the rest of the Committee for their report and all of the work that they have done. I cannot pretend to understand all about AI. I am probably the oldest of the old school when it comes to those things. I agree with what the Committee has said about how human rights should be first and AI second. I thank the Committee for its clear focus on that.

I also welcome the recommendation that there should be a new AI Bill. That is the right way to do it, because as we look forward, and move forward, we want to ensure that those things happen. Will the regional Assemblies across the United Kingdom, particularly the Northern Ireland Assembly, but also those in Scotland and Wales, be notified and advised of the technology and what the Committee has said? It is really important that individual human rights are protected. Indeed, I believe that they are sacrosanct. Human rights should be first. They should take precedent every time over the technology that is coming through AI.

speaker: Alex Sobel
heading: Joint committee on Human Rights
text:
First, AI may have the potential to replace many things, but it will probably never be able to replace the hon. Gentleman’s intervention at the Adjournment debate. We can probably rest assured of one thing in terms of AI development.

I am glad that we now seem to have cross-party support from the hon. Gentleman and his party for a new AI Bill with human rights at the centre. What he says about human rights is absolutely correct. I always say that human rights are universal, inalienable, indivisible and apply everywhere in the world. Our Committee’s remit is for the UK, but this is an international issue. I am sure that the Minister has heard all that we have said.

Sitting suspended.

speaker: Laura Kyrke-Smith
heading: Defence
text: Whether the threat is from Russia, Iran or rogue AI agents, keeping our country safe is the precondition for growth and progress here at home. Protecting ourselves means protecting the critical national infrastructure on which our constituents’ lives depend, whether that is our banking systems, road and rail networks, or electricity grid. As the Chief of the Defence Staff and the Secretary of State have said, we face a society-wide threat, and we must prepare and respond with a society-wide effort. Will the Secretary of State say more about what he is doing with Cabinet colleagues to protect our critical national infrastructure, and will he advise my constituents on what they can do to play their part in keeping us all safe?

speaker: Steve Yemm
subheading: Manufacturing Skills — [Sir Christopher Chope in the Chair]
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Sir Christopher. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Isle of Wight West (Richard Quigley) for securing this important debate at a time when our economy is undergoing transformation. AI, robotics and automation are changing how we manufacture and the skills that our businesses need. If we are serious about reindustrialisation, we have to make sure that our workforce is ready to seize the opportunity that those changes will bring. For places like my constituency of Mansfield, that means rebuilding the connections between education, local employees and employers, and skilled employment. Further education providers, including colleges like West Notts college in my constituency, are critical to delivering that.

On constituency visits, I have been fortunate to see the great work that is already being done by employers working in partnership with West Notts college and Nottingham Trent University. One such visit was to a local aerospace and nuclear electronics company, Glenair, which has recently taken on 60 new apprentices in Mansfield. Often, people consider apprenticeships as an option for school leavers, but what I find in my area is that those opportunities exist equally for adults who want to retrain, change careers or develop new skills. I am therefore very encouraged that Mansfield recorded 680 new apprenticeship starts in 2024-25, more than half of which were taken up by people over the age of 25.

The backdrop to this discussion, as Make UK has reported, is that there are almost 50,000 live vacancies across UK manufacturing. Three in five small or medium-sized manufacturing enterprises identify a lack of the right type of technical skill as a key barrier to recruitment. That apparent weakness can also be seen as an opportunity. For areas like mine, reindustrialisation and the ideas around it represent a real chance to build on our proud industrial heritage and create a new generation of skilled and well-paid jobs, but we have to make sure that local people have the skills to take on those opportunities, whether they are young people starting their careers or adults looking to retrain and learn something new, and skills for a new economy. If we get that right, as a Government and as a country, we can make sure that the industries of the future bring investment, opportunity and prosperity to places like Mansfield and that local people are properly equipped to play their full part in sharing our economic future.

speaker: Ian Sollom
subheading: Manufacturing Skills — [Sir Christopher Chope in the Chair]
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Sir Christopher. I congratulate the hon. Member for Isle of Wight West (Richard Quigley) on securing this important debate.

I start with some numbers we should celebrate: UK manufacturing produces output worth £220 billion and supports 2.6 million jobs, paying on average 8% more than the rest of the economy, and it accounts for 42% of our exports and almost half of all business research and development. It is a sector of skilled, well-paid careers that we are rightly proud of, but it is also a sector that could do more if it had more of the skilled people it needs.

Skills England identifies advanced manufacturing as having the third highest proportion of skills shortage vacancies of any sector, and projects that 84% of the additional jobs in its priority occupations to 2035 will need qualifications at level 4 or above. The businesses in Cambridgeshire that kindly shared their insights with me in advance of this debate described problems that I suspect Members from every part of the country will recognise. One electronics firm, Cap Air, told me that although electronics is the largest manufacturing sub-sector in our region, the county is a dead spot for the sort of technical education it needs, with training necessitating travel outside the county. There is no occupational standard for much of the work the company does. As Cap Air put it,

“You cannot fund a course for a job the system does not recognise.”

That is a national problem for Skills England, but lack of local provision is something places could fix for themselves. I hope the Prime Minister’s well-known enthusiasm for devolution extends to giving areas like ours the skills, powers and capital funding to do it.

Another manufacturer in my constituency, ZEISS, which makes electron microscopes, makes a related point about the future. Advanced manufacturing now combines traditional mechanical and electrical engineering with automation, software, data and AI, and we need to build those capabilities now before they become critical shortages, not just fill today’s vacancies. In 2024-25, there were over 46,000 starts in engineering and manufacturing in England, but level 2 manufacturing starts fell by 80% in the five years to 2023-24. That is a significant problem in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough.

The Liberal Democrats have long called for the apprenticeship levy to be replaced, so we welcome the Government’s move to a more flexible growth and skills levy, but we recognise that progress has been slow. Apprenticeship units have been available since April, yet the skills charity Enginuity found that a fifth of manufacturing SMEs have never heard of them, and only one in 10 think that they will fill their skills gaps. On the Department’s own forecasts, apprenticeship spending is due to fall after this year, even as levy receipts rise.

Employers tell me that the system needs to be straightforward for employers to use, responsive to changing industrial needs, and attractive to young people as a genuine alternative to university, but too often it is none of those things for smaller firms. The apprenticeship model may work for large employers, but a firm of 20 cannot easily release a young employee for two or sometimes three days a week to a college that might be miles away. It is also difficult for them to carry the paperwork that comes with. Another manufacturer in my constituency, Domino Printing Sciences, pointed out that employers pay into the levy but cannot use it to cover much of the real cost of employing and developing an apprentice, as the funding bands for many engineering apprenticeships simply do not cover the cost of delivery. As a result, we have employers with skills gaps, young people who need good routes into careers, and apprenticeship funding that is not fully used.

As hon. Members might expect me to say, there is a lot that the Government could take from Liberal Democrat policy. We would like to introduce skills tax credits with enhanced relief for priority sectors to reflect the fact that skills are an investment. We would also establish structures for skills co-operatives—I know the Prime Minister likes co-operatives—so that smaller firms can pool training resources and even rotate apprentices between them. We would also expand higher technical routes, such as higher national certificates, higher national diplomas, foundation degrees and higher apprenticeships, building on the investment already made in FE colleges and institutes of technology.

We would like Skills England to be a truly independent body with employers at its heart. Already in its short life, it has been moved from the Department for Education to the Department for Work and Pensions. It remains an Executive agency in that Department and is not the independent voice for skills that employers really need, so I urge the Government to look again at giving it genuine independence.

I have three questions for the Minister. First, levy receipts are forecast to be £4.5 billion this year, but after the devolved nations’ share and England’s £3.3 billion budget, about £700 million will not be returned to the skills system but will stay with the Treasury. On the Government’s own spending predictions, that will rise to about £1 billion next year. Will the Minister commit to ensuring that the money raised for skills is spent on skills and is not clawed back by the Treasury?

Secondly, will the review of funding bands address the shortfall of up to £8,000 per apprentice that employers face in engineering and manufacturing? Thirdly, will the Minister press Skills England to develop occupational standards for a wider variety of manufacturing roles, such as printed circuit board assembly, which the system currently cannot see? Nyobolt, a battery manufacturer in my constituency, put it well: the opportunity now is to make sure the skills pipeline develops at the same pace as the technology.

Skills, like manufacturing investment itself, require multi-year, long-horizon decisions. Industry needs a long-term, stable plan from the Government, and I hope the Minister will tell us that it is coming.

speaker: Angus MacDonald
text:
I beg to move,

That this House has considered long duration electricity storage systems.

It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Sir Christopher. I am glad to have been able to bring forward this debate on long duration electricity storage systems. I would like to focus on pump storage and the cost-benefit of hosting that technology in the highlands of Scotland.

The highlands and islands hope to benefit from the new Prime Minister’s growth in every postcode plan, however we do not have a defence, artificial intelligence, tech or financial industry to rely on. Our major industry is tourism, which suffers from a short season and low pay in hospitality. It is a struggling industry.

I recently wrote to the Prime Minister and laid out some harrowing facts. Remote Scotland has a 30% higher cost of living and a 10% lower income than urban Scotland. We have seen a dramatic drop in school rolls and a 71% increase in the number of people over the age of 75. I represent Inverness, Skye and West Ross-shire and it would be difficult to find another part of the UK with a greater interest in renewables.

speaker: Lord Hannan of Kingsclere
heading: Technical Education: University Technical Colleges - Question
text: My Lords, ours is a services-based economy: legal services, financial services, call centres. We are uniquely exposed to the changes coming as a result of AI. Is there not a particular urgency in teaching the kinds of skills in which UTCs excel, such as advanced circuitry, logistics, electronics and so on? Should there not be a presumption that, where there is demand—the noble Baroness mentioned Doncaster; it is already oversubscribed—people should be allowed to create these excellent schools with their excellent records? To declare my interest, I once spent a day at the JCB Academy. I have a paperweight, a sagging lump of metal, which I keep on my desk as a reminder to never again think of welders as semi-skilled. They are artists behind those scarred visors, flicking their flames as Vermeer flicked his paintbrush.

speaker: Perran Moon
subheading: Royal Mail: Performance — [Emma Lewell in the Chair]
text:
Meur ras, Ms Lewell. It is an honour to serve under your chairship. I thank the hon. Member for Lagan Valley (Sorcha Eastwood) for securing this debate and for her excellent speech.

The performance of Royal Mail in Camborne, Redruth and Hayle, in the south-west of Cornwall, has been simply woeful. Constituents regularly tell me that they have gone weeks without post and, like other hon. Members’ constituents, have received a large backlog all at once.

Sharon from Hayle had waited a year for an operation when she received a call from the hospital asking whether she intended to attend. The appointment letter, together with the swabs required pre surgery, had never arrived. Thankfully, the arrangements were later confirmed by phone and email, but the letter itself was delivered three days after the operation had taken place. Another constituent was sent a letter for a hospital appointment 19 days after it was scheduled. Such delays risk causing vulnerable people to miss essential treatment, and place a burden on our overstretched NHS.

In Cornwall, our remote coastal geography and patchy digital connectivity—to say the least—mean that many of us still rely heavily on the universal postal service, but I worry that the situation will only get worse. In recent weeks, several Royal Mail workers have contacted me with concerns about the new delivery model 26. They report unmanageable workloads, experienced workers leaving, morale at rock bottom and substantial volumes of mail sitting undelivered. Three workers completing four rounds does not sound a credible way to improve reliability and restore public trust in Royal Mail. I echo the points made: the issue is not one of posties; it is one of management. Nor should Royal Mail continue to respond, if at all, to our constituents with template responses or hide behind impossible-to-navigate AI chatbots, while the reality on the ground slips further behind.

I therefore ask the Minister what discussions the Government have had with Royal Mail about DM26, and what action will be taken to ensure my constituents receive a postal service worthy of the word “royal”. If Royal Mail is going to treat this House and elected Members with such arrogance, the Government must take direct, firm and urgent action.

speaker: Ben Maguire
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Ms Lewell. I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Chichester (Jess Brown- Fuller) on securing this important debate. I pay tribute to my excellent policemen and women, who do a fantastic job in keeping us safe.

We Liberal Democrats have long called for a return to proper community policing, and the visible, trusted police presence that it provides for our constituents. During the previous Conservative Government’s programme of cuts, local community policing across our country was torn apart. We have heard from some Government Members who may need educating on the concept of a coalition in which the junior partner makes up 15% of the MPs, and so does not have total control over every Government policy. Since Labour came into government, more than 1,000 officers have been cut from our streets. I am sure that the hike in national insurance contributions has not helped that at all. My force, Devon and Cornwall, has faced a 50% cut to its recruitment budget.

The politicisation of the police service through the introduction of police and crime commissioners has done untold further damage to that trust. I was glad when, in November last year, the Government embraced a long-running Lib Dem campaign by announcing the scrapping of PCCs entirely. That will save the British taxpayer an estimated £100 million a year, £20 million of which can be funnelled into neighbourhood policing.

For rural areas such as my North Cornwall constituency, neighbourhood and community policing focus heavily on tackling the scourge of rural crime. I have prioritised the fight against rural crime on behalf of my constituents by introducing the Rural Crime (Strategy) Bill and consistently pushing the Government to develop a full strategy to address it countrywide. For many countryside communities up and down the country, thefts of farm machinery, tools and livestock can be devastating. At a time when family farms are being hammered by rising costs, a botched sustainable farming incentive payment system, a rise in inheritance tax, bluetongue outbreaks and a severe drought, the loss of just one all-terrain vehicle or expensive piece of farm machinery can set them back tens of thousands of pounds. Sadly, many of my farming constituents have told me that they have altogether lost confidence that such crimes will be dealt with seriously, so they no longer report them.

It is clear that many forces still lack specialists to deal specifically with these types of rural crimes. The Home Office is planning £365,000 of funding for the entire country’s rural crime units, which works out at around £8,500 pounds on average per police force. From my own work on the Home Affairs Committee, I have had the opportunity to quiz officials on police visibility in communities, and specifically on the effectiveness of reopening front desks. I was told by one police official from Buckinghamshire that the reopening of a police station in a town there saw a 19% overall reduction in crime, not just because people reported crimes more, but because it gave the local community a more visible police presence. I have been requesting that Launceston, in my constituency, has its police station’s front desk reopened, but Devon and Cornwall’s police and crime commissioner has refused time and again to do so. That refusal is especially disappointing when the cost is around £100,000 and the cost of suspended Devon and Cornwall police officers is currently around £1.3 million a year.

We have clear opportunity to bring back this policing visibility and confidence, yet the requests of the community are being ignored. One way to ensure that frontline officers are left to focus on the communities they serve is to prevent them from being pulled away for other types of crime that fester online. Our Liberal Democrat proposal is to establish an online crime agency, funded by £250 million per year—a levy on the big tech and AI firms that too often enable this online crime to take place. Our local officers would be freed up and sent back out to our towns and high streets, where they belong, combating thefts, shoplifting and the other types of local crime that hon. Members have mentioned.

Will the Minister commit to ensuring that every community across Britain has a police counter by using spaces such as libraries, shopping centres and town halls and reopening front desks where feasible, and to establishing an online crime agency so that deepfakes, revenge porn and other online crimes are tackled by specialists? Will she also ensure that the proposed police reorganisation does not further reduce community policing, and build on the NPCC rural and wildlife crime strategy, to tackle the scourge of rural crime?

speaker: Lord Nagaraju
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: To ask the Senior Deputy Speaker what consideration the Procedure and Privileges Committee has given to introducing greater procedural flexibility to ensure that the House is able to undertake effective scrutiny of significant and fast-moving policy areas, such as AI and emerging technology.

speaker: Lord Nagaraju
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: My Lords, I beg leave to ask the Question standing in my name on the Order Paper. In doing so, I draw attention to my AI and digital interests set out in the register.

speaker: Lord Ponsonby of Shulbrede
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: My Lords, our procedures allow flexibility, including topical Oral Questions, Private Notice Questions and Questions for Written Answer. The Government also offer regular statements, and Urgent Questions asked in the House of Commons are often repeated in your Lordships’ House. The noble Lord himself has used a number of these avenues to raise matters related to AI. The Procedure and Privileges Committee has not discussed scrutiny of AI and emerging technology. However, it is open to considering any proposals.

speaker: Lord Nagaraju
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: My Lords, September brought UN findings, the Prime Minister’s G20 AI pledge, international warnings and an AI agent breaching Australia’s Medicare statistics portal days apart. My balloted options were weeks away. Taking up the committee’s invitation for proposals, will the Senior Deputy Speaker help the UK set the global standard for parliamentary scrutiny of AI by proposing at its next meeting a pilot for one sitting term to have a protected weekly AI session of up to 30 minutes with cross-government updates and questions on opportunities, risks and delivery on commitments?

speaker: Lord Ponsonby of Shulbrede
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: I will ensure that this proposal is drawn to the attention of the Procedure and Privileges Committee. As noble Lords will be aware, the Committee needs to balance a range of demands on the House’s time, and any proposal for dedicated scrutiny arrangements on one policy topic must be considered against other important policy areas. Artificial intelligence is clearly of great importance. Noble Lords will have an opportunity to debate one aspect of this issue—the impact of AI on children—later today during the debate in the name of the noble Lord, Lord Patel.

speaker: Lord McLoughlin
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: My Lords, it is incumbent on us all to try to understand artificial intelligence and use our own intelligence to get around it. Will the Senior Deputy Speaker do all he can to draw to the attention of other Members of your Lordships’ House the availability of digital training on AI and the way in which the House provides those facilities for all to take advantage of?

speaker: Lord Ponsonby of Shulbrede
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: I thank the noble Lord for raising that and pointing it out to the House, which he did extremely effectively. I think many Members of the House, if not all, have at least dabbled—if I can put it that way—in AI. Last week, I was in Rome at the Council of Europe’s European Conference of Presidents of Parliament, which addressed AI. It is true that parliaments across Europe and the world are using AI in different ways. We are all finding our way in this; it is an ongoing learning experience. I thank the noble Lord for drawing that training to the House’s attention.

speaker: Lord Grocott
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: Does the Senior Deputy Speaker agree that we could have far better consideration of a number of issues, including AI, if the House started sitting at a more sensible time? Has he seen the views—I am sorry to see them, because they are the views of very senior Members—of the Procedure and Privileges Committee? It simply suggested two options: do nothing or do as little as possible. Does the Senior Deputy Speaker agree that we would be far better off if we started most days—not Monday, but the rest of the week—at 11 am?

speaker: Lord Alton of Liverpool
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: My Lords, the Senior Deputy Speaker will be aware that, in September, the Joint Committee on Human Rights published a 94-page report on AI and human rights, which was unanimous. It has not yet been listed for debate in your Lordships’ House, because it cannot be until the Government respond. Will the Senior Deputy Speaker look at that procedure so that, when Select Committees publish reports, the House can be informed at the earliest possible time? Please can he also encourage the Government to respond, so that such a debate can take place?

speaker: Baroness Harman
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: Picking up on the question the noble Lord just asked, does the Senior Deputy Speaker agree that we need to look at overhauling the procedure of how we legislate on AI, because AI moves so fast? Even when agreement is reached about what needs to happen, the legislative process is so slow that, by the time the legislation has come into force, new problems have arisen. Does the Senior Deputy Speaker agree that there could be a joint committee of this House and the House of Commons that could have delegated powers to legislate on AI? That way, we would keep up with the speed of AI, which is currently bringing this legislature into disrepute, because we always seem to be behind the game.

speaker: Lord Ponsonby of Shulbrede
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: The noble Baroness makes a very fair point. This issue is not limited to AI; it affects many other areas. In my previous area of justice, there was a constant frustration that the legislative process was proceeding very slowly. Nevertheless, the noble Baroness makes a specific recommendation about creating a joint committee to look at AI, and I will bring it to the attention of the PPC.

speaker: Baroness Hayter of Kentish Town
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: Will the noble Lord assure us that our staff, not just ourselves, are able to use AI where appropriate, particularly in dealing with, for example, responses to consultations and Select Committee inquiries?

speaker: Lord Ponsonby of Shulbrede
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: Yes, I can give that assurance. The staff within the House use AI in a number of ways and there is ongoing training, I understand. There is also training for Members of this House.

speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra
heading: Cyber Security: PHP Vulnerability - Private Notice Question
text: The incident regarding PHP identified vulnerabilities ahead of potential exploitation. That is one of the potential benefits we can see of frontier AI, although of course we understand that frontier AI, and AI in general, can also increase and augment potential threats. In respect of the Bill, MSPs will be brought into it. As SMEs rely on the sort of underlying systems and websites that may be supported by PHP, the fact that MSPs will be brought into the Bill will mean that more of the economy will be covered: in particular, companies that do not manage their services directly. In addition, under the security and resilience requirements, there will be further requirements on patching, and requirements for critical patching within defined timelines. In those ways, the Bill will support what we are seeing in terms of new threats and the identification of vulnerabilities.

speaker: Baroness Northover
heading: Cyber Security: PHP Vulnerability - Private Notice Question
text: My Lords, experts warn that it is not a matter of if an organisation is going to be attacked, but when it will be attacked, and that is what we are seeing here. For small businesses, as I think the Minister knows, a cyber incident can be existential. Some 60% of SMEs that fall victim to a cyber attack go out of business within six months. Does the Minister think that the Government are being sufficiently proactive in what she has outlined in terms of protecting the whole of our economy? Given that frontier AI can now find such flaws at such speed, will she be giving the AI Security Institute statutory powers of inspection and mitigation?

speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra
heading: Cyber Security: PHP Vulnerability - Private Notice Question
text: The noble Baroness raised a series of very important points. In respect of this vulnerability, while we have seen exploitation activity in scanning being reported internationally, we are not currently aware of any confirmed compromise of central government systems resulting from these vulnerabilities. As we have previously noted, frontier AI allows for the identification of vulnerabilities. As the head of the NCSC and others have alerted industry and, indeed, government, this means we need to be more vigilant and quicker in readying ourselves to apply patches and other mitigations. That is something that we all need to prepare for, including SMEs. In this example, most probably SMEs will be relying on their managed service providers. I recommend that they talk to their managed service provider to assure themselves that the services that they rely on have been updated, as advised by the NCSC.

speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra
heading: Cyber Security: PHP Vulnerability - Private Notice Question
