text: The NCSC was briefed by OpenAI last week on this potential specific vulnerability and has been working to ensure that disclosure happened in a co-ordinated way with vendors, so there was sufficient preparation to protect customers. It is regarded as best practice to be able to mitigate the impact to prepare and disclose in a co-ordinated way.

speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra
heading: Cyber Security: PHP Vulnerability - Private Notice Question
text:
In terms of the assessment that my noble friend mentioned, we are monitoring the situation closely alongside NCSC. While we have heard reports of exploitation activity in scanning internationally, we are not aware of any compromises in the UK public sector, or in the UK as such.

In respect of cyber resilience more generally across the public and private sectors, our message is that with the increased threats that we are seeing from the augmentation of AI, we recommend that the public sector, including education, and the private sector, all of industry, increase their cyber resilience by taking the measures we have suggested, including board leadership, signing up to early warning systems, understanding fully their supply chains and ensuring that they all meet the requisite standards of cyber resilience.

speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra
heading: Cyber Security: PHP Vulnerability - Private Notice Question
text: The noble Lord asks about the responsibilities of tech companies but also the impact of technological developments on cyber security. In this incident, the effect has been to be able to identify vulnerabilities which can then be mitigated and patched. In respect of the cyber security Bill that is coming forward, it will include sectors such as data centres and managed service providers within the regulatory ambit. The Government continue to believe that regulating AI at the point of use is the right approach. The Minister for AI set out last week the many further efforts that we are taking to harden our defences and address both the opportunities and threats that AI presents.

speaker: Lord Patel
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, it is a pleasure to open this very important debate on the effects of AI, screen use and social media on children. Your Lordships will excuse me for using a screen to fulfil my screen time.

Before I start, I sincerely thank the noble Baroness, Lady Lloyd of Effra, for making time to respond to this debate on behalf of the Government; I appreciate it. I also thank all noble Lords taking part in this debate and very much look forward to all their speeches. I particularly welcome the previous Lord Speaker, the noble Lord, Lord McFall; I think this is the first time since he relinquished office that he is taking part in a debate. I thank him for doing so.

I thank the Library for its excellent briefing paper and POST, the Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology, which has produced several well-researched, evidence-based publications with expert contributions on the subject. POST reports do not often get a debate slot, despite being well-resourced, high-quality publications. Much of my speech is based on its excellent findings and I thank all who contributed to its work.

Anybody who travels on the Tube, buses or trains will see, as soon as they get on, that everybody is looking at their tablets or their phones. It is not just children who get addicted to looking at them; all of us do. The rapid integration of digital technologies into the everyday lives of children and young people has led to the question of its consequences for the health, education and development of children.

While my focus today may be on the negative aspects of AI, tablets and social media, I recognise the great benefits that they can have if they are properly used. Comprehensive reviews by POST and in international publications, professional journals and government reports have all highlighted that while digital technologies offer opportunities in education, creativity and community building, excessive and harmful content that is designed to get children and young people addicted to both content and technology is leading to serious harm in children.

I will briefly look at the evidence regarding the effects of AI, screen use and social media, hopefully good and bad, based on the evidence that has been published. Screen use and AI use are increasingly embedded in children’s daily lives. Screen exposure begins early in life in the United Kingdom. Studies show that 98% of children aged two use screens on a daily basis. Use of generative AI—so-called gen AI—is increasing rapidly among young people, for not just education but for social interaction.

The impact of screen use on children is based predominantly on observational studies reflecting the ethical and methodological challenges in establishing a causal relationship. While screen use and AI can support education, creativity and social connection, it displaces face-to-face interaction and excessive use leads to poor social and emotional outcomes.

What is screen use? Screen time—time spent using screen-based devices—remains the key measure of children’s screen use but is a poor indicator of the potential benefits and harms of digital engagement. A systemic review of over 600 studies looked mainly at screen time use and not at other factors such as the age and development stage of a child, type of content—which is becoming more diverse with the use of AI—and context: whether it is supervised and the time of day at which the screen is used by children. All are factors which have an effect.

What is AI use? AI tools are increasingly embedded into digital devices and online platforms and used for information seeking, content creation, communication and learning support. The pandemic, changes in education and leisure activities, and greater availability of devices and technology have led to an increase in children’s screen use. The 2026 Ofcom data shows that screen time at the age of two years is about 127 minutes per day. It increases to several hours per day with older children. Children who observe parents’ frequent use of screens themselves start using screens at an earlier age. Tablet use is common in early childhood—80% of children aged between five and 11—with smartphone ownership rising from 56% of 10 year-olds to 83% of 11 year-olds. The use of smartphones therefore is now more common than the use of tablets.

The use of AI, particularly gen AI, is also increasing. Ofcom data suggests that 86% of those aged between eight and 17 have an awareness of gen AI and that 11% use it regularly. Higher screen use associated with poor socio-emotional development is more common in children with existing emotional difficulties. The use by parents of digital devices to manage distress, tantrums or challenging behaviour in children leads to increased screen time.

Internet Matters found that 23% of vulnerable children reported using AI chatbots because they did not have anyone else to talk to. Concerns have been raised about AI companions, particularly following high-profile legal cases in the United States—where an $18 billion settlement was agreed—where it was alleged, as POST states, that

“conversational AI systems formed emotionally significant relationships with ‘vulnerable’ young users and responded inappropriately to discussions of self-harm and suicide”.

Concerns have been raised too about addictive patterns of use, particularly in gaming. A 2016 systematic review suggested that gen AI tools may support cognitive processes but can reduce opportunities for independent thinking, deep learning and skills development. The health impacts of screen use relate to obesity, risk and sleep deprivation, especially if screens are used in the evening and late at night, which in turn leads to emotional well-being and behavioural problems.

There is some evidence of the benefits of use of AI-based mental health apps. A 2025 survey suggested that one in four teenagers have turned to gen AI chatbots for mental support with some benefits.

UK qualitative data shows that those aged between eight and 17 are actively spending money online, with persuasive design features influencing spending and contributing to financial harms. Studies also show that adolescents who purchase “loot boxes” have four to six times higher odds of developing problem gambling behaviours. Children also face high levels of embedded advertising online, which is often integrated into game-play or entertainment content, so making it difficult for them to spot.

Children encounter a range of harms through digital platforms, including cyberbullying, grooming, image-based abuse, fraud and scams, and exposure to hate speech, misogynistic content, violence against women and girls, pornography, forms of violence, suicidal ideation and self-harm content. With the advent of more immersive platforms, novel forms of tech-facilitated abuse can emerge which are more difficult for children to identify.

On social media, children and young adults use social media for a variety of reasons—entertainment, relaxation, social integration and seeking support. Research by Ofcom in 2025 found that 97% of those aged between 13 and 17 had a profile on at least one social media platform and that 93% of parents felt concern about potential harms to their children from social media. Studies and reviews of the harms of social media to children and young people have led countries to develop legislation to deal with it, including the United Kingdom, Brazil, the European Union, France and Australia. Alongside national policy, social media policy intersects with child and human rights frameworks such as the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. The range of potential impacts of social media use relates to mental health, physical health, safety, financial harms behaviour and social interaction. Elements of social media platform design intensify this problem, such as the infinite scroll function, autoplay, the push notifications that continuously appear on the screen, and “like” and “dislike” comments. Adolescents are particularly vulnerable because of the stage of their brain development.

POST research also highlights some of the benefits—education and creative thinking, social and community interaction and positive material on physical and mental health. A longitudinal study of adolescents at 31 London schools found that of those aged between 11 and 12 who used social media for more than three hours daily, 70% were more likely to experience depression and 60% more likely to experience anxiety. Self-harm-related images on social media are associated with harmful effects such as increased self-harming behaviours, anxiety and depression. At the same time, possible benefits included emotional support.

While social media platforms have the tools to detect and remove harmful content, such content continues to reach young users online through algorithmic content recommendations, something that the media platforms could easily handle. Research published by Ofcom in 2026 showed that social media was a leading online space where children were exposed to child sexual abuse material. Children who experience online abuse often end up experiencing poor mental health, self-harming and having a feeling of disempowerment. Ofcom’s study also showed that 62% of its sample of 11 to 17 year-olds reported seeing bullying content, while 51% reported seeing hateful content.

Let me now turn briefly to the most important part—the area of most concern to me. We have all seen recent reports in print media and Sky News on the investigation into violent and extremist networks that target vulnerable children and young people. The FBI, the National Crime Agency and the NSPCC have all mapped out how these groups operate to pull minors into illicit networks. They identify vulnerable children with anxiety and who are feeling isolation on mainstream gaming consoles—the likes of Roblox, Minecraft and TikTok—and, after initial contact, posing as friendly teenagers, inserting avatars into the game, they switch the child to encrypted apps. Their ideology is nihilistic self-mutilation and violence. Eventually, it leads to self-harm, violence against others, suicide and possibly even worse.

This is so serious. In the process of finding this out, I tried to do my own research and spoke to some children, aged seven to 13, in front of their parents with the parents’ permission. I was horrified to learn that children as young as seven knew about this and often came across it, and the smart ones avoided it. One particular one, whose mother did not allow them to use headphones so that she could listen to what they were following, had to ask the child to turn it off, because they were being led to the dark side of the internet—being asked, “can you now send a photograph of yourself?” At that point, the mother stopped it. These are nihilistic and serious things on the dark side of the internet that we must stop. We need parental education, wide media alerts, law enforcement and legislative action, aggressive prosecutions, international co-operation, gaming industry responsibility, restriction of cross-platform migration—which they use to migrate children from legitimate gaming consoles on to the dark internet—and much more.

In the context of this, I do not have any other questions, except one. Following the Statement by the Secretary of State on 8 September, I ask the Minister this: what further measures, legislative and non-legislative, do the Government intend to bring to protect children from online harm—particularly young children from the dark internet? I beg to move.

speaker: Baroness Barran
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for securing this extremely important debate and for his very powerful speech. I particularly associate myself with his last remarks about the nihilistic behaviour of predators approaching our children online and the ability of the large tech companies to sort many of the problems themselves. We heard during the passage of the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act that we were playing catch-up as a country on protecting our children from harms, particularly from smartphones and social media in that case. I think we find ourselves in the same position again but with a much more terrifying prospect of trying to play catch-up in the age of AI.

The evidence of harm to children is widespread, perhaps most disturbingly in relation to child sexual abuse material: we have seen an explosion in AI-generated child abuse videos. More broadly, we have seen reports of three year-olds spending hours every day on a screen, with visible—forgive the pun—impact on their eyesight, as well as pupils being issued with one-to-one devices at school without evidence of the impact of that. As we heard from the noble Lord, Lord Patel, and as I am sure we will hear from other noble Lords, we know that children are seeing harmful material on social media and meeting potential predators online. That is not to say that there are not safe and useful things that can be done online, of course, but the situation currently is that the lack of regulation means that the harmful is far outweighing the good.

Will the Minister clarify whether the Government plan to adopt the precautionary principle in future? We would never let a medicine reach our children on the promise that harm would be measured later. Will the Minister confirm that products used with children, including educational technology and AI, must show evidence of safety and benefit before they can be marketed, particularly where they are being bought with public funds? We know that the Law Commission is bringing forward a very welcome consultation on changes to product liability legislation, but that is a painfully slow process and not fast enough to safeguard our children.

Most recently, 150 clinicians wrote to the Secretary of State for Education, citing their concerns and asking for health checks on classroom technology. They cite research associating each extra hour of daily screen time with a 21% higher odds of short-sightedness. Can the Minister update the House on whether work is taking place on an early warning system, similar to the National Child Mortality Database, which would allow us to pick up patterns of harm before full evaluations come forward? Finally, do the Government have plans to equip health visitors, GPs, school nurses, optometrists and paediatricians with the training they need on digital risks and the impact of screens so that they can be part of an effective national response? Building a system that is agile and resilient is crucial if we are to protect our children from these harms. I hope the Government will consider these suggestions.

speaker: Bishop of Peterborough
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, it is a privilege to speak on a subject so critical to the flourishing of young people. I welcome this debate. I too wish to focus primarily on the role that emerging technologies might play in our schools and how we, as the shepherds of those who attend them, can ensure that such technologies are integrated safely, usefully and with humanity in mind. At its heart, a school is a place of preparation, and a good school system must equip young people to confront the challenges of life. But I ask your Lordships to consider whether we have given enough thought not just to preparing young people but to preparing and resourcing those we charge with educating them.

To give one example, there is a Church of England primary school in Peterborough diocese with just 99 pupils on its roll. It is not uncommon for a Church of England school to be even smaller than this. The governance challenge presented to such schools by the emergence of AI is enormous. How do we ensure its use is safe? How do we integrate it in a way that guarantees the security of children’s personal data? These are great philosophical questions, as well as governance ones. As a nation, we bear a responsibility to build a consensus that aids our schools with practical advice and support in navigating this new aspect of our world. We owe it to our educators not to expect them to conjure specialist knowledge on AI integration from thin air but to equip them so that they can prepare our children for lives where they can use these technologies safely.

The philosophical question of what it means to be fully human is one that the Church has been seeking to guide on for as long as it has existed. In our Church schools, we place the concept of human flourishing at the heart of what we do. We have a vision of a school as a place where pupils bloom into the human being they will become for the rest of their lives. These technologies have the potential to enhance our human relationships, experience and intellect, but, as we have heard, they also have the potential to replace, displace or diminish the humanity in our daily lives. Which of these paths we take is ultimately a very human choice. Whether AI and technology used by or in the service of children enhances or diminishes a human purpose is, to us, the central and critical question of our time.

At the National Society for Education, we are already exploring both the challenges and the opportunities of AI in Church schools. First and foremost, this is by working with schools and the diocese to understand their needs. Nothing can replace that first-hand experience from those who know their students so well, and I encourage the Government to look at similar consultation as they set their own policy. We have a solemn responsibility to prepare the next generation for a future where the widespread use of AI is their reality. As a nation, we must properly equip our educators to do so.

speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I am grateful to the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for his comprehensive introduction to this debate and his observation that “screen time” is a phrase that encompasses very many different activities. How many of us, in preparing for this debate, were not helped by AI, either by design or by default? I have no doubt that the resulting speeches will demonstrate that it may be artificial, but it is certainly intelligent.

The impact of AI is immense, and its potential to improve human lives is too. I do not believe that children should be prevented from having complete access to it, but they also need to be taught about its potential harms and to be extremely alert to that. Until they are fully prepared to cope with its downsides—my goodness, we have already heard about how deep those downsides are—then children’s access to AI should ideally be limited.

The same is true of social media. Although many of us may shun most social media, the family WhatsApp group is now a vital part of life for many of us, and of communication for those whose parents, or grandchildren, may be a long way away. My young granddaughter got to know her American family courtesy of a screen, and it did not do her any harm—the absence of that might well have done—but there is no denying the harm that some social media sites are delivering. The big tech companies could do so much more to stop that. In an ideal world, most people would want to see their children completely protected from such things.

I have supported the concept of tight restrictions on young people’s access to social media, but we must be realistic about how effective this can be. Early evidence from Australia is that the ban has had only limited effect. It is, after all, being imposed on a cohort of youngsters who are incredibly tech-savvy, and they are finding ways around the ban. Any effectiveness will depend very heavily on the stance taken by parents, and that, inevitably, will vary. That is not to say that we should not do our best to impose restrictions, but we need to be realistic about the impact they will have.

I want to concentrate my remarks on the area in which Government can and should have a real impact, and that is the classroom. The noble Baroness, Lady Barran, explained how schools do not even vet the quality of, and the damage that can be done by, the products they buy. Although it is essential that schools equip our children for this technological age, it means teaching them digital literacy and to be on the alert for the harms that lie in wait for them. But in many schools, it means putting them in front of a screen. In some schools, there are now children who learn all their lessons from a tablet. This is not the way that relationships can be built. Most of us will know of a teacher who had a lasting impact on our lives. Indeed, my speech will be followed by one such teacher, and I am sure he will be remembered by many of his pupils. Screens should be limited in schools. Indeed, perhaps the example of Winchester may be taken note of: the best-achieving school has banned tablets in class.

speaker: Lord McFall of Alcluith
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I feel nervous about the introductions that I have had. This is the first time for 10 years that I have spoken in the House of Lords as a Back-Bencher, and it is a delight. I thank the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for that insightful speech and the interest he has had in this subject for many years.

In 2012, along with the late Lord Lawson, the Archbishop of Canterbury and Andrew Turnbull, the then Cabinet Secretary, I represented the House of Lords on the Parliamentary Commission on Banking Standards. That was established by the Prime Minister of the day, David Cameron, now the noble Lord, Lord Cameron, in light of the global financial crash. It was a joint House of Commons/House of Lords committee, not a Select Committee but an independent body reporting to the Prime Minister and the Chancellor with our own staff, outside experts and a very wide remit. It was tasked with providing legislation solutions for banking in the UK, managed by a brilliant House of Commons clerk, Colin Lee. We delivered on its mandate, new legislation was duly implemented and the House of Lords played a huge part.

Quite simply, today I am calling for such a commission for AI to be established along similar lines to the Parliamentary Commission on Banking Standards, commissioned by the Prime Minister. Why? Because the seriousness of the situation confronting our children, society and humanity today is without parallel. We need the authority and the imprimatur of the Prime Minister to foster a national conversation, in the first instance, to demonstrate that government, Parliament, industry experts and civil society are facing up to the real-time problems we have. That is what politics has failed to do to date—we are always behind the curve. We must rid ourselves of that passive approach.

Let me give an example. When Lord Speaker, I invited the world-renowned Stanford University expert in AI and computing, Stuart Russell, to deliver a lecture on defence and security. His concluding remarks were that he was the bearer of bad news: namely, that industry regulation did not exist, and one could start a war from one’s bedroom. Today, the lethality of drones in Ukraine, the Iran war and Gaza illustrate his remarks. That speech by Stuart Russell took place four years ago, in October 2022. His warnings went unheeded. In the intervening period, we have witnessed the transfer of sovereignty from our countries to a small number of private tech companies, and we are at their beck and call. The Musks, the Altmans, the Bezoses, the Amodeis—they are the AI masters, and we are subservient to them in every respect.

What are some practitioners in the AI industry saying today? For example, Brad Smith, the president of Microsoft, says that AI is less regulated than milk or washing machines. Bill Gates says that, left unchecked, the technology could cause a billion deaths, and added that no weapon today is more powerful than the combination of AI and malign actors. Sir Ken McCallum, head of MI6, referred last week to bioweapons and nuclear war threats. So it is crystal clear that a culture of safety does not exist in the AI industry.

If Bill Gates’s chilling comments do not incentivise us all to get round the table, with parliamentarians in the vanguard, nothing will. My challenge is for the parties, Parliament, Mr Speaker and the Lord Speaker, using their authoritative voices, to convince the PM of the need for such a commission. Presently, we are drowning in information but starving in wisdom. Let us foster that campaign to ensure that we acquire wisdom before it is too late.

speaker: Lord Brooke of Alverthorpe
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
I express my gratitude to the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for bringing us this debate and for his outstanding introduction to it.

The more that we debate AI and climate change, the more we will reach the point where we need somebody on the Cross Benches to give us a debate on the future of humanity, because these are very fundamental issues that we are tackling. We need effective regulation and protection against the addiction, exploitation and damage to children’s development that are arising with AI and related issues.

That of course could all be reduced, as I have argued previously, if, like other countries, we were prepared to develop our own sovereign AI entity. I pressed this previously, and said that I believed many parents would support it. We would control much of what was around us, we would take charge and I believe we could persuade people to invest in this if we were willing to consider creating a whole new public/private partnership to fund its introduction. So I ask my noble friend the Minister: is there any movement on this front?

We also need to distinguish between the dangers of unregulated social media and the potential benefits of properly designed artificial intelligence. At Kenward House, a residential recovery centre in Kent, we are developing for trial an AI companion to support people recovering from addiction, alcohol and drug problems and, increasingly, gambling. As Ministers know, we are also exploring the possibility that this could, if successful, be equally applied in prisons, and it could be run over a wider front too.

The essential principle is that AI should support human relationships, not replace them. Could we develop appropriately safeguarded AI companions to help children struggling with obesity, loneliness, poor self-esteem or difficulties in forming relationships? Rather than encouraging more screen dependency, could we help them develop healthier lives and stronger relationships with other people? Such applications would of course require independent evaluation and appropriate professional support.

I give another example. This House sent a Select Committee to Blackpool when it was undertaking a review of obesity, diet and how we could affect changes. In the north-west, we found particularly heavy growth of obesity among children. We have been weighing and measuring children since 2008, yet they get bigger and heavier. We found in Blackpool that the social services people were saying, “We do the measuring and weighing, but we do not do any follow-through to assist them because we don’t have the resources”. Is this not an area where potentially we could explore the use of an AI companion with children to give them guidance about food, calories and so on? These are areas worth looking at.

The other area that is developing—we wait with interest to see the report that is coming on employment—is how we start to prepare, if possible, for the different style of working that will be needed in the future and the extent to which we can use AI. AI is going to destroy many jobs that we have known, and what we have called “growth” may have to be redefined in the future, with a shift from the material and more towards—here I look to our Bishops’ Bench—the caring professions and towards teaching people about the importance of service as opposed to producing goods. This is an area where we do things better than AI or indeed any technology could do. We should look to the strengths in humanity and start increasingly to try to pass on the message to children and to train them and find all the tools we can, including AI, to make certain that we are effecting this very important shift that will replace many of the traditional approaches to employment.

speaker: Lord Tarassenko
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, it is a pleasure to be speaking, for the second time in just over a month, in a debate secured by my noble friend Lord Patel. If we want to minimise the harmful effects of AI in children through the misuse of AI chatbots, for example, we need to teach them how to use AI properly, and that should happen in schools. Sir Anthony Seldon was characteristically blunt about this issue a month ago when he wrote that Britain was falling behind other countries in its use of AI in education. He went further and said that the DfE should be put in special measures over its handling of AI in schools.

I am not sure that such headline-grabbing statements are helpful, but the pace with which the DfE is taking up the challenge of AI in education is far slower than it needs to be. For example, it is still yet to announce the consultation, promised more than six months ago, on the approach to certifying the safety of edtech in schools. Earlier this year, it advertised a new post—director general for digital, AI and infrastructure—with a £200,000 salary, the highest within the department. Unfortunately, it was able to make only a temporary appointment, and a permanent role has now been readvertised. There are worthwhile initiatives which have started but these are standalone projects. In June, eight companies were awarded contracts to design classroom-ready AI tutoring tools, aligning with the national curriculum and covering years 9 to 11 in English, maths, science and foreign languages. As of last month, year 12 students in seven schools are piloting the level 3 qualification in data science and AI, which I and Cambridge University’s Professor Peyton Jones proposed last year. It is now designed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation as the preparation for an extended project qualification or EPQ topic. There are other initiatives, such as the AI product safety standards, but there is no overall coherent strategy.

I am therefore in agreement with my noble friend Lord McFall. The Government should set up a commission, but perhaps with a narrow brief. The commission should have an independent chair and cross-departmental representation and be given a brief to develop an overall strategy for schools, integrating existing DfE initiatives but also identifying gaps where they exist. The commission should work at pace to inject a sense of urgency and create a road map for the rollout of AI teaching and digital literacy in schools, with a clear implementation plan, which would then be the responsibility of the director-general for digital, AI and infrastructure.

If this country is not to be left behind Estonia, Singapore or China, we cannot afford to wait. Independent schools are not waiting: dedicated heads of AI education or directors of AI posts have been created in elite independent schools such as Brighton College and The Perse School. We need a coherent strategy for AI in education in the state sector, with a timetable for delivery measured in months, not years. Therefore, I ask the Minister whether she will commit to taking such a proposal to her ministerial colleagues in the Department for Education after this debate.

speaker: Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for securing this important debate. I declare my interest as a member of the advisory board of Arāya Ventures, which invests in AI technologies.

Countries across the world are wrestling with the same question: what will it mean for our children’s future to grow up in an age of social media and artificial intelligence? I know that noble Lords across this House agree that we must do everything in our power to protect children from harm and to stop those who seek to inflict it.

Today I wish to focus on my concern that a blanket ban on social media may lead us towards more harm and not less. As many noble Lords have highlighted, the UK is introducing a ban on social media for under-16s. I am not totally opposed to this, but I am concerned that this approach is not nuanced enough. Australia banned social media for under-16s in December 2025, and yet research by the Molly Rose Foundation, published in April this year, found that 61% of 12 to 15 year-olds who held accounts on restricted platforms before the ban still have access to at least one. Of the children who used these platforms before the ban, 51% said that it made no difference to their online safety, and a further 14% now feel less safe. These findings are sobering. I acknowledge that the ban may need more time to bed in, but my concern is that a ban in the UK may put the onus solely on parents, when we should be using the Online Safety Act to hold platforms accountable and ensure safety by design.

The recent Meta settlement in California has shown what can be done when a platform is held to account, with a deal struck that limits notifications to children and allows them to choose a feed that is not driven by algorithms. Yet this judgment applies only in participating US states and Meta has not announced whether these essential protections will be extended to the UK. Any ban that is too porous could take the pressure off social media companies to deliver safety by design. British children could therefore end up with fewer protections than their American counterparts. Children in Cardiff deserve the same protections as children in California.

Turning to artificial intelligence, our instinct must not be fear alone. AI has an extraordinary ability to democratise knowledge. While we must always scan the horizon for potential harms to children, we must also embrace its benefits and equip our children with the skills needed for an AI future. Imagine every child in this country having a personalised tutor, one that picks up on the gaps in their learning and can repeat concepts they struggle to grasp over and over without losing patience—not as a replacement for a real in-person teacher, but in addition to it. Imagine the potential of this technology for children whose families cannot afford private tuition, and the potential this could unleash for our STEM industries to have a generation growing up with the curiosity for learning and the confidence and skills to use AI.

It is vital that we mitigate the worst impacts of social media and AI on children, but we must take a pragmatic and nuanced approach. Let us continue to strengthen the Online Safety Act, ensure that tech companies operate with safety by design and ensure that Ofcom acts swiftly where they fall short. Most of all, let us ensure that the decisions we make today do not limit our children’s skills, knowledge and opportunities for the future.

speaker: Lord Alton of Liverpool
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I join others in thanking my noble friend Lord Patel for initiating this important Cross-Bench debate drawing attention to how AI systems can harvest, scrape and process personal and biometric data, often without meaningful consent or awareness from young users. These tools also risk making inaccurate assumptions or misidentifying children as adults.

AI risks are identified in the last report on my watch as chair of the Joint Committee on Human Rights, Human Rights and the Regulation of AI, which was published last month, including risks for young people and children in whose lives AI is ubiquitous. Over 14 months, I chaired 10 oral sessions. Witnesses included major tech companies—Google, Meta and Microsoft—regulatory bodies, academics and the AI Minister, Kanishka Narayan. That inquiry received over 70 written pieces of evidence. It led to our unanimous 94-page report and 59 recommendations. We called for a wide-ranging stand-alone AI Bill, including some outright prohibitions, strengthened GDPR safeguards and independent oversight. In written evidence, 5Rights Foundation cited its children and AI design code. It said:

“Government policy on AI has largely overlooked the distinct opportunities and needs for children”.

I therefore ask the Minister what assessment is being made of the nine criteria listed in that code and of the concerns of the Children’s Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza, and indeed of our JCHR report.

In the 1990s, in another place I moved amendments to safeguard children from gratuitously violent video material. The murder of a two year-old boy, James Bulger in Liverpool, finally led Parliament to act, but the same phenomenon has now emerged in new technological clothes. Through my noble friend Lady Kidron, I met the grieving parents of Sewell Setzer, a 14 year-old boy who took his own life because he had been befriended by a chatbot. His mother said it was like having

“a predator in your home”.

Similarly, a 13 year-old autistic boy was groomed by a chatbot which criticised his parents, encouraged him to run away and offered an explicit relationship which could be consummated in the afterlife.

Commercial drivers have no compunction in aggressively amplifying high-quality, visually compelling AI-generated material relating to suicide, self-harm and violence, which is targeted at vulnerable young people. Platforms leverage persuasive AI-designed features optimised purely for screen time and engagement; some involve compromising deepfakes. How AI and social media intersect is important because it is in an area where generative AI has already had a colossal and largely unremarked impact.

In the influencer arms race, in which an ever-evolving set of tactics are used to maximise the virality of what they write to gain exposure and ad revenue, generative AI is the equivalent of giving a medieval knight a Kalashnikov. Influencers can now churn out hundreds of posts a day, all hyper-optimised for engagement; there is money to be made, and so they do. Society is now saturated with mobile social media where nothing can be taken at face value, and the impact on children can be profound. Some material is insanely addictive; it is linked to advertising revenue and companies have spent a great deal of money making it as addictive as possible. Addictive technology is more analogous to a slot machine than a communication method, with children especially vulnerable.

The Government must insist on AI systems that are made developmentally appropriate, safe, fair, transparent and accountable. Governments, who are the guardians and gatekeepers, have been lagging behind tech giants whose market valuations exceed those of entire nation states. That must change.

speaker: Baroness Bennett of Manor Castle
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I join the chorus in thanking the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for securing this debate, and for his powerful introduction. I will take a different approach to many speeches already made: a broader, systemic, historically informed approach.

I begin with a quote:

“The Manufacture of this Nation hath been of late Years hindered … by the misspending so much Time as the poorer Tradesmen do, in going about from one Coffee-House to another, poring upon Seditious, Heretical and Treasonable Papers”.

As the language might hint to your Lordships’ House, that is from the very early 18th century. The presence of new technologies, and wide access of ordinary people to them, has long been of concern to elites, and to elders about the young. Technological determinism is a common claim and a handy alibi for those profiting from a society directed to the benefits of the few at the cost of the many. Technology never determines the direction of a society; it is a human creation that can be, and is, directed by humans for good or ill—as is the state of our society.

I will start with screen time. The noble Lord, Lord Patel, asked an entirely appropriate question about the health impacts—my spine can attest to that—but what alternatives do young people have? Is there a youth club for them to go to? Almost certainly not. Is there a flourishing, healthy green space to attract them? No. Does their school in some giant academy chain employ tech instead of trained teachers, so that, despite the lack of evidence of any benefits, it relies on edtech?

Earlier this week, at a meeting of the APPG for Woods and Trees, I heard a nurseryman lamenting the decline of horticultural and agricultural education: the colleges that should be preparing young people for crucial, healthy jobs. How often do we hear Ministers or the Prime Minister speaking about this, compared with them waxing enthusiastically about the possibilities of artificial so-called intelligence—promoting it, and suggesting that it is an inevitable part of future jobs, so directing young people towards it?

We have extraordinarily well-funded and powerful voices, some of them owning and directing the very technologies we are talking about, who promote AI and social media at every turn. We have them funding so-called think tanks—better called lobbyists—following the models of political influencing developed by the fossil fuel companies and the tobacco merchants of death. As the noble Lord, Lord Addington, and the noble Baroness, Lady Wheatcroft, have said, this tech can be, and is, used for good. It can be a democratising force—yes, I am a fan of Bluesky.

These days, it is common to complain that there is too much information; Duran Duran sang about that in 1993—although, when you look at the lyrics of the song, it is actually about advertising. That is a reminder that a lot of the toxic material our young people are encountering—the promotion of ultra-processed food-like substances, fast fashion, and tech itself—is from giant multinational companies. Blame them, not the technology.

Finally, we come to the question of the environmental footprint of these technologies. Some communities on these islands and around the world are increasingly aware of this issue and are campaigning against it. These technologies are not in the cloud; they are very much down to earth, causing real damage to the already greatly depleted world our young people will inherit. Are the Government considering how much of all these technologies our environment and the environments of the world can support?

In conclusion, we have a toxic artificial intelligence and social media environment that harms adults and children. That comes from a toxic society. What to do? Listen to the children: nothing about us without us. They are the experts. As in so many areas of life, allowing more people to input into decisions, rather than the few dictating, is the route to a better society.

speaker: Baroness Greenfield
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
As a neuroscientist, I congratulate the noble Lord, Lord Patel, on drawing attention to this timely issue. I declare an interest as founder and CEO of a biotech company, Neuro-Bio Ltd. Most recently, in collaboration with senior psychiatrists, we have been attempting to develop the first ever biomarker for depression, and we have done this in young people. This experience, working with clinicians and disturbed adolescents, has confirmed views I flagged in your Lordships’ House as far back as 2009 that digital technology was offering an alternative environment for the human condition.

Environment is key to individual development. Our species occupies more ecological niches than any other on the planet because of the superlative ability of our brains, compared with those of any other animal, to adapt to our surroundings. Even if you are a clone—an identical twin with the same genes—your brain becomes personalised through the development of unique configurations of connections between neurons that characterise the growth of the human brain after birth, curating a highly individual mind that is in constant dialogue with, and updated by, your unique life experiences.

Even before AI, it was increasingly apparent that screen usage would bring problems. It is not just the effects of not sleeping, not escaping the crowd and not having time to exercise that can facilitate obesity and bullying; the digital lifestyle can in and of itself prove deleterious. The more we depend on screen technologies as intermediaries for interpersonal relations while young, the less we learn the skills needed for effective communication and empathy in real-world interactions.

All too familiar are reports on how video games and social media can be deliberately crafted for commercial purposes to become addictive. The neuronal mechanism of addiction is an enhanced release of the chemical messenger dopamine, which underlies the anticipation of reward, raises arousal and is the hallmark, neurochemically, of recreational drugs. Dopamine inhibits a part of the brain—the so-called prefrontal cortex—that moderates emotional responses and dampens impulsive reactions. This region, just behind your forehead, is not fully operational until late teenage years or even the early 20s. Until then, characteristic features will include recklessness, a short attention span and, most significantly, overdependence on external stimulation. This mindset could well be exaggerated further by the perfect storm of a still immature prefrontal cortex coupled with unprecedented surges of inhibitory dopamine driven by a 21st-century screen lifestyle.

So we are faced with a set of dilemmas. Society desires young people to master and harness technology for the good of humanity, yet technology simultaneously drives mood deterioration, social exclusion, exploitation and trauma. The online world offers connection. AI holds promise at national and global levels, yet its unregulated integration into young people’s lives risks creating an entity increasingly alien to human emotional experience. The education system demands conformity to model answers, yet the modern world increasingly places a premium on creativity, independent thought and collaboration—skills the current system structurally undermines. Young people need community, shared purpose and belonging, yet the pull of influencer culture and online identity draws them away from real-world participation.

My psychiatrist colleagues were keen to suggest solutions—inevitably, with more money and more regulation. But perhaps we first need to agree on what the ideal teenage lifestyle would look like in the coming years. It is easy to list what we do not want but, unless we can decide on what we wish to achieve, it will be hard to attain it. Commonplace activities such as eating together, exercising, reading stories to children and immersing yourself in a novel may seem simplistic and nostalgic as solutions. Indeed they are, and they are not in themselves the answer, but they can be the bedrock for the development of emotions, intuition, empathy, morality, spirituality and, above all, spontaneous curiosity—a quintessential human profile not seen in AI systems. If you like, it is not a digital lifestyle but an analogue one. Let us ask not what will happen to us in the AI future but rather how we can shape a future where AI is neither an anthropomorphised spectre nor a saviour but a means towards the valued end of young people realising their full potential.

speaker: Lord Loomba
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for this important debate. There is no doubt that artificial intelligence, social media and digital technology are changing childhood in ways that would have been unimaginable only a generation ago. Much of our discussion today is rightly focusing on the risks. We are all aware of growing concerns about excessive screen use, harmful online content, cyber bullying, misinformation and the impact these can have on children’s mental health, well-being and development.

We must, therefore, expect technology companies to take greater responsibility for the products that they create and the environments they expose young people to. Children cannot be expected to navigate complex digital spaces without proper safeguards; protection must be built into the systems they use. However, I would like to focus on another aspect of this debate which is sometimes overlooked. For many children around the world, technology is not simply a source of entertainment; it can be a gateway to education, opportunity and hope. That is where technology has enormous potential. A child living in a remote village should be able to access quality educational material, regardless of geography. A child who has fallen behind should be able to receive additional support. A child whose family cannot afford private tuition should still be able to learn, progress and aspire. Artificial intelligence may help to make that possible. Used responsibly, it can provide personalised learning support, help explain difficult concepts and offer educational assistance beyond a classroom.

The challenge before us, therefore, is not simply how to protect children from technology. It is how to ensure that technology serves children. We must protect them from exploitation, harmful content and unhealthy digital environments. At the same time, we should ensure that children from disadvantaged backgrounds are not excluded from the educational opportunities that new technologies can provide. I hope that the Government will continue to promote digital literacy, support online safety and encourage partnerships between technology providers and educators. The true test of artificial intelligence will not be how advanced the technology becomes—it will be whether it helps to create a fairer society in which every child, regardless of income, geography or family circumstances, has the opportunity to learn, to develop their talents and to fulfil their potential.

speaker: Baroness Prashar
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I too thank the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for securing this debate and for his comprehensive, chilling and sobering introduction. As he said, digital technology is now part of children’s education, friendships and everyday lives. Research identifies genuine opportunities for learning, creativity and social connections but, as the noble Lord said, it also highlights concerns about mental health and emotional well-being, behavioural issues, sleep deprivation, and online harm and safety.

The issues raised by AI differ from those raised by social media and screen time. The benefits and potential of AI should not be underestimated, as we have heard, but there are legitimate concerns about AI replacing independent thinking, inhibiting cognitive development, blunting critical thinking and judgment, encouraging excessive engagement and simulating emotional relationships.

Ethical use of AI is also a concern. Although the Government have taken some welcome actions in supporting the development of AI tutoring tools for disadvantaged pupils, most of the other actions, particularly in response to the dangers of social media, have come too late. We are moving towards a predominantly—of course, necessary—stronger regulatory environment, but we need to make sure that the regulation is proportionate and that it does not stifle autonomy and learnings such as self-discipline, self-management and children’s development.

We need safer technology and to hold companies responsible and accountable for making their products safe, and Ofcom must police them with rigour. Above all, as other noble Lords have said, we need better media and digital education, with parental involvement, if we are to harness the benefits of those technologies and avoid their downsides. We have not done enough on AI digital literacy or educating children about how best to use AI and social media. We need to empower young people to learn how to self-regulate and establish their own boundaries.

Protecting children requires more than just addressing online harm. It requires spaces and initiatives that encourage offline activities, children’s healthy development, and activities that build resilience and effective personal relationships. Here I associate myself with the comments made by the noble Baroness, Lady Greenfield, about making sure that we concentrate on young people’s self-development.

We have not equipped schools with capacity, resources and know-how. The response has been reactive rather than proactive. As the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, said, there is no coherent strategy. I was, however, pleased that a school in Scotland—probably the first one to do so—has appointed a dedicated principal of AI literacy, who will focus entirely on helping pupils and staff to understand the risks, and so on. That is an encouraging development, but will the Government learn from this initiative?

Furthermore, the implications of AI will have a profound effect on society and the economy. Are we assessing the skills that children will need to navigate this fast-changing landscape and job market? Are we doing enough in this area? Acting on AI is more important than just advocating it or promoting it. It is important that we do not make the same mistakes that we made with social media, where we are behind the curve and engaged in catch-up. The Government cannot afford to repeat the mistakes and delay action regarding AI.

My questions to the Minister are: what broader initiatives are the Government taking to promote AI and social media literacy and to empower young people to self-regulate in schools? Will the Government bring the currently unregulated AI chatbots within the online framework? If so, when? Are companies being held accountable for ensuring that their products are safe? This is probably the most revolutionary development of our time. How we respond to these significant challenges will determine the future security and resilience of youngsters in our society.

speaker: Lord Nagaraju
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for securing this important debate. I declare my interests as a technology consultant, AI adviser, and director of AI and AI policy companies. My concern is children’s ability to direct their own attention. Counting hours in front of a screen cannot tell us enough. An hour speaking to family is different from an hour of passive scrolling. A 2025 study demonstrated how attention fragmentation, caused by rapid cuts of short-form content, results in diminished focus and mental fatigue in students. Using AI to understand the problem is different from using AI to avoid thinking about it. We must distinguish between general time online, the activity undertaken and the design of the service.

Ofcom spoke to 40 children aged eight to 16 who felt they spent longer online than intended. They described how endless scrolling, autoplay and personalised recommendations made stopping difficult. These interviews cannot tell us how widespread that experience is. They do, however, show why design deserves our attention. The Royal College of Psychiatrists recommends that the responsibility for children’s online safety should sit not only with families but with government, regulators and technology companies, and calls on them to promote stronger safety by design by regulating addictive design features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and engagement-driven recommendation systems. I therefore urge the Minister to consider requiring platforms to turn off autoplay by default, to create meaningful stopping points in endless feeds, and to limit notifications that exploit fear of missing out.

Conversational AI raises further questions. It can support learning, but completing homework is not the same as understanding it. Learning sometimes means staying with a difficult task when the answer does not come immediately.

Chatbots should never be designed to create emotional dependency. Those targeted at children are designed with custom names, avatars, voice-enabled features and excessive anthropomorphic features aimed at promoting engagement. Safeguards should address simulated attachment, pressure to continue chatting and interactions that discourage children from seeking human support.

The Government have announced restrictions on social media for under-16s, protective defaults for 16 and 17 year-olds and mandatory chatbot breaks for under-18s. The task now is to ensure that these measures work in practice. I therefore ask the Minister three questions. First, how will Ofcom assess whether they reduce prolonged or compulsive use? Secondly, what enforceable safeguards will prevent conversational AI services cultivating emotional dependency or steering children away from trusted adults? Thirdly, will the promised independent evaluations measure the prevalence of binge-scrolling behaviour on children’s sleep, attention, learning and ability to stop, alongside overall time spent scrolling short-form content online? Will they also examine children’s ability to question AI’s answers and follow their use of conversational AI over several years?

Our responsibility is to protect children’s capacity to learn, form relationships and make choices of their own. That requires services designed to respect their developing independence and evidence that the safeguards we introduce make a difference.

speaker: Baroness Murphy
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, the noble Lord, Lord Patel, always likes to give us a challenge when he sets a debate, and this is certainly one of the greatest challenges we have had, in terms of its widespread topic. I will just pick out a few things; so much has been said and it has been a very interesting debate.

The rapid rise of generative AI systems, particularly conversational chatbots such as ChatGPT, has of course sparked new concerns regarding their psychological impact on all users, but especially children. I stress that, while there are legitimate concerns, about which we have a heard a great deal, the real problem in my view is that children are missing out in their lives when they are stuck in front of a highly addictive screen: friendships, social activities, physical activity and family time. Although of course I appreciate there is an amazing ability for children to reach out to relatives in other countries, to talk to friends on screen and so on, but what they get from generative AI systems can be very harmful.

When you introduce a young child to reading books, you do not just plonk a book in a child’s hand say, “Here you are, read that”. You read with them, getting them to know gradually what the words mean, how they connect and how to grasp a story. The parent supervises the child before letting them loose on any old book. The same surely should be true of AI and the internet in general. As many people have said, parents need to be educated about it themselves if they are to help their children. Teachers above all need to know about this stuff in the classroom, and perhaps we are very far behind several other countries in getting to grips with that. So my question to the Minister is: what is the Government doing to ensure that the Department for Education is preparing its teachers, and teachers are preparing parents, for activity in this area?

While these AI tools offer unprecedented access to educational information and opportunities to learn, learning is not a solitary activity. Being part of a class with a good teacher is worth a hundred hours of unguided self-learning. Interestingly, the Minister of Education in China mandates AI literacy and tech courses starting in elementary school. Middle and high school students tackle machine learning, ethics and model design. They regulate AI exposure quite fiercely and perhaps it is time that we thought about that as well.

In the UK, the Scottish Government published their own—I have to say, rather vague—policy in March, but left everything open to local flexibility. In England and Wales, although AI usage has skyrocketed, we have not produced a similar policy on how to develop this stuff. In fact, UK students boast some of the highest generative AI adoption rates globally, using it for nearly half of their academic work. Teachers are permitted and encouraged to use it, but where is the guidance and regulation? Where is the education for teachers?

It is the companionship from AI chatbots that poses a real problem: the anthropomorphic nature of them. There is a growing body of evidence that these objects may induce or exacerbate psychiatric symptoms in vulnerable children and adolescents. False social attachments can lead to some serious harms indeed, and we have already heard from the noble Lord, Lord Alton, about the tragic case of Sewell Setzer in the States, who died by suicide following months of intensive interaction with AI chatbots.

I have come to the end of what I can say about this. We need to understand the mental health implications, but we also need parental and teacher education to get this stuff in the curriculum, too.

speaker: Lord Rees of Ludlow
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, until a decade ago, the IT revolution seemed a social good. We acclaimed the amazing technology that allows people anywhere in the world to communicate with each other and to access the world’s knowledge. But ambivalence set in. We became anxious about the impact of fake news, the amplification of extreme views, and the shoddy and often obscene content that young children were enticed to scroll through and on which some spent several hours per day.

The pace of advances in the past three years—the release of ChatGPT, followed by its increasingly powerful successors—scares us all. The apocalyptic scenarios and the overdominance of a few globe-spanning mega-companies should be high on the political agenda.

Today’s debate is a chance to address more domestic issues: the extent to which we should allow AI to invade our domestic lives. To take a very simple example, every child could now have a mobile device that can answer all its questions in its mother’s voice. Some find this distasteful, rather like delegating childcare to robots. But anyone mindful that some five year-olds enter reception class not toilet-trained and barely able to speak must agree that such a phone could have eased their deprivation. It has some pluses.

AI cannot completely replace a real teacher, except maybe for adult professional education, but it can be a genuine aid for all but the very best teachers. For instance, the Khan Academy website, already 15 years old, produced a library of simple videos showing a hand writing as though on a blackboard, with an unseen voice offering a clear exposition of, for instance, simple geometry or mechanics. There would still be a teacher monitoring the class but, if each pupil had a tablet or simple laptop, they need not all go at the same speed. A range of simple programmes such as this could enhance basic teaching in the developing world, and indeed in this country, too.

The Khan Academy allows pupils anywhere in the world to benefit from a small number of outstanding expositors. Likewise, those who offer fine lectures at school or university level should spread their impact wider via AI, just as writers of good textbooks do.

It is crucial to ensure that students develop their own knowledge and skills, not becoming overreliant on AI-generated content. There is concern about what is called cognitive offloading: students delegating problem-solving to AI rather than nourishing their own intellectual development. We must guard against that. AI’s role will also surely become more crucial at college level, if, as one expects, the three-year full-time residential model of education becomes less dominant and is replaced by a more flexible structure.

speaker: Lord Hampton
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the clerks for allowing me to speak in the gap. I join the chorus of thanks to my noble friend Lord Patel for securing the debate, and for his wise words. I congratulate my noble friend Lord McFall of Alcluith on his first speech following his 22-yard walk from the Woolsack to the Cross Benches. I thank my 15 year-old daughter Cecilia for her help with this speech, and for being a sounding board.

I am a working teacher. I have talked about mobile phones so many times. They have no place on the way to or in schools. Children need to learn without them. Mankind managed 500,000 years without them. If you need to know where your child is, give them an AirTag.

We kid ourselves that AI and screens are an issue for the young; they are issues that affect us all. By the time we finish this debate on AI, it will already be out of date. Jimmy Carr said:

“If you listed me the attributes of God … you would say: ‘He’s omnipotent and he’s all-knowing … and he lives in a cloud and he can make miracles happen’. Those are the attributes of a deity … I think we were not made in God’s image, but I think we so wanted there to be a god that we built one in our image. That is what I think about AI”.

A friend of mine, who is the CEO of a data company, has a theory that when you ask an AI engine to do a task, it first makes an obvious error and then apologises, and he thinks that is deliberate to make it seem unthreatening, so that we underestimate the power that is going on behind us.

On screens, we need to make sure that no one can accidentally or deliberately access harmful content, as my noble friend Lady Manningham-Buller said so powerfully. I commend the work of the charity Tender in educating people on how to communicate. It educates on what is acceptable. Fundamentally, if we want to get young people off screens and somehow keep them offline, we need to make the offline world that much more interesting.

speaker: Lord Clement-Jones
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I warmly thank the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for securing the debate and for the authority with which he opened it. We have heard a series of outstanding speeches on a very broad range of issues, as the noble Baroness, Lady Murphy, pointed out. Like the noble Lord, Lord Hampton, I was absolutely delighted to hear from the noble Lord, Lord McFall, who was a very technology-savvy Lord Speaker, understanding both the opportunities and risks of tech for this House during his tenure.

On many occasions, I have asked whether this technology will be our servant or master. Today, that question has a rather sharper edge: is this technology serving childhood, or are our children being shaped to serve a business model built on attention? Are we being invaded in our domestic lives, as the noble Lord, Lord Rees, said; or, as the right reverend Prelate the Bishop of Peterborough said, is it serving their humanity?

The debate is no longer about whether to act; it is about whether what we do is well-designed, grounded in evidence and able to keep pace with AI. At its heart is one principle: safety by design. The question is not only which children we keep off which platforms but whether the products themselves are built with children’s well-being in mind.

What does the evidence tell us? The POST briefings were mentioned by the noble Lord, Lord Patel. They were published in August and show the scale of the situation. By the age of 2, 98% of children use screens on a typical day, and 97% of 13 to 17 year-olds have a social media or messaging profile. Some harms are found consistently: disrupted sleep, sedentary behaviour, obesity—mentioned by the noble Lord, Lord Brooke—myopia and the security risks mentioned by the noble Baroness, Lady Manningham-Buller.

However, POST is equally clear that most studies take a snapshot at a single point in time, so they show a link, but not a cause and effect. The harm lies, therefore, not just in the content but in the functionality of the product: infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks and recommender systems tuned for engagement, and recommender systems tuned to maximise engagement rather than well-being, triggering the brain effects mentioned by the noble Baroness, Lady Greenfield.

These are deliberate design choices, and they can be designed differently. A ban asks children to stay away from unsafe products; safety by design, as the noble Baroness, Lady Owen, advocated, requires companies to stop building them. However, we should not forget the benefits, which were mentioned not only by my noble friend Lord Addington but by the noble Baronesses, Lady Wheatcroft, Lady Owen and Lady Bennett, and the noble Lords, Lord Loomba and the Lord Rees. The OxWell survey found that one in eight students use social media for mental health support, rising to around a quarter among some of the most vulnerable groups.

Australia’s early evaluation, also mentioned by the noble Baronesses, Lady Wheatcroft and Lady Owen, found a fall in accounts on restricted platforms, but that many children had kept access. A blunt instrument can miss its target and hurt the very children it is meant to protect. We should listen to the children’s charities here. The NSPCC has warned us that a complex problem needs more than a blanket solution. The risk is that children are pushed through VPNs into less regulated spaces, where they are harder to protect, and then meet the full force of the most addictive features the day they turn 16. The Secretary of State acknowledged that cliff-edge concern, but the same thinking should apply to younger children too, because many will get round the ban or use services it does not cover, and safer design is what protects them there.

That is why we on the Liberal Democrat Benches have argued for film-style age ratings for social media. Platforms with harmful content or addictive algorithmic feeds would be rated over-16, and extreme content 18-plus, while educational sites and family messaging would stay open. No child should be banned from Wikipedia for their homework or from the family WhatsApp group. We have also called for health warnings on apps and a cap on doom scrolling. There is a range of views about the right age threshold, but we share the same goal. The Government’s package reflects some of the thinking behind our approach, and the noble Lord, Lord Nagaraju, set some of that out—targeting harmful features rather than screens alone, and safer defaults for 16 and 17 year- olds. They have chosen a blanket ban where we would have preferred ratings, but a ratings approach should still shape how the ban is defined and enforced, so that it is the riskier services that are caught.

Let me turn to artificial intelligence, which has been mentioned by so many noble Lords and which I fear will be the next frontier of this debate, long after a social media ban has bedded in. As the noble Baroness, Lady Prashar, says, we need to act now. Ofcom has said plainly that chatbots are not regulated at all where users interact only with the bot, and that extending its powers is a matter for government and Parliament. The Online Safety Act regulates services, not technology, and generative AI exposes that gap.

The Government’s fix is welcome, but too narrow. Illegal content duties and an age limit on romantic companion bots leave untouched the sycophancy, emotional dependency and manipulative design of general-purpose chatbots, which children increasingly treat as friends, tutors and confidants, as we have heard from noble Lords today. POST also notes potential risks to attention, language development and independent thinking. AI should strengthen children’s thinking, not substitute for it. These are design choices, too. A chatbot that flatters, never ends a conversation and presents itself as a friend has been built that way. Will the Government look at default design duties rather than relying on illegal content duties alone?

I suggest four steps. The first should be the adoption of the proposals in the recent report from the Joint Committee on Human Rights, of which the noble Lord, Lord Alton, was chair. This would involve mandatory children’s algorithmic impact assessments before AI products were likely to be used by children. Secondly, there should be a statutory children and AI design code, building on the age-appropriate design code. Many noble Lords have mentioned the opportunities for AI in education, but there should be human-in-command standards for AI in schools and edtech. I commend strongly the recent book by Daniel Susskind, What Should My Children Do? and, of course, all the work that Sir Anthony Seldon and Michael Stevenson are carrying out at Wellington College on human flourishing and education. Fourthly, there should be age assurance that protects privacy and is built on open standards. I should also mention, as the noble Lord, Lord Rees, did, the importance of avoiding cognitive offloading in higher education in particular, and the steps that need to be taken to make sure that we use AI tools but that we also educate in a way that forces people not to be able to use AI tools but keep the critical thinking that is so vital.

I have some questions for the Minister. First, will the Section 214A regulations be made by affirmative procedure, with a draft published for consultation, and will the end of the year timetable hold? Secondly, which services are in and which are out? YouTube disputes that it is social media, and WhatsApp sits outside the ban. Will there be an independent risk-based rating mechanism rather than a ministerial list? Thirdly, how will privacy be protected in age assurance and how will VPN circumvention be handled? The Government also said they would legislate for age verification at device level if their recommendations were not adopted by September this year. That deadline has passed. Can the Minister tell the House what has happened and whether legislation is now coming? Fourthly, will the regulations and Ofcom codes impose positive design duties so that services likely to be used by children are safe by design, as the Online Safety Act’s own objectives require? As the noble Baroness, Lady Armstrong, asked, what about digital inclusion? Other noble Lords talked about media literacy. The new RSHE guidance taught from this September covers online misogyny, AI and deepfakes. What support will teachers get to deliver it with confidence, and will independent evaluation be built in from day one?

Childhood should not be a product optimised for engagement. Our aim is not simply to keep children out of the digital world but to require that it is built safe for them from the start: technology that serves childhood rather than dominates it. As the noble Lord, Lord McFall, said about what Stuart Russell had to say when he came to the Lords about the power of tech companies, we should heed him. We need a culture of safety, and we need regulation to back it up.

speaker: Earl of Effingham
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, we are most grateful to the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for securing this important debate.

Throughout the passage of the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, my noble friend Lady Barran successfully argued that social media, mobile phones and screens in general were largely detrimental to children, a view which we steadfastly hold. We drew on evidence from teachers, parents and experts which concluded that the use of these devices risked worse social skills, worse mental health and worse results.

The Government acknowledged that conclusion, and from the start of this academic year, schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default. Regulations will soon be laid to ban under-16s from the negative effects of social media. In both these measures there is an implicit acknowledgement that screens in fact do not benefit children but have the potential to cause active harm.

For that reason, it is of grave concern that worrying elements of educational technology remain in the school system. The government guidance is clear: no mobile phones in schools. Additional guidance states that anything other than this should be by exception only. With the presence of edtech in classrooms, screens are anything but an exception. Now 11% of pupils use an individual device in every lesson, while nearly 40% use screens in schools every day.
