The noble Baroness, Lady Wheatcroft, was quite right that this is not the way that relationships are built. The noble Baroness, Lady Armstrong, referenced this as a nuanced subject, which is right. To be clear, we are not conflating mobile phones with educational technology. There are notable exceptions when edtech helps—for example, with special education needs pupils. However, the medically proven distractions that are considered detrimental in respect of use of mobile phones are too often prevalent in the edtech that is supposed to facilitate learning.

Homework apps may prioritise interaction over learning and treat schooling as a reward-based enterprise versus essential learning for self-improvement. This would be no issue if using screens produced better learning and better results. However, these devices have proven the exact opposite. Studies have found that students spending two-thirds of every hour off-task while using a laptop in educational settings is a regular occurrence and that it can take students up to 20 minutes to refocus on a task following a distraction. This is a well-known fact.

The noble Baroness, Lady Wheatcroft, highlighted a school which uses no devices for teaching. It is a fact that comprehension increases by up to 60% if students read on print rather than digitally. Benefits to mathematical learning become pronounced only in the upper secondary school years after students have developed sufficient foundational knowledge and cognitive maturity to engage productively with the demands of virtual experimentation. Again, this is a fact.

I greatly enjoyed the excellent contribution from the noble Baroness, Lady Greenfield, with her neuroscience background. Her fellow neuroscientist, the best-selling author, Dr Jared Horvath, has demonstrated that independent schools in England and Wales, which use relatively the most educational technology, have been declining in PISA scores by 21% per decade—a phenomenon which is offset by improving state schools, which have, unfortunately, less access to some of the edtech.

This outcome should not be a surprise to noble Lords. While no consensus has been reached regarding edtech’s benefits and only 7% of companies have conducted controlled trials, schools have been left with the responsibility of weighing the costs and benefits of procurement in line with their longer-term strategies. The right reverend Prelate the Bishop of Peterborough argued that we owe it to our educators. The noble Baroness, Lady Murphy, rightly challenged the Minister on the very same subject. Schools are left to navigate an uncontrolled experiment while edtech companies have little oversight of their actions.

These are big tech companies. The noble Lord, Lord Alton, flagged that some of them have larger market capitalisations than the entire GDP of many national economies. The noble Lord, Lord McFall, reminded us that AI, bizarrely, is less regulated than milk or washing machines. As a minimum, the industry must have some kind of centralised oversight. Will the Minister commit to such regulatory scrutiny, in line with the request of the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, to be measured in months, not years?

There is, rightfully, much interest around the benefits that new technologies can bring to learning and working. We are not suggesting that technology cannot be used to improve schooling, or children’s lives in general, but simply that it must be rigorously tested before it is rolled out and then overseen when it is.

On artificial intelligence, 90% of children already use AI for entertainment, while 85% use it for schoolwork. There are undoubtedly benefits to introducing children to new technologies as they enter into a world built by them, but, surely, unfettered access and use can be incredibly damaging during a child’s core development years. Studies show that early protracted exposure to AI can interfere with long-term memory and learning processes. More generally, there is a risk that AI creates a generation of children dependent on outsourcing their thinking, which has been referenced by many noble Lords. Much like educational technology, AI must be most beneficial when its users have acquired the foundational knowledge and maturity needed to deal with that very technology.

The Government are implementing an AI strategy in schools as evidence emerges, but we would suggest to the Minister that we need more. The pace of change in this sector is like nothing we have seen before, and other countries are acting: the OECD and the European Commission have co-published the AI literacy framework, and over 35 US states now have official AI guidance. When will this Government follow their lead?

I will end on concerns of AI becoming edtech by the back door. There are a number of schools already using AI learning assistants in lessons. It is so incredibly important, as was referenced by the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, to give children the best start in life, and the Government’s approach must be evidence based and balanced. The education sector is facing a torrent of new and untested technologies. Some will be beneficial, but others will not, and it is surely absolutely critical to get this right for everyone involved.

speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Patel, for securing this important debate and for his introductory speech, expertly setting the scene through facts and situating children’s experience in the context of the rest of their lives. I also thank those across the House for their valuable contributions. There were so many excellent points made, and I will seek to respond to those; for those I do not manage to get to, I will write afterwards.

I can reassure your Lordships’ House that the Government take this issue incredibly seriously. There is nothing more important than keeping our children safe, both offline and online, and the Prime Minister has set a clear ambition that the United Kingdom will have the strongest online child safety laws in the world. It was a privilege to hear the excellent contribution by the noble Lord, Lord McFall, today, who asked for the Prime Minister’s leadership, which, indeed, he is setting out, because artificial intelligence, screen usage and social media all pose unique challenges for children today. We know that 99% of eight to 17 year-olds are online, and Ofcom’s latest data suggests that nearly three-quarters of children aged 11 to 17 had encountered harmful content in the previous four weeks. That is why we are determined to put children’s wellbeing first and give them the best possible start in life.

As we heard from the noble Lord, Lord Addington, these technologies can be personally transformative, and there are genuine opportunities—a point underlined by the noble Lord, Lord Loomba. We know they have great potential to support children’s learning and development when the conditions are right. My noble friend Lady Armstrong so rightly highlighted the importance of digital inclusion, which we are working on across the whole of government to ensure that that is embedded as a foundation, specifically in education. That is why through the AI tutoring tools pioneer programme the Government are working with educators, experts and developers to co-create and trial AI tutoring tools. The £24 million edtech testbed programme, delivered in partnership with the Education Endowment Foundation, is building the evidence base on what works in education technology, including AI-enabled tools.

As many noble Lords stressed today, how we adopt education technology in our schools is critical. The noble Baroness, Lady Barran, made this point very eloquently, as did the noble Lords, Lord Tarassenko and Lord Rees, the noble Baroness, Lady Owen, and my noble friend Lord Brooke. Our focus should be on the quality of technology use. We need sensible guardrails around children’s use of technology while recognising that digital tools can improve outcomes when used effectively. Excellent teaching remains at the heart of education. Technology should enhance and support great teaching, not replace it. A school should be empowered to use digital and non-digital approaches according to what works best for their pupils. To help children and young people benefit from edtech and AI safely in their education, this autumn we are consulting on introducing new safety certification of technology used in early-years settings, schools and colleges. This will help educators and parents have the confidence that tools meet clear, trusted safety standards.

A number of noble Lords, including the right reverend Prelate the Bishop of Peterborough and the noble Lord, Lord Hampton, have stressed the critical role of teachers. The DfE has published practical AI support materials for teachers covering opportunities and risks of AI, which was updated in May 2026, and is developing a new digital and data skills pathway for the education workforce, setting expectations for skills needed to use tech, data and AI safely. The Department for Education’s policy paper Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Education sets out our approach to the opportunities and risks of generative AI in education and provides advice on using AI safely, effectively and responsibly. These guardrails are incredibly important for the correct adoption of AI technology in our classrooms.

A number of noble Lords, including the noble Baroness, Lady Prashar, highlighted the importance of media literacy. That is why we published A Safe, Informed Digital Nation, the UK’s first cross-government media literacy action plan. It sets out a shared framework for action across government to deliver these aims.

However, as many noble Lords have highlighted today, the technology poses risks. That is why the Government are delivering on the Online Safety Act 2023, placing tough legal duties on platforms to keep their users safe. The strongest protections in the Act are rightly reserved for children. The child safety duties came into effect in July 2025. They require platforms to prevent children accessing pornography, self-harm material, suicide content and eating disorder content. The Online Safety Act also requires providers to protect children from harmful content such as violent content and bullying and abusive content, such as that referred to by the noble Baroness, Lady Manningham-Buller. When something does go wrong, parents and children have simple, clear ways to report it. The Government have given Ofcom the powers to enforce the Act, and that is our expectation.

We know that technology and online harms continue to evolve. We will therefore keep the legislative framework under review and we will not hesitate to take further action to ensure children are protected online—a reassurance, I hope, for the noble Lord, Lord Nagaraju. Indeed, we have already done so. Earlier this year, the Government ran a national consultation, Growing Up in the Online World. It was one of the largest engagement exercises the Government have recently conducted, receiving over 116,000 responses. This included the views of at least 54,000 parents and 14,000 children. As the noble Baroness, Lady Bennett, highlighted, it is important to listen to the voices of young people.

The results showed an overwhelming demand for action. Some 90% of parents who responded to the consultation supported an outright ban on social media for under-16s, and two-thirds of young people agreed that under-16s should not be allowed to use at least some social media platforms. That is why the Government have acted. Like Australia, we are banning social media companies from offering their services to children under 16. However, we are going further by banning under-16s from livestreaming, stopping unknown adults communicating with children through online services, including gaming services, and switching off harmful features for 16 and 17 year-olds by default. This will protect children from platforms’ online features that create the most harm. The first regulations on the social media ban will be laid before Parliament by the end of this year, and the restrictions will come into effect from spring 2027.

A number of noble Lords raised the importance of AI chatbots. My noble friend Lord Brooke highlighted the potential for AI chatbots to help young people learn, explore new ideas and find information. However, as the noble Lord, Lord Alton, highlighted, there are risks that we are acutely aware of. They can expose children to harmful content or encourage an unhealthy reliance on technology. That is why Britain will become the first country in the world to ban chatbots that offer sexualised content to under-18s. We will restrict this functionality on general purpose chatbots, too.

The Government have committed to introducing mandatory breaks in AI chatbot use for under-18s, to encourage healthier online habits. We have also taken a delegated power in the Crime and Policing Act to bring currently unregulated AI chatbot services within the scope of the Online Safety Act’s illegal-content duties. This is a rapidly developing area so, where new evidence of chatbot harms does emerge, the Government will not hesitate to take further action where necessary to protect children.

To the question asked by the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, on the commitment that the Government have made to be the first country in the world where it is impossible for children to take, share or view nudity online, last month we announced that this Government will introduce legislation requiring tech companies to strengthen protections on devices and platforms, and we are working to introduce that as soon as possible.

We have heard about the impact of screen use on children, and the noble Baroness, Lady Murphy, highlighted the importance of parents in this picture. We know that long periods of time spent on screens can get in the way of activities critical for development, such as sleep, physical activity, creative play and interaction with parents. The Government recognise the need to balance embracing technology with promoting the health and development of younger children. That is why the Government have published advice on screen use for parents of children aged nought to five on the Best Start in Life website. It offers practical, non-judgmental support to help families to balance screen use with other activities. It is underpinned by the findings of an expert panel led by Professor Russell Viner and the Children’s Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza. Following the guidance for under-fives, DHSC is now working with DfE to develop practical advice for parents and carers of five to 18 year-olds.

A number of noble Lords highlighted the importance of the offline world and how we cultivate the right atmosphere for children to grow offline, including the noble Lord, Lord Hampton, and the noble Baronesses, Lady Greenfield, Lady Prashar and Lady Bennett. What type of society are we building? We are working across government to ensure that children and young people have access to safe online spaces. Specifically through Youth Matters: Your National Youth Strategy, the Government are investing more than £500 million to ensure that all young people have somewhere to go, something to do and someone to talk to. This includes a £450 million Youth Matters fund to deliver significant long-term change in youth provision in the most underserved areas of England.

As I said at the outset, there is nothing more important than keeping our children safe. That is why the Government are delivering on the Online Safety Act and building on it where necessary to protect children online. In addition, where there is evidence, the Government have not hesitated and will not hesitate to go further. We will continue to listen to those making contributions in this House and to reports such as those referenced today, as well as reports such as those cited by the noble Lord, Lord Alton, from the JCHR. This is how we will deliver our ambition for the UK to be a world leader, keeping children safe and providing them with the protections and support they need in an increasingly online world.

speaker: Lord Patel
heading: AI, Screen Usage and Social Media: Effect on Children - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the Minister for her response. She may not have had the opportunity to pick up some of the points that were made, particularly about developing an AI policy, either through a commission or through other routes, and maybe she can reflect on that again.

There were some important points made about the important role schools could play: developing material by themselves for themselves. This may benefit vulnerable children in particular, or enable those who have greater demands to better participate in educational activities though developments in the use of available technology.

Many important points were made about how the Government can have a bigger role, aside from regulation—which is, of course, an important issue that we should address. I was pleased to hear the Minister refer to more legislation about controlling the tech industry and making it take responsibility for some of the issues that were raised that are detrimental to the development of the children, including the ability to migrate from responsible gaming platforms to the dark web. They should not be allowed to do that. There are issues about regulation that the Minister addressed, and I am glad to hear that more regulation may be required and that the Government are keeping an eye on it. However, the debate raised the subject of opportunities to use AI to benefit children, although much of the discussion, including my contribution, focused on the harm that is being created. I hope we might return to these points and that the Minister might reflect on them.

It is customary to thank all noble Lords who took part in today’s debate. I am not doing so because it is customary but because I sincerely mean to thank all noble Lords for their exemplary contributions. It was a well thought out deliberation. And I am glad that the teacher, the noble Lord, Lord McFall, is back. He spent a lot of his time teaching but now he is back and I was delighted by his contribution.

Motion agreed.

speaker: Lord Frost
heading: Puberty Blockers and Cross-sex Hormones - Question for Short Debate
text:
My Lords, it is a pleasure to follow the noble Baroness, Lady Cass, on any subject, but particularly this one. I am grateful to the noble Baroness, Lady Deech, for securing this very important debate. I have not spoken much about this subject in public, but I have followed it closely; I feel strongly about it. I wanted to speak today because I simply fail to understand the logic behind what is going on and what we are allowing to proceed. I support what the Government have done so far on this general issue—the bans and the indefinite pauses on puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones. The Government deserve credit for this, particularly given the strongly held opposition from a narrow group of their own supporters on this subject.

However, what I cannot quite follow—I have learned that many other people cannot follow it either—is what is happening now. The Government have judged these drugs too uncertain to give children in the ordinary way of things, but are now prepared to support giving them to 11 and 12 year-olds as an experiment. We know that the MRHA, as a regulator, had misgivings about this and suggested a minimum age of 14—still too low, in my view—but somehow, it has been persuaded to change its mind and think that 11 or 12 is okay. It is not clear entirely why; perhaps the Minister could shed some light on that.

One must ask why this trial is necessary at all. As far as I can see, the only reason one might want to do it is to learn whether we might one day be able to administer such medicines to children who feel gender dysphoria; of course, we already use them in other extremely limited circumstances. If we do not ever wish to do that, why would we want the trial? I recognise that others may not share my view, but personally, because of my own convictions about the nature of reality and sexual difference, I cannot imagine circumstances in which we would ever want to do this. The view that we might rests on the much-disputed premise that a child can have a gender at odds with his or her sex, and that if so, it is the body rather than the beliefs should change. I am afraid I simply do not accept that. I know others will, but I do not.

By the way, in passing, I worry that if the Government’s conversion practices Bill ever made it into law, what I have just said would become quite a risky thing to say in quite a lot of circumstances. Gender dysphoria clearly is a real thing, and children who suffer from it deserve all kinds of psychological and social support—the best we can possibly give. But by crediting the belief that in certain circumstances the body should change to reflect the psychology, we surely make dealing with it harder not easier, because that appears to offer a way out.

I do not accept the logic behind the trial at all. I just do not understand it. As I have said, I recognise that others may take a different view on the nature of gender and sex differentiation. We live in a free society, of course—but it is a free society for adults, and we have a duty to protect children. In the previous debate we heard the Government saying they were banning sexualised chatbots for children under 18, presumably because they think children under 18 cannot deal with that sort of content. Surely, therefore, we must protect children from irreversible medical treatment, decided on at an age at which no reasonable person would think they could reasonably consent, even in a trial. I do not see how we can, in conscience, proceed with such a trial involving 11 year-olds.

I experienced some of the Covid pandemic from the inside of government, more as an observer than a participant. I am afraid I learned from that period that sometimes the cleverest scientists and the most highly respected medical authorities could not see the wood for the trees, and ended up supporting things that were, I think, indefensible. We need to stick to principles sometimes, and one of my principles on this is that it is wrong to administer irreversible treatments to 11 and 12 year-olds. To be honest, I find it shocking and disgraceful that we can do it. It should be opposed in every way possible.

speaker: Lord Carter of Haslemere
heading: Written Constitution - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, it is a privilege to follow so many distinguished speakers. The primary purpose of a constitution is to establish the fundamental legal framework for governing a state. In the United Kingdom, two key facets of this are protecting and strengthening our democracy and providing a framework for effective government in accordance with the rule of law. I would measure the arguments for a written constitution against these two benchmarks.

So, would a written constitution be more or less democratic? Jonathan Sumption pointed out in his Telegraph article of 9 August this year that a written constitution would

“hand enormous political powers to the courts”,

which would have the power to interpret it and overturn Acts of Parliament if they did not measure up to the courts’ interpretations. That point was echoed by the noble Lord, Lord Howard of Lympne, just now. Extending the role of our unelected judges in this way would distort our finely balanced separation of powers, weakening parliamentary sovereignty and thereby our democracy.

Parliamentary sovereignty provides the flexibility to reform and strengthen our democracy. One can point to many of our statutes, such as the European Communities Act, the Human Rights Act, the Constitutional Reform Act and the Fixed-term Parliaments Act, when Parliament has legislated in a constitutional way. The same is true of devolution in the United Kingdom, which the Prime Minister thinks should be extended throughout the country by a written constitution.

The beauty of our current system is that parliamentary sovereignty has enabled these constitutional statutes to be enacted and then to be repealed or amended subsequently through a normal legislative process, as has happened in the case of every single one of them. A written constitution could not so easily have achieved this, since the whole point, as has been said, would be to entrench it and give it a higher status than primary legislation, deliberately making it harder to amend or repeal and transferring power from elected politicians to the judiciary in the process.

There has, of course, been social and political angst in the debates leading to the enactments and repeals I have mentioned, but take a moment to imagine the discord which the nation would endure in trying to decide what a written constitution should contain. There would certainly be calls for it to go wider than the Cabinet Manual. One has only to consider the recent heated debates on economic and social issues, such as whether a person is a man or a woman, which migrants should be allowed to stay in the United Kingdom, or the duties of the state to provide welfare and social care. The list goes on, and one could see some people arguing passionately for their inclusion in a written constitution, leading to fresh divisions in society. Far better, in my view, to rely on Parliament to decide such issues as and when necessary, in line with manifesto and other policy commitments, and to override unintended judicial interpretations by fresh legislation.

I turn to the second purpose of our constitution—to provide a framework for effective government. Advocates of a written constitution might point to the ineffectiveness of our current system to get anything done. One is spoilt for choice, but just look at the seeming inability to deliver infrastructure projects such as Hammersmith Bridge, which has so far been closed for seven years and will not fully reopen until 2035. The Chinese replaced their multilane Sanyuan Bridge in 43 hours. Look at the massive cost overruns and delays of HS2, the broken prison system and the procurement failures and lack of investment in UK defence. Tempting as it is in the face of these failures to seize on anything which might make things better, it is not the fault of our constitution that some Governments over the past 15 to 20 years have failed to govern effectively or responsibly. A written constitution would make no difference.

Ministerial accountability is already part of our unwritten constitution, for which the Prime Minister holds ultimate responsibility, and it can be enforced by means of the Ministerial Code and parliamentary scrutiny mechanisms such as Select Committees. The Public Office (Accountability) Bill, once implemented, may help to add statutory weight to the principle of ministerial accountability. In addition, there is political pressure, which, at an election, punishes ministerial incompetence or irresponsibility—or earlier, if our leaders are forced to quit. Seven Prime Ministers in 10 years speaks for itself. This and other political dramas in recent years show how our constitution can weather the fiercest storms.

Some would say that a written constitution would be more transparent than our current convoluted statute book. They have a point. AI states that there are around 6,000 statutes in force, many totally incomprehensible because of extensive amendments to previous Acts. The Representation of the People Bill is a case in point. However, the answer is not a written constitution but a programme of legislative consolidation, which would vastly improve everyone’s understanding of what the law actually is. There is little hope of that.

In conclusion, let us cherish the jewels in the crown of our unwritten constitution: parliamentary sovereignty, the separation of powers and ministerial accountability, which have protected our democracy for so long and which are the envy of written constitutions around the world.

speaker: Chi Onwurah
heading: Science and Technology Committee
text:
Thank you so much, Ms Furniss. I am really grateful to the Backbench Business Committee for allocating time for this statement on the Science and Technology Committee’s report entitled “Rewiring the state: Delivering digital government” and to discuss the Government response. I place on the record my thanks to the Committee Clerks and specialists who supported this complex inquiry, as well as to all those who gave evidence, in person or in writing.

Both the previous Government and the current one have spoken of their ambition to make the UK a truly digital state, transforming citizens’ experiences of the health service, the education and justice systems, and indeed all public services, increasing productivity and efficiency and reducing costs. I am a tech evangelist; I believe that technology should make the world work better for people, and my Committee welcomes and supports the Government’s ambitions, but our report raised serious concerns about how achievable they are.

In our report, we identified four building blocks for successful digital transformation. The first is money. Money always matters, but we found that inadequate data on digital spend prevents the Government from making informed decisions or holding those responsible to account. The second is people. Do we have the right people and skills to deliver digital transformation and cultural change to ensure that skills are valued and embedded in leadership roles? For example, how many permanent secretaries have the digital experience required? The third is information and data security. There are serious data hygiene failures across the public sector. Public bodies hold public data on trust; it needs to meet the highest standards. The fourth is delivery. We need a detailed and measurable plan to ensure the success of the digital transformation agenda.

We also identified four barriers to realising the benefits of digital transformation. The first is hype. Both tech companies and the Government are guilty of this. Tech companies hype their solutions, often without reference to the problems, and the Government talk up the impact, such as the supposed £45 billion annual productivity saving from digitalisation. Hype undermines the credibility of the Government’s arguments, confuses and demoralises civil servants, and encourages the belief that over-optimism, rather than achievement and honesty, will be rewarded.

The second barrier is legacy systems. Outdated, obsolete or unsupported IT infrastructure, systems, hardware or processes pose an unacceptable level of risk. Our report found that, without a plan to address legacy systems, the Government’s digital ambitions will struggle to be achieved.

The third barrier is vendor lock-in. If significant costs or reductions in functionality are associated with changing vendors, we have vendor lock-in, whereby vendors can hold the Government hostage, raise prices, require additional contracts or reduce performance. The public sector depends on a small number of large digital and technology providers—such as Palantir, Microsoft and Amazon Web Services—and the Government appear to be worryingly comfortable with that.

The fourth barrier is lack of technology sovereignty. While the over-reliance on a small number of foreign vendors exists, the Government cannot set out to deliver their own sovereign digital agenda for the United Kingdom or fully support a competitive UK tech ecosystem. The Government should set out a public sector definition of sovereignty.

Palantir is a case study in three of the four barriers. Palantir’s relationship with the NHS began during the covid-19 pandemic when it was paid a nominal £1 fee to provide what its chief executive Louis Mosley described to us as “aggregating data”. It is now hyped as being uniquely essential to the NHS’s mission to save lives. It is a clear example of growing vendor lock-in as well as an over-reliance on foreign tech giants. Our report called on the Government to commit to exercising the February 2027 break clause in the federated data platform contract.

I thank the Government for their response, which came from the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, although I understand other Departments were involved, so it is a welcome example of cross-Government working. Some parts of it are excellent, particularly the commitment to develop a strategy within the Government Digital Service to end vendor lock-in. That is a real step forward, as is the commitment to strong central co-ordination to drive progress on fixing legacy systems across the public sector, which is what we recommended.

An action plan is promised, as well as a remediation plan, subject to security considerations. The Government also reveal that 36 tech company employees have had access to either the federated data or specific datasets assigned by NHS England when initially Palantir said that none of its employees had access to it. So there is more transparency.

Other parts of the response are less encouraging. Significantly, in response to our recommendation that GDS develop and publish a framework to evaluate the performance of digital spend, we are told that they cannot count spend by Department. So as we embark on a complete digital transformation, we do not know how much is being spent and on what. How can we ensure that Ministers make informed decisions and can be held to account? Every single Government Department might be buying the same cloud services from the same vendor, and we will not know or be able to assess our resilience or performance.

Despite repeated data breaches, the Government refuse to share which public bodies and Departments meet basic data hygiene practices. That is due to “security considerations”. So we cannot hold Government to account for bad data management because it might alert the Chinese—I fear they know our limitations better than we do. Rolling out AI-driven public services over bad data infrastructure is a recipe for disaster and will require strong, rigorous standards and implementation to address it.

On open source, the Government are inconsistent and contradictory. They agree it is an important tool against vendor lock-in, but reject our recommendation that public bodies prioritise open-source tools and technology over proprietary offerings, citing the “essential commercial accountability” offered by suppliers of proprietary software. So is open source a good or a bad thing? The Government did not even engage with our request to provide impact assessments relating to the US CLOUD Act 2018, under which US headquartered companies can in principle be compelled to provide the US Government with access to UK customers’ data held in their UK data centres. The Government accept the need to strengthen sovereign capability and they promise updates, but reject a cross-Government strategy on sovereignty or a definition. They confirm efforts to support UK start-ups and scale-ups through procurement.

Two further key issues: we learned for the first time that the digital inter-ministerial group has been replaced by an official-level bimonthly digital executive committee, which sounds like a significant downgrade, just as digital is moved from the centre of Government—the Cabinet Office—to DCMS. Yet there is no commitment to appointing a dedicated Cabinet-level Minister responsible for driving effective digital transformation across the public sector.

Yesterday in the Committee hearing with Ministers on the machinery of government changes, the diffuse nature of responsibilities was apparent. Ministers and officials spoke repeatedly about working together effectively, but it does not give confidence that digital transformation will be achieved when there is not one person accountable for it or able to impose digital standards.

Finally on Palantir, the Government state that if a decision is taken not to extend Palantir’s contract, then the contract includes measures to support transition and continuity of services. I have since had a letter from the Minister for Health Innovation emphasising the significant costs associated with moving to another vendor while denying that there is vendor lock-in. I am seeking further clarification.

The British people deserve a modern, flexible digital state designed to meet their needs, with public services that improve their lives. Trust is essential to achieving that and bad data hygiene, outdated systems, vendor lock-in, hyped solutions and lack of sovereign capability is a recipe for failure. Without clear leadership that can drive and deliver the scale of change needed, we remain very concerned that there will be no successful digital rewiring of the state.

speaker: Chi Onwurah
heading: Science and Technology Committee
text:
I thank the hon. Gentleman for his questions, which go to the heart of the matter: the relationship between the public sector and business, and that between the public sector and the people it is meant to serve.

On business, the public sector should be able to call on the support of businesses as they themselves adopt digital products and services. It should be able to include many different businesses, from Northern Ireland to the north-east of England and across the country, rather than being reliant on a small number of often monopolistic providers. That is a point that we make very strongly in our report. It is important that the interface between the Government and business be open and competitive and not be monopolised. That is one of the things we think that the Government’s response to our report, in terms of looking to ensure the end of vendor lock-in, should help to promote.

On the interface with the public, the hon. Gentleman is absolutely right: the public should not need to be digital experts or super-knowledgeable on AI. The responsibility falls within Government to ensure that people’s data is safe and secure and that the public can trust the Government in handling that data, and to ensure that we have the best digital infrastructure, and transparent providers and suppliers as well.

speaker: Sally Jameson
heading: Civil Service Pensions
text:
I wish to provide the House with an update on the administration of the civil service pension scheme. I must declare my own interest as I hold a civil service pension with His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service.

As we know, the previous Government awarded the contract to Capita in 2023. Earlier this year, in response to significant performance issues, the Government intervened to increase scrutiny and oversight of the scheme’s administration. Capita committed to recovery milestones for April and for June, both of which it failed to meet. In June, we exercised our contractual rights and mandated Capita to produce a rectification plan and—at Capita’s expense—appoint a remedial adviser to assess the plan. The Government also appointed an independent auditor to assess the effectiveness of Capita’s operational arrangements up to July.

Capita committed to the House to deliver recovery milestones in September, which it states it has achieved. However, I want to be clear that that does not reflect members’ lived experience or my own correspondence. Those were self-imposed, self-determined and self-assured targets. Many hon. Members, unions and scheme members have written to me asking why, if Capita has met those targets, they still do not have their quote, their pension remains unpaid and they are struggling with no income despite years of commitment and public service. Building on the good work in holding Capita to account undertaken by my predecessors, my right hon. Friend the Member for Torfaen (Nick Thomas-Symonds) and my hon. Friend the Member for Southampton Test (Satvir Kaur), I have taken further clear and definitive action to continue that work and ensure that Capita has its feet held to the fire.

We have seen some small improvement on priority cases, with Capita now processing more than it receives, and I acknowledge that Capita staff on the ground are working hard in difficult conditions. We are also seeing some slow improvement on technology, with Capita confirming that increased volumes are being managed through automation. It is also rolling out new tools that allow eligible spouses and dependants to view pension payslips and make online inquiries.

However, the question remains: why has it taken this scale of Government intervention to force Capita to act? Since taking up this role, I have met the CEO and his senior team twice, and on both occasions expressed in no uncertain terms my outrage at their performance throughout this contract. We were promised

“the most AI-enabled Pensions service”.

It is fair to say that Capita has comprehensively failed to deliver on that commitment. The progress overall has been abysmal. Complex issues remain unresolved for too long—1,800 cases for more than a year. Although some individuals have more than one case, too many members and family are still left waiting in limbo. The administration issues have also had a knock-on effect on the progress of Capita’s work on the McCloud remedy. I will update the House on that issue next month.

The House will be aware that my predecessors rightly directed Capita to appoint a remedial adviser and Cabinet Office to appoint an independent auditor through the Government Internal Audit Agency. My officials have this month received the remedial advisory report and the auditor’s interim report, giving independent and objective perspectives. It will not shock this House that the independent adviser’s report clearly shows that Capita’s rectification planning was wholly insufficient, its technology was weak, and its ambition was falling well short of restoring the quality services that members deserve. Poor performance has been evident, but the reports now provide detailed and actionable recommendations, including a new recovery plan for the whole service, with a road map for technology and a focus on data.

The remedial advisory report concluded that, in a service whose success firmly relied on automation, Capita did not deliver the promised technology, that it had not been applying the right techniques to understand demand, productivity and capacity, and that it had not put in place effective mechanisms to detect and escalate failure. Well, I have certainly detected a lot of failure, as have many in this House. For the sake of the dedicated people who are waiting for their pensions, we must not allow the service to fail them further. It is clear that Capita cannot do that on its own. A new plan is needed.

I agreed with Capita executives that Cabinet Office officials would work with Capita to develop a credible, workable and realistic recovery plan for which Capita alone will be held to account. I can confirm that, for the first time, Cabinet Office officials now have full access to Capita systems and data. I have put in place expert teams to work alongside Capita to agree priorities, improve quality and processes, and ensure that pensions are paid correctly.

The new recovery plan is made up of five workstreams. The first three workstreams look at cases of differing levels of complexity, the fourth ensures that significant exercises such as the McCloud remedy are not overlooked, and the fifth, on technology, tackles issues around infrastructure that support delivery. We will require Capita to evidence its focus on fixing complex cases, ensuring that this plan makes the difference that Capita’s original plan could not. Capita has committed that every member with a complex case will be written to in the next month, ensuring that they understand where they are in the system and how they will be supported. Old cases will no longer be allowed to sit on backlogs without progress. Any stuck quote or payment will be actively managed through revised complex case management.

Capita’s new plans will be further supported by challenge and advice from a new group of senior experts, drawn from across the civil service and led by the Cabinet Office. These problems were not created by civil servants, but it will be through the expertise, commitment and perseverance of the civil service that operational delivery is supported and we shape the solutions with Capita. Capita must be open and transparent. We will be publishing fortnightly scheme updates on the pension scheme website, with the number of outstanding complex cases broken down by age, the service levels for straightforward cases and the number of other tasks that are outstanding. We will do so until performance has been stabilised.

I want to be clear that while we are leaning in with expertise, Capita remains absolutely accountable for service delivery. It will need to deliver its contractual obligations and pay for its failures. We will continue to apply commercial levers to recover costs incurred, including holding back nearly £10 million of statements. Throughout this crisis, hon. Members have shown why they and their teams are so valued by their constituents. To support that, we have delivered over 1,300 surgeries for more than 320 MPs. I will provide further updates on the progress of our recovery plan in the coming months.

In addition to the immediate ongoing recovery plan, I want to update the House on the longer-term strategy for the scheme. Following our previous commitments to Parliament, my officials have led an extensive programme of engagement with trade unions, practitioners and experts. The evidence from those sessions was clear: restoring operational resilience and member trust must be the approach. I have instructed my officials to evaluate the viability of a range of future delivery options, including insourcing all core business operations.

There are a number of different insourcing models in operation across the public sector that we will learn from, and we will consider which is the best approach to take for the civil service pension scheme and all the other schemes that it interacts with. Once those assessments are complete, I will return to the House to provide a further update, but in the here and now, Capita must deliver.

This Government inherited a broken, outsourced administration. We cannot replace a complex pension operation overnight, but let me be clear: this Government will hold Capita to account and continue to apply the most stringent commercial levers, and we will not rest until every civil servant receives the pension they are entitled to. I commend this statement to the House.

speaker: Sally Jameson
heading: Civil Service Pensions
text: I am sorry to hear of Elizabeth’s experience. It is totally unacceptable, as are so many of the cases that we have heard about today—and so many that we will not hear about, too. As the hon. Member will know, the Cabinet Office supplied nearly 150 staff in a surge team to help support Capita in processing the backlog. We also now have senior Cabinet Office officials working every single day with Capita to ensure that it is dealing with the complex cases that need serious expertise to be processed. We will continue to support Capita in any way we can. The remedial report noted that the technology let Capita down in a big way. It has now put some further resource and money into the technology, so automation should help process some cases faster. The biggest learning from the report is that while Capita said it would be an AI-enabled pension scheme, that just was not the reality.

speaker: Claire Young
heading: Civil Service Pensions
text: Another weekly surgery, another Capita complaint—this time, a constituent was told on one of her many calls to Capita that she would have to wait while they accessed the spreadsheet because someone was already using it. When the Minister talks about some slow improvements in technology, one can only imagine that Capita’s starting point was a typewriter and abacus. Even with the support of officials, does the Minister really trust Capita to safely deliver an AI-enabled service to our constituents?

speaker: Sally Jameson
heading: Civil Service Pensions
text: I agree with the hon. Member. I am not a tech expert, but I certainly know there is nothing AI about the system that Capita has been using. It is totally unacceptable that Capita suggested that the system would be AI, when clearly it was not ready to take on this level of automation. The technology was not available to Capita at the time. Cabinet Office officials are working on the Capita systems day in, day out to make sure that we are holding Capita to account and challenging it. As I have said, there have been some improvements to the technology, and I have told Capita that those improvements need to continue. Whatever it is putting in, there is more it can do, and I continue to tell Capita representatives that every time I meet them. As far as I am concerned, things will never be good enough until every single person affected has the pension that they should have and the compensation to which they are entitled.

speaker: Karen Bradley
heading: Home Affairs Committee
text:
I am grateful for this opportunity to highlight the Home Affairs Committee’s new inquiry on work-based immigration and to explain the innovative approach we have used with this inquiry. I thank the Backbench Business Committee for allowing time for this statement. I know that the Chair of the Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Harrow East (Bob Blackman), was staying just for that thank you; he is welcome to leave now. [Laughter.]

When I was elected Chair of the Home Affairs Committee, one of the things I talked about was wanting to have a more informed and considered debate on immigration that recognises the distinction between legal migration—visas for work, family, study and humanitarian purposes—and irregular migration, which primarily means small boats nowadays, where the numbers are much lower but the attention much higher. We want a debate that digs into the reasons why net migration numbers have followed the path they have and how reducing those numbers, which is the stated aim of successive Governments, can be achieved in a fair way that serves our economic and national interests.

To do that, the Committee decided to commission a series of deliberative workshops. Instead of relying on opinion polls or surveys, which can only give a snapshot of views, we partnered with the think-tank Demos to design and deliver a rigorous deliberative process, and I thank the Liaison Committee for supporting us financially. This process is one where ordinary people, selected to reflect the make-up of the local population, learn about the issue, discuss it with one another, and work towards agreeing conclusions.

We chose work-based immigration as the focus of these workshops because it is an area of ongoing contention, the policy is constantly under review and therefore open to influence, and, importantly, the Government have effective levers to determine who is allowed to come to the UK on a work visa. So that people could better understand the complexities and the trade-offs in policy making, we wanted to hear from people in different parts of the country. We chose North Tyneside, Leicester and Renfrewshire. We wanted to share with them the kind of conversations that go on within Whitehall.

We know these questions are hard to resolve. I have been a Minister in the Home Office, and I know that it is hard—I sympathise with the challenges faced by the current Minister, the hon. Member for Bassetlaw (Jo White). Earlier this month, the Home Secretary revealed that she gets almost weekly requests from other Ministers to provide visas for foreign workers in different sectors. This is at the heart of the issue: the extent to which we want to rely upon migrant labour and skills, and the weighing up of the economic and social factors that influence the decision.

The report produced by Demos on the results of the workshops was published on 7 September, and it is available in the Vote Office. I hope it will be of interest to hon. and right hon. Members and to other Select Committees whose remit includes areas affected by immigration.

Between them, the 89 participants at the three workshops produced a list of 13 principles that they thought should underpin policy on work-based immigration and ranked them. It was striking that the No. 1 priority at all three workshops, in three totally different parts of the country, was that the Government should focus on training, upskilling and employment opportunities for UK residents, especially young people, before relying on migrant labour. The second-highest ranked principle was the need to ensure that local infrastructure can support migrants and existing residents. The third and fourth principles were the need for better workforce planning and for migrant workers to be protected from abuse by employers.

The fifth principle was about promoting an honest and balanced public conversation about immigration. That was our intention when we started this work, and I am pleased that the members of the public who participated at our workshops agreed with that aim. It is now up to us, in this House, to help promote that honest conversation. I am pleased that the Prime Minister has now joined us in calling for an honest discussion on this subject, although freedom of movement was not a question on the table when we started this work.

We are also reliant on the media to move away from the soundbites, simplistic characterisations, misleading memes and social media disinformation that only serve to polarise and infantilise. While there was more support for restricting numbers of low-skilled migrant workers than higher skilled, there was also some support for restricting neither. Similarly, there were differing views on whether we should prioritise short or long-term work visas. The most common view was that we need both, but the discussions revealed interesting nuances. For example, participants who prioritised greater integration found themselves arguing for longer-term work visas, which was not necessarily their starting position. They saw how policy design can have wider impacts and considered the interaction between competing objectives in reaching conclusions. That is the value of this deliberative approach.

When we received the report on the results of the workshops, we considered how best to use the conclusions to inform our future work on immigration. At the launch event for the report in Portcullis House on 7 September, I announced our intention to hold an inquiry based on the principles identified through the workshops. Our inquiry will focus on the top principle agreed in the workshops: to focus on training, upskilling and employment opportunities for UK residents, especially young people, before relying on migrant labour. We announced the full terms of reference on 15 September. These outlined the detailed questions that need to be answered in order to deliver an outcome that respects that principle.

The Government have undertaken to link their immigration policy to skills. We will scrutinise how they propose to do that. We will also examine the role that migration does and should play in responding to labour shortages, and how that can be more firmly linked to skills. We will look at the Home Office’s approach to managing the skilled worker visa, and how that links to wider skills policy. We plan to scrutinise the Labour Market Evidence Group—the agencies that advise on work-based migration policy—and test how the different objectives of different Departments are managed and how judgments relating to shortages and skill levels are made. We also plan to hear the views and voice of the public throughout our evidence sessions—both through the evidence we gather and from what we learned from the workshops.

Artificial intelligence is affecting pretty much every aspect of life and will continue to do so. Consultations are no exception. Most of our inquires attract large volumes of written evidence. We value that evidence and draw heavily on it to inform our thinking, conclusions and recommendations. We depend on it to do our work, but there are signs now—I am sure that colleagues are seeing this in their constituency correspondence and in other Committees—that AI is increasingly being used to generate lengthy submissions that do not necessarily add anything new to the evidence base. There are resources implications for handling large volumes of written evidence, and questions around its value.

Work is going on among Select Committees to look at how we can secure high-quality contributions to our inquiries: the experiences from those at the sharp end of policies and, when warranted, the considered views of an informed cross-section of the public. There are of course resource implications here as well, but I hope that the Liaison Committee might consider how best we allocate resources to best support our scrutiny of difficult policy issues in the age of artificial intelligence.

Those of us who observed the workshops and spoke to the participants learned that, even on a subject as sensitive and divisive as immigration, people are capable of having a reasoned, respectful and constructive conversation. Not only that, but they obviously valued the opportunity to engage with each other—different communities that do not always mix—and with the political process, in a meaningful way. They valued being listened to, and at the end, their views on our political process were more positive.

I look forward to returning to the House with the conclusions of the inquiry, and the Government response to it, in due course. In the meantime, I am happy to respond to any questions.

speaker: Lord Markham
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, although we are grateful for the way in which the Minister has listened and modified the Bill on many of the things we say, I think it is probably the feeling of most noble Lords that the Bill is very much piecemeal in nature—or maybe, as the noble Viscount, Lord Colville, said earlier, it is a bit of a whack-a-mole plan for tackling cyber security, rather than setting out a comprehensive strategy for cyber security. Amendment 77, in my name and those of my noble friends Lord Camrose and Lord Holmes, seeks to address this by trying to have a strategic review of which entities should be brought into scope and which should not.

Amendment 163, tabled by the noble Lord, Lord Birt, and signed by the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, and me, seeks to build on this. As ever, the noble Lord, Lord Birt, has made some very thoughtful and insightful points, and I know that much work has gone into this. Through Amendment 163 we are trying to require a regime-wide effectiveness review, looking at which sectors should and should not be included, and at how we can use our world-class AI safety institute to play a crucial role in cyber security. In all this, Amendment 163 is critical in building a comprehensive cyber security strategy and action plan—or, dare I say it, a national cyber action plan. Given that the Minister said earlier that DCMS is in the process of preparing such a plan, I hope that this is something the Government are prepared to support. If it is not, and if it is something that the noble Lord, Lord Birt, wishes to divide on, we will support him in testing the opinion of the House.

speaker: Lord Birt
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
Amendment 163 is in my name and those of the noble Lords, Lord Markham and Lord Clement-Jones, and the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron. I think the earlier stages of this Bill have seen this House on all sides at its very best, with Members bringing real-life experience and serious expertise to bear in a considered and non-partisan way on the grievous challenge that the cyber threat presents to our country. That scrutiny has demonstrated, I am afraid, just how limited this Bill is in addressing that grievous challenge. It has almost been forgotten in our debate today that it focuses on only a small fraction of the economy and the public sector, not on the lessons of JLR, M&S, TfL or the Department for Education. It fails to appreciate the enormous complexity of technology platforms and the origin of their vulnerabilities.

Just a few days ago, a leading CTO, in the midst of negotiating a contract to be supplied with data services by a leading provider, read out to me one of the legal conditions of that supply: “We shall not be responsible for any damage caused to the customer’s computer or to customer data, or for any bugs, viruses, Trojan horses or other destructive code”.

Extraordinarily, and this has been touched on more than once today, the draft of the Bill that reached us did not even mention AI. Can that be believed? It is a Bill that creates a multiplicity of cyber regulators, an estimated 18 in all. In Northern Ireland it is the Department of Finance that will be the designated regulator, not just for energy but for health, road and rail and drinking water. How could 18 regulators possibly amass the necessary skills to regulate in this deeply complex and ever-evolving environment? Week by week, as we have considered the Bill, the ever-darkening cyber storm-clouds gather. Last week, as we all will have noticed, the PHP incident affected 70% of the world wide web, with 10 million servers identified as at risk.

Our amendment seeks to see the Bill as a work in progress. It would require the Government, over the coming 12 months, to address the whole of the challenge identified throughout our proceedings and to conduct and publish a review, inter alia, of the appropriate regulatory framework for cyber, which we manifestly do not have; a review of which organisations have a material impact on the economy and society in both the public and private sectors and should be brought into scope; a review of what obligations should be placed on those organisations to promote cyber resilience; a review of what obligations to provide safe services should be placed on technology suppliers, and noble Lords should remember the quote I have just read out; a review of what scale and nature of cyber professionalism the UK needs; a review of what incidents should be reported and to whom; and, critically, a review of the powers of the AI Security Institute or another regulator in relation to frontier AI systems—a matter that has come up over and over again today—to make AI a safe technology for us all to deploy.

Our hope is that this Minister will welcome the opportunity that such a review would present to address all the many questions that have arisen but not been properly answered today, and that it would speedily promote further legislation that would enable us to grip this challenge in a way that the Bill in its present form simply does not.

speaker: Lord Tarassenko
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I too support Amendment 163 in the name of my noble friend Lord Birt. It has not attracted much notice, but the series of incidents in the last few months in which frontier AI models broke into the systems of several organisations is beginning to generate some sort of response among the culprits. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are reported to be planning to launch their own standards authority for frontier AI, which would establish qualifications for independent auditors of the models and labs.

We have the best independent auditor in the world in our AI Security Institute. We should not leave it to the frontier AI developers to mark their own homework or decide who audits them, so I welcome the additional £120 million investment in AISI announced on Saturday. The director of AISI told us today that it is £120 million over four years, which is very much needed to keep AISI at the forefront of frontier AI evaluation.

We should also acknowledge that the Government have moved since Committee. Their Amendment 70 gives the Secretary of State powers where a compromise may be attributable to loss of oversight or control of an AI agent. However, as we have already noted, Amendment 70 operates after the event. It also does not mention the AI Security Institute, yet AISI is the only body in the UK with the technical capability to determine before a model is deployed whether it can attack the systems that the Bill protects. Today it has that access because developers choose to give it. The suspension of that access for three weeks at the request of the US Government shows that it can be withdrawn overnight.

With frontier AI capability advancing every few months, should our critical national infrastructure rely on good will alone? That is the question that proposed new subsection (5)(d) in Amendment 163 asks. It would require the review to consider whether AISI should have powers over frontier AI systems that pose a material risk to our essential services, to audit them before deployment, to set standards, to inspect them and to require or recommend their suspension.

Amendment 163 proposes a review, not new regulation, and I therefore hope the Government will not find it too difficult to accept. However, a review is only as good as its conclusions. I would therefore be grateful if the Minister could give the House two assurances: first, that the Government will reach a clear conclusion, and not simply keep the matter under review, on whether AISI should have a statutory role before deployment; and, secondly, that the power in Clause 29(1), which the Government’s Amendment 70 will now use for AI, could give it that role without further primary legislation. Amendment 163 is critical. If my noble friend Lord Birt chooses to test the opinion of the House, I shall support him.

speaker: Lord Clement-Jones
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, we have had three persuasive and excellent speeches in support of Amendment 163. I thank the noble Lord, Lord Birt, for tabling this extremely comprehensive cross-party amendment. I wonder whether the Deputy Speaker has the details of some of the typos in the amendment so that we do not vote on something that will have to be changed at Third Reading.

The amendment covers the scope of the Bill, which, as has been explained, is not adequate. The food and essential goods supply chain could be under review, as could local government and democratic infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, software as a service and cloud intermediaries. It would create a structured evidence-based review, with a mandatory interim report at six months and a comply or explain mechanism requiring the Government to state publicly why any excluded sector was not being brought into scope. Crucially, as the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, says, it would require the review to examine the institutional architecture, including whether the AI Security Institute should have formal audit powers over frontier AI systems deployed in essential activities.

We risk leaving our primary technical watchdog equipped only with voluntary oversight, while the capabilities it is charged with scrutinising outpace the law. We face an era of persistent cyber warfare: we cannot leave our food supply, our local democracy and our advance industries unprotected. If the Minister cannot accept having this review in the Bill, we on these Benches will strongly support the amendment of the noble Lord, Lord Birt.

speaker: Baroness Berger
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: To ask His Majesty’s Government whether they intend to publish a single, government-approved list of artificial intelligence tools that meet minimum safeguarding and data protection standards for use in schools.

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: My Lords, the Government are focused on ensuring that technology used in education is safe and trustworthy, through generative AI product safety standards, updated guidance and a planned consultation on introducing safety certification for higher-risk products. Such certification would lead to a published list of child-facing generative AI tools which have been certified as meeting safety criteria, including data protection and safeguarding, for use in education settings.

speaker: Baroness Berger
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: My Lords, edtech is largely untested and we do not yet know the full impact of it on our children in schools. A school choosing an AI tool can struggle to judge whether it meets those safeguarding and data protection standards. A recent ICO audit of 28 edtech providers found that around 70% of their agreements with schools lacked the legally required detail. The edtech businesses could not provide evidence that the schools using their platforms had authorised reuse of student data for their own purposes. Can my noble friend the Minister, in light of her reply, say what additional practical support the Government can provide today to schools to ensure that children’s safety is not harmed by these tools?

speaker: Baroness Barran
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: My Lords, the Minister mentioned that the Government plan to consult on the certification of edtech and generative AI products. Can she give us a timetable for that consultation? Similarly, the Government announced that there would be sovereign education benchmarks, but no timetable that I am aware of has been announced. Can she confirm that AI products used in education will be independently assessed against those benchmarks?

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: We intend to launch the consultation and certification framework very soon—this autumn. I will come back to the noble Baroness about the AI sovereign benchmarks. I understand that they are already operationalised, but I will respond specifically respond to that point.

speaker: Lord Clement-Jones
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: My Lords, I declare an interest as an adviser to DLA Piper on AI regulation and policy. A list of safe tools can tell us what to avoid. What is the Government’s vision for what AI in schools can achieve for children? Will they adopt a human flourishing test for AI in schools? That would mean asking not just whether a tool avoids harm but whether it independently improves children’s learning, curiosity, critical thinking and agency.

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: I wish the noble Lord a very happy birthday. Of course, he is right. That is why we need different elements of protection and, as he rightly said, promotion. The certification would enable schools more quickly and easily to see the edtech products that met the standards. In January, we strengthened our product safety standards both to reflect emerging risks and developments in AI technologies and to ensure that AI supports genuine learning and does not undermine children’s ability to think, learn and develop independently. The certification scheme enables the development by legitimate edtech companies of the type of technology which will help to support children’s learning.

speaker: Bishop of Hereford
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: My Lords, a number of noble Lords have already asked questions about the regulation of AI in schools. Would it be Ofsted that inspected schools and how they govern their use of artificial intelligence, including the safeguards they have in place to protect pupils and manage the use of personal data? If so, what steps are the Government taking to ensure that Ofsted inspectors have the expertise and guidance necessary to make such assessments effectively?

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: Of course, Ofsted will have an important role to play in ensuring the safeguarding responsibility of schools with respect to AI as well as its appropriate use in the classroom. There is also a role for the Information Commissioner’s Office in the protection of data. As I have already identified, it would not be appropriate for Ofsted, for example, to be the organisation that holds the certification process. That is another area where there will be support for ensuring that what happens is right, safe and effective, and a way of ensuring that schools are following the certification and the guidance that already exist.

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: Yes, of course it is the case, but we need to ensure that we harness the positive opportunities that come from AI and educational technology and avoid the risks—which certainly need to be managed very carefully—in our schools. That is the reason for the breadth of initiatives being taken by the Government. It is the reason for the update of the generative AI product safety standards, which have specific protections relating to cognitive development, emotional and social development, mental health and manipulative design, reflecting areas where children may be particularly vulnerable. I do not believe that there is anybody in this House who does not believe that there are opportunities that AI can bring into our schools for teachers and learners. The Government are working hard to get that balance right.

speaker: Baroness Bull
heading: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Schools - Question
text: My Lords, alongside their positive role within the education system, many parents and children will choose online and AI tools to support their learning outside of the classroom. My noble friend Lord Tarassenko has pointed out that it is a bit of a minefield. It is difficult for parents to assess which of those tools are likely to be the most efficacious. Are there any plans for the Department for Education to help parents by perhaps rating those tools on their effectiveness in supporting children who have particular educational needs?

speaker: Lord Ravensdale
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I declare my interest as the chief engineer working for AtkinsRéalis and start with my Amendment 3. Very briefly, the central problem remains that if I am a small or mid-sized enterprise—an SME—I cannot tell with any confidence whether I am in the scope of the Bill as a critical supplier. That uncertainty creates a cost, because firms delay investments and can overprepare or even walk away from public service contracts altogether because they do not want to fall within the scope of this legislation. I go back to the impact assessment, which could not say how many SMEs will be designated within the powers of the Bill. I simply ask the Minister whether she can provide any further clarity on SMEs and critical suppliers, and who exactly is in within the scope of the Bill, because that would be tremendously helpful for all small and medium-sized businesses out there that are concerned about whether they will fall within the scope of the Bill.

My other Amendments 58 to 60 all relate to quantum computing and quantum cryptography. Noble Lords have quite rightly focused on AI within the scope of the Bill—that is the zeitgeist and the issue of the moment. However, AI does not fundamentally change the rules of the game in terms of protection of our information, but quantum computing fundamentally does. We are talking about a technology that can potentially break the public key crypto that we rely on across financial services, energy and telecommunications.

This technology is advancing tremendously quickly. In Committee, I brought up the example of the Willow chip that Google has produced. Industry is now analysing, or has come up with, a fully compiled end-to-end resource estimate for a 20,000-qubit system. That is the class of system that can really break the 256-bit encryption that we use across many of our services.

We look across this more broadly in terms of what organisations and Governments are doing. Google is now saying that by 2029 it is going to complete transition to post-quantum crypto. In fact, earlier this year, the USA brought forward an executive order that brings forward its federal migration timeline by four to five years. Previously, the target was 2035 and now it is 2030.

This indicates the case for action from all the organisations cited on how fast this technology is advancing. The Minister will point to the NCSC and the timescales we have published in the UK, but there is a good opportunity within this Bill, or within the guidance to the Bill, to ensure, first, that regulators are aligned in the approach they are taking on post-quantum crypto, and, secondly, that the priority of post-quantum crypto migration is set out in the Bill. I am after some confidence from the Minister on how the Government will work towards those objectives within the framework of the Bill. Quantum is the elephant in the room when we are talking about specific technologies in the conversations we have had about AI, so I would welcome some comments from the Minister on how the Bill’s supporting documents will work towards the objective of protecting our most sensitive information against these threats.

speaker: Baroness Morgan of Cotes
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I will speak to Amendments 62 and 69, which I have tabled in this group, and Amendment 78, to which I have added my name. The noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, is right to say that this is quite a disparate group. That just shows how complicated the issues in the Bill are and how fast moving this area is, as the Minister will know extremely well. I thank her for her engagement on these amendments and the conversations we have had.

Amendment 62 is about being guided not just by the size of a provider but by the risk that it presents. It reflects an amendment that was discussed in Committee. I moved it to Clause 29 at the suggestion of the Minister, because she pointed me to that clause. I had not spotted it, but Amendment 3 from the noble Lord, Lord Ravensdale, is perhaps another way of looking at this. I totally understand the point that he is making: SMEs need to know whether they are caught by this Bill and similar provisions in future. It may not be quite as easy as telling them whether they are in or out, but the issue—we are talking now about cyber security resilience—really has to be about the risk that these services pose to our essential or national infrastructure. As we saw just last week with the PHP attack, the reality is that it might be the smallest element of software that causes some of the greatest harm. I will return to these issues that Amendments 62 and 69 capture because I do not think that any Governments have yet worked out how to legislate on the basis of the risk posed by these services. It is exactly the same as the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, said in the debate on the Online Safety Act about categorisation of platforms; it is an issue that is not going to go away and that we will return to later this week.
