The smallest platform or service can present the greatest risk. We have to work out a way to legislate or pass regulations that reflect this.

The regulations under Clauses 29 and 30 could bring in smaller providers, but the power is discretionary, there is no risk test and it comes with no commitment to use it. I am interested to hear the Minister’s response to that. The Government’s revised Part 4 extends national security directions to persons beyond regulated persons, regardless of size. Risk-based reach does therefore exist in the Bill, but only for national security and not for wider resilience risks.

Amendment 69 is about corporate governance, which might not seem the most exciting of subjects, but the Bill is about the regulation of essential activity. In Clause 24, “essential activity” is defined as activity

“essential to … the economy of the United Kingdom or … the day-to-day functioning of society”.

I do not think we can get much more essential than that. I think we will know about it if those activities and services are somehow massively undermined because of a lack of cyber resilience. This is an issue that I will return to. I do not necessarily intend to test the will of the House today on this, but I think it is now impossible for the culture of organisations to change or for senior-level accountability to exist—I have discussed this with both the noble Baroness and the AI Minister—without there being board-level accountability for the services being provided by the companies those boards are responsible for, and a clear understanding of the risks that those services might provide.

The noble Baroness suggested when we spoke that perhaps governance could be addressed in codes of practice. I am not sure that goes far enough, but it could be a start. Is a general duty of board oversight sufficient? I am very happy to discuss this further with both the noble Baroness and her ministerial colleagues. The Government have indicated that they think Clause 29 already allows regulators to address governance in codes of practice. They will not accept an individual fiduciary duty, but a general duty of board oversight may be acceptable. I would be interested to hear what the Government’s position is, but this is going to be relevant for all related tech or cyber resilience legislation.

On Amendment 78, to which I have added my name, I support the principle that large businesses should report on cyber security and resilience plans. I am not sure that it goes far enough, but I think it starts the point where boards and senior managers actually take responsibility for what their services are doing. It would be a welcome step forward, and that is why I was pleased to add my name. I look forward to hearing the Minister’s response on these issues, and I would very much welcome further conversations with her because these issues are not going to go away.

speaker: Baroness Harding of Winscombe
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, there are a lot of amendments in this group that attempt to fill the AI-shaped hole in the Bill. I probably speak for everyone who engaged in Committee when I say that we were all intensely frustrated by the absence of AI in the Bill. It is in danger of proving correct the people who think that you cannot regulate AI, because we are not even trying.

This is quite a complex group. I extend my support to Amendment 65 in the name of the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, on “last-resort” powers; Amendment 66 in the name of the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, on AISI audit powers; and Amendment 67 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, on AI red lines. I will not speak to them, because I know that everyone wants to move at pace.

I will focus my remarks only on Amendment 41. My amendment is not techy or complex; it is very simple. It would require frontier labs to report to essential services and their relevant regulator if one of their AI agents or models gained unauthorised access to UK essential services and/or their data. The reporting requirements would be similar to those imposed on the essential services—the 24/72-hour piece that we have just been discussing. By way of example, if a frontier lab’s AI agent accessed NHS data without permission, once the frontier lab became aware of this, it would be required to report the incident within 24 hours, update within 72 hours and issue a final report within 14 days.

This is currently not happening, as witnessed in Australia quite recently. OpenAI accessed Australian Medicare data in June. It did not inform the Australian Government until September via an unmanned email address, such that the Australian Prime Minister was at the UN General Assembly rallying support for the innovative growth potential of AI while OpenAI knew that it had accessed his country’s health data and he did not.

Other countries are already requiring this basic thing. In New York, the RAISE Act requires AI frontier labs to report within 72 hours if one of their agents has gone rogue. In California, it is within 52 hours. The EU AI Act requires it without undue delay. The AI labs themselves agree that clear reporting requirements would be helpful. In front of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee in the other place only last week, representatives of OpenAI and Anthropic, including my noble friend Lord Booth-Smith, representing Anthropic, supported the idea of required reporting, at least in principle—that is an important “at least”, I suspect.

I know there is concern that this could be seen as international overreach and that all AI regulation needs to be global. That is one of the favourite tropes of tech companies: “Do not do anything locally; it has to be done globally”. Those of us who have campaigned for regulation of social media have been fighting that battle for more than a decade. But this really is an instance that does not need to be global. This is about UK services and data being illegally accessed. It does not matter that it might be an American company doing the accessing—it is accessing our data illegally. This surely should be the purview of this House. I believe the Minister agrees with me. I think the Government’s AI Minister in the other place also agrees with me. In fact, he has said in public that it is important to have these reporting requirements. However, I cannot see it in this Bill.

I support government Amendment 70 in this group, but that just puts even stronger requirements on the essential services that might have had their data hacked, not on the companies whose AI agents would have done the hacking. I very much hope that the Minister can explain to me and all of us in this House how the Government intend to require AI labs to report incidents and when this is likely to come into effect, if not through this amendment. It is simple common sense that if these agents access our data, they should be under a legal obligation to tell us. We should not be leaving that to chance; we should be making it the law. I beg to move.

speaker: Baroness Berger
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I have added my name to Amendment 41 because it identifies and addresses a significant gap in our approach to cyber security: the growing capacity of frontier AI models to interfere with systems on which our essential services depend. This amendment would ensure that there is a corresponding duty on developers to report such incidents and to do so in a timely fashion. This has been put forward as a cross-party amendment because technology is advancing so rapidly and the security of our critical infrastructure is a shared responsibility. It demonstrates that, by working together, we can address what is a very serious emerging risk.

If it was not already clear, the urgency of this issue has been brought into sharp focus by recent events, even since we last met in Grand Committee to scrutinise this Bill. The past month, as noble Lords may be aware, has been named “Black October” after advanced AI models accelerated the discovery of critical, long-standing security flaws, most notably in the PHP programming language, triggering global emergency patches and widespread server shutdowns. On 22 October, the Government confirmed that 32 government services had been taken offline as a precaution following the discovery of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, which is a programming language underpinning an estimated 70% of the world’s websites. These vulnerabilities were identified with the assistance of frontier AI, and cyber security companies have subsequently reported millions of attempts to exploit them. To be clear, the Government have said that these precautionary shutdowns did not mean that those websites had been hacked, but this incident demonstrates how AI can help uncover long-standing vulnerabilities at unprecedented speeds and how quickly that discovery can trigger a global security crisis. Cyber security experts are warning us of a new era of AI-enabled hacking.

This technology has a dual nature. AI can strengthen our defences, but it can also lower the barriers to finding and exploiting weaknesses in systems on which we all depend. This is not a theoretical concern. In July, the UK AI Security Institute identified an incident during frontier AI testing in which AI agents took sustained, unauthorised actions against real people and organisations. In the most serious case, an agent attempted a software supply chain attack, submitting malicious code and creating fake accounts to pressure a software maintainer into accepting it. Although no real-world harm resulted, the incident demonstrates exactly why we need effective safeguards and clear reporting obligations when AI systems behave in unexpected and potentially harmful ways.

We already know the consequences when our digital systems fail. The cyber attack on Synnovis disrupted blood testing and forced the cancellation of hospital appointments and operations. The ransomware attack on the British Library caused extensive disruption to its services, with recovery requiring a prolonged effort. These attacks pre-dated the latest developments in frontier AI, but we must take seriously the possibility that AI will make future attacks faster, more sophisticated and more damaging.

The question before us is therefore straightforward. If a frontier AI model gains unauthorised access to or interferes with a regulated organisation’s systems, who ensures that that incident is reported promptly? We know from the example that has been set out that it took 84 days for OpenAI to inform the Australian Government about its model’s breach, and just this weekend Anthropic slipped out an announcement to let us know that Claude has accessed publicly available voter data without any human authorisation. These events are taking place on a daily basis. The organisation affected may not know that AI was involved. The developer, meanwhile, may hold crucial information about the model’s behaviour, the nature of the threat and the steps needed to mitigate it. Without a clear reporting obligation, that information is not reaching the people who need it when they need it.

This amendment addresses that gap. It would require an initial notification within 24 hours, a fuller account within 72 hours and a final report within 14 days, and ensure that the affected organisation, its regulator, the relevant cyber security incident response team and the AI Security Institute receive information essential to containing an incident and preventing its recurrence. These are practical and proportionate requirements. They would not prohibit innovation but establish a basic principle of accountability. Those developing powerful technologies must at the very least take responsibility for reporting serious incidents involving their models when an incident has occurred. Without meaningful penalties for non-compliance, these obligations risk being little more than words on paper.

During last Thursday’s Cross-Bench debate on AI and children, a point was repeatedly made that is worth repeating here. AI is currently less regulated than milk. The risks to children and the risks to our critical infrastructure and government systems are of course different, but the underlying principle is the same. Our regulatory frameworks must keep pace with increasingly powerful technologies. We are already at the point where harm has become widespread. We need to establish reasonable safeguards, clear responsibilities and effective oversight.

speaker: Lord Tarassenko
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I declare my interest as senior adviser to the Alan Turing Institute. I wish to speak in support of Amendment 41, in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, to which I have added my name, and then briefly about my own Amendment 66 in this group. We heard during Committee not only about the out-of-control behaviour from agents running AI models from OpenAI, Google and Meta but about the unacceptable delays before the incidents were reported. Contrast that with our own AI Security Institute. When it found unsanctioned agent behaviour during its testing this summer—and this was confirmed to us by Henry de Zoete at a meeting in Portcullis House today—it immediately declared a security incident and contained it within an hour of the alert being raised, with all relevant machines isolated within that time. That is the standard we should be expecting.

With Amendment 41, the developer must notify the affected organisation and its regulator within 24 hours. The duty applies where the developer is aware, or ought reasonably to be aware, so no company can avoid it by not looking. The report must say whether the model acted autonomously or was used by someone else.

On 12 October, the Government said that they would look at strengthening this Bill so that serious AI incidents are reported. Their Amendment 70 gives the Secretary of State powers to investigate where control of an AI agent is lost. However, no one can investigate an incident they have not been told about. Amendment 41 is what makes Amendment 70 work. I would therefore be interested to find out whether the noble Baroness will be minded to accept Amendment 41.

I turn briefly to Amendment 66 in my name, to which the noble Lords, Lord Clement-Jones and Lord Holmes of Richmond, and the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, have added their names. This amendment would require the AI Security Institute to audit frontier AI products before they were used in the network and information systems that run our hospitals, our energy networks and our water supply. Developers would submit their evaluation results using methods and thresholds set by AISI, with evidence of a tested means of suspending the system in the UK. Where the institute found a serious risk that was not mitigated, the Secretary of State would have to decide within 14 days whether to act and give reasons.

As I have already said, I welcome the Government’s Amendment 70, which accepts that loss of control of an AI agent is a risk to essential services that should be addressed in this Bill. However, it operates after the event and does not mention the AI Security Institute. I would be grateful, therefore, if the Minister could tell the House what role the Government see for the institute—AISI—in assessing frontier models before they reach our critical systems and whether the power in Clause 29(1) could give it that role.

speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I too rise to support Amendment 41 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, and to support Amendments 65, 66 and 67, to which I have also put my name. As the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, said, to have a Bill with “cyber security” in the title and not mention AI seems to have been a huge error. The Government seem to have recognised the great lacuna in some of their amendments in this group, which is most welcome. Also, we must welcome the Chancellor of the Exchequer’s low-key announcement over the weekend that the Government would invest £120 million in the Artificial Intelligence Security Institute. Surely this Bill should be an opportunity to ensure that AISI investment is used as effectively as possible and that, just as this country recognises the importance of AI in keeping our technical leading role, this new, incredibly powerful technology has new frontier models that need to be investigated prior to release.

Amendment 41 is an important step forward in ensuring that AI developers notify the relevant authorities when things go wrong, so if the noble Baroness decides to take this amendment to the vote, I will support her. I am surprised that not all parties think that the measures in this amendment need to be supported. AI frontier models have proved to be a threat, and we need to face up to it. The AI providers’ own safety report tells us of the threats posed by new models. Google wrote that a person outside the company had attempted to use its AI tool, Gemini, to obtain

“a complete, step-by-step technical guide for synthesizing weaponized biological agents”.

An Anthropic report found that there were five case studies of actors using its models in a way that could support biological weapons development. There were also reports of the terrorist group, Boko Haram, using frontier AI, including ChatGPT, to plan attacks and design explosive devices. Surely these concerns should encourage the Government at least to look at my noble friend Lord Tarassenko’s Amendment 66, which would have safety against terrorists and biological attacks, among other things, built into new AI frontier models and put AISI in a stronger position to be a third-party evaluator of frontier models.

I had such hopes when the 2023 Bletchley Park summit announced that AISI and the model providers would work together and voluntarily submit their new models to the directorate, but this is decreasingly happening. Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5.1 was withdrawn from AISI last month. There are other cases such as Claude Opus 5.5, which was reportedly withdrawn from AISI’s pre-release evaluation in September, as was the OpenAI and GPT-6 Luna model.

I hope that your Lordships will listen to the chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee in the other place, who this month during an evidence-gathering session with AI leaders announced that AISI lacked compulsory access to models and a power to stop new models coming to the market. I call on the Minister to address these concerns.

This brings me to Amendment 67, in the name of my noble friend Lady Kidron. As many other noble Lords have said during the passage of this Bill through the House, this is a defensive Bill. Surely the best way to stop new frontier models from going rogue is to be proactive in putting guardrails around their design. Otherwise, we are just going to play a game of whack-a-mole. The principles in the Online Safety Act were to try to instil safety by design into the algorithms of online content providers. Surely the same needs to happen to AI frontier models. Amendment 67 sets out to provide guidelines for how the design of AI models might be kept in check.

I ask His Majesty’s Government to ensure that safety is built into new AI model designs and that the highly respected AISI is given sufficient power to ensure that they are safe. The Minister must know that the world would be grateful if new models were safe by design and properly evaluated before release.

speaker: Lord Holmes of Richmond
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, there is a huge hole that has already been identified through all stages of this Bill, and that is the absence of AI. As we have gone through each stage of this Bill’s process, that hole has become wider and deeper. As we have gone through this process, external events have only highlighted that.

Amendments 41, 66 and 67 in this group, which I support, do something that is practical and effective about this. Specifically on AISI, does the Minister think that citizens up and down the United Kingdom are in a better situation now that AISI is the “security institute” rather than the “safety institute”—more than just a question of a change of word, but a change of emphasis and change of impact in terms of every citizen in this country?

As has been rightly mentioned, milk is more regulated than AI. With this in mind, does the Minister agree that, when it comes to cross-sector, cross-economy AI legislation, the Government need to discover the bottle to bring forward a Bill?

speaker: Lord Clement-Jones
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, as the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, and other noble Lords have said, this group confronts what was termed in Grand Committee the “AI-shaped hole” in our national cyber security architecture. At Second Reading and in Committee, the Government maintained that AI sat outside scope of this Bill, yet recent events have shattered any illusion that AI is merely an emerging hypothetical threat. Frontier general-purpose models and agentic workflows are supercharging offensive cyber capabilities, discovering zero-days and exploiting vulnerabilities at machine speed. Indeed, we have seen this unfold directly in front of us, and the noble Baronesses, Lady Harding and Lady Berger, and the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, have all described extremely cogently what has been happening over the last few months.

I welcome the Government’s Amendments 70 and 74, which introduce provisions addressing loss of control of an artificial intelligence agent. It is an important concession: a first acknowledgement by the Government that it is not enough to be technology-agnostic and that agentic AI risks must be addressed. However, the Government’s approach remains entirely reactive and diagnostic: gathering information only after the horse has bolted.

The cross-party and Cross-Bench amendments in this group, which I have been pleased to sign, establish a comprehensive, forward-looking governance framework. First, Amendment 41 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, which was so brilliantly introduced by her and which I have signed, places a direct reporting duty on developers of frontier AI models to report to regulated persons, the NCSC and the AI Security Institute within 24 hours whenever an AI model gains unauthorised access to or interferes with critical systems. We must close the loophole where victim organisations bear all the reporting burdens while frontier developers remain unaccountable. On these Benches, we will support the noble Baroness if she presses her amendment to a vote.

Secondly, Amendment 66, in the name of the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, which I have signed, and Amendment 79 in my name, empower the AI Security Institute. Some of us had an impressive presentation today about the work of AISI. However, it is time now, in principle, for the institute to be placed on a statutory footing, with powers to conduct pre-deployment audits of frontier models before they are deployed in critical infrastructure, set safety standards and recommend that the Secretary of State restrict or suspend unsafe deployments. Can the Minister give the Government’s response to a very clear set of recommendations in this respect from the Joint Committee on Human Rights? I recognise that the Government’s response is due in a few weeks’ time, but it would be useful if the noble Baroness could give us an indication of their approach.

Thirdly, Amendment 67, in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, and myself, establishes clear statutory red lines against autonomous AI systems executing cyber attacks, evading human shutdown or self-replicating uncontrollably.

Finally, Amendment 65, standing in my name and also tabled in Committee, provides the ultimate indispensable emergency backstop: statutory “last resort” powers for the Secretary of State to direct the shutdown of data centres or large-scale AI deployments during a catastrophic AI emergency. As former Technology Secretary Liz Kendall rightly noted, true digital sovereignty requires the means to contain an emergency on our own soil. Crucially, Amendment 65, the so-called “kill-switch” amendment, wraps this emergency power in rigorous constitutional safeguards: a 24-hour continuous necessity review reporting to Parliament within seven days, pre-tested emergency communication protocols, and an immediate right of appeal to the High Court, with power to cancel orders and award compensation.

We must empower the AI Security Institute, hold frontier developers accountable and equip the state with court-supervised emergency backstops.

speaker: Viscount Camrose
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I am grateful for the Government’s amendments and for the clarity that they have given us following, I think, some confusion in Committee.

None of us can be blind to the need to ensure that AI is made safe by appropriate safeguards: regulations. We support any activity that moves us towards the global implementation of AI safety rules, whether via national routes or not, but in the context of always driving economic growth and maintaining our attractiveness as an investment destination.

We have to recognise the challenges of designing rules that govern technologies rather than products and do so in a rapidly changing environment. However, for the effective development of AI regulation, a necessary if not sufficient condition will be continuing to have direct conversations between the Government and industry. Those conversations are evidently taking place, as I hope the Minister will confirm when she gets up to speak. Given these government amendments and the words of the AI Minister over the past few weeks, we on these Benches feel that it may not be helpful on this occasion for Parliament to impose policies as they are in the process of being formulated—although I think I am not alone in wishing they could be formulated a little faster.

I turn briefly to the Government’s Amendment 70, granting the Secretary of State the power to intervene in a loss of control incident. TechUK and others have raised a number of concerns about this, including a lack of definition of the terms used, the lack of transparency to third parties, and the frankly odd decision to name agentic AI as a specific technology in the Bill. I urge the Minister to take these concerns seriously and to see what can be done to address them while retaining the amendment’s intended results.

Finally, there is an important conversation to be had surrounding the role of the AI Security Institute, as the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, and others compellingly pointed out. I am grateful to AISI for its briefing to noble Lords earlier today. The evolving direction of AISI is a difficult question. We would support this being reviewed, which is part of the reason why we support Amendment 163 in today’s final group. I look forward to it being debated then.

speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
I thank noble Lords for their engagement on the important issue of addressing AI cyber risks and I share the concerns raised by this House and the public. The Government take the safety of the British people incredibly seriously.

AI risks are trans-national threats. The best response to a global issue is a global response. At the UN General Assembly in September, the Prime Minister set out that the UK will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure that AI development is safe and will make AI a central focus of our G20 presidency next year. It is important to situate this Bill and its important yet targeted role within the Government’s broader approach. We will legislate where necessary, alongside all the other tools at our disposal.

I will now set out how the NIS regime currently covers AI risk and applies to some AI digital services. The Bill takes an all-technologies, all-threats, all-hazards approach to protecting regulated services. This means that essential services need to manage cyber and physical risks associated with AI systems underpinning their services and protect themselves from threats. Many digital and managed services within scope of the regime are enabled by, deploy or help to deliver AI capabilities. This includes cloud computing services, which provide software, platforms and infrastructure services that many organisations across the economy rely on.

Commercial AI services are often delivered under similar digital service models and so are likely to be in scope. This includes AI assistance delivered via software-as-a-service models, AI platforms, and infrastructure used for AI workloads. Where an AI digital service falls in scope, the provider will have to take steps to manage the security and resilience of their services and the systems that underpin them, just like any other regulated entity.

I have met with the CEO of the Information Commission. We agree on the importance of guidance to provide industry with clarity on these definitions. The regime is not designed to provide a comprehensive framework for AI governance, including frontier AI capabilities which have not been released to customers, or wider safety or societal impacts. These are important issues that need addressing at the global level, as well as through the AI Taskforce and regulation at point of use in the UK.

Where AI-centred digital services are in scope of the NIS regime—for example, registered as cloud computing—our national security powers of direction could be used to direct those regulated organisations, subject to meeting strict legal tests. The direction power allows government to direct regulated organisations to take specific action where a security or operational compromise, or threat to their NIS, creates a national security risk. Directions must be necessary and proportionate. Where the legal tests are met, the direction powers enable the Government to require certain actions in an AI loss of control scenario; this could include actions such as isolating systems, restricting data flows or suspending automated actions being taken by an affected AI system.

AI models are often distributed across different data centres and jurisdictions. A broad power to shut down AI systems could have implications for investment, growth and our digital sovereignty. It must be very carefully thought through. If there is a loss of control scenario that compromises a regulated entity and poses a national security risk, directing the entity to take certain actions is more proportionate and, likely, more effective in containing the risk. This addresses the underlying risk raised in Amendment 65 tabled by the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones.

I turn to Amendment 41 tabled by the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, and spoken to by my noble friend Lady Berger, the noble Viscount, Lord Colville, and the noble Lord, Lord Holmes of Richmond. Where AI digital services are regulated under the NIS regime, the providers of those services will have to report incidents that have affected the security and operation of their systems. This includes incidents where there is a loss of control of an AI system used to provide a regulated service and where that loss of control disrupts the provision of that service, compromises user systems or has other significant impacts on the functioning of the UK’s society and economy. We will bring forward a consultation setting out further detail on how the incident reporting regime will work, including how the regulated organisations should assess whether an incident is significant. This will consider how the framework applies to emerging technologies such as AI.

However, I would like to reassure noble Lords that the Bill’s reporting requirements already provide the underlying framework for identifying and reporting significant incidents involving AI systems used in regulated services, as well as other cyber incidents affecting those services. Indeed, these requirements place the onus for reporting on the regulated entities affected by an incident. This is in keeping with the overall principle of the NIS regulations, which are about how the UK’s most essential services can manage risks to their systems. It is also one of the reasons why I cannot support Amendment 41 from the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, which would place the onus for reporting on developers of frontier models rather than regulated entities.

Regulating the developers of frontier AI is a different question, and I do not believe that this Bill is the right legislative framework in which to answer it. The Government will, of course, continue to take action where necessary to keep the UK safe, but these risks and technologies are global. Placing duties on developers operating in the UK will not by itself keep us safe from developers and models elsewhere in the world.

Turning to how we plan to strengthen the Bill and the NIS regime to better understand and protect against AI cyber risks to our essential services, the Government have tabled an amendment to the delegated powers in the Bill. Clauses 30 to 35 list examples of what provisions may be made under Clause 29 and set out certain requirements and restrictions. Amendment 70 expands this to clarify that future regulations may enable the Government to use in-house expertise, such as AISI, and gather information on why agentic incidents in our essential services happen. Our intention is for the information to then be shared with relevant stakeholders to help prevent similar incidents. Detail on how this function could work will be consulted on.

I will also bring forward three further measures in secondary legislation to manage the risks posed by agentic AI. These will be consulted on. To the question raised by the noble Viscount, Lord Camrose, I have seen the questions raised by techUK and undertake to continue to consult with industry on these matters. The measures are: first, to include technical and organisational requirements within the proposed security and resilience requirements to reduce the risk of agentic incidents affecting regulated services; secondly, to preserve information that regulated entities hold on incidents that stem from agents malfunctioning, so that others can use that information to understand why incidents happen; and, thirdly, to require regulated entities to tell other organisations—for example, suppliers—if agents used by the regulated entity are negatively impacting those organisations’ operations when an incident is occurring.

Finally, the changes I mentioned today on developing a voluntary framework for regulated entities on near-miss reporting will also be a meaningful step to developing our understanding of why and how this type of incident takes place. The commitments I am making today are an example of us responding with speed and precision to address potential harms to the UK posed by novel AI risks. I strongly consider this to be the right approach. I understand that there are diverging views on how fundamental AI regulation should take place, and there is a debate to be had on this, but the Bill is not the place for it.

The amendments tabled by the noble Lords, Lord Tarassenko and Lord Clement-Jones, and the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, would provide the AI Security Institute with a statutory role to regulate the deployment of frontier AI models in the UK. These amendments would not be effective in making our essential services safer. AI is a dual-use technology. Malicious actors could use frontier AI capabilities to attack the UK, but defenders can use the same capabilities to protect it, as my noble friend Lady Berger pointed out. Delaying essential services’ access to the latest tools would leave them less well defended, while attackers would face no such delay. These amendments could hold back adoption for up to 10 weeks in a field where new models come out every few weeks.

The scope of this Bill is also not right for AISI, or the regulation of frontier AI models. In particular, a regulatory role for AISI would undermine its voluntary partnership with leading AI developers, which give it early access to the most advanced models and on which its vital work to inform government depends. This is in contrast to the EU’s regulatory stance and lack of access to frontier models.

Finally, as I have said, the risks from frontier AI do not respect borders. We believe that the most effective response, as the Prime Minister committed to, is agreeing international standards. This Government remain committed to making sure that AISI is equipped to fulfil its vital role, and will keep the House updated on its work. In response to the question from the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, I will not pre-empt the Government’s consideration of or response to the Joint Committee on Human Rights; the response will be published in due course.

I thank noble Lords for their contributions. Through the commitments I have made today and the commitments made by the Prime Minister, the Chancellor and the Minister for AI in recent weeks—which, critically, seek to build UK capability through our sovereign AI fund and other measures—I hope I have been able to show that the Government are absolutely committed to ensuring that we will do whatever it takes to keep the British people safe.

speaker: Lord Clement-Jones
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I will speak to this group and move Amendment 61 on behalf of the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, alongside speaking to Amendment 158 in my name.

Amendment 61

“requires the Secretary of State to prepare, maintain, and lay before Parliament a Digital Sovereignty and Resilience Strategy”.

In modern cyber defence, we must know not just how we will defend our networks but whose technology we are relying on to do so. The strategy establishes a statutory digital sovereignty dashboard developed in consultation with the NCSC, the Competition and Markets Authority, the ONS and the AI Security Institute. This dashboard would monitor foreign state dependencies, supply chain bottlenecks and the security of core sovereign data assets, including NHS records, BBC archives and meteorological data. It will provide the evidence base needed to reform government procurement, promote resilient UK-developed technology and safeguard critical open source software. We cannot build genuine cyber resilience on borrowed or vulnerable foundations.

The Government cannot continue to substitute a disparate list of commercial partnerships and piecemeal initiatives for an overarching, statutory digital sovereignty strategy. True digital sovereignty is not merely a question of data residency, of where servers happen to be located; it is about decision rights, operational agency and jurisdictional immunity. When key public functions, policing databases and essential national infrastructure are underpinned by foreign-owned platforms, subject to extraterritorial levers such as the US CLOUD Act, the UK exposes itself to acute single-point-of-failure vulnerabilities and sudden regulatory hostage taking. Relying on the good intentions of overseas boardrooms or transient administrative commitments is a fragile foundation for our national resilience.

Amendment 61 provides the clarity and coherence we currently lack. It would require Ministers to audit our strategic dependencies, benchmark foreign ownership across critical systems and ensure that Britain retains the statutory levers, open technical architectures and domestic capability needed to control its own digital future. This amendment mirrors the amendment so powerfully championed in another place by my honourable friend Victoria Collins, alongside our honourable friend Freddie van Mierlo. As she warned, in an unstable world, true cyber resilience cannot exist without a statutory strategy to confront foreign supplier dependency and build sovereign capability. It is in that same spirit of transparency and digital integrity that I warmly welcome Amendment 165, tabled by the noble Lord, Lord Moraes.

I turn next to Amendment 158, which stands in my name and that of the noble Lord, Lord Holmes of Richmond. This new clause would

“place a statutory duty on the Secretary of State to review, within 12 months, whether a statutory defence under section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990”

should be introduced for legitimate, “good-faith cyber security researchers” and threat intelligence practitioners, and to report the findings to Parliament. I made the case as strongly as I could in Grand Committee.

Competitor jurisdictions, including the United States, France and Belgium, have already updated their laws to provide legal certainty for ethical research. The Pro-innovation Regulation of Technologies Review from the noble Lord, Lord Vallance, explicitly recommended introducing a statutory public interest defence. Amendment 158 does not write the defence into law today. It would simply place a statutory obligation on the Government to conclude their discussions with the CyberUp campaign and industry within 12 months and lay concrete proposals before Parliament. It is time to untie the hands of our cyber defenders. I beg to move Amendment 61.

speaker: Lord Holmes of Richmond
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I apologise for not getting to my feet before our Front Bench. I was clearly so moved by the eloquence and erudition of the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, that it slowed my motor function, and by the speed of my noble friend Lord Camrose, who clearly has his Asics on today. I very much support Amendment 61. There is so much talk about AI sovereignty, data sovereignty and digital sovereignty with it potentially meaning different things to each speaker of the sovereignty spiel. We need greater clarity across this. In the Bill before us, having this comprehensive clause covering what is required when it comes to digital sovereignty for the United Kingdom makes complete sense.

Moving to the Computer Misuse Act, the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, my noble friend Lord Arbuthnot, I and others have pushed various Governments over at least a decade on this issue. Our cyber professionals, those who do so much to keep us safe, often and understandably in silence and in the shadows, deserve our support. It cannot be that they are still on the wrong side of a statute that is racing towards its 40th birthday. We should update the Computer Misuse Act. The noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, has offered a pragmatic solution in his proposed new clause, with a 12-month period to bring this to fruition. Our cyber professionals do so much; they deserve our support. This proportionate amendment should be accepted by the Government and put in the Bill.

speaker: Lord Moraes
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lord, I shall speak briefly to Amendment 165 in my name. This amendment was introduced because the scope was quite difficult in Committee, and the question of end-to-end encryption is so fundamental to cyber security that it needs to be discussed.

Any weaknesses or access points that can be exploited by hackers and hostile threats can make us less safe and undermine the whole purpose of the Bill. It is a difficult one. The Government issue technical capability notices, and they have back doors into encryption, but this is an extraordinary issue. We are discussing AI machine-learning attacks, but if systems are vulnerable because the encryption has broken down, which happens every time there is a TCN or a back door, we have a real problem. This issue is not discussed enough, so I wanted to get it into the discussion on the Bill. I hope this will be addressed at some future point.

The amendment asks simply for a level of scrutiny. Is it really necessary to have the back door? Can it be scrutinised, for example, by the Intelligence and Security Committee of Parliament? That is what the amendment asks, and I hope that end-to-end encryption will be taken seriously as we move ahead.

speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
I thank noble Lords for their contributions. I will begin with the amendment tabled by the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, on digital sovereignty, which was spoken to by the noble Lords, Lord Clement-Jones and Lord Holmes of Richmond, and the noble Baroness, Lady Morgan—I hope I have not missed any noble Lords out.

I assure noble Lords that entities in scope of the NIS regime are already required to manage and mitigate the risks posed to their systems that deliver essential services. As set out in the Government’s response to the Science, Innovation and Technology Select Committee report in September on science diplomacy, this Government recognise and are actively working through the issue of digital and technical sovereignty, but we do not think that a fixed statutory public strategy is the appropriate vehicle. It remains this Government’s opinion that the rapid development of new technologies means that a fixed statutory strategy would reduce our flexibility to respond to new developments and might require the publication of sensitive material, including commercial information.

The Government do not see digital sovereignty as total independence. It is about capitalising on our domestic capabilities, achieving strategic resilience and building trusted interdependence. This has been set out in current strategies, including the Modern Industrial Strategy Digital Technologies Sector Plan of 2025 and the Cabinet Office’s June 2026 Procurement Policy Note 025, which recognises AI as one of four key sectors critical for national security and outlines new guidance to prioritise contracts for British businesses to protect national security.

Actions were announced by the Competition and Markets Authority to improve competition in cloud services following last year’s investigation. These will support greater choice for UK businesses and the public sector and include voluntary steps agreed by Microsoft and Amazon, safeguards to personal data through UK GDPR and legal and regulatory frameworks and continuing to encourage organisations to follow the UK Software Security Code of Practice and relevant international standards to manage cyber risks, including those related to open-source software components. The current approach remains the most proportionate and effective, providing the Government with the flexibility they need to respond to emerging developments.

Most importantly, we need to act to build UK capabilities, just as we are through investment to grow our domestic capability, including £500 million for the Sovereign AI Fund, £1.1 billion for the AI hardware plan and support for a £2 billion investment in quantum computing. This weekend, the Chancellor announced further investment to boost the UK’s ability to build our own chip design and cyber defences. By making active choices about how we harness AI, we can ensure that this technological revolution benefits our society and economy more fully than the Industrial Revolution.

Turning to the amendment tabled by the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, and spoken to by the noble Lord, Lord Holmes of Richmond, and the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, I thank the noble Lord for returning to this important subject. I share the view that the UK should have the right legislative framework to tackle cyber criminals. The Home Office has already carefully reviewed the Computer Misuse Act and proposes to introduce a defence to Section 1 for accredited cyber security researchers when carrying out certain cyber security activity that would currently be unlawful under that section. The Home Office has worked closely with NCSC, law enforcement and the cyber security industry to refine these proposals.

As my noble friend the Minister set out in Committee, the Home Office recognises that legislating in this area is a priority, and will do so as soon as parliamentary time allows. As the noble Lord will be aware, the King’s Speech in May included a commitment to a national security-focused Bill, with measures to update the Computer Misuse Act. This legislation is in development. While I understand the objective behind this amendment, reforms to the Computer Misuse Act extend well beyond the sectors covered by this Bill and are better taken forward through this wider programme of reform.

I thank my noble friend Lord Moraes for his amendment, which seeks to create a requirement to assess risks relevant to encryption. I recognise the intention behind this amendment, but I do not consider it necessary. The Government support strong encryption and robust privacy protections.

The Investigatory Powers Act 2016 is world-leading legislation that helps keep the public safe while protecting privacy. It contains important and extensive safeguards, oversight and scrutiny arrangements in relation to the exercise of investigatory powers, including powers that may engage encrypted services. Decisions under the Act are subject to statutory tests, independent oversight and, where appropriate, approval by judicial commissioners. This includes duties to consider impacts on privacy and system security.

The amendment would duplicate existing considerations of security and privacy and wider impacts, while creating an additional reporting process alongside the framework established in the Investigatory Powers Act. Creating a parallel statutory assessment regime through this Bill would not materially add to the existing and robust safeguards and oversight.

Finally, on the amendments tabled by the noble Viscount, Lord Camrose, regarding the national cyber action plan, I can assure him that the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport is working closely with the Cabinet Office to develop the action plan, and that the Government remain committed to publishing it shortly. We will update Parliament on the publication and implementation of the plan in the usual way. The action plan will make it clear that cyber security is a shared responsibility that requires action from government and businesses, including delivering this Bill to secure the UK’s most critical systems. With those reassurances, I hope that noble Lords will feel able to withdraw, or not move, their amendments.

speaker: Lord Clement-Jones
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I thank the Minister for her cameo appearance today on this group, and for having the temerity to give an undertaking on behalf of the Home Office. I hope that the Home Office will deliver in due course. That was as expected as regards Amendment 158. I very much thank the noble Lord, Lord Holmes, the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, and the noble Viscount, Lord Camrose, for their support. We will look forward to that Bill when it comes forward with that provision in it.

As for digital sovereignty, I think we are on the same page in not believing that this amounts to total independence. But it does mean, as the noble Baroness indicated, having resilience across the full stack involved in the development of AI in particular.

If circumstances were different and we had more time, we might be pressing further on this amendment. I am certain that if the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, were here she would be wanting to do that, but I think we are anxious to move to the next group. In the meantime, we will be holding the Government’s feet to the fire, in terms of their AI sovereignty strategy in particular. I beg leave to withdraw Amendment 61.

Amendment 61 withdrawn.

Clause 29: Regulations relating to security and resilience of network and information systems

Amendment 62 not moved.

speaker: Ali France
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Continuing on from earlier, these laws are about protecting people from harm. They're about setting basic standards and giving social media users more choice over what they see. It will require big tech to provide a safe online environment, in particular for our kids. Our country needs this; our kids need this.

This month, the AFP has told us about and spoken of online child exploitation and victimisation, like on nudify apps. They've also spoken about online abuse and accounts; the manosphere; images and videos that glorify violence, porn and misogyny; and content that encourages eating disorders. Suicide is having a devastating impact, and all of this content is having a devastating impact on our kids. It has real-world consequences.

I spoke earlier about the number of comments that I receive on my social media accounts. If you had a side look at my socials for a minute, you'd see that, over the last 18 months, I've had tens of thousands of comments threatening my personal safety, calling me 'peg leg', calling me 'NDIS scum' and telling me that they hope my other son dies. Last week, one person wrote:

know where your family lives, run or burn

which was reported to the AFP. In the week before, Adrian said:

you are a delusional—

bleep—

retard that needs a hot poker shove up your—

bleep. John said:

jump off a building already—

bleep bleep. Jamie said:

I prefer assassinations.

Leroy said:

Someone shoot this dopey—

bleep. And, on the day after Helen's attack, Josh said:

are you gonna get the AFP to knock on my door for 'intimidating you'

We know that words and other content online and in the media fuel violence, threats and abuse in real life, not just for MPs but for teachers, health workers and retail workers. The Minister for Social Services, Tanya Plibersek, said yesterday that the explosion in social media tracks the explosion of sexual violence and strangulation. It's frightening. Kids, vulnerable people and people with mental health issues read those comments. They see and they feel the hate. They follow and are fed destructive content. There are millions of social media accounts that promote and normalise violence, misogyny, extremism and dangerous behaviours—porn.

We must demand better from big tech and the online environment. That is at the core of this legislation. If you run an online service in this country, you have a duty to keep the people using it safe. If you build it and put it online, you are responsible for the risks to users. And it's not just about social media; the games, the apps and the AI chatbots are all covered by this bill, as are nudify apps, which we heard today over 200,000 people have downloaded in Australia. That's scary.

We know what algorithms feed our young people: content that promotes eating disorders; content that glorifies dangerous behaviour, violence and suicide; and content promoting misogyny and the abuse of women. This content is seeping out of the screen and into our schools, our homes and our relationships. These are accounts that are, overwhelmingly, set up to menace and harass. Teachers are telling us about it. Young female teachers are now copping abuse in the classroom. They are telling us about attitudes that walk through the school gate straight off a phone or an iPad. It is content that radicalises, pushing young people towards extremism and violence.

This bill creates a single, overarching obligation—a digital duty of care. It requires the providers of online services to take reasonable, practicable steps to keep the people who use them safe. A duty of care is not a new idea; it is one of the oldest ideas in our legal system. We already ask an employer to take reasonable steps to keep their workers safe. We ask the builder to make safe homes and the manufacturer to make safe products. All this bill does is apply the same well-settled principle to online services that are now as much a part of our daily life as any workplace or public square The standard is not perfection. The standard is what is reasonably practicable—reasonable steps matched to the risk. That is a deliberate choice, because for too long the approach to online safety in this country has been to just politely ask the platforms, 'Do better,' with a set of basic online safety expectations and industry codes. They were a start. But, as we all know, that approach has been a big fat fail.

This bill replaces that with one clear, enforceable duty, set by this parliament, that every provider must meet. For young people, this bill goes further still. Providers must take particular care to protect Australians under 18 from the harmful material they promote. Where a platform breaches that duty of care it will face penalties of up to $109 million, enforced by the independent eSafety Commissioner. The bill also gives the eSafety Commissioner strong tools to act on the harms that are hurting Australians right now. It sets minimum standards for how complaints and disputes are handled so that, when an Australian reports something, they get a proper process and a real response, not a bot and a dead end.

This builds on the work the Albanese Labor government has already done to make Australians safer online with the social media minimum age and our crackdown on nudify apps and undetectable tracking tools that are used to stalk and control women. Then there is the part of the bill that hands Aussies back some direct control. We call it My Feed, My Way. Under the bill, social media services will have to notify their users—new users and existing users alike—and offer them a real choice over what drives their main feed, an opportunity to shut out the garbage, to switch it off. You can absolutely keep the algorithm and swallow that garbage if you want to, but if you don't want to you can choose not to: your feed, your choice. This bill gives you the power to make it social again, to make it about your friends, your family, your favourite charities and the businesses you want to follow.

Now, you would think that a law to protect Aussies from this would be a no-brainer, but we know that those opposite and One Nation will tell you this bill is censorship. They'll call it Big Brother. They will say that the government is coming for your freedom—which is just rubbish. Adults can still access what they want. The real freedom is in the ability to switch off the algorithm. We would not accept the harms caused online in other environments and other contexts. We demand that a car is safe before it is sold. We demand that a medication is tried and tested before it is put to the market. We demand that a toy is safe before a child can play with it. We should demand nothing less of the platforms Australians use every single day.

At the centre of this bill is one simple principle: that the best interests of Aussies should come first. On this side of the House we are choosing the wellbeing of the people who use these platforms over the profits of the companies that run them. Anyone who votes against this bill is choosing something else. They are choosing profit. They are choosing outrage. They are choosing harm. I know which side I'm on, and I commend this bill to the House.

speaker: Tanya Joan Plibersek
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I want to thank the member for Flinders for that contribution, because I think she made a number of compelling points based on her experience in the industry. Can I suggest to her that the minister herself has said on multiple occasions she is very keen to have specific amendments from the opposition to do what I hope we all want to do, which is provide some protection from the way that the online environment is harming particularly our children at the moment.

Right now, we have an information environment which is force-feeding billions of people a steady diet of outrage. It monetises hate. It drives division. It severs social connections, and it spreads the kind of disinformation that makes us all less safe. Nearly 39 per cent of Australians aged 16 to 24 experience a mental illness every year, according to ABS data—figures that have risen sharply when you compare them to the pre-smartphone era. It takes just 23 minutes for an account mimicking a 16- to 18-year-old boy to be fed misogynistic content on social media. The tenor of public discourse is now so vitriolic that nine in 10 female politicians in this country are experiencing persistent abuse or violent threats on a regular basis. These are just some of the examples that people have been canvassing in recent days, but the point is clear. Social media platforms are deriving enormous profits from unsafe products—products that harm our children, our democracy and our health while eroding any sense of common ground and pushing our community to extremes.

Our Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 will change that. It will ensure that tech giants are held to basic safety standards, just as toy manufacturers are, just as car makers are and just as food companies are. No-one should be able to sell faulty products in Australia that harm consumers or promote criminality. It will force platforms, gaming sites and AI chatbots to protect under 18s in particular from violent pornography, from hostile ideas about women and gender equality, from content that encourages eating disorders and from content that glorifies criminal activity or causes serious distress, including abuse and bullying. Of course, our greatest focus is on those under 18s because we know that they are the ones at greatest risk, but all Australians should be protected from content which depicts, encourages, promotes or incites child sexual abuse, which promotes sexual or gender based violence, which circulates fake nude material created without consent or which promotes or incites extreme violence or cruelty or involves explicit threats of violence, including death or rape threats. As we've been discussing these issues in recent days and weeks, I think most Australians would be shocked to know some of the content that we are proposing to deal with. They wouldn't believe that such things exist on the internet.

The other crucial thing that this bill does is give back users control over what they see in their feeds. Some of us are old enough to remember what social media was when it was first introduced. It was a great place to catch up with what family members were doing, particularly if they were in different parts of Australia or around the world. It was a great way to catch up with friends, particularly friends who'd moved away, or check out whether your high school boyfriend was now single. But, in recent years, it has really morphed into an environment where algorithms are shoving violence, misogyny and body dysmorphic content down users' throats. Research consistently shows that content that's divisive can radicalise users and prey on their most intimate insecurities. The bill seeks to give Australians back their agency online by allowing them to either opt in or opt out of recommender systems.

Many of those opposite are trying to pretend that this is somehow the government controlling what people see. It is the exact opposite. This is allowing people to choose the people they want to follow, the businesses they want to follow and the organisations that they care about—their local footy team, the coffee shop down the road, the community group that they're part of or their local church. They can choose who they receive content from. They don't let absentee oligarchs in Silicon Valley make that choice for them. That's what's happening now, with no transparency around it at all. Anyone in this chamber trying to frame this choice as censorship needs to ask themselves the question: what am I so determined for people to see online without giving them the choice that they can opt out of seeing it? Algorithms are built by tech bros who have no concern for Australia or for Australians. They themselves—those tech bros—are not champions of free speech. They use free speech arguments when it suits them, and then they use billions of dollars to shut down criticism whenever it criticises them. They're not champions of free speech. They're champions of their own speech. They worship at the altar of profit and they have proven time and time again that there is no low they won't sink to in order to keep eyeballs glued to screens.

Social media, of course, can be a tool for good. The member for Flinders was providing great examples of where it can be used for good. It can be a source of connection. It can be a way to enhance community. It can be a way to celebrate self-expression. If you're a small business, it can be a way to get connected to new markets and new buyers. But, as things stand at the moment, we have not got the balance right.

Our world-leading social media ban for under-16s has gone a long way already in shielding young Australians from the harms that some of these platforms inflict, while giving them back their childhoods. We're hearing great stories about kids playing in the playground more and talking to each other more, but technology changes rapidly. A digital duty of care will ensure that every Australian is entitled to safety online; that products, websites and platforms which violate those standards face consequences; and that users choose what they see on social media, not billionaires based in Silicon Valley.

The legislation has my full support because we know that online harms are rapidly spilling into the real world and because, in the words of Molly Bannister, who lost her beautiful 14-year-old son Olly to suicide after he was constantly and ruthlessly fed body-dysmorphic content on social media, Molly said:

For too long we've asked everyday people and parents to somehow outsmart the most sophisticated technology companies in the world.

This bill changes that. It gives more power back to parents. It gives more power back to social media users. As the minister in charge of the next plan to end violence against women and their children and as a mother, I back that. I implore those opposite to join with us to put the needs of children first, to put the safety of Australians first and to back our digital duty of care.

speaker: Gabriel Ng
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I thank the member for Fowler for her contribution. The Albanese government is continuing its international leadership on online safety. We led the world with the under-16s social media ban, which has been taken up in countries around the world, including in the UK, Spain, Malaysia and many other countries, and we're leading the world again with establishing a digital duty of care.

This legislation sets basic safety standards for those engaging in the digital tools we use every day. It's fundamentally about two things: safety and choice. The idea that businesses have a responsibility for the products that they create is one of the oldest obligations in law. Negligence is founded in the concept of businesses having a duty of care for their consumers. It's something that we expect in things that we use every day, from food and drinks to the cars we drive, to the buildings we live and work in. This bill extends these obligations to online services, like social media, online games and AI chatbots.

This is not about limiting freedom of speech. There's already, I fear, misinformation out there about this bill. We've received emails from constituents concerned about restrictions on freedom of expression. We understand that freedom of speech is absolutely vital to our democracy, and I reassure those people that have written to us that this bill will not restrict freedom of speech. It will not prevent you from criticising the government or our policies, or from engaging in public debate about a range of issues. It will not stop you from disagreeing even strongly in the public sphere. This is about keeping people, particularly young people, safe online. It's about putting the obligation on social media companies to take reasonable care to prevent foreseeable harm. It's also about giving people more choice in what they see online.

There were many speeches yesterday that touched upon the online environment, how the anger and aggression that has, sadly, become endemic in Australian society finds its worst expressions online and how the online environment even fuels it. This anger and its symptoms—the worst being violence against retail and hospitality workers, hospital workers, paramedics, teachers and politicians, at every level of society, it seems—is not going to be solved by this bill alone, but I believe this bill is part of the solution.

Our under-16s social media ban, which passed with bipartisan support, has already shown that effective regulation can help improve safety online. It's already resulted in over five million accounts being deactivated. We recognise that not every account that is held by a young person has been deactivated, and that they often find ways around it; they're very resourceful in that way. I think it's particularly difficult for the generation that had social media and have been asked to delete their accounts. But, as a parent, I know it will be easier to say no to my kids signing up for social media. My daughter is becoming a teenager now and we haven't let her sign up for social media because there is that norm in society now that teenagers, that young people, can't sign up for social media in the first place—and their friends won't be online, so we won't have that group pressure. As a result of the under-16s social media ban, we're hearing about some good outcomes. Teens have reported greater engagement in sport, better sleep and a reduction in bullying online just since our reforms took effect. We're making meaningful progress, but there's still more work to do, and that's what this bill is about. This digital duty of care is particularly focused on strengthening the safety of young people.

Under this legislation, all online services, including games and AI chatbots, must protect people under 18 from harmful content like pornography and material or conduct that encourages, promotes or instructs disordered eating; that encourages or promotes hostile attitudes towards women or gender equality; that glorifies crime or encourages dangerous stunts or seriously harmful practices; and that involves abuse, harassment or bullying, or any other material or conduct or combination of material and conduct that may cause serious harm to children. Under-18s will also be protected from design features that will have negative behavioural impacts, like addictive features that cause kids to stay up late and to lose sleep.

These steps address concerns that I hear from parents and people across my community. Algorithms that have targeted vulnerable children and young people come up amongst teachers and parents chatting at the school gate or at the local footy, and they come up with young people themselves. Young people know about the harm an unfiltered and unregulated social media presence can have on them and their friends. Often they're even more aware of it than adults are. I've spoken to students at East Doncaster Secondary College and Box Hill High and with our youth advisory committee, who understand online harms all too well.

As I said, one of the harms we're addressing is disordered eating. These laws will require platforms to prevent minors and users from being targeted by material that promotes eating disorders. In Australia, over 1.1 million people are living with an eating disorder. Twenty-seven per cent of these people are aged 10 to 19—and that's a figure that's doubled since 2012. Eating disorders are amongst the deadliest forms of mental illness, and for those that seek help it takes an average of one to six years to recover. A 2015 study of teen girls reported that social media users were significantly more likely than non-social media users to have internalised a drive for thinness. Now, 10 years later, the risk of young people being fed targeted and harmful messaging that can exacerbate eating disorders is significant. Robb Evans, who lost his daughter, Liv, to anorexia, has spoken about the ways in which social media can magnify mental illness. Liv, after searching for low-calorie recipes, was fed reels providing her advice on how to survive on just 200 calories a day. Her feed actively directed her towards more extreme and harmful content. Thanks to the bravery of people like Robb who have shared their stories, we now have an opportunity to protect vulnerable young people in the future from these exacerbating factors.

We've also heard in the House from the Minister for Communications and the Minister for Education how algorithms' bias towards misogynistic content means that accounts registered to teenage boys will be directed towards antiwomen, dehumanising content within just 23 minutes of being created. Within two to three hours, a teen boy's feed will be filled with videos promoting violence and sexist attitudes and war cries like 'your body, my choice. This is material they are force-fed purely because of their age and gender, and it tells them that social and personal frustrations are caused by gender equality. It is not woke to want our young men to have healthy, respectful attitudes towards women and to want to have healthy, respectful, equal relationships. It is a foundation of a decent society. This is especially the case in an environment of rising sexual violence and negative attitudes towards women.

This bill will also require that online services, including games, must protect under-18s from being exposed to pornography. Young people shouldn't be getting their sex education from pornography that normalises things like choking or violence or degrading acts. Online services will also need to protect young people from content that glorifies crime or dangerous stunts. Research done by the eSafety Commission showed 46 per cent of children have seen dangerous online challenges. In recent years, trends like the skull breaker challenge and the squishy toy microwave trend have resulted in significant harm for many Australian children and young people who are exposed to them. This includes spinal cord injuries, seizures, severe burns and head trauma.

When we consider the capacity of social media platforms to cause serious distress, the story of Emma Mason and her daughter Tilly comes to mind. Tilly Rosewarne was 15 when she died by suicide, and her mother, Emma, says:

This was death by bullying but it was enabled by social media.

Tilly's family are all too aware of the real-world harm that can be generated from online abuse, as Emma has so powerfully said. She has taken her Let Them Be Kids campaign to the UN and shared her story across the world. Now the world knows that tech companies are all about the algorithm and not the human cost of what's going on. As long as social media companies are the ones setting the rules, the safety of our children will not be the priority. As Emma has said, these reforms will save lives, and they will keep more kids safe.

This bill also places greater obligations on big tech companies to ensure their products are safe and gives adult Australians greater choice about what they see online. Social media companies like Meta and TikTok, online games like Roblox and more recent technologies like AI chatbots all have had ample responsibility to fulfil their social responsibilities, and far too often they have failed to do so, even when compelled. This bill will require them to do annual risk assessments of the harms the features on their services could cause Australians and put systems in place to prevent those harms.

Very importantly, this bill will give Australians the option to opt out of the social media algorithm. The option must be accessible, prominently displayed and not make your feed harder to navigate. If people choose this option, it means they'll only see content from friends, family, businesses and content creators that they choose to follow. Again, this is not about restricting freedom of speech. It does the opposite. It is about giving people more choice. For too long, big tech companies have avoided their social obligation. This bill puts the onus back on them. It will give Australians more choice. It will make them safer and it will make our young people safer. I commend this bill to the House.

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
For several years now, Australians have been increasingly concerned about the impact of the online world on the welfare of children and on the cohesiveness of our society. A movement for change, begun and led by brave parents who saw their children's lives taken by cruel and highly addictive social media, created a remarkable period of bipartisanship that put Australia in the forefront of global movements to bring about online safety. It enabled the government of Malcolm Turnbull to create the world's first online safety watchdog, the Children's eSafety Commissioner, whose remit was later extended to adults. Then, in 2024, the parliament came together again and legislated a minimum age for social media. We did it for Rob Evans and Liv, Emma Mason and Tilly, Mia Bannister and Ollie, Wayne Holdsworth and Mac, and for every young person who has lost their life or been damaged by the experience of social media and the online world—and we did it for their parents—so all children and adolescents would be protected from unnecessary harm.

It has had positive impacts on the welfare and happiness of our children and adolescents. Five million underage social media accounts have been deactivated, removed or restricted, and surveys have found that many young Australians are now spending more time playing sport, getting more sleep, being less exposed to inappropriate and violent content and suffering less from bullying. Despite the fact there are still too many under 16s using social media, it was a highly promising start and it attracted global attention, respect and support, which is why it is being replicated right around the world. It demonstrates that Australia can lead the world on truly important issues. Its failure to achieve even greater success can be put down to one overriding cause: noncompliance by the online platforms, some of whom have evaded their responsibilities under the law. We strengthened the compliance requirements recently through the Online Safety Amendment (Strengthening Enforcement for the Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2026, and, empowered by this, the eSafety Commissioner is currently investigating noncompliance by five platforms: Instagram, Meta, TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat.

Too many children, though, are still at risk and are still being harmed.
