There is a growing body of research pointing to the reality that, as a result of the deliberate design of its algorithmic features, social media is changing our society in harmful ways, turbocharging anger to the detriment of our social cohesion and our democracy. It is promoting misogyny, building an aggressive and sometimes frightening manosphere and driving a wedge between men and women, leading to an increase in gender based violence. Algorithms discourage nuance. They deliver increasing levels of angry content into the devices. At its most extreme, this is contributing to the normalisation of aggressive behaviour. The negative consequences are being felt by everyone, not just by politicians but also by nurses, doctors, ambos, teachers, shop workers, hospitality workers—in fact, people from all industries and all walks of life. It is affecting all of us in ways that are becoming increasingly negative and unpleasant. The problem has gone on for far too long.

The nation's security and police leaders have warned us that the level of potential danger is increasing. ASIO chief Mike Burgess warned:

Social media is … promoting discord and inflammatory rhetoric, exacerbating polarisation, and creating a permissive environment for violence.

AFP commissioner Krissy Barrett has said that the National Security Investigations team is charging almost one individual every week for targeting Commonwealth parliamentarians and public officials. The AFP, she said, is recording growing volumes of online abuse, threatening rhetoric and intimidation. This level of harm must be addressed and must be reduced.

The onus is not on children or parents to act. It is on the companies to act to ensure their services are safe. It is doing harm to our kids and to our society, and we must call time on it. We have given the tech companies years to address these serious problems caused by their products, but they have failed to do so repeatedly. By not meeting their social responsibility properly, the companies have been undermining their social licence. The time is up. Their social licence must now be expressed through legislation, and these technical companies, run largely outside of Australia, can make a difference.

I recently met with Tim Cook, the CEO of Apple. The new Apple phone has features on it designed to protect children and designed to empower parents to act more decisively in the interests of their families. So it is possible for companies to act responsibly, but the truth is that we have a responsibility as well to act, and this is the moment for this parliament to act, to make the social media and the online world safer, to pass the government's digital duty of care bill, and, by doing so, require tech companies to take responsibility for the safety of the products and services they provide that have made them hundreds of billions and trillions of dollars of profit.

This bill puts a positive obligation on big tech to provide a safe online environment where Australians are protected from seriously harmful and illegal content, adults are given a meaningful choice about what they see on their feeds and under-18s are protected from content and features harmful to young people. It will set safety standards for the digital services we use every day, just like we do for motor cars and food and children's toys. If we can do it for all of those products, why is it hard for us to do it for something that has a much greater and regular impact on families?

It will require companies to undertake risk assessments of their services, put systems in place to address their risky features from doing harm and provide people over 16 with empowerment tools that give them choice about what they see in their feed. Crucially, online services, like social media, online games and AI chatbots, must protect under-18s from harmful content that promotes eating disorders and hostile ideas towards women and gender equality, pornography, material that glorifies crime or dangerous stunts, and content that causes serious distress, including abuse and bullying.

The bill will also protect under-18s from addictive features that cause kids to stay up late and lose sleep. It will ban nudify apps, which cause so much distress and harm to young people. Our children simply should not have to live in this poisonous and unhealthy environment. They deserve better. Their childhood should not be spent glued to a device. They should be playing outside with their friends, off their phones and on the footy fields and cricket pitches, the tennis and netball courts, in the swimming pool, trying any sport that grabs their interests, reading books, and engaging with human interaction with real people. The stories we hear about people identifying a chatbot, a nonperson, as their best friend should be a huge wake-up call for every member of this parliament to be prepared to act. Young people need to be able to figure out who they are, free from the pressure of the entire world to act in a certain way.

The bill will also protect all Australians, including adults, from material that promotes child sexual exploitation or child sex abuse, grooming, sexual violence, extreme violence or cruelty, the menacing or harassing of individuals and the encouragement of terrorist acts. Importantly, it will halve the length of time that digital service providers have to respond to cyberbullying complaints from 48 to 24 hours, and it will empower eSafety to go undercover to make sure that companies are complying with the law. Failure to comply with this digital duty of care will result in a fine of up to $109.2 million, which is in line with other Australian penalties designed to protect Australian consumers.

Let me be clear: under the digital duty of care, online services will be required to have systems in place to protect all Australians, including Commonwealth officials, from death threats, threats of rape, threats of violence, terrorism and material or conduct that can cause serious harm by menacing or harassing an individual. Some have suggested this is about censorship. Nothing could be further from the truth. This is not about preventing mean comments or political debate. It is about preventing serious harm. It is not about controlling what adults do online. It's about giving people back power and choice. Rather than someone in the United States deciding what they see, they get to decide themselves. That is what this legislation is about. It is about increasing choice, because it will require platforms to give us more choice over the content and the features that we use, including the feeds that we choose.

I urge the parliament to support this bill. This bill, if we carry it, will be replicated around the world, just like the bill banning under-16s from social media has been. This is an opportunity for our country to lead, and lead we should. At its core, the legislation brings together 17 existing industry made codes into a single overarching legislative framework in a way that makes them easy to understand and enforce. The complex and contradictory nature of these codes has made them difficult to enforce and easy to evade. It makes them a lawyer's picnic. Put the power back in the hands of our constituents and away from the multinational companies and the tech giants. That is what this is about. The evasion has gone on too long. This bill will put an end to this subterfuge and will help to keep our people safe.

The bill in essence is a much-needed but moderate and commonsense response to a problem that is becoming more serious with every passing day, a response to a rising chorus of concern across society about what social media is doing to our children, our relationships and our social cohesion and community behaviour. It's backed by academic experts and by our intelligence and police leaders. It's endorsed by important organisations that support the rights and welfare of children, young people and young adults—headspace, Project Rockit, the Butterfly Foundation, SmackTalk and Teach Us Consent, whose impressive young leader Chanel Contos I met with yesterday to discuss this issue. I want to thank all of them for their advocacy. I want to thank the parents who have taken personal grief and channelled that into not wanting other parents to go through what they have gone through with the loss of their son or daughter.

Ultimately, this bill is, of course, in the interest of the digital media platforms and social media companies themselves, because it is the best way for them to actually retain their social licence, which is fast losing public support, and avoid a potential backlash. Australian parents and the Australian people want the measures in this bill passed. I say to everyone in the House and the Senate please examine your conscience, please examine what is in this bill, and please do not be distracted by what is not in this bill as well. This is sensible reform, and I commend it to the House.

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Imagine you could travel back in time 50 years to the 1970s. Imagine telling someone about the internet, about the mobile phone and about social media. 'Within 50 years,' you could tell this person, 'nearly everyone on Earth will carry a device in their pocket that gives them instant access to the sum of human knowledge—every book, every paper, every fact available in seconds. That same device will allow you to communicate with friends and family around the world in an instant. You'll be able to send messages, hear their voice and see their face. The tyranny of distance will be no more. You'll even be able to communicate with almost anyone on Earth. You'll be able to share stories, photos and videos. You'll be able to message people you've never met before with similar interests and ideas.' What would you have thought at that time, hearing about the promises of the future? The possibilities would have felt so bright and exciting. Access to the world's knowledge would surely drive productivity, new inventions and rising standards of living. The ability to connect with anyone at any time would surely drive greater connection and thriving families and communities, and the ability to share ideas with strangers would surely drive greater democratic participation and exciting new collaborations.

But fast-forward 50 years to the present and consider that productivity and living standards have plateaued or are going backwards. Families and communities feel even more strained and disrupted, and, around the world, democracies are backsliding towards authoritarianism. How has this happened? How has the technology that promised so much, which could have unlocked incredible possibilities, failed so badly? What went wrong? Our online spaces are now vectors for incredibly harmful material—child sexual abuse material, suicidal content, aggressive bullying, radicalisation and racism. Social media fosters anger and division. It causes anxiety and mental illness. It drives a constant feeling of negativity and helplessness. Social media is fraying our social fabric. We welcomed this technology into our lives, enamoured by its promises, without thinking about the harms it could cause. And now, decades on, we find our lives intrinsically intertwined with the digital world, and we find ourselves with the almost infinitely impossible job of unpicking the harms caused by social media and digital platforms, piece by piece.

The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 is one of those really important pieces. It places a digital duty of care on online services. They must take appropriate action to provide a safe online environment. For the first time, responsibility will sit with the companies that design these services and not only with the parents and children whose attention is being monetised. My electorate supports this. In a survey of my community of Curtin, more than 90 per cent of the 1,200 respondents supported the idea that social media companies should have to take more responsibility for the harms they cause. Importantly, the digital duty of care will extend beyond social media to other online services like search engines, AI chatbots and app stores.

The bill is strong when it comes to protecting children. Under the digital duty of care, online services would be obliged to protect children from content such as pornography, abuse, misogyny and the promotion of eating disorders. For adults, online services are required to protect people from serious harm, like content that promotes child sexual abuse, extreme violence, suicide and terrorism. What does this actually mean in practice? It doesn't mean you will no longer see harmful content online, but it means that platforms have to take appropriate action to limit it. That means doing risk assessments to identify the risks in advance, rather than waiting for harms to occur, and it means putting in place systems to deal with those risks. That could include better screening of extremely violent content, faster responses to content reported by users or dialling down algorithmic echo chambers that show extremist content.

Perhaps the most important step in this bill is that it goes beyond content. The bill requires services to look at the design features that cause harm to children and serious harm to adults. This means companies will have to consider the impact of algorithms and of addictive design features, content moderation systems, content monetisation processes, ad approval systems and beyond. This is an acknowledgement that it's not just individual pieces of content that cause harm; it's also the systems designed by social media companies. To give you one example, it's alleged that Meta, the owner of Instagram and Facebook, previously had a 17-strike policy before it suspended accounts engaged in the trafficking of humans for sex. You could give 16 indicators that you were sex trafficking, but only on the 17th would you be banned. Under the digital duty of care, systems like this are also under the spotlight.

The bill makes two further important changes. Firstly, it includes important transparency measures, which will allow researchers and the eSafety Commissioner to understand what safety measures these companies are actually putting in place. Secondly, it enables the minister to require user empowerment tools to give Australians greater control over their online services. The government has announced that it will use this power to require all social media companies to give you the choice to opt in or out of your algorithm.

The bill is very welcome. We need it, and I commend the government. It signals an important cultural shift as we start to expect more from social media companies. But it can be better, and I am proposing some improvements. The first is to introduce a private right of action. This would give Australians a way to take direct action when they've been harmed to take the pressure off regulators and to take the politics out of enforcement. It would then be Australians, not just the Australian government, holding international tech companies to account. This is complex drafting, and I haven't attempted it in the House, but I strongly encourage the government to move it and the Senate to consider it. The second is to increase the penalties. The current maximum penalty for breaching the duty of care and for failing to carry out risk assessments or provide user empowerment tools is $100 million. That might sound like a lot, but this would be about one-twentieth of one per cent of Meta's revenue last year—too small to change behaviour. Other jurisdictions have seen this. The EU, the UK, Canada and New Zealand have fines that range from three to 10 per cent of global revenue. I propose changing the maximum to 5 per cent of global revenue. If we want to change behaviour, there need to be consequences that mean something.

Another important amendment that I'm proposing deals with a harm that this bill doesn't address. Psychologists are telling us that AI chatbots and companions create a risk to children's long-term psychological development and human attachment through what's called attachment hacking. This is where AI systems like chatbots and companions simulate emotional intimacy, fostering a child's dependence on it instead of human relationships. As the PM mentioned in his speech a few minutes ago, we're seeing children confiding in AI chatbots and companions rather than in a friend, a parent or a teacher. An AI companion tells you what you want to hear, not what you need to hear to make sense of the world and sense of yourself. This can create a critical disruption to psychological development and a child's sense of reality. This bill would be improved with my amendment to include this type of harm. My fourth amendment is simple. User empowerment tools must be prominent and accessible, and this should be written into the act. It's meaningless to give adults a choice about their algorithms or future more sophisticated user empowerment tools if that choice is hidden deep in the settings menu. We've seen the EU struggle with this malicious compliance, an algorithm opt-out that's technically available but hard to find. Australians must have a real choice about what they see that's prominent and accessible.

I want to turn to free speech or, more accurately, our implied right of freedom of political communication. I've heard the concern from my community and from this chamber that this reform is about censorship—the government deciding what you see online now. I commend the government for listening to concerns and removing the minister's power to extend the categories of harm. This was a power that could theoretically have been used to threaten freedom of communication. I believe that this change should have quelled most concerns related to censorship, but I've still heard some pushback, which I want to address. If anyone is controlling what you see, it's the social media companies. Their algorithms decide what lands in your feed, and they are designed to make a profit by keeping every one of us scrolling for as long as possible. They are monetising our attention. We are the product, not the customer.

This bill shifts some of this control from the platform not to the government but back to the user. The bill doesn't make a single post unlawful. What changes is how services are designed. Reducing this important piece of legislation to a scare campaign about censorship is exactly what the worst of these platforms want. They want users to defend their ability to design platforms to keep those users hooked and angry so the platforms can sell your attention to advertisers.

Passing this bill is the start of the work, not the end of it. I want to make three points about what comes next. First, this bill will come down to compliance and enforcement. A duty of care is only as strong as the regulator that enforces it. The eSafety Commissioner will be asking some of the best resourced companies in the world to explain their algorithms and their safety systems. Ensuring that the commissioner is well funded and empowered is critical for the digital duty of care to succeed.

Second, we should design more user empowerment tools, and we should design them with the people who use them. I held a workshop on the digital duty of care with students from the University of Western Australia earlier this month, and the word that kept coming up was 'control'. Young people who grew up with social media told me that, rather than a binary choice about recommended content, they want to be able to dial it up or down—for example, by increasing the ratio of discovery to personalised content on their feed. They want to know what a platform has decided about them. The opt-in and opt-out choice is a good first tool, but it's blunt, and many will choose not to opt out. We should be thinking about other, more nuanced user empowerment tools that can help people combat echo chambers and doomscrolling to give Australians more control over their own experience of social media.

Third, we need to think harder about the more insidious role of social media in our public life. Australia has seen a rise in anger over recent years, with recent examples of anger spilling over into real-life violence. There's a broad recognition that social media has a role to play in the amplification of anger, negativity and outrage. Social media rewards short, emotional posts and punishes balance. Algorithms drive echo chambers, where people become more and more set in extremist views. Addictive features keep people online for longer, degrading mental wellbeing, disrupting families and keeping people disconnected from other people in the real world. Anonymity and the separation of a phone screen allow people to say things they would never say in real life. Social media is not the only reason for the rise in temperature, but it's a big reason and one that we've not dealt with before. Australia has gone through difficult economic times, international shocks and periods of polarisation, but we've never dealt with social media before.

These are issues that go beyond this bill. This bill deals with serious harm—not anger, outrage and anxiety for adults. It's about the relationship between the online service and the user, not about the broader impacts of social media on families, friends, communities and society. The next step in our journey must be to unpick the broader, negative impacts of social media on our society: the constant amplification of anger and negativity and the fraying of our social fabric. We must understand the impact so we can make our own choices about who we want to be, not just assume that this is inevitable.

To conclude, digital duty of care puts responsibility where it belongs: on the companies that design these online services. It looks at how services are built and not only at what's posted. It gives people some control over their own experience. Until now we have not made a considered choice about the role that digital platforms play in our lives. We can make one now. I encourage the government to seriously consider my amendments. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Jo Briskey
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
More than five million underage accounts have been deactivated, removed or restricted since our government set a minimum age for social media. At the time we were told it couldn't be done—that the technology did not exist and the kids would find a workaround within a week. Most notably, we were told that Australia was going to embarrass itself in front of the world for trying. But our government persisted, and now more than 30 countries either have legislated or are considering legislating similar laws.

Five million is a significant number, but perhaps what is more significant are some of the following numbers. A YouGov survey found 30 per cent of young Australians aged 13 to 15 are now spending more time playing sport, 27 per cent are spending more time with their families, online bullying in that age group is down nine per cent and exposure to inappropriate and violent content has fallen by 18 per cent. These are early numbers, but they all point in the one way and they are the result of a law that some of the loudest voices in this debate said was unworkable.

We know there are still too many under-16s on social media. Nobody in this government is pretending otherwise. But it's not the law failing; it's the platforms who are failing to comply with the law. That is a different problem with a different answer. The eSafety Commissioner right now is investigating noncompliance by five platforms: Instagram, Meta, TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat. Some of the largest and best-resourced companies in human history, who can comply, have decided themselves the pace at which they will. It is this arrogance and disregard for the safety of our children that is the case for this bill.

For the better part of 20 years, we have asked these companies to do the right thing through the codes they wrote themselves and then chased individual pieces of content around the internet long after the damage was done. Australia's digital duty of care sets basic safety standards for digital services that we use every day, just like we do for food, for cars and for kids toys. Nobody thinks it's an assault on the free market that a pram has to meet a standard before it can be sold. Nobody expects a parent to test the brakes of that pram themselves. We settled that question a long time ago. The person who builds the thing carries the responsibility for whether it is safe, and the parliament sets the floor so the operator doing the right thing is not undercut by those cutting corners.

The duty in this bill is lifted almost word for word out of the work health and safety law—taking reasonably practicable steps to provide a safe environment. It is the benchmark for best-practice regulation in this country. It is what the European Union and the United Kingdom have both landed on, and there is nothing truly novel about it. The only novelty is that we are finally applying it to an industry that has spent the last 20 years insisting it was worth a special exemption. Under the duty, services will have to do annual risk assessments of the harms their features could cause, put systems in place to stop those features causing harm and give people real choice about what lands in front of them. Failure to comply carries a penalty of a $109.2 million, in line with what we already impose on companies that rip off Australian consumers. There is an efficiency argument here too. One duty set by this parliament in language Australian businesses already understand is simpler to comply with and simpler to enforce than the 17 overlapping codes it replaces.

I have two daughters, aged 12 and nine. My eldest, Gweny, and her mates will be 16 before this duty is fully bedded down. The point of this bill is that it is not my job, it is not my husband's job and it is not the job of Gweny's friends' parents—it's not our job alone, at the kitchen table, to work out whether a product or an online product is safe for our kids. That has never been a fair fight. So here is what this duty requires for children, because a great deal has been said about this bill that's not actually in it.

Every online service—social media, online games, AI chat bots—will have to protect under-18s from pornography, from material that encourages or instructs disordered eating, from material that promotes hostile attitudes towards women and gender equality, from material that glorifies crime or encourages dangerous stunts and from abuse, harassment and bullying. They will also have to protect kids from the design features that keep people, young people, scrolling to all hours of the night. Anyone in this chamber seeking to ignore this aspect of the bill in favour of made-up hysterics is only making our kids' lives harder.

The chatbots are a part of this bill that public debate has not caught up with. I'm currently chairing the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, and we have heard from researchers, unions and industry as well as from the people who build these systems and the people who study them. The honest summary is that these products are being put in front of kids faster than anybody can test or understand what they do to them. That is the most concerning part. The rapid development of AI means that, if we write a law today that covers only the platforms we happen to be concerned about today, we'll be back in this chamber in the years to come writing something again. A duty of care does not need a new industry code every time a new technology appears. That is the whole design of the thing.

The same logic covers the disgusting apps built to generate fake nude images of real people. This bill empowers the eSafety Commissioner to take down apps and websites designed or predominantly used for that purpose, and it defines fake nude material as seriously harmful, so every service has to protect every Australian from it. On average, one in 33 children has reported someone creating a nude image of them, using AI—that is a terrifying thing to read as a parent—and one in 25 Australians has reported being victimised by deepfake pornography. For adults, the duty is narrower, and it goes to serious harm—child sexual abuse material, grooming, sexual violence, image based abuse, incitement to extreme violence, explicit threats of rape and death and terrorist-and-violent-extremist material.

Beyond these incredibly vile behaviours, this bill does not tell a single Australian adult what they can look at. The digital duty of care is not about controlling what adults do online; it is about requiring platforms to give us choice. That is the most underrated part of this bill. These companies make an extraordinary amount of money out of our information and out of our attention. We are asking that, in return, they let us decide what is in our own feeds. If you want your friends and the creators you choose to follow—the app has to let you do that by default, rather than throwing you into an algorithm full of people you will never subscribe to. I think that's a modest ask of an industry that has never once been asked for much.

We can all recall a time when we have been scrolling through a platform and something popped up that made us question why it had. I can remember a few times when something gruesome or awful came across my screen unwarranted. When something does go wrong, people are entitled to better than a web form and silence. This bill cuts the required response time to cyberbullying and abuse complaints from 48 hours to 24 hours and lets eSafety set minimum standards for how complaints and disputes are handled, because an automatic confirmation email—and then nothing else—is not a response.

Last week, the member for Indi was attacked outside her electorate office. While the details of what led to this attack are still to be fully understood, we know—the women in this chamber especially know—that online platforms are not safe. They allow people to live in bubbles that make them angrier and angrier. The people charged with keeping this country safe have also spoken plainly about the environment we are all now living in. The ASIO Director-General, Mike Burgess, has warned that social media is 'promoting discord and inflammatory rhetoric, exacerbating polarisation and creating a permissive environment for violence'. The AFP Commissioner, Krissy Barrett, has said her National Security Investigations team is charging almost one individual a week for targeting Commonwealth parliamentarians and public officials. We've also heard from workers and their unions about the rising abuse that is directed towards them. I'm talking about our frontline workers, nurses, teachers, retail workers and care workers.

This isn't about mean comments or robust political debate; we are talking about serious harm and serious harm only. If an individual can be held accountable by the police for their behaviour, a company that built something that carried it and made it money through amplifying should be accountable too. If you build it, you're responsible for it. That has always been the Australian way.

For a decade, online safety in this country has been bipartisan. The world's first online safety watchdog was built here by those opposite. That was good work, and that deserves to be said aloud in this place. In 2024 this parliament came together again and legislated a minimum age for social media. Every one of these reforms passed with bipartisan support, because some things matter more than politics. That is why the position the coalition has taken on this bill is utterly— (Quorum formed) I appreciate that it's hard to be held accountable for your decisions, Opposition. The claim that this bill censors Australian adults is absolutely false. The claim about test counts is even worse and in my opinion rather dangerous, because it is an argument against truly holding these big tech companies accountable. The test accounts are not about policing what people see online. They're about making sure the tech companies are adhering to what we expect of them.

So right now our government stands on the side of parents and their kids, whilst those opposite appear to be content with siding with big social media platforms. I implore the opposition to reconsider their position. It is not too late for there to be a bipartisan approach, in the same way that we have delivered progress in this space as a parliament over the last couple of years. It is so important that we get this right, not just for our kids but for all of us. We deserve to see a safer, better place online. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Nicolette Boele
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Consider the influence that social media companies have over you. Consider the way they shape the news you read, the jokes you listen to and the people with whom you interact. When your feed was chronological, simple and all about the people you actually knew feels like a distant memory. Most of us—at least, those my age—joined social media to connect with friends and family. Today, the algorithm can be fun, interesting and even informative, but it can also be divisive, isolating and radicalising. It exercises enormous power over us, and we barely understand how it works.

Governments have allowed tech companies to cultivate this power with minimal oversight, and for too long a handful of tech billionaires have written their own rules. They've had years to fix the problems themselves, and they have chosen not to. These multinational companies have discovered that the most effective way to increase their profits is to hook us—and the best way to hook us is to inflame us, to drive us further apart from each other into echo chambers and digital worlds that are often dark, dangerous and divisive. In just 13 minutes, an account mimicking a 16- to 18-year-old boy will be fed misogynistic content. Too many children in my electorate are experiencing these harms, and parents write to me frequently to express their concerns. They feel powerless to protect their kids from these formless, invisible algorithms that manipulate their kids' minds and distort their development.

Social media is the Wild West, and the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 tries to bring some law and order into the digital world. It's time for government to crack down on the tech-bro cowboys and govern to protect the people who put them in this place. At its core, this bill puts a legal duty on online services to take appropriate action to keep Australians safe. That covers social media, websites, messaging and online games. For the first time, companies will be required to protect us from serious harmful materials and conduct resulting from the products they sell. These serious harms include child sexual abuse material, grooming and image based abuse. In addition, companies must protect children from specific harmful material, including content promoting eating disorders, self-harm, misogyny and dangerous stunts.

Tech companies will need to give users new tools that increase an individual's ability to control what they see, rather than be subject to the invisible whims of the algorithm. At least once a year, they will have to assess the risks their own products create and act on them. The cost of taking action is no excuse. There'll be fines for breaching the duty of up to $109 million. These could and should be higher, and that's why I'll be proposing a sensible amendment to calculate penalties as a percentage of revenue. This would make our legislation consistent with similar legislation in other jurisdictions which places higher penalties on companies, recognising the enormous quantum of profits that these companies enjoy.

The bill also gives the eSafety Commissioner new powers to take down nudify apps. It halves the time platforms have to act on cyberbullying and abuse complaints before the eSafety Commissioner can step in, from 48 hours to 24 hours. It starts to prise open the black box of platforms so that independent researchers can finally look into how those algorithms actually work.

Opponents of this bill claim that it's about censorship, that government wants to control what you see and read. The obvious response to that objection is: if there's someone controlling what you see, it's the social media companies that develop the algorithms, with no scrutiny or guardrails—and they do so entirely in pursuit of profit. This bill is about giving you more control to determine what you watch, what you listen to, what you read and, therefore, how you think and feel.

Let's just take a step back and remember what it is that's being restricted here—child sex abuse material, terrorism, nonconsensual fake nudes, rape threats. Which of these do you want to allow unrestricted? For children, preventing their exposure to pornography, to material that encourages disordered eating or to attitudes hostile towards women seems, to me, eminently sensible and reasonable. I welcome the government's decision to drop the power for a minister to add new categories of harm without first coming back to the parliament. Limiting this ministerial discretion, I believe, is an important step and should put to rest the claims that this bill is about censorship.

The bill could be stronger. I'm going to support the amendments put by my colleagues from the crossbench. It should ensure that opt-in to algorithms is the default, and that's what the campaign led by Chanel Contos of Fix Our Feeds is calling for. It would mean that you have to intentionally choose to use particular algorithms rather than being nudged into them by the tech companies. The bill could include amendments to protect children from AI companion chatbots, including attachment hacking where tech companies manipulate people into emotional connections with AI. I applaud, in particular, the member for Curtin for her leadership on this issue, showing what constructive, courageous leadership from the crossbench can look like.

More broadly, this bill doesn't address every harm caused by social media and other online services. We still have so much more to understand about how these services and the companies operating them drive radicalisation and polarisation. The bill's own explanatory memorandum points to research showing social media can accelerate young people's paths into violent extremism. We see the same forces pulling our politics further apart, making it harder to talk with one another, disagree respectfully, trust each other and find common ground. If we want safer and more connected communities, it's time to put the platforms in their place and the people in control. I commend the bill with the amendments brought by the crossbench to the House.

speaker: Tom French
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
The coalition has launched a petition to kill the bill. Apparently, the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 is government censorship. That is an extraordinary description of legislation that gives Australians more control over what they see online while requiring technology companies to take responsibility for the products they design. I've been on Facebook since around 2008 and on Myspace before that. I'm starting to give away my age! Then again, back then it was a terrific way to keep in touch with friends and family, particularly while I was travelling overseas. When I returned to Australia, it helped me stay connected with the people I'd met along the way. I could see their photographs, hear their news and maintain friendships across thousands of kilometres. It was simple: you followed someone because you wanted to hear from them, and, for the most part, you did.

These days, Facebook is a different experience. Posts from friends and family are still there, but they're sprinkled throughout my feed like salt and pepper in between a sponsored post, videos from strangers, arguments I never asked to join and advertisements for things I have no intention of buying. I joined Facebook to keep up with people I actually know; now, I spend more time scrolling past people I don't. Apparently the algorithm knows what I want better than I do.

The technology writer Cory Doctorow has explained how platforms arrive at this point. At first, a service offers something genuinely useful. It connects friends, helps small businesses find customers and allows people to share information. We join because it works. Then, when enough people depend on it, the company starts prioritising advertisers and paying customers. The experience changes. What we choose to see competes with whatever keeps us looking at the screen. Eventually, the platform starts squeezing those businesses too. A local business spends years building an audience only to discover it may have to pay to reach the people who already chose to follow it. The experience gets worse, but leaving becomes harder because our friends, customers and communities are all still there. That is not just a complaint about the advertisements; it is about the enormous power platforms acquire over connections Australians have built themselves.

It brings us to My Feed, My Way. Under the proposed rules, Australians over 16 will be able to choose whether their primary social media feed contains posts from accounts they follow or personalised recommendations selected by an algorithm. If you like the recommendations, you could opt in. If you prefer posts from friends, family and chosen creators, you could choose that instead. The choice should be clear, easy to make and persistent. A platform should not quietly reverse it each time you open the application or make the alternative impossible to use. It should not take a science degree, six settings screens and the patience of a saint to see what your friends are posting.

The detailed feed requirements are proposed through a legislative instrument enabled by the bill, not spelled out word for word in the primary legislation. That distinction's important and parliament can scrutinise how the rules operate, but the underlying principle is straightforward: the person holding the phone should have a meaningful say in what appears on it. The coalition calls this censorship, but I struggle to see how giving someone the choice to reject recommendations silences the person whose content is not recommended. Nobody has the right to appear in a stranger's feed simply because a company's algorithm predicts that an argument will generate engagement. And, if choosing your own feed is censorship, what should we call a system in which a technology company chooses it for you?

There is another question we need to ask. For years, social media companies have presented themselves as platforms where people post content, but those services are not passive noticeboards. They select, rank and recommend posts. They decide which video plays next, which controversy is amplified and which content reaches people who never asked to follow its creator. Those are decisions about distribution. They can have commercial and human consequences. Traditional publishers carry legal responsibilities associated with what they publish. The High Court's decision in Voller demonstrated that facilitating third-party comments can, in particular circumstances, amount to publication for defamation law. That decision did not declare every technology platform a publisher of everything it hosts, and this bill does not do so either—but the policy question remains. When a business activity recommends and amplifies content for profit, what responsibility should accompany that power? There is a difference between allowing someone to speak and deliberately putting their words in front of a million strangers.

I do not suggest that every recommendation amounts to an editorial endorsement—a newspaper editor and a recommendation system are not identical—but we cannot ignore the decisions made by the people who built and tune those systems. They determine the incentives, the measures of success and the way content travels. If a company can optimise its system to maximise advertising revenue, it can also be required to assess how that system exposes people to foreseeable harm. That is a more useful discussion than pretending the platform has no role once someone presses 'Publish'. The digital duty of care begins to address the risks created by the system doing the amplification, and the principle should be familiar to anyone who has worked in an industry where safety is taken seriously. In workplaces across Australia, employers have duties to identify hazards and control risks. They cannot simply wait for a worker to be injured, hand them a complaint form and declare the system successful. We apply similar expectations to cars, food and children's toys. If a product has a foreseeable defect, the company designing it has a responsibility to act. Online services should not get a different rule simply because their products apply on screens.

This bill requires providers to assess the risks arising from their services, including risky design features, and take effective measures to reduce them. It is about prevention, not just removing a harmful post after somebody has already been hurt. It also changes the way online safety is regulated. Today there are 17 industry developed codes and standards spread across different services and obligations. The bill replaces that complicated framework with an overarching duty of care after a transition period. Rather than waiting for the industry to draft a new code each time technology changes, providers must assess new risks and respond to them. Companies remain responsible for designing their services, but safety is not simply left to rules written by the companies being regulated. The duty applies to specified serious harms affecting adults, including child sexual exploitation, explicit threats of violence, intimate image abuse and material encouraging suicide or serious self-harm. Children receive additional protections against pornography, material encouraging eating disorders, dangerous stunts, bullying and hostility towards women, as well as design features associated with harmful behaviour. This is not about outlawing political disagreement; it is about defined categories of harm and appropriate steps to reduce the risk that online services expose Australians to.

The government has already introduced the social media minimum age of 16. According to the updated government figures, more than five million underage accounts have been deactivated, removed or restricted. That does not mean the job is finished. There are still underage accounts, and the eSafety Commissioner is investigating possible noncompliance by major platforms. (Quorum formed) The answer to noncompliance is to enforce the law, not to abandon the expectation that that platform should follow it. The figures also describe survey respondents reporting more sport and better sleep, alongside reduced exposure to some harmful experiences. These are early findings, not a declaration of victory. The responsibility remains on platforms to meet the law and on regulators to test what is happening in practice. The risks to children extend beyond social media accounts. They use online games, messaging services and artificial intelligence chatbots, including products that imitate a friend or adviser. Parents cannot expect every interaction or understand every feature of every new product. Children should not be expected to recognise unsafe design before the provider has any responsibility to intervene.

The bill also addresses a particularly disturbing use of artificial intelligence: apps that generate fake nude images without consent. A perfectly ordinary photograph can be turned into an intimate image the person never agreed to create. For the person targeted, especially a child, the damage can be devastating. The commissioner will have powers to require action against apps and websites predominantly designed and used for generating that material. When serious cyberbullying or adult cyberabuse is reported, the bill reduces the waiting period before the commissioner may intervene in relevant cases from 48 hours to 24 hours. Australians should not have to submit a complaint into a digital black hole and wonder whether anybody has read it.

There is another issue that those opposite have become particularly excited about: sock puppet accounts. It sounds sinister, but in reality these regulated test accounts are rather like mystery shoppers for the internet. If a shop says it checks identification before selling an age restricted product, an inspector can test whether that actually happens.So why should regulators have to accept a technology company's word that its safety systems work? Can an adult profile contact a child through an online game? Can a younger teenager open an account without age checks? How does an AI service respond to attempts to produce abusive images? Those are practical questions. A test account can help answer them.

These provisions allow appropriately regulated testing and provide a pathway for approved researchers to obtain relevant safety data. They are not a licence for government to plant political opinion in people's newsfeeds. They are a means of checking compliance. We do not let companies mark their own homework, and there is no reason to start with big tech.

The coalition has also criticised powers that were removed before this bill was introduced. The proposed ministerial power to add new categories of 'harmful material' was removed. The final bill contains protections for professional news material. It does not establish a general regime for deciding whether political claims are true or false. Those are facts about the legislation before parliament, whatever a petition might suggest. Nor does the duty mean a neighbourhood florist's basic website will be regulated as if it were one of the world's largest social media platforms. The framework is risk based, with minimal obligations intended for low-risk services and guidance to be provided by the eSafety Commissioner. Technology should serve the people who use it, not the other way around. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Tracey Roberts
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
() (): The incorporated speech read as follows—

I would like to speak in support of the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026. This bill is about a simple but powerful principle: the companies that build the digital spaces where Australians live, learn, play and connect have a responsibility to keep those spaces safe. For too long, we have asked parents, teachers, young people and community organisations to carry the burden of online harm on their own. This legislation shifts that responsibility back to where much of it belongs—with the platforms and services that design the products, set the algorithms and profit from our attention.

In Pearce, I hear about this every week. I hear from parents in Butler, Tapping, Yanchep, Clarkson, Banksia Grove and Quinns Rocks who are worried about what their children encounter online. I sit on multiple school boards within Pearce and hear from teachers and school leaders who see the effects of cyberbullying, sleepless nights and harmful content flowing into classrooms the next morning. I hear from local sporting clubs, youth groups and community organisations who do extraordinary work keeping young people connected, active and supported but who know that the online world can undermine that good work in an instant. Pearce is one of the largest and fastest-growing parts of Australia. Our community is full of young families, new schools, new suburbs and new opportunities. That growth brings energy and optimism, but it also means many parents are navigating the challenges of raising children in a digital age while trying to work, run households and keep up with technology that changes faster than any of us can reasonably expect. They should not have to become experts in algorithms, privacy settings and platform design simply to keep their children safe.

The Albanese Labor government has already taken world-leading action to protect Australians from online harm, particularly young people. We began by establishing a minimum age for social media accounts, because we recognised that children deserve a childhood that is not shaped by endless scrolling, targeted content and commercial pressure. The early results are encouraging. More than five million under-age accounts have been deactivated, removed or restricted. A YouGov survey found that 30 per cent of young Australians aged between 13 and 15 are now spending more time playing sport. Twenty-seven per cent report better sleep. Online bullying is down nine per cent, and exposure to inappropriate and violent content has fallen by 18 per cent. These are not abstract statistics. For a young person in Pearce, that can mean more time at footy training, netball, surf lifesaving, dance or cricket and less time lying awake at night with a phone in their hand. It can mean a better night's sleep, a better morning at school and a better chance to simply be a kid.

But we also know there is more to do. There are still too many children under 16 on social media. That does not mean the law has failed. It means some platforms are failing to comply with the law. The eSafety Commissioner is currently investigating alleged noncompliance by five platforms: Instagram, Meta, TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat. Australians expect the rules to apply to everyone, including the largest technology companies in the world. This bill strengthens the framework so that safety is not treated as an optional extra or a public-relations exercise.

The next step in our mission is the digital duty of care. This bill will set basic safety standards for the digital services Australians use every day, just as we set safety standards for food, cars, medicines and children's toys. When we buy a car, we expect seatbelts, airbags and brakes that work. When we buy a cot or a toy for a child, we expect it has been designed with their safety in mind. We do not accept that a manufacturer can say, 'We built the product, but what happens next is not our problem.' Yet, for too long, that has effectively been the approach of parts of the digital economy. The digital duty of care will require platforms to protect Australian children from harmful content and harmful features. It will also give parents better tools to keep their families safe online. Importantly, it is not about telling adults what they can and cannot do online. Adults should be free to access lawful content and make their own choices. What this bill does is require platforms to give people more control over the content and features they use while ensuring that services are not designed in ways that cause serious harm.

At the heart of the duty is the creation of a safe online environment. All Australians should be protected from seriously harmful and illegal content. Children and young people under 18 should receive additional protection from content and features that can harm them. For the first time, the bill sets minimum standards for the features digital companies use. Services will need to conduct annual risk assessments of the harms their features could cause to Australians. They will need to put systems in place to prevent risky features from causing harm. And, for social media services, they will need to provide user-empowerment tools that give people over the age of 16 genuine choice about what appears in their feed. These are practical, sensible obligations. They ask companies to think about harm before it occurs, rather than waiting for a tragedy, a complaint or a headline. They ask companies to design safety into their products from the beginning. That is what we expect in every other industry, and it is what families in Pearce rightly expect from the apps their children use.

The protections for children in this bill are comprehensive. Online services, including online games and Al chatbots, will need to protect under-18s from harmful content such as pornography; material or conduct that encourages, promotes or instructs disordered eating; material that encourages hostile attitudes towards women or gender equality; content that glorifies crime or encourages dangerous stunts; and abuse, harassment or bullying. The bill also captures any other material or conduct that may cause serious harm to children. Children will also be protected from design features that have negative behavioural impacts. We know that some features are deliberately engineered to keep young people engaged for as long as possible: infinite scroll, constant notifications, streaks, rewards and recommendation systems that learn exactly how to hold attention. These features may be good for engagement metrics, but they can be terrible for sleep, concentration, mental health and family life. When a child in Yanchep or Two Rocks is losing sleep because an app is designed to keep them awake, that is not an unavoidable feature of modern life. It is a design choice, and it should carry responsibility.

The bill also protects adults from seriously harmful content. It addresses child sexual exploitation and abuse material, grooming, sexual violence, non-consensual intimate images and fake nude material, extreme violence and cruelty, explicit threats of physical violence, gender based violence, menacing or harassing conduct, content encouraging suicide or self-harm, animal cruelty, terrorist content and violent extremist material. These harms are not hypothetical. They affect real people, real families and real communities. Every member in this place will know of constituents who have been targeted, threatened or traumatised online. The digital duty of care is not about controlling adults. It is about choice. When someone buys a new appliance, government sets minimum safety standards, but the consumer still chooses what to buy. In the same way, this bill sets minimum safety standards for digital services while preserving lawful choice for adults, provided that choice does not cause serious harm to others.

One of the most important reforms is My Feed, My Way. Algorithmic recommender systems and doomscrolling cause real harm to young people, which is why we have set a minimum age of 16 for social media. But, for people over 16 and for adults, social media platforms make substantial profits from using our information and shaping what we see. They should give us choice and follow basic rules, just like every other industry. Under this bill, social media platforms will have to give Australians choice over the primary feed they see when they first open an app. People should be able to opt in or opt out of the algorithm. If someone wants a feed made up of friends, family and creators they have chosen to follow, the platform must allow that by default. No-one should be forced into an algorithm filled with content from people they do not follow or subscribe to. And, if someone is happy to receive recommended content, they should be able to choose the kinds of content they do and do not want to see. This is a meaningful change. It recognises that people are not merely products to be sorted, targeted and monetised. It gives users back a degree of agency over their own attention.

The bill also takes decisive action against nudify apps. There is no place in Australia for tools designed to create non-consensual deepfake images or child sexual abuse material. These tools are abhorrent. The bill empowers the eSafety Commissioner to take down apps and websites that are predominantly designed or used to generate fake nude material. It also defines fake nude material as seriously harmful, requiring platforms to protect all Australians from it. The scale of this problem is deeply concerning. On average, one in 33 children have reported that someone has created a nude image of them using Al. On average, one in 25 Australians have reported being victimised by deepfake pornography. Behind those figures are young people who feel humiliated, frightened and powerless. In a connected community like Pearce, where young people know one another through school, sport and local networks, the damage can spread quickly and be devastating. This bill sends a clear message: technology that facilitates this abuse has no safe harbour.

The bill also strengthens complaint and accountability mechanisms. It reduces the required response time for cyberbullying and abuse complaints from 48 hours to 24 hours. It empowers the eSafety Commissioner to set minimum standards for complaints and dispute processes, because too many people have submitted an online form only to receive no meaningful response. It allows the commissioner to use sock-puppet accounts to test whether services are complying with the law, and it gives university-accredited researchers access to data about online safety. Better evidence means better policy, better enforcement and better protection. Failure to comply with the digital duty of care will attract penalties of up to $109.2 million. That is consistent with other Australian penalties designed to protect consumers. It is not about punishing companies for the sake of it. It is about ensuring that safety obligations have consequences. A fine that is too small becomes merely a cost of doing business. A meaningful penalty changes corporate behaviour.

This legislation is not anti technology. It is pro safety, pro family and pro choice. It recognises the enormous benefits of digital connection while refusing to accept serious harm as the price of innovation. It supports parents who want their children to benefit from technology without being exposed to its worst excesses. It supports young people who deserve to learn, create and connect without being targeted by predators, bullies or harmful algorithms. And it supports adults who want transparency, control and basic safety from the services they use every day. For the people of Pearce, this bill is about dignity and protection. It is about a parent in Alkimos being able to trust that the apps on their child's phone meet basic safety standards. It is about a teenager in Butler having more control over what appears on their screen. It is about a local sporting club knowing that young members are less likely to be drawn into harmful online content after training. It is about a community that wants technology to serve people, not exploit them.

The Albanese Labor government is taking world-leading action because Australians deserve nothing less. We have started with a minimum age for social media, and we are now building the next layer of protection through a digital duty of care. This bill asks digital services to do what every responsible business should do: identify foreseeable risks, act to prevent harm, respond when things go wrong and put people before profit. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Sophie Scamps
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise to speak on the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026. In this House on Monday, Helen Haines's husband, Phil, asked for us to ensure that the horrific attack she endured last week would mean something. The attack on our dear colleague last week brought into sharp focus the toxicity of online environments and the abuse and threats that not only politicians but Australians across the country are facing every day. It shone a spotlight on the intentional stoking of online outrage, grievance and anger by AI algorithms that are designed to drive profits for the tech bro billionaires. Quite simply, outrage sells. This growing online rage is dividing our nation and our communities. As this culture of abusive rhetoric becomes increasingly normalised online, it's now spilling out into the real world. Vulnerable people, people with mental ill health, are being radicalised with a rapidity never before seen and at younger and younger ages. This is not healthy for individuals, and it is not healthy for our nation. As Phil Haines said, we have a choice right now. We can choose to inflame this toxic rhetoric or tame it.

So the introduction and debate of this bill is extremely timely. It presents a critical opportunity to protect Australians from the growing harms of an increasingly toxic and harmful digital world. It is our opportunity to finally hold big tech accountable and put the wellbeing of Australians ahead of the profits of some of the most powerful multinational tech companies in the world. Quite disingenuously, the coalition and One Nation will try to argue that this bill is about restricting freedom of speech and expression. Nothing could be further from the truth. It is, in fact, about putting the power and choice back in the hands of Australians. And, at its heart, this bill is about prevention of harm to Australians. It would place a duty of care on digital platforms to identify and reduce foreseeable online harms. It would require platforms to take reasonable steps to safeguard their users with stronger protections for children and young people. It would also give Australians greater control over what appears in their social media feeds. Importantly, it would strengthen the powers of the eSafety Commissioner and introduce penalties for companies that fail to meet their obligations.

These are important reforms, and I welcome them, but we must ensure this legislation is as strong as possible and does in practice what it is intended to do. For too long we have allowed the big tech companies to operate unfettered and without boundaries we would expect of all other industries. We would never accept children's toys or bikes, for example, being sold without proper safety standards. Yet we've allowed social media platforms into our homes, our schools and our children's bedrooms without demanding the same duty of care. Research shows that 63 per cent of Australian children aged 10 to 17 years were exposed to harmful online content in the previous year and 74 per cent have been exposed at some point in their lives. Exposure to cyberbullying, online abuse, self-harm content and other harmful material is recognised by the eSafety Commissioner and mental health experts as a risk factor contributing to youth mental ill health and suicide risk.

Too often it is shock, outrage and anger that keeps us engaged, so that is what the tech bro algorithms serve up constantly. I see it firsthand. This toxic online culture is getting worse, and it's becoming normalised. People talk in a way they would never do face-to-face. A quick look at my own Facebook page is case in point. Comments say: 'Bullshit clown', 'Look at you. All stupid and shit', 'Stupid bitch'. These are just a handful of the comments I, and so many others here in this House, receive on a regular basis. As a member of parliament, I accept that public scrutiny and robust debate are an important and crucial part of this job. Freedom of political expression is fundamental to our democracy, and we must defend the right to disagree. But intimidation, harassment and abuse should never be the price of participating in public life. It weakens our democracy. Research commissioned by Women for Election found that nine out of 10 female politicians and candidates had received abusive threats online, including those of a sexual nature. Of course, this has a chilling impact on our democracy. Freedom of speech does not mean tech companies should have a free pass to amplify abuse and division for profit.

This bill is not about suppressing legitimate debate or unpopular opinions. It's about making big tech responsible for the systems they design and the harms they can prevent. Nowhere is this responsibility more important than when it comes to our children. Parents across my electorate of Mackellar are deeply concerned about the impact of social media on their kids, and, yes, they're still getting around the limits. A mother of a young girl wrote to me recently. She said she was horrified by the onslaught of violent and misogynistic content across social media, and how these key messages feed back into our community and our schools. Her concern is one I hear repeatedly. Parents are worried about what their children are seeing online. Many children can circumvent that 16-year-old limit and find themselves immersed in an online world that is uncensored and harmful.

We know that young people who spend more than three hours a day on social media face double the risk of mental health problems, including symptoms of depression and anxiety. We know that harmful content, unhealthy comparisons, cyberbullying and sleep disruption can and do affect young people's wellbeing. We know that algorithms can repeatedly expose vulnerable users to material that reinforces their insecurities. Prevention must be at the heart of our response.

Very recent research from the eSafety Commissioner shows that almost 50 per cent of Australian kids have been exposed to offensive, sexist or hurtful content about women and girls, fight videos, dangerous challenges, content encouraging unhealthy eating or exercise, and hate based content targeting identity groups. In 2024, researchers from the University College London examined how TikTok's algorithms delivered misogynistic content to accounts modelled on teenage boys. They found that, after just five days, misogynistic content increased from 13 per cent to 56 per cent of recommended videos. The boys were not necessarily searching for hatred towards women. Some accounts began with interest in fitness, self-improvement or loneliness, but the algorithms increasingly directed them towards content built around anger and resentment towards women. This is deeply disturbing because it demonstrates that young people do not have to actively seek out harmful content to be exposed to it. I have two sons, and, like many parents, I don't want them logging on to social media to watch sports highlights or fitness videos only to be automatically exposed to content that demeans women or promotes harmful ideas about masculinity. This is particularly concerning because adolescence is the time when young people are forming their identities and are highly susceptible to influence. They are learning what healthy relationships look like and developing their understanding of respect, consent and equality.

The consequences of harmful content do not stay on our screens. A recent study conducted by the University of Melbourne found that young men are more likely to hold hostile attitudes to women. Amongst other alarming findings, it found that 24.7 per cent of teenage boys believe that feminism is damaging to society and should be resisted with violence if necessary. Toxic and extreme attitudes are becoming increasingly normalised online and are now spilling into our real-world interactions, including in schools and in classrooms. This is not just an online safety issue anymore. This bill is also about preventing abuse of and violence against women.

We're also seeing the devastating consequences of so-called nudify apps. These AI-powered tools can turn an ordinary photograph of a young person into a sexually explicit image without their knowledge or consent. Girls and young women are overwhelmingly the targets. These images are being used to humiliate, bully, harass and even blackmail children, with devastating consequences for their mental health. In 2025, Australia's eSafety Commissioner took action against nudify services attracting around 100,000 visits a month from Australians. These services had been used to create sexually explicit deepfakes of Australian schoolchildren. This technology is facilitating sexual abuse, and we have a duty to ensure that these companies prevent these types of harm.

The government's proposed My Feed, My Way reforms are a welcome step, allowing people to choose between algorithmically recommended content and the content from the people and pages they choose to follow. Algorithmically recommended content should be opt-in, not opt-out. This is especially important for young people. We cannot expect a child to understand how a sophisticated recommendation system is shaping their emotions, interests and beliefs, and we should not put the entire burden on parents to fight algorithms developed by some of the world's most powerful technology companies.

We must also confront the addictive nature of social media. These platforms are not designed to simply entertain us. Many are deliberately designed to keep us coming back. Infinite scrolling means there is never a natural point to stop. Autoplay delivers the next video before we have decided whether we want to watch it, and notifications draw us back into the app. Likes and comments encourage us to keep checking. There are striking similarities between these techniques and the psychological mechanisms used in poker machines. We regulate poker machines because we understand the dangers of their design and intention. Why should we ignore those same risks with digital platforms? We should not wait until harm has occurred before we act.

Then there's the prolific and violent pornography that our sons and young men are frequently being delivered by AI algorithms and exposed to day in, day out. This has led young people to believe that strangulation is a normal part of sexual relations. This had devastating consequences in my electorate of Mackellar not long ago, with the tragic loss of a beautiful young life recently. Also increasingly commonplace is anoxic brain injury.

The organisation It's time we talked has spent almost two decades working to prevent the harms of pornography on children and young people. It warns of the growing normalisation of sexual strangulation. Amplified messages on social media that portray dangerous sexual practices are contributing to this normalisation. It's time we talked are seeing the consequences of the large-scale promotion of gender inequality, sexual aggression and violence. They are calling for stronger action to prevent the normalisation of harmful sexual practices. They want a regulator with the authority and the tools to hold digital platforms accountable. I support that call. We cannot allow engagement algorithms to help normalise dangerous behaviour while companies evade responsibility for foreseeable risks, and we cannot continue to treat the online world as though it's disconnected from the real one.

But strong obligations must also come with strong accountability. Australians need access to free and independent external dispute resolution when digital platforms fail them. While the bill provides for stronger internal complaints and dispute resolution processes, an internal complaints process alone is not enough. For many Australians, dealing with a large digital platform can feel like shouting into the void. Accounts are hacked, businesses are locked out of platforms they rely on and harmful content is reported but not removed. Complaints are met with automated responses, endless online forms or no meaningful response at all. And when the platform fails to resolve the problem, where does the consumer turn? Too often there's nowhere to go. We should expand the jurisdiction of the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman to cover the digital world. The TIO is an established and trusted scheme. Expanding this model would give Australians a practical avenue for redress, and I will be moving amendments to that effect.

Today's bill is about the kind of world we want to create both online and outside—one where teenagers are manipulated by addictive designs built by teams of engineers or behavioural experts, one where people cannot be targeted simply because outrage, division and engagement are profitable and one where we can engage respectfully and robustly in debate without doing harm. We have a responsibility right now to Helen, to Phil and to all Australians. This is our duty of care, and we must uphold it.

I move the amendment as circulated in my name:

That all words after "House" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:

", whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading:

(1) notes that:

(a) people, small businesses and community organisations need an accessible and affordable avenue for redress when they are in dispute with large digital platforms, including where their accounts are suspended or terminated, or they are otherwise adversely affected by a platform's decisions or conduct;

(b) an independent ombudsman is needed to provide accessible, independent and effective dispute resolution for users of online services; and

(c) there is strong support for expanding the remit of the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman to cover digital platforms, including from the public, consumer advocates, legal and community organisations, academics and parliamentarians; and

(2) calls on the Government to:

(a) require appropriate online service providers, as determined by a legislative instrument, to join and abide by an External Dispute Resolution scheme operated by the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman; and

(b) expand the remit of the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman to establish an Online Services Ombudsman, providing independent, accessible and effective dispute resolution for users of digital services".

speaker: Julie-Ann Campbell
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Every parent wants to believe that when they send their child out into the world, that child will be safe. Every parent knows the fear of not being able to protect them from everything the world might throw at them. That used to mean waiting with bated breath on the porch, as the sun came down, for them to ride in on their bike. But the world our children are growing up in has changed. Their lives extend far beyond the school gate, the local park or the sidelines of a weekend sport.

The online world is now woven into how children learn, socialise and come to understand themselves, who they are and the world around them. But that connection comes with risks. Through social media, online games and other digital platforms, children can be exposed to harmful content, online bullying and dangerous influences that can affect their safety and wellbeing. It has quietly slipped into their pockets and into their bedrooms. We cannot leave parents on the digital front line to fight by themselves.

The companies that design and profit from these platforms must take responsibility for the harm their services can cause. If big tech can spend billions of dollars to get you hooked on an algorithm that keeps you coming back for more, it is not too much to ask for those same companies to keep you safe from harm. The question is not whether children should be able to participate in the digital world.
