It is whether the companies shaping that world should be required to take greater responsibility for the harm their services can cause. If you build it, you have to be responsible for it. The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 builds on our social media minimum age reforms by setting clearer expectations for online services, requiring them to take a more proactive approach to safety and giving Australians greater choice over their online experiences.

I think about this issue not only as a member of parliament, but also as a parent. My daughter is three years old. She is at an age when the world is full of things to discover every day—questions to ask and new experiences to explore. Like any parent, I want her to grow up with the freedom to learn, to make friends, to develop her interests and to find her own place in this world and in this country. I also want her to grow up in a society that takes her safety seriously. Technology will continue to change, and the online world she encounters as a teenager will almost certainly look different from the one that we know today. I hope that is because of a Labor government introducing a digital duty of care.

We have the opportunity to set a clear standard for the world that she'll grow up in. Companies that profit from digital services must take responsibility for the harm they cause. This is not a new concept at all. In the 18th and 19th centuries, unscrupulous bakers used to put chalk and sawdust in bread to thicken it out—to make more of it. That doesn't happen anymore, and it doesn't happen because we have standards, because there are rules and because those who made the bread needed to be accountable for it. We see those standards in every facet of our lives, from cars to manufacturing and retail.

This is the extension of that into the digital world. These platforms are not neutral spaces that live in a vacuum. Companies make decisions about what appears in a feed, what gets recommended next, how long people are encouraged to stay online and how easily they can report abuse. Those decisions shape people's experiences. Harmful material can affect how young people see themselves and others. Features that encourage prolonged engagement can interfere with sleep, and online bullying can follow a child beyond that school gate; it can follow them home. Adults, too, can experience threats, harassment and the non-consensual sharing of intimate images. These are not problems that can be solved simply by telling people to log off. That's not how the world works. We need to address the risks at their source, where digital platforms have the capacity to prevent harm.

This government has shown that it's prepared to act. In December last year, the Albanese Labor government introduced Australia's social media minimum age law, setting a minimum age of 16 for accounts on covered platforms. Since then, more than five million underage accounts have been removed, restricted or deactivated. A YouGov survey earlier this year found encouraging figures among 13- to 15-year-olds. Thirty per cent reported more time playing sport, 27 per cent reported better sleep, online bullying was down by nine per cent, and exposure to inappropriate and violent content fell by 18 per cent. You don't have to listen to what is happening; it's there in the numbers.

These results ask us to answer a bigger question: what kind of childhood do we want our children to have in Australia? One where they face constant threats from an ever-present digital world? Or one where they have more time to play, better sleep and less exposure to harm? The social media minimum-age law was an important first step. But protecting young Australians online means going further than just setting that age limit. We must also address how digital services operate, the content they promote and the features they use to keep people engaged. The eSafety Commissioner is already investigating whether major platforms are meeting their existing obligations. We must ensure that those obligations are enforced while building on that work to make online services safer by design, day by day. That is the next step: a digital duty of care that requires digital services to take greater responsibility for preventing harm.

The purpose of this bill is pretty straightforward. The bill will establish basic safety standards for online services, including social media platforms, online games and AI chatbots. Services will have a positive obligation to protect Australians from seriously harmful and illegal material and conduct and to protect people under 18 from material conduct and features that are harmful to young people. The bill shifts that focus towards prevention, stopping harm in its tracks before it becomes a reality.

Providers will need to assess risks associated with their service's features and put systems in place to prevent harm, including through annual risk assessments. In other words, companies should not have to wait until someone is harmed before asking whether a feature is safe. They should be considering those risks when they design their services and when they decide how those services should work. What is the impact on our young people? What is the impact on people streaming on their services? We expect manufacturers to consider product risks and to act when they identify those problems. Digital services should not be exempt from that basic principle that has been around for a very long time. The bill strengthens protections for young Australians against content that promotes eating disorders, glorifies crime or dangerous stunts, causes serious distress, or encourages hostility towards women and gender equality.

We want young Australians to learn, connect and participate online, but not at any cost, and not in an environment where harmful material circulates without safeguards, where seatbelts have never been required to be installed. The bill also addresses design features that can encourage children to stay online late into the night and to lose sleep. This is not about eliminating every risk; it is about requiring technology companies to take reasonable, proactive steps to reduce the harm that we know is happening.

The bill also empowers the eSafety Commissioner to take action against apps and websites that are predominantly designed or used to generate fake nude material. These so-called nudify services can be used to create intimate images of people without their consent. The consequences for those targeted can be deeply distressing. Services designed to facilitate this kind of abuse shouldn't be able to operate without meaningful consequences. The bill reduces the required response time for cyberbullying and abuse complaints from 48 hours to 24 hours and empowers the eSafety Commissioner to set minimum standards for platforms' internal complaints and dispute-resolution processes. It also allows the commissioner to use covert accounts to test compliance and enables university accredited researchers to access online safety data. This helps assess services' performance rather than relying solely on what the companies say.

The bill is also about giving people more choice. Through the My Feed, My Way initiative, social media services will be required to give Australians aged 16 and over a choice about the primary feed they seek. People will be able to choose a feed based on the pages and the people they follow, rather than relying only on algorithmically recommended material. Those who prefer personalised recommendations should also have choices about what they see. In my household, my partner, Mark, doesn't tell me what I can watch on television. Why should I let Mark Zuckerberg tell me what I can scroll on my phone if I don't want to? This is not about the government deciding what adults should think, what they should read or what they should watch. It is about giving people greater control over their online experience while requiring services to take responsibility for serious harm. In short, this ain't about freedom of speech; it's about freedom from harm.

Obligations mean nothing if there are no consequences for failing to meet them. Under this bill, failure to comply with the digital duty of care can attract penalties of up to $109.2 million. That is substantial—and appropriately so. Online safety obligations are serious legal responsibilities because they not only affect our kids, our young people and every Australian but impact on our society as a whole. At the same time, strong safety standards must have clear boundaries. The government has listened to concerns raised during consultation and made changes to the bill. Protecting people from serious harm is not the same as censoring legitimate debate. There is a difference between expressing unpopular opinion and threatening someone with violence, just as there is a difference between lawful discussion and the non-consensual creation of intimate images. We can uphold freedom of expression while requiring companies to take reasonable steps to address those serious risks. For the bill itself, as it progresses, we should consider genuine improvements constructively while keeping its purpose in view.

The question is whether we are prepared to establish reasonable standards and hold big tech accountable. I believe that we are right to do so. Australians have strengthened safety standards in workplaces; we've strengthened safety standards in cars and in everyday products. The social media minimum age law was an important step in online safety, and the digital duty of care is the next. It puts Australia at the forefront, as a world leader in this space, and we watch as the rest of the globe looks to us for that leadership. It will require online platforms to assess risks, prevent harm, protect young people, respond quicker to complaints and give users greater choice. Most importantly, it makes clear that responsibility for online safety cannot rest with parents alone. We must hold the companies creating these platforms to account.

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I'd like to begin by sharing the experience of a mother in my electorate of Griffith who contacted me many months ago about the devastating impact an AI companion chatbot has had on her family. Her experience is deeply confronting, and it demonstrates why we cannot leave the safety of Australian children in the hands of technology companies that have repeatedly failed to protect them.

This mother said:

I am writing to you first as a mother.

My eldest daughter was seriously harmed by an AI companion chatbot when she was 12 years old.

I am also a technology founder who builds privacy compliance infrastructure for regulated industries, so I come to this issue from both sides: as a parent living with its consequences, and as someone whose work is in regulatory compliance and who understands what is at stake in getting it right.

In December 2024, my eldest daughter, then 12, was harmed by an AI companion app called Talkie AI.

She was first introduced to an AI roleplay website around the middle of 2024, at school, on a friend's phone.

From there it escalated quickly, and the harm built over an extended period of conversations rather than a single exchange.

During those conversations an AI character told her she was worthless and made references to self-harm.

Reading the exchanges back afterwards, they had the clear hallmarks of grooming and gaslighting.

This is not a historical event that we have moved past.

My daughter is in regular therapy.

The experience affects her every day.

She recognises it as a problem and does not know how to stop returning to it, and what we are managing at home now has the characteristics of an addiction.

Minimising her access helps, but it does not undo the harm already done.

Despite building close to a best-case home environment, including a physical device lockbox, a router with DNS-level filtering, device-level controls, a browser-free phone, and more than 100 AI roleplay and companion domains blocked manually, my children can still reach these platforms.

My younger daughter has since also been exposed, this time at home, through her older sister.

The responsible-parent ceiling is not high enough.

Debate interrupted.

speaker: Jim Chalmers
heading: BILLS
subheading: Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 4) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I move:

That this bill be now read a second time.

Today, the Albanese Labor government is delivering on our commitment to boost innovation and investment through the tax system.

The reforms we are introducing today are part of our comprehensive plan to support businesses and grow our economy.

They are a key part of our ambitious tax reform package, which is also making it easier for Australians to buy their first home, cutting income taxes for workers again and again and better aligning the tax treatment of work and asset income.

A thriving private sector is the key driver of economic growth.

Our long-term growth agenda is built on that fact, and the reforms we are introducing today are as well.

These reforms give the private sector tools and tax concessions to help them succeed in an increasingly competitive world.

The bill provides more certainty for investors and more incentives for innovation, building on the $3.8 billion in new tax relief and concessions for businesses and start-ups.

These reforms will mean our tax concessions are targeted at starting a new innovative business and investing in a new build, helping Australians to invest their money, grow their wealth, and boost growth.

Importantly, the bill also provides more flexibility for businesses to meet their tax obligations.

Cash flow is crucial for small businesses which is why we're providing more options to pay tax in a way that works for businesses.

And reforms to better target support for electric vehicle uptake will make existing tax breaks fairer and more sustainable.

Schedule 1 to the bill implements the innovative business capital gains tax concession.

The concession supports early investment in innovative businesses by providing eligible founders, employees and investors with access to a 50 per cent capital gains tax discount on equity investments.

This means early investors in innovative startups that begin with a low or zero cost base still receive a significant discount on a future capital gain.

This will support investment in innovative Australian startups, and the continued growth of Australia's startup and venture capital system.

Critical technologies like artificial intelligence, quantum computing, robotics and clean energy will play a critical role in driving our nation's future economic growth, productivity and jobs.

Schedule 2 to the bill simplifies and refines the research and development tax incentive to better target government support for business R&D in Australia and drive innovations and productivity gains.

This schedule simplifies administration and better targets the incentive to genuine innovation, including by increasing core R&D offset rates by up to 50 per cent.

It extends access to the refundable offset for young, growing firms for longer by increasing the turnover threshold from $20 million to $50 million, reduces the R&D intensity threshold so that firms that invest more substantially in core R&D can benefit from higher offset rates, and it increases the maximum expenditure threshold.

In addition, the changes in this schedule recognise the longer regulatory approval processes and product development timeframes of biotechnology and medical technology firms by providing access to the refundable offset for up to 15 years for eligible firms.

Older firms' eligibility for the higher offset rate is maintained through a non-refundable tax offset.

It also improves integrity requirements around small claims, with expenditure claims below $50,000 requiring a partnership with a research service provider or cooperative research centre to be eligible for the incentive.

This schedule also introduces an instrument-making power to allow a treasury minister, in consultation with the industry minister, to prescribe eligible R&D activities as being integral to core R&D.

This will futureproof the incentive and allow governments to modernise the definition of R&D as markets, businesses and technologies evolve over time. Overall, these reforms are expected to lift investment in R&D by young firms by $400 million a year. These reforms form part of the government's response to the Ambitious Australia report, and we thank its authors.

Schedule 3 to the bill expands the venture capital tax incentives to encourage more investment and support early-stage and growth businesses.

These changes increase existing thresholds to reflect modern company valuations. This will allow venture capital investors to invest larger amounts over a longer period in startups that find it difficult to access traditional forms of finance.

Schedule 4 to the bill allows taxpayers required to report and pay pay-as-you-go instalments on a quarterly basis to elect to pay on a monthly basis instead.

This will provide individuals and businesses with more flexibility to meet their tax obligations.

It's one of several initiatives that we're rolling out that will ensure instalments better reflect real-time business conditions.

It also empowers the Commissioner of Taxation to require taxpayers with a demonstrated history of non-compliance to report and pay instalments monthly to strengthen the integrity of the system.

Schedule 5 to the bill adjusts the electric car discount settings to ensure they remains fiscally sustainable. It incentivises the supply of more affordable options and provides more targeted support for EV drivers.

This measure has been successful in boosting uptake of EVs while reducing transport emissions and contributing towards more fuel security as well.

The discount has helped take EVs from one in every 50 sales when we came to government to roughly one in every eight in 2025.

Now, we are ensuring these settings are sustainable for the future as well.

From 1 April 2029, a 25 per cent discount for electric cars up to the fuel-efficient threshold for the luxury car tax will be applied to the 20 per cent fringe benefit tax statutory formula rate that applies to all other cars.

The full 100 per cent fringe benefit tax discount will continue to apply to electric cars valued up to $75,000 from 1 April 2027 to 31 March 2029.

All eligible electric cars will retain the fringe benefit tax treatment that was in place when the last relevant commitment commenced.

Full details of the measure are contained in the explanatory memorandum.

I acknowledge the many groups and individuals, and colleagues, who have contributed to this bill.

Like all big tax reform, implementing details relies on constructive feedback and expert insights, and I thank everyone who has helped us to get this right.

There has been a lot of collaboration between ministers and members of this place on these proposals as well, and I acknowledge their role as well.

This is a bill that recognises the hard work of Australian businesses and helps them to succeed.

It encourages entrepreneurship and economic growth.

The changes are sensible, but they will make a positive difference to the businesses and start-ups that employ Australian workers and make our economy stronger as a consequence.

And that is why I commend this bill to the House.

Debate adjourned.

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Moments ago, I did share the words of a local mother from my electorate of Griffith, and I have thought about those words a great deal. Here is a parent who has done everything a parent could do—monitored her children's internet use, invested in safety tools and sought professional support—and still the negative impacts of technology have found their way into her daughters' lives. What chance does the average Australian parent have against companies developing increasingly sophisticated technology designed to keep people engaged? This mother has since taken her advocacy beyond her own family, speaking at a national and international level about the urgent need for better safeguards. I thank her for trusting me with her family's experience and for her determination to protect other children from the same harm.

Parents have a responsibility to teach their children about online safety. They're conversations that we have in my household with my children, aged 11 and 13, almost daily. As parents, we set boundaries, we discuss risks and we help young people make sound decisions. But we as parents cannot inspect algorithms, anticipate thousands of private chatbot responses or block every new dangerous feature a company introduces. The companies developing these products must take responsibility for their safety. We already expect manufacturers to meet safety standards for children's products and employers to protect their workers. Businesses must take reasonable precautions against foreseeable harm. Digital services should have clear responsibilities too.

The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 will require online service providers to take reasonable steps to protect Australians from serious harm. Instead of relying solely on the removal of dangerous material after someone reports it, companies will need to identify risks, assess their consequences and act to reduce them. Those obligations extend beyond social media to services such as online games and AI chatbots. As technology changes, our protections must keep pace. A company should not wait until a child is harmed, a family makes a complaint or a damaging exchange is shared publicly before examining the dangers built into its product. The obligation must begin when a service is being designed and continue as its features change.

This bill builds on this Albanese Labor government's work to establish a minimum age of 16 for social media accounts. That reform recognised the growing evidence of harm associated with children's early exposure to social media. It was a major change and one that many parents had been calling for, and we are already seeing encouraging results. More than five million under-age accounts have been deactivated, removed or restricted. I know in my house, with preteens, we had talked for quite some time about when they could have social media accounts, and I had kicked that ball down the line for so long, saying, 'We'll talk about it when you get to high school.' But then, as my eldest started high school, I realised that that time had come up so quickly, and I did not feel that he or we were ready for that. These laws now have actually given my own children several more years without this presence in their lives. Indeed, 30 per cent of young Australians aged 13 to 15 reported spending more time playing sport, and 27 per cent reported better sleep. These are promising findings, but we know the system still needs improvement. Too many children under 16 continue to hold social media accounts, and our government is determined to hold platforms accountable for complying with the law.

But protecting children from online harm cannot end at the age of 16, and restricting access to social media does not address the risks children face through other digital services. A young person using an online game can encounter strangers, bullying or harmful material. A child using an AI companion, as we heard in the example I shared, can develop an emotional attachment to a program that imitates friendship or affection. A teenager can be exposed to dangerous material through recommendation systems and repeated promotion of similar content to them. Digital duty of care addresses these broader risks.

I want to address directly the suggestion that introducing this legislation is somehow an admission that our social media minimum-age laws have failed. Some have argued here in this chamber and even this evening that if the under-16 restrictions were working we wouldn't need a digital duty of care. But this argument fundamentally misunderstands what each of these reforms is designed to achieve. The social media minimum age restricts access to accounts on certain platforms for children under 16. Digital duty of care places responsibility on technology companies to make their services safer for all Australians, regardless of their age. They address different problems, and it has always been intended that they will work together alongside one another.

We should recognise what the minimum-age laws have already achieved. Millions of underage accounts have been removed, deactivated or restricted. That is important progress. But we know that some platforms have not done enough to stop children from accessing their services. The eSafety Commissioner has been investigating possible noncompliance, and the government has strengthened enforcement powers and increased the penalties that platforms face. We are holding technology companies to the responsibilities parliament has already placed on them. Even if every platform complied perfectly with the social media minimum age we would still need this bill. A 12-year-old could still encounter harmful interactions through an AI chatbot, a 14-year-old could still face grooming or bullying through an online game, and a 17-year-old could still be exposed to dangerous material promoted by a social media algorithm.

Adults face serious online harms, too, including threats, abuse and the creation of intimate images without consent. None of those risks disappear simply through restricting social media accounts for children under the age of 16. And of course young people do not suddenly become immune to online harm on their 16th birthday. That is why the government is taking this next step. The minimum-age laws address when children can access certain platforms. Digital duty of care addresses the responsibility of those platforms and other services to keep their users safe. We need both.

AI has enormous potential. It can assist students with learning, help people access information and support new developments across health care, research and education. But AI companion technology raises particular concerns. These services can simulate human conversations and relationships. They can remember personal details, respond to emotions and create the impression that a user is speaking with someone who understands them. For a young person who is experiencing loneliness, anxiety or difficulties at school, that interaction can feel deeply personal. The eSafety Commissioner's research paints a concerning picture. In a survey of children age 10 to 17, almost 80 per cent had used an AI assistant. More than half of children who had used an AI assistant or companion reported using it for personal or social reasons. And one in five children who had used these tools reported potentially inappropriate or harmful interactions. That includes harmful advice, bullying and controlling behaviour. This bill will require providers to assess the harms associated with their services and take reasonable steps to prevent them.

The bill introduces specific protections for Australians under the age of 18. Online services will have a responsibility to protect children from material and conduct that encourages eating disorders, promotes harmful attitudes towards women, or exposes them to bullying and harassment. It covers pornography, content that glorifies dangerous behaviour and material that can cause serious psychological harm. Crucially, it addresses the design features of online services. Consider the way that some platforms encourage people to keep scrolling, watching or interacting. A young person begins watching a video about healthy eating. They go from one video to another and another, and gradually their feed becomes filled with increasingly restrictive dieting advice, extreme body ideals or material promoting disordered eating. We know that these are design features that are intended to prolong engagement, and they can encourage compulsive use and interfere with sleep, study and relationships. Under this legislation, companies will have to undertake risk assessments and introduce safeguards for features that create foreseeable harm.

We know that men and women often have very different experiences online, and I'm confident that female colleagues from across this chamber could speak firsthand about the vile threats, abuse and harassment they have endured simply for participating in public life, but it's not just politicians who are exposed to this. It's women across our community. That is why I particularly welcome the provisions of this bill addressing online violence and abuse against women and girls.

We have seen disturbing developments in the use of artificial intelligence to create intimate images of people without their knowledge or consent. The images can be used to humiliate, threaten and intimidate victims. Young women and girls are particularly exposed to these forms of abuse. This bill will give the eSafety Commissioner stronger powers to restrict access to websites and applications predominantly designed or used to generate fake nude images.

Another important element of this legislation is My Feed, My Way. Most Australians who use social media will recognise the experience of opening an application and finding a feed filled with content they never asked to see. Some of it comes from friends or people that they follow, but much of it is selected by an algorithm that predicts what will keep them watching. These systems can be useful. They can help people discover new information, communities and interests, but users deserve more control over their own experience.

These reforms have been shaped by years of advocacy from parents, researchers, community organisations and people with lived experience in online harm. I particularly want to recognise the work of the Butterfly Foundation. They have welcomed the government's decision to identify content promoting disordered eating as a harm that online platforms must address. There are so many other organisations who have also welcomed this legislation, like the Alannah & Madeline Foundation and John Hartman at the Minderoo Foundation. They have said that this bill is a much needed step when it comes to protecting women and children, who experience disproportionate harms in the online world. Wayne Holdsworth from SmackTalk lost his son Mac to suicide, and he said that they wholeheartedly support the digital duty of care.

We cannot keep asking families to manage risks that technology companies have created and know how to prevent. The Albanese Labor government is taking practical action to change this. This legislation will set clearer expectations, strengthen accountability and give Australians greater control over their online experiences. It builds on our social media minimum age reforms and recognises the rapidly changing risks associated with AI. Companies that develop products for Australians must take reasonable steps to protect the people using them.

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise to speak in support of the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026. It is really urgent that we have this in place, and I want to thank at the outset so many who have campaigned for this and done a lot of work, particularly Chanel Contos with her Fix Our Feeds campaign, to give users back that control and autonomy of choosing what you see and what you switch out of in your feed. Many organisations have championed this because it's an area that is really the hallmark of this generation: how exposed they are to this online world. Yet it's an area that has been devoid of proper protections, so I do welcome the fact that we are finally here with a digital duty of care legislation.

It is time to rebalance responsibility for online safety in Australia. For too long, the burden of navigating online harms has fallen on individuals and families. We need to prevent the harm before it happens, rather than leaving individuals and families to deal with the consequences. The list of harms is long. When it comes to mental health, eating disorders, violence, sexual assault, intimidation and discrimination against women, we know that the online world has given rise to this environment where harm is allowed to go unchecked, and it's led to major issues when it comes to suicide and eating disorders. There is another area, though, that this bill does fail to address, and that's the growing threat of AI deepfakes, which use people's images, voices and identities without their consent. We know deepfakes can spread misinformation, fuel hate and damage reputations and public trust. Yet, despite the events—despite everything that we are discussing at the moment around rising threats and violent commentary online—this bill is failing to address what I would say is a major area that should be addressed.

We know the internet has transformed how we communicate, how we learn, how we do business and how we participate in public life. It has created extraordinary opportunities for connection, innovation and democratic engagement, but we also have to acknowledge the serious harms that can arise from these technologies. Social media platforms can amplify harmful material, recommend it to vulnerable users and spread abusive content at a scale unimaginable a generation ago. That's why it is so important that that control in relation to the feeds be given back to the user.

We can't expect individuals, especially young people, to bear the full responsibility for protecting themselves from highly sophisticated systems designed to capture and keep their attention—that's the really important bit. This is not innocent technology; this is highly sophisticated technology that is creating significant harm.

We can't leave families alone to deal with the consequences or navigate the risks alone. We've had so many stories of families absolutely devastated by tragedy as a result of the pernicious and damaging influence of social media—the algorithm and the pushing of harmful content—with no real action coming in return. Busy, exhausted parents should not have to rely on settings that are difficult to find and confusing to use or be sent through opaque and impersonal reporting and complaint processes that all too often result in very little change.

Technology companies have access to the data, expertise, resources and the technical capacity to identify and mitigate foreseeable risks at a scale that individuals simply do not. That is at the heart of the requirement of this legislation, and that is why it's important. They have the tools and the capacity. They must use those to mitigate foreseeable risks.

That's why this is important reform. It establishes a clear principle: online services should take reasonable steps to protect their users from serious harms arising from the use of their services. We accept that of every other business. For every other business, even if it's a supermarket that you walk into and buy a product from, we expect there to be compliance when it comes to duty of care—that a product can't cause harm. There are consequences when the risks are ignored. We know that, too often, big tech companies wait for harm to occur and only act if they're really forced to. Even then, it is a convoluted process. I welcome this move to a model where platforms must identify risks and prevent foreseeable harm in the first place.

The people of Warringah are highly digital aware. They appreciate the opportunities presented by digital technologies and AI, but they are also concerned about the harms. Since before this bill was introduced, my office has been contacted by many people who want to see greater protections in the online space. They want to see a digital duty of care passed. They believe that it will create a safer online environment, particularly for young people and vulnerable groups.

The age limits that the government proposes to pass are simply not sufficient—I've said that from the start—to keep young people safe online. In particular, young people in Warringah have told me loud and clear that they want online safety to be prioritised. A 16-year-old in the electorate wrote to me just a few days ago to urge me to support this bill in the hope that it will build a safer online world.

The push for a digital duty of care has been building for some time. Former member for Goldstein, Independent MP Zoe Daniel, in fact helped bring the idea into parliament, introducing her own private member's bill in November 2024. It would have required major online platforms to identify and manage the risks their services pose to Australians. The bill lapsed when parliament was dissolved in 2025, but the legacy continues. I welcome the Albanese government's developing this digital duty of care with the same principle at its heart: online platforms should do more to prevent foreseeable harm. I've long argued that online safety must involve meaningful accountability for the companies that design and profit from these systems. Remember, they are the ones that benefit from algorithms that keep pushing dangerous content.

But the details matter. We need legislation that delivers real safety and accountability and greater choice for users. Of course, everyone fearing this legislation has been hiding behind smokescreens of 'freedom of speech', 'freedom to choose' or 'government intervention'. In fact, I would argue that it's the complete contrary. This is giving choice back into the hands of users. They can control their feeds, and they can no longer be preyed on by these billion-dollar-making companies who benefit and profit out of pushing content through these algorithms.

We know that as the technology evolves so must our approach to the harms it can create. We have the opportunity in this legislation to ensure that it addresses not just the risks that we already understand but also address emerging threats. One such risk is the spread of highly realistic AI generated audio, images and video depicting identifiable people without their consent. I've been trying to get the government to engage on this when it comes to truth-in-political-advertising legislation and to cover deepfakes in that, but it goes broader than just political advertising. It's actually everyone. Why should anyone in Australia have their image or likeness used in a way that is contrary to their wishes and without their consent to do something that can be very harmful? The amendment that I intend to move will address this issue.

Artificial intelligence can make someone appear to say something they never said. It can create a scene that never happened or make a fabricated event look like a genuine news report. We do not have to look far to see examples of these risks in Australia. Consider the AI generated videos released by Sportsbet featuring high profile AFL players Lachie Neale and Will Ashcroft. The videos depicted the athletes saying things they had not said and were made without their consent. The videos were reportedly intended to help Sportsbet attract new gambling customers, and the AFL instructed Sportsbet to take them down. They were able to do that because they had that power, but an individual in the community does not have that same power to ask for a deepfake to be taken down.

A deepfake video depicting Tasmanian Senator Jacqui Lambie has also recently circulated on social media. It portrays her making statements that she never made, including comments criticising another party's voters, which then led to increased threats against her because they then were outraged by the perception that these comments have been made. These are the risks we face and the dangerous environment in which we are in. These examples raise a fundamental question should someone or an organisation or an account overseas be able to use artificial intelligence to put words in another person's mouth and use their identity, image and likeness to deliver a message they never agreed to deliver? I think any right-minded Australian should say a firm no to that.

AI can also be used to create fabricated scenes that appear realistic. Earlier this month, the One Nation Victorian branch aired an AI generated video featuring a man of African appearance wielding a machete and a suicide bomber who appeared to be of Middle Eastern descent. This is incredibly dangerous content. The video used fabricated imagery to portray threatening scenarios, stoke hate, provoke fear and create a highly racist and dangerous environment. It demonstrates how synthetic content can influence public perceptions, particularly when viewers may not realise that the scenes are artificial. As AI tools improve, the distinction between authentic and synthetic content becomes increasingly difficult for ordinary viewers to make. This material can also be produced, copied and distributed at an extraordinary speed. The consequences can extend well beyond the original post. They can affect personal safety, professional reputations, public trust and the quality of our democratic debate. Australian law must respond to these risks in a way that is practical, proportionate and capable of adapting as the technology develops.

The European Union has introduced transparency requirements intended to make AI generated and manipulated content easier to identify. Since August this year, the EU's AI framework has required certain deepfakes to be disclosed as artificially generated or manipulated. The framework also includes requirements concerning machine readable markings of some AI generated content. These European laws recognise that people should not have to guess whether what they are seeing or hearing is genuine. The European approach also recognises that art, fiction and satire should not automatically be treated in the same way as content pretending to be authentic. Transparency requirements are not the same as a blanket ban on deepfakes. What we should do is seek to avoid people being deceived while allowing legitimate uses of AI to continue. We need to look at that, and the framework, to recognise the benefits of innovation while ensuring that people affected by fake content are not left without meaningful protection.

We need to ensure that deepfakes which depict an identifiable person without their content and are likely to cause serious harm are captured within this bill. That means content that depicts you, Madam Deputy Speaker Garland, and any other member in this House but also members of the public. We should not have the right to use someone's image, voice or likeness in AI generated content without their consent. It's not about prohibiting artificial intelligence in creative works or preventing Australians from commenting on public figures, but we cannot pass that off as being authentic content. We need to address the specific risks where AI generated content that uses a real person's likeness without consent is capable of misleading viewers into believing it is genuine and is likely to cause serious harm, not just misinformation. I commend my amendment to the House as incredibly important if we genuinely want to make this environment safe.

Social media platforms are responsible for assessing and managing risks associated with this material. This would force them to consider and take reasonable steps to reduce that risk. It would also give the eSafety Commissioner the power to order the removal of harmful online content. Platforms shouldn't wait for a victim to suffer consequences before taking reasonable steps to address a foreseeable risk. It's particularly important because deepfake content can spread so rapidly. In fact, we saw it in the aftermath of the Bondi terror attack, where we saw fake content generated online; that should be banned. Once a video or image has been widely shared, removing the original material may not be enough to undo the damage.

The bill recognises that AI generated abuse is a serious and growing problem. The proposed powers concerning fake nude material are an important example of the need to act before harm spreads, before the person is depicted, because it's so devastating. But we need to go beyond just that because the harms are much greater. I support the principle, but I ask the government to look for all AI generated fakes. Many are worried about freedom of expression, which is front of mind. Satire and political commentary are a legitimate and valuable part of democratic life, but they are not a licence and we shouldn't be creating a framework that enables us to abuse and take on the image, likeness and content of another person. I commend the bill to the House in relation to the digital duty of care, but I urge the government to go further.

speaker: Basem Abdo
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise to make a contribution on the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026. The online services we use and increasingly depend on have reshaped so many aspects of our everyday lives—how we stay connected with one another, how we stay informed, how we work, how we learn and how we interact with services. Given the significant role these services play in our everyday lives, it is only appropriate that we establish a set of basic safety standards to protect Australians as they go about their lives online. This should not be controversial. We impose basic safety standards across so many aspects of everyday life, and we have a responsibility to ensure that our online services meet those same fundamental standards of safety. We are committed to ensuring that online services meet appropriate safety standards and that technology companies fulfil their responsibilities to keep Australians, particularly our children, safe online. We are taking world-leading action, with our approach and learnings being closely watched by countries right around the world. This bill forms part of that action to keep Australians safe.

At the heart of this bill is the establishment of a digital duty of care. This will ensure that Australians are protected from serious, harmful and illegal content while under-18s are protected from content and features that are harmful to young people. Another key element of the digital duty of care is giving adults greater choice and agency over the content they see and the features they use online. For the first time, the digital duty of care will establish minimum standards for the features used by digital service companies. These standards will require digital service companies to undertake annual risk assessments of the potential harms associated with features on their services, put systems in place to prevent those features from causing harm to Australian users and, in the case of social media platforms, provide user empowerment tools that give people a 16 and over greater choice and agency over what they see in their feeds, and, if platforms and online service providers fail to comply with the digital duty of care, they can expect the fine of $109.2 million. This will bring penalties for this sector in line with the penalties that apply in other sectors on which Australian consumers depend.

One of the key objectives of the digital duty of care is to protect Australian children from content and features that are harmful to young Australians. We are placing a positive responsibility on platforms and online service providers to protect children and act in their best interests online. The digital duty of care will protect Australian children across online services, particularly those popular with young people, such as online games and AI chat bots. It will address harmful material including abuse, harassment, bullying, pornography, content that promotes eating disorders, content that promotes hostile attitudes towards women and gender equality, and other material that causes harm to children.

Another form of harmful content this digital duty of care will seek to tackle is content that glorifies crime or encourages dangerous stunts. Regrettably, we have seen young men in particular engage in criminal activities after being exposed to content that glorifies a life of crime. Having spoken to parents, local community organisations and schools, I have seen the very serious and lifelong consequences for those who have fallen into that life. Those consequences are not limited to the individuals themselves. They affect their families and they affect the wider community, and, of course, there is the impact on their victims, who are often other young people. It is critical that we dismantle the ability of criminal organisations to use online platforms to recruit vulnerable young people into a life of crime. As a member of the Joint Committee on Law Enforcement, I've seen evidence of the consequences of predatory behaviour online and the harm it does to children.

The digital duty of care will also take action to protect Australian children from design features on digital platforms that can have negative behavioural impacts, including addictive features that encourage children to stay up late and lose sleep. As a father to a young child, I share the concerns of many parents about screen time and its impact on our children, particularly the younger ones. We all know how important it is for young children to spend time away from screens and maintain healthy habits, so I am pleased to see action being taken through this bill.

The reforms in digital duty of care bill before the house today build on the other actions the Albanese Labor government has taken to protect Australian children online, including the minimum-age requirements for social media accounts. The Albanese Labor government introduced and passed legislation establishing a minimum age of 16 for social media accounts, with the laws coming into effect in December last year. It's been less than a year since those laws came into effect, and they're already having a significant impact, with more than five million underage accounts deactivated, removed or restricted.

There is still more work to do in this space. Despite millions of accounts being deactivated, we know there are still far too many under-16s on social media. That is why the eSafety Commissioner is investigating platforms that have failed to comply, including Meta, TikTok and Snapchat. Even so, there is a strong start, and we are seeing positive signs for young Australians. Exposure to inappropriate and violent content is down by 18 per cent, online bullying is down by nine per cent, 20 per cent of Australian children are reporting better sleep, and 30 per cent of young Australians aged 13 to 15 are spending more time playing sport. It's no wonder that other countries have looked to follow Australia's lead, with the United Kingdom, Canada, Indonesia and the European Union all considering or adopting similar policies.

The digital duty of care is not just intended to protect Australian children, it is intended to protect all Australians, including Australian adults. I belong to a generation that grew up as the internet was becoming part of our lives, long before it became the dominant force it is today. The internet and the digital services that now shape our everyday lives are a far cry from what they were when I was younger. The internet has become more advanced and more deeply integrated into our lives. That has brought many benefits, but it also brought new risks and harms.

The bill before the House will work to address the harms Australians are at risk of being exposed to online. It will require online services to protect Australians from a range of harmful content, including sexual violence, child abuse, animal abuse, content that incites or promotes extreme violence, content that promotes physical violence, death threats, rape threats, gender based violence, self-harm, material supporting a terrorist organisation and other harms. The bill will also provide additional powers for the eSafety Commissioner to take down platforms that create non-consensual deepfake images. It is critical that we protect all Australians from exposure to harmful content online.

This is not neutral technology. Algorithms are designed to feed us more in a way which has amplified harmful content. As the Prime Minister said today, big tech are failing to meet their social responsibilities. The companies have been undermining their social licence, and their time is up. Their social licence will be expressed by this legislation. We have seen the devastating impact the online world can have on young people, including driving them towards self-harm. We have seen bullying take on new and more damaging forms. We have seen how people can approach, manipulate and exploit children without ever meeting them in person. And we have seen how children can be manipulated into causing harm to others and, tragically, to themselves. Parents suffer, families suffer and children suffer. On platforms where people can manipulate children anonymously, the harm inflicted on a child can be broadcast to their community and to the world.

Social media is a unique service and market. In most other markets we have a choice about what we want to consume. If we are on a streaming platform, we choose what movie we watch. If we are watching television, we choose the channel. If we are listening to music, we choose the song. But social media platforms are different. That is because algorithmic recommender systems feed us content from people and pages we have not chosen to follow. Social media companies make a lot of money from our information and our attention. Therefore, users should have a say in how their experiences are shaped on these platforms. Our feeds can be crowded, with content being recommended to us rather than the people we actually want to see and follow. But this bill is not about removing the algorithm. It is about choice.

Having worked in the tech space for most of my professional life, I've seen how much the digital landscape has changed. Our cyberthreats have evolved, but so too has the way we interact with online platforms. We all remember when our social media feeds were largely made up of posts from our friends, family and the people we chose to follow. Today it is becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish between the content we have chosen to see and the content platforms choose for us. For us as users, it is not always clear how much control or agency we have over the experiences that these platforms create for us. These experiences are shaped not simply by neutral technological choices but by business models in which engagement and attention generate revenue. That is why giving Australians greater choice over what they see online is so important.

The bill before the House will introduce My Feed, My Way. Under the digital duty of care and My Feed, My Way, social media platforms will have to give Australians a choice over the primary feed they see when they first open the app. It will allow Australians to opt in or opt out of algorithmic recommendations as they wish. It is about choice, not restrictions. If you want to continue using algorithmic recommendations, you can opt in. If you no longer want to use them, you can opt out.

Those who oppose these reforms have characterised them as an attempt to control what Australians can and cannot see on social media. It's simply not the case. It is about giving Australians greater agency over what they see and do on their social media accounts and bringing this industry into line with so many other markets where Australian consumers have a choice. So it is interesting that those opposite, who so often advocate for individualist approaches, suddenly seem opposed to the principle of individual choice. When it comes to social media, why shouldn't Australians have the same agency over their own experience that we expect in so many other parts of our lives? It's not telling people what they can and cannot see. It is about giving people the freedom to decide for themselves.

The bill before the House will bring about an important set of reforms to protect all Australians online and build on our world-leading action to protect Australian children through the under-16 social media minimum age requirements. We are holding big tech companies to account while making sure that Australian consumers have the same opportunities for choice and protection that they would normally expect in other parts of our economy. I am proud to be part of an Albanese Labor government that is taking action to address the serious challenges in this space.

Australia's digital duty of care is about giving adults more choice over their feeds and protecting kids online. We're acting and we're making sure big tech and the tech companies take more responsibility for the online environments they create. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: GRIEVANCE DEBATE
subheading: Warringah Electorate: Ocean Safety, National Disability Insurance Scheme, Aged Care
text:
One of the most important responsibilities we have as members of parliament is to listen to our communities, understand their challenges and ensure their concerns are heard here in parliament. My office receives a significant number of emails from Warringah constituents about issues directly affecting their families and lives. Whether it's changes to the NDIS, delays in aged care, concerns about artificial intelligence or keeping our beaches safe, people want clear information, guidance and accountability, and they want to be heard. I take this opportunity to raise some of those issues here today.

As we move into summer, the safety of beachgoers remains front of mind for my community in Warringah. Over the past year we've been reminded of just how vulnerable we can be in our waters. Late last year there was a tragic and fatal attack on Merc Psillakis at Long Reef Beach in Dee Why, and earlier this year there were two more attacks in Manly and Dee Why. That has shaken our community. I tried to address that earlier this month, because we know that it not only impacts obviously beach goers and safety in the water but also impacts our local businesses. It changes tourism, and it changes confidence. So, earlier this month, I convened a roundtable with our lifesaving clubs, local businesses, academics, industry groups and Surf Life Saving NSW to discuss these safety concerns and how we can best work with our natural environment and our local communities. We discussed shark safety, ocean education, emerging technologies and the growing responsibilities placed on local councils and lifesaving organisations. There were practical proposals ventilated and discussed, which are very much worth pursuing.

First and foremost, we need to review whether the current CASA drone regulations adequately support beach safety operations. What we heard was that drones are increasingly important for monitoring sharks and assisting lifesavers, yet the existing restrictions can limit their deployment in busy coastal areas. We heard from local businesses who are taking on the responsibility of having drones themselves to ensure their ongoing business models—for example, for learn-to-surf schools. But they identified the restrictions of the current regulations prohibiting or preventing them from being able to get drones in the air in a timely way and in a way that would be of assistance.

We also need stronger evidence to guide investment in prevention, education and shark risk management. Local councils and lifesaving organisations carry significant responsibilities, and the federal government has a role in supporting those consistent standards, research and funding across our nation to make sure that goes better. There were a number of further suggestions, and I will provide further information to the community. I want to assure local businesses and local stakeholders, neighbouring MPs and relevant ministers that we are going to all work together to progress these issues because they are so important.

Another issue that I'm often contacted about, as I'm sure many others are in this place, is the NDIS and Thriving Kids. Families need certainty. Families across Warringah are deeply concerned about the proposed changes to the NDIS and the uncertainty surrounding the rollout of Thriving Kids. Parents are worried about what changes to eligibility and support will mean for their children, particularly those who rely on early intervention services. There's considerable uncertainty about what services will be available, who will qualify and whether appropriate supports will be in place before changes are made. The community understands the objective of Thriving Kids. They understand that it's important. Every child deserves access to timely developmental support and families should be able to access early intervention before challenges escalate.

I support the principle of providing more accessible, community based services for children with developmental needs, but good intentions must be matched by clear implementation and services that families can actually access. I'm increasingly hearing from constituents who are worried about the growing gap between what has been announced by government and what is available on the ground in reality. Families are being told that new supports are available, while clinicians report uncertainty about whether to refer children who do not access NDIS but still require developmental intervention. That leaves parents in the middle, trying to navigate a system that is changing without clear information about what will replace existing supports. This is all whilst the development and the timeline for their children is very much at stake.

These are families who are already managing significant pressures and should not be left searching for answers about their child's care. The message from Warringah families, clinicians and community providers has been the same. They want assurance that children will not lose access to existing assistance before appropriate alternatives are available—or all those hard-won gains will be lost. The government must provide clear referral pathways, realistic implementation timelines and transparent information. Early intervention can make an enormous difference to a child's development, education and wellbeing, so we need to get these settings right.

Finally, another issue that is frequently raised is around aged care. There's a very real human cost to delays. We know there's enormous distress for constituents in Warringah around the issue of access to aged care. Too often, I am hearing that aged care plans are approved but that incredibly long delay in actually then accessing plans means that families are left incredibly vulnerable.

The new Aged Care Act commenced on 1 November 2025, introducing a rights based framework intended to put older people at the centre of their care, but the reality being experienced by far too many older Australians is deeply concerning and not consistent with that commitment by the government. Last year, around 6,400 older Australians died while waiting for home-care support. That was a 34 per cent increase on the previous year. Current estimates suggest that between 198,000 and 266,000 older Australians are waiting for assessments or approved funding. It's just not good enough. The government has made changes on how it reports on waiting lists, including those receiving interim funding, but changing how you describe or calculate a waiting list and how it's reported does not resolve the underlying problem of shortage of timely care.

In Warringah, I regularly hear from older residents and families struggling to access support. Some are waiting months for funding already approved, and they simply don't understand. If the government has been able to proceed with approving the requirements, surely that can then proceed to actual funding. Yet in reality they wait for months. Others rely on family members to fill gaps in essential services, often at enormous personal cost. So these delays can lead to loss of independence and increased pressure on family carers.,

The concerns go well beyond waiting times. Since the implementation of the new aged-care reforms, there's been an ongoing concern around AI decision-making built into the system, and I've continued to raise with the government the concern that the automated aged-care assessment system lacks adequate safeguards and produces unfair outcomes. My office continues to hear from constituents battling with this system that the automated funding system is unfair and not fit for purpose. Yesterday the Commonwealth Ombudsman released a deeply concerning report that agreed with that assessment. It found that decisions cannot be overridden by assessors even where those assessments are shown to be clinically inappropriate. That has to be a red flag for all members of the government.

There are real concerns about transparency and equity as well as oversight of the system. While the government has made steps by legislating an escalation pathway for exceptional cases and commissioning an independent review, we have to remember it's only exceptional cases, so it's not capturing all of these instances. It's not enough. The escalation pathway creates more questions about what the criteria will be for it to be deemed urgent, and another review means more lengthy delays to meaningful changes. We should have learnt the hard lessons from robodebt: automated government decisions require transparency, human oversight and clear rights of review. In June I met with Minister Rae to raise concerns about people in their 90s facing waits of up to nine to 12 months for approved funding. I thank the minister and his staff and the department for the engagement on tricky cases, but it's just crazy to think that a 90-year-old who has been assessed as needing care can reasonably be expected to wait another year.

speaker: Tim Watts
heading: GRIEVANCE DEBATE
subheading: Australian Defence Force Parliamentary Program, Artificial Intelligence
text:
'Everyday people doing extraordinary things'—that's the way Commander Paul Hardman described the work of his outstanding crew on HMAS Choules, who generously hosted me recently as part of the Australian Defence Force Parliamentary Program. I couldn't agree more with him, and I was proud as an Australian to have the opportunity to see it up close in person.

The ADF Parliamentary Program allows members of this place to step into the shoes of the Australian servicemen and servicewomen who we ask so much of as a nation. It gives MPs a meaningful insight into the day-to-day operations of the ADF through practical, immersive experiences. We get the opportunity to experience their workplaces, share their daily routines and gain a much deeper understanding of their lives and the responsibilities that they carry on behalf of Australia every day. I've participated in the program four times now, and I've always walked away with a feeling of deep pride in being able to see Australians in the ADF executing what they have been trained to do in the field.

I also want to put on the record that, in the decade that I've participated in the program, I've personally observed the way that the culture of the ADF, like this parliament, has changed. I was proud to see the diversity of modern Australia reflected in the young service men and women that I saw on this program. Real progress has been made on this front, and I want to recognise it here in this place.

This year in the ADFPP, I joined the ADF personnel taking part in exercise Keris Woomera 2026. Exercise Keris Woomera is a major bilateral military exercise conducted between the Australian Defence Force and the Indonesian National Armed Forces, and it was established by this government in 2024. The name Keris Woomera tells a story. The kris is a traditional Indonesian dagger, the woomera a traditional Australian spear thrower. Together they symbolise two distinct traditions working together towards a common purpose. That symbolism is important because this exercise is about far more than military exercises. It's about trust. It's about understanding. It's about building the habits of cooperation that allow two neighbouring countries to work effectively together when it matters most. Around 1,000 ADF personnel and over 1,200 TNI members participated in the exercise and conducted complex training across maritime, land, air and cyber domains. It's a significant exercise and a key element of our broader Indo-Pacific Endeavour program. The exercise is designed to strengthen interoperability, enhance combined operational capabilities and further deepen defence cooperation between Australia and Indonesia.

As part of KW 2026, I bunkered down with the REM on HMAS Choules, embarked on amphibious vehicles to land on the east coast of Java near Banyuwangi, slept in barracks with an artillery unit and experienced the South-East Asian heat in uniform with protective gear.

KW 2026 was a significant exercise for multiple reasons. It was the first time Australia's High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, HIMARS, was deployed and fired overseas. KW 2026 was also the first time that RAAF No. 4 Squadron deployed aircraft into South-East Asia since the Second World War. It was also the first time that Australia conducted cyberintegration training with Indonesia.

Participating in exercise Keris Woomera gave me the opportunity to observe something that's increasingly important in Australia's security and prosperity: the partnership between Australia and Indonesia. Australia and Indonesia are good neighbours and close partners. We're bound by strategic trust, mutual respect and a shared interest in a peaceful, stable and prosperous region. Earlier this year, Prime Minister Albanese and President Prabowo signed the Australia-Indonesia Treaty on Common Security, the Jakarta treaty. That treaty reflects a close friendship, partnership and deep trust between Australia and Indonesia. At its core is a simple idea: to keep Australia and Australians secure, we have to anchor our security in our region. Exercises like Keris Woomera show what that looks like in practice. They deepen understanding between our people and help build the habits of partnership that contribute to peace, stability and security across the region.

What struck me most during the exercise was not the equipment, impressive though it was, nor the complexity of the planning. It was the people. The Australian Defence Force and TNI are building something that no agreement or exercise directive can create on its own: trust—trust that comes from training together, solving problems together, spending time together. I had the opportunity to speak to both ADF members and TNI personnel throughout the exercise, and again and again I heard the same thing: they genuinely enjoy working together as partners. They value the opportunity to learn from one another. They appreciate the different perspectives each side brings. They recognise that every exercise strengthens relationships that may one day prove critical when our countries are called on to work together.

I acknowledge and thank all those who made my participation in exercise Keris Woomera possible. I want to thank my in-country liaison officer—makasih pak. I thank Lieutenant Alec Fuller for sharing an early-morning picket with me in Java. I thank Colonel Mark Tutton, Commander Landing Force of the Australian Amphibious Force; Captain Christopher Doherty, RAN, Commander Australian Amphibious Task Group; Commander Paul Hardman, the commanding officer of the HMAS Choules; Bombardier Max Vaughan, who demonstrated how to make things go bang on Java; and all of the ADF personnel who hosted us throughout the exercise, including my cabinmate on the Choules, Lieutenant Elliot Mitchell. Thank you also, as always, to Lieutenant Colonel Andy Martin, who does the important work of preparing all Australian parliamentarians to participate in the program. And I want to recognise Lieutenant Colonel Brett Edmonds, who I hosted in my office as part of the ADF parliamentary exchange before his departure. You're a credit to the ADF. Thank you also to all the Australian service men and women for our country.

Deputy Prime Minister Marles recently said that artificial intelligence is 'as big a sovereignty inflection point as we've seen since the Second World War'. He's right. A commitment from a frontier AI lab to train their models here could be the foundation of a new Australian-based AI industry that powers our security and prosperity in the decades to come. Hosting the training of frontier AI models in Australia could greatly expand the range of choices available to Australia in the rapidly changing and uncertain world we are seeing emerging around us. But the terms of that investment matter. Done right, it could commit the labs to invest in Australian researchers, put compute in the hands of Australian universities and start-ups and deal Australia into a seat at the table where the rules on the regulations and safety of frontier AI get written.

If Australia hosted an internationally significant share of the world's training compute, our voice would carry further with the labs and with other governments. We'd be wired into the supply chain of an industry that will shape the coming decades. We'd make ourselves indispensable. None of this will just happen, though. The labs have choices about where they invest. They weigh energy, talent, law and politics, and other countries are courting them. Winning this investment will take what Australia used to do best: an approach of our own—one that shapes things in the Australian way.

The Prime Minister has stated that the work with his framework on Australian standards for AI is intended to do this. The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence has backed it. A letter to the Prime Minister from the committee on 12 October, signed by the chair and the deputy chair, said that Australia should not merely be 'a consumer of AI technologies developed elsewhere, but a trusted, competitive and strategically capable partner of the global AI industry'. The letter asks that any deal with the labs reserve compute for national security and our universities. It asks that the Australian Signals Directorate be given early access to new models.

But the committee also heard that there's a real obstacle to being able to realise investment in frontier AI model training in Australia. In my first speech in this place, in 2013, I noted that Australian intellectual property law was throwing sand in the gears of digital innovation and limiting Australian productivity growth. American copyright law has built the most rewarding economy for content creators in world history. Home to the biggest film and music industries in the world, Hollywood and the Grammys, as well as a video game industry bigger than both of them put together, it's a great place to be a filmmaker, musician, writer or artist. But US copyright law also allows transformative uses of content—using existing work to create something completely different. This kind of transformative use is the foundation of digital innovation, and there may be no better example of this transformative use than generative AI.

Generative AI doesn't substitute or compete with the products that it learns from. It learns from them and creates something completely new. American courts have ruled on training for generative AI and so far have found it to be a fair use. Australian law has no similar legislative protection for transformative uses. As a result, the work of Australian artists, musicians and journalists is currently being used to train generative AI models in the United States—in the words of the committee's letter to the PM—'without adequate control or payment'. At the same time, it's also why no frontier AI labs are training models here.

The evidence before the committee is clear: the status quo doesn't work for anyone—not the creators, not the labs, not the Australian national interest—nor does it maximise our sovereignty. And that's what the committee's letter to the PM said. It asked the government to re-examine our copyright settings so that creators keep control and get paid to build a better outcome for Australia—one that, if we can reach it, will be a world-leading settlement. Last month, at the National Press Club, former prime minister Kevin Rudd warned that Australia could slide into becoming a second-rate country. Missing opportunities like this is what would make us one.

speaker: Basem Abdo
heading: GRIEVANCE DEBATE
text:
The Australian Signals Directorate has today released its Annual cyber threat report 2025-26. In my time in the technology sector, I saw the impact of cybercrime on businesses and organisations, including the significant financial costs and operational disruptions that can follow from an attack. Cybercrime poses a serious threat to Australia's national security and our economic security. Cyberattacks are carried out by a range of actors, from organised criminal networks to state sponsored entities seeking to exploit vulnerabilities across our increasingly interconnected digital economy. As modern supply chains become increasingly reliant on data processing, digital infrastructure and the digital exchange of information, cybercriminals are exploiting these connections to compromise systems and disrupt operations. The impacts can extend well beyond individual organisations, interrupting supply chains, affecting critical infrastructure and harming the consumers and communities that rely on them.

Importantly, these threats are not confined to large corporations. Small and medium sized businesses, local organisations and not-for-profits are also vulnerable to cyberattacks and often have fewer resources and less capacity to prevent, respond to and recover from them. This highlights a common vulnerability across interconnected supply chains in which attackers can exploit weaknesses in one organisation to gain access to others. Even when larger organisations have invested heavily in their cyber defences, attackers may target smaller businesses and third-party suppliers with weaker security measures as an entry point into broader networks. By exploiting these vulnerabilities, cybercriminals can gain access to systems, data and operations well beyond the business they initially compromised. That is the evolving nature of a cyberattack.

The Minister for Cyber Security recently highlighted just how rapidly the cyberthreat landscape is evolving. The scale of that change is concerning. It reflects the growing speed and sophistication with which cybercriminals can exploit technological advances. He illustrated this with a striking example. The time between a hostile actor identifying a vulnerability and exploiting it was once measured in years. Today, that window can be as short as 10 hours, compared to approximately 2½ years previously.
