The ASD's report released today recognises that artificial intelligence has been the defining force in the cyberthreat landscape over the past year, allowing malicious actors to identify vulnerabilities faster and exploit them at an unprecedented scale, speed and sophistication to conduct espionage, steal money and disrupt systems. In this environment, our approach to cybersecurity must continually evolve alongside the threats we face. We must ensure that government institutions and critical infrastructure operators have the strongest possible cyber defences to protect essential systems, safeguard sensitive information and keep Australians safe.

Cybercriminals are constantly looking for new ways to exploit weaknesses, whether through sophisticated scams, outdated technologies or software vulnerabilities found in businesses and service providers. They employ a variety of tactics to target Australian small businesses, including phishing messages and suspicious links or QR codes, fake websites and advertisements, business email compromise, malware, ransomware, denial-of-service attacks and deceptive requests to install software. Importantly, effective cybersecurity requires more than simply investing in technology. It also means ensuring employees can recognise suspicious activity and understand the potential risks of communications that impersonate legitimate third-party suppliers and service providers. These are practical measures that can make a real difference in reducing an organisation's exposure to cyberthreats.

As our economy and services become more interconnected digitally, an attack on one organisation can quickly create risks for others, particularly where supply chains and digital networks are closely connected. For small and medium sized businesses, having clear and accessible guidance is particularly valuable. Many operate with limited resources while facing the same increasingly sophisticated threats as larger organisations. Helping them strengthen their cyber defences is essential to protecting their operations, their customers and the broader economy. That is why I'm encouraged by the Albanese Labor government's work to support Australian businesses in navigating these growing challenges and ensuring Australian organisations can operate confidently and securely in an increasingly digital world.

The Albanese government is working with public and private sector organisations to strengthen their cyber resilience and continues to invest in our cybersecurity through project REDSPICE, the largest investment in the ASD's history, strengthening Australia's capacity to detect, prevent and respond to cyberthreats. We are asking all entities to lower thresholds for reporting to the ASD and to prioritise security over service availability. Australia's cybersecurity landscape is becoming increasingly complex, and as businesses, government agencies and essential services become more dependent on digital systems, protecting those systems is critical to our national security and our economic resilience.

As a member of the House Select Committee on Cyber Security for Small to Medium Sized Businesses and Organisations, I recognise the importance of understanding the challenges these organisations face and identifying practical ways to address them. The committee is looking to the cybersecurity maturity of Australian small and medium sized businesses and organisations, including not-for-profits, and assessing the adequacy, appropriateness and accessibility of government provided cybersecurity guidance. These considerations will also help assess how an organisation's level of cybersecurity maturity affects its ability to participate in government and large corporate supply chains. I want to thank the chair, the member for Reid, for her work in chairing the committee, and I acknowledge the deputy chair, here in this chamber today. I look forward to contributing to the committee's work, designed to help Australian businesses and organisations strengthen their cyber security and participate confidently in an increasingly digital economy.

I want to congratulate a local, young athlete from Craigieburn in my electorate, Divjot Singh. At just 19 years of age, Divjot is currently representing Australia at the 2026 Commonwealth Kabaddi Championships in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, in India, making him one of the youngest competitors in this year's tournament. For those unfamiliar with the sport, Kabaddi is an ancient contact sport which combines elements of tag, wrestling, strength, strategy and agility. The game is played between two teams of seven players. Divjot has been selected as a raider—a position that requires him to enter the opposing team's half of the court alone, tag as many defenders as possible and return safely to his own half. The defending team, meanwhile, must work together to tackle the raider and prevent his return before time runs out. It is a sport that demands courage, tactical awareness, quick decision-making and extraordinary physical ability. There are parallels with the strategies of warriors, requiring infiltration, spatial awareness and the physical skills and tactical thinking associated with combat sports. We make them warriors in our part of the world. The competition represents an exciting opportunity to showcase this ancient sport on the international stage, with the potential for Kabaddi to feature on the main Commonwealth Games program.

What makes Divjot's journey particularly special is where it began. He first developed his tackling and defensive skills playing Aussie rules football. He went on to train at the James Hird Academy, associated with the Essendon Football Club. During his time playing footy, Divjot demonstrated strong tackling and defensive ability. Those skills caught the attention of people who recognised his potential in Kabaddi, and he was encouraged to take up the sport. There is always a great sense of pride when a young person represents our community and our country on the international stage, and Divjot has not stopped at Kabaddi. His ultimate goal is to play AFL, and we are cheering him on and hope to see him achieve that ambition.

Beyond his sporting achievements, Divjot has also demonstrated a strong commitment to giving back to his local community. For a number of years, he has served on the Kalkallo Youth Advisory Council, which plays an important role in empowering young people to participate in policy-making and civic life. It is wonderful to see a young person balancing sporting ambition with a commitment to helping others and making a positive contribution to the community. I want to congratulate Divjot on his contributions to sport at the local, national and international levels as well as to our local community. At just 19, he has already given us plenty of reasons to be proud. We are proud to see him representing Australia on the international stage and will continue cheering him on as he pursues his ambitions in both Kabaddi and Australian Rules football. Divjot, congratulations on your achievements so far. We wish you every success in the championships and in pursuing your goals both on and off the field.

speaker: Libby Coker
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026
text:
No matter where I go across my electorate of Corangamite, people are coming up to me and voicing their serious concerns about online safety. Whether they be parents, teachers or small-business owners, people are united in their view that social media has become the Wild West, with few constraints, and that the tenor of online debate is harmful, particularly for young people. It's why the Albanese government created a minimum age to have a social media account, and, so far, more than five million underage accounts have been deactivated, removed or restricted. As a result, YouGov has reported a nine per cent drop in online bullying, and exposure to inappropriate and violent content has fallen by 18 per cent.

This is welcome progress, but we know there's more to do—and that work is happening right now, with the debate underway on a digital duty of care bill. This bill is all about creating safety standards for the digital services we all use. It will force platforms to protect Australian children from harmful content and will ensure parents have the tools they need to keep their family safe online. For the first time ever, tech companies will need to do annual risk assessments of the harms their services can cause to Australians. They'll need to put systems in place to prevent risky features from causing harm, and, if they don't, they'll face serious penalties of up to $109 million.

That's significant, but so too are the provisions designed to tackle doomscrolling. We know doomscrolling causes real harm to young people. Locals tell me this all the time. Teachers speak to me about how young people are increasingly seeing more and more misogynistic and inappropriate content online. We know it's impacting their relationships with peers and, at times, their mental health, which is just so heartbreaking and so concerning. It's why we're backing the My Feed, My Way approach as part of our bill. It'll give Australians a choice. They can either opt in to the algorithm, or choose to only see content from accounts they follow. Social media platforms make significant profit from using the information of its users, so it's only fair that they give Australians some choice and follow the same basic rules as every other industry.

The bill also puts a stop to nudify apps. That means we're giving the eSafety Commissioner take-down powers to remove platforms that allow for generation of deepfake AI-generated nude images.

In closing, the bill in the House responds to so many of the concerns I've been hearing right across my electorate. I call on the parliament to unite in support of the digital duty of care bill. It's good for children, teachers and parents, and it's good for all Australians. It's about time that social media platforms are no longer the Wild West.

speaker: Melissa McIntosh
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading

speaker: Richard Donald Marles
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for his question and acknowledge his great work on the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security. Today the government has released the Australian Signals Directorate's Annual cyber threat report. It reveals that in the last financial year ASD responded to 1,500 cyber incidents, which is an annual increase of 20 per cent. By historic standards, that's a big jump. What's going on here is that malicious actors are using artificial intelligence to locate vulnerabilities in the IT systems of companies and organisations much more quickly. We are living in a more contested cyber environment.

But, in turn, ASD is engaging with companies and organisations around the country in a much bigger way, alerting them to threats, providing advice as to how to secure their IT systems and then doing just that. As a result, in this report there is some good news. For larger companies, which have good cyber defences in place and which are working with ASD, the average cost of a cyber event has come down by 27 per cent. The not-so-good news is that for medium-size companies the average cost has gone up by 45 per cent. So they are very much now the focus.

Today ASD has three really important messages. First, if you have an old IT system connected to the internet, that is a gateway for malicious actors; you need to replace it. Second, it's important to take the time to secure and harden your IT systems, even if that means that you go offline for a couple of days. And third, while AI represents part of the challenge here, AI is also very much part of the solution. You need to use AI to harden your systems. There are a lot of great AI products out there now and, through cyber.gov.au, ASD is providing a lot of advice about how to use those tools. In a more contested environment it is possible to meet this challenge and to win, and ASD is there to help. I am very fortunate to see firsthand the incredible work undertaken by the men and women who serve in the Australian Signals Directorate and who each and every day are providing for the cyber defence of our country.

speaker: Mr Tony Stephen Burke
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
Thank you to the member for Cunningham for raising this issue. The cyber threat landscape is always changing, but the fact that we are under attack is constant. The defence minister just referred to the Annual cyber threat report from the Signals Directorate, where we had 1,500 cyber security incidents last year, an increase of 20 per cent.

This is happening at the same time that artificial intelligence is being used by those who would want to do us harm. We need to remember that artificial intelligence is not creating vulnerabilities. What it's doing is finding vulnerabilities and finding them faster than they would otherwise be found. The gap between a vulnerability existing and it being exploited used to be about 2½ years. It's now 10 hours. Artificial intelligence is supercharging the pace at which these vulnerabilities are being found.

The vulnerabilities continue to exist in three key areas, all of which are being dealt with and addressed in horizon 2 of our cyber strategy. The first deals with legacy technology, and when we talk about legacy technology it's not necessarily old technology. There can be old technology that we don't call legacy because you can keep patching it and you can keep updating it. But any technology or edge device that's not capable of continuing to be updated is legacy and carries risk. The second is the issue of the human firewall. So many cyberattacks involve social engineering where somebody is tricked into opening the doors wide—sometimes an employee, sometimes an individual. The final vulnerability is links that can exist within an entire supply chain.

Just as those who want to do us harm are using artificial intelligence to find and exploit these vulnerabilities, we need the same capability to provide the protection. The change that people will start to see as businesses and government are using the best technology to find vulnerabilities as quickly as possible is that patching of software is going to have to happen and happen fast. We've got used to systems with a whole lot of the businesses that we interact with where you wait for Saturday night, and Saturday night between 2 am and 4 am is when the update occurs. We are going to start to see occasions where sites that we are used to having available for us constantly look like they're shut down for a time. Overwhelmingly, they won't be examples, by and large, of successful attacks. They will be examples of companies taking cyberdefences seriously. We need to use every single edge that is being used against us. Our entire world now—our electricity, our water and every household device—is capable of being connected, and we need to make sure that we have the defences Australians need.

speaker: Anika Wells
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Griffith for her question and for joining the Minister for Social Services and me recently to announce the Albanese government's $3.5 million investment in the Preventing Tech-based Abuse of Women Grants Program. Social media promised to create a village square that would create community and inspire creativity and encourage the discussion of new ideas. Instead, it has become a cesspit.

When dehumanising language online becomes normal, it lowers the barrier to harm in the real world. Over the past year, the Australian Federal Police have recorded growing volumes of online abuse, threatening rhetoric and intimidation. ASIO's chief, Mike Burgess—a person of great repute in this place—has warned that social media is 'promoting discord and inflammatory rhetoric, exacerbating polarisation and creating a permissive environment for violence.' The eSafety Commissioner—a person appointed, and reappointed, by the coalition—cautioned that online content can surface real-world intent, shaping attitudes, behaviours and actions, including radicalisation, violence and hate. The AFP Commissioner—someone who we all respect in this place—shared that the national security investigations team is charging almost one individual a week for targeting Commonwealth parliamentarians and public officials. The question before us all this week is: how are we, as elected members of parliament, going to respond to these clarion calls from our most trusted security and safety experts?

Just as individuals are accountable to the police for their behaviour online, platforms must be accountable for enabling it. The digital duty of care is built on the principle that if you build it, you are responsible for it. It applies the same standard to big tech that we expect of every other industry in Australia. The digital duty of care will require platforms to have systems in place to proactively protect all Australians from threats of violence, death and rape, and menacing or harassing behaviour, because it's not good enough to wait until threats escalate or a person gets hurt.

This is not about censoring political debate. This is not about avoiding the criticism of policy. This is not about misinformation or disinformation. If social media platforms, forums, online games and AI chatbots know that the tools they make money from can be used to seriously harm Australians, they should put systems in place to stop it. We don't always agree in this place, but surely we can agree on this.

speaker: Gordon McKee
heading: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
text: For a decade we have rightly been worried about the impact of misinformation on social media fuelled by hostile foreign states, but now millions of people get their information from AI chatbots. What work is the Secretary of State doing with European allies to protect the information provided by AI systems during elections here and overseas?

speaker: Ed Miliband
heading: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
text: My hon. Friend raises an important issue. I recently read the Foreign Affairs Committee’s report on these issues, and that was an important document. He is absolutely right about countering all the threats we face from AI, as well as taking advantage of the opportunities. That is something that the new centre the Prime Minister announced will definitely do.

speaker: Uma Kumaran
heading: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
text: I thank my hon. Friend for raising this important topic. The Government are taking action at home and internationally to tackle appalling online abuse towards women and girls, including AI-generated deepfakes and the sharing of intimate images without consent. The UK has introduced some of the strongest measures against this abuse, including making the creation and sharing of deepfakes a criminal offence. We are co-developing a model national framework to reduce opportunities for offenders to exploit differences between jurisdictions. There is a global partnership for action on gender-based online harassment and abuse. I will continue to raise this issue with international counterparts and at our summit next year.

speaker: Fred Thomas
heading: Strengthening Community Resilience
text: I welcome the Government’s Be Ready campaign, which I will champion in my patch in Plymouth. I thank the Minister for his continued endeavours, over the last several years, to knot together different bits of Government agenda and Departments to grow greater resilience. Can he assure the House that this will encompass AI and emerging technologies as well, and can he give us a sense of what new endeavours are being stood up, given the massive acceleration of the threat to our national resilience in that space?

speaker: Dan Jarvis
heading: Strengthening Community Resilience
text: I am grateful to my hon. Friend for his kind words and his observation about the importance of drawing the campaign together from across Government. There needs to be a response that is balanced across Government Departments in order to ensure wider societal resilience. My hon. Friend is right to reference AI. I tend to focus on the significant challenges that AI brings, but there are also significant opportunities, including in this area. I work closely with the Minister for Artificial Intelligence in this endeavour, and I would be happy to discuss that with my hon. Friend further.

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: Public Service Delivery: Devolved Governments - Question
text: The Council of the Nations and Regions has met twice. The UK Government work in partnership with the devolved Governments and mayors through a range of fora, including the mayoral council and the National Economic Council, to deliver on shared priorities. At the council’s first meeting, in October 2024, the priorities were inward investment and economic growth. In May 2025, the council discussed principally the opportunities of trade agreements that the UK Government had concluded, as well as the challenges of artificial intelligence. One aspect of that second meeting was bringing together for the first time the chief data officers of the devolved Governments and the mayoral strategic authorities. We will look at a number of ways of taking this type of work forward.

speaker: Lord Clement-Jones
heading: Meta: AI Development - Question
text: To ask His Majesty’s Government what assessment they have made of Meta’s updated Commercial Terms, which from 30 October authorise it to crawl the websites of UK business users for the purposes of AI development.

speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath
heading: Meta: AI Development - Question
text: The Government recognise the concerns raised by businesses and rights holders about Meta’s updated commercial terms. Meta has delayed their introduction until 20 November, and the Competition and Markets Authority is engaging directly with Meta. We are committed to ensuring that creators can control the use of their work. In our March Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, we committed to publishing a review of mechanisms for creators to control their works online, including technical standards and best practice on input transparency. This will inform whether there is an appropriate role for government.

speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath
heading: Meta: AI Development - Question
text: I assure my noble friend that the Government recognise the concerns raised about Meta’s updated commercial terms and are committed to ensuring that creators can control the use of their work. UK copyright continues to apply to the use of protected works in AI development and training. Where an activity requires permission under copyright law, that permission must be obtained unless an exception applies.

speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath
heading: Meta: AI Development - Question
text: Meta has publicly stated that website owners can use robots.txt to indicate their preferences about its crawlers, and has reiterated this in our engagement on creator control and transparency. However, we recognise the concerns raised by publishers about whether these assurances provide meaningful and enforceable control over their content. On publishing before 20 November, we recognise that the removal of the word “train” has not resolved the concerns raised about the revised terms, particularly on whether the remaining provisions could still permit content to be used for AI training. Meta disputes that interpretation, and we expect the response shortly.

speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath
heading: Meta: AI Development - Question
text: We recognise the importance of ensuring that publishers and smaller creators can control and benefit from the use of their content, and we further understand that news publishers rely on traffic, advertising and subscription to support their work. Concerns of the sort that the noble Baroness mentions have been raised about the effects of AI systems accessing and using their content, which is why in March we committed to establish a working group to consider how the Government could support independent and smaller creative organisations in licensing their work, including in journalism. This sits alongside our review of creator control and input transparency.

speaker: Viscount Camrose
heading: Meta: AI Development - Question
text: My Lords, perhaps we cannot really blame Meta for exploring the limits of the policy vacuum created by the Government’s continued inaction on AI and copyright. With that in mind, could the Minister tell us what progress has been made on the Government’s review of creator control and transparency, in particular the technical standards that could enable rights holders, particularly journalists, to protect their own work?

speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath
heading: Meta: AI Development - Question
text: The noble Viscount will not be surprised to hear that I disagree with his description of the Government’s strategy, work and progress on this issue. It is very clear that DCMS is in charge of AI and copyright and works across government, including with BIST on growth and the economy, and very closely with the Cabinet Office, which has the lead on the AI strategy. We are progressing our review of creator control and input transparency at pace, and are engaging extensively with stakeholders to assess the effectiveness of existing mechanisms and whether there is an appropriate role for the Government. We hope to publish our findings in the first part of next year.

speaker: Lord Lemos
heading: Courts and Tribunals Bill - Second Reading
text:
My Lords, I thank all noble Lords for what has been, as the noble Lord, Lord Marks, said, a powerful, thoughtful and thought-provoking debate. There is much for us to continue to discuss. Before I respond in detail to some of the points that have been made, I join other noble Lords in congratulating my noble friend Lord Stace on his excellent maiden speech and will comment on his rich and varied career. I do not think I ever imagined I would meet someone who was both chair of the Prison Reform Trust and the former CEO of Saga. I wonder which of those jobs is the more entertaining. Anyway, I congratulate him and I very much welcome him to our Benches. I am sure he is going to make a powerful contribution. I endorse my noble friend Lady Chakrabarti’s comment that his speech was humble and humane and, in that sense and in many others, entirely admirable.

At the heart of this Bill are principled reforms designed not simply to address the pressures that face our courts today but to ensure that our justice system is fit for the future. A number of noble Lords have spoken to me about some of the provisions in the Bill already, and I am grateful to them for their measured and constructive approach. I say to the noble and learned Lord, Lord Keen of Elie, that I promise to engage very fully not just with the Official Opposition but with all Members of your Lordships’ House, as I have already done on this Bill. I will continue to work constructively with all noble Lords who are interested in this. I do not underestimate what is at stake here, and nor do the Government.

I will address some of the points that were raised most frequently—as it were, the biggest concerns. If I do not get the chance to address every issue that has been raised, I promise to write in detail and will continue to engage. I will try to mention noble Lords who have raised these points, but I fear I will not be able to remember everyone and apologise in advance for that.

The constitutional importance of jury trial and the right to elect for a jury trial has been raised several times by noble Lords, including my noble friends Lady Chakrabarti and Lady Kennedy of The Shaws, the noble Lords, Lord Howard and Lord Ashcombe, and, from rather different perspectives, my noble friend Lady Levitt and the noble Lord, Lord Carlile. The Government agree that the right to a fair trial is a fundamental constitutional principle. However, a defendant’s ability to choose the mode of trial is not a constitutional safeguard. Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and allocating cases to the most appropriate venue supports that objective. The right to elect is not a universal feature of the common law system, as the noble Lord, Lord Carlile said; indeed, Scotland does not operate a general right of defendant election, as the noble Lord, Lord Macdonald, pointed out.

That said, when determining venue, magistrates will continue to apply the Sentencing Council’s allocation guidelines, considering the seriousness and complexity of the case alongside representations from both the prosecution and the defence. The constitutional principle we are protecting is the right to a fair trial before an independent court, and that principle remains fully intact.

The noble Lord, Lord Marks, raised the question of good character and the right to elect. In the Government’s view, allocation should be determined by the seriousness of the alleged offending and not by the personal characteristics of the defendant. Magistrates’ courts already deliver fair and impartial justice in the overwhelming majority of criminal cases. A Crown Court trial is not inherently fairer. There is no statutory or straightforward definition of “good character” for these purposes, and introducing such a test would add greater complexity and subjectivity to allocation decisions.

The question of legal aid was raised by a number of your Lordships, including my noble friend Lady Mallalieu, the right reverend Prelate the Bishop of St Edmundsbury and Ipswich and the noble and learned Lord, Lord Thomas. We acknowledge, as noble Lords have noted, that the Bill will result in more cases being heard in the magistrates’ court, where the legal aid means test is less generous than in the Crown Court. However, having looked into this, we are confident that the majority of defendants currently charged with “either way” offences will be eligible for legal aid in the magistrates’ court under the existing financial eligibility rules.

For individuals who do not qualify, however, support is available through the hardship review mechanism, as well as the free duty solicitor scheme, which may provide legal representation at the first hearing. We have listened carefully—this is an important point—to concerns about legal aid eligibility in the magistrates’ court in the context of the Bill’s reform to the right to elect. In light of this, the Government have accepted in principle recommendation 155 from the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, to increase the legal aid income threshold at the magistrates’ court. Final decisions on income threshold levels will be taken once the reforms have been implemented, subject to future funding decisions and operational considerations. I hope noble Lords take some reassurance from that.

There was a theme that ran through the entire debate today about the question of whether we were putting too much strain on the magistrates’ court system. It was mentioned by my noble friend Lord McNicol, the noble Baronesses, Lady Brinton and Lady Mallalieu, the noble and learned Lord, Lord Bellamy, the noble Lord, Lord Carlile, and, notably, the noble Lord, Lord Macdonald. The Government’s view is that the magistrates keep the system turning; they already handle more than 90% of all criminal cases, completing around 1.5 million cases each year, more than 11 times the number in the Crown Court, and deal with cases triable either way four times faster than the Crown Court. We of course recognise that additional demand will have an impact, and that is why we are increasing funded sitting days from 114,000 last year to 125,800 next year, rising to a target of 131,000 sitting days by 2028-29.

We have launched a multi-million pound recruitment campaign, and through this we are increasing the size of the magistracy by around 50%, as I said in my opening remarks. We are also increasing overall capacity through the recruitment of legal advisers and district judges, with recruitment programmes expected to provide sufficient judicial and legal adviser capability to support the increase in funded sitting days by 2028-29.

The noble Baroness, Lady Fox, asked about magistrates and whether we have asked them if they support these measures. The Magistrates’ Association is on the record as saying it supports these measures, and it is in our own Library briefing that it is supportive of them. I note the comments of the noble Baroness, Lady Sater, and I very much look forward to working with her, as we are working on other issues too. She clearly has extensive experience. I particularly note the points that she and a number of noble Lords made about training, which is obviously critical. It is a statement of the obvious that recruitment is one thing, but getting people trained and functioning effectively is something else.

The noble Lord, Lord Macdonald, asked me about models and assessments; the noble Lord, Lord Ashcombe, and the noble and learned Lords, Lord Thomas and Lord Keen of Elie, also asked me about this. We are confident that the remaining package of reforms, combined with record financial investment and our work on efficiencies, frees up enough Crown Court time to turn the tide on the backlog and to start delivering swifter justice for victims by the end of this Parliament. My honourable friend Minister Sackman has made that commitment many times. In fact, without the operational challenges of creating the Crown Court Bench division that would introduce juryless trials for less serious offences in the Crown Court, we shall be able to act quicker to implement other reforms and begin reducing the backlog sooner. We have published modelling that I have circulated to noble Lords who have attended various engagement meetings I have had.

That modelling shows that our remaining package of reforms, when combined with investment and our work on efficiency, sees the backlog peak in 2028 before starting to fall rapidly over 2029. With the accelerated implementation of the measures removing the right to elect, and of the magistrates’ court sentencing powers, we can go faster and turn that tide sooner. Our model suggests that, in fact, the backlog will peak in 2027 before starting to fall. That means that we should be able to get the backlog down sooner in this Parliament.

I want to be completely clear with your Lordships about this. The data has been published and we will keep it under review. I shall be happy, as we go through Committee, to discuss this with noble Lords and to be clear about it. We want to be transparent. Obviously, we want the magistrates to have the capacity to deal with the extra burden. We have published our models, as I said, and I will continue to discuss those with noble Lords. The noble Lord, Lord Macdonald, asked me about the Institute for Government’s observations. I understand that it has endorsed our model and said that it agrees with the analysis that we have set out of when the backlog will come down.

I thank the noble Baroness, Lady Jones, and my noble friend Lady Mallalieu for their contributions on the court estate. Obviously, we know that this is an important question; a number of references have been made to buckets and so on. We need to address the inefficiencies in the system. We must pull every lever, not just for structural reform but for investment and efficiency, as the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, encouraged us to do—in parallel, rather than choosing between them.

We have started to modernise our courts through greater use of technology and AI, and we are developing specialist case progression staff in every Crown Court centre, expanding appropriate remote hearings and investing over £17 million in virtual remand hearings. Pilots to help reduce delays and improve court productivity are under way. Again, efficiency in the court system is something we will have to think about as we go through these debates, and, indeed, beyond. We will continue to think about ways in which we can make the physical, as well as the technological, infrastructure of the court system more robust.

I turn to the questions raised by the noble Lord, Lord Russell of Liverpool, among others, about diversity in the judiciary and the magistracy. For all the reasons noble Lords have given, diversity in the judiciary and the magistracy is vital to maintaining public confidence, widening the pool of talent, and ensuring that the justice system benefits from the full range of skills and experience across society. Significant progress has been made for new entrants. This last year, women accounted for 55%, and 16% of new entrants to the judiciary were from ethnic minority backgrounds.

That is a positive, but there is clearly much more work that we can do, and need to do. That is why the Lord Chancellor and the Lady Chief Justice are co-chairing the Judicial and Legal Diversity Board, which looks across the whole system to improve diversity while maintaining appointment on merit. We think that is very important. I have also mentioned that we are engaged in a major magistrate recruitment campaign, targeted outreach and streamlining recruitment processes so that we can attract a broader and younger range of candidates to the magistracy, and ensure that it better reflects the communities it serves.

The question of appeals was raised by a number of noble Lords, including the noble Lords, Lord Murray and Lord Carlile, and my noble friend Lord McNicol. The noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, identified that an automatic right to a full rehearing impacts adversely on victims and witnesses, who may not be prepared to return to court a second time. We know that some appeals succeed not due to an identified error in the original trial but because victims and witnesses feel unable to relive the trauma with a second trial at appeal. We would all agree that this is not how we want things to operate.

Magistrates already give their reasons for their decisions, and these will be recorded and available to the judge to decide on the merits and scope of possible appeals. I note the comments that have been made about training and access to legal advisers. I also note the comments about the Law Commission. The Law Commission’s report was commissioned in 2023, and the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, has reported since.

I now turn to “judge alone” trials, which are an important aspect of the Bill for complex and lengthy cases. This was raised by the noble Lords, Lord Marks and Lord Howard, and the noble Baroness, Lady Kennedy of The Shaws. We have heard concerns that Part 2 of Schedule 1 to the Bill could be used, over time, to expand the scope of Clause 4 beyond fraud and financial offending. Amendments to the schedule can be made only through the affirmative procedure—I confirm that for the noble and learned Lord, Lord Keen of Elie, who asked me about it—which means a successful vote in both Houses. Offences cannot be added to the schedule without Parliament’s consent. This provision has been included to allow the system to respond flexibly, as criminal offending evolves over time. Any added offences would also have to comply with the statutory safeguards for the policy: a preparatory hearing; a public interest test; exclusions for homicide and indictable-only sex offences; and judicial decision-making.

On the same subject, I was asked by noble Lords about dishonesty. This change is not about who understands dishonesty better; it is about reducing the burden on ordinary people’s lives from sitting on long trials. Disclosure and case management of fraud cases must improve, and the Government have agreed in principle to many of the recommendations of the Fisher report and those made by the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson. This measure follows a long line of similar recommendations made by distinguished judges and independent reviewers, including those by Lord Justice Auld in 2001 and by Lord Roskill in the 1980s, as mentioned by noble Lords.

I am running out of time, but there are two important issues I want to deal with now; I will deal with the others in writing. I will address the question about victims, which was raised by a number of noble Lords. The case mentioned by the noble Baroness, Lady Brinton, and the noble Lord, Lord Russell, of Emma—I realise that that is not her real name—was heart-rending, and I am very grateful to them for bringing it to our attention. We all agree that we do not want the delays facing victims today to continue. We believe that the changes in the Bill, not just to speed up these trials but in tackling harmful myths and the admissibility of evidence, matter. The special measures that are also addressed in the Bill make enlightened and principled reforms that will be of great benefit to victims.

On the specific question that the noble Lord, Lord Russell, asked, my understanding is that the judiciary’s national listing framework will put an end to the practice of “floating” lists. Along with these reforms, we are investing record levels in victim support services and consulting on a new victims’ code, as we have discussed before in your Lordships’ House.

I will say just a few sentences about rape and serial sexual offences in the courts. I note the comments made by a number of noble Lords about this very important initiative, particularly those of the noble Baroness, Lady Brinton. We can do this without legislation, so we are rolling it out. I am very happy to discuss that with her further.

Finally, on repealing the presumption of parental involvement, we heard powerful contributions from the noble Baroness, Lady Barran, and the noble Lord, Lord Farmer. I absolutely undertake to discuss in detail those matters with them and others. This is a subject very close to my heart. I take it very seriously and I very much look forward to working with them on it. We have received divergent advice from your Lordships on this subject, so we need to work our way through it, but I think everyone agrees that we want to do what is best for the child.

I really have run out of time now—in fact, I have gone well over. I just want to say one other thing, which is to note the comments of the noble Lord, Lord Marks, about out-of-court disposals and the comment from the noble and learned Lord, Lord Keen, about getting to the root causes, endorsing the comments by my noble friend Lord Stace. I too think those are things that we should discuss further.

With thanks to your Lordships for a powerful debate and apologies for exceeding my time, I look forward to discussing these matters with your Lordships in Committee and, indeed, in engagement between now and then.

Bill read a second time.

speaker: Allegra Spender
heading: BILLS
subheading: Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 3) Bill 2026, Income Tax Rates Amendment (Minimum Tax on Discretionary Trusts) Bill 2026, Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 4) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I want to put my objections to the process on the record at the start. I understand the pressure the government has to pass these reforms this year, but, yesterday, we were asked to debate and pass a bill in the same day that it was introduced. The government has given us another 24 hours, but this is a small concession. This is treating the House and those people who sent us here with contempt, and the government is making it a habit. I'd now like to turn to the substance of the bill.

Rebalancing our tax system was an overdue debate left in the too-hard basket by generations of Labor and coalition governments. I give the government credit for taking it on. It's hard and it takes guts. The government has acted to try and increase homeownership, and I support that, but, looking at the packages before this parliament, I have two significant concerns. First, the government is not lowering income tax rates. That has, honestly, been the entire point of the work that I've been doing on personal income tax. Problems with trusts and CGT discounts would be significantly reduced if the top marginal tax rate was lower. Whether the government is saving this for an election or is wary of inflation, the $77 billion left unallocated in this year's budget because of these tax changes should have been committed in legislation to lowering marginal tax rates, even if they came in after a number of years. Secondly, the package the government has put forward in previous bills and in this bill fail on innovation and business investment, particularly because of CGT. They are delivering the opposite. I hear from people in my electorate about investments falling apart and entrepreneurs leaving the country because of the CGT changes. And while the IBCC that is included in this bill makes it better, this is not a fix. The government must do better.

Let me take these bills in reverse order. Tax reform No. 4 will introduce an innovative business CGT concession allowing qualifying companies to retain a 50 per cent discount. It will, secondly, reform the R&D tax incentive in line with the Denholm review and, thirdly, enhance venture capital investment vehicles. Fourthly, it will make FBT less generous for electric vehicles. I support the venture capital changes, and I have been pushing them. I support making FBT less generous for electric vehicles, and I think the government could potentially go further on this because of the great uptake in electric vehicles driven by the Iran war. But unfortunately the things that particularly are there to drive investment are overshadowed by the CGT changes. I want to put on the record that I remain deeply concerned by the government's indexation approach to the CGT discount when it is applied to businesses and shares. Its proposed fix for innovative businesses, the IBCC, is I think better than nothing but far short of what it needs to be.

I am on the record as someone who supports changing the CGT concessions. I am on the record so visibly. If it is driving reductions in marginal tax rates, that is the point. I think this is important, and I think these messages need to be sent, because we tax people the most heavily when they are least able to pay. That is indicated by two types of household, one over the age of 65 and one of working age. The working-age household pays, on average, twice the tax when their two householders are earning 100 grand compared with the retired household. That makes no sense, given that the working-age household probably has HECS debts, probably doesn't own their own home or has a big mortgage, and is maybe paying childcare costs.

We need to rebalance the system, because young people are being left behind. We have seen in the decade up until 2016 that the wealth of older households grew by around 50 per cent and the wealth of younger households flatlined. That is a problem, and it's a structural problem. And we have a structural problem with an ageing population. We used to have, in the 1980s, around six people of working age for every person over 65; now it's down to four, and in the future it's going to be down to under three. These are the reasons we do need to rebalance the system.

But I want to come back to the fact that I think changing the CGT model through indexation is wrong, because it is focused on fairness, which I support, but it is not doing what it needs to do on prosperity, and I think it is genuinely hampering the prosperity that we need to grow in this country. The Treasurer has acknowledged the indexation limitations for high-growth, low-capital companies, both in his budget papers and in his second reading speech on tax reform No. 1. And I think it is relevant that only one other major economy, and that is Israel, uses this methodology. But it has a top marginal tax rate on capital of around 30 per cent, not around 47 per cent. I know the government is trying to fix this, and I know the government has done genuine consultation on the IBCC and has responded to feedback on this.

But let's be honest: the IBCC doesn't fix all the problems here. Even in its current form, the IBCC proposal is complex. It is still administratively onerous. It doesn't work for genesis kinds of innovations, such as biotech. With those time limits it may not be appropriate. It doesn't work for publicly listed companies that are very innovative or taking high risks, such as minerals exploration and, again, some biotech. I think those reasons alone say that the IBCC itself should be better. But the problem is that even if we fix those challenges with the IBCC on those specifics, the IBCC and the indexation model are still not right for businesses and for shares. For one, they are complex, and that is an issue when it comes to tax. Adam Smith said simplicity should be part of the ambition for any tax system, and he, hundreds of years ago, was absolutely right. It is unfair. You don't have to be innovative to take enormous risk to start and grow a business. Many businesses in our economy are low capital and so are particularly disadvantaged by indexation but would not fall under this innovative sort of definition. It's just not fair. We do not want to penalise people who are taking risks who don't fit a government definition of innovation. We need to recognise that there is enormous uncertainty in starting and growing a business. That is why it deserves a discount.

Finally, this is internationally uncompetitive. We have businesses in this country that could be subjected to tax rates on CGT well into the 40s, compared to other countries. It's uncompetitive. We don't have to have the lowest CGT rates in the world, but we do have to be in the zone of competition or we will lose some of our best and brightest overseas. I think the government's current proposal could do that.

I am going to put forward a different proposal because I do believe there is a chance for the government to make substantial changes here that could make a difference. What I've been trying to do is ask, 'What could the government do, given the legislation that has passed, given the legislation that's in front of the parliament at the moment, to try and fix this?' I'm arguing that the government should, for businesses and shares, go back to a flat discount, and I'm arguing that we should use the 'active asset' definition—which is currently well established and well understood—from various CGT concessions, with some small modifications, and make that discount 40 per cent instead of 50 per cent. That would raise about the same amount of revenue, according to the PBO analysis that I have done, but it would be substantially superior.

These are the arguments why. Firstly, it would ensure that any company, regardless of its innovation potential, would get a guaranteed flat 40 per cent discount instead of indexation, and it would keep our top capital gains tax rate at around 28 per cent, which is competitive internationally. It's not the lowest, but nor is it the highest. It is in the zone of play. It would allow the government to keep indexation on housing, which I think is appropriate. I accept that there are some very good reasons there. The businesspeople I talk to have a wide variety of views in terms of how we should tax capital. But where I do think many of them are united is in saying that taxing at 40 per cent across the board on active assets, which would also benefit risk-taking in shares, is a better outcome than trying to do the 50 per cent only through the IBCC and have everybody else subject to indexation. I think the government really should look at this.

Finally, this bill reforms the R&D tax incentive based on the Ambitious Australia report. Again, I'd say that the intention is worthy. I recognise that the government has done some very good things here, including the higher offset rates for core R&D. But I'll be honest: I'm concerned on two fronts. One is about removing support of R&D. We know that they've expanded the definition of core R&D through the offsets, but we don't think they will be completely offset. The second thing is the time limit in relation to these R&D tax incentives. I understand where the government's coming from here, but I still think, particularly for biotech or deep tech, that 15 years isn't enough. I met Dr Julian Freitag today, whose company, Magellan Stem Cells, is 17 years old and in Phase III trials. It's exactly that sort of company that would not be able to get this important R&D tax credit under the current changes. So I'm urging the government to reconsider this.

I'll turn to Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No.3) Bill 2026. This bill delivers the budget commitment to a minimum 30 per cent tax rate on trust distributions. It includes rollover relief for those structuring out of a discretionary trust and a new electable regime, the excluded election trust. It also clarifies how CGT applies to trusts and defines 'new residential dwelling' for the CGT and negative gearing changes already passed. It's been a really hard time for small businesses and restructuring is one more thing to deal with. I think the timing of trying to get businesses to restructure is wrong. Certainly, while I support principles of managing trusts in a more effective way, I've never thought we should actually deal with the trusts directly because of the complexity of restructuring. Regardless of this, I do believe we should be working towards a tax system on the principle where, if money is earned, the tax rate that is applied is pretty consistent, regardless of the structure that you individually are able to use.

I want to admit that there are very many genuine reasons for trusts, including managing succession in family businesses—and my own family has those trusts in place—but it is very clear also that trusts have really ballooned in recent times for reasons outside of business succession and through income splitting in different ways. I don't blame anyone using these structures. I keep on coming back to the fact that we need to cut the top marginal tax rates, when the incentives to use these sorts of structures would be significantly reduced, which would be beneficial to the overall economy. I recognise that many people in my electorate use these structures for things that really matter to them, like helping their young people through uni or topping up an older parent's income. I take the point that these are really positive things, but I recognise that they aren't open to everyone, and therefore I think it is appropriate to consider these restructures, though I have to say I'm really concerned by aspects around stamp duty, because the states haven't guaranteed that they're going to waive stamp duty, and I think that is a really significant challenge with this piece of legislation.

I'm going to finish off with some broad observations on tax reform. Tax reform is essential in this economy—and, I think, with low productivity and real challenges on housing and opportunities for young people to get ahead, it's critical. But we need to be clear on the why and clear on the principles on which you judge a reform. We need all the taxes on the table and we need a transparent process that allows us to properly manage the trade-offs and build community support. And I do not believe that the government has delivered any of these effectively in this bill. In the green paper I first did on tax, I outlined six objectives for tax reform that I think are still relevant: lower income taxes, rebalance the tax settings in favour of homeownership, which I agree the government has done, boost productivity and growth, stabilise our revenue base so that it can endure changes to demographics and consumption patterns, support the energy transition through better tax settings, and implement institutional reform. There are also six principles which build on Adam Smith's principles of efficiency, fairness, simplicity and adequacy which are important to the tax system. One, tax reform should encourage economic productivity and growth. Two, it should raise revenue with the least cost to society by minimising distortions in the way we work, consume, save and invest. Three, it should encourage behaviours that benefit individuals, society and the environment. Four, it should treat people and organisations with the same capacity to pay in the same way and raise more tax from those with greater capacity to pay. Five, it should be easy to understand and simple and cost-effective to comply with. Six, it should provide a stable tax base over time given changes in the economy and society.

There are always trade-offs against these objectives and against these principles, but I still think they stand the test of time. And I think that this is where we need to go from here, because the tax reform that is in front of the parliament at the moment should be better, but it also should not be the last word. We have minerals that are undertaxed. We have stamp duty that taxes mobility. We have no credible way of pricing emissions. We have communities worried about jobs and AI, yet we tax people who employ people. These things don't make sense. We need to drive better outcomes across our society. The tax system is a critical part of this, and that is why we need broader tax reform but with principles and with purpose that are clearer than where we are today.

speaker: Ed Husic
heading: BILLS
subheading: Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 3) Bill 2026, Income Tax Rates Amendment (Minimum Tax on Discretionary Trusts) Bill 2026, Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 4) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I thank the member for Wentworth. A lot was covered off by her there, but I want to recognise that she's done a mighty lot of work in talking with people that we both know and have great regard for when it comes to building a stronger economy by thinking differently, coming up with new ideas and being able to convert those ideas into commercial practice. Again, I think these contributions are really important. If there's anything this parliament can do with more of, it is thinking about how we generate new enterprises and how to grow them and make them much more solid, particularly enterprises that are trying to change the nature of the economy.

The reality is our world faces three big issues in particular. We have the impact of global warming, the rise of artificial intelligence and the breakdown of the international rules based order that deals with those things. When it comes to global warming, for a country like ours that has been dependent on resources for so long and made so much money, particularly from fossil fuels, as the world starts pivoting away and we start seeing lower demand, what will happen is that we will earn less money off those things as a nation.

That requires us to think differently about how we make our income and about the jobs that we create, and it does require us to think really deeply about the economic complexity of the nation. We have too many eggs in a few baskets. The parliament, as I said before, needs to think about the types of firms that emerge, but the parliament also needs to think about the face, shape, operations and the economy not just in an election cycle but for many years ahead—dare I say, decades ahead.

On top of those three things that I mentioned, there will be things that come out of the blue, that are unexpected and that also challenge and pressure economies. We lived through it. A once-in-a-generation pandemic really highlighted for this nation how dependent we were on just one country for all our goods and services. We recognised that we were vulnerable to dysfunctional supply chains. We realised that so much of the stuff we took for granted required importation. The things we needed the most weren't there when we needed them most, and we said, particularly as an incoming government, that we would reimagine what we do so that we can ensure that, on those key things—those national priorities and the goods that are really important to us—we'll able to do a lot more of that work ourselves.

These things are very big. They're big, hairy problems that are very difficult to solve. To do that, we need ideas. We need people to think differently about how to solve those problems. For instance, if we want to reimagine how we reduce our dependency on overseas supply chains and how we make more of our own goods, how we do so, when others have perfected the production process and we haven't got that ourselves, requires smart people—researchers and scientists—to start thinking of the ways to get this done. It also requires entrepreneurs to join with that effort to convert an idea from a lab benchtop into a production process and turn that into a commercial reality. We need a lot of people to do it.

In any nation, the key to all that I'm describing is having a healthy base of research and development. In Australia, we often celebrate really smart people who have done incredible things. We are, for example, right on the cusp of curing one of the most terrible conditions that has affected women: cervical cancer. We are now immunising young women from cervical cancer using Gardasil. Gardasil was created—it came out of an Australian mind in Dr Ian Frazer, and we owe him a big healthy dose of gratitude for what he's done to transform the lives of women and prevent them dying early from cervical cancer. It was an Australian who did it, but it was an overseas company that made the products and took all the gains.

We see this time and again, and I am so frustrated that an idea that began in an Australian mind is finished with hands on another side of the planet. We can do this work, and we can make it happen here, but R&D is critical as part of that process. In this country, as much as we have some really great minds, we've got a really bad way of supporting those great minds. If you look at R&D investment, it fell from 2.24 per cent of gross domestic product to 1.69 per cent in just 15 years.

In the OECD, we performed terribly on R&D. We have got to do better, but it's not an easy thing to fix. In the last term, as an industry minister, I pushed a number of times. It may come as a big surprise, but I can be a bit persistent! I did continue to badger my way into making sure we got a review of R&D in this country, and it ended up being called the Strategic Examination of Research and Development. It was designed to maximise the value of public investment in research. It was looking at harnessing and growing business investment in R&D. It looked to leverage our scientific strength to help address national priorities and, importantly, to foster new industries.

This is really important. As I said earlier, we have too many eggs in one basket. Our economy is not complex enough. We need to come up with new industries that make money. I'll give you an example. We can do this. People in this chamber would probably be unaware that we export a product that earns more money than some agricultural products that we currently ship overseas. There'd be very few people in this place that would think that software licensing is creating a lot of export dollars for us, but it's actually doing much better than most agricultural products in this country. Australians are coming up with software that is being bought by other people overseas, but that takes a lot of work, and we can't just have a few of those examples. But we are creating those new sectors in this country.

The SERD, as it became known, was headed up by Robyn Denholm, a terrific Australian, who is now chair of Tesla internationally. She came from the western suburbs of Sydney, made her way through different jobs and has been recognised for great business acumen, particularly in a company that has had to rely heavily on R&D, to change the way we drive cars and produce them. We had Professor Ian Chubb, former chief scientist, on there. We had Fiona Wood from WA, who was the instrumental person in the development of spray-on skin, which was critical when we had victims of the Bali bombing who had suffered terrible burns. She was able to help them repair their skin. We put her on the SERD panel. Someone who I've got great admiration for is Kate Cornick, who headed up LaunchVic and has been involved in helping start-ups in Victoria for many, many years. A great mind, she is now involved as the CEO of the Tech Council of Australia.

I want to formally, on the record, thank those people for their work. Their work has been absolutely critical in outlining how we can improve the way in which we invest in R&D in this country. To be completely frank, I would much prefer a much more developed and detailed response to SERD than a sporadic attempt to deal with some of those things. The review has been mentioned a number of times in terms of underpinning the changes that are being debated in this amendment today, but we do need to have a much more comprehensive response. I imagine the panel is keen to do it, and they've done a mighty job for this nation with the work that they've done, but it is critical work to think about how we invest more in this process.

The government has done a lot here to try and think this through. I know that there's been a focus on core R&D. Core R&D is important, but so is the supporting effort as well, particularly if you're developing hardware. Hardware does require the translation of a concept in the core phase, where you think of an idea, you think it might work, but when you go from a prototype you realise it may not actually stack up commercially and no-one will buy the product in the way that it's being put forward. Supporting R&D takes the time to do that. It's why, for example, the idea of capping—how long it takes or how long you can claim the R&DTI—has had such resistance, particularly in areas of biotech. But I also think of people in the climate tech space who are helping us reduce emissions with new hardware. It takes them ages to get that sorted, so we do need to see a bit of flexibility around that.

There are a lot of changes in here. I know there are people in the startup sector who've reached out to me who are happy with the level of engagement that the Treasurer and Treasury have undertaken, but they still have some concerns. Obviously, we are trying to work through some of that moving forward.

But I do get tired, I have to say; it took me a while to get the SERD up. When it comes to R&D, it's not the first time that there have been moves to change it. Under the former government, there was a move to cut $2.4 billion out of R&D—and before then, when we were last in government, there was a move to change the capital gains tax arrangements on employee share ownership, which, frankly, was disastrous. We get the advice from the same two departments. It doesn't matter, as I keep saying, who is on this side of the House; we get advised by the same people—the hive mind that is built between the Department of the Treasury and the Department of Finance—that do not look at Australian R&D as an investment. They see it as a cost and they see it as a way to cut, and they always put forward these types of ideas to cut costs. We can't afford that in this country. Treasury in particular have made public statements where they believe that it's better for us to just adapt someone else's technology than to develop here in this country. This is selling out our country terribly—absolutely awful.

We need those people who are stuck in ideological permafrost to recognise that, if we want to get the economy ready for the long-term, if we want to learn the lessons of the pandemic, if we want to ensure that not all our eggs are in one basket, if we want to not be dependent on vulnerable supply chains, we need to back R&D. But if we listen to Treasury and we listen to Finance, they're always going to be looking for a quick save—and we can't have it, because they don't have faith in Australian innovation. Like I said, when we were last in office it was they that suggested we tax unrealised gains in employee share ownership—terrible for start-ups, and we backed the last government in fixing it. The last government had a revolt in its own ranks about changes to R&D that were pushed, and I have to congratulate Senator Hume in leading that charge in government to convince the Morrison government not to go ahead with massive cuts to R&D. But now we've had to deal with proposals yet again by Treasury and Finance that we make these changes to R&D—terrible.

If we want the country to be stronger longer term, on its own two feet, in a changing world, we need to not only back our scientists and researchers; we absolutely have to back those start-ups, those early-stage companies, to make sure that they can succeed in the best possible way. There are a lot of good changes in here, and I'm glad that a lot of work's been done, but we can absolutely do better into the future. The parliament needs to take the time to learn a lot more about the work of start-ups and the contribution they make to this great nation of ours.

speaker: Nicolette Boele
heading: BILLS
subheading: Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 3) Bill 2026, Income Tax Rates Amendment (Minimum Tax on Discretionary Trusts) Bill 2026, Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 4) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I'm rising to speak on the Income Tax Rates Amendment (Minimum Tax on Discretionary Trusts) Bill 2026, the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 3) Bill 2026 and the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 4) Bill 2026. The changes outlined in schedules 1 to 3 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 3) Bill 2026, which introduce a minimum tax on discretionary trust income, are significant. Indeed, they are a significant departure from the beneficiary taxation principles that have been in place for 90 years. These proposed changes are technical and complex. I note, with disappointment and at the risk of repeating myself, that we are once again not being offered the opportunity to review the outcome of that inquiry before debating the bills.

I want to talk about these discretionary trusts. I've heard from many small businesses in Bradfield that will be impacted and who rightly use discretionary trusts for fair dinkum purposes—family and commercial arrangements, quarantining investment risks, asset protection and succession planning, not to mention estate planning, about which some concerns and confusion remain. Treasury estimates that the additional regulatory compliance burden will be material, around $141 million per annum. While not all of this will be borne by those needing to restructure, it is an acknowledgement of the additional complexity being introduced in the tax system as a result of these bills. Rollover relief across an extended period to 30 June 2030 is therefore welcomed. However, this relief only applies to a small subset of potential costs and does not provide for the state and territory stamp duty that may be incurred in transferring real assets nor the cost of professional services and other advice that trustees will be required to seek to understand their restructuring options and what's required of them. One Bradfield small-business owner told me that she will be forced to close her business as a result of these changes. I think it's reasonable to expect that the federal government will work hard to negotiate with the states to introduce stamp duty exemptions for these businesses, and I'm going to continue to press them to do so.

In addition, despite the deliberate intention of these reforms being to, in effect, force taxpayers to migrate from one structure to another, any tax losses accrued in the original trust structure will be potentially stranded. This is a substantive economic cost being imposed on taxpayers who are only restructuring because government has made a midterm policy change. This is a question I'm being asked all the time. Surely the government could have worked to create a statutory mechanism to preserve tax losses during a government induced restructure. This is among many of the questions that my constituents have raised with me in relation to these bills. I think it points to a need for greater transparency from the government on other key issues also raised with me, such as the source of the $4.5 billion additional revenue allegedly generated from these changes, how much is going to come from income splitting and whether some of these arise because tax losses become stranded or unusable. Also, more transparency is needed about how the government settled on a flat rate of 30 per cent. While this aligns with the marginal rate that the average taxpayer pays, it's difficult to otherwise reconcile it to the average taxable income or the average tax paid.

There is another part of the bill that I would like to speak to as well, and that's the clarification of negative gearing exemptions for social and affordable housing. The bill defines affordable housing in line with the Income Tax Assessment Act, but the definition could be improved and made consistent across the country. My campaign for a nationally consistent definition of affordable housing is ongoing, and I introduced a private member's bill into the House last month to create exactly that. It sets affordable housing rent at the lower of 75 per cent of market rent and 30 per cent of household income for lower household incomes. The Treasurer has said that he agrees we need a consistent definition, and this bill is an opportunity to progress that agenda.

Today we're also being asked to debate another large tax bill, Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 4) Bill 2026, at the same time as the other two bills. I don't support lumping these together. I believe it dilutes the quality of parliamentary debate, but I have some remarks to make on this bill. I support the fact that the government is proposing to provide exemptions for CGT changes for innovative start-ups, as I've consistently called for since the tax changes were announced in the budget in May. I acknowledge the member for Wentworth has put forward different, cleaner proposals, and I support the fact that the government is considering these and hopefully doing something about this issue. The bill also makes changes to the research and development tax incentive. Previous reviews of the R&D tax incentive have found that the scheme has fallen short of its objectives of encouraging additional R&D and generating wider economic spill-overs. That's why I support the direction of these parts of the reforms, which seek to better target assistance towards core experimental research and provide stronger incentives for businesses undertaking genuinely innovative work. These are worthwhile reforms that respond to an important part of Australia's innovation challenge. However, one of the changes is the 15-year refundable offset for biotechnology and medical technology firms, which in my view is just not fit for purpose. Many medical technologies take much longer than 15 years to reach market, and that means the cut-off will come often during costly late-stage clinical trials, just when we need to be offering them support. We have biotech firms based in Bradfield, and I'm calling on the government to support the member for Curtin's amendment to this bill. Remove the 15-year age limit on the offsets for companies in this sector.

These changes also sit within a larger challenge that cannot be addressed through the tax system alone. Australia's total investment in R&D is now just 1.69 per cent of GDP against an OECD average of 2.72 per cent, and the Australian Academy of Science has described recent measures in the budget as useful whilst warning that they will not on their own reverse Australia's long-term research underinvestment. At a time when artificial intelligence, biotechnology, clean energy and other critical technologies are becoming central to our economic prosperity and national resilience, we cannot afford to allow Australians and their research capabilities and the talented people who sustain it to fall behind. So, while I support the direction of these particular changes, I encourage the government to see them as part of a broader national task—lifting Australia's research ambition, retaining and attracting talented scientists and ensuring that the technologies and industries that will shape our future are not simply invented elsewhere and imported here.

Finally, this bill implements the government's commitment earlier this year to phase out the fringe benefit tax exemption on EVs. As I said when they made this announcement, I think it's disappointing that, in the middle of a fuel crisis when every electric car on the road represents diesel and petrol that they don't have to import, the government should choose to roll this successful initiative back. We absolutely need to be prudent with how government funds are invested, but right now I think is not the time to wind this back. I think it's good that they aren't removing it entirely. EV sales are taking off around the country, and we should still be doing everything we can in our power to electrify our transport systems as fast as we can whilst this fuel crisis continues. These bills are far from good. They might in some places have good meaningful intent or not, but I hope by the time it comes back to this place that many of the crossbench amendments that have been made are considered and adopted—those from Wentworth, from Curtin and indeed from Mackellar. Without these changes, this is going to be a bunch of bills that will be tricky to support.

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
text:
'What is one big issue shaping our future, and what is a meaningful action you want parliament to take on it?' Earlier this year, Raise Our Voice asked that question to women and gender diverse people under 25 years of age. I'd like to read two responses to the question from two young people in my electorate. First, from Evelyn, aged 11, who argues that our school curriculum should not include artificial intelligence, especially where it impedes the mental health and cybersafety of our students. Evelyn says:

Data shows strong evidence that screens have significant effects on mental and physical health on children. The more they were engaged with screens, the likelier they were to develop socioemotional problems as screens are a coping mechanism, the socioemotional problems that would arise would be anxiety, depression, aggression and hyperactivity, which would lead to a damaged family relationship, behavioural issues, attention and self-esteem challenges.

It is time that our curriculum prioritises student health and cyber security with the same urgency as traditional subjects!

The second response I received was from Iris, who is 13 years old. Iris says:

To combat anti-immigrant sentiment in Australia, it would help to teach a more inclusive history to young Australians, they would be educated in the diverse histories of cultures beyond their own, increasing their empathy and understanding.

Australians need to know about the wrongdoings of the British empire.

They need to learn about other countries histories'; about minorities' histories, such as feminist history, the history of other races and religions, and queer history.
