Iris then suggested that parliament could review the curriculum, reconsidering how historical events are taught with an increasing focus on critical thinking for all year groups. She believes this is necessary for the general education and betterment of society. I couldn't agree more. Thank you to both Evelyn and Iris for your youthful responses.

I'd also like to take the remaining time to thank the group of young adults and students from the Australian Youth Climate Coalition action groups who visited me recently. In fact, some are in parliament today with their report to the special rapporteur around climate action and the trust gap between the Australian government's commitment to the Pacific nations around care and climate and continuing to make the problem worse by approving coal and gas. I thank young people for being engaged in their democracy and caring about their issues. Contact your local MPs. Make your voice be heard.

speaker: Patrick Gorman
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
text:
I am happy to once again participate in the Raise Our Voice campaign, which puts young people's voices on the record in parliament, helping shape Australia's future. Today I have the speech of a 16-year-old from the Perth electorate:

My name is Alexandra, and last year I spoke in my state's Legislative Assembly about the mental health crisis affecting our young people.

This year, I stood in that same room and gave a voice to this issue again.

Right before our eyes a national emergency is unfolding, and it's shaping the future of my generation.

39 per cent of young Australians aged 16 to 24 are experiencing a mental health condition.

That is nearly two out of every five young people.

It is time to realise the traditional system is not just failing to cure the problem, it is completely incapable of understanding it.

Meaningful solutions start with a fundamental shift in power.

Solutions made by youth—

A division having been called in the House of Representatives—

Sitting suspended from 11:03 to 11:14

Before I was democratically interrupted, I was reading Alexandra's speech:

Meaningful solutions start with a fundamental shift in power.

Solutions made by youth for the issues they face.

We don't just need more institutions; we need programs designed and driven by the very students who live with the daily pressure of life in our modern age.

Youth advocacy is vital and the missing link, but simply listening to us inside this room is no longer enough.

I call on this Parliament to mandate that all future youth mental health legislation and funding require a co-design strategy directly led by young people.

Let us turn our struggles into solutions and finally heal the heartbeat of this nation.

Thank you very much to Alexandra, who I recently met at a Fogarty Futures leadership forum. What struck me was her determination to stand up for young people and give them a seat at the table. It is a message we hear again and again. I heard it at my Youth Leaders Policy Dialogue that I hosted alongside the Minister for Social Services, the Minister for Youth and Senator Whiteaker. We heard directly from young people about everything from mental health, to housing, artificial intelligence, education, gender equality and the environment. Those students didn't just bring concerns; they brought forward practical ideas. They challenged assumptions about the way the world is and the way the world could be and have a high expectation of turning their input into action.

Finally, as I am doing a Raise our Voice in Parliament 2026 speech, I want to say a big thank you to the team who make all of this happen. They are an incredible bunch of volunteers, led by CEO and founder Ashleigh Streeter-Jones and a bunch of her team, including Nuria Olive, Declan Davidson and school teachers across this country who are embracing this program as a practical way to teach the next generation about how to engage in our civic institutions and make sure that we do indeed listen to the voice of young Australians. Thank you very much.

speaker: David Littleproud
heading: BILLS
subheading: Domestic Gas Reservation Bill 2026, Domestic Gas Reservation (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2026, Domestic Gas Reservation Levy Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
While I stand to talk about the Domestic Gas Reservation Bill, I have significant issues around this bill. This bill is about trying to address one key aspect in the gas industry, which is supply. To understand that problem, you have to understand our history and the industry. To understand that, you need go no further than the electorate of Maranoa, because the east coast market is underpinned by the Surat Basin, particularly around Chinchilla, Roma, Dalby and Condamine, which produces most of the east coast gas but also goes into much of the export market.

It's important to understand that, when that industry was developed, it was developed on the proviso and the condition of the then premier of Queensland, Anna Bligh, and former prime minister Julia Gillard that the gas that was drilled and developed in the Surat Basin was not to be put into the domestic market. In fact, it was to be exported. It was to be exported out of Curtis Island off Gladstone. To demonstrate that, there was a pipeline built from the Surat Basin to Curtis Island. The reason for that by the Queensland premier at the time was that the Queensland government made $1.5 billion in dividends every year out of energy generation and distribution. So that came from coal-fired power assets.

What they didn't want to do is add more supply to the east coast market, which would reduce the price of the dividends that they got in generation and distribution from their coal-fired power assets. So Anna Bligh said, 'You can go and develop these fields, but you must export it.' So, for politicians to come in and condemn gas companies for being greedy and exporting gas to other parts of the world, you need to understand history. That was the condition of the development of those gas fields—that the gas was not to be put into the domestic market; it was to be exported, and it had to go out in a boat. So we created those export markets, and Australia has enjoyed the benefits of those export markets in royalties and in income; in fact, even in my home town.

I grew up in a place called Chinchilla. We would never get more or fewer than 3,000 people. That's what we were always stuck on. There's now 7,000 people living in Chinchilla today because of what the gas industry has done for our community with long-term jobs, not just direct but also indirect. The economic impact that it's had on our economy is enormous, not just in export dollars. If you understand that this is a supply issue, you would understand that, in Queensland, where this gas was drilled and put out on a boat, our industry isn't traditionally fuelled by gas—and probably still isn't—it's fuelled mostly through our energy grid, through coal, because we have significant coal-fired power assets. The states that do rely on gas—New South Wales and Victoria—are the states that are constraining supply because they're not drilling for the gas that sits underneath their feet.

The irony in all of that is that they complain about the price because of the lack of supply, yet we'll allow Queensland to continue to drill holes—and I don't have any problems with that—but they're about to run out of industrial gas, while, as the previous member was just talking about with industries in her own electorate, they sit there and say, 'We need more supply.' Well, they only need to look to their own state governments to see what's underneath their feet. In terms of making sure that the gas companies must supply 110 per cent of the market, if you want to oversupply something, you might drop the price, but then no-one drills any holes and you find yourself back in the same problem you were just in.

If we don't understand the history of how we have found ourselves in this mess, we are going to perpetrate that even further by saying everybody has to provide 110 per cent. What that means is there will be no investment. The town that I now call one of my own in my electorate will see that investment taken away. The boards of these companies make investment decisions, and they will not go and spend money to continue to increase supply if they can't make money. In fact, they're going to lose money. That's just how business works. I'm sorry to explain it to those opposite, but that is the reality of what will happen if you impose such a draconian measure in this bill. Investment will leave this country. It will leave my electorate and I will lose the 3,500 to 4000 people that have come to towns like Chinchilla, because those gas companies will go to another continent and we will have to import our gas. That is the stark reality of economics and business. You can't run away from that through ideology, and ideology is what this bill is about.

This is about making sure that we open up our tenements. We have that supply, and there are some practical things we could do. There are small capacity constraints between the Surat Basin and those in New South Wales and Victoria. In peak periods, we could get more gas down, in addition to what we're already sending out on a boat and paying the bills for to sit here today in the privilege of the air conditioning and the lights in this beautiful building. We might get those royalties and those gas companies to pay those taxes. We could see more gas flow down into New South Wales and Victoria. That is if they don't have the courage to drill a hole themselves, if they don't have the brains to think, 'Wouldn't it be quicker and easier to drill a hole right underneath our feet and pump it into those businesses that sit here and tell us they are going broke because they have high gas prices because they can't get gas?' The further you have to transport it, the higher the cost—another revelation to those opposite about how business works. Lo and behold, if you drilled the hole and you pumped it straight up, you might get cheaper gas and you might solve that supply issue. That's before you even look at, if we had to, plugging in Beetaloo that is in the Northern Territory. That will go out in the export market, and it is an opportunity to work with the gas industry and to plug that into the east coast as well.

We have an abundance of gas, and what we are trying to solve with this bill is a supply issue. The supply is beneath our feet, but those south of the border of Queensland have not had the brains to drill a hole to get it and still want it. To sit there and compare us to Western Australia because they have a gas reservation scheme—that is the right policy for Western Australia. The forefathers of Western Australia that did that did the right thing. But understand that the east coast market is significantly different—a higher population and a higher industry base that has already established coal. Gas has played some part in it, particularly in the southern states, and that's why it's important that you don't compare a reservation scheme in Western Australia to that on the east coast. That is purpose-built for Western Australia, and it is the right thing, but it's not the right thing for the east coast.

The stupidity that we are finding ourselves in is that when the supply is there—and this is the basics of all we're trying to solve—it is simply about us taking it, not forcing companies to make investment decisions that put us up against other countries and other continents that are prepared to develop that asset and allow those companies to get that capital to flow into them, away from Australia. We'll be back here again in another five or 10 years sitting here wondering why our gas prices are so high and why we don't have any gas going to the whingers in New South Wales and Victoria because their industries don't have the gas and they're paying too much for it when it's sitting underneath their feet. This is where common sense has left the building, and this is where a government has overreached and will have significant impacts.

Think about what is coming at our country. We're walking ourselves into the fourth industrial revolution of humanity with AI and the data centres that will be required. To give you an insight into what an AI data centre will need, forget normal data centres; an AI data centre is significantly greater. There's one proposed out near Chinchilla, where I live, and it will need 2,600 megawatts of energy every year to run. That is a bit over a quarter of the total generation of energy in Queensland every year. That's just one.

I'm sure I'll hear—and our teal friends will be here soon telling us—that we need all this energy and renewables will do it all and we've got AI data centres and they should all be run by renewables. If you want to do that 2,600 megawatts with wind turbines, you need to multiply that by three. You need three times the energy generation with a wind turbine over gas or coal or nuclear. Let me tell you what that looks like for the people of my electorate, around Dalby and Chinchilla. To do seven to eight gigawatts of energy, you would need 1,400 wind turbines at 260 metres high swishing around our heads. The member for Warringah got all upset about eight wind turbines at North Head because the good people of North Head were upset they couldn't see the Pacific Ocean unabated. Well, you know what? What about the views of the people of Western Queensland? We don't want to look at the Pacific Ocean—or live in Sydney, for that matter—but we want to live where we live without the amenity of our lives being taken up by 1,400 of them. But it gets worse. If you want to do it with solar panels, it's 1.5 million solar panels across 20,000 hectares. That's probably about the size of the shire of Sydney or more. That is what you are asking us to bear with. But you put your head under a pillow and forget about us, because you can sit in your high-rises in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane and forget about what happens to us out there.

I don't want to turn away this AI data centre. I want to see these 1,400 new jobs come to the towns of Dalby and Chinchilla—new jobs, high-paying jobs. We do need to have AI if we want to be competitive with the world, but not at our cost. It should work. That is why, if you put these sorts of bills in place, you tear away the investment decisions of gas companies that are sitting there when there are three gas peaking plants sitting around one of these proposed data centres right at Dalby, which you could actually increase if you sent the investment signals to our gas companies to drill more. That is how markets work. That is the practical reality that happens outside this building. We might think we shape the world, but ultimately what happens is that the capital that flows from the decisions that we make determines what we actually pay, and that is what is lost in all this. We're going to force these companies to sell into certain markets, and we're going to tell them to oversupply, so the CEOs will go to their boards and the boards will say, 'We'll take our money elsewhere.' So we will be stuck with an energy grid that again depletes itself in the lived experience that Australians are already feeling—not that $275 reduction off their 2022 bills that they were meant to get in 2025. It's gone up by 1,300 bucks off their 2022 price.

So this is where physics and economics are catching up with this government. This bill is not well thought through. This will have a detrimental impact. It will have a detrimental impact on our economy but also on the environment, because you know what? You think about 20,000 hectares of native vegetation stripped away to put solar panels on to run a data centre. 'Oh, that's alright. I can still look at the Pacific Ocean. It's all good, because that's the only environment that I can see and that I care about.' Well, I don't really think that is a notion that Australia should predicate its decisions on.

This bill will do serious harm to an industry that has supported this nation and paid its bills. You talk about social licence. Let me tell you what social licence looks like. When Santos, Origin and Arrow turned up in western Queensland, I wouldn't feed them. They treated us like dirt. But we squared up with them, and now they are the best corporate citizens you would find in Australia. They spill more community support in Roma, Chinchilla and Dalby on a Monday before smoko than these wind tower companies give us in about 10 years. They're just throwing bits and pieces at us, thinking we can put up with 1,400 or 1,500 of these 260-metre towers. This is the reality. When you talk about social licence, the gas companies are the ones that actually are doing the right thing by us out there and by our economy. But what we are doing in this bill is saying to them: 'We don't care. We're just going to tax you and put market mechanisms that send you out of this country over you.'

I can tell you, London to a brick, that, if this thing gets through and it sticks long enough, I'll be back here again and we'll be fixing this, because this is just simple demand and supply. The Treasurer doesn't need to write 6,000 words of economic blah. I learnt in grade 8 at Chinchilla State High School from Mrs Hart about demand and supply. This is supply. Mrs Hart would be telling me, 'Increase supply.' Create the environment to increase supply and, lo and behold, you will actually have more stable and lower prices in the long-term. If you want to interfere in a marketplace, you will have detrimental outcomes that will not only strip supply but lead to perverse outcomes for prices into the future. This is just politics getting away from reality, and I fear that the people of Western Queensland who have worked with the gas industry and believe in the gas industry will have their futures stripped away because we believe that we can replace this with renewables, which will never be able to do what gas, coal and nuclear can, because of some ideology. This is dumb politics, this is dumb policy and we will all pay the bill.

speaker: Claire Clutterham
heading: BILLS
subheading: Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise today to speak in support of the Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026. We know that Australia's defence capability must be delivered differently to meet the demands of a more dangerous and unpredictable era where the consequences of delay, costs, and capability underperformance are more serious than they have been in generations. Legacy capability systems, optimised for deliberation and risk minimisation, are not well suited to an environment that demands speed, integration and disciplined execution.

In reflection of this changing need, on 1 December 2025 the government announced significant reform to capability development and delivery, including the establishment of the Defence Delivery Agency from 1 July 2027, with an interim step of the formation of the Defence Delivery Group within Defence from 1 July this year; the establishment of a national armaments director to lead the new agency, responsible for providing advice to ministers on the delivery of acquisition and sustainment projects following government approval; and the centralisation of capability development and contestability functions under the Vice Chief of the Defence Force to support clearer prioritisation, streamlined decision-making and accountability.

This announcement followed the 2023 Defence strategic review and the 2024 National defence strategy, and it was reinforced by the 2026 National defence strategy. This found that defence acquisition and sustainment arrangements were not fit for the scale, complexity or urgency of Australia's strategic circumstances.

The key pillars of the 2026 National defence strategy are clear, urgent and unavoidable. First and foremost is increasing Australia's self-reliance over the longer term. Now, self-reliance doesn't mean fighting or facing threats alone; it means having the homegrown industrial strength to sustain the fight. So inextricably linked to this is another critical pillar from the 2026 National defence strategy, which is to grow Australia's sovereign defence industrial base by shoring up our sovereign supply chain and an appropriately skilled and qualified workforce. Other features of the 2026 National defence strategy include strengthening our bilateral and multilateral security partnerships in the Indo-Pacific.

The government has also directed the ADF to maintain the capacity to defend Australia and our immediate region; to deter, through denial, any potential adversary's attempt to project power against Australia through our northern approaches; to protect Australia's economic connection to our region and the world; to contribute with our partners to the collective security of the Indo-Pacific; and to contribute with our partners to protecting and upholding global rules and norms. So what is required to focus on that is speed to capability. Speed to capability has two parts.

The first element of speed to capability is minimum viable capability. This phrase is sometimes misunderstood because of the word 'minimum'. In this context, minimum viable capability does not mean the bare minimum in terms of operational functionality. It does not mean procuring substandard or barely passable capability for our defence force. It doesn't mean that at all. Minimum viable capability means fit for mission, a capability that achieves a threshold capability effect inclusive of all fundamental inputs of that capability in the required time. Minimum viable capability delivers what Defence needs to achieve a military effect. It can be further developed, scaled and built up, and it includes materiel and sustainment elements so that the management, support and maintenance of the relevant military equipment and platforms can be achieved. In short, it's procuring something that can do the job well by the point in time it is needed.

The second element of speed to capability is minimum viable processes. Again, this does not mean poor or ill considered processes; it means the implementation of targeted and efficient processes that are smooth and that facilitate the delivery of the capability and its ongoing sustainment. Minimum viable processes can ensure that the capability is safe to operate, that it's fit for mission and that our Defence Force personnel have trust and confidence in it no matter the domain. It also ensures that risks and issues associated with that capability are always managed at the appropriate level within the organisation.

The reforms outlined in this bill have at their heart a focus on speed to capability. The development, testing and introduction of new capability just has to take place at a greater pace than ever before. A new capability has to operate in a meaningful and effective way with Australian industry and with our international partners. A framework to facilitate this requires careful thinking. In this respect, the bill establishes new legislative foundations that will enable Defence to develop and secure that capability at pace. It's a key enabler to the full implementation of the National Defence Strategy and the delivery of pillars I and II of the AUKUS trilateral security agreement and partnership with the United States and the United Kingdom.

A central objective of the bill in this respect is to replace fragmented and inconsistent legislative arrangements with clear statutory frameworks supported by defined safeguards, oversight and accountability mechanisms. The reforms improve transparency, consistency, accountability and certainty by establishing these transparent statutory decision-making processes that identify what activities can be carried out, the circumstances in which they may occur, the conditions that apply and the oversight mechanisms. The reforms reduce reliance on complex multijurisdictional exemptions, implied authorities and administrative arrangements that might otherwise be required to support defence activities. They're focused on defence activities, and they provide the legislative support to facilitate them. What does that look like?

Schedule 1 of the bill will create a defence capability framework, a fit-for-purpose capability development and testing framework including for activities conducted with industry and international partners. It is going to streamline the current patchwork of federal, state and territory legislation, which was not necessarily designed with defence purposes in mind and especially that need for speed to capability. Importantly, the framework will operate to remove legal and regulatory hurdles that adversely impact on that speed of capability development. The era of multiple exemptions, licences and approvals from different state and territory authorities for a single activity will come to an end under this framework and with it the corresponding delays, inconsistencies and uncertainties.

Australians expect a properly equipped defence force that uses the best available equipment that is fit for mission. It cannot be that the ADF and its defence industry partners are unable, or limited in their ability, to develop and test advanced capability here in Australia, because this limit would also have the effect of limiting or overly complicating the commercialisation of technology here in Australia, which does nothing to promote our competitiveness or provide incentives for industry to invest.

Importantly, the framework is also critical to enabling the delivery of AUKUS Pillar II signature projects—those being the development of cutting-edge payloads and enabling systems for uncrewed undersea vehicles—with delivery starting in 2027. These uncrewed undersea vehicles will support a range of missions, including to protect critical national seabed infrastructure; deploy cutting-edge surveillance, reconnaissance and strike capabilities; conduct logistics operations; and bolster superiority in antisubmarine and antisurface warfare, mine countermeasures, electronic warfare and contested littoral manoeuvre. All of this further enhances the asymmetric capability of Australia and its partners.

Pillar II often gets lost in the excitement of Pillar I, but Pillar II, with its focus on advanced capabilities and emerging technologies, offers a critical opportunity for Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States to pool resources, accelerate innovation, share technology and compete effectively with potential adversaries in areas such as cyber, autonomous capability and artificial intelligence. We've already seen what can go right in this respect, with the relaxation of export controls to enable smoother and faster collaboration and joint collaboration in a licence-free environment. Pillar II offers potentially more transformative impacts for the Australian defence industry and capability because, if it goes right, Australia will be in a position to develop world-leading defence capabilities, including autonomous capability, through growing its defence industrial base, encouraging innovation and then integrating this industrial base with that of its partners. Pillar II could transform the strategic balance in not only the Indo-Pacific but the broader Asian region, because it will illustrate that the world's leading liberal democracies, of which Australia is one, can innovate together to facilitate speed to capability, to deter aggression and to shape the future of warfare by detecting, deterring and responding to threats to critical infrastructure like undersea cables and pipelines.

With respect to Defence bases, the bill also establishes a modern Defence Security Zone Framework that consolidates and replaces a number of fragmented security regimes across defence legislation. The framework applies a consistent approach to security measures across Defence, ADF and relevant foreign partner assets, and it supports tailored security arrangements for Defence facilities, activities, infrastructure and capability. It also provides contemporary powers to address threats posed by drones and other uncrewed systems, including powers to detect, monitor, track, seize, recover, interfere with and, where necessary, neutralise uncrewed systems that present a security threat to Defence personnel, assets or sites.

The work that the men and women who are on our Australian Defence Force bases are doing is truly excellent, and it's non-negotiable that these bases, which house our personnel but also our assets and other Defence infrastructure, should be properly protected. This is urgent because the development of adverse drone and other uncrewed technology is happening rapidly, and our protection of Defence bases cannot lag behind this any more than it already does. Defence needs enduring legislative authority that allows personnel to protect Defence sites, Defence personnel and critical assets from drones and other uncrewed systems. This bill builds on the interim measures the Albanese government has already implemented through the Defence Amendment (Counter-UXS Measures) Regulations 2025.

The reforms in this bill move us further forward by modernising security arrangements currently spread across multiple Defence statutes and consolidating them into a single Defence Security Zone Framework. This provides a contemporary and consistent framework that enables Defence security zones to be established in order to protect locations, assets, personnel and capabilities, as well as foreign partner assets.

The reforms also support increasingly important security requirements associated with AUKUS activities, visiting US and UK nuclear powered submarines and major Defence industrial precincts. To be clear, the reforms do permit the detection, identification, monitoring, tracking and response to drones and uncrewed systems, including through destructive means if necessary, at defence bases that may be at risk, but this is entirely appropriate, and there are safeguards which provide that the action must be proportionate to the risk. The reforms in this bill will enable Defence to act before an authorised system compromises sensitive information, disrupts an activity or causes harm. Defence must work with other agencies including the Civil Aviation Safety Authority to ensure the safety of civilian aircraft when conducting these activities at shared facilities.

Australia's strategic environment is changing rapidly. It's characterised by increasing strategic competition, accelerating technological change, growing reliance on sovereign defence industry and deeper cooperation with allies and partners. The reforms in this bill are not only critical enablers of the National defence strategy and AUKUS. They support Australia's national security by facilitating speed to capability and giving authority to our defence personnel under rightly controlled circumstances to protect that capability and the defence bases on which they live and work in the interests of our country. I commend the bill to the chamber.

speaker: Matt Burnell
heading: BILLS
subheading: Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Australia's national security depends on our ability to respond to an increasingly complex and uncertain world, and ensuring our Defence Force has the capabilities, resources and protections it needs to keep Australians safe is one of the most important responsibilities of any government. But protecting Australia today requires more than maintaining the Defence Force we have always known. It requires us to prepare for the challenges of tomorrow and recognise that the nature of modern warfare is changing faster than ever before.

Across the world we're seeing new technologies fundamentally changing how military operations are conducted. Drones, autonomous vehicles, artificial intelligence and cyber capabilities are no longer technologies of the future. They're being used in conflicts the world over. As these technologies continue to evolve, Australia must ensure our Defence Force is equipped to respond, because we cannot expect our Defence Force to meet the challenges tomorrow while operating under legislation designed for the past. That is why the reforms before the House are so important. They will ensure Defence has the legislative foundations it needs to develop new capabilities, work more closely with Australian industry and protect our national security.

The Albanese Labor government understands that Australia is facing one of the most challenging strategic environments in generations. We're seeing increasing strategic competition across our region, rapid technological change and emerging threats to our critical infrastructure. Through the 2026 National defence strategy, our government is taking the steps necessary to strengthen Australia's defence capabilities and prepare for the challenges ahead. But delivering these capabilities requires more than investment alone. It requires legislation that supports innovation, rather than creating unnecessary barriers.

Right now, Defence can face a complicated combination of Commonwealth, state and territory laws when developing and testing new technologies. Many of these laws were never designed with modern defence capabilities in mind, and in some cases Defence must obtain multiple licences, exemptions and approvals simply to undertake a single testing activity. Different requirements can apply depending on where an activity takes place. This creates delays, additional costs and unnecessary uncertainty. At a time when defence technology is advancing so rapidly, those delays matter, because every unnecessary barrier can mean more time before an important capability reaches the people who need it, and every delay can mean a missed opportunity for Australian businesses developing the next generation of defence technology.

That is why this bill establishes a new defence capability framework that will provide a clearer and more consistent process for Defence to develop, test and evaluate new capabilities here, in Australia. It will support emerging technologies including autonomous systems, guided weapons, cyber capabilities and electronic warfare. Importantly, it will make it easier for Defence to work alongside Australian businesses and our trusted international partners. Take, for example, an Australian company developing an autonomous maritime vessel, which is a technology that could play an important role in surveillance, reconnaissance or protecting the water around our island home. Under existing arrangements, Defence and that company may need to navigate multiple layers of regulation before the vessel can even be tested, and these requirements can delay development, increase costs and make it harder for Australian innovations to become practical defence capabilities.

The new framework will help address these challenges by providing a clearer pathway for appropriate testing and development activities. This matters not just for Defence but for Australian industry because, when we make it easier to develop and test advanced technologies in Australia, we're creating opportunities for Australian workers and businesses. We're supporting researchers, engineers, manufacturers and the next generation of skilled workers, and we're strengthening Australia's sovereign industrial capability so that we're better equipped to develop and maintain the technologies our Defence Force relies on. This is particularly important when we consider the opportunities presented by AUKUS.

Our partnership with the United States and the United Kingdom represents a generational opportunity to strengthen Australia's national security. While much of the public discussion focuses on nuclear powered submarines, AUKUS extends well beyond submarine construction. Through pillar II, Australia is working with our closest partners to accelerate the development of advanced military technologies, including autonomous underwater vehicles, artificial intelligence, cyber capabilities and other emerging systems. But to take full advantage of these opportunities, Australia needs the ability to develop, test and integrate these technologies efficiently. We cannot afford to have Australian innovation held back by outdated regulatory arrangements, and we certainly don't want to see opportunities for Australian businesses move offshore simply because our legislation hasn't kept pace. These reforms will help ensure Australia remains an active participant in the development of the next generation of defence capabilities, and, importantly, they'll help ensure the economic benefits of these investments are realised here at home.

For my home state of South Australia, these reforms are particularly significant. South Australia is already playing a central role in Australia's defence future. From our naval ship building industry to the growth of advanced manufacturing and defence technology, South Australia is helping build the capabilities Australia will rely on for decades to come. While much of this investment is concentrated around major Defence precincts, the opportunities extend well beyond them. Across the northern suburbs of Adelaide, including communities in my electorate of Spence, defence investment has the potential to support local manufacturers and create highly skilled employment opportunities—opportunities for young Australians looking to enter the workforce, apprentices learning a trade or a small business looking to become part of Australia's defence supply chains. Because strengthening our national security and supporting Australian jobs are not competing priorities; they go hand in hand.

By strengthening Australia's ability to develop and manufacture advanced defence technologies, we are building a stronger economy and a more secure nation. But developing new capabilities is only one part of the challenge. We must also ensure that the people, facilities and infrastructure supporting those capabilities are properly protected. Increasingly, one of the most significant threats facing defence installations around the world comes from drones and other uncrewed systems. These technologies have become more affordable, more accessible and more sophisticated. While they have many legitimate recreational and commercial uses, they can also be used for surveillance, espionage and sabotage.

We've seen in conflicts around the world how relatively inexpensive drones can pose serious threats to sophisticated military equipment and critical infrastructure. As these technologies become more widely available, our Defence Force must have the tools necessary to respond. A drone operating near a sensitive Defence facility could potentially gather intelligence, disrupt operations or threaten personnel and equipment. Yet the legislation governing Defence's ability to respond to these threats has not always kept pace. That's why this bill establishes a modern defence security zone framework.

This framework will bring together and modernise existing security arrangements, providing Defence with clear authority to protect its personnel, facilities and sensitive activities. It will allow appropriate security measures to be applied to Defence bases, important industrial facilities and other locations where sensitive defence activities are being undertaken. Importantly, it will provide authorised Defence personnel with the ability to detect, monitor, track and, where necessary, neutralise drones and other uncrewed systems that pose a genuine security threat. Because Defence should not have to wait until sensitive information has been compromised or personnel have been placed at risk before responding to an emerging threat.

The framework also recognises that defence activities don't always take place within the boundaries of permanent military bases. There may be circumstances where sensitive equipment is being transported, where an Australian company is undertaking important capability trials or where an emergency requires temporary security arrangements. The ability to establish permanent, temporary or mobile and emergency defence security zones will allow security measures to be tailored to these different circumstances. This is particularly important as Australia continues to deepen its defence cooperation with the United States and the United Kingdom through AUKUS. As our partnerships expand, so too does the importance of protecting visiting military assets, sensitive technologies and major defence industrial precincts. We have a responsibility to ensure these activities can be undertaken safely and securely and that Australia remains a trusted and capable partner.

While these reforms provide Defence with important new authorities, they also recognise that those powers must be accompanied by appropriate safeguards. Strengthening national security should never mean abandoning accountability, and providing Defence with the powers necessary to respond to modern threats does not mean those powers should be unlimited. The defence capability framework does not provide a general authority for Defence to undertake any activity it chooses. Activities must fall within the legislative framework and be specifically authorised. It cannot be used to authorise domestic policing functions, compulsory acquisition of land or the use or threat of force against people in Australia. When authorising capability activities, decision-makers must consider whether the impact on people in Australia is reasonable and proportionate. They must also consider whether those undertaking the activities are suitable and whether appropriate safeguards are in place. These are important protections that ensure the development of new defence capabilities is accompanied by clear responsibilities.

The same principle applies to the defence security zone framework. Security zones must be geographically limited and no more extensive than necessary to achieve their intended purpose. There are also requirements for consultation with people who may be affected and time limits on temporary and emergency arrangements. Importantly, the legislation recognises the need for Defence to work with other agencies, including the Civil Aviation Safety Authority, to ensure that security activities don't unnecessarily compromise civilian aviation safety.

The bill also strengthens independent oversight through expanded functions for the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force, alongside parliamentary scrutiny through the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence, because Australians should have confidence not only in the capabilities of the Defence Force but also in the systems of accountability that govern its activities.

These reforms have not been developed in isolation. They follow a consultation across government, including with 19 Commonwealth departments and agencies, as well as a public consultation process undertaken by Defence in 2023. That consultation has helped inform legislation intended to balance the operational needs of Defence with the rights, interests and safety of the Australian community.

Ultimately, these reforms reflect a simple but important principle. If Australia is serious about strengthening our national security, we must ensure our legislative framework is capable of supporting the defence force we need for the future. We cannot expect our military personnel to operate with tomorrow's technology while navigating yesterday's laws, and we cannot expect Australian defence industry to compete internationally if unnecessary regulatory barriers prevent innovation from progressing here at home.

The Albanese Labor government is committed to building a defence force that is capable, adaptable and prepared for the challenges ahead; a defence force supported by advanced technologies, strong international partnerships and a growing sovereign industrial base; but also a defence force operating within a clear legislative framework, with appropriate safeguards and strong independent oversight. These reforms are an important part of delivering that commitment. They will help accelerate the development of new capabilities, strengthen the protection of Defence personnel and infrastructure. and create greater opportunities for Australian industry. As Australia's strategic environment continues to evolve, they will help ensure that our Defence Force has the authorities it needs to respond effectively, because, ultimately, our responsibility is not simply to respond to the security challenges Australia faces today; it's to ensure our nation is prepared for the challenges we may face in the decades to come. That means making the investments, building the partnerships and delivering the legislative reforms necessary to keep Australia safe. That is what these reforms seek to achieve, and that is why I commend them to the House.

speaker: Tania Lawrence
heading: BILLS
subheading: Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise to support the Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026. The bill should be understood as part of something much larger. It is yet another positive step in the transformation of Australia's defence posture that has been underway since the Albanese Labor government took office.

We are spending more on defence, but the challenge before Australia is not simply to spend more on defence. It is to identify the capabilities our nation needs, acquire them faster, build and sustain more of them here at home, reduce sovereign risk, firm up supply chains, work effectively with our allies and trusted partners, and protect those capabilities, the people behind them and, importantly, the places from which they operate. That takes investment, and this government is providing it at a level unprecedented in living memory. But it also takes strategy, industry, skills, partnerships, accountability and, saliently, laws that are fit for the strategic environment in which the Australian Defence Force now operates.

The bill establishes a new defence capability framework to support capability development, testing, evaluation and preparedness, alongside a defence security zone framework to better protect defence personnel, the facilities, the information, the activities and the capabilities. Importantly, the bill also provides for independent oversight by the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force.

I've spoken in this House before about Australia facing the most challenging strategic circumstances since the Second World War. In fact, there are more conflicts right now than there ever have been since the Second World War. This is not a slogan. It is the starting point for serious defence policy—policy based on our own needs and interests and the development of a sovereign capability.

Since 2022, the Albanese government has been systematically answering some fundamental questions: What kind of Defence Force does Australia need? What capabilities must it possess? How rapidly must we acquire them? What must Australia do to build and sustain ourselves? And how do we make our Defence Force, our economy, our infrastructure and our communities more resilient? There is a clear chronology to what then followed.

In 2022, one of the first actions of the Albanese Labor government was to commission the Defence Strategic Review, led independently by former defence minister and former foreign minister Professor Stephen Smith and former Chief of the Defence Force, Sir Angus Houston. I know both of these men, and I know the seriousness and the expertise they bring to their work. That review was commissioned within the government's first 100 days. We did not begin with an arbitrary spending figure. We began by examining Australia's strategic circumstances, determining the force structure needed to respond to them, and then identifying the capabilities required to make that force credible.

The Defence Strategic Review was released in April 2023. It identified six priorities for immediate action: nuclear powered submarines, through AUKUS; longer range strike and Australian munitions manufacturing; strengthening our northern bases; growing and retaining the defence workforce; translating disruptive technologies into military capability more rapidly; and deepening Australia's diplomatic and defence relationships across the Indo-Pacific. As I've said previously in this House, thanks indeed to the extraordinary leadership of ministers Marles, Conroy, Keogh, Kahlil and Thistlethwaite, a great deal has followed on from that strategic review process.

In March 2023, Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom announced the AUKUS optimal pathway. That pathway provides for increasing submarine visits; the Submarine Rotational Force-West, from as early as next year; Australia's acquisition of Virginia class submarines, from the early 2030s; and, ultimately, the construction of SSN-AUKUS. For Western Australia, this is very real. HMAS Stirling will sit at the centre of the Submarine Rotational Force-West, with a planned rotational presence from as early as next year of one UK and up to four US conventionally armed and nuclear powered submarines. That means infrastructure, engineers, apprentices, nuclear stewardship, security, maintenance, sustainment and Australian supply chains. It means the development of sovereign Australian capability.

In April 2024, the government delivered Australia's first national defence strategy, establishing a strategy of denial as the cornerstone of defence planning and directing the ADF towards becoming an integrated, focused force. Modern deterrence requires integration across maritime, land, air space and cyber domains. It requires intelligence, resilient infrastructure and supply chains, advanced technology and a strong Australian industrial base, and that requires investment. The 2024 National Defence Strategy provided an additional $5.7 billion over four years and $50.3 billion over the decade above the previous Defence funding trajectory. The Australian Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Plan committed $16 billion to $21 billion across the decade, including Australian manufacture of the Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System missiles and maintenance of the Naval Strike and Joint Strike missiles. Buying capability is one thing; being able to replenish it, repair it, modify it and sustain it in a crisis is another.

That same year, Labor also introduced legislation for a dedicated Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence modelled in significant respects to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, on which I serve, and able to deal with the classified information. A statutory Defence committee had been a bipartisan recommendation actually over several parliamentary reports. When we build capability, we also have to build proper parliamentary oversight. The coalition, unfortunately though, played politics and failed to support the bill at that time and delayed the establishment of the committee.

In 2025, much of this planning became increasingly tangible. In January, the government committed another $262 million to develop Australia's AUKUS submarine supply chain, supporting around 125 Australian businesses with the skills, security, accreditation, manufacturing, equipment and qualifications for international submarine supply chains. Then, in September, the Prime Minister announced $12 billion in new funding for the Henderson defence precinct in Western Australia. By then the additional Defence investment over the decade had reached $70 billion.

Henderson will support continuous naval ship building, AUKUS, surface-vessel sustainment and future submarine support, with the government projecting more than 10,000 local jobs. On any visit there, you will see the place and how it's transforming. The energy, the absolute dedication and focus across all tiers of government—local, state and federal—is actually an extraordinary example of how we can work fast and collaboratively where it's needed on such a priority project.

The Prime Minister spoke of investment in both our capability and our relationships. That is an important distinction. Sovereign capability does not mean strategic isolation. Australian capability becomes stronger when Australian industry and workers are connected to the technology, the expertise and the scale of trusted partners. We are also seeing emerging technology move from theory to practice. During Exercise Talisman Sabre in July 2025, AUKUS partners deployed autonomous and remotely operated underwater vehicles and advanced algorithms aboard an Australian P-8 maritime patrol aircraft. Later that year, more than 200 defence personnel, scientists and industry participants tested around 30 next-generation capabilities through Maritime Big Play.

In December, the government announced major reform of capability acquisition and sustainment, including the creation of a dedicated Defence Delivery Agency and Australia's first National Armaments Director. Labor also reinforced the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence legislation in October 2025, and it finally passed both houses on 4 March this year. So today Australia has a statutory Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence with legislative scrutiny and parliamentary oversight, and that matters. The larger Defence becomes, the more sophisticated its capabilities become and the more tax money we obviously invest, so a stronger case is made for rigorous parliamentary oversight. Supporting Defence and scrutinising Defence are not competing objectives. Strong accountability makes Defence stronger.

Then we come to this year. The government has again increased the scale and pace of reform. The 2026 National defence strategy and Integrated Investment Program bring the combined additional investment to $117 billion over the decade to 2035-36. The 2026 strategy places greater emphasis on self-reliance, sovereign industrial resilience, international industrial partnerships, national civil preparedness and resilience. Under the NATO methodology, Defence spending is projected to reach three per cent of GDP by 2033. That is why the acquisition reforms matter.

The Defence Delivery Group commenced on 1 July 2026, with reforms intended to provide clearer accountability, stronger contestability and better cost estimation and assurance as Defence transitions towards the Defence Delivery Agency. The government's Rebuilding defence capability report says that with increased investment comes a clear responsibility to ensure Defence has the structures, the skills and the systems necessary to turn that strategy into real capability for the ADF. That task, of course, is made more urgent by the speed of technological change. Artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, quantum technology, hypersonics, long-range strike, undersea warfare and directed energy systems are developing extraordinarily quickly.

That brings us directly back to the bill. Modern military capability is increasingly developed with Australian companies, scientists, universities, researchers, engineers, startups, major primes and international partners. The new Defence Capability Framework provides a statutory foundation for developing, testing, evaluating and sustaining that capability. But speed must not come at the expense of safeguards, so the framework does not authorise military operations, intelligence collection or law enforcement activity, nor does it create a general exemption from Australian law or remove environmental heritage or native title protections.

The Defence Security Zone Framework addresses the other half of the equation: protecting what we build. Existing Defence security laws were written in years past, and Defence has identified gaps and inconsistencies, including in responding to contemporary threats such as drone incursions. It makes little sense to spend billions developing sophisticated military capabilities while leaving the people, the places and the technology supporting them vulnerable because our laws have not kept pace. The bill addresses that gap.

I just want to return to WA, because for Western Australia sovereign capability is already becoming real. Henderson and HMAS Stirling, as I said, are central to the story, but so are Western Australian businesses. I've spoken previously in this House about Hofmann Engineering in Ashfield and Bayswater, in my electorate of Hasluck, becoming the first qualified Australian company to receive a request for a quote to supply parts into the United States submarine supply chain. The Hofmann story demonstrates what sovereign capability can mean. A business that began as a backyard operation developed into an internationally connected Australian engineering company—Australian engineering, Australian workers and Australian skills connected into one of the most sophisticated defence industrial networks in the world. That is what AUKUS can look like in an Australian suburb, and that is why defence industry policy is a national security policy. Our security depends not just on what Australia can buy but on what we can build, what we can repair and what we can sustain and replenish.

Amid all of these strategies, investment programs, submarines, missiles and technologies, we should never lose sight of one thing: Defence is ultimately about people. Before coming to this place, I served in the signals reserves, and that experience gave me an enduring appreciation of the responsibilities that come with service and of the people who put on our nation's uniform. Since coming to parliament, I have continued to maintain that connection, including through Exercise Pitch Black, the ADF exchange programs and hosting officers from the ADF through the ADF parliamentary internship program. I'm also engaged through the ANU national security program, and I encourage every MP and senator in this place to participate in the same.

So this bill matters. Capability matters because we may ask our Australian service men and women to use it. I will conclude by saying that we are working now to develop that capability faster and to protect the capability better. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Consideration in Detail
text:
Today I propose two substantive changes to the digital duty of care bill. I commend the minister and the government for engaging in good faith on this important legislation and for being open to reasonable improvements to it, like the ones I'm proposing today.

The first change is reflected in amendment (1). It adds a new category of harm to children that platforms have to consider—attachment hacking. This is where a service simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child's dependence on it in place of human relationships. It will apply to all online services. Most importantly, it will apply to AI companions, like Nomi and Chai, and to general chatbots, like ChatGPT and Claude, if they continue to simulate emotional intimacy and foster dependence. eSafety found AI companions offer humanlike, sycophantic and often sexually explicit conversations. About 200,000 Australian children aged 10 to 17 have used one. We've seen just how badly this can go wrong. Sewell Setzer, aged 14, Juliana Peralta, aged 13, and Adam Raine, aged 16, died by suicide after extended conversations with chatbots. Reporting on their chat logs suggests the bots discouraged them from turning to other people.

This amendment would also capture the slower, less obvious harms of AI chatbots and companions that pretend to be your friend. Psychologists are telling us that children are increasingly turning to AI instead of friends, parents and teachers. This is a significant risk to children's long-term psychological development. Human relationships are how children learn to form bonds, regulate emotions and form a sense of self. Relationships with strangely friendly or sycophantic AI chatbots are not. Because this harm is long term, the evidence is still emerging, but, from the social media experience, we've learnt that waiting for exhaustive evidence of damage leaves a generation of children impacted. Importantly, this doesn't restrict AI chatbots or companions being used by children, but it tells these AI companies that simulated emotional intimacy, sycophancy or pretending to be a friend or romantic partner is unacceptable.

The second change is reflected in amendments (2) to (8). This ensures that user empowerment tools such as the opt-in or opt-out setting that the government says it will require under this bill must be prominent, accessible, easy to use, functional, available on an ongoing basis and not affecting the functionality of the service or impairing the user experience. Why is this important? We know that tech companies will do what they can to exploit loopholes and keep users on their algorithm. After the EU required Meta to give users an option to switch off the algorithm, the company hid the setting, removed significant functions from the non-algorithmic feed and automatically switched users back to their algorithmic feed every time they closed and reopened the app. This malicious compliance is unacceptable. To ensure Australians have genuine control to switch their algorithm on and off, the setting must be prominent, accessible and easy to use and not affect the functioning of the app. Putting these standards in the primary legislation and not just in a ministerial determination strengthens these obligations and gives notice to social media companies that this is something they must comply with in good faith.

I also note that I had intended to move amendments to increase penalties for noncompliance with the digital duty of care. These amendments will now be moved by the member for Bradfield. The current penalties that apply to companies that do not comply with the digital duty of care are roughly $100 million. This would be about one-twentieth of one per cent of Meta's revenue last year—too small to change the behaviour of some of the wealthiest companies in the world. The EU, UK, Canada and New Zealand have either implemented or proposed fines that range from three to 10 per cent of global revenue. We should do the same. A big stick like this is essential to get these companies to change their behaviour. I would also like to see a private right of action added so that Australian users, not just the regulator, could enforce this new duty.

I would like to thank thousands of Curtin constituents who informed my work on this bill by responding to my community survey, the UWA students who attended my workshop on this issue and the many organisations across the technology ecosystem who engaged with me and my office. I commend the government for its work on this bill, and I thank the minister, who has indicated that the government will support these amendments. I commend these amendments to the House.

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Consideration in Detail
text:
I rise in support of the amendments moved by the member for Curtin and agree wholeheartedly on the importance of ensuring these attachment bots be included in relation to online harms. But I also have a question for the minister because, whilst there's a strong focus on protecting under 18s from harms online, there are other foreseeable harms that we're seeing occur and are not being addressed in this digital duty of care. My question for the minister in this consideration in detail process is: why has the government failed to explicitly include harmful AI generated deepfakes in its duty of care legislation? If the purpose of this legislation is to prevent foreseeable online harm, why are we failing to address one of the fastest-growing threats?

We've got an opportunity to get ahead of an emerging threat, yet the government is leaving a significant gap in online safety protections. Artificial intelligence can now make someone appear to say something they never said, do something they never did and participate in an event that never happened. We've already seen how this technology is being misused in Australia. Deepfake video circulating, for example, of Senator Jacqui Lambie was falsely depicting her criticising another party's voters. That results in threats from those voters back to her. At a time when we're talking about a heightened security environment for members of parliaments and the public at large, we're allowing this to continue to be legal.

The amendment I had wished to propose to this effect sought to address deepfakes depicting identifiable people without their consent where the content is capable of misleading viewers and likely to cause serious harm. We know the government has looked at this from the nudify apps perspective, but the harm goes beyond that. Harm to a person, whether they are under 18 or over 18, where their image, likeness and voice are used by AI technology to generate deepfake content that is then pushed through social media platforms and digital platforms and where there is no consent from that person that is readily identifiable should also be treated as a harm that these platforms should have to prevent and be aware of. So I ask the government to look at protecting all Australians, not just under-18s, from this use without their consent of their image, likeness and voice in relation to the creation of AI deepfakes. It is not just in the political space that this matters. This could ruin someone's business reputation. If someone is in the public eye in sport—we've seen Sportsbet do it with some actors as well. It is really important that the government address this gap.

I would also like to note my deep frustration with the process. This was an amendment that I had sought to get drafted, but, through lack of resources through the system, it has not been possible for the parliamentary drafting services to provide the draft of that amendment despite being asked to do this over a week ago. I find it deeply unacceptable for the parliament to not be able to provide adequate services to members.

heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Consideration in Detail
text:

They can be taken down by the eSafety Commissioner. That would include deepfake nude images. The duty would also require platforms to have systems in place to prevent the harm from occurring.

The member is correct in that material and content that does not cause serious harm is not the subject of this bill. We feel that the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence that is currently on foot is meant to be looking into these particular issues, and we intend to incorporate those informed findings into the forthcoming Australian AI standards, which we believe is the more appropriate place for them. Other feedback is noted. I also thank the member for Curtin for her amendments, which the government will support.

On user empowerment tools, the government recognises the importance of making sure that the primary bill mandates that the user empowerment tools are accessible, easy to use, prominently available on the service, and functional and available on an ongoing basis. We support that. On attachment hacking, we also recognise that the use of AI chatbots and companions are creating risks to children's long-term development and it's horrifying. As sociologist Sherry Turkle observed: 'Social media came for our attention. Chatbots are coming for our attachment.' I've spoken in this chamber before about the boy who was found to have 50 different tabs open seeking companionship, and whilst some of those chat—

speaker: Dai Le
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Consideration in Detail
text:
These amendments are about proportionality. They recognise that an ordinary small business's website is different from a platform that allows users to share harmful material, and they seek to give small businesses clarity about their obligations under this legislation. Think about the businesses in Fowler—a builder in Edensor Park displaying photographs of completed renovations, a bakery in Cabramatta showcasing its baked goods variety, a cafe in Liverpool accepting bookings, a restaurant displaying its menu, a mechanic in Bonnyrigg advertising Services. These businesses use the internet to reach customers and earn a living. A website used for those purposes should not be treated in the same way as a service that allows users to distribute pornography or generate new images using artificial intelligence. The law should recognise that distinction clearly.

My amendments make three changes. First, they establish a small business exemption using the small business entity definition in the income tax legislation. That exemption is not unconditional. It does not apply to services that allow users to post, share or send material to other users or otherwise communicate with one another. It does not apply to services that provide or link to pornography. It does not apply to services that generate or enable users to generate, provide or link to AI generated nudity, and it does not apply to services targeted at children. The amendments also allow the commissioner after inquiry to remove the exemption for a particular service when satisfied that it poses a material risk of serious harm to users in Australia. Business sites alone should not provide an ongoing exemption for a service with those features or risks, but an ordinary small business website should have a clear exemption where none of those exceptions apply.

Second, the amendments require compliance costs to be taken into account where a small business remains covered. That does not make it cost effective. It does not create an automatic defence. It ensures that the cost of an action or measure is considered when determining what is appropriate for a small business. A family business does not have the same resources as a multinational technology company. Recognising that difference is not an argument against online safety. It is an argument for obligations that are practical and proportionate.

Third, the amendments require an independent assessment of the likely cost to small businesses of complying with this part. The report must be tabled in both houses of parliament for small businesses that remain covered, the part would apply only after a further six months. To be clear, the deferral also applies to small businesses operating services excluded from the ongoing exemption, including services targeted at children and those involving pornography or AI generated nudity. It also applies where the commissioner removes the exemption. That is the transition proposed by these amendments. It should be considered separately from the question of which services qualify for an ongoing exemption. The assessment would give parliament and small businesses a clearer account of the likely compliance costs. The additional six months would provide time for affected businesses to prepare. I ask the government: How many small businesses does it expect to be covered? What does it estimate compliance will cost businesses operating ordinary, low-risk websites? Why should those costs not be taken into account when determining what measures are appropriate?

These are practical questions about how the legislation will operate beyond the major technology platforms. Small businesses deserve clear answers. We should distinguish between services according to their features and risks, we should consider the resources of the businesses expected to comply, and we should understand the likely cause of the obligations parliament imposes on small businesses. For anyone who has a small business in this House, they should understand how much costs have increased to operate a business since this government came to power. These amendments seek to put those principles into legislation. I ask the House to support them. I commend the amendments to the House.

THE HON D. M. DICK MP

Speaker of the House of Representatives

28 October 2026

speaker: Andrew Gee
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
text:
We are on the cusp of a massive data centre invasion across regional Australia. The tech billionaires think our country communities are fair game, and parliament is asleep at the wheel. I was out at Stubbo near Gulgong, where Firmus wants to drop a colossal data centre that will devour enough electricity to power hundreds of thousands of homes, but the unanswered questions here just keep piling up—zero answers on where the water is coming from, zero protection for our productive agricultural land, zero protection for the environment, public safety and privacy and zero say for our country communities. The tech bros are rolling in it while these mega projects are threatening our way of life and driving up power and water bills.

That's why I introduced my AI Kill Switch and Data Centre Control Bill 2026 to this House. We need an immediate halt to this unregulated rollout and a ban on these data centres until our laws catch up to protect the public and our regional communities. Parliament and the political parties of this nation need to wake up and act before it's too late. Our country communities are demanding action and there has not been enough of it in this House. We need to act now and bring these data centres under control because the future of our country communities depends on it.

speaker: Jerome Laxale
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026
text:
No-one would expect to see harmful content on their television, in print media or at the cinema. You'd never see deepfake news in the paper nor would you see instructions on how to commit suicide after the nightly news, but this vile stuff can be fed to you right now on your devices. Social media is unregulated. It's dangerous, and it's having a profound impact on our society.

Today, the House of Representatives has passed reasonable, sensible and important legislation which will put basic safety standards in place for digital media. This bill will require platforms to assess risks, prevent harm and give users over 16 real control over their feeds. This bill will keep Australians safe, and it builds on other world-leading reforms, like our under-16s social media ban. Australians have been asking for reform like this, and Labor is delivering it, but, inexplicably, the three right-wing parties opposed the sensible reforms today. They claim it's censorship. They cry that it's an attack on free speech. It's neither of those. They focus on what this bill is not about rather than what it is about. This bill is about protecting kids and adults from illegal and harmful content. This is about listening to parents, who tell me that they want this parliament to stand up to big tech and social media companies. Labor is listening to sensible parents, and it's time for the Senate to do so as well.

speaker: Jason Dean Clare
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank my friend the capital member for Canberra for her question—see what I did there? You can tell I'm a dad! There's no place for antisemitism or any type of racism or any type of hate in Australia. I think we all know we've got a lot of work to do here, and part of that is the work we do in education. That's why we set up the Antisemitism Education Taskforce, led by the great David Gonski. David is a towering figure in Australia, somebody I know is admired, respected and loved by people right across the chamber. They are working on how we combat antisemitism right across the education system. Following the Bondi attack we said we would review the National Curriculum, and that will be considered by education ministers when we meet next week.

But that's not the end of the work we need to do here. The truth is that it's just the start, because kids aren't born racist; kids aren't born with hate in their heart. This is something that's learnt; it's something that's taught. And I think if we're honest with ourselves we've got to look at what we can do to stop racism and hate fomenting in all its noxious forms. Part of it is what kids are taught at school, what's on the curriculum. But part of it is what kids are taught when they go online. I think Peter Dutton got it right this week when he called it a 'lawless jungle'. I will give you just a couple of horrific examples: people using artificial intelligence to make antisemitic songs and videos directly targeting kids; a Pixar-style animation set in a concentration camp; and fake news segments denying the Holocaust. All this was designed with AI, put online and then, with algorithms, sent to our kids—force-feeding our kids all this sort of rubbish, serving up hate on a plate to our kids.

I think we all know, if we look deeply into ourselves and think about this, that we need to do something about it. This is part of what the digital duty of care legislation that passed the House of Representatives today is about—doing something to crack down on these algorithms that are having this obvious impact on our kids. And it's not just me saying this; it's not just the government saying it. It's also the Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, Jillian Segal, who recently said:

My hope is that a digital duty of care will make it harder for algorithms … to dish up this sort of content to Australians, particularly children.

I say to colleagues who voted against this today: it's not too late to change your mind and to vote for this when it gets to the Senate.

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
This is what the RBA governor has said:

The conflict in the Middle East has re-escalated and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts.

… … …

In addition to the energy price shock, the AI boom and extreme weather events are contributing to upward pressure on a range of agricultural and technology-related prices.

… … …

We are not alone in being concerned about inflation—central banks in many other advanced economies are responding by increasing their policy rates or signalling they will do so if needed.

That was the Reserve Bank governor. I have respect for the RBA governor. We can't just wish away what has occurred, particularly since 28 February, which has been ongoing—a conflict that we were told would last for days or weeks and is indeed still going.

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: To the Prime Minister: a recent AI generated deepfake video targeting Senator Jacqui Lambie spread false statements in her name, resulting in increased threats to her. Sportsbet also did an illegal ad using AI generated images of real athletes without their consent. This technology is evolving fast. At a time of heightened concern for the safety and security of politicians, realistic deepfakes can damage reputations, inflame tensions and expose people to psychological harms and security risks. Will the government make the creation and dissemination of AI generated deepfakes illegal?

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
