They will not be able to livestream themselves or communicate with strangers on a wide range of services, including gaming. We call this the Australia-plus model because we are bringing in gaming, which is not included in the restrictions there. 16 and 17-year-olds will have those protections applied by default. There will be no cliff edge on the adult social media experience: when they hit 16, restrictions will be applied by default when they enter an account until they are 18.

We will introduce default protections for 16 and 17-year-olds on persuasive features on social media such as autoplay and personalised feeds to support young people to manage their time online. We will also apply default overnight curfews, including muting push notifications. Many Members have mentioned the other features and functions on social media that are addictive but may not be as harmful as the really extreme harms, such as child sexual exploitation or some of the other stories we hear. There is a spectrum of harms, including the addictive nature of social media, the lack of sleep from using it and the neurological difficulties it is causing in the adolescent brain—that is why social media companies design them that way. In fact, there is a Science and Technology Committee hearing tomorrow morning on the neuroscience of childhood and how social media is affecting children. It is worth looking into these big issues, and that is why we are applying overnight curfews to try to combat the impact on sleep and attention as part of the social media defaults, including muting push notifications.

These protections will sit alongside a wider package of measures including stronger safeguards around AI chatbots and measures to promote a more positive and educational experience both online and offline. We want children to enjoy the benefits of the online world but give parents the confidence that they can do that safely. We know that regulation alone is not enough. We must also help children and young people to build media literacy and critical thinking skills to navigate the online world safely and prepare them for an increasingly digital future.

I have spent a lot of time in schools in my constituency talking to 11 to 15-year-olds about the social media ban. I think hon. Members are absolutely right to suggest that we do not give young people enough credit for their understanding of dangers online. They understand when there are things online that they should not be seeing. They are very much aware of bullying and of those addictive features, and we do not give them enough credit for being able to navigate this themselves.

We are therefore strengthening digital resilience and media literacy through changes in the curriculum and practical support for parents and carers, while helping children and families to access high-quality online content. This is about building on the protections that we already have and going further where children need us to. The Government cannot and will not look the other way. We must move more quickly and decisively to keep people safe online, and nowhere is that responsibility more important than in protecting children from harm.

Since I took on my online safety role in the reshuffle, I have spent a lot of time with grieving families. I encourage all Members of this House—Ministers, Cabinet members, Back Benchers and those who are just interested in this issue—to spend some time with the grieving families to hear directly from them how social media has impacted their family life. They have some incredibly difficult stories that are harrowing to hear, but I think all Members should hear them. The test for the Secretary of State and me is that if we get to the end of this process and find that all these regulations would not have saved their children from the harms that led to their deaths, we will have failed their children and failed to protect the children of the future from harm. That is a very high bar, but it is a bar we have to meet, because the social media companies have not. Over years, if not decades, they have consistently turned the other way, and they are starting to take action only because they realise that legislation is coming to restrict accounts for under-16s.

Our job as a Government is to build an online world that is safer and more responsible, where platforms take responsibility. If we ask more of the online world, we should also offer more in the real world: stronger communities, better youth provision and more trusted adults around young people. Safety is not just about what we block; it is also about what we build, and we are determined to do that.

I will run through some of the interesting and important questions that hon. Members have raised. My hon. and learned Friend the Member for Folkestone and Hythe, who introduced the debate with a tremendous speech, talked about age-gating and the Australian example. What Australia has not done—we have been learning this from Australia—is have highly effective age verification. That is the gateway to making sure that the ban works. Many hon. Members have rightly challenged me, as the Minister responsible, on what that will look like. We are looking at this at the moment. Should it be at the app store level, as the shadow Minister said? Should it be at the device level? Should it be at the level of each individual social media platform? We are working through those issues to see what the most effective option is, but the principle for us is to ask, “What is the most effective system of age verification to ensure that under-16s are protected from social media platforms?”

My hon. and learned Friend talked rightly about the risky parts of gaming. We are bringing gaming into our approach, through features and functions. We will pass the under-16s social media ban this side of the new year, and it will come into effect in the spring of next year; we will then bring forward a host of regulations on features and functions, including stranger communications, which is the biggest problem with Roblox and some of the other issues that hon. Members have raised. That will allow gamers to continue to have the functionality of stranger pairing, but without the ability to talk to strangers in a gaming context. That should resolve some of these issues. A lot of the harms are where vulnerable people are taken from the gaming environment to other platforms, in order for grooming and exploitation to continue. That is a commitment of the features and functions part of this, which overlays the social media ban.

I will talk a little about isolating young people, because that is always on my mind; I know the Secretary of State thinks about it a lot as well. I pay tribute to my hon. Friend the Member for North West Cambridgeshire, who is the baby of the House—I was hoping to be the baby of this debate, but I have been beaten by probably everybody else in the Chamber—for telling his personal story, which is a very brave thing to do. Isolation is a concern, particularly for vulnerable communities, but from the data and information that we have, we are seeing that the most vulnerable young people are the most susceptible to being involved in these harms.

The balance here is about whether we have these spaces where young, vulnerable people can seek that advice or the communities that they wish to be part of and where they can have that enrichment, or whether we protect them. On balance, protecting people is probably the best place to be, while enriching the offer that we can give young people so that they are confident that they can go to safe spaces with safe people they can talk to about their experiences. This is not an easy thing to resolve. If anyone said it was, they would not be telling the truth.

Let us talk a little about the way back. Essentially, it all comes down to the scope of the social media ban. What we want to do with the ban, which we announced in June, is capture user-to-user platforms whose purpose is to enable online interaction and which allow users to post material, alongside having an algorithm. The Australian regime includes platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram and Facebook. We will not be naming platforms directly in the regulations. Ofcom will subsequently apply the regulations to the social media companies and then determine whether it will produce a list of the companies that are in scope. I will explain what Ofcom will do in the regulations and what the thought processes are. Social media companies that think that they are in scope and that have more than a certain number of users will have to self-notify to Ofcom as being in scope of the legislation, and then conform to the regulations. We are working through the detail of how we translate the Australian scope into the UK context, and it is really important to get this right within that.

Several hon. Members talked about the regulations, about meeting the criteria and about what the off-ramp is. Essentially, the off-ramp or the way back is for platforms to prove, through their design, that they meet the regulations. It is just a case of reversing the situation. If stranger communication is banned and your online platform is subsequently not to be available to under-16s but you have that functionality, it is quite clear that you do not comply with the regulations, so the way back is to comply with the regulations and fall out of scope. That is an easy thing to say but not an easy thing to deliver, but that is the principle with which we will go forward on this.

If there are services like Lego Play or—YouTube has been mentioned—YouTube Kids, are there ways in which you can stop the harms being created by the algorithms, the recommender systems, the commenting systems or the conversations that can be had with strangers? If you have created a service that complies with all the regulations, is it then available to under-16s? I would say that currently the Government’s position is that, yes, there has to be an off-ramp, and the Canada model is something that we are looking at quite closely in terms of its regulations.

speaker: Jonathan Reynolds
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text:
I do not want to say that the hon. Gentleman should listen a bit harder to the Chancellor when is giving a Budget, but he went into detail on that. I will expand on what the better regulation taskforce will mean.

Specifically on the employment rights agenda, we know that the Conservatives do not like it—that is not a secret—but I would simply say to the hon. Member that we have a manifesto commitment to address in particular insecurity in the workplace, including the 1 million people on zero-hours contracts. Let Conservative colleagues not forget that the premise of that particular measure is that where a person works a regular number of hours, they will receive, if they wish to, a contract for those hours—not additional costs. Additional costs are not present when someone get a contract that reflects what they are already working.

The rest of the agenda may not be popular with the Conservative party, but it is certainly popular with the country. And because of that agenda—[Interruption.] I know the Conservatives did not stick to their own manifesto commitments, but we will stick to ours. Because of that agenda, of course want to reduce burdens in other places; it is an entirely noble agenda and one that reflects the interests of British business. The hon. Member may be aware—the Chancellor did speak about this in the statement—that there is an aspiration to reduce business burdens by 25% over the course of this Parliament. That will be delivered through the new Better Regulation Executive. It brings together the power of the Treasury, the Cabinet Office and my Department to move us towards a more streamlined and proportionate regulatory system—one that spurs growth, investment and innovation across the country.

I also warmly welcome the Chancellor increasing access to finance for ambitious founders and entrepreneurs. In the Budget, he introduced a new founders relief to encourage a new wave of wealth creation. Founders and early investors will benefit from a 10% capital gains tax rate on up to £10 million of lifetime gains. Dom Hallas from Startup Coalition said:

“The chancellor has delivered the boldest action backing startups and scaleups of any government in years.”

Meanwhile, the trading allowance for people starting new ventures is being tripled from £1,000 to £3,000, and £700 million is going towards home-grown innovation, strengthening Britain’s sovereignty and ensuring that tomorrow’s technologies are developed and adopted right here in the UK.

On top of all that, the Budget gives the British Business Bank £1.4 billion of additional commercial equity capacity, allowing it to back specialist venture capital funds in strategic sectors and larger growth funds capable of writing the cheques needed to keep the UK’s fastest-growing companies scaling here. The package is expected to leverage around £4.2 billion of private capital and create 14,500 additional jobs. That builds on the landmark investments the bank has already made, backing businesses across the UK: from Optima Partners, the Edinburgh-based AI consultancy, to Pharos Marine, the Norfolk manufacturer of navigation aids for offshore wind farms and ports, to Oxford Space Systems, whose satellite antennas were launched into orbit earlier this year.

Our industrial strategy is also making a difference. It is an essential part of our ambition to reindustrialise Britain and back our own sovereign capabilities. It is delivering on industrial energy costs, reversing what we inherited from the previous Government, with the highest industrial energy costs in the developed world. We are slashing electricity bills by 25% for over 10,000 British manufacturers through the British industrial competitiveness scheme. We are cutting electricity costs for those businesses by up to £40 per MWh, bringing their costs closer into line with competitors across Europe, with eligible businesses also receiving a one-off additional payment in 2027 to cover the support that they would have been received if BICS had been in place from April this year, correcting years of Conservative failure.

We are channelling investment into the eight high growth-driving sectors of our economy, including life sciences and advanced manufacturing. The Budget confirmed over £1 billion of new life sciences investment, from Kindeva, Vertex and Convatec, backed by almost £70 million of Government funding. It gave the green light to a partnership that I am particularly proud of: a partnership with Rolls-Royce to develop its next generation of turbine engine technology here in Britain. This is the single biggest reindustrialisation opportunity that the UK has before it.

speaker: Jonathan Reynolds
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text:
I agree with the sentiment put forward by the right hon. Gentleman, on one of the most substantive issues that the House must grapple with. There is no inconsistency in being proud of the services-led nature of the UK economy while recognising the essential contribution of advanced manufacturing. There are sectors of the UK economy that could gain from the current phase of innovation in artificial intelligence in goods; for instance, robotics could reduce our wage differential with low-wage economies and return industrial functions to the UK.

The basis of British industry will, however, always be export led—that is key in the automative or aerospace sector. I do not see a tension between strengthening our resilience and our domestic industrial capacity and being an outward-facing, internationalist country to the rest of the world. I believe the two things must go together.

I give the right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) a specific example: our critical minerals strategy. We cannot reduce our dependence on other countries entirely, but we can reduce the degree of exposure to individual markets and use the levers of Government, through investing in tungsten or lithium mining in the south-west of England, looking at how the refining process works, and working with allies. It is a balance between the two things. I recognise absolutely the substance of the right hon. Gentleman’s question and its importance to this debate.

On the UK-EU summit, in addition to the premise of the deal we seek to strike, we want to make progress on electric vehicle rules of origin, steel tariffs and economic security, recognising that in many cases we share similar challenges. We face those challenges together, and we can overcome them together. To that end, the Prime Minister will say more later this year about options for our long-term relationship with the EU—one that strengthens our collective security and our collective prosperity.

speaker: Peter Swallow
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text: The Secretary of State makes an important point about our relationship with the EU. He will be aware that Bracknell is home to lots of companies that work in cloud technologies. Is he alive to concerns around the EU’s proposed cloud and AI development Act, and will he ensure that we address those concerns robustly as part of our negotiations in the summit and thereafter? We do need to get that right.

speaker: Neil Hudson
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text:
The theme of this year’s autumn Budget was said to be one of hope. It raised our hopes akin to the title of a “Star Wars” film, yet for many of my constituents in Epping Forest, and indeed for families and businesses across the country, that hope has been sorely dashed. I have huge respect for the Chancellor, who is a deeply honourable man. He resigned as Defence Secretary, calling for 3% of GDP on defence spending by 2030, but sadly, even his hopes for this clear commitment and plan have been dashed by this Government.

In Epping Forest we are fortunate to have fantastic local businesses, restaurants, cafés and pubs, yet many are struggling to stay afloat under this Labour Government. It is deeply regrettable that this Budget did not take up the sensible proposals from the Conservatives on scrapping the family farm tax and family business tax in full, abolishing inheritance tax on family homes and scrapping business rates for 250,000 businesses nationwide.

One thing my constituents in Epping Forest will have noted was the Chancellor’s talk of a British data centre covenant. Many of my constituents are rightly concerned about the implications and environmental impacts of AI data centres, including the proposal in Loughton, with major concerns about their huge water and energy usage. Also, a speculative and completely inappropriate proposal is being worked up for a data centre near Chigwell that will threaten our precious green belt. Many of my constituents have reached out to me, alarmed by the Chigwell proposal and by the fact that it comes in the context of a Labour Government who have outrageously taken away large planning decisions from Epping Forest district council and who are arbitrarily and spuriously moving to reclassify green belt as grey belt in order to achieve their development targets.

We have seen this, too, with inappropriate large-scale housing developments being proposed on green belt in Theydon Bois and around Epping, and with solar developments on farmland between Thornwood and Epping Upland. I urge the Labour Government to do the right thing, listen to my Epping Forest constituents, leave our green belt alone and pull the plug on these damaging top-down policies and inappropriate developments.

speaker: Preet Kaur Gill
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text:
“Fresh hope for the future” must mean something that people can recognise in their own lives: a young person finding a skilled job close to home, a patient getting a diagnosis sooner, someone waiting for an operation finally getting treatment and getting back to their life. That is how people will judge us, so I welcome this Budget’s determination to give families breathing space now while building a stronger economy for tomorrow. I want to focus on one opportunity that can help us achieve both: backing life sciences so that Britain can build a future here. That involves developing new treatments, manufacturing them in Britain and getting them to NHS patients faster, because a healthier country is a stronger country. The industries that help us live healthier lives can also create the jobs, investment and prosperity that our communities need.

I began working as a care assistant at 16. I became a social worker, working in child protection, and served as cabinet member for public health and protection. Those experiences taught me that public services are judged at the moment someone needs them. Can they get help? Are they listened to? Does someone take responsibility? As a Health Minister, I brought that same test to innovation. A scientific breakthrough is an extraordinary achievement. Approval matters, but success is a patient receiving treatment. Our ambition should be clear: discover here, make it here and deliver it here.

This Budget gives us something substantial to build on. I welcome the £100 million investment in robotic surgery, supporting the ambition to increase procedures from 70,000 a year today to 500,000 by 2035. For a patient, that could mean a less invasive operation, a shorter stay in hospital and getting home to their family sooner. I also welcome the life sciences investment in Manchester, Oxford and Loughborough, together worth more than £1 billion, supported by almost £70 million in Government grants. These investments should give businesses the confidence to build in Britain and patients the confidence that progress will reach them.

The next task is to make that partnership work across the country, and to connect investment with improvements that people can feel. Birmingham’s life sciences district shows what is possible when we bring our strengths together. The University of Birmingham, the Queen Elizabeth hospital and Birmingham Health Partners connect world-class research with frontline care, and our health innovation campus and precision health technologies accelerator help businesses turn discoveries into treatments. We should back this district as an engine of national growth, attracting investment, expanding manufacturing and opening routes into skilled jobs for local people. This is an enormous opportunity for our city to know that there could be a place for young people in my city as a laboratory technician, an engineer, a clinical researcher, a manufacturing apprentice or a specialist working with health data. Representatives of the University of Birmingham are here today in Parliament launching the Birmingham health and life sciences quarter.

As the Government develop their 10-year plan and prepare for the next spending review, three things should guide us. First, we must make the adoption of proven innovation a core NHS responsibility, because businesses and innovators need a clear route from successful evaluation to everyday use, with named responsibility, funding and a timetable. For a small British business, a successful NHS trial should open the door. It should not have to go begging every single trust to procure its product. We should measure success through patient outcomes, and the same discipline should apply to AI. I therefore welcome the Budget’s review of NHS productivity and AI. Its purpose should be practical: better care, less avoidable administration and more time with patients.

Secondly, we need to connect life sciences investment to British manufacturing and local opportunity. Thirdly, we must make prevention and earlier diagnosis central to our ambition, because the greatest gain is often the illness avoided.

This is a serious economic opportunity. Better health can help people remain in work, support families and reduce pressure on public services. Successful British businesses can bring investment, exports and skilled employment. The Prime Minister has opened a conversation about the country we want to become. My answer is a Britain confident enough to back its scientists, ambitious enough to build new industries, and determined enough to put their achievements into the hands of the people who need them; a Britain where a discovery becomes a treatment and an investment becomes a skilled job, and where a young person can see a future in the place they call home. That is what fresh hope for the future must mean.

speaker: Victoria Collins
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text:
I could not have put it better myself. On top of that there is the cost of hiring, as has been mentioned again and again. The Government have to tackle that for businesses.

If we truly want fresh hope for the future and for our wider economy, we need bold action. Supporting our entrepreneurs is key, and as Lib Dems who have pushed for a type of young entrepreneurs allowance for almost a decade, we are pleased to see that proposal and look forward to hearing more details. I would also push the Government to look at further work to support start-ups and scale-ups, including reviewing the seed enterprise investment scheme, tax on SEIS, tax credits and relief so that they work for businesses.

As for the founders’ relief, I ask the Government to work with the industry to ensure that it works. One founder said to me that they felt that if they stood on one leg and turned around enough times they might just about get close to getting some of it.

On incentivising innovation, the Government must take spin-outs from our world-leading universities across the UK more seriously. We are calling for the Government to quintuple proof-of-concept funding, create regional innovation centres and introduce standardised frameworks for negotiating intellectual property across the sector. As regards innovative spending, the extra £120 million for the Sovereign AI fund pales in comparison to the nearly £8 billion of active contracts with US tech giants or the billions spent on procurement. We call for a proper digital sovereign strategy to back our British businesses and to look at increasing research and development spending, so that we do not have to make decisions over Jodrell Bank, for example, and how that is impacting innovation.

Finally, we need a bold plan on Europe. We are calling for a growth and defence partnership with Europe, rejoining the single market and customs union. Not only can we cut taxes for families with that growth dividend, but inject real growth into our economy for families, businesses and our future.

speaker: Peter Prinsley
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text:
I welcome much of what the Chancellor of the Exchequer has said in the Budget, but tonight I will speak of our NHS, for we will not grow our economy if we are not well.

Norfolk and Suffolk foundation trust is the mental health trust that serves my constituents, and it has been transformed thanks to its brilliant staff and inspired leadership—I thank all of them. Last week I learned that some of the teams have been early adopters of AI, using it to transcribe patient consultations. More time with the patients and less time staring at computers—imagine that!

Some of us remain suspicious of AI in healthcare, but who here has not asked their phone about a symptom or a medical worry? Many GPs already use AI-assisted triage to tackle the dreaded 8 o’clock rush. I am therefore pleased to hear that we will fund the technology that will increasingly shape our health service. Let us embrace it, not fear it.

I welcome the Government’s approach to healthcare, but much remains to be done. Too many of our patients are being asked to be just that: patient. We have record NHS staffing and resources since the pandemic, yet activity has not increased proportionately. Why is that? How much genuinely improves people’s health? We know that health depends on housing, wealth and much else besides. Falling life expectancy in some of our communities and the problems in maternity services demand urgent political attention.

I welcome the Chancellor’s announcement of funding for surgical robots, having heard how they are helping patients at West Suffolk hospital, but frankly, if I were asked where I would invest taxpayers’ money, my answer would be: in primary care and neighbourhood health centres.

speaker: John Hayes
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text: Of course I respect the hon. Gentleman’s professional expertise, which I do not share, but much of what he has said so far is counterintuitive. My constituents tell me that what they want from the health service is personal interaction—to form a meaningful relationship with a GP, surgeon or specialist. That is how trust is built, not through machines, AI and robots.

speaker: Steve Witherden
heading: Budget Resolutions - Income Tax (Charge)
text:
This Budget is aimed squarely at people struggling with the cost of living—good! In a year when one in five UK households have experienced food insecurity and there are 9 million people in severe hardship, according to the Trussel Trust, the Government should make no bones about putting them first. The Government have identified where household budgets are being pinched the most and have redistributed wealth accordingly.

Slashing bills for 80% of households in England is no small thing, and I am glad that the Welsh Government have since announced that they will use the consequential funding to extend the benefits to my constituents in Montgomeryshire and Glyndŵr. A high proportion of my constituents are reliant on heating oil, so I especially welcome the fact that the payment will be applicable to those off the gas grid. That, when combined with the scrapping of import tariffs on kerosene, could amount to a real reduction in heating costs.

Let us hope, though, that the additional £450 million that the Budget allocates to the Welsh Government for public services is spent wisely, at a time when three out of four of Montgomeryshire’s hospitals face the loss of all their beds, all their X-ray services and all their minor injuries units. Returning to tariffs, I applaud their removal from a wide range of everyday goods. It is appalling to hear these measures spoken of as small fry by the Conservatives, when it is the poorest in our society who are affected most by such price rises. In providing that bit of breathing space, the 3.9% rise in the minimum wage is another positive step.

The surest way to improve our food security, however, is to produce more at home, and that means supporting our farmers, so I welcome the suspension of import tariffs on fertiliser and the extension of reduced duties for red diesel. These measures will make a difference to the agricultural sector, which has taken a body blow this year in the form of the Iran war driving up input costs, compounded by a summer of severe droughts and wildfires, and further compounded by an outbreak of bluetongue. Threats to our national security are compounding, too, from climate change, AI-enabled cyber-attacks and a new age of interstate conflict, but we cannot forget about the basics. As an island nation, we must have domestic resilience in food production. You will have to forgive me, Madam Deputy Speaker, but food security is national security.

Let me end on fiscal devolution. The experience in many parts of Wales is that devolution is unfinished business. Powers have been devolved to the Senedd, but not to our regions and communities such as north-east Wales or the Marches. I am happy to hear that English local authorities will start to retain more business rates from next year, but I would like to see greater detail on how the Government are working with the devolved Administrations to realise the benefits of regional governance across the UK. This Government, like any Government, will be judged on how they improve the material conditions of hard-working people. It is that target on which this Budget is rightly focused.

speaker: Lord Leong
heading: Business Hiring Intentions - Question
text: My Lords, I fully accept that the labour market is failing too many graduates. Repeated rejection wastes talent and damages confidence. We are investing £7.8 million in university AI courses and graduate traineeships and our £20 million early careers jobs alliance helps employers maintain routes into work as technology changes. The digital and technologies jobs plan targets 20,000 entry-level jobs annually. Our responsibility is to turn those commitments into interviews, paid opportunities and lasting careers.

speaker: Lord Leong
heading: Business Hiring Intentions - Question
text: I have not had a chance to look at the report, but I definitely will. AI is automating repetitive tasks, and we take the risk to entry-level jobs seriously. The £20 million for the early careers job alliance that I mentioned earlier is helping employers redesign roles while maintaining routes into work. Through our AI skills boost, we aim to equip 10 million people with practical AI skills by 2030. Our priority is adoption that supports workers, improves productivity and opens opportunities. Technological progress must give young people a better future, not close the door.

speaker: Lord Nagaraju
heading: Binance Security Breach: Consumer Exposure and Interim Safeguards - Question
text: My Lords, I declare my interests in AI and technology as set out in the register, and I beg leave to ask the Question standing in my name on the Order Paper.

speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
heading: Binance Security Breach: Consumer Exposure and Interim Safeguards - Question
text:
My Lords, I bring to the attention of the House my registered interests in AI businesses and digital assets.

Digital assets operate across borders, as do cyber security threats, as we have seen in the issue with Binance. Given the considerable progress being made internationally on regulatory co-operation, does the Minister agree that there should be an increased amount of discussion about that co-operation on regulatory compliance? Also, does the Minister agree that the Government should commit to making digital assets a security and regulatory priority as part of our G20 presidency next year?

speaker: Lord Patel
heading: Health Bill - Committee (2nd Day)
text:
My Lords, I strongly support the amendment in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Shawcross-Wolfson, and I have added my name to it. She spoke so eloquently and made her case so strongly that I have put aside what I have written down because it would have been a repetition of what she had already said. I am going to take a slightly different tack but make the same point.

The noble Baroness quite rightly linked education, training and workforce planning. You have to know what workforce you might require for the health service you plan to have. I guess one can say that the Government’s 10-year health plan and the 10-year cancer care plan outline the kind of health service that the Government wish to see develop over the next 10 years. If that is the case, we need to address what kind of training and education and what kind of people we will need to deliver that plan.

I am guessing now that the reason why the 10-year workforce plan is delayed is because the premise on which it was to be formulated was that technology such as AI and digital technology would free a lot of clinical time, and hence the headcount need not be so high. That is a false assumption. It is false because we need to train people to use AI and digital technologies. The assessment is that, if you use these technologies, you might free about 40 minutes a day for front-line clinicians. With the pressure that the NHS now faces and the needs of the workforce it now faces, that time will be used to deliver better care to patients, particularly as the 10-year health plan identifies that technologies such as genomics and personalised medicine will be the way healthcare will go. There is an ambition by 2040 to have 50% of patients with some idea of their genomics, and the treatment is therefore based on that.

If you add all these together, and the Secretary of State now has responsibility for education, training and workforce planning, you ask the question: why is the workforce plan delayed? It is delayed because maybe the penny has dropped that, if you do not count the numbers and do not present a case about how technologies will reduce front-line clinical time, then you cannot plan the workforce.

Furthermore, I wonder whether the Bailie review of productivity in the NHS is based on the premise that greater productivity will be delivered in the NHS because of using technologies such as AI and digital technologies. We do not know that that will happen, but we have to wait until the Bailie review comes out. I wonder whether that is another reason—the Minister might comment on that—why the workforce plan is delayed.

It might be political pressures, it might be fiscal pressures or it might be the pressures from not knowing how to get the workforce numbers that we would require to deliver the 10-year plan and the cancer care plan that are holding up workforce planning. However, as the noble Baroness, Lady Shawcross-Wolfson, pointed out, if we do not have a plan, things will get worse. We will introduce technology, which will not be across the board, and we will then look for workforce that is not trained to deliver it. I hope the Minister will give us some answers about where we are going.

speaker: Lord Kamall
heading: Health Bill - Committee (2nd Day)
text:
My Lords, this has been a crucial debate, and I am grateful to noble Lords for tabling and speaking to their amendments, which raise fundamental questions about the future of the NHS workforce, the quality of care patients can expect and the Government’s ability to deliver health service reform.

The amendments from my noble friend Lady Shawcross-Wolfson and the noble Baroness, Lady Pidgeon, go to the heart of a simple but vital question: how can this Government, or indeed any Government, credibly plan for the future of the NHS without an independently verified assessment of the workforce that we need? As my noble friend said, the previous Conservative Government, albeit belatedly, recognised the importance of this challenge when we published the first NHS Long Term Workforce Plan in 2023. This was a baseline step in establishing a long-term approach to workforce planning, with clear ambitions to expand domestic training, improve retention and reduce our reliance on international recruitment.

We recognised then, as we must recognise now, that workforce planning cannot be conducted from one spending review to the next. Training doctors, nurses and other healthcare professionals takes years, and decisions made today will determine the quality and availability of care for patients a decade, or decades, from now. Yet we are still waiting, as other noble Lords said, for the Government’s new 10-year workforce plan. The noble Lord, Lord Patel, offered some possible reasons for the delay.

Clause 7 of the Bill makes the Secretary of State wholly responsible for workforce planning and training. As my noble friend asked, will the Minister commit to ensuring that the workforce plan is independently verified and published? Is she in a position to tell us, as the noble Baroness, Lady Pidgeon, just asked, by what date the plan will be published, or by what decade even? As noble Baronesses, Lady Hollins and Lady Tyler, asked, what about a workforce plan for mental health services? In debates on the Mental Health Bill, and indeed on the 2022 health Bill, we asked for parity between physical and mental health. Have we learned that lesson when we are talking about a workforce plan that seems to focus mostly on physical health rather than mental health too? What safeguards are in place to ensure that the plan and training evolve as new technology is adopted and roles change? The noble Baroness, Lady Rafferty, remarked on the importance of continued professional development, and the noble Baroness, Lady Gerada, spoke about the value of district nurses.

I turn briefly to Amendment 240, from my noble friend Lord Blencathra, concerning sexual misconduct by healthcare professionals. Patient safety and public confidence must remain paramount. No patient should have to fear exploitation or abuse at the hands of someone they trust with their care. There are important questions about proportionality and the appropriate role of professional regulators, but the underlying concern raised by this amendment is entirely legitimate. Can the Minister explain whether the Government are satisfied with the current regulatory framework and whether it deals robustly and consistently with proven sexual misconduct? Will the Government consider whether further action is indeed needed to ensure that professionals who pose a serious risk to patients cannot simply return to clinical practice, perhaps to repeat the same offences?

I return to workforce planning and will make two or three points. We have heard much about the Government’s ambitions to shift care from hospitals to the community—something that all noble Lords would support. It is therefore appropriate to highlight that primary care is also suffering under this reorganisation. The Royal College of General Practitioners notes that GPs receive the lowest share of the NHS budget, estimated at around 8.3%, but GP workload continues to rise, albeit with some of the demographic challenges we see as we shift to a more feminised workforce, and some of the challenges women GPs face as they balance work and life challenges. We know that, as we shift more from hospital to community, primary care will face even more pressure. Do the Government intend to implement a commensurate shift of resources?

I worry that the Government are placing too much emphasis on reorganising the machinery of the NHS and too little on the workforce who need to deliver the necessary care. What assessment have they made of the impact of this reorganisation on the recruitment and retention of staff? The noble Baroness, Lady Barker, spoke about the retention of ICB staff and their morale.

We have more doctors and nurses than ever before, but demand continues to increase, as a result partly of our ageing population and partly of awareness of more conditions. As the noble Lord, Lord Patel, alluded to, former Secretary of State Wes Streeting suggested that the NHS cannot afford to carry on employing ever more people, and proposed that AI and technology could be part of the solution. What he did not say, but perhaps implied, was that recruiting ever more doctors, nurses and other clinical staff could lead to the NHS or even the state running out of money. If you accept this premise, not only will there need to be a better use of technology, but the NHS will have to be complemented by, or partner with, independent providers such as mutuals, co-operatives, friendly societies, charities, non-profits, social enterprises and other non-state providers in order to meet that increased demand.

These amendments raise important questions about the workforce and the capacity of our system of healthcare, and about how it will evolve as new technologies are adopted and demand increases. I look forward to the Minister’s responses.

speaker: Baroness Merron
heading: Health Bill - Committee (2nd Day)
text:
My Lords, I am grateful for the debate we have just had. Unsurprisingly, but not exclusively, a lot of it focused on the promised workforce plan, so I will address that straight off. There has been lots of thought about why it is “in due course”, and that is the situation. I am glad that the noble Baroness, Lady Coffey, appreciated the impact, without blame, of a new Secretary of State: she is well placed to speak to that point.

Let me say that, first, our absolute commitment to the workforce plan for the NHS remains. There is no shift in that. I also say that, as I mentioned, the reason we await it and it is “in due course” is that, as is absolutely reasonable and right, a new Secretary of State has to be allowed to provide views; that is the situation. I hope that clarifies the position.

With permission, I will address Amendments 28, 92, 240, 252, 253 and 279J together. Amendments 28 and 253 have been tabled by the noble Baronesses, Lady Shawcross-Wolfson and Lady Pidgeon. I absolutely agree that the health and care workforce is fundamental. It is fundamental to everything we are doing and to this entire debate, and it is fundamental to the interests of patients, which is why we will publish the 10-year workforce plan. As most noble Lords spoke to the plan, I will emphasise that the Secretary of State already has duties to ensure effective planning and the delivery of healthcare, education and training—as has been called for, rightly—and also has a duty to report on the system for assessing and meeting NHS workforce needs.

To the noble Lords, Lord Kakkar, Lord Stevens and Lord Kamall, I can say that an expert panel of external stakeholders has scrutinised the 10-year workforce plan approach to workforce planning. To the noble Baroness, Lady Hollins, I can confirm that sickness absence is indeed factored in to the workforce planning process. I heard the noble Lord, Lord Stevens, talking about the way in which the workforce has changed; that is absolutely right and, again, the plan will reflect that.

The noble Lord, Lord Kakkar, and the noble Lord, Lord Stevens, raised points about short-termism versus long-termism in workforce planning, and so on. I am sure noble Lords will understand that decisions about the education and training of healthcare professionals will continue to be driven by data, based on evidence and intelligence led. That will be through the new restructured system. The point here is to make sure that we have the right people in the right places, with the right skills, to care for patients when they need it.

The noble Baroness, Lady Hollins, asked about a bottleneck in medical training pathways. I can say on that point that noble Lords will recall the passage of what became the Medical Training (Prioritisation) Act, and we are easing competition for medical training by prioritising UK-trained graduates for foundation specialty training places, alongside some other groups. The recently agreed 2026 resident doctors deal also significantly expands specialty training places by up to 4,500 over three years, including 1,000 next year.

The noble Baroness, Lady Gerada, made a very strong, and correct, point about the role of district nurses, borne out by the noble Baroness, Lady Barker. Through NHS England, we are actively monitoring future nursing and midwifery student numbers and will continue to assess the 2025-26 graduate guarantee as a mechanism. There is a wide range of measures to support students, educators and universities with the transition into employment, including Student Hub, which offers guidance and resources for students and newly qualified practitioners.

To the point made by the noble Baroness, Lady Barker, I will be pleased to speak to colleagues in the Home Office about the supply of district nurses, if not directly then through the appropriate Minister.

The noble Baroness, Lady Shawcross-Wolfson, in her opening comments made reference to numbers of GPs. We have committed £292 million for GP recruitment this year, which translates to 1,600 GPs, and there are 4,100 more GPs than a year ago. It is important to note that, while we wait for a workforce plan, we have not waited in taking action. For example, we have resolved the long-running doctors’ dispute and we have published a set of core NHS staff standards.

On adult social care, and the point made by the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, that was another point I pushed when we last debated this matter and when we were in Opposition. There was also a comment about legislating on planning duties. That would pre-empt the vital work to develop a national care service which will follow from the recommendations of the noble Baroness, Lady Casey, which we will receive in the summer. That work will have important implications for the shape and skills of the future adult social care workforce. I agree with noble Lords: it is inextricably linked with the NHS workforce, which is a point I have made over a number of years. In the meantime, we will commit to publishing a workforce plan and we will set out immediate action to further support and develop the adult social care workforce.

My noble friend Lady Rafferty tabled Amendment 279J on continued professional development for nurses and midwives. I agree that that is critical for patient safety and outcomes. That is why we are investing in their professional development, with £181 million of continued professional development funding allocated for nurses, midwives, nursing associates and allied healthcare professionals in 2026-27 as part of a three-year cycle and to support equitable access to professional development. To respond to her questions, I can tell my noble friend that organisations are responsible for the planning and governance of their CPD, to ensure that staff have a fair opportunity to benefit from the funding. We expect employers to provide support, supervision and guidance, and to foster a culture of continuous learning, which, again, we would expect throughout the NHS.

On Amendments 92 and 252, tabled by the noble Baroness, Lady Hollins, I assure her that action is already under way. We have recruited thousands more mental health workers and our intent is to continue strengthening services for children and adults. The noble Baroness raised the recruitment and retention of psychiatrists. That is a responsibility for local organisations, in the same way that consultant recruitment and retention is the responsibility of local providers. There is a programme being run by NHS England that works with trusts to help them understand why staff have left. It focuses on better support for line managers, including a staff retention guide, improved support for new joiners to the NHS and, for example, enhanced support for staff going through the menopause. Workforce growth alone will not transform mental health support, but that is why we are working to develop the mental health strategy, based on the independent review led by Professor Peter Fonagy.

To the point made by the noble Lord, Lord Scriven, we recognise that there are shortages remaining in respect of learning disability nurses, and we recognise the difficulty that is causing. We are therefore strengthening the future learning disability nursing workforce. Planning should connect the identified gaps to those organisations responsible for recruitment, training and workforce development. I very much acknowledge the point the noble Lord made about the sad loss of his nephew, Myles, and the impact that staff can have on somebody in their care and the need to support those who are being cared for.

To the noble Lords who raised different groups of concern, I anticipate the workforce plan will include all staff groups. The noble Baroness, Lady Gerada, is quite right to talk about the shift to neighbourhood health. All of the shifts are going to require a different approach from workforce planning, which is what this workforce plan will do.

Lastly, I will address Amendment 240, from the noble Lord, Lord Blencathra. I assure him and the noble Lord, Lord Kamall, that we believe that serious professional misconduct should be robustly addressed. The protection and safety of patients and the public is absolutely paramount. We believe that certain offences are so serious that conviction is incompatible with registration as a regulated healthcare professional and should result in automatic removal from the register, regardless of the sentence imposed. That is why we are taking forward a programme of reforms to the legislative frameworks of the healthcare professional regulators, beginning with the GMC. The legislation for that was consulted upon earlier this year. As part of these changes, we are proposing provisions requiring the registrar to remove a registrant from the register where they have been convicted of a sexual offence listed in the draft order, regardless of the sentence imposed.

I will be pleased to pick up some of the points in writing. I can say to the noble Lords, Lord Patel and Lord Kamall, that we have an NHS Digital Academy in place to support the workforce to develop digital data and AI skills and to give them the confidence to use them, which is absolutely going to be needed for a future NHS.

speaker: Andrew Ranger
subheading: Young People and Work: Milburn Interim Report — [Esther McVey in the Chair]
text:
I totally agree; that is another thing that I will come on to in my speech.

It is now our turn to repay the debt that we owe young people. Many players will help us to solve this crisis, and one of them is business, both local and national. I want to recognise the businesses already meeting the challenge. Examples from my own constituency include Moneypenny. At national level, Sainsbury’s and Greene King, among others, are giving 100,000 much-needed opportunities to young people. Those are vital, but I ask all businesses to give young people opportunities. They may not necessarily have the skills on paper—on their CVs—but they are undoubtedly talented and will repay the chance that they are given. Spend the extra time doing an in-person interview with an applicant, who will gain much more than they would have in talking to an AI chatbot. Look past the gaps in their CV and see the potential behind it.

speaker: Peter Swallow
subheading: Young People and Work: Milburn Interim Report — [Esther McVey in the Chair]
text:
The Milburn review interim report was clear that in order for the support provided to be fit for young people to enter the workplace today, not only the welfare system but our health and our education systems need to be fundamentally rewired. Education has a critical role to play in preparing young people for the workforce and for life.

What we hear again and again from employers is that young people, even in entry-level roles, have not been able to develop the skills that are essential in any workplace, and indeed for life—skills like communication, problem solving and critical thinking. This is not just about the NEET crisis we are facing today—painful though it is already for so many—or bringing down the welfare bill, although that is vital too; it is about taking the opportunity now to grasp the even greater NEET crisis that may be coming down the track as we face the reality of an economy being fundamentally reshaped by AI.

It is clear that AI is the defining technology of our time. In just a few years we have seen it power breakthroughs in fields as wide-ranging and important as medical diagnostics and research, agriculture and mathematics. That is why it is so fundamental that young people develop the skills they need not only to use AI critically and thoughtfully, but also to exist in a world where things for which we have always relied on humans are increasingly being automated.

I have long argued that an education system rich in the humanities must be at the heart of preparing young people for the age of AI, not just because of the content they would learn, but because of the skills the humanities would encourage them to develop. As part of its research into the future of the labour market, the National Foundation for Educational Research found that it was skills such as collaboration, communication, problem-solving and information literacy that will be most needed by employees in 2035. That is why it is so important that we develop an education system that provides young people with those skills.

speaker: Lilian Greenwood
subheading: Young People and Work: Milburn Interim Report — [Esther McVey in the Chair]
text:
I can assure my hon. Friend that we are aware of that issue and we are setting about addressing it.

Alongside all those measures, we are reforming post-16 education so that young people can have clearer academic, technical and vocational routes. We are transforming the apprenticeship levy, backed by an additional £1 billion, supporting 50,000 more young people into apprenticeships. New foundation apprenticeships, fully funded apprenticeships for eligible under-25s and additional support for employers will all create more routes into skilled employment. As my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) rightly said, the skills needs are changing in the world of AI.

These reforms represent significant action, but we recognise that the Government must continue to listen and learn. Alan Milburn’s interim report set out starkly the scale and complexity of the participation challenge facing this generation. Our ambition is straightforward: wherever a young person starts from, whatever barriers they face, they should have a genuine route into education, training or good work. I hope that reassures my hon. Friend the Member for Stoke-on-Trent Central.

Achieving that ambition means intervening earlier and joining up services across departmental boundaries, as my hon. Friend the Member for Birmingham Selly Oak (Al Carns) said. It means working with employers, colleges and local organisations such as those highlighted by many hon. Members, including Saints Works in Southampton, the Spear Programme in York and Making It in Aylesbury, because, as my hon. Friend the Member for Southport (Patrick Hurley) said, place-based solutions show great results. It also means refusing to accept that any young person is destined to remain outside opportunity. I should have said that it also means better public transport, especially in rural areas, as my hon. Friend the Member for Hexham (Joe Morris) and my hon. Friend the Member for Derbyshire Dales (John Whitby) emphasised.

speaker: Stephen Kinnock
heading: Wales
text: I thank the right hon. Lady for that question, but again I am not sure that those on the Opposition Benches are clear about what the Budget will deliver. In addition to all the breathing space measures, which are making a clear difference to the cost of living, we have £30 million on Cardiff Parkway railway station, £2.5 million on new funding for M-Sparc, £11 million for the Aberavon bridge and £20 million to support reindustrialisation in AI sectors, and that is on top of all the work we are doing on nuclear power at Wylfa and revitalising the Welsh steel industry. With all due respect, she too should have another look at the Budget and come back when she has got her facts straight.

speaker: Fred Thomas
heading: The Prime Minister was asked—
text: Satellite capabilities and AI are essential to our security and economy, yet Britain still relies on allies and a handful of extremely expensive sovereign satellites. With advancing technologies and growing threats, these are increasingly vulnerable to disruption, no matter who we contract to deliver them. There is another way: a British-owned constellation with hundreds of cheap, commercially built satellites in low earth orbit using AI to analyse data in space. This would support our space sector, add resilience to our national security and drive growth. Combining artificial intelligence with real-time satellite data, Britain could develop its own planetary intelligence. Will the First Secretary meet me to discuss this capability?

speaker: Steve Barclay
heading: Sporting Events Bill [Lords]
text:
I rise to speak to amendments 8 and 6, on industrial action and single sex protections respectively. The point I wish to raise goes further than this specific Bill, because I think it is a perfect case study of the purpose of the Chamber. We have a Bill that, as the hon. Member for Southend East and Rochford (Mr Alaba) articulated, has broad support across the House and is not a controversial Bill. Colleagues on both sides of the House love sport and want our country to attract major sporting events to our shores, and they see sport as a force for good in unifying communities—I very much agreed with his sentiments on that point.

The Opposition have tabled two modest, reasonable and sensible amendments, one of which would simply build on the existing law and provide that if we are to use taxpayers’ money on events in the UK, they should surely comply with UK law. That is the very essence of a modest amendment. We have a consensual Bill, and the amendment simply restates the existing law and how it would apply to an international competition held in this country.

Such events are unique, by their nature—often, they are once in a generation. Indeed, the reason we have the Bill is the unique nature of the events. If they happened year in, year out, we would have a very different Bill. It concerns a rugby world cup, a football Euros, an Olympics. By their nature, they do not come around all the time. It is farcical for the Government to maintain the premise that normal industrial relations would be constrained by preventing strike action during events that are so out of the ordinary. That is not in the nature of routine industrial actions, yet that appeared to be the Government’s case in the House of Lords.

We had effective scrutiny in the House of Lords, with sensible amendments tabled, but the Government’s argument was, first, that this was not specifically in their manifesto—but we are talking about a unique set of circumstances—and, secondly, that it would somehow constrain the trade unions and normal industrial relations. But the very reason for the amendment is that strike action taking place during a global sporting event that is being held in the UK would not be business as usual. That would not be normal industrial relations; it would be a trade union trying to exploit that unique opportunity for leverage. That would not be in keeping with the spirit of the Bill.

The Bill states that it will be

“legislative provisions to be applied to major sporting events”

and will

“provide financial assistance in relation to sporting events”.

We have consensus on the Bill. The Government have a lot of support for attracting sporting events to the UK. We have had sensible suggestions from the Lords, and two modest amendments tabled by the Opposition. That is why I say it is an interesting case study of whether the Chamber is simply somewhere people come and read out a speech that someone else may have written, or has even been generated by AI, with their head down, reading it out without taking interventions. Have we ceased to be a debating Chamber? Is that really where debates in this place are going? [Interruption.] I am happy to take an intervention if the Under-Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, the hon. Member for Barnsley South (Stephanie Peacock), wishes to intervene on that point. Or will the House scrutinise legislation and make modest amendments, which would simply apply the existing law and ensure that if taxpayers’ money is used to host a sporting event, it is not hijacked by entirely separate industrial action?

Can the Government bring themselves to accept even the most modest and consensual amendment, or will anything tabled be routinely rejected? Has the ability of the House to scrutinise become so defunct that suggestions from the Lords are disregarded, and we refuse reasonable amendments to a piece of legislation on which there is broad agreement? I know it is the default position of all Governments—I have been in government—simply to reject Opposition amendments. But the amendments are extremely modest, they reflect the debates in the Lords, and I hope that Ministers will view them constructively so that the broad support for the Bill can be maintained.

speaker: Victoria Collins
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill (Carry-over Extension)
text:
The Liberal Democrats absolutely support this motion, but it is my democratic duty to highlight some things that I would love the Government to consider as we make this extension.

Let us look locally, nationally and internationally. In July, Hertfordshire county council raised its cyber-security risk to the maximum score on its register, 25 out of 25. That is exactly the kind of risk that this Bill should manage, yet the Bill excludes local authorities, even though they hold social care records on some of the most vulnerable people. Less than a fortnight ago, 32 Government services went offline while Departments patched critical flaws in widely used web software. That shows just how vulnerable the heart of our nation’s digital infrastructure and security is. On Sunday night, hackers attacked dozens of supermarket refrigerators and freezers in seven European countries, raising their temperatures to 50°C and spoiling millions of euros-worth of produce. That is the food we all rely on every single day, and the National Cyber Security Centre has warned:

“The UK’s cyber resilience is not yet where it should be.”

Our framework must not fall behind those of our closest neighbours. We should deepen co-operation with European Union agencies and member states. In a digital world, isolation only increases risk.

Those examples lay bare the crucial importance of the Bill and the devastating cost to businesses, consumers and our national security if we fail to get it right. The Bill cannot simply react to yesterday’s threats; we must ensure that our critical national infrastructure is prepared for the future, which means addressing over-reliance on high-risk foreign technology, and tackling the rapidly escalating threat of cyber-attacks powered by artificial intelligence, and on the internet of things, which is embedded in so much of what we use.

Digital sovereignty underpins everything else. We can no longer ignore the risks of over-reliance on American and Chinese technology, or rely on hostile, unpredictable states for our critical infrastructure. More than half of central Government organisations now run most of their systems on the cloud, and that all sits with just two companies, both American. The Government are the UK’s largest buyer of technology, but they almost never buy British. Since 2023, Palantir has won more than £420 million in public contracts across the national health service, the Met, the financial regulator, a city council and the Ministry of Defence. The latter’s £240 million contract was awarded without competition. Palantir is also an approved supplier on six public sector buying frameworks with a combined value of more than £9.7 billion—a route into Whitehall, the NHS, the police and our local councils.

speaker: Victoria Collins
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill (Carry-over Extension)
text:
I thank my hon. Friend for that. There is so much that highlights that this is the wrong approach from our Government, and that we need to look not only at our suppliers, but at the importance of backing British technology. We believe that a digital sovereign strategy would change things. We need to back British innovation, reduce our dependencies and make our critical systems more secure. We need to look at each level of the tech stack and have a strategy that is right for the UK. I put that proposal to this House in June through new clause 13, which received cross-party support, but the Government and the Conservatives voted it down.

Sovereignty is not about doing this alone; it is about working globally while backing British. It is about becoming and staying world leaders in technology. It is about securing high-quality digital infrastructure that embeds us in global supply chains and makes the most of our incredible talent and skills. That would give us international leverage, not isolation. The Government say that sovereignty is covered by Departments across Whitehall, and last week’s Budget put another £60 million in the sovereign AI fund, but a venture fund and a patchwork of departmental reports are not a strategy.

The new powers on high-risk vendors in clause 44 allow the Government to react once a risky supplier is already in our system, but a strategy needs to be proactive. It needs to build British capability so that we never get to that point. Even industry is calling for a strategy, so I urge the Government to bring forward their own amendments on digital sovereignty.

Secondly, amendment 107, which passed in the Lords—a Cross-Bench amendment that Liberal Democrat peers supported—requires a review within a year of Royal Assent, and every year after that, of whether the regime is working, which sectors it covers, the supply chains, the regulators and the AI Security Institute. Given the fast pace of change in cyber-security, we urge the Government to support the amendment and to look at expanding the scope to local government, which holds our electoral rolls and our social records, and to retail, because a country that cannot feed itself is not resilient. We welcome the Government’s commitment in the other place to reviewing whether all critical national infrastructure sectors should be covered by this legislation and the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018.

This week’s NCSC review warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to be used in ransomware attacks on our critical infrastructure by 2028, yet there is still no clarity on who oversees AI in our cyber-defences: a single regulator, the AI Security Institute, or another body that is exactly right for the task. Our constituents and businesses need that clarity, because where there is trust in the regulatory environment, there is investment. People need to trust the technology; that is both pro-business and pro-society.

The Government need a plan for who does what, and they need it sooner rather than later. As Europe calls for a leaders’ summit on AI, I call again on the Government to convene a global AI summit, and to look towards an international AI safety agency, headquartered in the UK and modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency, with a global treaty on pausing the development of super-intelligent AI.

Finally, none of this works unless those who are expected to deliver it can work. Small and medium-sized enterprises make up 99.8% of UK businesses and are often the most vulnerable link in the cyber-supply chains. This week’s discount on Cyber Essentials certification is welcome—the Liberal Democrats called for that—but it is time-limited; it ends in March, and the certificate must be renewed every year. Even the NCSC calls it only a starting point. SMEs need real support from a cyber-security support service when they are hit, to give them clear guidance.

On Second Reading, I compared this Bill to a house with stronger fences and a better alarm, but with its back door left wide open. The past few days alone have shown us why closing that door matters. I urge the Government to consider our amendments, for the communities and councils who rely on critical infrastructure, for the businesses integrated into every supply chain, and for every family who expect the services that they rely on to be there when they need them. We support the carry-over motion.

speaker: Christopher Vince
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill (Carry-over Extension)
text: Madam Deputy Speaker, you missed out on me making a very long speech, so you are very lucky. Will the Minister briefly touch on what liability there will be for frontier model providers, such as OpenAI, who breach their duties, for example I am thinking of the Hugging Face incident in July 2026?

speaker: Ian Murray
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill (Carry-over Extension)
text:
My hon. Friend from Harlow—I am surprised he did not mention Harlow in his contribution, so I thought I had better put it on the record or otherwise he will be struck out—makes a good point. However, we can also see that AI provides a good solution to this problem. Because of the PHP incidents in the past few weeks, we have identified that there were holes in that particular system and then those holes were patched and plugged, so while AI is a big cyber-security problem, it is also a big part of the solution. This Bill is here to give us better cyber-security and better resilience across all our economy.

Question put and agreed to.

speaker: Zarah Sultana
heading: Petition - Coventry City Council contract with Palantir Technologies
text:
I rise to present a petition on behalf of residents of Coventry South regarding Coventry city council’s contract with Palantir. More than 3,900 people have signed a related online petition. In September 2025, Coventry city council awarded Palantir a contract worth £500,000 to provide AI-related services in children’s services. The contract was renewed in February 2026 at a cost of £750,000, a 50% increase, bringing the total to £1.25 million.

There are serious concerns about Palantir’s involvement in military and immigration operations, including providing surveillance infrastructure to the Israeli Government, which are committing genocide in Palestine, as well as the handling of sensitive personal data and the growing privatisation of our public services. The petitioners therefore request that the House of Commons urge the Government to call on Coventry city council to terminate its contract with Palantir, to consult residents and trade unions and to ensure transparency, accountability and democratic public control over the use of data in our public services.

Following is the full text of the petition:

[The petition of residents of the constituency Coventry South,

Declares that Coventry City Council has renewed a £750,000 contract with the US firm Palantir for children’s services; further declares that there are serious concerns about Palantir’s involvement in military and immigration operations, including its provision of data surveillance infrastructure to the Israeli government, which is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, the handling of sensitive personal data, and the increasing role of private technology companies in public services; and further declares that Coventry residents, council staff and recognised trade unions should have a meaningful say in decisions concerning the use of AI and data in local public services before a contract is agreed and renewed.

The petitioners therefore request that the House of Commons urge the Government to call on Coventry City Council to terminate its contract with Palantir; consult residents and recognised trade unions on future AI and data decisions; and ensure transparency, accountability and democratic public control over the use of data in Coventry’s public services.

And the petitioners remain, etc.]

[P003257]

speaker: Lord Mann
heading: House of Lords: Relevance - Question
text: We know what we are, but we know not what we may be. AI will usurp the revising Chamber; that much is obvious. Is our future to be merely the hallucinators? The hereditaries flew their perch with barely a murmur, but what of us? Will we waltz into oblivion or quickstep into a brave new world?

speaker: Baroness Twycross
heading: House of Lords: Relevance - Question
text: Of all the questions I thought my noble friend would come up with as a supplementary, I was not anticipating one on AI. I am not convinced by my noble friend’s arguments about AI. Clearly, AI will have a wide range of purposes and will enable us to do our jobs better in so many ways. However, I believe that, with a modernised House of Lords, we will continue to have a purpose for many years.

speaker: Lord Shamash
heading: Representation of the People Bill - Committee (2nd Day)
text:
My Lords, it is a pleasure to follow my noble friend Lord Hayward. I woke up this morning thinking that I would love to quote Martin Luther King—that I had a dream. I will give a tiny bit of history. The Representation of the People Act 1983 is the core legislation that everything has sprung from. It was 18 years from 1983 to the creation in 2001 of the Electoral Commission, in which I, and maybe others here, was involved. It is now 43 years since the 1983 Act came into being, and there have been repeated amendments and additions: the Electoral Administration Act, the Elections Act, and so on. We are getting to the point where, to move election law, you need a pick-up truck. It is completely crackers that we are in this situation.

The most important thing, as mentioned by my noble friend Lord Hayward, is consolidation. I have discussed the possibility of that with others, including my noble friend the Minister, and it is a major undertaking. But there is a new kid on the block, and that is AI. We must get to a situation where we can do this, because it is impossible to operate. I should have declared my interest as a former election lawyer to the Labour Party for many years. Having to deal with this legislation is very difficult, and you can miss things out very easily. My plea to the Minister is to take this idea away to the officials, so that my dream can actually come true and we can have a bit of consolidation in this Act.

speaker: Lord Fuller
heading: Representation of the People Bill - Committee (2nd Day)
text:
My Lords, I support the comments made by my noble friend Lord Hayward and by the noble Lord, Lord Shamash. We have heard in the debate so far that we need a consolidation. The points made by the noble Lord, Lord Shamash, are very persuasive. Not only do we not have consolidation but the Bill contains all sorts of contradictory provisions and inconsistencies. I cannot wait to see what the government amendments will be—I am sure there will be several groups of them.

Almost impossible duties are being placed on electoral registration staff and returning officers to make quite detailed judgments without the benefit of documentary evidence. A lot of it has not been thought through. My main point, however, is that, as complicated as the situation is today, so much is still to be done through secondary legislation, for goodness’ sake. There is a fundamental conflict of interest in asking Ministers to change the legislation, on the basis upon which they themselves are elected, to suit themselves without Parliament scrutinising the detail.

I do not deny that secondary legislation has a role in all walks of life and in a lot of the work that your Lordships’ House considers. On democracy, which is the foundation of our society, the law should be clear in primary legislation, not with so much left for Ministers to set; otherwise, it is not just that the Government have a lack of trust in us but, in turn, the voters have a lack of trust in Parliament, which cannot be trusted to sort it out, be clear and make the electors’ voices heard. If there is a lack of trust there, democracy is imperilled.

I strongly support my noble friend and the noble Lord, Lord Shamash, in their claim that we should bring this together. The Bill, thick though it is, fails to address the fundamental problem, especially in a world of AI and the complexity of the electoral system, which I will not dwell upon again. I strongly support my noble friend.

speaker: Lord Hayward
heading: Representation of the People Bill - Committee (2nd Day)
text:
