I have heard some interesting comments from the Minister and, as I indicated just now, I appreciate her offer to have further conversations in relation to the specific matters. I think we all knew that, on the question of consolidation, sadly, we are going to have to live with Encyclopaedia Britannica, whether it is on AI or any other system, for the future. It is grotesquely challenging for everybody who is involved. However, on that basis, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.

Amendment 13 withdrawn.

Amendment 14 not moved.

Clause 7 agreed.

Clause 8: Exceptions from prohibitions on disclosure

Amendment 15 not moved.

Clause 8 agreed.

Clauses 9 to 13 agreed.

Clause 14: Interpretation of sections 7 to 13

Amendments 16 and 17 not moved.

Clause 14 agreed.

speaker: Anna Sabine
subheading: Violence against Women and Girls: Smart Glasses — [Pete Wishart in the Chair]
text:
I beg to move,

That this House has considered smart glasses and violence against women and girls.

A few months ago I was delighted, with the support of many women in the urban design industry and the Minister for Housing and Planning, to get women and girls mentioned in the national planning policy framework. Across the UK, 86% of women and girls aged 18 to 24 have experienced harassment in public spaces, and it seemed crazy to me that they were not going to be at the forefront of how we design those spaces and places.

Having won that victory just before the summer, I was horrified to see stories about AI glasses appearing all over the press. Adverts for smart glasses appeared across London. Online, celebrities sold them as a device to “stay in the moment” and enjoy “effortless connection”. A key selling point was that the glasses could be used to film discreetly. To me, that did not look like a fantastic new innovation; it looked like a device for filming women and girls without their knowledge in the very spaces we have been campaigning to make them feel welcome in. Planning policy had finally accepted that women’s safety matters in the spaces we build, but at the same moment technology was eroding women’s privacy and safety in those same spaces.

Sales of smart glasses are now soaring, and already my fears about their use are being realised. Women are reporting waking up after nights out to find that videos of them, filmed without their knowledge or consent by men wearing smart glasses, have gone viral online. The only indication anyone has that they are being filmed is a small LED in the corner of the glasses, but that is quickly disappearing, with “ghost Meta” shops offering to remove the light entirely so that no one in a public space knows they are being filmed. To me these devices not only have the potential to erode safety and privacy in public spaces, but raise really important questions about consent.

A few weeks ago, I met the campaign group Stop Smart Glasses. One of its campaigners is a secondary school teacher, and he told me that as part of his job he stands in front of teenagers and teaches them that consent must be sought proactively—that yes means yes and no means no. But increasingly those same children go home, pick up their phones and scroll on social media, where they see videos of girls who were filmed without even being asked or knowing. He pointed out the irony that if one of his female students is filmed by AI glasses in public, the onus is on her to approach the man doing the filming and ask him to stop. What are we teaching young people—that consent is something we learn in the classroom and abandon on the street?

Covert filming is not new, and my hon. Friend the Member for Bath (Wera Hobhouse) has done excellent work on tackling the problem in nightclubs and other public spaces, but smart glasses make it easier, and harder to detect and challenge. In Australia, one solution has been to ban the use of smart glasses in certain areas, such as swimming pools, but I feel that sends a message to women that they are safe only in certain places. Surely, we do not want that to become the case.

Waking up to a video of yourself online undermines perceptions of safety, but it is also a breach of privacy and raises real data protection concerns. According to Meta’s smart glasses terms of use, content captured by the glasses can be used to train Meta AI. The burden of consent allowing Meta to do that is placed on the person wearing the glasses. That means that if someone is filmed without their knowledge or permission, Meta can still use that content to train its AI, because the wearer has given de facto consent. I do not see how that squares with data protection law. GDPR says that companies need a proper reason to use our personal data, and an individual walking past someone wearing smart glasses in the street has not agreed to anything. Small discreet cameras make secret filming easier, and women and girls will be disproportionately impacted by that. More broadly, in the age of wearable tech, all of us, male or female, are losing a bit of our privacy every time we step outside. Despite that, I have heard nothing from the Government about how smart glasses should be regulated.

When I raise this topic in public, one main argument comes back as a justification for smart glasses: they provide huge benefits for people with accessibility requirements, including blind and partially sighted people. I completely understand that point of view. I met the Royal National Institute of Blind People a few weeks ago to hear from it directly. It was very clear that although technology can offer huge benefits to its community, it does not want to become a fig leaf for Meta to justify poor practice and surveillance technology, and that its members have the same concerns about the technology as everyone else. Furthermore, Meta glasses have not been made with blind people in mind. If they had, they would be vastly better at accommodating the range of needs that those with disabilities might have.

These glasses pose a threat to everyone’s safety and privacy in public spaces. Meta and other developers are breaching everyone’s right to privacy, while failing to be transparent about what they are doing with the data they have collected. As in so many other areas of life, this modern technology will undoubtedly have a heightened impact on violence against women and girls.

On Monday, I sat in this room for a debate on the social media ban, and it struck me how long all Governments of whatever flavour have put off acting on social media, even though the evidence of harm has been there for years. I do not want smart glasses to go the same way, where we only regulate once it is too late. We are only 50 days from Christmas, and we can expect these glasses to be sold everywhere in numbers. How can we put the genie back in the bottle once they are being worn everywhere? We have called for them to be banned on the parliamentary estate, but frankly, everyone deserves the same privacy that we should enjoy in this place.

I look forward to the debate, and I am thankful to everyone who has attended. I hope to hear from Members across the House who are concerned about the use of smart glasses and from the Minister, to understand what the Government intend to do about this potentially dangerous new technology.

speaker: Shivani Raja
subheading: Violence against Women and Girls: Smart Glasses — [Pete Wishart in the Chair]
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Mr Wishart. I thank the hon. Member for Frome and East Somerset (Anna Sabine) for securing this debate and for her remarks, which summarised the concerns and challenges around this important topic very clearly.

This debate comes at an important time. We live in a time of rapid technological advancement, which is exciting but also must be safeguarded. We have seen how these developments can threaten the safety of our women and girls with deepfake videos, stalking and monitoring devices, and wearable tech such as smart glasses. The hands-free technology of smart glasses promises crucial assistance to visually impaired people across the country, but the promise must be backed up with the right precautions and protections. We should not restrict law-abiding citizens from using this technology where it causes no harm to others. Our responsibility is to ensure that the innovations do not outpace the very protections that keep our women and girls safe in public spaces.

Unlike smartphones, which are clear and visible when in use, camera-enabled smart glasses allow covert recording to take place at eye level, completely disguised as regular human eye-to-eye contact. For many women who are already navigating public spaces with extra vigilance, that creates real unease. Ministers have rightly set out that recording individuals without consent in order to cause alarm or distress or for sexual gratification falls under existing criminal offences such as harassment and voyeurism. The legal position is clear: anyone who misuses this technology to intimidate or harass women must feel the full force of the law.

The real issue, however, is enforcement. Proving intent when someone is covertly filmed on a bus or a high street is incredibly difficult, and once that footage hits the internet, the damage to a victim’s privacy and dignity is already done. Expecting victims to rely on post-hoc takedown requests under GDPR or the Online Safety Act 2023 places the burden entirely on the wrong shoulders.

speaker: Shockat Adam
subheading: Violence against Women and Girls: Smart Glasses — [Pete Wishart in the Chair]
text:
I absolutely agree. We must ensure that they are tamper-proof. Somebody will always create something to supersede technology, which I will come to. A woman cannot move away from a camera if she cannot see it.

I also want to consider what these glasses could do in school changing rooms. We know children can be cruel. It could be devastating to record a child—girl or boy—in their insecure period, upload the footage and threaten them with blackmail.

Harm does not stop at the wearer. It was reported earlier this year that workers paid to label footage for AI training were viewing intimate recordings captured by these devices, including people using the toilet. The people in the footage had not consented and were not aware that it was being used for training purposes.

The National Centre for Violence Against Women and Girls and Public Protection told us last month that at least one in five flagged online VAWG crimes are image-based abuse, with almost 75% of the victims being female. Every digital form of this abuse is rising, yet when we ask how many arrests have been made for covert filming, the answer is that the information is not held centrally, so we are legislating in the dark. I would like a response from the Minister on that point.

This abuse is not restricted to cameras, because hearing technology is now arriving in spectacle frames. Hearing glasses with directional microphones are already in our practices, and the patients starting to lose their hearing are often the same patients who are fitted with varifocal glasses. Again, I welcome that because live captions, conversation boosting and real-time translations are incredible. I tried the technology and even though I was in a noisy room, it did not just help me hear the conversation I was having—I was able to hear somebody else’s conversation on the other side of the table. If we take all that into account, we have facial recognition, which manufacturers are reportedly exploring, and a device that can know who we are, where we are and what we say without us even knowing it is there. The wearer knows they are using the device; people around them do not.

What is the law doing about that? Filming in public is generally lawful and data protection laws do not apply to individuals acting in a personal capacity, but the Information Commissioner has said that doxxing is largely outside their remit, wearables are not regulated in any particular category and the Government’s own violence against women and girls strategy does not mention smart glasses. As Doughty Street Chambers put it,

“English law was not written with this technology in mind”.

The industry already knows what is good. At this year’s 100% Optical, EssilorLuxottica, which makes the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, told practitioners that devices should show people nearby that they are in use, that encryption is

“not nice to have, but an absolute must”,

and that only necessary data should be collected.

speaker: Jim Shannon
subheading: Violence against Women and Girls: Smart Glasses — [Pete Wishart in the Chair]
text:
Half an hour; I was hoping it might be 28 minutes. I am not going to speak for 28 minutes; I will try to keep my contribution as succinct and focused as possible.

It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Mr Wishart and I thank the hon. Member for Frome and East Somerset (Anna Sabine) for setting the scene incredibly well. This subject has to be discussed and highlighted, and the debate has given us the opportunity to do that.

This matter strikes at the very heart of the safety, dignity and privacy of our citizens, and most notably the protection of women and girls in our communities. We stand at a crossroads where technological innovation is outpacing our moral and legal safeguards. If we do not act, the consequences will continue to be felt by the most vulnerable on our streets. Other Members have made that point incredibly clear and I thank them for that.

Let us look first at the scale of what we are dealing with. We are not talking about a niche gadget or a far-off futuristic concept as some may think. The figures are stark. It is estimated that hundreds of thousands of these smart glasses have already been sold right here in the United Kingdom. They are flooding the market, and they are sitting on the faces of everyday passers-by—people we do not know. Although many people wear them innocently, we cannot blind ourselves to the reality that these devices are a powerful tool of surveillance, masquerading as ordinary eyewear.

As we rightly focus our efforts on eradicating violence against women and girls, we must recognise how this technology changes the very nature of harassment, stalking and intimidation. That is not just my observation; the UK’s leading domestic abuse charities are also sounding the alarm, and they are clear in what they say. Refuge has given the example of perpetrators weaponising these gadgets to covertly track and film survivors—the hon. Member for West Dorset (Edward Morello) clearly illustrated that—which has contributed to a horrifying 62% spike in tech-facilitated abuse. Furthermore, Women’s Aid has forcefully stated that pairing these glasses with AI facial recognition threatens the very safety of all women and girls and hands a digital toolkit to stalkers who want to identify and track strangers in real time without their knowledge.

For a woman walking down the street, the fear of being targeted is already a daily reality, but now the horror of upskirting is being magnified by technology that is completely hands-free and virtually invisible. A person could commit an act of visual violation without ever holding a phone, leaving the victim entirely unaware that her privacy, her dignity and her body have been captured and digitised.

speaker: Blake Stephenson
subheading: Violence against Women and Girls: Smart Glasses — [Pete Wishart in the Chair]
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Mr Wishart. I congratulate the hon. Member for Frome and East Somerset (Anna Sabine) on securing this very important debate, and I thank hon. Members from across the House for their very thoughtful contributions. Counterpoint Research estimates that global sales of AI glasses rose by 263% in the first half of 2026, and the market is predicted to reach $44 billion by 2032—like other hon. Members, I expect the stockings this Christmas to be filled with AI glasses. It is essential that we examine how to keep women and girls safe as this market expands.

Technological innovations are too often accompanied by consequences that harm people, including women and girls. As a catalyst, technology can take the worst behaviour that already exists in our society and accelerate it, whether it is the pervasive use of early cameras, which resulted in the exploitation of women and young girls in a way that we look back on in horror, or the explosion of the internet and smartphones, which created a new range of problems that I know the Minister and others are trying to combat, day in, day out.

There are, of course, design issues with these smart glasses—we have heard about some of those today—but that does not mean that the technology itself was designed to cause harm. Rather, the problems arise from how it is used and exploited by those with the worst motivations in our society. That is why it is important to recognise that smart glasses are part of that wider pattern and present acute problems that impact women and girls. There have been numerous stories, some of which we have heard today, that illustrate the need to ensure that these glasses are not being used to harass women and girls in our country.

speaker: Blake Stephenson
subheading: Violence against Women and Girls: Smart Glasses — [Pete Wishart in the Chair]
text:
I think the hon. Member is saying that in anything that they do, the Government need to strike the right balance, because there are perfectly legitimate uses for these glasses that are useful to society, but of course there are harms. The hon. Member for Rugby (John Slinger) also talked about some of the cultural issues and problems and the education that is needed, particularly for young boys. I hope that the Government will be looking to strike the right balance.

Covert filming and online harassment of women are real harms that deserve a serious response. It is particularly concerning that people have used these glasses to record young women without their knowledge, and then used that footage for their own benefit, including commercial benefit. That is an absolutely despicable violation, and it should not be tolerated. The hon. Member for Chelmsford (Marie Goldman) referred to it as “monetised misogyny”, and I agree with her entirely, so there is cross-party agreement on this issue.

Refuge has reported that referrals to its specialist technology-facilitated abuse and economic empowerment team rose by more than 62% in 2025. The Science and Technology Committee has launched a call for evidence on technology-facilitated abuse. I hope that the Committee will use this important opportunity to help us all understand the prevalence of abuse in our society.

It is important to recognise that this issue is complicated by UK laws on filming. As hon. Members will be aware, it is not inherently unlawful to take photos or videos of people in public without their permission, but it can, of course, cross over into criminality. That is why the Home Office worryingly released a poster warning illegal immigrants about the legality of recording people without their permission. The fact that such a poster needed to be produced by Government in the first place is difficult for many to comprehend. The criticism it received from the National Union of Journalists illustrates the challenge of balancing protecting existing rights with stopping the unscrupulous use of technology.

That makes it all the more necessary to examine the issue and work closely with companies to ensure that new technology does not increase the prevalence of crimes against women and girls. In 2019, Parliament considered the disgusting practice of upskirting and passed the Voyeurism (Offences) Act, which created targeted offences related to upskirting. That provides a useful example of Parliament addressing a particular harmful act without outlawing everyday cameras.

If changes to legislation are necessary, they must be based on evidence, and we must ensure that we create the best policies we can. I would therefore appreciate the Minister setting out what evidence the Government are gathering on the prevalence of covert filming with smart glasses, its harms and the effectiveness of existing safeguards. We must be able to recognise the public’s concern when they see people using these glasses, while also distinguishing between their wrongful use and their use for genuinely important reasons, as the hon. Member for Strangford (Jim Shannon) said.

I understand that the Norwegian Government recently announced their intention to restrict the use of these devices in specific locations. To the point of the hon. Member for Chelmsford, women and girls should be safe everywhere, but it is important that any action here supports clear policies for genuinely sensitive environments, such as changing rooms, schools and clinical settings. There are existing laws that cover some of those matters, but we must be explicit about how we keep people safe in those environments. If we do not, we undermine those who seek to use this technology to truly improve people’s lives.

One example, as we heard already this morning, comes from the Royal National Institute of Blind People. It has recognised concerns, as reflected on by the hon. Member for Frome and East Somerset, but has also commented on how some blind and partially sighted people use smart glasses to benefit from enhanced access to information. Paul Arnold, the chief executive of the Information Commissioner’s Office, spoke about his experience using these glasses as a severely visually impaired person. The combination of AI and audio feedback has helped him to better understand his surroundings, access information and navigate the world with greater confidence.

This technology may also help those suffering from other serious health conditions. CrossSense, which makes AI smart glasses, recently beat 174 other inventions from around the world to win the prestigious £1 million Longitude prize on dementia. Furthermore, it is easy to see the uses for journalists working in the public interest, or the potential long-term benefits if the police could use the technology in a similar way to body-worn cameras or use facial recognition technology, an effective tool for identifying and catching criminals who commit violence against women and girls. I do not seek to downplay the risks posed by these devices with those examples, but rather to encourage the Government to consider those beneficial uses before introducing any blanket bans.

I recognise that the Minister’s Department is committed to the violence against women and girls action plan and to working across Government to encourage safety by design in smart and connected technology, which was mentioned earlier by the hon. Member for Rugby. There are concerns about delivery, however, and my hon. Friend the Member for Leicester East (Shivani Raja) raised concerns about missed deadlines in the development of the plan. As Dame Nicole Jacobs told the Home Affairs Committee last week,

“I do not believe that, to date, this strategy has been implemented in a way that shows that it is at the top of the priority list, in terms of resource and all those things.”

Can the Minister set out what measurable progress has been made on that commitment? Presumably, it involved the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology—a Department that no longer exists given recent changes at the top.

To conclude, all too often we have seen new technology used in a manner that puts women and girls at risk. I hope that we can find proportionate, sensitive and sensible policies that enable the continued use of that technology, while ensuring that we can prevent it from being used to facilitate the abuse and exploitation that we have seen throughout our society.

speaker: Satvir Kaur
subheading: Violence against Women and Girls: Smart Glasses — [Pete Wishart in the Chair]
text:
I do, although I would add that tech companies are very clever, and while they may not intend harm, they absolutely should feel their responsibility when producing and designing these products to safeguard women and girls. I know the shadow Minister and I agree on that.

I was asked directly about this, so let me be clear: sharing or threatening to share an intimate image without consent is a criminal offence. That includes creating or requesting the creation of deepfake intimate images of adults without consent. The Crime and Policing Act 2026 strengthens those offences further.

speaker: Baroness Finlay of Llandaff
heading: Health Bill - Committee (3rd Day)
text:
My Lords, I have two amendments in this group, and I am grateful to the noble Baroness, Lady Pidgeon, for having referred to one of them.

My Amendments 247 and 250 would address genomics and radiotherapy, because there are fundamental weaknesses in how diagnostic genomic services and radiotherapy treatment services are planned and improved across England. In both areas, rapid advances are altering survival and avoiding toxicity from poorly planned treatments. Current international comparisons by the OECD place the UK 31st out of 43 countries for five-year lung cancer survival and 26th for colon cancer survival. Overall cancer mortality data place the UK 26th out of 36 countries. Following on from the questions from the noble Baroness, Lady Pidgeon, I ask the Minister two specific questions. First, why is the UK no longer submitting information to the OECD on cancers? Secondly, will we be renegotiating for our cancer research to become part of the EU4Health programme again?

Diagnostic delays and inadequate radiotherapy services are largely responsible for our poorer outcomes. In cancer genomics, only 3% of pathologists are always meeting the 14-day national target for lung cancer genomic testing. Pathology personnel shortages are particularly severe in genomics and genetics, causing delays, which are compounded by high sample volume workload, administrative inefficiencies, delays in sample processing, and outsourcing, as well as inadequate equipment.

Recently, almost half of healthcare professionals had to start urgent treatment before biomarkers were available. Around 1,000 cancers are diagnosed a day, but delays compromise timely treatment decisions, patient safety, access to targeted therapies and eligibility for time-sensitive clinical trials, while precious time is wasted by fragmented reporting pathways, poor IT interoperability and outdated laboratory information management systems, or LIMS.

Yet genomics is one of the major strategic transformational priorities for the NHS to improve cancer outcomes. Innovation in genomics is advancing very rapidly, and AI advances in analysing and interpreting large-scale sequencing data need digital infrastructure. Although many local pathology laboratories can deliver results within clinically useful timeframes, whole-genome sequencing at genomic laboratory hubs becomes essential for complex cases and inherited cancer syndromes. In addition, it supports research and new biomarker assay development when integrated with tissue pathology and imaging.

The NHS workforce plan, which we have already discussed, must consider training and workforce development in genomics and genetics, cellular pathology, clinical biochemistry, and molecular pathology; otherwise, a bottleneck in cancer and precision medicine pathways will continue to compromise cancer diagnosis and will eventually leave us with even worse outcomes.

Radiotherapy is crucial for cancer treatment. It is the second most widely used cancer treatment. It is needed by half of cancer patients and is key to 40% of cancer cures, and there is also palliative radiotherapy. Yet radiotherapy has the worst waiting times of the main cancer treatments, with significant inequalities in access. The latest NHS figures show that wait times for radiotherapy are far worse than for surgery or cancer drug treatments. Only 42% of patients receive their first radiotherapy treatment within 62 days. In some ICBs, this is as low as 10%, so only one in 10 patients receives their treatment on time—far away from the target of 85%.

Delays to radiotherapy are worse in the east of England, the Midlands and the north-east. Delays jeopardise survival. For some cancers, every four-week delay in treatment, as we have heard, brings a 10% increase in the risk of death. That is very serious. Government data shows that access to radiotherapy among lung cancer patients was as low as 11% in some areas. As the noble Baroness, Lady Pidgeon, said, the UK has only five radiotherapy linear accelerators per million people, compared with more than seven in France, Italy, and the Netherlands. International estimates suggest that 53% of cancer patients could benefit from radiotherapy, yet in England only 35% received it as part of their primary treatment.

Improving this requires a new approach. I, like everyone, welcome the national cancer plan, but a previous error in it highlights the need for this amendment. The cancer plan claimed that 28 replacement radiotherapy machines would enable an additional 27,500 patients to be treated annually, but the now corrected figure is for 27,500 treatments, not patients. Patients can receive dozens of treatments, so this could be a tenfold overestimate in capacity increase. It shows why radiotherapy expertise must be involved in policy, particularly horizon scanning advanced technology.

Radiotherapy services do not map neatly within ICB boundaries and operate within in the wider operational delivery networks. Most ICBs have no named lead, having only one or two radiotherapy centres in their area. So the ICBs lack the necessary specialist knowledge. Secretary of State support to ICBs would improve access to modern techniques, including stereotactic radiotherapy and proton beam therapy. The financial case is compelling.

Radiotherapy is our most cost-effective curative cancer treatment. A curative course costs around £3,000 to £7,000, and palliative treatment is a few hundred pounds. It accounts for just 7% of cancer expenditure in England, despite being second to surgery for cure rates. Radiotherapy investment makes clinical and economic sense for the treatment of cancer patients. We must improve. I suggest that these amendments are practical, complementary to the Government’s cancer plan, and essential.

speaker: Lord Patel
heading: Health Bill - Committee (3rd Day)
text:
My Lords, I have put my name to several of these amendments. Much has been said already, so I will try to be brief. I will focus on two or three main things. One is where the developments are likely to lead us, which will complicate the issues even more than what we are talking about today.

Let me come to cancer outcomes first. It has rightly been pointed out where England stands internationally in terms of cancer outcomes. Cancer outcomes are the ultimate truth: the truth in terms of one-year and five-year survival rates of any cancer. They are often what we use for international comparisons, but there is a system-wide reflection to be had. Poor survival outcomes are, often, a failure of several other processes, including when the diagnosis was made, the aggressive nature of the tumour—the later it is identified, the more aggressive it is likely to be—and whether the treatment was given at the right time. As was mentioned, delayed treatment increases the risk of mortality.

Although the outcome, survival-wise, is an important parameter, there are other issues that need to be considered when assessing cancer outcomes, and they often relate to the processes. The balance metrics of measuring cancer outcomes may well include process indicators; operational timelines, in terms of how many days’ treatment the patient has; patient-centred outcomes, which are not often mentioned; and risk-adjusted clinical outcomes, based on the nature of the cancer. The core outcomes that are reported should include not only survival rates, but mortality rates, stage of diagnosis and operational and access metrics. The purpose of reporting—that is the important part for commissioning issues—is that accountability be taken into consideration. It should hold regional health services and Governments responsible for funding allocations and clinical performance, highlighting the gaps, and guiding policies and clinical improvements. Unless we have these measurements of outcomes, measuring survival rates only will not be enough.

I will briefly mention genomics and radiotherapy. On radiotherapy, I get a daily, or sometimes weekly, bulletin from a medical oncology consultant whom I know extremely well; I will not name her. The important point has already been mentioned: it is not that we do not have the expertise in clinical capabilities, as Cancer Research UK has mentioned in its report; it is that bottlenecks occur in the processes afterwards. The surgery might be good, but there are bottlenecks in other forms of treatment. On radiotherapy, we have already mentioned the unmet needs, waiting times, regional disparities and workforce and equipment pressures. They will multiply with the advances that are coming in radiotherapy, which not all centres in England have implemented. It is good that NHS England announced a major rollout of stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, which reduced treatments for prostate cancers, for instance, from 20 to five. However, only a few centres now use advanced technology and AI together to further assist the planning of radiotherapy treatments, which can sometimes take days.

There are developments occurring in radiotherapy that will put further pressures on patient access. With FLASH radiotherapy, for instance, radiotherapy is given in a concentrated way in a millisecond—not minutes, not hours, not days, but in a millisecond. Through biologically guided radiotherapy, integrated PET scanners, mentioned by the noble Baroness, Lady Finlay, are combined with linear accelerator scanners. They can immediately diagnose the nature of the cancer and deliver the appropriate therapy on the spot. Through generative AI adoption, AI is used while the patient is on the treatment table to identify the nature of the tumour and whether it can take higher-dose radiotherapy. There is also radiogenomics, whereby personalised genomics are associated with the behaviour of the tissue and the machine can decide whether it can give a higher dosage at a concentrated level. All these developments will put further pressure on our capacity to deliver to cancer patients, which needs to be addressed.

There are lots of issues to be addressed but, finally and briefly, the Science and Technology Committee is about to produce a report on AI, genomics and personalised medicine, which identifies the role of genomics not only in cancer but in other areas too. Cancer, in particular, will require the rapid genomic analysis that the noble Baroness, Lady Finlay, mentioned. It is good that NHS England established seven genetic hubs that now do mutation screening and genomic screening, looking at the mutations in each and every cancer to see whether it will react to a particular treatment or not. They are building up a library, and it is important to continue building that library.

Importantly, the only way to develop personalised medicine vaccines for delivery to individual patients is to do the genomics mutation study as rapidly as we can. The cancer genomics 10-year plan has identified all the issues, but it has not identified a way forward for implementation. This debate has emphasised that we need to know how we are going to deal with all the developments, deliver the cancer treatments and improve outcomes globally.

speaker: Sarah Sackman
heading: Justice
text: I am proud of the work the Labour Government have done in introducing a once-in-a-generation piece of legislation increasing workers’ rights, but we must ensure that those rights are capable of enforcement. The backlogs in the employment tribunal are ones that I recognise, which is why reform will be necessary and why we are increasing capacity with additional judicial recruitment. We are also seeing additional challenges through the pressures that AI is bringing. Our response needs to be up to the task by ensuring that we introduce our own uses of responsible AI to meet that challenge.

speaker: Mike Martin
heading: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
text:
We on the Liberal Democrat Benches broadly support the Bill. Modernising a framework that has grown complex over decades is sensible and there is much here to welcome, from wider credit union membership to protecting in-person banking and tougher defences against financial crime.

I want to use my brief time to talk about a missed opportunity, and I hope the Government will take me up on it. It relates to the Chancellor’s former job. The Government rightly want to rebuild our defence industry, and small firms are one of the bedrocks of that goal. With the way that warfare is accelerating, the cutting, bleeding edge is with small tech firms innovating in things such as AI and autonomy. The Ministry of Defence works with around 12,000 small and medium-sized enterprises through its supply chains, and spends about £5 billion a year with them. It is further set out in the defence investment plan and the strategic defence review that the MOD wants to spend a further £2.5 billion with SMEs by the summer of 2028. That is where defence is moving—if we want to win wars in the modern age, we have to have a robust defence SME sector,

Every small business, no matter what sector it is in, knows how hard it can be to raise finance, but many defence firms face an extra barrier. They are often refused bank accounts, loans or insurance simply because they work in the defence sector. SC Group—formerly Supacat—has won MOD contracts worth tens of millions of pounds, yet it has struggled to get investment or loans because it is not seen as acceptable. Another example is 4GD, which uses AI and robotics to run training simulators for British soldiers; the company stopped attending investment meetings and was actually turned away from one once the host found out it was a defence firm.

A couple of years ago, 15 SME defence firms formally raised the issue with their trade body, ADS, as they had actually had accounts closed by UK financial institutions. Obviously, those were just the firms that were willing to speak up; there are plenty that will have suffered adverse reactions when seeking credit but have chosen not to speak out—because what firm wants to advertise that they are unable to get capital or credit? The crucial point is that this is not because of regulation. In March 2025, the FCA stated very plainly that:

“There is nothing in our rules, including those related to sustainability, that prevents investment or finance for defence companies.”

The problem is that many investment and financial services firms have environmental, social and governance policies that explicitly name defence firms as being unacceptable for investment. The Government know that, because in the MOD’s SME action plan, which was published in July, they commit to working with everyone, from venture capital to high street banks, to make it easier for the financial sector to back defence SMEs. But there is a difference between knowing about a problem and setting out a robust way of fixing it, and that is what I want to focus on.

The Bill started in the House of Lords, where my noble Friend Baroness Kramer tabled amendment 67, which proposed a practical step that might go some way towards solving the problem. The amendment essentially required the Financial Conduct Authority to review how easily SMEs in sectors critical to our national security can get finance. More specifically, that review would examine the availability and cost of finance for defence firms, whether the FCA’s rules create barriers, whether lenders’ ESG policies, sector exclusions or risk assessments are shutting defence firms out, and whether defence SMEs find it materially harder to get finance than firms in other industries. Crucially, the review would finish with the changes that should be made to improve access to finance for defence SMEs—it should speak to the problems identified in the review.

When my noble Friend Baroness Kramer presented the amendment, among a package of others, the Government declined, saying that the framework was already proportionate to SMEs. I think something has been lost in translation there. Proportionality is not the issue; the FCA has told us that its rules are not the barrier. The question is about what regulated investment firms are actually doing. At the moment, nobody is monitoring that, but amendment 67 sought to do so, by mandating the FCA to carry out a review on a regular basis—once every two or three years.

I urge the Government and the Economic Secretary to use the Bill to honour the commitment made by other parts of Government to support SMEs—including defence SMEs—to have access to finance on a level playing field with other sectors. This is not a party political issue: in March 2025, more than 100 Labour MPs and peers wrote to banks and investors about exactly this problem, and it has also been raised on the Conservative Benches. On Report, pursuant to any conversations that the Minister might like to have with me, I intend to re-table the same amendment and seek cross-party support. I am pretty sure there will be robust support across the House. I would welcome the chance to meet with the Minister to discuss the issue, because I think we have an opportunity to strengthen the Bill as it goes forward.

speaker: Gareth Davies
heading: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
text:
It is a great pleasure to close this debate on behalf of the official Opposition, and to follow on from my very good friend, the shadow Economic Secretary—my hon. Friend the Member for Wyre Forest (Mark Garnier)—who has done excellent work both in this Chamber and behind the scenes to engage extensively with the industry. Indeed, I am sure there is not a lunch table in the City of London that has not been graced by my hon. Friend—all, of course, in the service of his great country.

I draw the House’s attention to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, particularly my long career in asset management, my active involvement in the industry going back many years, and my current chairmanship of the APPG for blockchain, which is relevant to this Bill.

It has been a privilege to be joined by many Members from across the House who clearly have extensive industry experience. I firmly believe, as I have for a long time, that we need more people in Parliament who have worked specifically in this sector, and who understand its importance and its power to help and influence our economy and our communities.

I thank all Members from across the House for their contributions to the debate, but I will name a few in particular. The Chairman of the Treasury Committee, the hon. Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier) who is not currently in her place, provided a typically detailed and very thoughtful contribution. She expressed concerns about whether the pendulum is swinging away from consumer protection, as well as outlining her concerns about the reforms to the FOS. I do not agree necessarily with everything she said, but the House is better for the scrutiny that she and her Committee provide.

Let me pay tribute to our country’s longest-serving Economic Secretary, my right hon. Friend the Member for Salisbury (John Glen), who moved with grace from museums to MiFID back in the day. He spoke about his mixed views of the FOS. He acknowledged that it is—in his words—an unreliable path to resolution, and helpfully warned us that we need to consider the challenges posed by AI to the financial services sector.

I congratulate the hon. Member for Peterborough (Andrew Pakes) on his appointment as the Government’s co-operatives and mutuals champion. I have to say it is an appointment that passed me by, but I very much welcome it. One person who has always been a champion of co-operatives and mutuals is, of course, the hon. Member for Harrow West (Gareth Thomas), who spoke of the high cost and burden of credit, especially for those in poverty.

We on the Conservative side of the House want sensible deregulation. We want less bureaucracy in our system. We want lower burdens and more growth. Where the Bill does that, we will welcome it and we will help make it happen. The Chancellor was right in his opening remarks when he said that it is important to recognise the cross-party work that has gone on already with the Bill. He rightly echoed the views of those us on the Conservative Benches when it was said in the other place that the Bill moves us all in the right direction. Having said that—I am loath to depart from the happy and collegiate atmosphere of the debate so far—I am reminded of what Disraeli once said:

“No Government can be long secure without a formidable Opposition.”

So, if Members will forgive me, I have a job to do tonight. In certain areas, as my hon. Friend the Member for Wyre Forest set out, we believe the Bill does not go far enough. I would like to highlight two areas in particular.

First, on digital assets, the United States has legislated for stablecoin. South Korea and even the European Union have their own regimes. Our competitors globally are moving ahead. That matters because stablecoins could revolutionise the way we pay for goods and services. Blockchain technologies could transform the way we interact with companies and the state. The Bill was our chance to set out a more advanced vision and policy agenda in those areas, but the Government chose not to.

Secondly, ringfencing forces our largest banks to separate retail banking from the rest of their business. That was right after the financial crisis, but the world has now moved on and our resolution regime has moved on with it, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Salisbury pointed out. If we look at our competitors from New York, Amsterdam, Frankfurt and Paris, not one imposes ringfencing like ours—not one. We believe that we should not either. The Bill gives a little and takes a little, but there is a simpler option. If true deregulation is the aim, we believe the Government should adopt the Conservatives’ plan to scrap ringfencing altogether.

No matter how well intentioned the measures in the Bill are—and I believe they are very well intended— I am afraid that I must point out that they are being brought in alongside a barrage of anti-growth taxation and regulatory burdens imposed on our financial services sector and British business more widely. This afternoon, the Chancellor praised Britain’s financial services sector, and I welcome his words; 13 days ago, he spoke similar words but then doubled the bank surcharge—a £1.5 billion hit to the very companies and people he says he supports.

It is all about choice. The Chancellor could have chosen to cut welfare, which is spiralling above £400 billion, but he chose the easier route for a Labour Chancellor, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) said, and decided to tax one of our country’s most-important sectors. Be in no doubt that this will have an impact, and specifically, I fear it will lead to more bank branch closures on our high streets, which none of us in this House wants.

I have no doubt that the Economic Secretary will shortly reference banking hubs in her wind-up, speaking with pride about how the Government are rolling out more. She is right to welcome them—I welcome them too—but she should also be clear about who pays for them. Banking hubs are funded by the banks—every one of them. Cash Access UK is funded by the banks. The mobile libraries and the pop-ups in our communities are funded by the banks. We cannot celebrate banking hubs on a Tuesday and then the next day tax the companies that pay for them. I am in favour of banking hubs, but I would much rather the branches not be closed in the first place.

To her credit, the Economic Secretary understands the sector. She is respected in the City and she understands the importance of banks to our high streets, which makes it all the more disappointing for the sector that she did not act to prevent the latest tax raid. The high street bank tax is just one example, but we also have the hike to national insurance and higher taxes on carried interest. That all results in more jobs put at risk, more high street banks closing and investment and innovation heading elsewhere rather than contributing to growth here in Britain.

For the most part, the Conservatives of course welcome the Bill, and we have been clear about that. Sadly, however, it will do little to overcome the barriers and burdens that this Government have inflicted on the financial services sector over the past two years. Warm words cannot undo cold taxes. The world’s capital has a choice about where it goes, and the Government have not acted in our favour. The Chancellor has a choice: he can back the sector or tax it until it becomes uncompetitive, but he simply cannot do both.

speaker: Steve Yemm
heading: Justice
text: What progress his Department has made on utilising AI for innovation in legal services.

speaker: Sarah Sackman
heading: Justice
text: The Ministry of Justice has made significant progress on the responsible utilisation of AI in innovation within the legal services sector. I will offer two examples: first, our launch of the legal services advisory AI growth lab, which brings together Government, regulators and innovators to accelerate responsible AI adoption in legal services; secondly, our commitment to continue to fund LawtechUK, so that we can accelerate the adoption of AI usage across the country. That is what we mean by growth in every postcode.

speaker: Steve Yemm
heading: Justice
text: I thank the Minister for her answer. The Labour Government inherited record backlogs in the Crown court system, with victims waiting years and years to access justice. What more could the Government be doing to utilise AI and technological solutions to get the courts moving quicker to improve access to justice and, crucially, to deliver justice for victims?

speaker: Sarah Sackman
heading: Justice
text: I thank my hon. Friend for an excellent question. I am passionate about using technology and AI responsibly to address the problem of delays in our criminal courts. We are using AI transcription to improve open justice; we are using AI case readiness tools to help our judges to ensure that cases are ready to be heard on time; and we are using AI responsibly in the scheduling of cases. All those things will ensure greater efficiency over time in our courts.

speaker: John Martin McDonnell
heading: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
text: May I put on record again my concern that, as we may be facing a significant global crisis as a result of AI debt problems, now is not the time to undermine the protections we brought forward after 2008 and, in particular, the separation between retail and investment banking?

speaker: Alex Davies-Jones
heading: Justice
text: I thank my hon. Friend for raising this important point. It is vital that victims and survivors get closure from their cases. Victims of rape and other sexual offences, and bereaved families of homicide, can access their free sentencing remarks transcripts. Our ambition is that, from spring 2027, we will extend this free provision to all victims in Crown court cases, and we are exploring how AI can provide transcripts more quickly and cost-effectively while representing a true and accurate reflection of the case.

speaker: Josh MacAlister
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text:
With permission, Madam Deputy Speaker, I would like to make a statement on education technology and mobile phones in schools.

Today’s children are growing up in a world shaped by smartphones, social media and artificial intelligence. Technology can bring enormous opportunities, but schools remain—and must remain—a place where children can focus, learn and connect with one another. Technology’s role in education should be to support learning, not to get in its way.

Earlier this year, with support from across the House, the Government strengthened guidance on mobile phones in schools to back teachers and parents in making schools mobile phone-free. Since that updated ban started in September, many schools have taken great steps to tackle the disruption that mobile phones can cause, and I am grateful to school leaders and teachers who have worked hard to create calm, focused classrooms. However, many teachers and pupils tell us that phones are still being used under desks, in the toilets and in the playground. Department for Education data published today tells a similar story: only 16% of secondary pupils say that their school’s mobile phone rules are followed all of the time. That means that teachers are spending valuable time spotting phone use; that school leaders are having difficult conversations about enforcement; and, most importantly, that digital distraction continues to crowd out learning.

How schools choose to implement the existing policy really does matter. Leaders need to feel more empowered by Government to make schools genuinely mobile phone-free environments. In schools where pupils are allowed to keep their phone in their bag or blazer—those with so-called “not seen, not heard” policies—only 20% of school leaders report that the rules are followed all of the time. By contrast, in schools with mandatory collection policies, 74% of leaders report that the rules are followed.

That is why I am today announcing that we will update statutory guidance to make it clear that schools should have policies that ensure children cannot have unsecured mobile phones in their blazer or bag throughout the school day. This backs teachers and leaders by giving them the clarity they are asking for. It still gives schools the choice as to whether phones are collected at the start of the day, kept in secure lockers or stored in a lockable pouch, or any other strategy that ensures phones are not within reach of children. We—parents, teachers and Government—need to work together to change children’s expectations about what the school day looks like. It should be a time to get lost in learning and make friendships that last a lifetime, not to be stuck doomscrolling in the corner of the playground.

The revised guidance will come into effect from September 2027, although we encourage schools to move towards implementation sooner if they can. Schools will continue to be able to make reasonable adjustments and exemptions where appropriate, including for pupils with medical needs and those with special educational needs and disabilities. We will work closely with school leaders as the guidance is developed. We want to learn from schools that have already led the way on this issue, ensuring that the approach is practical, proportionate, and able to meet the needs of children and teachers in different settings.

The second plank of this change is a new approach to deploying technology in schools. Today, we are launching a public consultation on establishing independent safety certification of education technology, or edtech, in schools, colleges and early years settings in England. Well designed and purposeful use of technology can support teaching, learning and the smooth running of settings. We also have a duty to support children and young people to learn to use technology confidently and safely. However, technology should never get in the way of learning. It should enhance, rather than shortcut, cognitive development, and without question it must be safe. Children’s safety and their educational outcomes, human interaction and teacher-led direct instruction must remain at the heart of our education system.

The Department for Education already sets standards for the safe use of technology, but settings are often still left to make sense of whether technology products meet those standards. These can be complex and technical issues about data protection or content safety, for example. That is why we are launching today’s consultation, which will invite views on whether certification for specific categories of technology should be introduced. It will explore which types of technology pose the greatest risks, including through exposure to harmful content, the use of children’s personal data and the impacts on cognitive development or social and emotional wellbeing. The consultation will ask about the standards and criteria that should underpin any scheme. The aim is to reduce the risk of harm to children, remain proportionate for suppliers of all sizes, be robust over time and be useful for educational settings. Findings from the consultation will inform the design of any future certification scheme, including the appropriate timescales for its introduction.

The proposed change to mobile phone guidance and the consultation on edtech safety certification meet the Government’s wider vision for childhood and education. International evidence, including the latest results from the programme for international student assessment, shows the strength of England’s education system. We are determined to go further to improve reading, writing, oracy and numeracy; to strengthen engagement; and to make schools unmissable for children. We want to go further on the depth and rigour of reading, so that we can inspire a love of reading for all children.

PISA highlights the risks when technology begins to replace the challenge, rigour and human interaction that define great teaching and learning. Technology has a place in our classrooms, but it should always be in support of learning, not become a substitute for it. To quote directly from PISA’s recent report:

“Technology can be a powerful amplifier of learning, but only if students are equipped with the cognitive and metacognitive tools to use it wisely. That means protecting time for reading in the school day. It means designing digital learning platforms that reward reflection, not just reaction.”

This Government are determined to get ahead of these challenges by shaping the role that technology plays in children’s lives, rather than leaving children to be shaped by it. I commend this statement to the House.

speaker: Laura Trott
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text:
I am delighted to come to the House today to welcome a proper phone ban in place for schools. The Government have finally done the right thing, but they have been on what I would euphemistically describe as a journey. We should remember that the former Prime Minister told us that a legislative phone ban was “completely unnecessary”. The previous Education Secretary, the right hon. Member for Houghton and Sunderland South (Bridget Phillipson), stood opposite me here and, in her warm and friendly manner, dismissed it as “a headline-grabbing gimmick”. When I raised this topic at Education questions, a then Education Minister told me to think of something better to go on—not condescending at all. When I asked the Government in this House to rule out a “not seen, not heard” policy, they refused. The stats that the Minister is citing today are correct, but they are essentially the same as the stats we quoted a year ago in this House, and the Government refused to act on them.

Let me remind Labour Members how many times they voted against a legislative phone ban in schools: not once, not twice, but seven times. Even the Minister, who I am sure has agreed with me all along, was forced through the voting Lobbies time and again, and the new Education Secretary, who also voted against it, has clearly had a change of heart.

The Conservatives and, to be fair, the Liberal Democrats, who also supported the ban, were told by Ministers that the majority of schools had a phone ban in place and that the existing guidance was working. It was therefore quite something this morning to have facts that I was repeatedly told in this House were incorrect being used by the Education Secretary, in the media, to justify the new guidance. We must also remember that the guidance was put on a statutory footing only a month ago. One month, and already the Government have to come back and toughen it up. We could have saved a lot of time and confusion for schools if the Government had just listened to us in the first place.

The Minister has confirmed that the guidance will only come in next September. That is a self-inflicted whole extra year of lost learning time while schools have a previous set of guidance, issued only a month ago, that the Education Secretary admitted this morning is not working—all because the Government refused to listen to the evidence. That is at best frustrating and at worst chaotic.

We have got there in the end, however, and this is a significant moment. I pay tribute to the many campaigners who have fought for this, the many parents who have spoken out and the many pupils who have bravely spoken about their own experiences. Smartphones in schools are a disaster for learning, a disaster for safeguarding and a disaster for happiness. This is an important step forward in giving children their childhood back.

I welcome the news that the Government are consulting on an independent safety certification for edtech. Will the Minister clarify whether the review will look at all edtech products currently being used in schools or just new edtech products entering the market? Will he also confirm that the review will look at education outcomes as well as safeguarding? Does he have a timeframe for the consultation? How is the review consistent with rolling out unevidenced AI tutors for the most disadvantaged? Those are the very pupils who need evidence-led, teacher-led support. Will the Government commit to not rolling out the programme until they can guarantee the safety and efficacy of AI tutors?

I welcome the Government finally getting to the right place. A full phone ban in schools is the right thing for behaviour and attainment in our classrooms. It will keep schools as places of learning and will turn the tide on the pervasive screen creep that is destroying childhood. We must never accept that just because something is new, it is progress; just because it involves technology, it is automatically better; and we must never again allow anything into our classrooms that has not been proven to be safe for children.

speaker: Josh MacAlister
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text:
Well, we put it on a statutory footing because we had a piece of legislation.

The question that is worth a moment of response was about the educational outcomes being within the scope of the certification process. AI tutors are a real concern, but there is an opportunity there. The Government are funding some of the leading companies around the world to develop products. They will then go into a separate programme for which we have funding, led by the Education Endowment Foundation, to establish the impact on educational outcomes and attainment. It is entirely right to suggest that there should be no widespread deployment of this technology before we know its full effects on cognitive development. Of course, there are also safety issues.

speaker: Helen Hayes
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text:
I thank the Minister for his statement, and welcome the announcement of strengthened guidance on mobile phones in schools. It constitutes agreement with the Select Committee, which called for a policy whereby children have no access to their phones during the school day rather than a “not seen or heard” policy. The Committee also said that schools should be given the resources, where needed, to implement such a policy in full. For secondary schools, the cost of buying pouches can be as much as £20,000. How will the Government ensure that schools have the resources to implement the policy effectively?

The Committee is currently undertaking an inquiry on AI and edtech. We have received a vast amount of evidence about the complexity of this landscape and the challenges that schools face in respect of procurement and the deployment of technology, and understanding the pedagogical basis that underpins it. Standards should be set, and I welcome the Government’s consultation, but they should be set in relation to a clear sense of the educational purpose of the technology, a deep understanding of pedagogy, and an understanding of the technology itself. What work has been undertaken on those aspects to underpin the Government’s thinking in this area?

speaker: Josh MacAlister
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text:
I thank the hon. Lady for her long-standing campaigning and support for these issues, including the work that she has done in her role as the Chair of the Education Committee. The source of the Government’s confidence in recommending this as the approach that all schools should take from September next year is that 39% of secondary schools are already, from within their existing budgets, able to implement a full ban, which means that young people are not taking phones around the school in the middle of the day. They have found a number of means of doing that, which include pouches. We will work closely with school leaders very closely to ensure that this is implemented effectively next September.

The hon. Lady asked about the role of the certification process, and the deployment of AI tools and the need to ensure that they are effective. I completely agree with her description of the complicated landscape that headteachers and subject leads face when deciding what to use: that is exactly why we want the certification process to go alongside the trials and the evaluation work that we want to do, specifically on the use of AI tools in the classroom. We need to do that as quickly as we can, but, as the hon. Lady will know, the quality of these trials needs to be robust enough to provide schools with really clear guidance.

speaker: Peter Swallow
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: Parents across Bracknell Forest will welcome the strengthened guidance on mobile phones in schools and the fact that the Government are having a look at edtech. I agree with the Minister that we need to make sure that the guidance is implemented in an intentional way, guided by pedagogy. May I ask him to touch on data concerns? One of my concerns about AI being utilised in the classroom without clear guidance is that we need to make sure that the data is kept safe and secure. It should not be the case that foreign tech companies are profiting from sensitive data from our young people.

speaker: Julian Lewis
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: I presume it is too much to expect a Government Minister to admit that the shadow Education Secretary was right to propose this measure previously and that the Government were wrong to vote against it, so let me ask him something easier to answer. What does he think the measures will be in the evolutionary process that he describes when schoolchildren start returning to the classroom with long essays that have clearly been the result of the application of AI? It will put teachers in an extremely difficult position, and it would be good if we could be ahead of that particular curve.

speaker: Josh MacAlister
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: The right hon. Member asks excellent questions in this House, and I am very happy to answer the specific one about homework and AI. He is right to highlight that this is an issue to which we will need to return in years to come. In fact, in many ways homework has already been highly disrupted by the use of generative AI tools. The issue for school leaders and teachers is ensuring there are methods of assessment and pushing learning that have grit and friction. Often that will need to be in the classroom, where we can be confident that AI tools are not being used to do the cognitive offloading, meaning children miss out on the opportunity to grow and develop, which is what our schools should be all about.

speaker: Josh MacAlister
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: Yes, there is a wider set of issues to do with children and technology. The Government have taken action on a full social media ban, which will come into effect next year. Action has been taken against AI chatbots and nudification images, and there is of course the action we are taking today, which builds on action we took earlier this year. All of that taken together is this House and the Government trying to wrestle with the best way to move on this issue and get ahead of it. As I said earlier, I believe we will have to come back to this issue time and again to be ahead of the curve.

speaker: Josh MacAlister
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: The hon. Member has hit the nail on the head: that is the issue that schools need to navigate at the moment, and we need to help them. The edtech certification, on which we are starting the consultation, is designed to tackle exactly that issue and help school leaders navigate some of those choices, as are the trials and evaluations that we will put in place on AI chatbots. That is linked to the warnings from PISA about school systems elsewhere in the world, where technology has been left to let rip in the education system and has displaced books, reading, writing and some of the more tactile things that we know children need in school to have the right cognitive development.

speaker: Cat Smith
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: I welcome the Minister’s statement. On Friday, I visited Lancaster high school in my constituency; under the leadership of Colin Malone, it has seen its best-ever GCSE results. During my visit, I did not see or hear a mobile phone. It is an example of a mobile-phone ban ensuring that children’s educational outcomes are improved. Will the Minister join me in congratulating Colin Malone on his leadership? My question to the Minister is about changing technology. While we are talking about mobile phones, I am aware that technology is moving on, with AI glasses and smartwatches also in the mix. Does he have any thoughts on that?

speaker: Alistair Strathern
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: It was great to see local schools like the Priory and Hitchin Boys’ and Girls’ lead the way on keeping phones out of the classroom. Having campaigned with parents and teachers to make this a norm, I am delighted that the Government are leading on this issue. As others have alluded to, the growth of generative AI is threatening to tread on children’s learning in the same way that smartphones did; just as we did with smartphones, we should not treat that as inevitable or unavoidable. How does the Minister intend to support our schools to ensure that generative AI can be used as an effective tool to support learning, but kept out of the spaces where it can be harmful to learning?

speaker: Josh MacAlister
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: My hon. Friend is right to highlight this matter. He has been a massive campaigner on these issues in his constituency and in this House, as have others. My hon. Friend the Member for Beckenham and Penge (Liam Conlon) has also been a big advocate for these issues. Earlier this year I was in Estonia, which has a high-performing school system and is adept at making good use of technology. While I was there, I saw the care and thought that went into the development of generative AI models that could be Socratic with pupils—they could coach and teach back and forth. Anything like that would need to go through rigorous testing to ensure that educational outcomes would be improved, but that shows the care and thought that needs to go into the deployment of such technologies.

speaker: Sarah Russell
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools
text: I welcome the Minister’s statement on smart glasses, which I profoundly believe should be banned from all public buildings as a matter of urgency. In the Information Commissioner’s findings about edtech, it already has concerns about the data that those companies admit they are farming on children. My concern is about the totality of the information that can be gleaned about children from across both the technology they use at home—such as their smartphones, including their location, and from apps that they might have, such as menstrual trackers, where children might not understand the importance of the personal data that they are sharing—and edtech. I am concerned that by the time AI recruitment decisions are being made, when the current generation are 25, 30 or 40 years old, the totality of information that could be known about them online will be staggering. Will the Minister take an approach that involves high levels of scrutiny of the totality of information that could be held about children, both from the edtech sector and outside of it?

speaker: Meg Hillier
heading: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
text:
I agree with both the Chancellor and the shadow Economic Secretary, the hon. Member for Wyre Forest (Mark Garnier) that the financial services sector has an important part to play in our economy. As the shadow Economic Secretary said, the sector represents 3% of jobs in the UK, and it is important for growth and investment. It is therefore important that we understand its role and that we get things right. This Bill, in the Government’s terms,

“will modernise how the sector is regulated, and enable it to grow and lend more to businesses. It will also make consumer protections fit for the digital age”.

I do not think any of us would disagree with those intentions.

The Government have also set out clearly that they want to maintain high standards of regulation and oversight at the same time. There is a balance to be struck in leaning in to support a sector, while also protecting the many consumers—millions of our constituents—who are borrowing, investing and using the services of financial institutions. Having a strong and competitive financial services sector is important for driving growth, but the protection of consumers is important, too. The Treasury Committee has looked at that balance between the growth objective that the previous Chancellor set the Financial Conduct Authority and its role in regulation.

As a side point, I mention remit letters. The new Chancellor has not had a chance to write too many yet, but the number of remit letters that go to our regulators runs into quite high numbers. Those bodies then have to consider the “have regard to” comments in those letters in their work, and it makes for a very long list of things to do, some of which just cannot all be done at the same time. The Treasury could look to prune some of these requirements, or to decide what the key areas are at any point, so that those organisations know what they should be focusing on.

This Bill could be seen as moving the pendulum more towards the financial services sector and further from regulation to support consumers, and we should be careful about that. The Committee has made some comments on it, but for me, consumers should be front and centre. My question to the Government—the Economic Secretary may expand on this in her closing remarks—is: how far should that pendulum swing? How far is too far? Who is the arbiter of what level of protection constituents and consumers should expect? We have a number of bodies, and I will speak about the Financial Ombudsman Service a little later.

It is not just me or the Treasury Committee who have been raising these issues. Nikhil Rathi, the chief executive of the Financial Conduct Authority, said to us in July that the FCA needs a clear indication of the Government’s risk tolerance when it comes to markets. He is up for the challenge, but he needs to know as a regulator where to draw the line between promoting growth and consumer protection. We know that even a small increase in the percentage of customers harmed is a lot of people. One of the pleasures of our role as MPs is that we get to see people face to face at our surgeries. We see people in the raw. Whitehall is a long way from that direct contact, and it is us who will be picking up the problems if they arise. As this Bill proceeds through Committee, we need to be cautious and make sure that we are stress-testing that point about consumer protection at each stage.

The Government are encouraging more investment. In fact, the Economic Secretary, during her previous time as Economic Secretary, made a number of public statements encouraging people to invest more. I can understand the Government’s position. People can make a lot more money from savings if they invest them carefully and well, but it is about changing the language. There has been concern about investment, particularly since the financial crash of 2008—it is a bit like the “Smoking kills” signs on cigarette packets—so the Government are changing the language, but I need to ask what level of risk they are willing to take. As they change the language and encourage people to take not risky, but less safe approaches to managing their money, where will the Government draw the line?

My main concern is the changes to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which has been a vital consumer protection. It is popular with consumers, and the source of much complaint from the City. The shadow Economic Secretary highlighted some of those concerns, as did the Chancellor. We know that the Financial Ombudsman Service is not perfect. It has had a bit of a rocky ride in the past few years, but it is already undergoing some changes without the need for legislation. It is having to adapt to the modern world, and AI is no doubt causing it even more challenges, but it was dealing with a high volume and not always reacting quickly enough.

I have a couple of particular concerns to raise. One is the time limit on complaints. While 10 years sounds like a long time, some of the financial products that our constituents take out have a very long life, with pensions being the obvious example. When something goes wrong in that area, it can have a long reach back into the past. I understand the challenges for banks, such as we have seen with the motor finance issues. When the issue was payment protection insurance, I spoke to one bank that employed 10 people just to go through the complaints coming in from people who were not even customers of the bank. There is a lot to be done in that area. This partly relates to those online promising the earth to people if they take up a complaint, even if they do not have legitimate grounds. I do not believe setting the time limit at 10 years is the answer. The Economic Secretary might not be able to discuss it now, but perhaps she will meet the Committee or me—whoever—to talk about how the Government will protect people taking out long-term financial products, including pensions.

The Treasury Committee has heard evidence on the Financial Ombudsman Service from the Citizens Advice, which noted that although it believes that consumer protection and growth do not have to be competing objectives—I agree with that—this Bill reduces protections and access to redress for consumers. Which? wrote to the Committee and noted that the proposed referral mechanism in clause 6 risks making redress slower and more complex, creating additional barriers to redress for consumers. I know that the Chancellor answered that point to a degree in response to my question earlier.
