Clause 7 constrains the fair and reasonable test that the FOS has worked under for such a long time, which will make it harder for consumers to receive redress, even when they have been treated unfairly. I can see clearly what the Chancellor and the Government are trying to do here. We have heard the noise from the financial institutions, saying, “We adhere to the rules of the FCA. We take into account the consumer duty, as the FCA requires us to do. Then something goes to the ombudsman and suddenly it seems to be judged by a whole different set of rules.” Most financial institutions do a reasonably good job most of the time and treat their customers fairly, and the consumer duty weighs heavily on them. When something goes to the ombudsman and is not considered to meet the fair and reasonable test, it should be something that is egregiously outside that consumer duty. It is important to have that backstop for our constituents. The Financial Ombudsman Service is already, as I said, undergoing non-legislative reforms. We should focus first on improving the system, rather than adding more layers of legal reform. Perhaps giving it that chance to reform itself would be the best first step.

In March this year, the Committee wrote to the Government outlining the importance of the Financial Ombudsman Service’s independence. The perception of that independence is vital. I propose—I would like to talk to the Economic Secretary further about this—that we introduce a statutory lock for the Treasury Committee on the appointment and dismissal of the chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service. There is precedent; the Chancellor of the Exchequer may not know it, but he cannot appoint or sack a chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility without the agreement of the Treasury Committee. That is a lock on a mad, bad or dangerous Chancellor taking away the independence of that important body. We think that there should also be a lock on a mad, bad or dangerous Chancellor doing the same for the chair of the FOS.

speaker: John Glen
heading: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
text:
I am very grateful for the hon. Lady’s characteristic grasp of the detail of this subject, and she absolutely makes the point. Just removing a banner from a front office does not streamline, so I urge the Economic Secretary to retain a forensic view, as I know she will, of what processes faced by businesses and consumers are actually streamlined.

I note the streamlining of the senior managers and certification regime by abolishing mandatory annual employee certification below senior manager level. I note the comment of the hon. Member for Great Yarmouth (Rupert Lowe), who is no longer in his place, on that regime, which was, “Abolish everything.” I understand the frustration that leads to many people saying that, but I think we have some new challenges, which have not been properly addressed, when it comes to AI in financial services.

The Chair of the Select Committee mentioned this in passing, but AI, in automating the evaluation of which products would suit individuals, is transforming most consumers’ interactions with financial services. Following the Mills review, there does seem to be a bit of a gap in what will happen with appropriate regulation. It seems that the essence of the position of the FCA is that it does not want to slow down the pace of innovation and growth in financial services, so it will be very reticent to put in any regulation. That is not an unreasonable sentiment, but we must discuss where we as a society feel responsibility should lie. If a financial services firm essentially allows an AI regime to produce offers of products that are sold, somebody has to be responsible for the terms and the basis for such a product going to market.

I welcome the changes to the PRA to streamline the bank rules on ringfencing, but I was the Minister who commissioned the Keith Skeoch review, which essentially came to the conclusion that it was not really necessary, but because of the legacy of the global financial crisis, we had better keep it in place. I urge the Economic Secretary to ask this question: what does that ringfencing actually give us? Many senior people at the PRA told me that we do not really need it, and we have a resolution regime that would actually satisfy all our requirements. However, it has a totemic significance, because it is associated with that season of under-regulation that led to the global financial crisis. We must have an honest conversation, not one based on received wisdom about what happened 18 years ago. We should not be reckless, but we do not need to carry unnecessary burdens when they do not really add anything.

Time goes quickly in this place, and I respect the need for everyone to speak, but I would like to make two or three broader points. One is about the imbalance of power and expertise. When I became the Economic Secretary, I hardly slept for the first few weeks because it was just so complicated, after I had been the arts, heritage and tourism Minister. From museums to MiFID in one step was a big move, but I did my best to master it. Every six weeks or so, I met the head of the FCA and the head of the PRA. These are some of the most brilliant people in public service, who have at their disposal some of the most intelligent, numerate individuals who are aware of all the nuances of different conditions, the capital requirements of banks of different sizes and the different mitigations for them. I was trying to mediate all the representations I had had from TheCityUK, UK Finance, the Association of British Insurers, the London Market Group and all the consumer organisations, essentially to try to challenge them on the right way of liberalising the regime or having a strong and simple regime to, for example, make it easier for smaller banks.

I probably got that right sometimes and on other occasions did not press hard enough, while at times there was a reasonable expectation that I would be moved on. Indeed, since July 2022 there have been eight Economic Secretaries—I am glad the sixth one is now back again as the eighth one. I just do not feel that that is a grown-up way to deal with our financial services Minister—the person responsible for this industry that we have all said is so important in terms of the jobs it creates and the GDP it accounts for. There is well-meaning intent, when we come to this place, to mediate consumer groups’ concerns and the concerns of our constituents, but we need to think about how we can do this better. Perhaps there should be a joint committee of the Commons and the Lords, properly staffed with the sort of expertise and advice that would really allow us to take on our friends at the PRA and the FCA, but it is something that does need scrutiny.

The legacy of the global financial crisis is important. It obviously had an enormous impact on our country and our public finances. “Too big to fail” must never happen again, but we must recognise that financial services in this country compete on an international basis. Too often, when legislation is passed in this place, there is another “have regard to”. I have been in Select Committees where colleagues have asked about some piece of legislation—some provision or “have regard to” that I probably allowed to pass through the House of Lords because I wanted to be collegiate—that led the regulator to make assessments that were not going to go anywhere, but added significant compliance costs to our financial services industry with no material outcome. I urge the Minister to really think about what is a necessary legacy of the global financial crisis and what is a sort of received wisdom of defensiveness that does not serve us well any more.

My final point, which I alluded to earlier, is about the consumer reset. The Chair of the Select Committee rightly pointed to Nikhil Rathi’s challenge to us at the Select Committee that we, as politicians, need to be clear about what level of risk we are prepared to tolerate. That is a difficult question for us as Members of Parliament. We are never going to want to say to our constituents, “We are happy to allow lots of risk,” but we have to put it in context. The measures we put in place on risk mitigation, the mandate and responsibilities we give the FCA and the PRA, make quite a big difference to the way the industry functions and how competitive it is.

I welcome what the Government have done on financial education. The Economic Secretary and I were at the launch of a report by UK Finance this morning. I welcome the progress that has been made and needs to be made in that area, but we must get to a better place in terms of enabling people, when so much more information is available, to own the choices that they make. Of course the responsibility to look after consumer interest exists, but let us calibrate that appropriately for the age we live in.

Thank you for the opportunity to contribute.

speaker: Lord Macdonald of River Glaven
heading: Courts and Tribunals Bill - Committee (1st Day)
text:
My Lords, first, I agree with the noble and learned Lord that this is a critical amendment. In my limited experience of sitting as a recorder, there is nothing a judge hates more, or fears more, than a litigant in person, because it makes the case longer, more difficult and more complex to manage. I commend to your Lordships a recent paper published by the Nuffield Family Justice Observatory on the impact of litigants in person in the family courts relying on AI for their pleadings and arguments and refusing to accept the rulings and judgments of judges on the basis that Claude says something different. I would foresee a quite chaotic situation in the magistrates’ court were there to be an absence of lawyers to represent defendants facing terms of imprisonment.

The noble and learned Lord is quite right that, if there is a disparity in payment between the magistrates’ court and the Crown Court, those who currently have mixed practices will stop going to the magistrates’ court and people will stop practising in the magistrates’ court. I suggest strongly to the Government that the sort of equalisation of fees that this amendment speaks to is absolutely essential if their reforms are to work.

speaker: Lord Lemos
heading: Courts and Tribunals Bill - Committee (1st Day)
text:
My Lords, this measure is about reducing the ask we make of members of the public. I think we can all agree that being required to serve on a jury, not for the typical two weeks but for months, could have significant consequences for someone’s personal and professional life, and the impact is likely to be worse for someone self-employed or with caring responsibilities.

Clause 3 follows a long line of similar recommendations made by distinguished judges and independent reviewers, including Lord Justice Auld, in 2001, and Lord Roskill, as far back as the 1980s. Fraud and financial crime have continued to evolve since then, becoming enormously more complicated and with vast volumes of digital evidence, which are still dramatically increasing. That means that, for a very small number of cases, we need a new model that is fit for the modern age.

In relation to the comments made by the noble Baroness, Lady Jones, I want to make it clear that we are not suggesting this is going to save an enormous number of court days or reduce the backlog. This is about the jury experience, as I said in relation to the last group; it is not about jury competence. We do not think that there will be many of these cases. This is not about who can understand dishonesty better but about reducing the burden on ordinary people’s lives from sitting on long trials, with which I am sure the noble Baroness, Lady Jones, would agree, at least in principle.

I agree that disclosure and the case management of fraud cases must improve, and this Government have agreed in principle to many of Fisher’s part 1 recommendations and others made by the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson. However, even after effective case management, some trials are likely to remain highly complex or lengthy. This is for those exceptional cases—and I stress the word “exceptional”.

Finally, Clause 4 does not expand the circumstances in which a “judge alone” trial may be ordered. It is a technical provision that ensures that the wider statutory framework operates coherently and aligns the existing “judge alone” trial regimes with the new regime, by requiring reasoned judgments following acquittal.

Let me turn to Amendments 13A, 13B and 15A, for which I thank the noble Lord, Lord Marks. These amendments seek to ensure that only cases of appropriate complexity and length qualify for a “judge alone” trial. Amendment 15A would require the defence and prosecution to agree that the estimated trial length is at least five months before a decision for a “judge alone” trial could be made. The Government do not consider that a fixed five-month threshold is appropriate. Such a threshold would arbitrarily restrict the operation of the policy and could exclude cases that are exceptionally burdensome for jurors simply because their estimated length falls slightly below that figure.

For this policy, the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, recommended that:

“In deciding within the Crown Court allocation system whether trial by judge alone is appropriate, the judge would have to have regard to relevant factors which could be published in a new Criminal Practice Direction, and these would include matters such as the likely duration of the trial, the volume and complexity of the evidence etc.”.

The Government agree that rules and directions are the appropriate place for such factors and intend to work with the rule committee and the judiciary. In addition, the test refers to case complexity or length, rather than complexity and length, as this was the construction recommended by the noble and learned Lord, Lord Leveson, and used in previous legislation such as the repealed Section 43 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003.

I turn to Amendment 31, which would limit the offences that could be added to Schedule 1 to specified regulatory offences. I thank the noble and learned Lord, Lord Thomas of Cwmgiedd, for this amendment and his discussion of it with me yesterday. I know there are broader concerns across the Committee about the existence of this power, and we will have the opportunity to discuss that in full in the next group. For now, let me say this. The purpose of this power is to ensure that the system can keep pace as technological developments continue to change the nature of fraud and financial crime. Restricting the power to existing fraud and regulatory offences would limit the ability to respond to as yet unforeseen developments—for example, new offences enabled by the powerful capabilities of AI. We will return to this in the next group.

With that explanation, I hope that the noble Lord, Lord Marks, will agree to withdraw his amendment.

speaker: Baroness Chakrabarti
heading: Courts and Tribunals Bill - Committee (1st Day) (Continued)
text:
Once more I find myself in unity with the Privy Council Bench opposite. My friend may be only a mere Viscount but I join him in his campaign against Henry VIII. I declare an interest as a council member of Justice and a member of your Lordships’ Delegated Powers Committee. In that committee, the spirit of the late, great and learned Lord Judge does not just sit but is always in the room. He would do this better, more swiftly and more powerfully, but the committee was in total unanimity when it found this to be a completely inappropriate delegation of power. The committee said:

“It confers on the Secretary of State a significant power to amend, by order, principal aspects of the policy contained in the Bill. We are unconvinced by the Government’s justification for the power in the Memorandum”.

It should be removed. It was not a debate about procedure but a unanimous assertion that the power should be removed.

I am conscious that, on an earlier group, my noble friend the Minister made an argument that is often made in relation to Henry VIII powers: “This is the 21st century. There is technology, there is AI, so further offences might be created that we might want to add to this list that would potentially be appropriate for a trial by judge alone”. With respect, those offences would likely be created, I hope, by new primary legislation. That legislation could deal with the appropriate mode of trial. This is a completely unacceptable power.

This is an unelected, scrutinising second Chamber and the Bill is not a manifesto Bill. If the Chamber has a constitutional role, surely the campaign against Henry VIII and his powers is central to it. That is why I am so grateful to my friend, the noble Viscount, Lord Hailsham, and why I urge Members of the Committee, regardless of their views on the substance of “judge alone” trials in complex cases or on the Bill as a whole, to hold firm on this issue, as has the Delegated Powers Committee. By the way, being on that committee is one of the great privileges of my time in your Lordships’ House. It is not celebrated but it does very important work. Year in, year out, it publishes its reports, which are sometimes ignored. Its seminal report was called Democracy Denied? because Henry VIII powers in particular are about denying democracy. They are about asserting the power of the Executive over what should be parliamentary sovereignty.

Once more, I hope my friend the noble Viscount will forgive me—I hope to spare his blushes—but his father gave an important lecture, not in 2026 but in 1976, contrasting an elective dictatorship with the constitutional democracy that we all aspire to. Henry VIII powers over matters of such importance as this are a manifestation of an elective dictatorship, not the democracy to which we all aspire.

speaker: Lord Lemos
heading: Courts and Tribunals Bill - Committee (1st Day) (Continued)
text:
My Lords, Schedule 1 is an inherent element of “judge alone” trials for complex or lengthy fraud and financial cases, as it stipulates those offences that are in scope of the measure, and therefore should stand part of the Bill. I have heard concerns that Part 2 of Schedule 1 could be used over time to expand broadly the scope of Clause 3 —noble Lords have spoken very clearly and firmly about that. Let me be clear: it is already the case that amendments to the schedule can be made only through the affirmative procedure—and I note the comments that have been made about that—which requires a successful vote in both Houses. Offences cannot be added to the schedule without Parliament’s consent.

Amendments 30, 63 and 64, tabled by the noble Viscount, Lord Hailsham, would prevent the addition of further offences to the schedule. Amendment 29, tabled by the noble and learned Lord, Lord Keen, would go further by preventing any changes to the schedules at all, whether additions or deletions. As I have said, the purpose of this provision is to allow the system to respond flexibly as fraud and financial offending evolve over time. Technology continues to evolve rapidly, including developments in artificial intelligence. Cases involving any added offences will always have to comply with the other statutory safeguards for an order under Clause 3: a preparatory hearing, a public interest test, exclusions for homicide and indictable-only sex offences, and judicial decision- making.

I have noted the comments of the Delegated Powers Committee, and I understand that we will return to this on Report. With those comments, I ask the noble and learned Lord to withdraw his amendment.

speaker: Max Wilkinson
subheading: Antisocial Behaviour — [Dawn Butler in the Chair]
text:
I commend my hon. Friend’s comments to the Minister.

Confusing legal frameworks make many instances of antisocial behaviour difficult to police. E-bikes, which have already been mentioned, are a common complaint in towns and city centres up and down the country, including in my constituency. Public concern is growing over the dangerous misuse of illegally modified high-speed e-bikes on pavements and in pedestrianised areas such as the High Street and the Promenade in Cheltenham. This is a particular concern to older people and parents with young children, but it can certainly alarm anyone—I speak from personal experience. It is antisocial behaviour in itself, but the suspicion is that these e-bikes are regularly used by drugs gangs and in county lines.

The legal framework for e-bikes is confusing, outdated and rarely enforced. As the hon. Member for Gillingham and Rainham (Naushabah Khan) mentioned, high-power conversion kits and illegal bikes are readily available online with almost no regulatory oversight. That would be a good starting point for Ministers wanting to introduce measures to tackle antisocial behaviour. We must tackle illegal e-bikes, including by giving police forces updated training to spot, intercept and confiscate them. Will Ministers look at how these proposals might tackle antisocial behaviour?

We must also recognise that a huge quantity of serious crime has moved online, as Sir Mark warned last week. The latest strategic assessment from the National Crime Agency warned that rapid technological change is the primary driver in serious organised crime, with the threat set to increase. That change is diverting resources away from frontline policing, producing poorer outcomes for victims of other crimes, including antisocial behaviour. A dedicated online crime agency would ensure that online crime was treated with the seriousness that it merits and would free up officers’ time to focus on neighbourhood crime, including antisocial behaviour.

That online crime agency would be funded by a new online crime levy on the big tech and artificial intelligence companies whose platforms enable the most serious crimes that Sir Mark warned about last week: child sexual abuse, fraud and money laundering. It would stop neighbourhood police being dragged off their streets to deal with those forms of online crime, which in many cases they are not trained to deal with. Just last week, Sir Mark warned that the police risk heading for failure if reforms do not empower officers to keep up with modern criminals operating online. Will Ministers consider that proposal, which the Lib Dems have set out before, to establish an online crime agency in order to improve community response on our streets?

The Government have made positive steps on some of these issues through their neighbourhood policing guarantee, but the proof will be in its delivery, especially given the upcoming police reform legislation. They must get those reforms right, with a proper focus on community policing, or they risk placing communities at greater risk and harming public confidence in the system. If the merging of forces means that officers become more distant from the communities they serve and less able to respond to local crimes, the Government will be making a serious mistake. Worryingly, the agenda being set by the Home Office seems to run counter to the devolution direction being set by the Prime Minister, particularly in respect of the number of boundaries that will be set and accountability to regional mayors. When will we find out how police reform fits in with the Prime Minister’s flagship agenda?

speaker: Andy Burnham
heading: Prime Minister
text: The right hon. Gentleman asks about the Russian threat that we face today compared with the cold war. With rapid changes in technology, including AI, cyber-warfare and autonomous systems, we face new complex threats, which is why we are fully funding the defence investment plan and investing in the modern capabilities needed for the future.

speaker: Matthew Patrick
heading: Welfare
text:
I am a progressive. I believe in a social safety net to help people in their moment of need. That might be to manage a health condition or to deal with a moment of crisis, or it could be to support people through the natural ebbs and flows of employment, which I think we will see more of with the advent of AI. There is a challenge, however, in getting that support to work for people. It requires a safety net, which needs to be the right size. It needs to be wide enough to catch people when they fall, but not so wide that people cannot escape it. The modern safety net should not simply break someone’s fall; it should support them to get back into work.

The benefits of work are many, and those benefits can bring so much to an individual: self-esteem, money, mental health, physical health, resilience, routine, friendship, socialising and demonstrating to yourself and others that you can make a difference. I believe that the benefits are endless, which is why it is so heartbreaking when we see just how many young people do not have them.

One million young people are not benefiting from a job or not expanding their opportunities through education or training. Why? The Conservatives created the broken system that led to the outcomes we see today. They do not like to hear it, but it is true. Their system pushed people further away from the job market. They scrapped the Work and Health Programme, shut down Work Choice and left Access to Work in chaos. They made support so difficult that people were pushed towards the health component of universal credit to simply deal with the cost of living crisis.

What was the consequence of that? There was no requirement for those people to look for work, apply for jobs or do any work-related activity. The Conservatives’ system both cost more and pushed people further away from work. Their system told people that they cannot. We need a system that helps people see that they can. Members will forgive me if I do not look to the Tory party for a route to achieving that.

speaker: Sean Woodcock
heading: Welfare
text:
I start by disappointing Conservative Members: I agree with some of what they are saying. The welfare bill is too high, and too many young people are not in education, employment or training; it is morally indefensible. The problem is that Conservative Members seem to have forgotten who was in charge when those trends first took hold. In their final year in office, the welfare bill rose by a record £33 billion. Listening to some of the speeches this afternoon, one might think that Conservative Members had spent 14 years campaigning against Conservative Governments. They are right to highlight the growing number of young people who are not in education, employment or training, but it is not a new problem. It did not begin last year, or in July 2024; it grew on their watch, and yes, it has continued since. Frankly, that should prompt some humility, not self-righteousness from Conservative Members.

I also agree with Conservative Members when they say that we need to spend much more on defence. What puzzles me, however, is the argument that all we need to do is cut welfare, and the defence budget will somehow take care of itself. If it is that easy, why did they not do it? They had 14 years in government, and over those 14 years, welfare spending rose while, in the words of a former Defence Secretary, our armed forces were “hollowed out”. What exactly are Conservative Members asking us to learn from their example—that it is entirely possible to end up with a growing welfare bill and shrinking military capability at the same time? Anyone on the Opposition Benches can demand cuts, but it is the responsibility of the Government to ensure that reform actually works.

Earlier this year, I brought together a group of young people from my constituency who were not in education, employment or training. Not one of them told me that welfare was the reason that they were out of work. They talked about poor or non-existent careers advice; artificial intelligence and the rapidly changing labour market; and struggling to get employers to give them a chance, because they lacked confidence or soft skills, in some cases. In other words, they talked about barriers. We can ignore those barriers and make speeches about random, crude cuts to welfare, or we can try to deal with them. I would much rather do the latter. Real welfare reform is not measured by how much money leaves the Treasury; it is measured by how many people can enter and remain in work.

The Opposition are right to demand welfare reform and stronger defence, but they have no right to pretend that they bear no responsibility for the position in which this country finds itself on either score. After their 14 years in government, the welfare bill had risen and our military was hollowed out. The country needs welfare reform and stronger defence, but demanding change is not the same as delivering it. The real test is whether more people find work, whether barriers are removed, and whether our armed forces are genuinely stronger. None of those challenges will be solved by that lot on the Opposition Benches pretending that the previous 14 years did not happen.

speaker: Baroness Bennett of Manor Castle
heading: Health Bill - Committee (4th Day)
text:
My Lords, it is a great pleasure to follow two of your Lordships’ House’s real experts in this area, and I look forward to hearing from a third shortly. To extend the metaphor of the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, we are singing from the same hymn sheet, but just different parts. That is what this group of amendments is doing.

I will start with my Amendments 168, 169 and 172B, and I will deal with Amendment 268 at the end, which is somewhat different. These three amendments address different parts of the same problem. Who has access to NHS patient data? Who controls the infrastructure holding that data? Should the NHS should continue to rely on Palantir to provide that infrastructure?

I will start with the principle behind all three: NHS patient data belongs to a public health service under public control. It should not be accessible to commercial companies simply because the NHS has entered into a contract with them to provide the technology. The Government will no doubt say that patient data remains under NHS control and that Palantir acts as a data processor and cannot use the information for its own commercial purposes. Those are important contractual assurances, but they do not, as the other amendments in this group highlight, answer the issues that are raised. There is a difference between owning the data and having control over the systems through which that data is accessed, processed and managed. There is also a difference between a contractual promise and having the practical ability to guarantee that sensitive information remains beyond the reach of commercial contractors. In fact, we know that that is exactly what is happening.

NHS England has confirmed that three Palantir engineers have administrative-level access to the national data integration tenant, part of the federated data platform. A further 12 Palantir engineers have had more limited project-specific access for particular data sets and tasks. Now, this is not an allegation that Palantir employees are routinely browsing individual patient records, but administrative-level access to a system holding identifiable patient information is a serious responsibility. It raises huge questions about the boundary between public control and commercial access. I note that the National Data Guardian herself has questioned this. She said that the information about external contractors having access to identifiable patient data appeared to be inconsistent with the data protection impact assessment she had previously reviewed and she sought clarification from NHS England on this.

Amendment 168 addresses this directly. It would stop commercial entities and their employees, officers and subcontractors from accessing identifiable NHS patient data. That includes not just direct access to patient records but administrative and privileged access to databases, as well as access through software, support, maintenance and testing. We need this because we cannot allow the distinction between accessing patient records and administering the systems that contain them to become a loophole in the protection of confidential information. Commercial suppliers can still provide technical services. The amendment does not prevent the NHS from buying software or obtaining technical support, but it requires those services to be delivered using anonymised records. The NHS should be able to benefit from technical expertise without giving commercial companies access to identifiable patient information.

We come to the specific issue of Palantir, which is covered by both amendments. Palantir, as has already been alluded to, is not an ordinary technology supplier with no wider controversies. Its work with the Israeli military has drawn serious criticism from human rights organisations, including Amnesty International, which has documented the company’s links to Israel’s military activities in Gaza. It is also important to look at the ownership and the philosophy of this company. In March, Alex Karp said he believes AI will shift power away from

“highly educated, often female voters who vote mostly Democrat”

and towards working-class men.

I asked the Library to have a look at the ownership and control structures of Palantir. I thank it for its very detailed research, to which I am not going to subject noble Lords in detail. The key point is that Alex Karp, to whom I have just referred, co-founder Stephen Cohen, and chairman Peter Thiel have between them 49.99% of voting power because of the stock structure of the company. I note that the major institutional shareholders are Vanguard Group and BlackRock, Inc. They are not known for being companies that stand up for human rights, the rule of law or the public good. They have very distinct financial interests.

In particular, the company’s chairman, Peter Thiel, is known for his controversial views. At the Oxford Union in 2023, he said that the NHS makes people ill and should be privatised. I note also, in a broader context, that he is on the record as framing politics as an existential struggle against the Antichrist. Mr Thiel has named possible suspects for the Antichrist, including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Greta Thunberg and people who are critics of artificial intelligence. Now, that is quite disturbing. I would also note the fact that he was asked, in a video available online under the headline “Peter Thiel and the Antichrist”, whether he preferred the human race to endure. The interviewer said:

“You’re hesitating”.

Peter Thiel said:

“Well, I don’t know. I would … There are so many questions around this”.

The interviewer repeated:

“Should the human race survive?”

After 18 seconds, Mr Thiel said, “Yes”.

I have some questions to put to the Minister within the framework of the fact that the UN guiding principles on business and human rights make it clear that businesses have a responsibility to respect human rights. Have the Government properly considered those responsibilities when awarding and continuing this contract? Have they assessed Palantir’s links to breaches in international human rights law? Will the Government explain what human rights due diligence was undertaken?

I will jump to Amendment 172B. I stress that it does not say that we have to switch off Palantir immediately. It is a proposal for a transition away from Palantir, with patient care and data security protected throughout. The Government may point to the benefits that they say the federated data platform is already delivering. Of course, better use of data can help hospitals to manage waiting lists and make better use of resources, but none of that requires the NHS to surrender its control.

I come finally to my somewhat different Amendment 268, which is much broader and not specifically about software. It would put a clear duty on the Secretary of State to

“take all reasonable steps to ensure … health policy is independent of undue commercial influence and serves the public interest”.

It backs up that duty by asking for greater transparency and accountability. It would require an annual report to Parliament setting out the interactions between the Department of Health and Social Care, relevant NHS bodies and commercial entities when developing health policy, what steps have been taken to identify and manage conflicts of interest and disclose any breaches, and the actions taken in response. Secondly, it would strengthen the requirements on integrated care boards and other relevant NHS bodies to maintain public registers of interest, manage conflicts and ensure that commissioning and procurement decisions are transparent and based on the interests of patients and the public. Finally, it would require guidance on identifying the commercial forces that shape people’s health, making sure that public policy is not driven by the interests of companies.

We have become accustomed to thinking about health policy largely in terms of what happens when someone becomes ill and what treatment the NHS can provide, rather than all the other factors that make up our health. Of course, many businesses make a positive contribution to public health; others make money from products and practices that damage it. We need to understand that influence and make sure that it does not shape government policy. Those interests are there. A study of parliamentary groups found that pharma companies and industry-funded patient organisations provided more than £2.1 million to health-related APPGs, accounting for 30% of their total funding. People are always trying to strengthen the rules around APPGs, but there is a responsibility for the Government to make sure that the influence being put on them and the way they are considering and making decisions is not unduly commercially influenced. This is not or should not be a controversial principle, but it is one that needs to be actively protected.

speaker: Baroness Kidron
heading: Health Bill - Committee (4th Day)
text:
My Lords, I will speak to Amendments 53, 171 and 289 in the name of my noble friend Lord Tarassenko, and Amendment 160 in the name of the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, all of which I added my name to. I have my own amendment on NHS data as a sovereign data asset in a later group, which is remarkably poor organising on my part, but it does give the Minister two shots at saying we are right.

The primary difference between the amendments in this group and those in the later group is that these amendments focus largely on the use of NHS data by companies contracted and procured to provide services to the NHS, rather than primarily on how the benefits from technology trained on NHS data are retained in the UK. However, both sets of amendments cover the key elements and, whichever approach is finally taken, determining who has access to UK health data, and on what terms, is an extremely urgent issue.

During debates on the Data (Use and Access) Bill last year, I tabled an amendment on sovereign data assets, of which the NHS’s data was a key example but not the only one. At the heart of that debate, which I urge officials to look at, was a warning that has become only more urgent. The speed at which the Government are giving access to our data is swifter than the plans they have to protect its financial or societal value. We are nearly two years on and there is still no published strategy or government policy to maintain British control over valuable data assets. We do not have a clear plan for how our data or the systems that host it will be resilient to foreign interference. We do not have a clear strategy for building technological capability within the NHS for its data or ensuring that all the healthcare and economic value that comes from our data will indeed come back to the UK as a benefit.

Amendment 53 offers a road map for the conditions for access to NHS contracts, with a focus on control of data, building sovereign capability for data handling and reducing the dependencies and risks from foreign firms. This is not government data; it is data held in trust for the British public and they are being poorly served.

Amendment 160 looks at how contracts are awarded and ownership of the architecture that supplies services to the NHS. It singles out the way in which free or low-cost services are used to gain access, create dependency and result in vendor lock-in, which a number of noble Lords have already described well.

Amendments 171 and 289 would require the Secretary of State to publish a digital sovereignty strategy for the NHS, including control of systems that host data, control over the data itself, avoiding vendor lock-in and capitalising on our data to build technological capability and commercial value. It is an exhaustive checklist, but it mirrors those issues I laid in the Data (Use and Access) Bill and the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, and in the debate on digital sovereignty in July. It also aligns with multiple recommendations by committees of both Houses, including—I will try to say this very quickly—the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee’s report, Rewiring the State; the Commons BIST Committee’s report, Investing in the UK Economy, the Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy’s report on undersea cables; and the Lords Science and Technology Committee’s inquiry into financing and scaling UK science and technology. The Lords committee also has an open inquiry on innovation in the NHS and personalised medicine. How many times do we have to make the same recommendation? This is a flashing warning light.

We are not too late, but it is two years since we proposed these measures, and that is two years of wasted time, nursing dependency and failing to think strategically about how our most valuable technological asset could be a source of strength. It is two years in which this House has repeatedly warned, as the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, said, that this is the window in which to act. We are reaching a critical moment, and it cannot be that the Government seek to be at the forefront of AI and at the same time continue to undervalue the assets they already hold.

AI is only as good as the data it has, and the health data of the NHS is unparalleled. In fact, during last year’s debate on copyright, I had a call with one of the most senior global leaders in tech who, while conciliatory on the question of copyright itself, changed his tone entirely when I raised the question of NHS data. He said, “The Kenyans have kidneys too”. Of course they do, but they do not have the NHS’s extraordinary accumulation of longitudinal health data, built up over generations and representing such a broad and valuable resource for medical research and AI. It was a chilling moment, revealing the extent to which the unique value of our national data assets can be dismissed by those seeking access to them. This is a rich national inheritance, not the Government’s to give away foolishly but to be held in trust for us. We are undervaluing data in every part of our economy, and this is the data upon which the products and services of the future will be built. Harnessing its value will have consequences for the resilience of the NHS, its costs and quality of care in the future. The prize is better patient outcomes, a more resilient NHS and the development of British technological capability upon which ultimately our sovereignty depends.

speaker: Baroness Cash
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools - Statement
text:
My Lords, I thank the Minister for the Statement, which we on these Benches wholeheartedly welcome. The statutory guidance for schools is to be updated, so that from September 2027 schools must act to ensure that

“children cannot have unsecured mobile phones in their blazer or bag throughout the school day”.

The road to get here may have been somewhat longer and more tortured by late nights in Division Lobbies than desired by the majority in this House, but it is always to be celebrated when we achieve consensus in the end.

I would like to take a moment to pay tribute to my noble friend Lady Barran, who led on this issue in your Lordships’ House, despite the then Secretary of State, the right honourable Bridget Phillipson, calling a phone ban a “headline-grabbing gimmick”. In June last year, my noble friend tabled an amendment to the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill to ask for exactly what has now been announced. In February, this House agreed to that by 178 votes to 140. The noble Baronesses, Lady Kidron and Lady Cass, and the noble Lord, Lord Hampton, put their names to it. Peers across the House voted for it. In the other place, my right honourable friend Laura Trott pressed the case at every stage. I put on the record my thanks to them all.

It is such a positive change of heart for the benefit of children that I find myself in joyous agreement with the Secretary of State, Lucy Powell—a line you may not always hear me utter—who said yesterday:

“Children should not be using smartphones at any point during the school day, full stop”.

Amen. But the stronger guidance will not apply until September 2027, so pupils taking GCSEs this year will still have the grade-lowering distraction of their phones. Can the Minister please tell us why on earth the guidance cannot take effect more urgently?

While I of course welcome the Government’s consultation into independent safety certification for educational technology, the Statement is completely silent on the real issue: there is insufficient evidence to prove that educational technology improves educational outcomes at all, and growing, serious evidence to indicate the very opposite, that it can be a real detriment to learning. The evidence and the warnings are here now, yet the Statement is silent on the need to reduce time spent on screens in classrooms, and on the known damage of edtech already. Even on the Labour Benches in the other place, the concerns were being cited. The Minister, Josh MacAlister, warned that

“where technology has been left to let rip”

in other countries, it

“has displaced books, reading, writing

The Labour MP Alistair Strathern told the House that generative AI threatens to harm

“children’s learning in the same way that smartphones did

Be under no illusions that children having access to screens in any context in schools is going to facilitate both. In September, the OECD reported that pupils who use AI for tasks such as summarising texts score lower in science on average. A study of almost 1,000 secondary pupils found that those who practised maths with a chatbot scored 17% lower when they were tested without it.

The neuroscientist Dr Jared Cooney Horvath, whose book The Digital Delusion is essential reading on this subject and has just been published in the UK, told the United States Senate in January that this is the first modern generation to score lower than its parents on core cognitive skills. His review of almost 400 meta-analyses found that pupils read with less understanding on screens than on paper, and that the effect of edtech on disadvantaged pupils is the greatest of all. He reported that pupils on classroom devices can be off task, though they appear to be on their screens, for up to 38 minutes in every hour. Having teachers in my family, I know exactly how challenging that is, because they talk about it. Sweden has already reversed course and is spending heavily to put printed books back in its classrooms.

According to Dr Horvath’s analysis of PISA data for England since 2012, which is available on his Substack, independent schools, which sharply and more rapidly increased their use of classroom technology, found that their pupils’ results fell back, including once background is taken into account. State schools used far less technology, and their pupils’ results rose. I know the Minister shares my concern and real desire to see all our pupils do their very best and achieve their potential, and I know she will take seriously this mounting body of evidence that we must put the brakes on the use of edtech. But at the moment the department is going ahead with developing AI tutors for up to 450,000 disadvantaged pupils, the very children who most need a good teacher in front of them. The certification scheme announced yesterday has no timetable, and the department says it has no power to require schools to use it. As proposed, it would test safety but leave out whether a product actually helps children to learn.

On phones, this House gave warnings and the Government took two years to act. On edtech and AI, the warnings are being given here tonight, on the record. Will the Minister confirm that the AI tutoring programme will go no further than the Education Endowment Foundation trials until those trials report, and that certification will be compulsory and will test learning as well as safety? Will the Minister meet Peers from all Benches in this House who have raised these concerns before the consultation closes, so that this time we can get more quickly to the right answer for British children?

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools - Statement
text:
My Lords, in January 2026 the Government strengthened their guidance on mobile phones in schools, making it clear that all schools should have mobile phones policy that prevents pupils having access to their phone throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, break times and lunchtimes. This guidance was put on a statutory footing during the passage of what became the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, and schools have been required to implement it since September 2026. However, evidence and feedback from the sector—and from noble Lords in this House—suggest that challenges persist.

That is why the Government are announcing that we will update statutory guidance to be clear that schools should have policies that ensure children cannot have unsecured mobile phones in their bag or blazer throughout the school day. This backs teachers and leaders with the clarity that they are asking for. This may mean phones are collected at the start of the day, kept in secure lockers, stored in a lockable pouch, or any other strategies that ensure phones are not accessed at any point during the school day.

Noble Lords opposite raised points about the timetable. While the new statutory guidance will be introduced from September 2027, it is of course the Government’s wish—I believe evidence suggests that this will happen—that schools move more quickly towards the implementation of this policy. Of course, we have seen evidence in the last year with a near doubling in the numbers of schools that are ensuring that pupils cannot have any access to their phones during the course of the day. This answers the point made by the noble Lord, Lord Mohammed of Tinsley, about resources.

All the evidence about the different ways in which schools have approached this issue suggests that it is culture, leadership and clarity that are the most important elements in ensuring that schools are successful in carrying out this policy. We are confident that schools will be able to move more quickly than the beginning of the revised statutory guidance in September 2027. Of course, we will want to work with leaders and others within our schools to ensure that this policy is both supported by government and put in place in our schools.

The noble Lord made a particular point about young carers. It is quite tricky because, arguably, young carers, as much as any other child, deserve the opportunity to have a mobile phone-free experience in school. I am not sure that specifically exempting them is the most appropriate way forward, but we would expect schools to recognise the need for young carers sometimes to be able to phone home or to be contacted. Using the school office, for example, to facilitate that might be a good way forward.

Noble Lords raised points about edtech safety certification. Technology is now an integral part of education, supporting teaching, learning and the smooth running of schools, colleges and early years settings. It is essential that children and young people learn to use technology confidently and safely, so they are prepared for and can thrive in a rapidly evolving digital world.

However, technology should support learning, rather than get in its way, and it must be safe. The Department for Education has developed and already sets standards for the safe use of technology in education settings, including digital and technology standards and generative AI product safety standards, setting our expectations for the safe use of technology in education settings. However, schools and other education settings often have to make complex technical judgments when selecting technology without clear and consistent evidence about product safety. That is the thinking behind the consultation launched yesterday on proposals for edtech safety certification.

This is about getting ahead of the curve and ensuring that the Government are not passive to technological change but actively ensuring that it is safe for children and supports their development, and also supports schools with difficult decisions about appropriate edtech in a rapidly changing technological environment.

I do not think the noble Baroness, Lady Cash, really means that there should be no use of screens in classrooms. One of the things I regret from my time teaching is that I never got the opportunity to use a whiteboard, for example, in the imaginative way that is pretty well taken for granted in most classrooms now. Nor did I get to use technology to support group work and learning, in some of the ways where I think there is evidence that it supports, rather than replaces, pupils’ learning. Of course, it is important that we are clear about how it is used and that we agree that schools need good evidence about whether technology is effective.

We think that safety and effectiveness require different approaches. Safety can be assessed against clear expectations, while educational effectiveness depends on the pupils, the setting and how a product is used. That is why we are addressing effectiveness through the £24 million national edtech test bed programme, to build evidence about what works, for whom and in what contexts. We think that together these two approaches will help schools to make informed decisions about technology that is both safe and effective and, in doing that, provide the support and evidence that teachers need to ensure access to learning and the space to do that without being sidetracked by the use of mobile phones. That is what our children deserve.

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools - Statement
text:
I thank the noble Baroness; it is certainly the case that she has been tenacious on this issue. We have talked about lots of other things, and I am sure we will again in future. I am slightly fearful about what she will choose to get her teeth into next.

On the examples, in this House we have previously talked about specific assistive technology that might be important for young people and medical technology that is linked to a phone, for example for diabetes monitoring. Those would be the sorts of things that would fall into that category.

On the point about school trips, it is not the intention of the guidance that this policy will apply when children are travelling to and from school, so I feel it probably would not cover school trips. I will come back to the noble Baroness if I am wrong about that.

The noble Baroness makes an important point about future-proofing all this. The fact that we have updated the guidance and are taking further action around edtech demonstrates the situation we find ourselves in. Both the evidence and technology are developing fast, and of course we will want to keep up with that.

On the methods and gadgets that the noble Baroness discussed, we intend to produce AI in education guidance that will help identify some of the opportunities and issues in other areas. I do not know how long I will be here, particularly given the way I am feeling this evening, but I have no doubt that this will not be the last time I talk about how we are updating our work in government to ensure that the objective that all noble Lords share—that children need to be able to focus on learning rather than scrolling or the distraction that comes from screens—is at the heart of our work.

Her final point about health experts was a very good one. I will certainly take that back and consider how we engage with health experts as part of this work.

speaker: Baroness Kidron
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools - Statement
text:
My Lords, I too pay tribute to the noble Baroness, Lady Barran. Tenacity is a good word; I was thinking of something a little tougher earlier.

I really do welcome this Statement and join with others in regretting that we have had to fight so hard for it. I looked this up in Hansard and noticed that the first time we debated this was five years ago. The battle of last year, or a couple of years ago, was the culmination of us all coming together. I say that not to take anything away from that particular fight but to make a broader point about the things that we did not get in that Bill.

I thank the Secretary of State in particular for the Statement and for getting it over the line now. She has succeeded where others have failed. I really want to recognise that moment.

I welcome the Government’s commitment to independent certification of educational technology—something else that we have fought for over many years—and in particular its references to filtering and monitoring. I was very grateful for the letter from the early years Minister and his officials earlier in the week. However, I am concerned about the focus on safety; it is much narrower than I and other noble Lords have been calling for. I absolutely understand what the Minister here said about safety being a crucial factor, but it is a minimal bar: children flourishing in education is what we all seek and I think that would be a better bar. I am sure that we all recognise, just as with mobile phones, that the question is not simply whether technology is safe but “What is it replacing?”

I was at a conference about AI in education a couple of weeks ago, and the overwhelming evidence was—as the noble Baroness, Lady Cash, mentioned—that many of the AI products currently available produced better results in tests, but then the children failed to retain what they had learned. The response at the conference, which was largely focused on putting AI into schools, was simply that the tech would get better. That is tantamount to asking children to teach AI, rather than AI teaching children.

I am sure that the Minister will remember that I had amendments in the same Bill on edtech and on standards for efficacy, et cetera. I recognise that the Government have chosen to do this in guidance, but I ask that they take a broader view on what we need to look at in edtech. Schools are places where children grow, not just learn, and where relationships, confidence and agency matter just as much as passing tests and measurable outcomes. I will again say that I welcome the Statement, but I ask the Minister to ensure that independent certification and the Government’s wider approach to technology in schools protect the things that most matter for a child’s development and cannot be readily measured.

speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern
heading: Mobile Phones in Schools - Statement
text:
I thank the noble Baroness for the work that she has been engaged in, alongside our officials, in the scope of the certification scheme. That has been welcomed. On the point about whether the focus is only on safety, I think we have a broad conception of safety in the standards against which the certification will be made.

For example, as I said, this will be certification against the standards, including our world-leading generative AI standards, which recognises that cognitive development of children is an important aspect to be considered when thinking in broad terms about safety. I do not think that the certification will have quite the narrow scope that the noble Baroness suggests, but I reiterate the point that we are interested not only in certification of products but in research on what is effective, how and where, and for whom—we are investing money in that—and we are looking forward for other uses of AI in education, where we will produce further guidance.

speaker: Lord Kamall
heading: Health Bill - Committee (4th Day) (Continued)
text:
My understanding is that it is in this group, but maybe other noble Lords can confirm. There is a slight disagreement between my noble friend’s and my understanding of that.

I repeat that important point made by the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko: the cheapest initial purchase is not necessarily best in the long term. There is also a legitimate question about whether procurement requirements have become unnecessarily complicated, which the noble Lord, Lord Austin of Dudley, calls for in his amendment, around clarity and consistency about the objectives against which procurement decisions are assessed.

I turn to the wider concerns raised in this group about patient data, digital sovereignty and the security of NHS information systems. Patients need to have confidence that their data is secure and their privacy is respected. I quite often like to quote my favourite philosopher, Jimi Hendrix. I have cited this more than once. He talked about building castles made of sand that fall into the sea eventually. What we do not want is the single patient record or the federated data platform to be that castle made of sand that falls into the sea eventually because there is no confidence from patients and they want to opt out of the system. We have tabled our own amendments on the single patient record that speak directly to some of these concerns. I will return to those points when we reach that group.

The crux of the matter is Palantir, what people really think about Palantir and whether it should be here. When I was the relevant Minister, I was told quite clearly by my officials that Palantir had by far the best solution to deliver the federated data platform. We should acknowledge the contribution it has made in increasing discharges, reducing discharge times, identifying and contacting patients who need to come back, making sure cancellations are reduced, and all those sorts of metrics that we want to see.

But there is obviously a question here, and we should not shy away from it. That was the point of the debate between the noble Baroness, Lady Bennett, and the noble Lord, Lord Austin. What we are really debating here, with a company such as Palantir that supplied software to the Israeli military that may well have been used in Gaza against civilians, is whether that disqualifies it from supplying its solutions to the NHS. That, as well as the political views of the people at the top, is what the debate seems to be coming down to.

As the noble Lord, Lord Austin, said, we should remember that when the noble Lord, Lord Khan, as Mayor of London, tried to extract Palantir from the contract with the Metropolitan Police, not only did police officials complain and say that Palantir was by far the best solution but the noble Lord, Lord Khan, lost his case. We have to be aware of that when we call for what is being called for. The note of caution added to the debate on this by the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, should be listened to. If you are going to do it, be honest and up front about why you are doing it. Let us not hide behind other things but be frank—do you have a legal basis for doing that? In the case that you do, what replaces Palantir, given that it was highly recommended when I was in the department?

I will finish with the amendments from the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko. I completely agree, and we have had conversations about NHS England having a great record and the fact that we can build a sovereign NHS data model. But we have to remember that data that was collected during Covid, with specific permission to be used only during Covid, was reused after Covid for something that it should not have been used for, even though it was used for a good thing. NHS England and the DHSC do not exactly have a good record in this.

We have a real tension. We have civil liberties organisations such as medConfidential that have legitimate concerns about patient confidentiality and such issues, but we also have a research community and AI developers who seem to pay less attention to some of these issues. We have to be frank about that, and my plea to the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, and other developers is: please sit down with organisations such as medConfidential and have a conversation. You may face more barriers to achieving what you are trying to achieve. But when I was in the department, I got my officials to speak to medConfidential, and my officials said to me, “What they’re asking for is not difficult; we can give some of that”.

There is a solution to be found, but what I hear from AI developers and researchers is, “Don’t talk to medConfidential, they’re a bunch of liars”. I am sorry, but I think you have to sit down and have that conversation. If you do not have that conversation, you will get civil liberties organisations campaigning for people to opt out. Talking is the sensible way. It is a model that we all want to see. Clearly, we want to see the ambitions of the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko. That is all I would urge.

I have nothing more to add, noble Lords will be grateful to hear. I just wanted to make that point, based on my experience. We look forward, much more than to my contribution, to the Minister’s response.

speaker: Lord Tarassenko
heading: Health Bill - Committee (4th Day) (Continued)
text:
I thank all noble Lords who have spoken. I think we have mostly sung from the same hymn sheet, with perhaps the odd discordant note—maybe even a few bars, maybe even a whole movement, some people might argue. I am grateful to the Minister for her comprehensive reply.

I found it heartening last week to hear the Secretary of State speak positively about sovereign data and sovereign AI—those were her words. We now have an opportunity to go from concept to implementation within the next two years—namely, the single patient record contracts; that is, not the FDP contracts but the new contracts for the single patient record.

I believe, and I believe that many other noble Lords agree with me, that we have a highly capable—world-leading, I would say—UK medical technology and software sector, with companies that are often university spin-outs now ready to scale up. None of my amendments is in contradiction with the Procurement Act. I believe these companies can win these SPR contracts on merit. We are talking about supporting UK excellence, but we need to remember that the US spends billions to support technology in a radically different, profit-driven healthcare system, which often produces software that has a very poor fit to the NHS. I am sure the noble Lord, Lord Lansley, will be able to tell us that the original EPRs, the electronic patient records, from companies such as Epic and Cerner were a poor fit because they were designed for billing purposes, not for optimising patient outcomes. We made that mistake with the EPRs; let us not make the same mistake with the SPR.

In general, because the UK businesses are much smaller than the Oracles, the Epics, the Palantirs and the IBMs, we need a level playing field. I suggest that we need a signal from the Government to those companies that the Government are keen for them, as was mentioned by the Minister, to use procurement strategically to back UK business. I think that signal is the NHS digital sovereignty strategy, and I believe we will come back to it on Report. I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.

Amendment 53 withdrawn.

speaker: Adam Dance
text:
Sorry—I totally agree with the hon. Member. It is really good to have cross-party support. Just as the Prime Minister has argued that we need mayors as a force to drive change in local authorities’ areas, we need one person in Government to drive positive change on neurodiversity policy.

You are probably thinking, “Adam, that is all great, but how are you actually going to do it?” To put it simply, I am asking the Government to do three things: first, to make way for a new Minister by restructuring current posts or amending the Ministers of the Crown Act 1975 to expand the number of Ministers we can have; secondly, to give the new Minister funded statutory powers, by presenting Parliament with a cross-departmental strategy for neurodiversity that the Minister would be responsible for implementing, because this does not work if the Minister does not have teeth; and thirdly, to appoint a Minister for neurodiversity, which is probably the most difficult and political part of the whole process.

That is obviously easier said than done, but, as with most things, the answer is there: it just requires political willpower. Look at the new Minister for Artificial Intelligence post in the Cabinet Office. We see this time and again with Government: we are told, “Oh, that is too complicated,” or, “Oh, that wouldn’t be practical,” but then the public kick up a fuss, and, suddenly, it is not too difficult and can actually be done rather quickly. Let us not forget that this is about 20% of the public.

Obviously, though, the Minister today cannot snap her fingers and promise to do this—I would love it if she could. That is just not how this works, and I get that. Instead, I ask the Minister to commit today to starting the process by having civil servants review cross-departmental policy on neurodiversity and the merits of a neurodiversity Minister, and then to meeting me and campaigners to talk through the findings with us and hear our suggestions in more detail.

I know that this proposal is ambitious, but it is the lack of ambition on neurodiversity policy that has got us into this mess in the first place. It is only with bold action that we are going to make a difference, because I do not want to live in a country where the next generation of neurodiverse kids feel as I did when they tried to shut my youth club, and where decision makers just do not get it and just do not care. I thank everybody for listening.

speaker: Christopher Vince
heading: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
text: From Scotland to Harlow, Mr Speaker. Online news sites like Your Harlow, which has provided thousands of news articles to Harlow residents across the years, rely on people visiting their site for advertising revenue, but there is a danger posed by AI summaries, particularly when some of those summaries are wrong. What thought has the Minister given to the impact of AI summaries on local news sources like Your Harlow?

speaker: Ian Murray
heading: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
text: The Government are actively looking at this issue, because we know from experience—we always use the Southport example—that when there are incidents or crisis moments across the country, people turn to their local news outlets and the BBC to find the truth because they are sceptical of what they are reading. In the meantime, anyone who is reading these AI summaries online should double-check with their local newspapers and the sources they are given to ensure that that information is true. What happens, of course, is the old adage: a lie is halfway around the world before the truth has got its boots on. That happens much faster now with social media. I am delighted that my hon. Friend has broken his habit in the House by at least mentioning Harlow in his question.

speaker: Ian Murray
heading: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
text: Keeping children safe online is a top priority for this Department and the Government. That is why we are taking urgent steps to clean up our online spaces, including by raising the age limit for social media to 16, dealing with the risks of children livestreaming themselves, stopping unknown adults from communicating with children through online services, including gaming, and switching off harmful features for 16-year-olds and 17-year-olds. We will also prevent under-18s from accessing chatbots that offer sexualised content. I look forward to working with my hon. Friend to continue these discussions.

speaker: Ian Murray
heading: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
text: I could not agree more with my hon. Friend. He has recently launched a white paper on digital product safety, arguing that platforms, AI and social media should be subject to the same rigorous product safety frameworks as physical goods to protect the public without stifling innovation, and it looks at this from a hazards perspective rather than a harms perspective. It is an incredibly interesting piece of work. It is something that we are actively looking at, and platforms and social media companies should be looking at it to ensure that their products are safe by design for children.

speaker: Anna Sabine
heading: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
text: The Government are rightly trying to protect children’s safety online, but AI smart glasses risk undermining some of those protections. Children and adults, particularly women, are being filmed without their consent and the footage is being posted online and used to train AI. In the Westminster Hall debate I secured last week, the Minister for Safeguarding said that the Government are looking at options to restrict the use of smart glasses. Will the Minister for Online Safety confirm what measures are being explored and when they will be laid before this House?

speaker: Victoria Collins
heading: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
text: The AI teddy bear that said unprompted, “I can’t help with killing you”, shows that online harms are extending to software within toys. Will the Government consider the Lib Dem approach of having a framework of harm that can look online and at the software in products with these developing technologies?

speaker: Bob Blackman
heading: Business of the House
text:
I thank Mr Speaker for hosting a Diwali event in Speaker’s House last night.

In addition to the business that the Leader of the House has announced, on Thursday 19 November there will be a statement from the Education Committee on its report, and on Thursday 26 November there will be a statement from the Transport Committee on its report. Given that the second debate on 19 November is on the emerging risks of advanced AI and was squeezed out on a previous occasion, would the Leader of the House consider giving that debate some form of protected time, to ensure that the large number of Members who want to speak are able to do so?

In addition, the business in Westminster Hall is as follows. On 17 November, there will be a debate on the performance of the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency. On Thursday 19 November, there will be a debate on support in the NHS for patients with learning disabilities, followed by a debate on inequalities in access to therapy for disabled children. On Tuesday 24 November, there will be a debate on the role of an MP, and on Thursday 26 November there will be a debate on access to stroke services in remote areas, followed by a debate on Islamophobia Awareness Month. On Tuesday 1 December, there will be a debate on nursing staff.

I gently remind the Leader of the House that we are still one down on the Backbench Business Committee. That is very important, because a number of colleagues are away from the estate on parliamentary business next week, and the quorum for our meetings is very tight.

Madam Deputy Speaker, you will know that executions of political prisoners in Iran are frequent. Indeed, Iran is the centre of executions of people who just want to stand up for their human rights. Later this evening, I shall be presenting the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist to Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani. He has been in prison in Iran for six years for his part in the protests of 2019. He is on death row for the simple reason that he is a political protester. Can we have a statement to this House from a Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office Minister on what the Government will do to call out not only this potential execution but all the other potential executions of prisoners in Iran?

speaker: Samantha Niblett
heading: Business of the House
text: Plans for Drakelow 1 and 2 AI data centres, which are part of the midlands supercluster, far exceed the original proposals on the current site of Drakelow power station. They would encroach into countryside and— alongside solar, farm and battery storage—encircle the village of Walton-on-Trent. However, just up the road is the old Willington power station site, which has been redundant for decades and is crying out for its 227 acres to be redeveloped. My understanding is that the application will go in as a nationally significant infrastructure project, and so inevitably directly to the Secretary of State, effectively disabling any input from local people. Will the Leader of the House therefore help me to secure a meeting with the relevant Minister so I can raise my concerns?

speaker: Iqbal Mohamed
heading: Gaza: Humanitarian Situation
text:
I cannot recall another conflict where the occupying and illegally invading force has used adverse weather, starvation and hypothermia as a weapon of war. The comments from those on the Opposition Front Bench were absolutely disgusting. Our compassion should be equal for Israeli civilians and Palestinian civilians. We should not differentiate in our humanity based on ethnicity or nationality.

Israel has used Lavender AI systems to target and execute thousands of Palestinian children, women and men. According to the Financial Times, the IDF is now in talks to deploy 1,000 AI robots to police and potentially engage in combat in Gaza. The humanitarian crisis is only worsening, with the future of technology being used to annihilate the civilian population, while Israel’s tech sector is booming. What steps are the Government taking to ensure that the UK can no longer invest in Israeli companies or co-operate with Israel, as these tools are used to cause the misery and death of Palestinians?

speaker: Jayne Kirkham
heading: Backbench Business
text:
I want to talk about the Cornish men and women who were in the Somme and involved in the first world war. There were 6,300 deaths of people from Cornwall in world war one. Many of them signed up to the Duke of Cornwall’s Light Infantry. There were a number of battalions from Cornwall that fought in the Somme, and the 63rd (Royal Naval) Division fought in the latter stages of the war as well. There was an article in the Royal Cornwall Gazette on 26 October 1916, which was an account sent by someone from the front, who said that they were mocked by the Germans because they knew where they were from; the Germans asked them if they had any Cornish pasties. Even over there, the Cornish were known and recognised.

I thank my hon. Friend the Member for North West Leicestershire (Amanda Hack) for talking about the tunnellers. They were coalminers where my hon. Friend is from, but those from Cornwall were tin miners.
