The Royal Engineer tunnelling companies worked in silence so that they were not heard; they could hear the Germans above them, apparently sometimes talking about how long it was since they had held their wives—they were that close. On the first day of the Somme, 19 charges were detonated under German frontlines, many of those tunnels having been built by the miners from my constituency and my hon. Friend’s.

The saddest thing is that many of those who managed to survive the Somme and the first world war came back to Cornwall and carried on working in the mines, and only a year later, on 20 October 1919, five of them were killed in the Levant mining disaster, in which 31 people died when the mine collapsed. It is a terrible sadness.

I know some of those stories because last week I saw the historians of Penair school, who have won the Western Front Association Malcolm Doolin local history prize for bringing the stories to life in a magical way. They used AI to make films about some of the people who fought in the Somme and the first world war—tunnellers from Cornwall—and said they had become very close to the men because many of them were only a year or two older than they are now. The way they brought them to life was magical. I am proud of the historians from Penair. They have been here for the past couple of days; they went to the ceremony at the Cenotaph yesterday and paraded there.

I am contributing to this debate simply to remember the men of Cornwall who died in the Somme, of whom there were many, and to give our great thanks for all that they did and all that they gave.

speaker: Adam Thompson
heading: Nolan Principles
text:
I will be as brief as possible. I thank the hon. Member for Mid Dunbartonshire (Susan Murray) for bringing the debate forward—we are all very grateful.

Despite what the media might have us think sometimes, I think people in my constituency are not actually that interested in the to-ing and fro-ing of us here in Westminster. Instead, what they want to see is honesty and accountability in their politicians and their Government. They want some breathing space from the pressures of the cost of the living crisis, and they expect that those elected to serve them are focused on the issues that matter to them most. When I speak to people across Erewash, they rarely ask about the sparring that has happened that week in Prime Minister’s questions. What they actually want to ask me about is whether they can get a GP appointment, if their train will turn up on time, or how they will make ends meet at the end of the month.

People need to know that politics is working for them. When confidence in politics falls, so does our ability to tackle the challenges facing the country and improve people’s lives. That is why the Nolan principles matter. They are about restoring trust at a time when many people have lost faith that politics can deliver for them. Rebuilding that confidence requires those in public life to uphold the highest standards of honesty, integrity and accountability. The Nolan principles are not about party politics; they are the core of good public service, and they help to ensure that decisions are taken in the public interest. They set out the standards that British people have a right to expect from those who are elected to serve them.

In the era of social media, where misinformation can spread quickly and public confidence is easily eroded, standards of conduct are more important than ever. People hear a lot about politics, but they do not always see reasons to trust it. The rise of artificial intelligence of course has merit. However, it has created room for the rapid spread of disordered information and misinformation. With political deepfakes—often from accounts registered from abroad—seamlessly depicting Members of this House doing or saying things they have not done, it is unsurprising that people feel distrust towards politicians.

I remember the incident last year involving the hon. Member for Mid Norfolk (George Freeman)—I have notified him that I would be mentioning him today. A deepfake video was created in which the fake version of him announced his defection from the Conservative party to Reform, which, of course, the real hon. Member had not done. It was terrifying for all of us here, because of how close to reality the video was, despite it being totally fabricated. Fake news spreads six times faster than truthful content online, and 70% of people struggle to distinguish between real and fake news. Two thirds of Brits now see misinformation as the leading threat to our democracy, and with trust in politicians at an all-time low, that should concern us all. That is why it is essential that all politicians uphold the principles of openness, integrity and honesty. Where there is uncertainty in the information space, people should be able to look to public servants for clarity and not be met with falsehoods or ambiguity.

Every story of poor conduct makes it a little harder for people to believe that politics is working for them. Trust is hard to build, and easy to lose. Once it is lost, regaining it takes time. And it has been lost. Just four years ago, Liz Truss sent the currency crashing and interest rates soaring; six years ago, Boris Johnson broke his own lockdown rules to host parties in Downing Street; and this year, Reform UK has been investigated by the National Crime Agency for alleged dodgy dealings.

This morning on the Floor of the House I raised an incident with Derbyshire county council, which had placed engagement sanctions on our brilliant local democracy reporter, Eddie Bisknell. Although I understand that those sanctions are now lifted, I strongly agree with the Leader of the House’s comment that it sounded like they were running scared from basic scrutiny.

Public trust has been seriously undermined. It is up to us, as Members of Parliament and public servants, to adhere to the highest standard of professional and personal conduct. If we want the public to regain faith in politics and us, selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness and honesty are the life foundations by which we must abide. Public trust should never be taken for granted; it must be earned and maintained. That is why the Nolan principles remain as important today as they have ever been.

speaker: Lord Pitt-Watson
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, it is a privilege to open this Budget debate. I welcome the noble Baronesses, Lady Aglionby, Lady Kitching of Penistone and Lady Ussher, and the noble Lord, Lord Neri, and I very much look forward to their maiden speeches. I also pay tribute to the former Chancellor, the right honourable Member for Leeds West, for the work she led to create fiscal discipline and repair our public finances. She was ably assisted in that task by the noble Baroness, Lady Martin, and by my predecessor in this role, the noble Lord, Lord Livermore, whom I hold in high regard.

I intend to keep my remarks today as factual and to the point as possible and, in the spirit of your Lordships’ House, to avoid the kind of political point-scoring that dominates the debate in the other place. I know we have more than 50 speakers and I may not be able to respond in full at the end. I have asked my staff to prepare a note on which I will comment and which I will circulate among Ministers and senior management at the Treasury so that the value I know we will get from this debate is transmitted to the Government.

This Budget is part of a long-term programme of government, one that will reflect the vision articulated by the Prime Minister and the Chancellor in their speeches at the Labour conference, one which will find expression in the 10-year plan that we will publish in the coming weeks, and one that will be reflected in the spending review next year. This Budget is set at a time of considerable uncertainty in the world economy—two wars, a challenging ally in the United States, unpredictable oil prices and interest rates rising. As the Chancellor has made clear, we cannot wish these global economic storms away. We must instead set out a course to steer the country through them.

The Budget therefore seeks to do a number of things. First, it shows how we will live within our means, within the fiscal rules. Secondly, it shows how we will fund defence, to which this Government are unequivocally committed. More than that, the Budget seeks to give breathing space to British people and—along with the conference speech and the 10-year plan—hope for the future.

I will start with fiscal discipline. In this Budget, we have chosen to use some of the fiscal headroom established last year to absorb the impact of the Iran war to protect the economy, British businesses and family budgets. But let us be clear: we meet the fiscal rules in full, and for the first time since 2022, in the third year of the forecast. While there are challenges, we should be proud of the resilience of this economy. Today, the Office for National Statistics announced 0.7% growth for this third quarter; I hope I have done my arithmetic right, but I think that is 1.9% so far this year. This is stand-out resilience. Last year, new borrowing by the Government fell to its lowest level in six years as a percentage of GDP and will continue to fall across the forecast. While government debt is high and interest payments much higher than we would like, action is being taken. Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the IMF, has said that the UK stands out as a country and is one where

“action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively”.

It is a tough world, but business investment is up and people and businesses are resilient.

The Government aim to underpin this resilience by providing breathing space for families and businesses. I have been asked what breathing space means. Let me use a metaphor. I commute to the House on the Tube; sometimes it is excessively crowded and stuffy, and I am older than I used to be. From time to time, a younger person will stand up and give me a seat. This is breathing space for me, but it is also more than that, because I feel grateful that they have understood how I felt in giving me their seat. This Budget does not solve all our problems, any more than the person who offered me the seat stopped the train being crowded. The world is still uncertain, but we can, as a Government, offer some breathing space.

Here is one example. For British people, energy costs are a particular challenge, so we are delivering immediate measures to help with rising bills, including the £100 household energy payment paid directly to households living in council bands A to D in England. That is breathing space. This will be funded by a time-limited 3% increase in the bank corporation tax surcharge; I am grateful to the banks for making that possible. Alongside this, the Government are extending the removal of domestic VAT on electricity until July, extending the 5p cut on fuel duty and abolishing gas standing charges to give people more control over their bills. Overall, in 2026-27 households in England are estimated to benefit by an average of around £160 from the support we are providing on energy. The households on the lowest income are expected to benefit the most, with the bottom 20% benefiting by around £230, almost four times the top 20%. We know that higher energy bills are a challenge for businesses too, so we are reducing bills by up to 25% for more than 10,000 eligible businesses from next April through the British industrial competitiveness scheme. This will not solve every problem, but it does offer breathing space.

Beyond energy, the Government are taking further action to support our lowest paid workers by increasing the national minimum wage and national living wage from April. To help those who use their vehicles for work, we are increasing the higher mileage rate and making permanent the increase in the standard milage rate announced earlier this year. To back businesses and high streets, we are taking 70,000 small retail, hospitality and leisure properties out of paying business rates altogether. For all other businesses in these sectors, we are freezing their business rates in real terms. If you want to remember two statistics from this Budget, remember 20 million and 70,000. There are 20 million households which will receive the household energy payment, and 70,000 high street businesses are no longer paying rates.

These measures provide breathing space for now, but the only way we can keep British families and finances secure for the long term is through an economy that is growing strongly. We believe that needs a positive response from government and local government. For decades, decisions about economic growth have been taken by people who are miles away from the communities they are trying to serve. With the best will in the world, they cannot be responsive. As a result, Britain has become one of the most geographically unequal large economies in the world. So we will be delivering an ambitious devolution package, putting power in the hands of local leaders who know best how to drive growth in their areas.

The Fiscal Devolution Roadmap, published alongside the Budget, sets out a plan for business rates to be retained locally by the end of the decade, and for mayoral strategic authorities to be assigned a share of the income tax generated from their area by 2028. Additionally, we are extending devolution and the advantages that come with it to 10 more areas in England, so that 90% of England’s population will be covered by a mayoral or foundation strategic authority. Good growth funds—flexible funding for local leaders to invest in local communities—will be rolled out across the country, supported by £285 million of capital grant funding, so that mayors and local leaders have more flexibility to invest in their own growth priorities.

We are also delivering radical reform of our energy system, because our priority is to bring energy costs down and to help British businesses compete and British households cope. We will buy and build new projects only when they lower bills and can connect to the grid. We will break the grip of international gas prices on our bills by moving more of our old renewables on to fixed-price contracts. We will build cheaper, faster grid connections through GB Grid; and, crucially, we are putting an end to the practice of loading levy costs on to bills.

Thirdly, we are supporting entrepreneurs. If you have a micro-business, you were formerly allowed £1,000 of income tax-free; now it is to be £3,000. We are going to pilot an entrepreneur scheme for young people. If your company is ambitious, we want you not just to start here but to scale, stay and prosper in the UK. The new capital gains founders’ relief will provide a 10% rate on lifetime gains, up to £10 million, for the founders of and early investors in high-growth innovative companies. To mobilise private investment in the UK, we are providing an additional £20 billion of capital to the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank. That is no small package for entrepreneurs, large and small.

One final measure I should mention is that we are putting in £700 million to support artificial intelligence security, resilience, adoption and innovation in the UK. Complementing that, our new data centre covenant will introduce strict tests that strategic data centres must meet to invest in local communities, support local jobs and help to re-industrialise Britain.

Finally, I would like to talk about some other big challenges facing our country. On defence, I think this House is absolutely united in understanding that defence of the nation is the first duty of a government. This Government have driven the biggest boost in defence spending since the end of the Cold War. At the Budget two weeks ago, we took the decision to reprioritise budgets across Whitehall to fund the defence investment plan in full.

At the spending review next year, we will set out details of how we will meet our NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035. Crucially, this includes setting a target for 3% in 2030. The Secretary-General of NATO has welcomed our plans, confirming that they represent a credible path to meeting our commitments. He said:

“The UK role in transatlantic security is vital”.

This move puts Great Britain on a credible path

“to ensure we’re all investing what’s needed to remain ready and able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security”.

Alongside this investment in defence, the Government are delivering a multi-billion pound package of financial support for Ukraine, because we will continue to stand by Ukraine for as long as it takes.

Housing has become more difficult, and housebuilding is slower than we would have liked but we cannot give up on building. This Budget will put another £1.5 billion into social and affordable housing to deliver 10,000 additional homes. It will put £4.7 billion behind the Your First Home scheme for first-time buyers and cut unnecessary costs and delays for housebuilders. The focus is on getting more homes built and helping more first-time buyers through the door.

We have already promised everyone sleeping rough a route off the streets this winter, and the Budget confirms a further £430 million to keep that offer open for the rest of this Parliament—not just this winter, but every winter.

We will continue to invest in Britain’s public services. Since 2024, we have aimed to rebuild our public services. Our investment has made Britain’s streets and borders safer. It has fixed crumbling classrooms. It has helped restore the NHS. But there is still so much more to do.

As we look ahead to the spending review, we start with ambition, but there will be choices we must make about prioritisation. We must continue to deliver efficiencies, building on the £16 billion of efficiencies and savings generated last year. We must continue to deliver an effective, efficient state of which people can be proud.

On welfare, I think the Prime Minister and Chancellor have been clear that the bill needs to come down, but in a planned and sustainable way, following the guidance that we get from the Milburn and the Timms reviews.

This is a Budget to deliver good growth, with growth in every postcode. It is part of a wider programme for government and for the nation. It is underpinned by fiscal discipline, the bedrock of the economy. It funds defence. It provides support to families and businesses now, and kick-starts work on the big changes needed to put this country on a better course, with breathing space today and fresh hope for the future. I look forward to our debate.

speaker: Baroness Neville-Rolfe
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I thank the Minister for his introduction and his undertaking to respond to all noble Lords’ comments. I very much look forward to the maiden speeches of the noble Lord, Lord Neri, and the noble Baronesses, Lady Aglionby, Lady Kitching of Penistone and Lady Ussher. I also very much look forward to the contributions from such a large and distinguished gathering.

This was Labour’s third Budget in office and the first delivered by the new Chancellor of the Exchequer. He was dealt a poor hand by his predecessor but, in summary, he has done little in this Budget to improve matters. We are in a bad way. Today’s figures were encouraging, but growth has been weak for a long time. Inflation is high, real wages are stagnating, unemployment is rising, taxation is approaching historic highs and, above all, the national debt approaches 100% of GDP and debt interest is increasing, thereby consuming an ever greater share of public spending.

These are serious problems demanding serious decisions, yet what we received was a Budget of short-term fixes and promises of action tomorrow. This week, the NIESR warned that the Budget failed the credibility test. Its director, David Aikman, said:

“A plan that is not believed adds to the premium the Government pays to borrow”.

The OBR forecast growth of just 1.2% this year, falling to 1% in 2027. Inflation will remain above target until 2028, while the economy’s underlying productive capacity is expected to grow by only around 1.5% annually. The Minister cited the IMF’s endorsement of the Government’s deficit reduction plans, but the IMF did not give them a blank cheque; it told them explicitly to “stay the course” and warned against slippage. Since then, the OBR has revised borrowing upwards and reduced fiscal headroom to £15 billion, and the Government’s plans have not yet led to any reduction in the deficit, as we discussed in Grand Committee only last week.

Further, the OBR forecasts no real earnings growth in 2027, followed by only very modest increases in subsequent years. Real household disposable income per person is expected to fall in the near term and, even by the end of the decade, to stand only around 2% above its pre-pandemic level. Yet the Government plan to meet their financial targets by “planning”—the word must be in quotation marks—to reduce public expenditure significantly in the last two years of their term. They should pull the other one.

Taxation under this Government has increased enormously, mainly by freezing income tax thresholds and increasing national insurance in the Government’s unfortunate first Budget. Both eventually have the same effect as a tax rise on working people, whatever the Chancellor says. The Government have also imposed extra burdens on higher-rate taxpayers, but, in the end, part of that burden is also borne by those lower down the income scale.

Even the OBR warns that taxation at these levels risks damaging incentives to work, save and invest. On this side of the House, we have not forgotten the debilitating effect of the application of IHT on family businesses, farms and pensions; or VAT on school fees; or the new mansion tax that will be in the Finance Bill.

This Budget’s measures continue in the same vein, with a rise in savings and property taxes, so that a widow renting out a flat pays a higher rate than a footballer, and a tax surcharge on the banks, on which SMEs rely for investment. Britain cannot tax its way to prosperity. The way to the growth and prosperity that we all seek is to spend and tax less.

What of those people who are not in work? Unemployment is forecast to exceed 5% in 2027, vacancies are falling and young people in particular are struggling to find work. Yet the Government have made employing people more expensive through higher employer national insurance, rising costs and increasing regulation. Their answer is a jobs guarantee, but another government scheme is not a substitute for a thriving private sector.

We cannot afford a system in which fewer people work, those who do work pay ever more in tax, and the welfare bill continues to rise. Can the Minister point to where in this Budget the Government have seriously confronted this challenge? We on these Benches have struggled to find it.

However, despite record taxation and enormous borrowing, the Chancellor has left himself just £15 billion of fiscal headroom. The OBR puts his chances of meeting his fiscal rule at barely 56%. Indeed, a one percentage point change in interest rates could increase debt interest costs by £16 billion, wiping out the headroom. Meeting a fiscal rule by the narrowest of margins is not the same as restoring the fiscal responsibility we need.

In short, the great failure of this Budget was the absence of serious decisions on the greatest challenges facing our country. Where was the plan for welfare reform? Health and disability benefit spending alone is forecast to rise from £86 billion to £120 billion by 2031-32. This is plainly unsustainable, yet the Government continue to postpone the difficult reforms that are needed.

Where is the plan for defence? The Chancellor himself, when resigning as Defence Secretary, warned that failing to commit to spending 3% of GDP by 2030 makes Britain less safe. He has failed the very test he set himself and failed to explain how the 3% will be funded. The Chancellor has chosen to defer difficult decisions. Postponing these decisions does not make the problems disappear; it simply makes them more difficult for the Chancellor’s successors.

What would we have done? What should a serious Budget have delivered? First, a credible plan for growth. There are signs today that AI and services are helping, which is welcome, but today’s figures for construction are grim—down 0.7%. Job losses in the sector have also been reported today, and, as I have heard from the Institution of Civil Engineers, we see a disappointing government record on maintenance spending and delivery of infrastructure projects.

Secondly, cheaper energy has been the key to growth historically. The Government’s temporary measures, set out clearly by the Minister, do nothing to address the underlying costs facing households and businesses. We need to go further. Our cheap power plan would remove carbon taxes and levies and abolish VAT on household energy bills for three years, reducing average household electricity bills by an estimated £200 a year. We also need to see the Rosebank field approved and the Fingleton report implemented.

Thirdly, the Budget should have delivered action on housing. The OBR now forecasts substantially fewer homes being built than it expected in the spring. Unlike this Government, we would reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens, remove barriers to development and abolish stamp duty on primary residences.

Fourthly, we would make work pay. We would halve employer national insurance for workers aged 21 to 24 and introduce our get to work programme, helping young people into employment.

Above all, we would confront the question this Government refuse to answer: how do we control public spending without continually asking taxpayers to pay more? We have set out a programme of £71 billion in annual savings, including £36 billion from welfare reform. At least half would go towards reducing the deficit, with the remainder supporting lower taxes, enterprise and our national priorities. We would establish a funded path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, because economic security and national security must go hand in hand.

The British people need a Budget that would confront the underlying problems facing our economy; instead, they received a Budget which left the major decisions for another day. It again relied on rising tax receipts to reduce borrowing, while leaving the largest structural pressures on public spending unresolved. Overall, it was a missed opportunity. Our ambition should be to build an economy that grows faster, rewards work, encourages enterprise and offers every generation the opportunity to enjoy a better standard of living than the ones before. Unfortunately, the Budget did none of that.

speaker: Lord Hollick
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, this Budget is an important step on the painful journey to tackle Britain’s deep-seated economic problems and to create, I hope, a sustainable and growing economy. The Prime Minister’s first bold move was to reform the triple lock, much canvassed in this House, by increasing pensions in line with wages. This will save £50 billion by 2050, but none before 2030. The Chancellor’s decision to resist the temptation to change the fiscal rules has been well received by the financial markets and rewarded by a softening of yields on government debt and a reduction of the so-called moron premium inherited from the previous Government. A bank tax has funded a number of small but important and well-received measures to help the less well-off, the high street, some SMEs and entrepreneurs.

Overall, a key fiscal measure, the current balance—the difference between the current year’s government borrowing and spending—has fallen from a deficit of 2.5% in 2024 to a deficit of 1.5% in 2025-26, and is forecast to be in surplus in 2028-29, another UK achievement praised in the recent IMF report. The Chancellor has continued the vital work of his predecessor to increase the chronically low level of public investment which has placed the UK at the bottom of the G10 over the last 30 years. Public investment has increased since 2024 from 2.5% to 3.5% of GDP to provide a useful boost to profit.

I welcome the decision to devolve many of the capital investment decisions to the regions, which will have a better understanding of what is needed locally. But the increase in public investment, whether it is centrally or locally, reminds us that despite the excellent work of the infrastructure commission, the Government have a dire record of oversight of many capital projects; for example, the runaway cost of HS2 and the 20-year underspend on maintenance in the water industry. Beefed-up oversight is needed and should be provided by an independent, professionally staffed body with full statutory powers to investigate the projects, many of which are protected by their sponsoring ministry.

Private investment has also increased by 7.5%, but high energy costs, elevated interest rates and a heavy regulatory burden present stiff headwinds. The Chancellor’s commitment to delink the price of electricity costs from the market price of gas can reduce our energy costs, which remain the highest in Europe, but so far, the benefits of the measure to reduce the regulatory burden remain elusive.

Major challenges lie ahead. The results of the assured process of reforming welfare benefits to move funding from benefits to training are imminent. The Chancellor’s reaffirmation of the target to invest 3% in defence is welcome, but the funding plan will not be available until next year. That spending plan is also forecast to deliver an overall 2.6% reduction in spending, to be found by a challenging cut of 10% in non-protected areas.

The heart of the 10-year plan must be a radical plan for growth based on innovation, the measured adoption of AI and investment in skills. It must include tax reform to remove the many barriers to business growth; it must reform personal tax and benefits to make it fair and progressive and to reward productivity. The decision to freeze personal tax thresholds in 2022 means that each subsequent year more people are dragged into paying higher tax. An additional 1 million people this year will be paying more tax on their earnings, which have generally increased barely enough to meet inflation. On top of that many lose benefits. It is an unfair system which particularly affects the low earners, but it acts as a major disinvestment to all.

In my career, I helped to draft and deliver a number of long-term plans in both the public and private sectors. These plans were never short of ambition but, crucially, their success depended on early implementation. No plan can be delivered unless the necessary reforms and the tough financial decisions are tackled in the first 12 months. If that first year is done well, hope can indeed be transformed into reality.

speaker: Baroness Bi
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I would like to follow the noble Baroness, Lady Bottomley, in her bipartisan praise for my noble friend Lady Ussher on her excellent maiden speech. I am confident that this House will benefit from her expertise as a macroeconomist, her understanding of business and financial services, combined with her understanding of the needs of her former constituents. I also look forward to hearing the other maiden speeches today.

I will continue the congratulatory tone by congratulating my noble friend the Minister and my right honourable friend the Chancellor on a Budget that was able to deliver on its core aims of maintaining fiscal discipline while giving people some breathing space on the cost of living. The Budget has been criticised by some in this House for not being bolder, but it is important for us to remember, as my noble friend the Minister has said, that this Budget is part of a package of measures that includes the 10-year plan to be published later this year, and a spending review next year. It is right that this Budget is limited in the breadth of changes it made ahead of those announcements to come.

We should also congratulate the Government on the calm reception that the Budget received from the markets, which recognised the limited space that the Chancellor had to effect change in a global environment of high energy prices creating higher inflation and rising interest rates. It is not a given that that was the reaction we would get and we should be grateful that we did.

The OBR has also confirmed that the Government are on track to meet their fiscal rules and that the deficit is expected to halve by 2029-30, which is an impressive achievement in the current climate. As has been said, that was recognised by the IMF, which said that the UK is the only G7 country with a serious plan to reduce its deficit. We also received the good news today from the ONS that the economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter. That growth is likely to be bolstered by the provisions in the Budget, with the Government providing support to business and innovation through the introduction of founders’ relief, the removal of business rates for many in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors, the additional funding for AI, and the increased finance made available through the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, which, as the British Chambers of Commerce has said, will give entrepreneurs an opportunity to start up and scale up.

I also welcome the decision to time limit the increase in the bank corporation tax surcharge. Financial services are one of the sectors in which we are truly world-leading, but we operate in a competitive global environment. It is vital that we have a stable and predictable tax regime for everyone, including banks, which encourages investment and capital to come to Britain.

I also support the decision to restore the limit on cash ISAs, as it is vital that we encourage people to save for their futures. I wholly support the Government’s aim of encouraging people to invest in the equity markets, but I believe we can do that through carrots—such as removing stamp duty on UK shares, as was suggested by Dame Julia Hoggett of the London Stock Exchange—rather than the stick of reducing the cash ISA.

As we have heard, the Budget also contains a timely response to the challenges of defence, which have become ever more acute and which this Chancellor understands better than many of his predecessors. My noble friend the Minister kindly said that he is open to considering constructive ideas; as Christmas is coming, I thought this might be the time to put forward my wish list of ideas for the 10-year plan. It will need to prepare for a decade of unparalleled change, not least because of the likely impact of technology across our economy.

First, I welcome the commitment to simplify and modernise the tax code; I hope it will be a key plank of the 10-year plan. We have an incredibly complex system that is difficult to administer and is gamed by the unscrupulous. We must also use the tax system to encourage employment, especially of young people, which the Milburn report seeks to address. Secondly, I agree with the noble Lord, Lord Fox, that deregulation and the simplification of regulation must continue and at a faster pace, whether in financial services—where we are beginning to make progress, as is reflected in the Financial Services and Markets Bill—or in our commitment to build 1.5 million homes. The UK has some of the highest costs for infrastructure development compared with our European neighbours, and we are the slowest to approve new projects; that clearly needs to change.

The reality is that, if we give people incentives to invest, work, and build businesses, the Exchequer will benefit from the activity that will follow and we will achieve good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart. This Budget is an excellent start to ensuring that.

speaker: Lord Harper
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, it is a great pleasure to follow the noble Earl, Lord Russell. We are blessed in this debate to have four maiden speeches. I am delighted to have listened to two of them and look forward to the remaining two.

I want to say a word or two about the noble Baroness, Lady Ussher. I am sorry that she is not in her place to hear them. It is always good when someone says something nice about you if you are there in person, but I am sure that she will have the chance to read it afterwards. She was in the House of Commons from 2005 to 2010, which was my first term in the House of Commons. I saw her in action as a Treasury Minister, and I thought her speech today demonstrated her enormous experience from that role and her considerable economic experience in a number of roles since. I am sure she is going to make a tremendous contribution to the House.

My noble friend on the Front Bench, Lady Neville-Rolfe, in the time she had, was able to set out a comprehensive critique of the Budget. I agreed with everything she said, so it is not necessary for me to repeat much of it.

There are a couple of points I want to focus on. Budgets are fiscal events, front and centre, and that means we should judge them on their tax and spending measures. The Treasury and the Chancellor seem to be very cross that people are judging the Budget on the tax and spending measures, but that is fundamentally what a Budget is. The IFS came to the conclusion that the tax and spending measures were minimal and are not going to make a significant difference.

The other big opportunity you have in a Budget as a Chancellor is to drive forward significant supply-side reforms that are going to improve the performance of the economy and drive up growth rates. I am afraid there were none of them either. The Budget was a big missed opportunity. It kicked into the future decisions on welfare, social care and defence. Those were missed opportunities. If you are a new Prime Minister, as Andy Burnham is, with a significant majority, my experience is that you need to take those decisions early because they take time to come to fruition.

The key thing I want to talk about is where we go in our relationship with the European Union. I am afraid I draw the opposite conclusion from that set out by the noble Lord, Lord Liddle. If we look at the growth figures today and the growth in the economy this year, the fastest-growing sector has been information and communication. The OBR itself says that a lot of that is driven by investment in artificial intelligence and related industries. That says to us that the debate about the EU is in great danger of being backward-looking, looking at the industries of the past rather than the industries of the future. If this country is to have high growth, we will have to be successful in those industries of the future.

I will give one example. On artificial intelligence, the regulatory regime that we have chosen in the UK is one much more likely to deliver fast growth in artificial intelligence and fast economic growth as a result. The EU has taken, as it does in many areas of policy, a much more risk-averse, anti-growth policy framework. If we are to get closer to the European Union, we will end up regulating artificial intelligence closer to its model rather than to the much more successful model that we have. That will set growth backwards. There may be advantages to be gained from industries of the past, those that are not fast-growing, and we may get some economic gains there, but any economic gains in those areas will be dwarfed by the gains we will miss out on by regulating areas of the economy that will be fast-growing in the future.

The final thing I want to say—again, this is connected to the Government’s European Union approach—is about unemployment, particularly for younger people. My noble friend on the Front Bench referred to the OBR’s forecast for unemployment going up. The big issue of today and the next week will be Alan Milburn’s report about NEETs. It seems to me that the Government have made two policy choices that make that more difficult: they put up employers’ national insurance contributions, particularly hitting hospitality and retail, the sectors of the economy that employ younger people; and they have put £5 billion of costs on businesses through the Employment Rights Act. Then there is the impact of the youth mobility scheme, which is a terrible idea. If we sign up to a scheme that will potentially see up to 100,000 young people coming to the United Kingdom from Europe, there is no way that it will help get British young people back into work.

The Government are therefore in great danger of having a backward-looking European Union policy that will damage our economic growth prospects and the unemployment rate, and will not deliver the economic growth prospects for the future that all of us in this House want to see.

speaker: Lord Neri
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I congratulate my noble friend Lady Ussher on her incredible maiden speech, setting the tone as I make mine. I express my sincere gratitude to all noble Lords as I make my maiden speech. This is an unusual but very special place, and the warmth I have experienced from right across the House has been both generous and welcoming. To those noble Lords who thought they could trick me and have me vote in the wrong Lobby, I forgive you. This really is a precious moment, and words cannot convey my true appreciation.

My personal thanks go to Black Rod, the doorkeepers, the clerks and the wider teams right across the Palace. I would like to make a very special mention of Garter King of Arms, who left the best possible first impression on the journey I was about to undertake, and of my incredible supporters, my noble friends Lady Kennedy of Cradley and Lord Kennedy of Southwark.

My mum and dad were physically absent during my introduction, but not in spirit. They would have been so proud of their youngest. My Italian father became maître d’ of the Ritz and later the Savoy—places where service was of the highest gold standard, serving royalty, including the Queen and the Queen Mother, referring to him as Mr Bruno. In the 1980s and 1990s, he would reject famous celebrities for not wearing a tie. He would have been a great doorkeeper in this place. He knew exactly how to treat and respect people, and worked a long six-day week.

Meanwhile, my mother, born in Essex and true Labour, kept the house going with four children—and we were a handful. It was my mother who I saw work hard at first hand. She used the house telephone to make deals happen, from buying and selling shares to securing the best retail offers, all pre-internet. Learning from her negotiation skills and commerciality became a huge influence.

In his final 10 years of living with dementia, my father had a steady decline—a very difficult period for my family. It was heartwarming to hear the Prime Minister speak so passionately about reforming the care system. I could not have coped if it was not for my wife, Michelle. It was just too much. The most useful aid and relief during my father’s final years was the power of music. When he forgot his granddaughters’ names, or even mine, playing him Puccini, in particular songs from “La Bohème”, suddenly awoke emotion, rekindling memories and, most importantly for us, remembering who he was in the room with. For the past seven years I have been a trustee of Music for my Mind, a charity whose goal is to build the perfect music playlists for patients with dementia. The medical proof is available and we are now helping patients like my late father.

The power of music is also where my profession took me. In my 27th year of working in the music industry, I am currently chief executive at the Ivors Academy and a director at UK Music. I also sit on the British Copyright Council and wider creative industry groups outside of music. What benefits or hurts one sector tends to impact another. A current example is that a vast number of greeting-card illustrators have lost employment to generative AI. This has largely gone unnoticed. Let us heed the warning and protect our actors, musicians, composers and authors from being replaced—and, indeed, our British creative culture.

In 2024, the creative industries contributed the most in GVA to the UK economy at £145.8 billion. Let us be robust and protect the future of creators and the integrity of intellectual property, and strengthen our copyright framework with cross-party unity. Just as artificial houseplants lack oxygen, artificial intelligence lacks soul and emotion.

In parallel with AI comes the threat of a dwindling talent pipeline. Schools struggle to meet the requirements of the creative curriculum due to timetable pressures caused by external scrutiny of academic subjects over the arts. Let us not forget that to be a scientist or a mathematician you need to be a creative thinker. Creativity is the heart of what makes us human; without it there is no invention. Picasso famously warned us that everyone is a creator until someone says that they are not. Let that not be us. Since 2010, the total share of GCSE and A-level entries in arts subjects has shrunk by around 50%. Nottingham University recently closed down its music department, with others considering following suit.

To return to the debate, creators are entrepreneurs but are writing and performing alongside second or third jobs. The new measures taken in the Budget recognise that support is desperately needed. The tripling of the trading allowance of £3,000 will mean that those who are starting to turn their passion into a profession will be able to keep more of their money. Expanding parental pay will go to freelance creators for the first time. At a time of great need, it is also welcome to see that music venues will see a 20% reduction in their business rates.

Thank you for indulging me. I look forward to conversations regarding what I have opened with and to working with as many noble Lords from across the Chamber as I can.

speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I add my congratulations to the maiden speeches we have heard today. There have been some excellent contributions, but we have also had some strong contributions from old codgers as well.

A breathing space for today, hope for tomorrow: that was the slogan at the start of the Budget. The Minister provided us with his idea of what a breathing space might be, and I hope that younger travellers on the Underground will continue to give up their seat for him. However, the Budget delivered a breathing space for the Government and fear for most of the population of this country—business and ordinary working people. It delivered fear because we all know that the Budget did not address the real problems; it just kicked them further and further down the road. We all know that money is short and that, in the end, there is no escape from deep cuts in services and benefits, or big tax rises, or potentially a combination of the two. It will be painful. Fear of that is now tangible, even if it is not yet affecting the markets. People have been left in limbo. It is not so much a breathing space as a place of trepidation.

Meanwhile, the Government boast of a few cash bungs to households, many of whom will see far more cash than they are given being clawed back because of the stealth tax of frozen thresholds. As the noble Baroness, Lady Neville-Rolfe, explained, and others have added, everything is being put off. Even the government reviews that report do not result in action. Implementation is what we need. The spending review will surely be backloaded so that any genuine cuts come way down the line.

Then there is the 10-year plan. We can all dream, and long-term ambitions are no bad thing, but if a week is a long time in politics then a decade, and planning for one in the age of AI, is better left to Gypsy Rose Lee. What we and the country need is action, and we need it now. We need to know how we are going to deal with social care and we need to start doing it, rather than talking about it. We need to fund defence now and we need to know how it is going to be done, because the threat is real. In many people’s eyes, this country has been at war now for several years; we just have not acknowledged it. We cannot pussyfoot around any more. We need to deal with the problem and fund it. I hope that John Healey, having resigned once because he did not have the money he needed, is going to find it and tell us how.

If the Government really wanted to make it easy for people and give everybody a bit of breathing space, there is one very easy thing they could do: embrace the idea of simplification. Even in this anaemic Budget, there were almost 100 tax and fiscal changes. The Red Book says:

“The government recognises the importance of a stable and predictable tax system”.

They must be joking. Instead, what we get is constant change. Our tax system is ludicrously complicated. Tolley’s Tax Guide now runs to more than 1,000 pages. The amount of time and effort people must spend filling in their tax forms could be spent in so many more productive ways. I ask the Minister to let us know whether he will consider bringing back the Office of Tax Simplification and what he intends to do to simplify tax. While he is dealing with that, could he also address the problems in the probate system, which make life anything but easy breathing for a lot of people in this country, just at the worst possible moment in their lives, and give us all a real breathing space?

speaker: Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I will focus on two points: the NEETs crisis and the essential role of businesses and entrepreneurs in addressing the crisis. The NEETs crisis—the almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training—was conspicuous by its absence from the Budget, despite the Prime Minister’s welcome acknowledgement that it is an

“economic catastrophe and moral failure”.

We have the publication of Alan Milburn’s review into young people and work to look forward to next week, as my noble friend Lord Balfe referred to in his speech, but, having hoped the review would be published before the Budget, with key measures implemented in the Budget, I want to underscore the fact that this delay will have human consequences and urge the Government to act on the review at pace. In June, the noble Lord, Lord Wilson of Sedgefield, told your Lordships’ House that the report would be out

“some time in September or October

The media were briefed that it would be published ahead of the Budget to allow speedy implementation.

Having spoken to many young people about the difficulty they are having in finding work, I was disappointed that the Budget did not include any measures of substance to address the NEETs crisis, even if the publication of the full review needed to be delayed. We will now have a further six or 12 months of delay until Alan Milburn’s recommendations for the Treasury are actioned in either the Spring Statement or next year’s Budget.

The million NEETs are a cohort of people who have spent much of their lives waiting. They put their lives on hold for two years during the Covid pandemic. Now they are facing a potential two-year delay from the commissioning of the Milburn review until its implementation. And this delay is not costless. It has real impact on young people’s lives. Alan Milburn’s interim report found that two-thirds of young people who are NEET for less than a year return to education, employment or training the following year. One-third—a very significant number—do not. For those who are unfortunate enough to be NEET for over a year, just 25% stop being workless. That means 75% continue being workless. So the delay in announcing and implementing the review’s recommendations could be catastrophic for people’s lives.

With the review being published next week, I am sure the Minister will already be familiar with its contents. I am not expecting him to reveal the details in his response today, but can he share with us whether the Treasury is looking to implement them in the Spring Statement or whether we will have to wait until next year’s Budget for them to be actioned?

Putting the Milburn review to one side, I turn to the impact of the wider business environment on the employment prospects of young people. At the end of every journey from welfare to work is a job either being provided directly by a business or paid for by the taxes generated by businesses. High energy costs, rising employment costs and an expanding regulatory burden are all making it more difficult for businesses to create jobs. This shows up in the unemployment rate. Rewinding to the 2024 Budget, the OBR’s forecast for the unemployment rate in 2026 was 4%. The same thing in this year’s OBR forecast is 5%. Current unemployment this year is therefore set to be 25% higher than forecast in Rachel Reeves’s first Budget in 2024. This can be reversed only by encouraging and incentivising entrepreneurs to work hard and invest to create jobs for young NEETs and other jobseekers.

The Chancellor promised a Budget for “bloody-minded entrepreneurs”: what we got was thin gruel. The new flagship proposal in the Budget to support entrepreneurs was founders’ relief, but the bar for founders to qualify is hugely restrictive as it stands. I find it astonishing, for example, that DeepMind would not have qualified when it was sold to Google. At the other end of the spectrum, the attack on sole traders will have a devastating effect on those beginning their entrepreneurial journey, and the halving of the business asset disposal relief lifetime limit from £1 million to £500,000 will disincentivise people from starting their entrepreneurial journey. We should always remember that incentives matter. If you tax the risk takers, you lose the job makers, and we need more job makers to help the NEETs.

Some have described this as the “Do no harm” Budget, but inaction makes life no better for the 1 million young people still waiting. I hope they are not kept waiting much longer. It is time for action because, to quote the Prime Minister, inaction on the NEETs crisis is an

“economic catastrophe and moral failure”.

speaker: Lord Londesborough
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I rise a little warily as speaker 38 of 57. I suspect parliamentlive.tv’s viewing figures may not trouble the scorers for a six-hour debate on a Budget of little content that seeks to do as little harm as possible, admittedly having learned some of the lessons from the two previous Budgets. Indeed, the markets barely reacted. I will give some credit to the Chancellor for not disturbing our recent GDP growth momentum; today’s third-quarter figures are encouraging and underscore the need for an AI economic strategy.

I will focus on SMEs and the bloody-minded entrepreneurs, but first I will make some brief comments on our public finances. I will follow up on the comments from my noble friend Lady Wheatcroft about the term “breathing space”. To me, this is the act of tinkering at the margins while another year slips by without us addressing the pressing economic issues of our time: debt, deficits, borrowing and a tax burden lurching towards 40% of our GDP. Our interest bill has climbed from £40 billion to £120 billion per annum in the last five years alone, and the OBR tells us that this will structurally settle at between £160 billion and £190 billion in the 2030s—and remember that the OBR has a history of optimism bias.

From debt and deficits, let us turn to three other “D” words: defence, demography and dependency. We have pledged to increase defence spending by some 40%, and it is proving politically impossible to reduce our health, pension and welfare spending, given our ageing and increasingly unhealthy society. That brings me to the final “D” word: devolution. I thought that devolution was the central plank of the Prime Minister’s strategy for growth, but the Budget announcements were small fry: a £1.5 billion borrowing facility and £285 million for good growth funding next year, presumably to be spread to every postcode. Like the noble Lord, Lord Bridges, with all these “D” words, I detect a distinct lack of urgency.

I shall focus on our bloody-minded entrepreneurs. I declare that I was one once, my son is one now, and I work with a range of start-ups and scale-ups, ranging from online platforms to canine matchmaking and community pubs. If we are to turn the dial from 1% to 1.5% growth in GDP to that mission-critical 2.5%, we must nurture and incentivise our small and medium-sized scale-ups that have a vital impact on economic growth. This group has suffered a bloody period: huge increases in employer NICs, outsized minimum wage hikes, restrictive employment practices and soaring energy bills and business rates. This Budget spared them further punishment, but almost nothing has been done to make employment more affordable or to deal with energy bills. While the Minister has trumpeted the fact that business rates relief is going to apply to 70,000 businesses in the high street, what is happening to the other 400,000?

The Chancellor has signalled the return of capital gains tax founders’ relief, which I very much welcome. However, as the noble Lord, Lord Elliott, said, on reading the small print one discovers that founders qualify only if they have delivered three consecutive years of 25% growth in both revenue, which must exceed £10 million, and headcount. That will exclude the vast majority of deserving founders, including those who, despite these headwinds, have created scores or indeed hundreds of valuable new jobs at a steady and sustainable rate over many years. One entrepreneur texted me this morning: “It’s like being asked to reach for the stars after two years of knee-capping”. He points out that the 50% reduction in business asset disposal relief looks set to hit a much larger group of entrepreneurs. I would very much welcome the Minister’s comments on these important measures, because the devil is very much in the detail.

This Budget is an improvement on its predecessors and has taken care not to inflict more damage on SMEs, but tough decisions have been delayed yet again and we still await a strategy for enterprise and economic growth.

speaker: Lord Nagaraju
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I declare my interest as an adviser to and director of companies working in artificial intelligence, technology and AI policy. I congratulate noble Lords who made their maiden speeches today.

I welcome the Government’s investment in AI; it can help businesses to grow, improve public services and raise living standards. People need to see what its promise means for them. For a business, it means being able to adopt AI with confidence. For a young person, it means a fair chance of finding work. These investments should be judged by the security and the opportunity they bring.

First, there is the £40 million for the national agentic security unit. As AI agents take on more tasks, we need to be ready when they behave in unsafe or unintended ways. Will my noble friend the Minister publish an implementation plan setting out when the unit will be operational, which Minister will be accountable and how its readiness will be tested? That plan should give businesses and public bodies a clear route for reporting incidents, with regular progress reports to Parliament that protect sensitive information. Preparedness has to be tested before a crisis.

Secondly, there is the additional £23 million for the AI Economics Institute. For a young person seeking a first job, the question is simple: where will I gain the experience that employers require? Early research shows weaker entry-level hiring but does not establish that AI is the cause. The institute must help us to understand what is changing and why. In answering my Written Question this week, following the warning by the IMF of an AI tsunami, the Minister confirmed that further analysis would be published. Can he give us a timetable for that work on jobs and wages and explain how the findings will shape funded apprenticeships, entry-level opportunities and support for workers whose jobs will change? The Early Careers Jobs Alliance offers a way to bring employers into that effort. Young people need opportunities to learn on the job as work changes.

Thirdly, I welcome the National Cyber Security Centre’s new AI centre of excellence in Manchester. Its expertise must reach the public services that need it. A council or hospital adopting AI needs people who can assess security risks and help staff use it safely. Will my noble friend set out how the centre will be funded, how public bodies will access its expertise and how the Government will assess the difference it makes?

These investments deserve to succeed. We should be able to show how this money is making services safer and helping people find their place in a changing economy. The measure of our leadership should be the security and opportunity that it brings to people’s lives.

speaker: Baroness Nargund
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I too congratulate all the maiden speakers on their brilliant speeches. I look forward to working with them. It is a pleasure to have the opportunity to speak on the Autumn Budget.

My first point is about the NHS. As a doctor, I welcome the additional £190 million for winter pressures. We must, however, make sure that it reaches every community, particularly the most disadvantaged and vulnerable in our country. I also welcome the zero rate of VAT on qualifying donated medicines and the £100 million investment in robotic surgery. This innovation will improve recovery time and outcomes and benefit our patients.

The NHS 10-year plan has committed to a shift from treatment to prevention. I particularly welcome the Budget’s commitment to a new category of ring-fenced preventative spending at the next spending review. This has also been welcomed by the King’s Fund and the Health Foundation.

Technology will be central to a more productive NHS, and I welcome the independent review of NHS productivity and AI, which will report early in 2027, and the £15 million AI challenge prize, whose first competition will focus on NHS challenges. From the outset, partnerships must have clear governance on data access, intellectual property, clinical responsibility and the route from pilot to wider deployment. Critically, innovation must reach all patients and improve patient safety.

My second point is about the social determinants of health. As I have said before in this House, health is not created in hospitals or GP surgeries alone. Housing, employment, poverty and education are all determinants of our health. That is why I welcome the £1.5 billion additional investment into social and affordable housing and £432 million additional investment to tackle rough sleeping. These are not simply housing measures; they are investments in prevention, social justice, human dignity and good growth.

My third point is about women and girls. As a long-standing campaigner to end misogyny, I welcome the Government’s continued commitment to end violence against women and girls. The £55 million to tackle violence against women and girls and the £15 million investment in the misogyny prevention fund illustrate the Government’s ongoing commitment to this cause. Extending paternity leave and pay to self-employed fathers is the correct step towards the fairer sharing of caring responsibilities and promoting gender equality, both at home and in the workplace.

My fourth point is about supporting female founders and entrepreneurs. As an entrepreneur myself, I welcome the overall commitment to promote entrepreneurship in our country, in particular for women founders. Some £200 million will come from the British Business Bank, doubling its previous support. When only 2p in every £1 of venture capital reaches women-founded businesses, this is truly welcome news. Closing the funding gap could unlock £310 billion for our economy. That represents equality of opportunity, ambition and economic growth. I ask my noble friend the Minister: how will the Government ensure that this support reaches every woman in every postcode who wants to start and grow a business, regardless of their ethnicity, disability and caring responsibility, not just those who already have the networks and investor connections to find it?

This Budget invests in our health and prevention of ill health, tackles inequalities that hold people back, and supports female founders who will grow our economy, all while providing people across the country with the breathing space they need. As a doctor, innovator, entrepreneur and founder, I am proud to support this Budget. I would like the Minister to ensure that good health in every postcode and promoting gender equality for economic prosperity will remain at the heart of our 10-year plan.

speaker: Viscount Stansgate
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I welcome the Budget. One of the advantages, if I can put it that way, of being so far down the list in today’s debate is that I can say with certainty that I have been able to listen to all the excellent maiden speeches. None of the maiden speakers are in their places at the moment, but I congratulate them all. They will enrich the House in the years to come, and I am sure they all feel much better for having made their speeches.

In the short time available, I want to concentrate on a single question: will this Budget succeed in helping science and technology businesses scale up in the UK? Why is that important? It is because it goes to the very heart of how we can get growth in the UK economy. As the House knows, we have many interesting committees, they produce many interesting reports, and we have many interesting debates. Top of the list of reports that have not yet been debated by this House is the report of the Science and Technology Committee from an entire year ago on the question of scaling up businesses. We entitled it Bleeding to Death because we wanted to make an impact and to make it hard-hitting.

One of the specific examples in our minds as we considered our report was the case of a quantum start-up—I do not know whether anyone remembers the name, Oxford Ionics—that was eventually bought out by an American company for £1 billion because it could not find the scale-up capital necessary to grow in Britain. We cannot allow this type of case to go on, time and again. We have to find better ways to allow businesses to grow and scale up in the UK, ending the endless talk about the valley of death, with which this House has been familiar all too often over the decades.

Today’s debate gives me an opportunity to make the case for the views of the committee, given that there were lots of positive messages about innovation in the Budget speech. I may as well say right at the beginning that I was encouraged to learn that an additional £20 billion is being allocated to the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank. My noble friend Lord Eatwell touched on this. However, I am discouraged to learn that it may take several years before this injection becomes a reality.

In addition, I am hoping that the Mansion House Accord will succeed in unlocking around £25 billion of additional investment into UK private markets. I believe I am right that about £2 trillion-worth of assets are managed by UK workplace pensions. Whereas 30 or more years ago pension funds invested 50% or more in UK equities, this figure has slumped to about 2%.

The challenge we face is to accelerate the deployment of capital into innovative S&T, scaling up businesses and supporting the UK’s scale-up ecosystem. On a smaller scale—I know the Minister mentioned it in his opening speech—I hope the planned pilot of a young entrepreneurs’ allowance proceeds as soon as possible.

In our Select Committee inquiry, we had occasion to discuss whether we need what you might call a concierge service that would enable and guide scale-up businesses through the different stages, from start-up to scale-up and beyond. Is this, in effect, the idea behind Scale UK, as mentioned in the Budget Red Book? If so, when will the Scale UK-Connect regional pilot programme, designed to help 200 high-growth firms, begin?

About a month ago, the Prime Minister made a speech at the Innovation Nation Summit in Manchester—where else?—in which he spoke of a

“globally significant cluster in every region”

of the UK. He sees devolution at the heart of a renewed growth strategy. For this to happen we need to nurture the creative sector, the advanced manufacturing sector, fintech, photonics, clean energy, space, automotive engineering, quantum, cyber, compound semiconductors and AI. AI has, after all, established itself as a foundational technology, and the UK’s presidency of the G20 and the G7 gives us a chance to advance the AI for Good agenda.

Can my noble friend confirm that the UK will press for a global code of standards and guardrails to safeguard the global economy and guard against the much-discussed risks of AI, the sheer scale of which we are only beginning to understand? When it comes to international co-operation, a collaboration that is absolutely vital to R&D, what will this mean for future relations with the EU? These questions may go beyond my noble friend’s brief at the Treasury, but they are vital to our future.

I want to briefly highlight one other point about the reallocation of capital budgets across departments, designed in part to pave the way for the defence investment plan. I ask the Minister, as does the Campaign for Science and Engineering, whether there is a risk that R&D budgets might end up being disproportionately targeted. Can the Minister give any reassurance on this point?

I commend the Government for their commitment to ensure that the immigration system supports a dynamic labour market and innovative firms, and, to that end, want to deliver the most pro-business migration system in Europe for high-skilled workers. I put it to the Minister that, when our visa policy is considered, I hope the Home Office will enable this to happen rather than hinder it. I hope that there will be joined-up government, because the visa system was described to us on the Select Committee as “insane”; we took the view that it was an act of national self-harm. I very much hope that the Minister can give us some reassurance that this will be a feature of the years ahead, in support of growth.

speaker: Baroness Moyo
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I begin by recapping the serious economic situation in which this country finds itself: slow economic growth, forecast to fall to 1% in 2027, followed by years of flatlining growth and living standards—this notwithstanding the comments made today on the OBR announcement. Structural unemployment was also mentioned, with close to 1 million young people persistently out of work, even before the projected job displacement that AI will incur takes hold. We have high energy prices—at 40 cents per kilowatt hour, the highest across our G7 peers. There is an unsustainable welfare bill, which is now close to 10% of GDP. I wish here to emphasise the precariousness of time and why it is now urgent that we address these challenges.

The Prime Minister has promised a 10-year plan that will address the cost of energy, better water infrastructure and a long-term industrial strategy. But for here and now, what we know from the Chancellor of the Exchequer’s Budget is that it scarcely mentions economic growth. I appreciate that we heard about individual policies that can be said to support economic growth, such as the £20 billion for the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, and greater rates relief for high street businesses. However, taken together, these are not of sufficiently significant size or scale to catalyse economic growth; nor do they reflect a much-needed economic growth strategy. Without a credible economic plan, Britain is increasingly vulnerable to exogenous shocks such as cyber attacks, extreme weather events and escalation of geopolitical conflicts.

A credible economic agenda will need to address three points. First, it must present a clear vision that meaningfully reduces policy uncertainty. Greater certainty of the policy agenda would ease volatility in the financial markets, especially in gilt yields. As has been mentioned, the UK has the highest cost of capital among its peers in the G7. Ten-year gilt yields trading at over 5% reflects, at least in part, the fear that this country does not have a clear economic direction. Worryingly, since the Budget the OBR has cautioned that uncertainty is hindering the fiscal outlook. Policy certainty is urgently needed on scaling back the unsustainable fiscus, reducing the cost of energy and cutting the public debt so that less government money goes towards paying interest costs and more funds public services.

Secondly, the plan must convincingly show that Britain will commit to policies that drive long-term economic growth. For example, AI will be the greatest engine of economic growth over the next decade. This year alone, AI will lead to at least a 0.5% uplift of US GDP growth. Britain must aggressively lean into this unfolding AI super-cycle. The 10-year plan must not only be about risks and the regulation of technological development but must also demonstrate that Britain will invest substantially in emerging technologies that will drive growth. The absence of a believable long-term plan heightens the risk of continued short-termism in resource allocation decisions taken by both government and business, which further limits the economy’s upside.

The third point concerns implementation, which has been mentioned. There must be an easily observable and measurable timeline of policies. An opaque process with a lack of clarity on implementation prolongs uncertainty and only holds back the economy further. For example, domestic and international investors remain largely unattracted to the UK, with UK pension funds allocating around 5% of UK equities in their portfolios, down from 50% 25 years ago.

For too long, Britain has been coasting and delaying hard decisions, many coming at the expense of economic growth. In an era of ever greater complexity, we must re-architect economic thinking and design policy that ensures economic success and does not shortchange future generations. Britain is not immune to a full-blown economic crisis, as we know from living memory with the IMF bailout of 1976 and the run on sterling in 1992. That is why we must urgently pivot from the current precarious economic path. This requires long-term policy that, at a minimum, offers confidence, transparency and credibility.

speaker: Lord Pitkeathley of Camden Town
heading: Autumn Budget 2026 - Motion to Take Note
text:
My Lords, I draw the House’s attention to my registered interests as chief executive of the Camden Town and Euston Town business improvement districts. I thank my noble friend the Minister for his opening remarks and revel in the joy of sharing this debate with not one, two or three but four maiden speeches. How lucky we are. They were expertly delivered, and we look forward to hearing more contributions from all new noble friends. Being the last Back-Bench speaker, I have the last word among the Back Benches—a very temporary distinction in this House.

In my other office, I am a short walk from Euston station, and the rather expensive hole in the ground beside it. I believe that what happens there next should be more interesting than what has happened so far, but first, to the Budget.

The Budget offers breathing space for high streets. We have heard this many times today. Raising the small business rates relief threshold will take more qualifying retail, hospitality and leisure properties out of rates. Extra relief for Camden’s pubs and live music venues is welcome. I spent much of my youth in these venues, chasing a big break that never came. I am glad that the Government are being kinder to those venues than the music industry was to me—though I am pleased that my new noble friend Lord Neri had better success than I did in the music industry. However, we should also acknowledge that, in London, higher rateable values mean that many businesses will see less of this difference. BIDs—business improvement districts—know that local decisions need predictable funding, and I welcome the direction in the Budget on devolution.

As we have heard on OpenAI, I welcome the AI Economics Institute’s work on jobs and living standards. I have previously raised in this House the risk that job displacement will outpace job creation. The Budget cites an OECD estimate that AI could add up to 1.3 percentage points to annual UK labour productivity growth over the next decade. That is at the upper end and is dependent on adoption, and evidence lags the technology. In AI models, even a few years is a long time, and we must pay attention to that.

The Government are building capacity through the AI Security Institute and the new AI biosecurity lab. Once established, their location and collaboration will be harder to change, which brings me back to Euston. The Budget says that a tax increment financing—TIF—mechanism based on a business rates retention zone will be implemented at Euston, subject to a business case. It is intended primarily to fund London Underground upgrades. TIF links that investment to future growth. So, the question is: what do we put at Euston to ensure that we get that growth?

After years of disruption, pessimism is understandable—I have heard it said that in some cases HS2 is where some civil servants go to die. But Euston brings trains from Birmingham, Manchester and beyond into the Knowledge Quarter, by the Crick Institute, UCL and AI firms such as DeepMind, OpenAI and, shortly, Anthropic. If any part of London belongs to the rest of the UK, I suggest it is Euston.

Now a Londoner, though born in Manchester, I know that proposing London as the home for national institutions is not the surest route to popularity in your Lordships’ House. But I am suggesting an AI campus network starting in Manchester, Birmingham and Euston with other cities joining later. Institutions could share space, build on local strengths and bring researchers, businesses and skills providers together. Mayors could shape the work with devolved powers and funding. In short, we could get the dispersed regulators within Whitehall into a system that can move at the pace and relevance this new world needs.

I ask my noble friend the Minister: will the Government develop this idea with the Mayors of Greater Manchester and the West Midlands, as they work with the Mayor of London on Euston? Will they treat the location of the state’s AI capability as a decision to make, not one left to chance?
